Reading edition · RyanLPeterman

The Engineering Judgment Library

Conversations on building software, growing a career, and deciding what matters.

106 of 107 transcripts included; 1 excluded; 0 pending.

Good engineering depends on more than producing code. It involves understanding the mechanism, choosing an appropriate design, making progress with other people, and deciding which outcomes deserve your effort. This reading edition brings together the Ryan Peterman transcript collection around those questions.

Each source has its own section. Interviews retain the sequence of substantive questions and answers, with follow-ups attached to the discussion they extend. Spoken repetition, opening montages, sponsor messages, and channel housekeeping are condensed so the argument and examples can be read as prose. Source links return you to the relevant point in the original conversation.

Read from foundations toward systems and organizational work, or use the contents and search to follow a particular question. Related-section links connect short clips with full conversations and contrasting views. The guests’ observations, predictions, and career experiences are presented in their own context; this edition does not turn them into one universal rule. Diagrams labeled editorial synthesis organize an explanation without pretending the speaker supplied that exact framework.

Part

Thinking, learning, and explaining

Clear reasoning starts before implementation. These conversations connect writing, mathematical models, teaching, and the habit of understanding what sits below an abstraction.

Section 01 · interview

Include performance in the definition of maintainable code

Casey Muratori argues that abstraction rules should explain their compiler costs so engineers can make deliberate, recoverable tradeoffs.

QWhat do you mean by putting “clean code” in quotation marks?

Casey Muratori

Muratori is criticizing particular prescriptions associated with the book Clean Code, rather than readability or maintainability as goals. Different programmers mean different things by “clean” or object-oriented code, so the label alone cannot resolve the argument.

He focuses on a combination: hiding concrete types behind interfaces or base classes and requiring extremely short functions. Either practice can have a rationale, but together they can keep a compiler from seeing what code actually does. He does not think a function becomes unmaintainable merely because it is 30 or 50 lines long, or that knowing concrete types makes source inherently hard to read.

The cost is not chiefly that one virtual call is catastrophically slow. Small functions can be inexpensive when the compiler can inline them. When the target remains opaque, the compiler may lose opportunities to combine code, remove work, unroll loops, or use SIMD. The degree depends on language, visibility, prediction, and compilation or linking capabilities. His objection is to teaching the structure without teaching that consequence.

Source: 00:00–04:58 ↗
The compiler tradeoff Muratori emphasizes
Design situationWhat the compiler may knowConsequence to consider
Small visible function with known typeIts body and target can be identifiedInlining may erase the call boundary
Small function behind an unknown virtual targetThe implementation may remain opaqueInlining and broader loop transformations can be blocked
Maintainable code with explicit performance reasoningThe engineer understands constraints and a future pathA cost can be accepted deliberately instead of discovered too late
Source: 01:10–04:48 ↗

QWould you tell engineers not to read Clean Code?

Casey Muratori

He calls it a mixed bag rather than simply forbidding it. Clear variable names are one example of advice he agrees with. His criticism is that rules need an honest explanation of likely performance costs and the difficulty of later repairs.

He objects to using “premature optimization” as a reason to omit performance from design education. Deliberately accepting a known cost because it will not harm the product is different from deciding to ignore performance until the end. He similarly criticizes broad assurances that refactoring-related performance concerns will usually be fine.

He speculates that this judgment may become even more useful when directing AI to structure code: performance constraints could be part of the instructions. He explicitly says he does little AI work and might be wrong, so that extension should remain a tentative inference.

Source: 05:00–08:44 ↗

QWhat low-cost performance knowledge has the highest value?

Casey Muratori

Learn the basic performance characteristics of the machine and system you are building for. Knowing the difference between network latency and throughput, for example, can lead to batching rather than a deeply serial design that cannot use the network effectively.

Muratori favors education and awareness over prematurely tuning every detail. With enough understanding, you can notice when there is no credible path to making an architecture run well and revisit the decision before it becomes expensive. If you can explain how later optimization will work, most implementation-level optimization can wait.

The objective is to avoid a design corner in which the only fix is a rewrite. He does not supply a benchmark or a universal list of forbidden abstractions; he asks engineers to retain a reasoned path from the current design to the required performance.

Source: 08:46–11:16 ↗

Section 02 · interview

Learning the foundations pays off even when you stop using the syntax

David Malan explains why CS50 uses C before moving to higher-level tools.

QWhy begin with C when teaching programming?

David Malan

Malan sees C as a useful teaching balance: it is close enough to hardware to reveal how programs work, but has more approachable syntax than assembly or machine code. Loops, conditions, functions, variables, and return values make it possible to introduce procedural programming through a relatively small language.

Its limited standard-library support creates a deliberate learning opportunity. Students build data structures rather than immediately instantiate them from a library. In CS50, that includes hash tables, linked lists, trees, tries, stacks, and queues. The purpose is not to make everyone write those implementations repeatedly throughout a career. It is to understand the representations and algorithms underneath the convenient interface.

That understanding has three benefits in his account: better choices when designing data structures, the ability to diagnose failures from first principles, and a foundation for using higher-level languages intelligently. Moving from a substantial C hash-table implementation to a Python dictionary in one line makes the abstraction visible. Malan acknowledges that Python-first teaching can be productive and that CS50 has used it for some audiences; the C-first route serves the course’s broader goals of engineering understanding and technological literacy.

Source: 00:00–03:08 ↗

QWhat would you say to someone who argues that a future web engineer does not need these low-level topics?

David Malan

Malan rejects the conclusion that knowledge is useless because the corresponding language will not be used every day. He distinguishes knowing the underlying principles from literally using a particular implementation tool. Someone describing themselves as a full-stack engineer, in his view, should understand the layers in that stack.

He uses his own teaching as an example: he works in C during a limited part of the course, and Scratch during an even shorter part, while using other languages more frequently. The earlier material still helps him reason about performance, system behavior, and the design of a new solution. His standard for engineering is therefore understanding and creating beyond simply producing code. It is an educational argument, not a requirement that every engineer use C for every task.

Source: 03:09–05:35 ↗

Section 03 · interview

P versus NP asks whether recognizing a solution makes finding it easy

Avi Wigderson uses a computational question to explore the difference between discovery and verification.

QWhat is P versus NP, and why connect it to the limits of human knowledge?

Avi Wigderson

Wigderson deliberately gives an intuitive explanation rather than a formal definition. Computer science studies which problems computers can solve, and efficient algorithms turn some questions into things we can actually know. A navigation application is his example: an efficient shortest-path algorithm makes a useful answer available rather than merely imaginable.

He describes P through efficient solution-finding and NP through efficient checking: even when we do not know how to find an answer, someone might supply a proposed solution whose validity is comparatively easy to verify. The distinction is between discovering the answer and recognizing that an answer is good. NP in this explanation does not mean a class known to be impossible or necessarily hard to solve.

To connect this to human inquiry, he argues that a serious search normally has some way to recognize success. A mathematician can inspect a proposed proof; a scientist can compare a theory with observations; an engineer can check whether a design satisfies the assigned constraints. His examples include physical and monetary constraints, so a design that violates them fails even if it is impressive in other respects.

Wigderson interprets these activities through the discovery-versus-verification lens and asks what would change if efficiently recognizable solutions were also efficiently findable. In that philosophical framing, P equaling NP would collapse a major barrier between what we want to know and what we can discover. His expansive examples, including scientific cures, convey the scale of the question; they are not a claim that the clip supplies a practical algorithm for every human problem. The interview does not resolve P versus NP or establish a literal formal classification of all human endeavors.

Section 04 · interview

Use risk and trust to set review depth

An Instagram engineering leader distinguishes core-system scrutiny from fast peripheral changes and explains the conditions behind accepting with required fixes.

QHow do you decide how deeply to review a code change?

Guest

The guest allocates review effort according to risk. Live production code and the core architecture receive close examination. A gated, noncritical leaf component may receive only a high-level review, including a check for serious problems such as security risks, because the blast radius and cost of rewriting it are smaller.

His trust in a known teammate is part of the calculation. This is not a philosophy he applies automatically to a new colleague, nor one he claims all Meta engineers share. He separates correctness and architectural risk from forcing every implementation to match his personal style.

Do colleagues push back on quick approvals?

Yes. His team knows it can explicitly request a deep review in the description or test plan, or return an approved change to review. The author may know that a superficially small component has a subtle performance or design issue. That signal changes the reviewer’s time allocation even if the component is still peripheral.

QWhy ask how to accept a change instead of how to reject it?

Guest

He wants to identify what truly prevents safe progress: major architectural problems and critical bugs. He is less interested in making another engineer write the code exactly as he would. Greater experience can make reviewers more comfortable with several valid approaches.

He takes conditional approval unusually far. If he spots a bug that would break production, he may leave a clear warning and approve while explicitly requiring the author to fix it first. He says trusted colleagues have not landed such a known defect in his experience. For someone new, or a fix he doubts they can make correctly, he asks to be contacted again before landing.

The title and opening excerpt can obscure that condition. He is not claiming that deliberately shipping a known production-breaking bug is acceptable; he is relying on the author to resolve it before shipping. His reported track record does not prove that this convention is safe in every workflow.

Source: 04:07–06:12 ↗

Speed is adjusted through feedback

The guest applies a similar idea to rollouts: if a small release produces healthy metrics and little adverse feedback, he may expand more quickly, then pull back when negative signals appear. He and the host accept some risk as the cost of learning and progress, while agreeing that repeatedly breaking production means moving too fast. This is a judgment based on system risk and visible feedback, not a fixed rollout schedule.

Source: 06:07–07:34 ↗

Section 05 · interview

Write to expose the gaps in your thinking

Leslie Lamport explains how hierarchical proofs make hidden reasoning steps visible.

QWhy does writing help us think?

Leslie Lamport

Lamport begins with the ease of fooling oneself. While proving increasingly complicated concurrent algorithms correct, he found that his usual mathematical proof style made it hard to track every detail and check whether each obligation had been satisfied. A convincing overall impression did not give him a reliable way to account for all the steps.

His response was hierarchical structure. A proof consists of steps; each step has its own justification, either a paragraph or another sequence of smaller justified steps. The writer identifies which earlier facts support a particular conclusion. If the conclusion does not follow from those facts, the proof is wrong even if the theorem itself happens to be true. Breaking the argument into layers makes those gaps inspectable.

Lamport says the approach worked for proofs of programs and then for ordinary mathematical theorems. He also recalls an unexpectedly angry response when presenting it to a small group of mathematicians. He interprets their reaction as fear that they would have to write proofs for a computer program. That interpretation is his account of the experience, rather than evidence of what every participant actually believed.

He stresses that hierarchical organization does not automatically demand more formal notation. The change is to organize the argument and identify the facts each step uses. It does create more work when it reveals things the author has not actually stated: what felt obvious in thought may turn out to be a missing step on paper. Writing therefore tests whether apparent understanding survives a clear explanation.

Source: 00:00–04:02 ↗

Section 06 · interview

Casey Muratori: Premature Optimization, Clean Code, and the History Behind Software Slogans

Casey Muratori traces the history behind the premature-optimization slogan, argues that object hierarchies and Clean Code rules misread older ideas and hide performance costs, and shares career and AI views.

Muratori's view: slogans need their history, and design needs contact with reality

Casey Muratori, a game-technology programmer who also researches computing history, argues in this interview that software slogans lose their meaning once they are cut off from the context that produced them. In his account, the "premature optimization" line was aimed at programmers who obsessed over cycle-shaving, not at programmers who ignore performance. He argues that object-oriented domain-model hierarchies took the wrong lesson from Sketchpad, and that the Clean Code rules about tiny functions and unknown types carry performance costs the book does not disclose. His remedies are basic performance education, bottom-up development grounded in working code, and reading technical papers. The conversation then covers his career, the parts of a game engine, and his views on AI-assisted programming. Everything below is Muratori's own view or recollection. His historical claims come from his research for conference talks and are not independently verified here.

Source: 01:08–1:56:44 ↗

QWhere does the line "premature optimization is the root of all evil" come from, and why does it matter?

Casey Muratori

Muratori says the phrase matters mainly because people keep repeating and reinterpreting it, so its effects reach far beyond anything Knuth meant in context. Some readers take it with nuance. Others take it bluntly to mean that performance can be ignored until the end of a project, when the slow spots will be found and fixed. He notes that it is about 50 years old, which he calls an incredibly lasting impact for a rule of thumb. He gave a conference talk on its history because earlier reading had shown him how much he did not know. He calls this kind of computer-history digging dumpster diving and says he enjoys it. He adds that he is not a professional historian, so even a thorough read for a talk is shallow compared with what access to personal papers would allow.

Muratori traces two threads that converge around 1974. The first is the software crisis of the late 1960s and early 1970s. Early hardware was simple, so programming meant translating a straightforward description of a computation into machine instructions, close to what hand-optimizing assembly is today. As computing power grew in the 1960s, people wanted payroll systems, data analysis and graphical displays, and programmers were not ready. Abstractions that now go unnoticed, such as calling a library function to load a JPEG, required a cultural shift. The crisis was the recognition that existing methods would not scale.

The second thread is Knuth at Stanford learning to use execution profiles to see where a program spends its time and to guide where development effort goes. Muratori stresses that sampling and instrumenting profilers were brand-new concepts then, not tools everyone assumed they could have. He says Knuth and some students instrumented Fortran programs in 1970, though not very rigorously.

Knuth was also committed to structured programming, which Muratori describes as a set of ideas for improving the situation rather than a neat solution. In Muratori's reading, Knuth's message was that programmers could not spend all their time on tightly optimized assembly. They had to pick their battles and accept concessions to maintainability, and a routine that accounts for little runtime should not be obscured with hand-unrolled loops. Muratori adds that no optimizing compiler like LLVM existed, so such transformations were done by hand. He says the 1974 paper on structured programming with go to statements is the first print appearance he knows of, though Knuth may have said it in lectures earlier. He reads the passage as nuanced: be seriously concerned about efficiency, but know that an optimization matters before applying it, because needless optimization adds a cognitive burden for maintenance and debugging. Muratori reads the phrase as Knuth's way of reminding himself to think before deciding, and he cautions that he does not want to put words in Knuth's mouth.

So is this an engineering trade-off, with the lesson being to be mindful of where the cost is paid?
Casey Muratori

Muratori agrees, and adds that the audience determines what counts as the root of all evil. Today many programmers give optimization little or no thought, so the phrase sounds like encouragement to ignore performance, and he would highly dispute it as a good thing to say now. In the early 1970s, he says, the problem ran the other way: much of programming was clever assembly tricks to shave a cycle. To an auditorium full of people absorbed in that, the line corrects a pendulum swung too far in one direction. In his view it was still hyperbole, but less of an exaggeration then than it would be now.

Source: 14:16–16:31 ↗
Source: 01:08–14:12 ↗

QDid anything surprise you in the research behind your talks?

Casey Muratori

Muratori says constantly, and first names the personal side of the history. The people involved were friends and competitors, and that is lost when computing history is told in a sterile way. His example is Dijkstra, who kicked off the structured-programming line of thought, though Muratori declines to call it a revolution. Dijkstra's typewritten notes on structured programming were written at a low point. Muratori says Dijkstra and a part-time team at the Eindhoven university had done pioneering distributed-computing work, now widely recognized. Because they sat in a mathematics department that did not see it as math, the department disbanded the team, and Dijkstra was unsure what to do with his life. Muratori avoids calling that an existential crisis, preferring to quote the historical figures. His advice is to read what such people wrote beyond their technical papers, because it makes the story felt.

Two smaller finds did not make the talk. The first is a handwritten-annotated note by Tony Hoare about an idea he chose not to pursue, because after Hoare raised it at a conference, Peter Naur replied that multipass compilers are easy and he had just written a nine-pass one. Muratori says that, perhaps overreading with hindsight, the note pretty much describes static single assignment form, a standard compiler technique developed in the 1980s. He wonders half-seriously whether Naur accidentally set compiler science back by roughly 15 to 20 years.

The second is Margaret Hamilton's published defense of the Apollo flight software. Critics had pointed to its alarms as a failure, but Muratori says, from memory and without recalling the venue, that the computer was being used in a configuration it was not meant for and, instead of crashing, switched to backup modes and landed. He sees that as a triumph of fault-tolerant engineering. He says the episode shows that the more things change the more they stay the same: a successful project would draw the same pile-on on Twitter today.

What made you conclude that Dijkstra was depressed?
Casey Muratori

Muratori says Dijkstra was a straight shooter, so no interpretation was needed. In a handwritten retrospective from later in life, Dijkstra says outright that he was very depressed in that period and gives his reasons. Muratori adds that Dijkstra could be wrong about the source of his depression, so he does not claim it is true just because Dijkstra said it.

He also observes that academics of that era produced a voluminous record and benefit from being forthcoming. It would be much harder to learn what people at a company such as Lockheed were thinking, he guesses, because of classification and because they have no habit of writing everything up.

Source: 24:32–26:16 ↗
Source: 16:33–24:30 ↗

QWhat is the people side of Dijkstra's "Go To Statement Considered Harmful"?

Casey Muratori

Muratori calls the story relatively simple and gives it as Dijkstra told it. At a conference in Tennessee, Dijkstra was talking outside with Brian Randell and others, the equivalent of the bar conversations at modern conferences, and gave an example of a problem with goto. Muratori says it involved enumeration and that he can explain it later, but the interview does not return to it. The listeners urged him to publish, since arguments over goto had been growing since about 1959. Dijkstra wrote it up under the title A Case Against the Goto Statement and sent it to Communications of the ACM.

Niklaus Wirth, whom Muratori describes as a language designer and the creator of Pascal, was the editor in charge. As Muratori tells it, Wirth did not want to wait for refereeing, so he ran the piece as a letter to the editor and retitled it Go To Statement Considered Harmful. Muratori says that confrontational title was not Dijkstra's own plan.

The reaction was bad. According to Knuth, Dijkstra received abusive and even threatening letters, much as would happen today. Muratori adds that by all accounts Dijkstra enjoyed pushing people's buttons, and he names Alan Kay, who liked Dijkstra, as the best source for that. Muratori therefore treats the letter as a flash point rather than the first attack on goto, and he calls Wirth's title a clickbait doozy.

How did these arguments play out in print, compared with social media today?
Casey Muratori

Muratori explains that it was a periodical, usually soft-bound, with a table of contents and a letters section. Some historians have digitized personal papers, and he says one can find online a personal exchange between Dijkstra and an advocate of functional programming that reads like a flame war conducted on paper, since there were no quick Twitter replies. Knuth's contribution was different. He published open letters to the authors of the book Structured Programming, including Dijkstra, reviewing it and saying what he did not find compelling. Muratori says it reads as respectful, so he does not count it as a flame war.

He adds that Dijkstra numbered his writings with EWD labels himself, and some non-technical ones, such as trip reports, are online with personal anecdotes. For a real heart-to-heart he found nothing beyond what appeared in papers. He laments that computer historian is not a job anyone pays for, and says he would almost take it.

Source: 32:03–35:08 ↗
Source: 26:17–32:02 ↗

QWhat is the 35-year mistake in your talk?

Casey Muratori

Muratori says the idea came from a practical problem. In editors such as the 3D graphics editors he has worked on, a user can multi-select a mix of objects, say text, shapes and hand-drawn strokes, and the interface should show which properties can be edited across them, such as color, and apply the edit to all. Many programs never solve this architectural problem and are frustrating as a result. While rewatching a demo of Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad, a light-pen graphics program from the early 1960s, he wondered how Sutherland had solved it in assembly with almost no tools. Sketchpad could constrain two lines to be perpendicular, a feature he says AutoCAD offered only around 2007. Reading the thesis and code, he realized the design was essentially an entity component system, which he calls the state of the art for real-time architecture, operating on one property across many different things at once.

His editorial point is that object-oriented teaching struggled with this problem for a long time. He says the pedagogy was to build a domain-model hierarchy, such as employees divided into contractors and full-time or part-time staff, and that this architecture does not suit cross-cutting operations. He says he documents this fully in the talk. The irony he calls the mistake is that Sketchpad's architecture showed the solution, one that could arguably be framed in an object-oriented way, yet the 1980s and 1990s took away a different lesson. In his account Alan Kay looked at Sketchpad and took from it the ability to hold a shape without knowing what it was and ask it to draw, which Muratori finds much less interesting and rarely architecturally useful. He softens the claim: bad is too strong in the absolute, since sometimes high-level Smalltalk-style thinking is appropriate, but it was bad in the way it was applied.

Why doesn't a class hierarchy work for this problem?
Casey Muratori

Muratori says it is easy to see. In a hierarchy modeled on the real world, a shape has derived circles and triangles, and encapsulation is drawn around the most derived class. A circle has a radius but a shape does not. When something has to work across many shapes, such as changing scale or color, it cannot know what is inside those encapsulated classes. The usual fix is to add accessors and iterators at the top that probe the lower classes. That in effect rebuilds the Sketchpad-style architecture on top of the hierarchy and leaves the hierarchy doing nothing for you.

He does not say deriving is useless, since saying one thing is like another and borrowing its implementation can help. His objection is to teaching people that building the hierarchy makes the architecture work. Most real needs are cross-cutting operations over data inside the derived classes, and virtual functions at the top of a tall hierarchy are a poor fit. His alternative is still object-oriented, but the first-class objects are the things shapes are built from, such as a radius or a center, not the on-screen triangle and circle. He believes many object-oriented programmers already think this way and would not object.

Source: 41:29–45:42 ↗
Why not put color in the base class and let each shape use it?
Casey Muratori

Muratori says that is what tends to happen. Base classes accumulate every property any derived class might need, which he says were once called fatty base classes, with accessors for primary, secondary and tertiary colors. Nothing is wrong with running a program that way, but then the hierarchy gives no encapsulation benefit because everything was forced into the base, and a single class called shape would do.

On the entity-component alternative, he says he does not personally use ECS and does not want to advocate it. The idea is to turn the design on its side. The physics system knows how physics data is stored, and any entity that participates holds a handle valid across systems, so encapsulation stays around the system. Something can have several physics handles, or none, in which case the physics system simulates nothing for it. Whether it is the world's best architecture he will not argue, but he says it is a lot better than domain-model hierarchies.

Source: 45:45–48:53 ↗
Source: 35:10–41:28 ↗

QHow does your "Clean Code, Horrible Performance" video fit this trade-off, and why is Clean Code in quotes?

Casey Muratori

Muratori says the quotes are there because clean code, like object-oriented programming, means different things to different people, and two programmers rarely agree on whether code is clean. His video targeted the specific advice in the book Clean Code. One piece is that code should not know the types it operates on, so it works through base classes, effectively dynamic dispatch in many languages. The other is that functions should be very small, with numbers he calls strange, around four or five lines.

In a compiled language such as C++, he says, tiny virtual functions on types the compiler cannot see, or that live in another module, are a toxic combination. The compiler can inline a four-line function it can see, but not one behind a virtual call. He also corrects a misreading of the short video. He does not think virtual calls themselves cost much, since the cost depends on prediction and is less than people think. In a hardcore optimization scenario you would avoid them, but that was not the bad part. The real cost is that the compiler cannot merge code, inline, remove waste, unroll loops or widen them to use SIMD, because it cannot see what is on the other end.

He says the video was not an attack on readable or maintainable code. He has no trouble maintaining functions of 30 or 50 lines, does not find five a magic number, and finds it easy to write code where types are known at compile time without making it hard to read.

Would you recommend that software engineers read Clean Code?
Casey Muratori

Muratori calls it a mixed bag and says he does not disagree with everything in it. Giving variables understandable names, for example, is good advice he follows himself. His objection is to handing out rules of thumb without telling readers about the problems that come with them.

He sees a tendency, rooted in the misuse of "premature optimization is the root of all evil," to treat performance as something books and courses need not discuss. He says the book Refactoring opens by saying performance concerns are usually fine, which he considers fundamentally untrue. In his view such books should discuss in detail the performance problems their advice is likely to cause. A reader who understands the trade-off can decide it is acceptable, which he says is a different engineering approach from not worrying about performance until the end.

He adds that he does not really do AI work, but suspects this matters more now, since people instructing AI tools on how to structure code should include performance trade-offs in those instructions. He allows that he could be wrong about that.

Source: 54:48–58:32 ↗
Source: 49:47–54:47 ↗

QWhat are the high-value performance considerations that cost little to think about?

Casey Muratori

Muratori's first answer is awareness: roughly understanding the performance characteristics of the hardware, and of the network if there is one. A little awareness goes a long way. For example, someone who knows that network latency and throughput are different things can batch work properly up front, whereas someone who does not may get far into a project before discovering that the whole design is serial and can never run well over a network.

The lowest-hanging fruit, he says, is to get some education in how a machine works, what makes it fast or slow and what it struggles with. He calls that the highest-impact, lowest-cost step, because the training is done once and then acts as an alarm bell when he cannot see a path to a design running well. As long as the team can see how they would optimize it later, optimization work can be delayed, and they will not paint themselves into a corner where only scrap and rewrite remains.

Source: 58:34–1:01:31 ↗

QWhere does bad code come from?

Casey Muratori

Muratori says that in everything he has seen on past projects, bad code comes from roughly one source: not dealing with the actual thing that is happening. He finds that upfront design, making many decisions without implementing anything, universally leads to the worst code. He says he personally cannot hold all the details of complex software in his head, including what happens when instructions reach the CPU. A design worked out ahead of time forgets important details, which produces the hilarious APIs where one must create many objects, connect them, build a filter graph and call compile, when all that was wanted was one function that low-pass filters a buffer. The cause, in his view, is that the designers never looked at what the real code looks like when solving the problem.

Maybe some people have brains large enough to do it upfront, but he has never met one. A narrowly specified problem such as a single mathematical operation with known inputs and output can be worked out on paper. For something like a web browser, he says, the details are where the complexity lies, and designing without them gives bad results.

How do you avoid writing bad code?
Casey Muratori

Muratori tries to start from actual solutions and work up, bottom-up rather than top-down, though he notes that top-down is not quite the same as upfront design. If a project needs a rasterizer, he builds one, sees what it does and how it is most straightforwardly called, and makes an API out of that. Abstraction then comes from working code instead of being pushed down from the top, only to discover that it is a poor way to use a rasterizer. This guarantees an architecture that is at least good for one use. To make it reusable, he builds several varied users of the rasterizer together and makes abstraction decisions that work across all of them. He would question anyone who says they can design a rasterizer API for many people without writing any of it, unless they have written many before and so have already done what he describes.

Source: 1:04:41–1:06:15 ↗
Is the design-doc-before-code process common at large companies a terrible idea?
Casey Muratori

Muratori calls it an absolutely terrible idea, but says a slight modification would satisfy him. If the time before coding is spent writing experimental test code, such as a little rasterizer, and the document records which API those experiments showed to be good, that follows his procedure almost exactly. He does not usually produce upfront documentation because he works on smaller teams, but it seems reasonable for communicating research to a wider audience, as long as the due diligence of checking that it works in practice was done.

Source: 1:06:17–1:07:57 ↗
So the design is a kind of paired prototyping, building as you go to get a sense of reality?
Casey Muratori

Muratori agrees. He would be comfortable with a team that wants to document before developing, perhaps a very large organization with good reasons, provided the process is not just typing on paper. The API decisions should come from usage code the team has actually implemented, at least experimentally. He does not want to hear that the team thought it all the way through, because he has seen people believe that, himself included, and then forget an important thing and make a really stupid design.

Source: 1:07:59–1:09:12 ↗
Source: 1:01:36–1:04:40 ↗

QWhat is "the only unbreakable law" in software engineering?

Casey Muratori

Muratori says he gave that lecture while trying to name one thing about architecture that is probably not wrong, since most architecture ideas are observations, not laws. The only one that feels like a real law to him is Conway's law. He says a physicist would laugh at calling it a law and that it is more a hypothesis than a theory, but it is the software-engineering claim he would bet on being validated if we ever could test it.

His version of the argument applies to any set of workers, human or AI agents, whose communication with each other is slower than each one's internal computation. To gain from parallelization you must decide who works on what. In his car example, one person designs the body and another the wheels. That decision locks in that iteration across the boundary will be slower than within either part, so the degree of harmony between the two designs suffers. The consequence Conway's paper points out, which Muratori places in the 1960s at least and possibly the 1950s, is that products come to resemble the structure of the organization that produced them. The boundary will be visible in the object, because the interface between parts is not as good as the parts themselves. The pithy form is that products look like the org chart, which he calls a downstream consequence of the rule.

Is this the idea that shipping your org chart is a bad thing at big tech companies?
Casey Muratori

Muratori says part of why he treats it as unbreakable is that it is somewhat unavoidable. It is something to be aware of and mitigate. Where lines are drawn has consequences for what ships, so over time one should try to place the boundaries where they hurt the product least. He suspects the same will become true for AIs, which will need to partition problems in ways that respect that lower communication bandwidth. He also finds it a good explanation for why something is not integrated into something else: because they were two different teams, and integrating them would cost much more.

Source: 1:14:06–1:15:56 ↗
Source: 1:09:14–1:14:02 ↗

QHow did you get into programming, and what have you worked on?

Casey Muratori

Muratori says he started programming very young because his father worked at Digital Equipment Corporation, maker of the PDP-11 and the VAX. He describes the company as a case study in how failing to adapt to a technological change leads to demise, with parts absorbed by Intel and Compaq. He grew up on the east coast, got a Microsoft internship while pretty young, and came west around 1995, before everything was on the web. He has worked in the game industry since, almost always on technology, and says he is famously terrible at game design.

He is proudest of a character animation system he wrote at Rad Game Tools, apart from a texture compressor written by Jeff Roberts. He says the first version, released in 1999, was awful because he was new. The second, around 2001, he thinks was done well, at a time when people thought licensable game technology of that kind could not meet performance and integration demands. He says it is still in use with a largely unchanged architecture and that he recently learned Larian uses it in Baldur's Gate 3. He adds that it is not a product one would make today, since engines are now monolithic. He also worked briefly on the walk system for The Witness, by Jonathan Blow and team, of which he thinks the design was good and the implementation partly janky.

What drew you toward games and away from a Microsoft career?
Casey Muratori

Muratori says the full answer is probably all BS, and that he is more affected by the people around him than he used to admit. He was only ever an intern. The group he was to join had a manager who had a massive flame-out with upper management and walked out the week before the interns arrived. The interns were handed to a test lead and a colleague, and his first task was a parser for animated cursor files, which he found meaningless. He did not know assembly at the time, and says that with a team that taught him to write device drivers in assembly he might still be at Microsoft.

Instead, he says, a brash youngster gravitates toward people doing impressive or technologically interesting things. The people he found impressive were colleagues leaving Microsoft to do a startup, and if they had stayed, he thinks he might have too. This is his best reconstruction in hindsight.

Source: 1:20:44–1:25:50 ↗
Moving across the country for a startup sounds risky. Why did you do it?
Casey Muratori

Muratori agrees it was risky, and says a startup then meant scrappy people in a crummy office, not venture funding and free sodas. He did not really know why he did it, other than having had bad experiences with education, wanting no more school and wanting to work, and this was the easiest way.

He does not regret it. Later work let him spend months on things like a linear least-squares solver or the walk system, which he sees as the kind of deep, single-problem work, with paper reading and a small novel contribution, that people do in a master's or PhD thesis. He says he was lucky to get that, and had he not, he could imagine regretting skipping graduate study.

Source: 1:25:51–1:28:19 ↗
Was there pay at that startup, and what did you take from it?
Casey Muratori

Muratori says it was pretty rough and did not last long. He soon moved to an actual game company and then to Rad Game Tools, where he stayed for quite some time. His negative takeaway is that startups are hard and probably not worth doing without many people and lots of funding.

The positive one is that he worked with Chris Hecker, to whom he gives basically complete credit for teaching him to read technical papers. Before that he thought math was stupid and had no idea what to do with a SIGGRAPH proceedings. He learned to use CiteSeer, a precursor to Google Scholar, and to crawl references. He says without that experience he would not have given the two talks discussed here, since they consist of him crawling every reference back and back, and he does not know whether he would have learned that without someone conveying the importance of reading the scholarship.

Source: 1:28:21–1:30:42 ↗
Source: 1:15:57–1:20:41 ↗

QFor someone young, should they take the common big-company path or the chance on a startup?

Casey Muratori

Muratori calls it a really tough question and says the advice is to think about what you want to do every day. The things he regrets are times he chose or had to do things he was not happy doing daily. Both paths are blind bets: a startup might work out and a big company might be interesting, or not. So optimize for the day-to-day experience you want, and keep checking. If six months in you do not like what you do every day, get out.

He suggests imagining honestly what working at a startup will be like: is it thrilling, being on the edge, collecting war stories about pulling off the demo? If that sounds exciting, he says you should do it, even if you expect the startup to fail, much like backpacking across Europe or playing guitar at a nightclub. The question is whether you will look back and be glad you did it. He thinks most people, if honest and free of motivated reasoning, can guess better than his advice would.

The big-company side may suit someone who values security or stability, for example while dating, looking for a partner or starting a family, because not everything fulfilling in a life centers on computing.

Source: 1:30:44–1:34:50 ↗

QWhat are the big software pieces in a video game?

Casey Muratori

Muratori says the biggest mental shift from the input-process-output model taught in programming is that a game or any simulation keeps a world state and updates it at a regular interval. Nothing waits for input; everything is always happening in real time. The components are built around this idea, with the depth depending on sophistication. For networked games, the client's world state may be provisional: the authoritative simulation runs on a server, and the client predicts motion forward from the last information it has to avoid waiting on latency. The host relates this to online-game lag, where other players keep moving and then jump into place when the connection catches up, and Muratori confirms.

Source: 1:34:52–1:39:55 ↗
Main components of a game, as Muratori describes them
ComponentRole as Muratori describes it
World state (entities)Stores what is in the world, where it is, what state it is in and what it is doing now.
Update stepAdvances the world state. Can include physical simulation and game AI such as pathfinding or deciding whether to attack the player.
RendererPresents the world state. Traditionally a major part of big-budget games, where visuals are a selling point, and much smaller in indie pixel-art games.
Asset streamingLoads textures, models, world data, physics and collision models on demand from disk and caches them for the renderer and physics, instead of loading everything up front.
Audio and musicTriggers sounds, ambient effects and music from the world state, using streamed assets.
NetworkingLets clients talk to a server that runs the authoritative simulation. Clients predict world state forward to hide latency, which matters for competitive multiplayer.
Source: 1:35:48–1:39:41 ↗

QWhy is it "not even slightly crazy" that NASA does not allow recursion?

Casey Muratori

Muratori explains that in a procedural language, calling a function gives you storage on the program stack for locals and saves the return address so execution comes back to the right place. Neither is something you could not implement yourself: you can break the work into pieces, use a state machine, or keep your own stack and push data onto it. Recursion only lets you reuse code someone already wrote, which is convenient because it is built into the language.

The catch, he says, is that using recursion assumes there is room on the stack, with no real way to check. One could try to compute how many recursion levels remain, but a compiler change to the stack layout would invalidate the calculation. If NASA wants astronauts not to crash into the moon, it is far more logical to turn the algorithm into a loop with an explicit stack and a state machine. That can be reasoned about clearly, gives exact bounds and behaves the same regardless of the compiler. He assumes NASA is not doing this for fun but because lives, or at minimum millions of dollars of equipment, are at risk, and a stack overflow there is not just a restart.

Source: 1:39:57–1:43:09 ↗

QYou replied to the vibe-coding tweet that software would get a lot worse. Has that proved accurate?

Casey Muratori

The host places the tweet in February 2025, about a year and a half earlier. Muratori says the "whole lot worse" part depends on something that may not happen: that typing a request into a computer and shipping the result to production becomes a common way of working, including for people without a computer-science background. He says a person well trained in computer science using AI today can make substantially better code than someone who knows nothing about the field using the same tool, and that the difference is dramatic from what he has seen. His concern was that nobody who knows computer science would check the code, and in the worst case some random person in marketing types a request and crosses their fingers.

He frames it as a race between two curves. One is how good and autonomous AI becomes, able to make better decisions without the user. The other is how quickly it is adopted by people who are less capable and pay less attention to its output. If the AI is always good enough for what it is being adopted for, software need not get significantly worse. If the curves go the other way, he says, there is a lot of trouble. He feels the situation is on a knife's edge and offers no prediction.

Muratori hopes the AI curve wins. He understands people who dislike AI and want it to fail, and says he is no fan of AI himself. But with so many people using it, he thinks it would be bad if it stopped improving now, as he believes would have been true six months ago and is probably still true. For software not to be terrible, he says, one has to hope the AIs are significantly better again in six months, which he sees as the only way out of the current situation, though he is unsure whether that is fair.

Source: 1:43:11–1:47:29 ↗

QWhy did you reply "slopify" to Shopify's internal AI memo?

Casey Muratori

The host reads the tweet as leadership pushing the adoption curve harder than the AI's capabilities. Muratori says he also just liked the pun. What he finds most unfortunate about how companies adopt AI is their reasoning that not getting in early would be a disaster, so everyone must adopt now, before they know whether it can do what they want or whether the outcomes will be good. He understands why they believe it is critical.

To him it is terrifying, because the sane approach with any technology is to measure its capabilities, see whether it solves your problems faster than your current method, and put it into a workflow once it is a net positive. A team whose job is to assess it is a good idea, but he does not think everyone should be told to use a ton of tokens, or that people should be running 3,000 agents on a cluster talking to each other. He does not think adoption has gone in the best way for software quality.

He tempers this with a caveat he adds to most AI criticism: software was not exactly a five-nines industry to begin with, and its quality was pretty low going into the AI era. Some AI uses may make things worse, but he calls the narrative that software was amazing until AI ruined everything completely ridiculous and untrue.

Source: 1:47:30–1:50:21 ↗

QDo you have a top technical book recommendation for engineers?

Casey Muratori

Muratori says no, and uses the question to pitch reading technical papers, both historical and current. He says the industry would benefit from people being more aware of what is happening in their field. It is daunting at first: papers are confusing, hard to find, and seem to take too long if you do not know how to skim them to decide whether a section is worth your time. But he says that a few months of reading a paper at night or on a lunch break gets you your bearings. You learn where the good papers are and where they are published, and how to spend your time on them.

He thinks this is tremendously valuable in nearly all fields, perhaps excluding a few small ones where people do not write many papers. He says he finds it so rewarding that he reads papers in disciplines he does not work in, such as security research, even though games rarely involve that kind of threat model, simply because there is so much good material to learn from.

How would a generalist find a first paper worth reading?
Casey Muratori

Muratori suggests pulling up the proceedings of USENIX, finding a paper that sounds interesting, or trying the best-paper award of a conference, which he says USENIX tends to have. He says those proceedings usually cover operating systems and systems design, topics most people can relate to. By contrast, he says, opening a SIGGRAPH proceedings would turn up something like neural networks for cloth simulation, which someone outside graphics cannot relate to.

Another option is Google Scholar. If you are curious about a consensus algorithm such as Paxos that came up at work, you can type it in and get a list of papers with cited-by counts, which he says is, to a certain extent, an indicator of how influential a paper was. He adds that it will not be for everyone and some people may bounce off, but it is worth a try.

Source: 1:52:04–1:54:26 ↗
Source: 1:50:24–1:52:03 ↗

QIf you could advise yourself at the start of your career, what would you say?

Casey Muratori

Muratori says he would tell himself to get into low-level programming earlier. By his rough estimate he did not learn to analyze or write assembly properly until roughly the last decade (the captions garble the year). He had always wanted to know how, and the advice would have been to go down the hall and ask someone to show him how they write this.

He thinks many young people fear appearing not to know things, and that this is a real impediment to learning. He says it was probably true of him. Saying "I don't understand this, please explain it to me" is among the most useful things you can do, and most people will happily oblige if they are not unkind. Some very good engineers are poor at explaining what they do, so the first explanation may not be good, but if you keep asking you will find someone who can explain clearly. He adds that today he would not need this advice, because the internet has so much good information and he could have taught himself, which was not possible when he started.

Section 07 · interview

David Malan: Teach the Principles, Make the Learning Memorable

CS50’s instructor explains long-form teaching, learning the layers beneath abstractions, AI tutoring, open education and the value of exploring beyond a planned path.

QHow did you first discover computer science as a student?

David J. Malan

Malan entered Harvard expecting to study government, following his interest in constitutional law. Familiar subjects felt safer, so he did not try CS50 until his sophomore year in 1996, when Brian Kernighan taught it.

The course changed his relationship with homework. He looked forward to returning to his dorm on Friday evenings and working through the problem sets. Enjoying that demanding work was a signal to change direction, rather than evidence that he had arrived already knowing how to program.

Why did your first Hello World assignment lose points?

He remembers a small, easily corrected mistake. His preserved assignment demonstrates that even the person who later taught the course did not begin with a flawless submission.

Source: 02:22–02:43 ↗
Source: 00:57–02:21 ↗

QHow did you go from student to teacher?

David J. Malan

As a senior, he taught an introductory computers-and-internet course at Harvard Extension School to a room of adults. At about twenty-one, he was younger than his audience and tried to project maturity, but the experience chiefly revealed that he enjoyed teaching.

He later returned for a computer-science PhD because that qualification would open teaching opportunities. As he finished in 2007, his adviser moved into a dean’s role and CS50 needed an instructor. Malan was initially intended as a one-year replacement. His long tenure grew out of that opening rather than a predetermined career plan.

Source: 02:45–04:12 ↗

QDid you immediately plan to transform CS50 into a major online course?

David J. Malan

No. Malan describes an evolution. His Extension School teaching already involved distance education: early classes were filmed on VHS, sometimes by undergraduate friends operating the camera. Later the team distributed streaming audio and video, then downloadable podcast files that students could use during a commute or at the gym.

The initial aim was convenience for existing students, especially freedom from a constant internet connection. Video podcasting expanded those uses. Unexpected popularity and repeated bandwidth limits then revealed a wider audience. That encouraged the team to make the material accessible to people who could not attend because of geography or resources.

The historical dates are informal recollections. The causal lesson is that solving an existing student need exposed a broader opportunity over time.

Was the public material originally a supplement for students who had paid to enroll?

Yes, and giving it away created some campus tension. Malan distinguishes knowledge from the support, credit, transcript and credential that a formal enrollment provides. He thinks withholding the knowledge itself serves society poorly.

Source: 07:45–08:17 ↗
Source: 04:13–07:43 ↗

QDo short-form internet hooks shape the design of your lectures?

David J. Malan

They shape some social content, but not the basic lecture format. Interviews, project-fair excerpts and occasional topical material can help new students notice the course. The lectures remain substantial sessions rather than a sequence of tiny clips optimized for scrolling.

Malan distinguishes engagement metrics from educational outcomes. Online learners can pause, rewind, search and pursue a question in another tab, so a long recording need not be consumed in one sitting. He prefers to give students that control, including taking longer than the nominal lecture time when necessary. He acknowledges downsides to long lectures without concluding that shorter is always pedagogically better.

Source: 08:19–10:34 ↗

QHow do you keep people engaged through a three-hour lecture?

David J. Malan

The team creates memorable moments tied to concepts. Tearing a phone book in half dramatizes binary search. Having students open lockers to find a number makes the difference between linear and binary search visible. Asking students to sort themselves brings sorting algorithms into physical space.

Those demonstrations also expose prerequisites and costs: binary search requires sorted data, so sorting must be understood before treating the search improvement as free. Simple algorithms can be valuable teaching tools even when faster library implementations would be used professionally.

The aim is a memory anchor. An overwhelmed beginner may forget terminology but remember a roommate acting out bubble sort, then reconstruct the idea from that scene. Malan wants at least one such moment in a class, for remote and in-person students alike.

Source: 10:35–13:39 ↗

QDoes that theatricality sacrifice technical depth?

David J. Malan

Yes, there is a tradeoff. Experienced students may not need ten minutes on linear search or a lengthy physical demonstration of binary search. Malan deliberately spends disproportionate time on some concepts because they motivate beginners and help them see the meaningful problem behind hours of implementation and debugging.

He treats the balance between density and memorable presentation as a design problem, not something automatically solved by enthusiasm. At the same time, a dry recitation is a weak reason to gather people in one room: a book or written message could convey the same words. The lecture should offer interaction and a reason to care.

Source: 13:41–15:27 ↗

QWhere does your energetic delivery come from?

David J. Malan

Malan partly attributes it to the insecurity of not wanting to stand before a bored audience. Bringing energy is a way to earn students’ attention and communicate the excitement he found in the field.

He also sees it as an obligation. Students should encounter the subject in a form that lets them decide whether they love it, rather than judge it only through an uninspired presentation. That excitement connects to the actual work they will do outside class, rather than performance for its own sake.

Source: 15:31–16:54 ↗

QWhy not share the strongest teaching materials across institutions instead of duplicating every course?

David J. Malan

Malan sees substantial duplication in preparing lectures, assignments and grading systems. Sharing that work could free educators for the more personal parts of education: mentoring, supporting and interacting with students. His aim is not to eliminate educators but to make their effort more valuable.

He describes collaborations with Yale and Oxford as exceptions rather than the normal structure of higher education. During pandemic teaching, he hoped institutions would let students take one another’s courses more freely, but found little appetite for it.

He does not propose one monopoly introductory course. Healthy competition and different modes of instruction remain useful. He imagines a smaller collection of strong shared resources that other teachers can adopt and adapt as an educational buffet, instead of repeatedly recreating all the same material.

Source: 16:56–20:46 ↗

QWhat prevents a college from using another institution’s better resources?

David J. Malan

He suspects a combination of institutional pride and fear of making one’s own work seem unnecessary, while acknowledging that others could explain their motivations better. He encountered a desire for Harvard to offer only what Harvard itself created, even when nearby institutions had richer catalogs in some areas.

Research collaboration across campuses is normal; educational collaboration can feel more personal or threatening. Malan would rather let institutions specialize, share resources and provide different local support experiences. In that model, borrowing a strong course is a way to improve service, not an admission of failure.

Source: 20:48–22:36 ↗

QWhy retain C in an introductory course when many students will use higher-level languages at work?

David J. Malan

C predates Malan’s leadership of CS50, and he chose to keep it because it exposes hardware and memory while retaining readable programming constructs. It offers loops, conditions, functions and values in a relatively small language, without requiring assembly as the starting point.

The limited built-in conveniences are useful educationally. Students implement structures such as lists and hash tables instead of merely instantiating a library object. That makes representation, performance and failure modes tangible. The purpose is not to make them repeatedly hand-build those structures in a job, but to give them a basis for engineering decisions and diagnosis.

The transition to Python then has meaning: a large hash-table implementation becomes a one-line dictionary construction, and the student understands what the abstraction is providing. CS50 aims to develop engineers and informed citizens who can reason from first principles, not only people who can use the current interface.

Source: 22:38–26:11 ↗

QWhat would you say to someone who thinks full-stack developers do not need to understand the lower layers?

David J. Malan

Malan distinguishes not using a low-level language every day from not benefiting from knowing how the system works. He uses C only for a limited portion of the course, yet that understanding informs his use of higher-level languages, performance choices and design.

He thinks a full-stack engineer should be able to reason across the layers. Familiarity with Scratch, C or another teaching tool can be valuable even when the literal syntax is rarely used later. The aim is to solve new problems and understand symptoms, particularly when generating routine code is increasingly easy.

Source: 27:06–29:32 ↗

QWhat can an introductory course teach about AI in a single session?

David J. Malan

The AI session is a broad introduction, not an attempt to compress a full AI curriculum into an hour. On campus it coincides with family weekend. It supplies context for a technology people hear about and for the virtual rubber-duck assistant students use in the course.

It also prepares students to use general AI tools more effectively for their final projects. Malan distinguishes that permitted project use from the more restricted policy for ordinary course assignments; the rules reflect different educational purposes.

Source: 29:34–31:05 ↗

QWhat is the ideal relationship between introductory students and AI?

David J. Malan

The course’s virtual rubber duck is intentionally less willing to provide answers than a general chatbot. It should lead a student toward a solution like a tutor, rather than complete the assignment. Malan had already seen code-completion tools generate a known problem set from little more than a familiar filename.

Open teaching materials can appear in model training data, which makes general tools especially good at giving away those answers. The duck is an effort to retain useful assistance while reducing the temptation to bypass the thinking the assignment is meant to develop.

Is that mainly a system prompt and scaffolding that asks the model to teach rather than answer?

Broadly, yes. Malan also values the clear interface and policy boundary: students may use the course assistant, while ordinary assignments prohibit general tools that can do the work for them. Asking each student to paste and maintain a special prompt in a general chatbot would be clumsy and easy to ignore. A dedicated tool makes the expected behavior easier to follow.

Source: 32:57–34:07 ↗
Source: 31:07–32:55 ↗

QHas AI increased cheating, and can you detect it?

David J. Malan

Malan says detected academic dishonesty has not increased statistically in the course’s observations. Historically, comparisons among submissions and with public repositories or transcribed videos led to administrative action for roughly five to ten percent of students per semester in his account. That is a reported detection and discipline rate, not a measurement of every act of cheating.

AI makes evidence harder to present. A copied answer once had a specific source URL; a model may blend patterns from many sources. Experienced staff can still notice unexpected sophistication, inconsistency with prior work or an answer to an older version of an assignment, but such signs are different from a clear copied-source match.

He hopes explicit boundaries, course culture and support keep most students acting appropriately. He acknowledges that some misconduct inevitably remains undetected, so a stable detection count cannot prove an unchanged underlying rate.

Does a five-to-ten-percent rate still feel high?

It did to him earlier in his teaching career. After seeing similar results repeatedly, he is chiefly relieved it is not higher. That reaction does not remove the need for fair evidence in individual cases.

Source: 37:17–37:35 ↗
Source: 34:10–37:15 ↗

QWhat would you tell a student afraid that AI will make learning programming pointless?

David J. Malan

Focus on learning to solve problems. Malan treats language syntax as an implementation detail that supplies representative tools and teaches underlying principles. Methodical reasoning remains valuable within technology and in other fields.

He welcomes automation of work such as repetitive tests or documentation lookup, while continuing to value system design, user experience, database choices and decisions about what information a business needs. A more technological world still presents problems requiring judgment.

He illustrates both the benefit and limit with an AI-assisted prototype: the tool handled much of the implementation, but confidently proposed an operation the API could not support. His knowledge let him challenge it using the documentation. He expects error rates to improve, but uses the example to explain why people need sufficient understanding to remain in charge.

What if the tools become much more accurate than they are today?

Malan does not claim to know the ultimate capability limit. His educational objective remains worthwhile even with much more automation: helping students teach themselves, reason algorithmically and become better-informed citizens. That argument does not depend on predicting how many lines humans will type.

Source: 41:28–42:15 ↗
Source: 37:37–41:27 ↗

QIs AI reducing enrollment or interest in computer science?

David J. Malan

Malan says recent interest appears to have declined, but places it after a downturn in recruiting opportunities that began before general AI tools were ubiquitous. He thinks AI-related uncertainty has exacerbated that concern.

He expects fluctuations rather than a simple permanent decline, recalling earlier swings around the dot-com era and other technologies. His broader observation is that the technology and investment worlds often overreact before finding a more balanced assessment of a tool’s value. This is an interpretation of current campus experience and a forecast, not a universal enrollment dataset.

Source: 42:16–44:39 ↗

QHow does free online learning compare with attending college in person?

David J. Malan

It depends on the goal. Malan sees significant value in credentials, the admissions filter, networks, relationships and life experiences at a university. Those benefits are not the same as access to course information.

For knowledge and practical learning, he thinks an online course can offer an excellent experience, sometimes improved by pause, rewind and the ability to investigate questions immediately. He does not claim that receiving the same lecture produces all the same social opportunities or outcomes as campus attendance.

Source: 44:40–46:22 ↗

QWhich concept consistently gives students the most difficulty?

David J. Malan

Pointers in C. Malan remembers struggling himself and then experiencing a sudden realization during a conversation with a teaching fellow: a pointer was an address. The simplicity of that phrase did not make the concept immediately intuitive.

Memory is unfamiliar to someone who has only experienced a computer as a black box. The anecdote makes room for delayed understanding, even when several people have already given the apparently correct explanation.

Source: 46:24–47:29 ↗

QHow do you help someone understand a difficult concept?

David J. Malan

Use a familiar metaphor or a memorable physical example. A phone book, a contacts application or doors with hidden numbers can make search behavior visible. The learner may discover that an apparently arcane algorithm resembles something they already do.

Likewise, explaining decimal place values before binary makes the new system a variation on a known pattern: ones, tens and hundreds become ones, twos and fours. Malan wants that recognition to bring learners into the conversation, rather than leave the subject feeling reserved for people who already belong.

Source: 47:31–49:14 ↗

QCan anyone learn computer science, or should persistent struggle sometimes suggest another direction?

David J. Malan

Malan does not offer an unlimited promise. If repeated attempts over a long period produce neither understanding nor enjoyment, exploring another field may be sensible. But struggling after only a few attempts should not immediately become a verdict on a person’s ability.

Change the approach: another class, instructor, teaching assistant or book may explain the same idea in a way that clicks. His own teaching style will not suit everyone. Time is another adjustable variable. An online learner need not finish in twelve weeks if twenty-four or fifty-two better fits the demands of their life. The numbers illustrate patience and flexibility, not a precise threshold for giving up.

Source: 50:03–51:48 ↗

QWhat comes next for CS50?

David J. Malan

He expects tooling and presentation to evolve with AI, while the introductory problem-solving backbone remains. Comparing past and upcoming syllabuses reveals substantial conceptual continuity despite very different lectures and assignments.

The team is also expanding a curriculum around the core course, including gentler starting points and later study. Malan describes planned work with an Oxford colleague on mathematics, with broader STEM and potential arts-and-humanities collaboration of interest. These are directions and plans described in the interview, rather than a claim that all the proposed courses have already shipped.

Source: 51:51–53:52 ↗

QHow do you think about other educational resources such as Khan Academy?

David J. Malan

Malan welcomes healthy competition if it encourages new teaching approaches. Different resources can serve different learners, and more accessible educational material benefits the world.

How might a parent choose between styles of online course?

He describes differences in presentation rather than declaring one universally superior. CS50 tries to maintain a recognizable aesthetic and lecturing style across its courses. Khan Academy’s early handwritten explanations offered a different, compelling experience. Familiarity with a style can help a learner know what to expect.

Source: 54:22–55:10 ↗
Source: 53:55–54:20 ↗

QWhat is your biggest career regret?

David J. Malan

Malan wishes he had calmed down and explored more. He arrived at college with a plan for all his courses and spent too much attention crossing requirements off a list. Later experiences in Latin, theater and archaeology revealed how much he enjoyed subjects outside his expected path.

Professionally, he wishes he had spent more time in industry before remaining in academia. A later semester as a professor in residence at GitHub let him observe team meetings, issues, feature requests and design conversations. He found it rewarding to experience the working environment his teaching discussed. The regret is about missed exploration, alongside appreciation for the career he did have.

Did you ship code during the GitHub residency?

He does not think he contributed production code. His role was an educational voice, supplying issues, bug reports and feature requests and explaining what teachers and students needed from the products. Contribution can take that form even when it does not appear as an authored code change.

Source: 57:48–58:27 ↗
Source: 55:12–57:47 ↗

QWhat stands out as having gone well during your leadership of CS50?

David J. Malan

Open courseware became a meaningful mission. Malan credits earlier work at MIT as an inspiration, and describes stories from learners about professional transitions, family support and discovering a field they thought was inaccessible.

Those are anecdotal impacts, not a controlled outcomes study, but they make the work personally worthwhile. He hopes the course’s openness and production offer an example others can use, with more mutual sharing still a missed opportunity.

Source: 58:29–59:42 ↗

QWhich books would you recommend?

David J. Malan

His personal favorite is The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy. For technology, he fondly remembers the illustrated How Computers Work and How the Internet Works books as accessible explanations, while noting that their contents have aged.

For deeper low-level C techniques, he mentions Hacker’s Delight. He also values books designed for broad beginners, including familiar introductory series, because a textbook should not require someone to have already taken the course to understand it.

CS50 does not require learners to buy a textbook. That supports the commitment to remove financial barriers to the material rather than making one particular book a prerequisite.

Is there a required textbook for the on-campus Harvard course?

No. He identifies computer and internet access as requirements, without a separate mandatory textbook purchase.

Source: 1:01:40–1:01:50 ↗
Source: 59:45–1:01:39 ↗

QWhat advice would you give yourself at the beginning of your career?

David J. Malan

Explore more and experience additional jobs. Malan thinks another year or two between undergraduate and graduate study might have broadened his perspective, or an industry period after the PhD could have done so.

He also recognizes the timing tradeoff: leaving campus might have meant missing the CS50 opening. He is not rewriting the past as a clear mistake, but encouraging more deliberate experimentation alongside an attractive academic path.

Source: 1:01:52–1:02:46 ↗
