Section 08 · interview

Modularity makes correctness a problem you can reason about

Barbara Liskov traces data abstraction and distributed systems through practical problems, research freedom, and ideas that became invisible through success.

QHow did you enter programming when graduate education could exclude women?

Barbara Liskov

After completing an undergraduate mathematics degree, Liskov applied to graduate programs. Princeton sent a postcard saying it did not admit women. She had known about its undergraduate restriction but had not realized the graduate program was also closed to her. Berkeley did admit her, but she decided she was not ready for a mathematics PhD and wanted to work first. The best job offer was programming, which she calls a fortunate accident that brought her into computer science.

The host notes that she had been a strong student and still faced a closed door. Liskov contrasts that institutional exclusion with Berkeley’s environment: her mathematics classes had few women, but the university did not treat the subject as something women were prohibited from doing. She separates low representation from an explicit denial of access rather than turning the story into one undifferentiated description of every institution.

Source: 00:31–02:51 ↗

QWhat was the software crisis, and what made large programs fail?

Barbara Liskov

Liskov recalls reports of organizations spending large sums and hundreds of person-years on systems they ultimately discarded because the programs did not work. The missing discipline was modular design: divide the system into components whose interfaces explain the service they provide, while hiding their implementations.

With an appropriate decomposition, correctness can be reasoned about one module at a time. But procedures were the main mechanism offered by languages of that era, and a procedure did not naturally represent a stateful service such as a filesystem or a database. The problem was not simply how to cut a large file into smaller files. It was finding a module concept that matched the design of a real system.

What were the early proposed solutions, and how did you find data abstraction?
Barbara Liskov

Researchers talked about modularity without a clear account of what a module was. Some treated a module as a chunk of code of a particular size, which Liskov did not consider a sufficient design rule.

Earlier work at Mitre had given her a more complete mechanism. A small team was building a complicated system, and she wanted to keep the programmers from interfering with each other. A component exposed a collection of operations while its internal data remained inaccessible. She eventually recognized that this could represent a set, sequence, or other abstract data type. In hindsight, she saw related papers as close to the idea: it was a moment when several pieces were ready to fit together.

Source: 04:58–07:05 ↗
Source: 02:53–04:55 ↗

QHow did this work in CLU influence programming languages beyond the research project?

Barbara Liskov

Liskov and Steve Zilles wrote a paper outlining abstract data types and how a language could support them. It had an immediate effect in the research community, and CLU then developed the language-level ideas further.

She chose not to turn CLU into a commercial product. She preferred research, and companies of that period generally wanted an organization standing behind a language rather than downloading an independently shared project. CLU still had users, but broad adoption also came through later languages. She identifies Ada as a prominent language designed with data abstraction and Java as another later step in the influence of the underlying ideas.

Source: 07:07–09:00 ↗

QWhat concerned you about Python’s modules?

Barbara Liskov

Liskov’s criticism is about encapsulation: code outside a module can interfere with its internal state. She regards protection of that boundary as essential to modularity, especially when many programmers work on a large system. Compiler-enforced restrictions can prevent a weak implementation or misuse from undermining the whole team. She also acknowledges that Python serves other goals and says she no longer considers herself a programming-language expert. The argument is her view of the tradeoff, not a comprehensive evaluation of Python’s current ecosystem.

Source: 09:03–10:16 ↗

QWhat drew you into distributed computing?

Barbara Liskov

A paper by Bob Kahn described programs composed of pieces on different networked computers, at a time when how to build those systems was still unclear. Liskov saw an important open problem while looking for a new direction. Her first project was a language for distributed programs; subsequent work followed the problems that project exposed.

What was that language, and how did it manage a computation spanning machines?
Barbara Liskov

Argus was influenced by CLU. A guardian was a module on one machine, and guardians communicated with remote procedure calls. A computation using several guardians needed to complete as a whole or leave no effect. Liskov borrowed transactions from databases so those computations could run atomically. That work led toward storing replicated data with correct behavior and availability when enough nodes and the network remained operational.

Source: 11:03–12:30 ↗
What does a viewstamp represent?
Barbara Liskov

It lets the system identify sufficiently recent state when a node fails and another must take over. The goal is to continue without losing already completed work. The clip gives the intuition rather than a full protocol specification.

Source: 12:32–12:51 ↗
What happens when clocks disagree?
Barbara Liskov

The mechanism does not depend on synchronized wall clocks. Liskov says the views are numbered: one view is followed by the next numbered view. The host recognizes this as passing and incrementing logical numbers rather than comparing clock readings.

Source: 12:53–13:07 ↗
Source: 10:17–11:02 ↗

QDid you develop this work together with Leslie Lamport?

Barbara Liskov

No. Liskov says they independently reached essentially the same underlying idea: her Viewstamped Replication and Lamport’s Paxos. She is describing a shared core rather than claiming every presentation and implementation is identical.

Are there significant advantages and disadvantages between the two approaches?
Barbara Liskov

She says there are technical details one can vary, but regards the main mechanism as substantially the same. She recalls a former student recognizing Viewstamped Replication in Google’s filesystem-related work while the people using it described it as Paxos. This is her account of recognizing the common idea.

Source: 13:33–14:15 ↗
Source: 13:09–13:32 ↗

QHow did parallel work on object-oriented languages lead to the substitution principle?

Barbara Liskov

Liskov describes simultaneous but partly separate research streams: CLU, Smalltalk, and Alphard. When preparing an OOPSLA keynote, she read work based on Smalltalk and noticed an unresolved connection between implementation inheritance and type hierarchy.

Her own teaching with John Guttag emphasized module specifications, abstract data types, and correctness. It began with what a component meant; its implementation remained hidden. By contrast, some class descriptions she read explained how an implementation differed from its superclass. Thinking in terms of behavior gave her a way to state the required relation: a subclass used where a superclass is expected should behave appropriately for that context.

That insight became associated with the Liskov substitution principle. Liskov says her later paper with Jeannette Wing formalized behavioral subtyping. The interview’s account emphasizes expectations and meaning rather than treating reuse of a superclass implementation as sufficient proof of substitutability.

Did you give the principle your own name?
Barbara Liskov

No. She discovered the name when someone emailed her in the 1990s asking whether an interpretation of the “Liskov substitution principle” was correct. By then she was working on other topics and had not been thinking about the idea’s growing visibility.

Source: 17:58–18:29 ↗
Source: 14:17–17:56 ↗

QWhy do some names and ideas become better known than similar work?

Barbara Liskov

Asked why Paxos became more familiar than Viewstamped Replication, Liskov recalls Lamport’s explanation that he gave the talks while she implemented the work. She acknowledges his presentations and papers as a source of visibility. When the host wonders whether the catchier name also helped, she agrees that it is a appealing name without treating naming as a proven causal explanation.

She also reconnects the technical history to transactions: an ordinary transaction leader can become a serious problem if it fails, whereas the replication protocols had to move to a new leader safely. That change was the important advance she and Lamport reached independently.

Source: 18:32–20:38 ↗

A new failure model requires a new protocol

The conversation then distinguishes crash failures from nodes that act maliciously while appearing healthy. Liskov describes work with Brian Oki on Viewstamped Replication and later work with Miguel Castro on Byzantine-fault protocols, prompted by interest in attacks on networked systems. The captions mislabel one protocol in this passage; the discussion’s contrast between crash handling and Byzantine behavior is retained without assigning the inconsistent label to Castro’s work.

Source: 19:41–21:43 ↗

QDid you meet Dijkstra, and what mattered about his argument against goto?

Barbara Liskov

Liskov met him several times but did not work with him. She notes that the famous goto text was a letter to the editor, and regards its importance as a statement about reasoning: correctness was not trivial just because someone could write code. At a time when computer science was dismissed as simple programming, that was a substantive argument for taking the discipline seriously.

Why was the argument controversial?
Barbara Liskov

Some people needed goto because their languages, including assembly, lacked the structured constructs familiar today. Others worried that less direct control would produce inefficient code because compilers were weaker. Skilled programmers could also feel personally criticized. Liskov adds that Dijkstra’s manner was not especially diplomatic. The controversy involved practical limitations as well as offense; later languages and compilers changed the context.

Source: 23:08–24:46 ↗
Was he as blunt in person as in his writing?
Barbara Liskov

She says he was not always as tactful as he could have been, while also acknowledging his distinction as a researcher.

Source: 24:49–25:02 ↗
Source: 21:44–23:06 ↗

QWhy stay in academia rather than move permanently into industry?

Barbara Liskov

Liskov enjoyed research and working with students. Although teaching was not her favorite part, she saw it as closely tied to research. She also points out that the boundary between professors and startups was different when she was young; founding a company alongside academic work was not the default path she saw.

She briefly worked in a startup in the late 1990s and preferred research. Academic freedom let her follow the zigzags visible across her career. She calls that freedom both a gift and a curse: it allows a researcher to choose a direction, but also makes deciding what is worth doing their responsibility.

What keeps a researcher from pursuing a useless direction?
Barbara Liskov

Her blunt answer is that a researcher may not receive tenure. The freedom to choose a problem still operates within evaluation by a research community.

Source: 26:32–26:36 ↗
Who judges the value of that work?
Barbara Liskov

The research community is important. A research university cares substantially about how its faculty members are regarded by others in their field.

Source: 26:40–27:06 ↗
Source: 25:04–26:31 ↗

QWhy are teaching and research so closely connected?

Barbara Liskov

Teaching from first principles demands a deep understanding of what works, what fails, and which assumptions are being made. Liskov sees good research as requiring the same reasoning process. Explaining a foundation and investigating it are therefore closely related intellectual work.

Source: 27:07–27:29 ↗

Find a good problem, not just more work on the same one

When the host emphasizes choosing the right research direction, Liskov advises graduate students not to remain in a pattern of tiny incremental improvements. The goal is a good problem that admits a plausible solution and matches the researcher’s skills. Recognizing when a direction is productive—or is not—is part of the work, not something guaranteed by effort alone.

Source: 27:31–28:30 ↗

QWhat role did luck and setbacks play in your career?

Barbara Liskov

Liskov sees both luck and hard work. After her PhD, she wanted a faculty job but did not receive a good offer. Returning to Mitre gave her several years to change direction from AI toward systems without simultaneously taking on teaching and student responsibilities. A disappointment became a useful period of transition.

She also connects later academic opportunity with institutions opening more broadly to women. The recurring image is a set of doors: some close, another opens, and the person must decide whether to step through. She does not claim every setback is beneficial; she describes continuing to work through the available choices rather than letting one rejection halt her career.

Source: 28:32–30:37 ↗

QWhy did some people question the significance of your Turing Award work?

Barbara Liskov

Liskov first challenges the host’s assumption that only she faced negative comments. Her husband happened to read those comments online; she thinks other recipients may have encountered similar treatment if they looked.

Her more interesting interpretation is that some of the work had become so fundamental that people could no longer imagine the previous world. Even her graduate students had not fully grasped that abstract data types and the modular-programming mindset had to be invented. A specific protocol is easy to identify as an invention; a way of thinking that permeates ordinary practice can become part of the unnoticed background.

She therefore viewed the dismissive comments, despite their intent, as a kind of compliment to the broader research community that created those foundations. The impact had become difficult to see precisely because the ideas were taken for granted.

Source: 30:39–33:43 ↗

Section 09 · interview

Ryan Williams: LeetCode, P vs NP, and Fine-Grained Lower Bounds

Ryan Williams explains fine-grained complexity, the strong exponential time hypothesis, and a space-time simulation, and argues that doubted hypotheses still guide useful research.

Ryan Williams's view: bold hypotheses, even doubted ones, drive progress in complexity theory

The host introduces Ryan Williams as an MIT professor who won the Gödel Prize for theoretical computer science. Williams argues that researchers understand polynomial-time computation less deeply than they think. Algorithm results keep surprising people, while lower bounds usually match what researchers expected but are hard to prove. Williams also argues that a hypothesis can be useful even when Williams doubts it, because trying to refute strong ETH leads to new methods. Editorial note: the conversation moves from a LeetCode three-sum question to fine-grained complexity, SAT and its variants, space-time simulation, and research habits. The host is not named in the transcript.

Source: 00:00–1:11:42 ↗

QCan three-sum be solved in less than n squared time?

Ryan Williams

Williams first describes the standard methods. Brute force tries every triple and takes n cubed time. A faster method sorts the numbers, then for each number runs a finger search with one pointer at each end of the remaining list. That gives n squared time overall.

Williams says beating n squared is possible, though not obvious. The improvement applies the finger search to small groups of neighboring sorted numbers rather than single numbers. A preprocessed lookup for pairs of groups lets the search skip work. Williams uses an n to the 1.5 preprocessing cost as an example, and says the approach starts from the finger search and speeds up its moves.

Is the unit of work a single integer or a group of integers?
Ryan Williams

A group. Williams says the lookup is more involved than a simple table. The method works in a model called the linear decision tree model, where Williams says an n to the 1.5 solution is possible. The core idea is preprocessing that makes the finger moves faster.

Source: 06:45–07:23 ↗
What is the intuition behind the faster three-sum bound?
Ryan Williams

The host reads out a bound with logarithm factors raised to the two-thirds power and calls it crazy. Williams says several algorithms of this kind exist. They all modify the n squared method, using different lookup tables and compression tricks, and then speed up the search with preprocessing.

Source: 07:26–08:26 ↗
Source: 00:42–08:26 ↗

QWhat is fine-grained complexity, and how does it differ from P versus NP?

Ryan Williams

Williams says fine-grained complexity studies canonical problems that are taught to undergraduates. Their canonical algorithms have resisted major improvement for decades, so the question is whether those algorithms are optimal. The focus is the exact running time a problem needs, not only whether it is polynomial.

Williams contrasts this with P versus NP. P allows any polynomial, even one with a huge exponent, so showing that a problem is outside P only shows that it needs super-polynomial time. Fine-grained work asks whether an n cubed algorithm can be improved to n to the 3 minus epsilon, and whether a small gain on one problem can give a small gain on another.

The main tool is a reduction that carries speedups. Williams's example is subset sum, which has an obvious 2 to the n algorithm. Williams reduces it to a two-sum instance with about the square root of 2 to the n numbers. Williams says two-sum can be solved in linear time on that list, which gives a square root of 2 to the n algorithm for subset sum. Williams says this relates problems that look unrelated under P versus NP.

Why is it acceptable for a reduction to blow up the instance?
Ryan Williams

Williams says the reduction is not required to be polynomial-time. What matters is that a faster two-sum algorithm would give a faster subset sum algorithm. The host restates it as a small time loss that is smaller than the overall gain, and Williams agrees that the whole chain is what counts.

Williams compares this to a surprise. Sorting and binary search give a shortcut for finding a pair of numbers with a given sum, which avoids trying all pairs. Williams says that kind of shortcut can then be used to get a subset sum algorithm that avoids trying all subsets.

Source: 13:58–16:58 ↗
Source: 08:27–13:57 ↗

QWhat is the strong exponential time hypothesis, and why does it matter?

Ryan Williams

Williams calls strong ETH a severe strengthening of the P versus NP question. P versus NP asks whether SAT has a polynomial-time algorithm. Strong ETH says that SAT, and the k-SAT version with clauses of width k, cannot be solved much faster than 2 to the n time. Williams says the exact details of k-SAT matter less than the overall claim.

Williams notes that SAT is solved well in practice and used heavily for verification. The worst case is different: no known algorithm solves it much faster than 2 to the n. Williams says the hypothesis is far stronger than P versus NP, since it says the cost is close to 2 to the n, not just super-polynomial.

Source: 17:00–19:09 ↗

QDoes Williams believe strong ETH is true, and why?

Ryan Williams

Williams says the answer is no: Williams is on record as not believing the hypothesis. Williams began thinking about it as an undergraduate, and early in graduate school tried to solve CNF-SAT faster than 2 to the n. Other NP-complete problems, such as subset sum, already had faster algorithms, and 3-SAT does too. Williams saw no clear reason SAT should be the exception.

Each attack Williams tried on the hypothesis failed in a ridiculous way, with no real chance of solving the original problem. Williams says studying those failures led to other results. Williams says the truth value of strong ETH matters less than its effect on research. Believing it is false pushes Williams to discard natural algorithms and think in new directions. Williams finds that very useful, even without a refutation.

Williams calls this a minority view. A close friend who helped propose the hypothesis stressed that it was deliberately not named a conjecture. It was put forward as a lower bound to get people thinking, more controversial than other widely discussed statements such as P versus NP. Williams says hypotheses at the edge of understanding can be enlightening.

Why might someone still believe strong ETH?
Ryan Williams

Williams says the hypothesis gives a convenient world view. SAT can be reduced to many problems that look unrelated, such as edit distance and various pattern matching problems. Those problems have natural polynomial-time algorithms. An improvement on any of them would also give a faster-than-2 to the n algorithm for SAT. So believing the hypothesis makes those textbook algorithms look optimal.

Source: 23:39–24:35 ↗
Source: 19:09–23:36 ↗

QWhat are the main forms of SAT?

Ryan Williams

Williams says the most common form is conjunctive normal form, or CNF. Modern SAT solvers read it from DIMACS CNF files. Each line is a clause, which is an OR of literals. A literal is a variable or its negation. The formula is an AND of the clauses. The width of a clause is its number of literals, and k-SAT limits every clause to width k.

Williams lists other forms. Formula SAT allows any expression built from ORs, ANDs, and negations, with nested parentheses. Bounded-depth circuits, called AC circuits, use layers of ORs and ANDs with a constant number of layers. Williams notes that the name refers to alternating ORs and ANDs, not electrical alternation. CNF is a special case of such a circuit: an AND of ORs.

Does the best known exponent change as k grows?
Ryan Williams

The host states that improvements over 2 to the n exist for small values of k, and that larger k is harder. Williams agrees that this is the intuition. Williams says the best known algorithms all approach an exponent of 2 as k grows, moving from values like 1.99 toward 1.999. The curve drops quickly, and the exponent behaves predictably for known algorithms. Asked whether the curve has been plotted, Williams describes its shape in words.

Source: 28:13–29:22 ↗
Source: 24:38–28:11 ↗

QWhat is the intuition for beating 2 to the n for 3-SAT?

Ryan Williams

Williams starts with one clause on three variables. Exactly one of the eight assignments to those variables makes that clause false. Only that one is ruled out, and the other seven could still be part of a satisfying assignment.

Williams says a simple algorithm tries one of those seven assignments and recurses on the remaining formula. A naive search would branch eight ways. Using the clause gives seven branches, which removes three variables at the cost of seven recursive calls instead of eight. That is a slight improvement over 2 to the n. Williams says better algorithms exist, using the same general idea of setting variables to force constraints that rule out many assignments.

Source: 29:24–31:29 ↗

QAre there analogies between SAT circuits and neural networks?

Ryan Williams

Williams says a majority gate can replace ORs and ANDs, and that the resulting model is basically equivalent. A majority gate outputs one when at least half of its inputs are one. With majority gates and negations, Williams says a constant number of layers of a typical neural network can be simulated. Williams calls these threshold circuits.

Williams says threshold circuits still work on Boolean inputs. Once inputs are real-valued, lower bounds become a different kind of problem and can be stronger. Williams gives an example: some functions need depth three in a neural network and cannot be computed at depth two. Williams says the real domain gives a very different picture from the discrete one.

Source: 31:30–34:02 ↗

QWhy did Williams assign only 80 percent confidence that P is not equal to NP?

Ryan Williams

Williams says the figure first stood near 75 percent. A college classmate, Scott Aaronson, challenged that number, and Williams settled on 80 percent. The host notes that most people state much higher confidence.

Williams's main point is that researchers do not understand polynomial-time computation as deeply as they think. Algorithms keep surprising people with unexpected speed. Lower bounds, by contrast, usually match what researchers expected, though they are hard to prove.

Williams says intuition about P versus NP has often been revised over the years. Williams asks whether, in such a field, confidence about the answer was simply misplaced. Williams says complexity theory is full of statements that are easy to write down and very hard to settle.

Source: 35:12–38:08 ↗

QWhy does Williams give NEXP not equal to EXP only 45 percent?

Ryan Williams

Williams confirms the 45 percent figure. Williams says the belief is that NEXP equals EXP is more likely than the two being different. Williams frames the question as a special case of P versus NP, restricted to SAT instances that are highly compressible.

In that case, a small machine, exponentially smaller than the instance, outputs the character at a given line and column of the CNF file. The question is whether such an instance can be decided in time polynomial in the decompressed size. Williams offers one hypothesis for why SAT solvers work in practice: the real world is structured and governed by a few rules, so the instances that arise are very compressible.

Williams calls the conjecture overkill, since it is not even a well-formed mathematical statement. The hypothesis is that highly compact representations can be solved efficiently, which would make such instances special rather than arbitrary.

Source: 38:24–41:49 ↗

QWhy was the 80 percent NEXP versus coNEXP estimate so contentious?

Ryan Williams

Williams starts with NP versus co-NP. Co-NP holds the complements of NP problems, such as unsatisfiability. Checking unsatisfiability costs the same time as checking satisfiability, but no short proof of unsatisfiability is known in general. Williams says most people do not believe NP equals co-NP, and that NP differing from co-NP would imply P differs from NP.

Williams then describes the exponential analogue with a little birdie, meaning advice. The advice is the total count of yes-inputs of a given length, which takes about n bits to write down. An NEXP machine can guess the no-inputs, verify each one, and check the guessed total against the advice. Once that is done, every input is accounted for, so the rest must be yes-inputs. Williams says this is how advice would let NEXP handle co-NEXP questions.

Where would the little birdie's advice come from?
Ryan Williams

Williams says the advice might itself be constructible in NEXP. If it is, the machine could compute the advice and use it to settle the question. Williams presents this as an open possibility, not a result.

Source: 46:21–46:58 ↗
Source: 41:51–46:58 ↗

QWhat was known before Williams's time and space result?

Ryan Williams

Williams says the problem is this. Given an algorithm that runs in time T, can it be simulated with much less memory than T while still computing the same result? For an arbitrary circuit, the natural method uses about T space as well as T time.

Williams says that in 1975, Hopcroft, Paul, and Valiant, building on work by Patterson and Valiant, showed that time T algorithms in a multi-tape Turing machine model can be simulated in space T divided by log T. The result was extended to random-access models and other models in the late 1970s and early 1980s, so T over log T was known for reasonable models.

Williams says the saving came with a hidden cost: the space-efficient simulation needs exponential time. Many researchers therefore expected T over log T to be close to the best possible, and did not expect something like T to the 0.9 space.

Williams calls it a big surprise that any time-T algorithm can be simulated in about square root of T space, again with exponential running time. Williams says this holds for any such algorithm, including ones that produce pseudorandom or cryptographic output, and that this was not obvious.

Source: 47:00–51:52 ↗

QWhat was the trick behind simulating time T in about square root of T space?

Ryan Williams

Williams says the key was reading the tree evaluation paper by James Cook and Ian Mertz very carefully, alongside the earlier work on space-bounded computation. Hopcroft, Paul, and Valiant modeled space-bounded computation by writing pieces of computation into blank memory, which means erasing memory first. Williams says that model turned out to be more restrictive than its authors expected.

Williams uses a swap example from basic programming. Swapping two registers normally needs a temporary register, but XOR-ing the registers, or adding and subtracting them, swaps them in three steps without one. Williams says this is the starting point for asking why it matters to always write into erased memory.

Williams says Cook and Mertz studied tree evaluation with a small stack, and their computation wrote into erased memory. They realized that allowing computations to XOR bits into existing memory saves a lot of space. Careful XOR operations let useful content be recovered without storing everything at once, and unneeded content cancels out. Williams describes this as the high-level idea, not the full argument.

Is the square-root version just an extension of the same method?
Ryan Williams

Williams says the square root is the optimal trade-off in this tree evaluation setting. The computation is split into intervals of about square root of T steps, so there are about square root of T intervals, each with about square root of T steps. The simulation keeps only a constant number of these interval records in memory at any time. Williams says this is not obvious, and that the square root is a sweet spot where the trade-off balances.

Source: 56:45–57:43 ↗
Source: 52:14–57:43 ↗

QWhat was it like to become convinced the square-root result was correct?

Ryan Williams

Williams says long experience has taught Williams to distrust one's own ideas, since one can be deceived by oneself many times. The first two or three times the idea came up, Williams judged it impossible and set it aside. Convincing oneself was slow, and Williams suspected either a bug in the Cook and Mertz work or a misreading of it.

Williams says the only way through was to write the argument down again and again in different ways, adding detail, shortening it, and explaining it differently. When Williams submitted it to a theory conference, Williams was still not fully confident it was correct, and was exhausted. Williams sent it to two trusted colleagues. One did not read past the abstract. The other said a footnote was where the argument began to be believable.

Williams then turned that footnote into a fuller part of a later revision, which Williams called the warm-up. Williams wanted the argument to be airtight so that others would believe it, and says it took a long time for Williams to believe it.

Source: 57:44–1:01:00 ↗

QWhat keeps Williams working on hard problems?

Ryan Williams

Williams says the aim is to avoid bashing one's head against a wall. If Williams does take on a hard problem, Williams wants the process to be enjoyable. Williams enjoys the grind of understanding something, and without that enjoyment Williams would not do it.

Other work is mostly opportunistic. Williams takes something new, integrates it fully with what Williams already knows, follows every consequence to its logical end, and sees what happens.

Source: 1:01:02–1:02:24 ↗

QHow does Williams pick a good research direction?

Ryan Williams

Williams says the best kind of direction is one where the researcher cannot lose. Williams sets up a hypothesis H, so that if H is true good things follow, and if not-H is true other good things still follow. Williams calls such opportunities a win-win, and says they are hard to find but important.

Williams says Williams often looks at a method or technique rather than one specific problem. Williams asks what else can be done in that space of ideas, and often solves problems by taking an idea from one place and putting it somewhere else.

Is there a concrete example of a win-win direction?
Ryan Williams

Williams describes a research program on the orthogonal vectors problem. If that problem can be solved in nearly linear time, SAT could be solved in about the time of subset sum, which Williams says would break strong ETH in a radical way. Williams has also shown earlier that improving SAT running time can give circuit complexity lower bounds.

Williams says the hypothesis in that program is technical. If it is true, Williams gets a fast algorithm for orthogonal vectors, an algorithm for SAT, and circuit lower bounds. If it is false, it can be used to prove a different circuit lower bound. Either way, Williams says, a new limitation is proved.

Williams says the usual path is less clean. Williams reads an algorithm idea, tries to apply it to SAT, and it fails. Williams then studies the failure, extracts what can be used, and often finds another kind of algorithm. Williams says this is how Williams proved circuit lower bounds that first helped earn a job at Stanford: an attempted SAT algorithm worked for a large class of circuits, including some with no known lower bounds.

Source: 1:03:59–1:07:12 ↗
Source: 1:02:26–1:07:12 ↗

QWhat books would Williams recommend for learning complexity theory?

Ryan Williams

Williams says the answer depends on how deep the reader wants to go. Williams first recommends Avi's book, which Williams calls really nice.

For a gentler introduction, Williams suggests the early chapters of Lance Fortnow's The Golden Ticket, which imagines a world where P equals NP. For a more technical book, Williams mentions The Nature of Computation, which Williams recalls as by Mertens and Moore. Williams also recommends Sipser's Introduction to the Theory of Computation as a concise, well-written textbook.

Source: 1:07:13–1:08:28 ↗

QWhat advice would Williams give an earlier self, knowing what Williams knows now?

Ryan Williams

Williams says one lesson came by accident: no one needs permission to work on very hard problems. In complexity theory, few people know what to do beyond simple structural results, which levels the field. The knowledge is open, so younger researchers can learn it and think about it without anyone's say-so.

Williams says another lesson is to avoid inertia. Researchers should now and then ask where they are heading and whether their current direction will lead where they want to be. Williams says this applies to life generally, not only research.

In research, Williams reevaluated each year's work by comparing what was known then with what is known now. Williams says this self-evaluation matters in a PhD program, because there are no easy metrics for progress. The only option is to compare the past self with the present self.

Source: 1:08:32–1:11:42 ↗

Section 10 · interview

Technical excellence needs a clear user and a useful problem

Adam Ernst explains code-driven influence, successful iOS infrastructure, and the lessons from a technically accomplished framework that failed to gain adoption.

QWhat was your middle-school software company?

Ernst began programming young, spending time with computers in his teacher mother’s classroom. His first commercial product was online-testing software, sold internationally through a cross-platform BASIC-inspired development tool. He remembers the project as an accessible way to make something useful, despite the tool’s limitations.

What made the development environment accessible?

A drag-and-drop canvas let him place buttons and fields directly, then attach code to interactions. Unlike writing a textual UI description first, that immediate visual feedback was easy for a beginner. It was less suited to scaling large applications, but suitable for his first product.

Source: 01:51–02:56 ↗
How did you sell software internationally before modern payment APIs?

An existing software-store service handled cards and license-unlock codes. He also accepted mailed checks from teachers and emailed their codes back. The service name is uncertain in the captions and is not essential to the example.

Source: 02:56–03:40 ↗
Did your parents know?

Yes. He is unsure what they thought, but says they knew about the business.

Source: 03:40–03:47 ↗
Source: 00:50–01:50 ↗

QWhat did you join Facebook to do, and at what level?

He believes he joined as E5 because of prior self-employed iPhone development experience, arriving shortly before the 2012 IPO. The iOS engineering group was still small enough to meet in one room. Its rewrite from an HTML5 approach to native code had won organizational support, creating both opportunities and scaling problems as new features accumulated.

Source: 03:50–05:14 ↗

QWhat storage problem drove your staff-level work?

The native rewrite used Apple’s Core Data, which Ernst considers useful for a small application team but unsuitable for their rapidly expanding organization. As the engineering group grew from roughly fifteen or twenty to hundreds, product teams wanted native features while the infrastructure team feared the storage layer would fail.

The migration had to be incremental because feature work could not simply stop. Their new immutable model system made mutation and thread-safety reasoning easier. His account illustrates a scaling constraint involving both technical architecture and the number of teams sharing it.

Why was adoption difficult?

Core products such as feed had obvious performance gains, but the remaining teams sometimes saw little benefit compared with their other priorities. Some iOS engineers also strongly preferred built-in Apple frameworks. Ernst had to repeatedly explain the particular limits at Facebook’s scale rather than assume everyone valued replacement for its own sake.

Source: 06:46–07:56 ↗
Source: 05:16–06:44 ↗

QHow can an IC influence other engineers without formal authority?

Speak in person or over video when possible; nuance and tone can be easier to convey than in writing. Begin sympathetically: he too would prefer standard Apple frameworks if they solved the problem. Then provide concrete evidence of why they do not.

The team investigated Core Data’s otherwise opaque implementation, including disassembly, to explain initialization costs. Research gave the argument more substance than a preference for a new framework.

He also often performed migration work himself. Asking someone to approve a completed improvement is easier than asking them to spend their own time adopting scaffolding. He qualifies the tactic: Meta’s later codebase became too large for one person to finish such migrations, making broader alignment more necessary.

Source: 07:57–10:18 ↗

QWhy spend so much time reviewing code?

Code review supplies a concrete opening for influencing engineering habits. Ernst can discuss an actual design rather than issue an abstract company-wide message. He tries to explain concerns flexibly, allowing a reasonable differing choice or helping the author make a necessary change. Authors who understand the reasoning may carry it into their future work and their own reviews, spreading the influence organically.

What makes a good review comment?

Explain why a change matters instead of merely ordering X to become Y. Admit that context may be missing and ask whether it would change the recommendation. If it does, encourage including that context in the diff summary so others can review the decision on its merits. Flexibility does not mean abandoning concerns; it means making them intelligible and revisable.

Source: 11:43–12:53 ↗
Source: 10:18–11:42 ↗

QWhy did you build ComponentKit?

Around 2014, rapidly growing news-feed code suffered crashes, layout errors, and performance problems. Ernst credits Lee Byron with asking how React’s concepts could work in an iOS-oriented form. ComponentKit was his response.

It used components, immutability, conceptual re-rendering, and view reconciliation. Instead of manually coordinating view objects, product code declared what should appear and the framework managed the native views. He is proud of the balance among syntax, performance, and the business need.

The work included inventing the framework, introducing it into feed, and spreading it to other products. He places it before the later mainstream SwiftUI and React Native options in the historical context he remembers.

How did you convince engineers to adopt an unfamiliar declarative model?

Examples showed much less code; performance demonstrations showed work moving off the main thread. Some engineers remained unconvinced, so more senior engineers helped mediate. React’s established reputation internally also helped. Ernst acknowledged awkwardness in the Objective-C++ approach rather than deny its costs, and repeatedly explained the benefits for this application.

Source: 15:33–17:03 ↗
What general lessons did the disagreements teach?

Allies could persuade in ways his own style could not. Compromise also mattered: another team’s Panels framework was meant to be the next UI direction, and the overlap was painful. Incorporating part of its data-source technology into ComponentKit created a shared win. He recommends bringing people into the solution rather than insist on every detail being his own.

Source: 17:03–18:25 ↗
Source: 12:53–15:33 ↗

QDid strong pushback make you doubt ComponentKit?

He remained convinced for news feed, while rejecting it as the only acceptable UI architecture. A mostly static scrolling list with complicated nested content suited declarative rendering. A highly dynamic drag-and-drop interface might feel much less natural. Conviction about the intended application coexisted with awareness of paradigm tradeoffs.

Source: 18:26–19:34 ↗

QWhy build ComponentScript, and what happened?

The next ambition was cross-platform UI without separately writing iOS and Android versions. In Ernst’s opinion, React Native at that time worked better when it controlled an app than when small cross-platform pieces were embedded throughout a complex native app. He explicitly leaves open that later architectural changes improved this.

His first attempt to implement React above the existing native frameworks proved too difficult because React’s surface was large and complex. A smaller React-like JavaScript API became ComponentScript. It supported real features, full screens, and nested native and scripted components.

The project nevertheless failed after about two years. It satisfied the infrastructure group’s technical requirements but did not generate enough sustained adoption. He distinguishes a working implementation from a successful offering.

What did the postmortem identify?

It had no clear target engineer. iOS developers did not want to learn JavaScript, while JavaScript developers preferred actual React Native to an unfamiliar React-like API.

He insisted on GraphQL-based data consistency, but its tooling was slow at the time. A competing server-driven approach could skip that burden for products that did not require consistency and handle the exceptional cases individually. He sees his refusal to compromise as part of the failure.

He also approached many individual engineers rather than securing one committed team. Scattered experiments did not build momentum. A team finally wanted broad adoption when he was ending the effort, but he believes that was already too little and too late.

Source: 22:52–25:53 ↗
Source: 19:34–22:51 ↗

QWhy publish such a candid retrospective?

Writing it was cathartic, answered repeated questions about the project, and explained the failure once without continually reliving the conversation. He hoped others would recognize the same traps before repeating them. He does not clearly remember whether someone also encouraged him to write it.

Source: 25:53–26:39 ↗

QHow did the failure affect performance reviews?

A “meets most” rating helped him realize that the project needed to stop. He thinks a new manager’s fresh view was useful and that the performance process did its job.

He then helped every dependent team move to native code, React Native, or another chosen option, and deleted the framework completely. He did not leave a permanent remnant for someone else to maintain. He believes taking responsibility and publishing lessons gained goodwill afterward.

His advice is qualified: responsibly winding down a failed project can be better received than indefinitely dragging it out. This is his experience, not a guarantee about another organization’s evaluation.

Were there signs you could have acted on earlier?

For the last year he sensed that the project was going badly and sometimes lost sleep over it. His habitual response was to write more code and migrate more features. In retrospect, that treated an adoption and strategy problem as a coding shortage. He wishes he had accepted the signal earlier and found another useful problem.

Source: 28:28–29:02 ↗
Source: 26:39–28:28 ↗

QHow did you know management was wrong for you?

He strongly prefers writing code and thinks he is better at communication tied to a concrete technical problem than at broader direction, documents, or organizational alignment. Managing would distance him from the part of the work he enjoys most. He describes himself as an extreme example and says the choice depends on the individual.

Source: 29:04–30:07 ↗

QWhy stay in iOS rather than switch domains?

The path emerged rather than being planned. Reorganizations shifted his placement, but he liked the people, mobile work, and available opportunities. Staying let him acquire deep knowledge across the surrounding systems. He admires people who switch into areas such as AI or AR/VR and might choose differently as a new engineer today, but does not regret his own fit.

Is depth or breadth better for reaching very senior IC levels?

He sees multiple successful patterns and considers himself to have both. When GraphQL blocks his work, he investigates many layers of code instead of immediately handing the problem to its owners. He either fixes it or arrives with a precise diagnosis, saving them time and learning a new system. Repeating this problem-driven investigation builds broad, deep knowledge organically rather than through a predetermined checklist of systems.

Source: 31:54–33:31 ↗
Source: 30:09–31:54 ↗

QHow do you make sure your coding meets IC9 expectations?

He stopped trying to judge each piece of code by its level. Instead, he regularly checks with his manager that he is solving important organizational problems and does work he enjoys. ComponentScript is his reminder that he can become attached to a direction that no longer matters; feedback should then cause him to listen and adjust. He does not advocate ignoring business relevance or management input.

Source: 33:33–34:56 ↗

QWhat makes other senior engineers exceptional?

Ernst admires several different strengths rather than one archetype: high-volume implementation, diagnosing unexplained metrics deep in unfamiliar systems, repeatedly starting complete useful projects, clear writing, and cross-team or cross-company alignment.

One colleague’s project-starting ability included not just code but deployment, documentation, naming, and multiple platforms. Other colleagues made complicated messages clear enough to become examples for engineers improving communication. He particularly respects a collaborator who manages the difficult Apple relationship—work Ernst lacks patience for himself.

The examples make complementarity explicit. A senior engineer who writes little code may still contribute through coordination that a productive implementer cannot supply. Several names are unclear in the captions, so the summary preserves their roles and contributions without inventing identities.

Source: 34:56–37:37 ↗

QWhat would you tell yourself just after graduation?

He would avoid changing a path that worked well for him. He nearly applied to Facebook in 2010 but discarded its puzzle-style process; joining later meant arriving at the native rewrite instead. He cannot know whether joining earlier would have been better. His broader advice is to find work one enjoys that intersects with industry needs, while recognizing the luck involved. Enjoying problem-solving does not mean every moment of debugging is pleasant; it supplies motivation for difficult work.

Source: 37:40–39:41 ↗

Section 11 · interview

What computation can know, prove, and conceal

Avi Wigderson connects complexity, randomness, zero-knowledge proofs, quantum models, and the daily practice of theoretical research.

This conversation moves from the difference between finding and checking a solution to a deeper question: what resources make knowledge possible? Wigderson repeatedly changes the model or the resource being measured. The resulting distinctions matter: worst-case hardness differs from practical performance; computational unpredictability differs from true entropy; an interactive proof differs from an ordinary algorithm that decides a problem. The explanations below retain those boundaries and the assumptions behind the surprising results.

Source: 00:49–01:07 ↗

QWhat is P versus NP, and why connect it to the limits of knowledge?

Avi Wigderson

P concerns problems that can be solved efficiently; NP concerns problems for which a proposed solution can be checked efficiently. Here, efficiency means polynomial growth in the input size. The question asks whether efficient checking always implies efficient solving.

Wigderson gives a philosophical interpretation: many serious searches aim at something we expect to recognize when we find it. A mathematician checks a proof, a scientist checks whether an explanation fits data, and an engineer checks whether a design meets its constraints. Finding an answer can be much harder than recognizing a satisfactory one.

He therefore presents P versus NP as a question about the reach of discovery. If the two classes were equal, efficiently verifiable solutions would also be efficiently findable in the formal setting. His references to human knowledge and a cure for cancer illustrate the significance he sees in the question; they should be read as a broad analogy, rather than a claim that every medical or human problem is literally an NP decision problem.

Source: 00:49–06:37 ↗

QWhich answer do you expect, and why?

Avi Wigderson

He expects P and NP to differ, while stressing that the reasons are intuition, rather than a proof. Looking for lost keys feels harder than recognizing them once someone points them out. Many independently motivated optimization, logic, and verification problems have resisted attempts to find efficient general algorithms over decades.

NP-complete problems connect these searches: an efficient algorithm for one would give efficient algorithms for all problems in NP through reductions. Many appear to require searching an exponentially large space, and researchers do not see a general way to compress that search enough.

Those observations are suggestive, but a new idea could overturn them. His uncertainty is part of the answer: a long record of failure to find an algorithm is not a theorem that the algorithm cannot exist.

Source: 06:39–10:21 ↗

QDoes NP-completeness mean practical software can do no better than brute force?

Avi Wigderson

The formal question requires an algorithm to be correct and efficient on every instance in a family. Real applications often produce a restricted set of instances with extra structure. A method can work very well on those instances while remaining poor in the worst case.

He uses protein folding as an illustration. A general energy-minimization formulation can be hard, while natural proteins need not represent arbitrary instances of that formulation. He suggests that evolution may have selected proteins with useful structure, and explicitly does not claim to know the biological explanation.

Similarly, verification formulas can contain structure that a SAT solver exploits. The simplex method offers another example: its worst-case running time can be exponential, despite strong practical performance. The existence of efficient general algorithms for linear programming is a separate point. Practical success and worst-case complexity answer different questions.

Source: 10:22–14:47 ↗

QCan relaxing exact correctness make a hard problem easy?

Avi Wigderson

It can help, but there is no universal guarantee. AlphaFold’s success on natural protein instances belongs to the structured-instance discussion; it does not settle the general worst-case optimization problem, even if its predictions work well on those inputs.

Approximation is another natural relaxation: accept a solution within a factor or percentage of the optimum. Wigderson explains that the PCP theorem and subsequent results also establish limits on approximation for many constraint problems.

For the MAX-3SAT example he describes, a random assignment satisfies a clause with probability 7/8. In the relevant worst-case approximation setting, guaranteeing even a small improvement beyond the 7/8 threshold is NP-hard. The striking point is that a modest-looking improvement over a simple baseline can already capture the difficult part of the problem.

Source: 14:48–20:06 ↗
Three different kinds of success
QuestionWhat success establishesWhat it leaves open
Does a heuristic work on useful inputs?Good performance on the instances being tested or encountered.An efficient correct method for every possible instance.
Can an approximation meet a guarantee?A specified distance from the optimum in the stated setting.A better guarantee beyond a hardness threshold.
Is there a polynomial-time general algorithm?Efficient solution across the formal input family.Whether it is the simplest or fastest choice on a particular application.
Source: 10:22–20:06 ↗

QWhat is the wider landscape of complexity classes?

Avi Wigderson

Classes organize problems by resources and models. Time is one resource, but memory, communication between parties, energy, and parallel computation also matter. A problem can require different amounts of these resources, and adding more computers does not automatically make every computation immediate.

There is also a boundary before efficient computation: some problems are decidable at all, while others are not. P and NP describe a particular part of a much larger landscape.

Reductions relate problems even when their precise complexity is unknown. An efficient translation can turn a solver for one problem into a solver for another. His Sudoku example concerns the generalized family of growing puzzles, not a single fixed-size puzzle. Such relationships produce an ordering of difficulty and explain why very different-looking problems can belong together.

Source: 20:09–25:37 ↗

QHow can very different problems reduce to satisfiability?

Avi Wigderson

Many basic reductions are relatively simple, although some major results, such as approximation hardness, require much deeper tools. The key intuition behind the foundational satisfiability reduction is that computation is local.

Imagine a proposed table of a machine’s states over time. Each step makes a small permitted change. Constraints can check the local transitions, the initial input, and the accepting outcome. A satisfying assignment then describes a consistent computation. What looked like an entire execution becomes a collection of small conditions that must all hold.

Other problems already have local constraints: graph coloring asks adjacent vertices to receive different colors. Factoring also illustrates verification: multiply proposed factors and check the product. Encoding that multiplication gives a satisfiability instance. Reducibility to SAT does not by itself say that factoring is NP-complete.

Source: 25:39–30:34 ↗
Editorial synthesis
Source: 26:42–30:34 ↗

QIs there a general theory of trading time against space?

Avi Wigderson

Yes, but the answer depends on the problem and the model of computation. Some results force a tradeoff between small memory and fast execution; other problems permit both. Models that are equivalent in what they can compute need not be equivalent when exact resource costs matter.

A basic observation is that a computation running for t steps cannot visit more than t memory locations. He then describes space-saving simulation results: earlier work improved the direct bound, and a result by Ryan Williams achieved a much larger, roughly square-root-scale saving in the Turing-machine setting. The time cost of these simulations can become very large. This is a statement about what a model permits, rather than a ready-made optimization for arbitrary programs.

Does that result apply to a general computation?

He specifies Turing machines and cautions that the same statement may not apply to random-access machines. The model is part of the theorem.

Source: 34:29–34:42 ↗
Is there an intuitive example of how such unexpected space savings work?

Instead of unpacking the newer proof, he gives an older example associated with Barrington: a majority decision can be represented using a very small internal state and an appropriate sequence of repeated accesses to input bits. The surprising question is whether there are more zeros or ones, rather than the task of printing their exact count.

The explanation uses noncommuting permutations: rotating and then flipping can differ from flipping and then rotating. Carefully arranged operations can simulate logical gates. He offers a picture-hanging puzzle as an analogy: loop a string around two nails so removing either nail drops the picture. The interview poses that puzzle but does not work through its solution.

This is an explanation of a particular branching-program viewpoint. The small internal state does not mean that every ordinary computer can inspect an arbitrary input with no addressing or control resources.

Source: 34:34–41:46 ↗
Is the information encoded in the sequence of operations?

That is the intuition, with an important output distinction. A yes-or-no majority answer is small; printing an arbitrarily large count would itself require enough bits to represent that count. He adds that this line of work has useful applications, including in cryptography, rather than being only an abstract curiosity.

Source: 41:46–43:05 ↗
Source: 30:35–34:28 ↗

QWhy use a SAT solver if translating the problem can enlarge it?

Avi Wigderson

A translation may indeed make the instance larger. But satisfiability has received an enormous amount of practical optimization. Heuristics select influential variables whose assignments force other choices, sometimes producing a cascade that sharply reduces the search space.

Those methods exploit structure rather than escaping all worst-case hardness. He also mentions the stronger conjectural expectation that difficult satisfiability instances require exponential time. That is an expectation about hard cases, not a description of every formula.

For verification, the translation is often convenient because specifications already look like sets of constraints. The cost of moving into SAT can be outweighed by the maturity of the solver and the fit between the specification and its input language.

Source: 43:06–45:51 ↗

QWhy treat randomness as a computational resource?

Avi Wigderson

Random choices can make algorithms effective; randomized primality testing is one historical example. Their analysis commonly assumes perfectly unbiased, independent bits. Actual computers need a source for those bits, and obtaining high-quality randomness has a cost.

Physical noise, traffic measurements, deterministic generators, and digits of a mathematical constant are different proposals, not interchangeable proofs of ideal randomness. Quantum measurements offer another source in the physical model, but a real device still costs money and has imperfections.

Once randomness is a resource, researchers can ask how many bits an algorithm needs, what quality it uses, and whether its error can be reduced or its random choices removed. Sometimes the analysis requires far less independence than it first appears to require. He describes the discovery of deterministic primality testing as an example of understanding the way randomness was being used, rather than simply supplying more of it.

Source: 45:53–53:47 ↗

QHow do you quantify the quality of random bits?

Avi Wigderson

For pseudorandomness, quality is relative to a test or observer. The goal is for the relevant algorithm not to distinguish a lower-entropy generated distribution from the ideal random one. Different algorithms can require different kinds of pseudorandomness.

For some analyses, pairwise or limited higher-order independence is enough. A much smaller seed can then generate the distribution the algorithm needs. The practical question is what the analysis actually demands, rather than whether the output is random by every possible definition.

What makes randomness depend on the observer’s computational power?

Consider predicting the landing of the same tossed coin. An unaided observer has little basis for doing better than a guess. A laptop alone may not help in the tiny time window. Sensors and sufficient computation, in the thought experiment, could measure the conditions and predict the motion.

The event has not changed; the observer’s ability has. This illustrates computational uncertainty. It does not say that physical entropy itself changes because a faster computer is present.

Source: 55:48–1:00:14 ↗
Source: 53:49–55:47 ↗

QUnder what assumptions can randomness be removed from efficient algorithms?

Avi Wigderson

He describes the hardness-versus-randomness connection: sufficiently strong computational hardness assumptions can yield pseudorandom generators and imply P = BPP, meaning efficient bounded-error randomized computation can be simulated efficiently without randomness.

The assumption he describes concerns strong circuit hardness, such as exponential circuit requirements. It is stronger and more specific than merely stating P ≠ NP. The surprising relationship is that an assumption about difficulty, with no randomness in its wording, can support the removal of randomness.

He also explains that the connection has converse forms: successful derandomization can imply hardness results. The exact relationship depends on the version of the theorem; he does not present one unconditional equivalence covering every setting.

Source: 1:00:18–1:02:31 ↗

QWhat is the intuition connecting hardness and randomness?

Avi Wigderson

A computationally limited observer cannot always determine the answer to a hard problem, so there is uncertainty relative to that observer. But having a few hard instances is not enough: the construction needs answers that are difficult to predict on average, almost like fair coin flips. Hardness amplification strengthens that unpredictability.

Producing one unpredictable answer from many random input bits still does not expand randomness. A generator must do the reverse: use a short seed to produce many outputs that look random together.

He describes the Nisan–Wigderson approach at a high level: evaluate a hard function on carefully chosen subsets of a short seed. The output bits may be mathematically correlated, yet the restricted observer cannot detect the correlation. The guarantee remains conditional on the relevant hardness and the observer’s computational limit.

Source: 1:03:24–1:07:15 ↗

QWith unlimited computation, would nothing be truly random?

Avi Wigderson

An unrestricted observer could distinguish an expanded low-entropy seed distribution from a fully uniform one. That shows the limit of a computational pseudorandomness guarantee.

It does not eliminate information-theoretic randomness. A task that demands a genuinely random bit or a specified amount of entropy is asking something different from fooling a limited test. He uses secrets and security as motivation for caring about entropy itself. The correct notion depends on the task; the coin-prediction analogy does not establish that unlimited computation can predict every physical phenomenon.

Source: 1:07:18–1:10:18 ↗

QHow can weak sources produce better randomness?

Avi Wigderson

Randomness extraction is a different, though related, theory. A weak source can contain uncertainty while also having bias and correlations. Weather is an intuitive example: tomorrow is not fully predictable, but it is correlated with today. Feeding arbitrary weak bits directly to an algorithm that expects independent fair bits can make it fail.

The difficult part is that the entropy may be present without its location or structure being known. A universal deterministic procedure cannot simply turn every arbitrary single weak source into one perfect output string.

He describes a way around that obstacle for running algorithms: generate a collection of candidate blocks, with most having the useful randomness guarantee in the relevant construction, run the algorithm on the candidates, and combine the answers by a majority vote. The details depend on the extraction model and assumptions. This is an intuition for computational use, rather than an instruction for manufacturing a secret by choosing any one candidate.

What is the idea behind constructions with several sources and sum–product structure?

With several independent weak sources, the goal can be to combine them into a source with more useful entropy. He relates this to arithmetic combinatorics. Adding every pair in an arithmetic progression may produce little growth; multiplying every pair in a geometric progression may also produce little growth. Sum–product results capture the fact that the two operations cannot both remain similarly unproductive in the relevant setting.

Mixing multiplication and addition, such as multiplying two source values and adding a third, can exploit that tension. A full proof must analyze distributions and entropy, not just count distinct values. He explicitly separates this multi-source intuition from the harder arbitrary single-source problem.

Source: 1:15:59–1:21:19 ↗
Source: 1:10:10–1:15:59 ↗

QWhat is a zero-knowledge proof?

Avi Wigderson

First enlarge the idea of a proof. Instead of sending one written object for a verifier to check, a prover and a randomized verifier can interact. A sound protocol makes the chance of accepting a false claim very small.

Zero knowledge adds a privacy requirement: the verifier becomes convinced of the claim without learning the secret proof or witness beyond what the claim itself reveals. A cryptographic participant might need to show that a public number was produced by multiplying two primes, while keeping those primes secret. More generally, participants want assurance that others followed a protocol without exposing their private inputs.

Wigderson recalls how implausible this initially sounded. His work showed the broad reach of the idea for efficiently verifiable claims under the required cryptographic assumptions. The surprise is that convincing someone and revealing the underlying secret need not be the same act.

Source: 1:21:20–1:27:45 ↗

QHow can a proof be checked without revealing it?

Avi Wigderson

The explanation assumes suitable one-way functions: easy to compute in one direction and hard to invert. These support commitments with two important properties. Hiding prevents the other person from learning the committed value; binding prevents the sender from later changing the value they claim to have committed to.

For the example, both people know a graph and the prover knows a legal three-coloring. The prover commits to a color at every vertex. The verifier randomly chooses an edge, and the prover opens the commitments at its endpoints. The verifier checks that both colors are allowed and are different.

If the graph cannot be legally colored, every proposed coloring has a defect. Random checks have a chance of exposing it, and repetition makes the chance of undetected cheating very small. But reusing the same coloring would gradually disclose it. The prover therefore randomly renames the three colors before each round. The two opened colors then look like a random pair of different colors, rather than pieces of one stable secret assignment.

Finally, reductions make the example broadly useful. A reduction must translate the original instance and its witness into a graph and a corresponding legal coloring. An efficiently checkable proof can be handled through that representation. The interview gives the intuition; the formal zero-knowledge definition and security proof require more care than this sketch.

Can the verifier ever be completely certain?

The completeness side can be exact: an honest prover with the required witness succeeds. Soundness against a dishonest prover can retain a nonzero error probability, reduced to an arbitrarily small level by repetition. Those are different guarantees.

Source: 1:37:47–1:38:16 ↗
Source: 1:27:46–1:37:46 ↗
Editorial synthesis
Source: 1:31:16–1:37:46 ↗

QHow has quantum computation changed complexity theory?

Avi Wigderson

Quantum computation adds operations inspired by quantum mechanics, including superposition and interference. Interference permits contributions to reinforce or cancel; the interview’s analogy with negative numbers is about that behavior, rather than negative probabilities. Measuring suitable quantum states also supplies random bits, so the model includes randomized computation.

Shor’s efficient algorithms for factoring and discrete logarithms made the significance concrete. They threatened specific assumptions used in important public-key systems and stimulated both hardware work and cryptographic research. Building the machinery is a separate challenge: maintaining quantum states, controlling noise and decoherence, and correcting errors are difficult engineering problems.

Cryptography must ask which assumptions survive a quantum adversary. He distinguishes plentiful intuitions about one-way processes from the rarer structures needed for useful trapdoor systems. He discusses lattice-based problems and learning with errors as candidates for which efficient quantum algorithms were not known in the conversation’s context. Lack of a known attack remains an assumption, rather than a proof of security.

The effects extend beyond cryptography. Quantum models bring computer scientists and physicists together, suggest algorithms that can sometimes be translated back into classical approaches, and create new questions about proof systems.

His most striking example is MIP* = RE, involving multiple entangled provers and an efficient verifier in a particular interactive proof model. That model can verify claims connected with undecidable problems. It does not give an ordinary algorithm that decides the halting problem. He emphasizes that the techniques also resolve important mathematical questions: a model that initially seems remote can produce useful new proof methods.

How can a verifier handle something described as undecidable?

He does not offer a short derivation. The result depends on a very substantial body of work combining quantum proof systems with classical techniques, coding theory, algebra, and PCP ideas. The long proof adds more tools on top of that foundation. The remarkable claim belongs to the specific interactive model, whose assumptions must remain visible.

Source: 1:52:45–1:53:57 ↗
Source: 1:38:18–1:52:42 ↗

QHow does the community verify an extremely long, surprising proof?

Avi Wigderson

Carefully, and sometimes over years. Wigderson compares the process with other major mathematical proofs that required extended checking, corrections, and explanatory work. For the quantum proof-system result, he describes an early bug that was fixed, ongoing refereeing at the time of the conversation, and later papers that reused the tools or supplied alternative and stronger results.

Confidence comes from people examining and extending the argument, rather than from the size or prestige of the initial paper. He also points toward formal proof systems such as Lean as a possible way to make parts of verification more explicit and machine-checkable. His remarks about the paper’s review status are historical to the interview.

Source: 1:53:58–1:56:24 ↗

QWhat is the relationship between mathematics and theoretical computer science?

Avi Wigderson

He sees the field as having two parents. Mathematics contributes rigorous theorems, proofs, and aesthetic questions. Computer science contributes the central object of computation and questions motivated by technology, industry, and natural systems.

The field asks what can arise from sequences of simple local steps and what resources those steps require. Similar questions can be posed about software, biological processes, and physical systems. Living between the two disciplines gives researchers both a supply of useful models and the freedom to study models for their own structure.

Source: 1:56:25–1:59:28 ↗

QWhat motivates you when an application is not the immediate goal?

Avi Wigderson

He first corrects the emphasis on solving problems: creating models, definitions, and questions is itself a central contribution. The computational definition of pseudorandomness is one example of a definition opening an unexpected line of work.

His interest in computation is intrinsic and grew through a computer science education. He regrets not having studied more mathematics earlier, because he had to learn it later. He also values a lively, collaborative community in which colleagues have become close friends.

Applications can be surprising. He originally expected the general zero-knowledge protocol to be too expensive for implementation; motivated researchers found more practical approaches and different assumptions. The broader lesson is to investigate a natural theoretical question without demanding that its first formulation be immediately deployable.

Some foundational questions still have no direct system implementation. Establishing strong hardness results could move cryptography from assumptions toward theorems, but the limits of efficient computation remain poorly understood. He regards the field as being early in its understanding, despite the substantial structure it has already built.

Source: 1:59:32–2:08:15 ↗

QWhat is it like to make rare major discoveries?

Avi Wigderson

The experience is exceptional, but most progress consists of small contributions from a community of researchers. Papers strengthen bounds, adapt techniques, or clarify one piece of an argument. He considers that incremental work essential.

A breakthrough need not settle a famous decades-old question. It can expose an unexpected possibility, as in the small-state majority example: he recalls that the researcher had been trying to prove an impossibility when the new approach appeared.

The day-to-day practice matters more than a distant prize. Many days end without solving the intended problem. Failed attempts can still teach something that later becomes useful. The work suits people who enjoy thinking, trying ideas, and learning through that uncertainty; it will not satisfy everyone in the same way.

Source: 2:08:16–2:12:16 ↗

QWhat advice would you give a beginning researcher?

Avi Wigderson

He would not change much about his own path, which he attributes partly to luck: excellent mentors, collaborators, and a community welcoming to young researchers. As a first-year graduate student, he remembers a senior figure taking genuine interest in the problem he had studied.

His actionable advice is to explore a variety of areas and work on the problems you enjoy most. A prestigious target may not match your affinity. Reading across areas and trying several kinds of problems helps reveal both interests and capabilities; the work you enjoy can also be the work you do best.

Source: 2:12:16–2:14:46 ↗
