Section 28 · interview

Database architecture follows the workload

Mike Stonebraker traces relational databases, argues for specialized implementations, and examines the transactional demands of production AI.

QHow did you begin building database systems?

After arriving at Berkeley, Stonebraker realized that continuing his doctoral work would not give him a promising research direction. A mentor, Gene Wong, proposed exploring databases shortly after the publication of the relational model. Stonebraker describes this mentorship and timing as consequential accidents, rather than a fully planned career.

Existing network and hierarchical systems tied programs closely to physical organization. Pointer-following made programs difficult to debug and schema changes could force extensive rewriting; hierarchical trees required awkward additions to represent more general relationships. The relational proposal offered a cleaner separation, so the team began Ingres in 1972. It became his main tenure project.

He distinguishes a demonstrable university prototype from a system others could actually run. The team invested the additional effort to make Ingres reliable, and roughly a hundred universities adopted the free Unix implementation. Commercial adoption exposed another obstacle: Arizona State could tolerate unsupported Unix and an unsupported database, but its COBOL shop could not proceed without COBOL on Unix. A company, formed in 1980, supplied support and a port to a commercial operating system. Technical quality alone had not supplied the surrounding ecosystem customers needed.

Source: 00:39–06:47 ↗

QHow could Oracle compete with a technically stronger Ingres offering?

Stonebraker attributes Oracle’s competitive success to Larry Ellison’s sales ability, while making strongly critical allegations about the accuracy of its promises. These are his recollections and judgments, rather than independently established findings. His example is referential integrity: he says Ingres implemented it while Oracle documented the standard definition with a note that it was not yet implemented.

The host brings up customers’ concerns after Oracle acquired MySQL. Stonebraker credits that concern with helping PostgreSQL become a preferred open-source relational database. His account connects adoption to trust and business behavior as well as engineering.

Source: 06:51–09:04 ↗

QWhat could PostgreSQL do that Ingres could not?

The original academic Ingres project was supposed to support geographic information. Its fixed set of integers, floating-point values, and strings did not efficiently represent points, lines, polygons, and groups of lines. Although successful as a general database, it failed at this motivating application.

A later commercial customer revealed the same limitation from a different direction. Bond calculations treated each month as thirty days; subtracting two Gregorian dates therefore produced the wrong financial interval. The customer had to retrieve dates into application code, calculate there, and write the answer back, at an estimated two- or threefold efficiency cost. He wanted to overload subtraction with the semantics of his own domain.

PostgreSQL’s central response was an extensible type system: users could introduce useful domain types and their operations inside the database. Other experiments included inheritance and time travel. Stonebraker explicitly says the time-travel implementation was poor and was eventually removed, so extensibility should not be mistaken for a claim that every original feature succeeded.

Source: 09:05–14:31 ↗

QHow do you identify extraordinary engineers?

Stonebraker judges accomplishment against his understanding of the difficulty of the work. A student who completes roughly three times what he considers a reasonable amount is conspicuous. This is a personal screening heuristic, dependent on an informed evaluator’s technical judgment.

Source: 14:33–15:04 ↗

QHow do you evaluate whether someone understands technical work deeply?

He asks progressively specific questions about a candidate’s own thesis or project: what was built, exactly how it worked, how errors were handled, how many processes were used, and why threads were not chosen. The useful method beneath his blunt language is to test understanding through implementation choices and failure conditions, rather than accept impressive project labels.

Source: 15:05–15:51 ↗

QDoes one database architecture fit every workload?

His argument began with three very different architectures: conventional relational row storage, stream processing, and column storage for warehouses. Each specialized implementation could be an order of magnitude faster for its intended workload. He maintains that this distinction still matters, including for vector workloads.

A common parser can sit above multiple physical implementations. He criticizes PostgreSQL’s lack of a built-in column store and multinode warehouse support in the context of very large analytical systems. These are his assessments of the offerings discussed in the interview, not a current product survey.

He nevertheless recommends PostgreSQL as a practical starting point for many ordinary applications: it is free, has a large community, offers many extensions, and makes hiring easier. His boundary is scale and workload fit: the ease of starting with a general-purpose system does not prove it remains the best design for a million transactions per second or a petabyte warehouse.

Source: 15:54–19:10 ↗
Editorial synthesis
Different database requirements imply different architectures
RequirementReason the choice changes
Ordinary application developmentPostgreSQL offers a practical ecosystem and easy starting point.
Large analytical warehouseColumn storage and multinode execution may matter more than general-purpose convenience.
Uniform accelerator-friendly workGPU parallelism helps only when dependencies and transfer bandwidth permit it.
Nonnegative inventory or coordinated money transferAtomic transactions preserve constraints that asynchronous reconciliation can violate.
Source: 15:54–26:47 ↗

QDo GPUs create new opportunities for databases?

Probably, but Stonebraker sees important architectural constraints. A GPU’s single-instruction, multiple-data execution fits uniform parallel work better than dependent pointer traversals. Storage bandwidth and the CPU-to-GPU connection can also become the bottleneck, so simply attaching an accelerator does not ensure useful speedup.

Why does indexing fit SIMD poorly?

Finding a person’s salary in a B-tree requires choosing a branch at the root, following a pointer, and repeating the process several times. Each next step depends on a preceding memory access. That dependency chain does not expose the broad, uniform parallel work that a GPU needs.

Source: 20:10–21:05 ↗
Source: 19:13–20:07 ↗

QWas the original Ingres implementation written from scratch?

Yes. Stonebraker says the original system was implemented from scratch, including its underlying structures.

What was the hardest component, and why?

The query optimizer was the hardest component. He calls it algorithmically difficult and says experienced database engineers would still commonly give the same answer. The interview does not develop a more detailed optimizer explanation.

Source: 21:12–21:45 ↗
Source: 21:05–21:10 ↗

QWhy did you object to MapReduce’s popularity?

Stonebraker believes many adopters inferred quality from Google’s reputation instead of comparing architectures. He and collaborators already understood distributed database systems and argued that they could greatly outperform Hadoop; he points to their 2011 comparison as the basis for this criticism.

He extends that criticism to enthusiasm for eventual consistency. In his view, the approach addresses a narrower set of application requirements than its advocates implied. This is a forceful participant’s evaluation, and the section preserves it as such.

What problem was eventual consistency intended to solve?

Synchronously committing a transaction across distant replicas requires network round trips. Asynchronous updates avoid that immediate coordination cost: each coast updates locally and sends messages that eventually reconcile the replicas. The difficulty appears when both sell the last item at the same time. The eventual state may be negative stock, and one buyer cannot receive the promised item. Applications that permit overselling can accept this; systems that require stock to remain nonnegative cannot. He cites Spanner’s use of conventional transactions as evidence that stronger guarantees remain valuable.

Source: 23:45–26:47 ↗
Did you discuss these disagreements with Google?

Before the 2011 paper, his group proposed working together, but Google declined. The interview supplies no account of Google’s reasoning beyond that refusal.

Source: 26:47–27:24 ↗
Source: 21:45–23:44 ↗

QDo you disagree with other large companies’ database strategies?

He says he told Amazon that maintaining approximately fifteen database systems was excessive—about twelve too many—and that they had not retired them by the time of the interview. He sees this as a consequence of company culture and portfolio decisions.

Why should fifteen systems become roughly three?

His criterion is whether a system is sufficiently performant in a sufficiently large market to justify maintenance. He regards dedicated graph storage as rarely the best performer and suggests presenting nodes and edges through a layer above a relational implementation. This is his design judgment, not a universally demonstrated result for every graph workload.

Source: 28:09–29:15 ↗
Source: 27:24–28:07 ↗

QWhy influence industry from academia rather than work at a large company?

An industry role brings a boss, company rules, publication restrictions, and reduced access to information competitors might share with an academic. He values the freedom to investigate and criticize across organizations.

He also prefers startups. After the commercial PostgreSQL effort was acquired by Informix, he worked part time in a company of about two thousand people and felt unable to make much difference. Bureaucracy and executive authority frustrated him. He openly acknowledges that corporate politics and interacting with people he does not respect are personal weaknesses.

Source: 29:15–30:54 ↗

QWhat is DBOS, and how did its operating-system idea become a company?

The academic project began around 2019–2020 with a scheduling problem at Databricks. At very large scale, existing operating-system schedulers did not meet the requirement. Storing scheduling data in PostgreSQL suggested a broader hypothesis: much of an operating system is managing state at scale, and database technology could provide that state management.

The research explored replacing the upper part of Linux while keeping device drivers. A language interface then made programs inherit database properties by keeping application state in the database: durability, transactions, and failover. Venture investors doubted that a startup could displace Linux but liked the programming model, so the 2023 company focused on that opportunity.

He describes integrations for TypeScript, Java, Go, and Python and a workflow model whose steps are transactional and whose completed progress is durable. Whole-workflow atomicity is described as something the system could support if there were market demand, not as an unqualified existing feature. He says customers include startups and increasingly larger organizations, and that roughly two thirds were working on agentic AI.

Why would agents need stronger workflow guarantees?

Many early agents produce read-only recommendations. Stonebraker expects applications that change real state to require database guarantees. Transferring one hundred dollars between two accounts requires the debit and credit to commit together or be rolled back together; separate agents do not remove that requirement. He presents growing read-write agent use as a forecast and a business opportunity for DBOS.

Source: 38:23–39:38 ↗
Source: 30:58–39:38 ↗

QWhat tradeoffs appear when an operating system’s state lives in a database?

Stonebraker claims that the research file system outperformed Linux’s, that scheduling was competitive, and that database-based state made failover available across the system. He argues there is no inherent downside in replacing the upper operating-system components while retaining device-driver code. The interview does not provide benchmark details or investigate counterexamples, so these remain his claims about the research.

How did operating-system researchers respond?

He recalls researchers feeling that database specialists were encroaching on their territory, and similar reactions from programming-language researchers to database-backed runtimes. He also cautions that adoption can be slow, using Java’s roughly decade-long path to broad acceptance as an analogy.

Source: 41:16–42:10 ↗
Source: 39:40–41:16 ↗

QWhich unsolved database problems interest you now?

His first focus is text-to-SQL on production warehouses. His group obtained actual workloads from four warehouses and reconstructed the natural-language requests behind them. He contrasts those tests with Spider and BIRD, on which he says leading systems scored around eighty to eighty-five percent.

On his group’s benchmarks, the tested language models scored zero percent; retrieval and other additions raised that to about ten percent. Giving the actual FROM tables and join clauses raised accuracy to roughly thirty-five percent. These are the results he reports for the systems and benchmarks in this interview, not timeless capabilities of all language models.

He identifies four differences: proprietary warehouse data is absent from general training material; real queries can reach about a hundred SQL lines rather than ten or twenty; production schemas have cryptic names and redundant materialized views; and business concepts can be idiosyncratic, such as MIT’s January term. Together, these make clean demonstration benchmarks misleading for his target problem.

His group released the anonymized BEAVER benchmark and is exploring simpler retrieval units containing table and join information. For requests spanning structured databases, he prefers preserving tables and using SQL joins rather than asking an LLM to execute the joins. A Munich transportation example combines schedules, traffic-light sequencing, intersection CAD, and national and city regulations. Their research direction is to turn these into tables and use query optimization to join them. His second focus is transactionally correct read-write agents.

What does text-to-SQL mean here?

The user asks a question in ordinary language, such as identifying professors at MIT who won the Turing Award, and a model constructs the SQL needed to answer it. The important comparison is whether it can do this over a real production schema, not merely generate plausible SQL syntax.

Source: 43:26–44:02 ↗
How well would a human perform on the difficult benchmark?

Once the natural-language request is disambiguated, a knowledgeable SQL programmer with the schema should achieve very high accuracy, Stonebraker says. The host suggests ninety percent or more, but the guest does not supply a measured human benchmark score.

Source: 50:52–51:35 ↗
Source: 42:10–50:50 ↗

QWhat should someone study to understand databases deeply?

He recommends Readings in Database Systems, the Red Book he edited with Joseph Hellerstein, followed by influential research papers. He notes that the edition discussed was about eight years old, so the later literature matters for newer developments.

Source: 51:38–52:26 ↗

QWhat advice would you give your younger self?

Beginning a database system without knowing much about databases or implementation was, in retrospect, a very ambitious gamble. He encourages unusual ideas and learning by making them work, rather than assuming useful projects must follow prevailing fashion.

He distinguishes this from advice to students choosing a field now. He speculates that computer science may cease to be a growth industry, regards health care and building trades as safer, and is unsure he would recommend the same degree choice. Those are his predictions, not established labor-market facts.

For a new PhD graduate, he recommends the most prestigious available role, a willing mentor, and a research direction outside the main flow. He also acknowledges a tension in telling children to follow their passion while doubting that money necessarily takes care of itself.

If money may not work out, why still encourage passion?

His wife wanted to teach children, but her parents urged a better-paid path and she studied computer science. He says she continued to regret abandoning teaching. His point is about satisfaction: passion may not make someone wealthy, but work that feels like more than a trade can improve life. He enjoys his own work regardless of whether it pays a great deal.

Source: 54:43–55:50 ↗
Source: 52:26–54:42 ↗

Section 29 · interview

Leslie Lamport: Concurrency, Paxos, Byzantine Generals, and Thinking by Writing

Lamport explains how algorithms, invariants, and written proofs shaped his work on concurrent and distributed systems, from the bakery algorithm to Paxos.

Lamport's view: write the algorithm down, state the invariant, and prove it

Lamport argues that the reliable way to understand a concurrent or distributed system is to state an algorithm, name an invariant about its state, and write the proof down. He says informal code hides the issues that matter for synchronization. The conversation follows his key work in order: the bakery algorithm, the paper on ordering events, Byzantine faults, Paxos and Raft, then writing as a thinking tool, LaTeX, and his view of his own abilities. The host introduces Lamport as a Turing Award winner.

Source: 00:00–1:09:22 ↗

QWhat problem does the bakery algorithm solve, and how did Lamport first come across it?

Leslie Lamport

Lamport says Edsger Dijkstra introduced the problem in a 1965 paper, which Lamport treats as the start of concurrent programming theory. Dijkstra structured a program as semi-independent tasks that must synchronize. Time-sharing made this urgent, since a shared printer could produce garbled output if two programs used it at once. Dijkstra's answer was a critical section, a piece of code arranged so that at most one process runs it at a time.

Lamport says he first learned of the problem in 1972, from a Communications of the ACM article that gave a solution.

How did the bakery idea develop after Lamport's first attempt?
Leslie Lamport

Lamport's simple two-process algorithm had a bug, which the editor pointed out in a letter. The lesson was that concurrent programs are hard to get right and need a proof of correctness. The bakery idea came from a deli counter, where customers take numbered tickets. Dijkstra's version had no central server, so each process had to choose its own number.

Source: 03:55–06:27 ↗
Why was the bakery algorithm notable, and who doubted it?
Leslie Lamport

Lamport says its proof showed a surprising property. Mutual exclusion was assumed to need atomic reads and writes of shared registers. Bakery did not need that, because each shared value had one writer. A reader overlapping a write could see any value, and the algorithm still worked.

His colleague Anatol Holt found the result so remarkable that he did not believe it. Lamport wrote the proof on a whiteboard, and Holt went home convinced it must be wrong. He never found a flaw.

Source: 06:30–08:27 ↗
Source: 01:25–03:50 ↗

QWhat was unsatisfactory about Dijkstra's solution, and why was bakery different?

Leslie Lamport

Lamport says Dijkstra's original solution allowed starvation. If many processes kept trying to enter the critical section, one might never get in. Lamport recalls that the next solution, by Donald Knuth, measured efficiency by how long a process might wait. He believes bakery was the first with first-come, first-served order: if one process picked its number before another, it entered first. He also thinks bakery was simpler than the alternatives.

Source: 08:44–09:58 ↗

QWhat was the month in the Netherlands with Dijkstra, in 1976, like?

Leslie Lamport

Lamport says Dijkstra wrote short papers, called EWDs, and sent them to colleagues. One described the first concurrent garbage collection algorithm, by Dijkstra and associates. Lamport saw that the free list could be part of the regular data structure instead of needing its own coordination. That simplified the algorithm, and Dijkstra made him an author on the next version.

Lamport says the idea seemed obvious to him but was not obvious to most people. Dijkstra told him he had a remarkable ability at abstraction, which Lamport says he only came to appreciate in recent years.

What came out of the visit?
Leslie Lamport

Lamport says the month produced one published result, a variant of the bakery algorithm. It came from weekly discussions with Dijkstra and a colleague.

Source: 13:41–14:11 ↗
Source: 10:18–13:37 ↗

QWhat is the story behind the paper on time, clocks, and the ordering of events in distributed systems?

Leslie Lamport

Lamport says a paper on distributed databases executed operations as if they occurred in a sequence that could differ from their actual order. He drew on special relativity, where one event can influence another only if a signal could travel between them below light speed. He applied the same idea to messages: one event happens before another if the first could have affected the second through messages actually sent.

Lamport says this happens-before definition surprised people, and it was the first of his papers he would call a scientific result about distributed systems. He admits it broke a rule he had been warned about, since it put two ideas in one paper.

Why did the state machine idea matter, and why did readers miss it?
Leslie Lamport

Lamport says the paper's ordering algorithm let any distributed system be described as a state machine, where each command changes the state and produces a value. He calls this the practical idea in the paper, yet readers ignored it. Twice people told him the paper said nothing about state machines, so he reread it to be sure.

Source: 17:57–20:08 ↗
Why does Lamport prefer invariants to reasoning about sequences of events?
Leslie Lamport

Lamport says a concurrent program is best understood through an invariant, a Boolean property of the state that holds at each point and guarantees the right answer. Reasoning about sequences is hard, because the number of possible executions grows exponentially with the number of processes. Lamport says the work in an invariant proof grows roughly quadratically, so invariant proofs are easier to get right.

He says much distributed-systems theory spent years on partial orderings. That approach produced many papers but is not the practical method, apart from exceptions such as bakery.

Source: 20:12–23:24 ↗
Source: 14:57–17:55 ↗

QWhat is the story behind the Byzantine generals problem?

Leslie Lamport

Lamport says his ordering work assumed no failures, but a distributed system should keep running when a computer fails. He assumed the worst case, that a failed process might do anything. His algorithm implemented a state machine under that assumption, using digital signatures so a faulty process could relay messages but not forge another's signature.

When Lamport joined SRI, colleagues were working on the same problem. Few people knew of digital signatures in 1975, but Lamport knew of them through Whit Diffie, a friend and co-author of the Diffie-Hellman paper. He says Diffie called building them an open problem, and he sketched a first signature algorithm on a napkin. By his rough estimate it needed about 128 bits to sign one bit, but signing a hash of the document made it workable.

How did the SRI approach differ, and why did it need four processes?
Leslie Lamport

Lamport says the SRI group framed the problem as agreement on one command, repeated for each command, which he found a nicer abstraction. Without signatures, their algorithm needed four processes to tolerate one fault, against three with signatures. The original paper contained both algorithms, and Lamport co-authored it. Marshall Pease wrote the general algorithm, which Lamport calls brilliant and nearly incomprehensible.

Source: 26:54–30:21 ↗
Why was the algorithm largely ignored?
Leslie Lamport

Lamport says the SRI group had a contract to build a multiprocess computer for flying airplanes, so they took malicious failures seriously. Each three-process design could be defeated by some plausible sequence of failures. Lamport adds that digital signatures were expensive at the time, which is why the algorithm was largely ignored.

Source: 30:24–32:42 ↗
Why did Lamport choose a story about generals?
Leslie Lamport

Lamport says Dijkstra's dining philosophers problem was not especially interesting in itself, but its story made it popular. Lamport decided his result needed a story too. In his version, four generals must agree on whether to attack or retreat, and one of them might be a traitor.

Source: 32:43–34:08 ↗
Source: 24:28–26:48 ↗

QWas there an earlier version of the problem, called the Chinese generals problem?

Leslie Lamport

Lamport says Jim Gray had described a related problem as an impossibility result, which gave Lamport the idea of using generals. He first thought of Albanian generals, since Albania was largely closed to the outside world. His boss pointed out that Albanians exist, so Lamport chose Byzantine, since there are no Byzantines around.

Source: 34:22–35:23 ↗

QWhat made the Byzantine problem worth extra work?

Leslie Lamport

Lamport says the problem mattered because computers would fly airplanes. In the 1970s oil crisis, designers wanted fuel-efficient planes with smaller control surfaces, which were aerodynamically unstable. A pilot could not make the constant adjustments needed, but a computer could. People assumed three computers could tolerate one fault, without realizing that arbitrary faults needed four. Lamport believes that result needed to be well known.

Source: 35:25–37:00 ↗

QHow does Lamport choose problems, given that most of his work was in private companies?

Leslie Lamport

Lamport says he worked for private companies, not in academia or government. Some problems came to him when an engineer had a need. Paxos was one such case, because someone actually wanted an algorithm that did what it did.

Source: 37:03–38:01 ↗

QWhat is the story behind Paxos?

Leslie Lamport

Lamport says Paxos addressed the same problem as the Byzantine work, building a fault-tolerant state machine. By then, industry cared most about failures in which a computer simply stopped, and Paxos handles that class of faults. Lamport joined Digital Equipment's Systems Research Center in 1985. Its group had come from Xerox PARC, had built one of the first distributed operating systems, and had invented Ethernet.

The group's system kept shared storage consistent across computers. Lamport did not believe that was possible, and he tried to write an impossibility proof. He eventually concluded that the group's code was itself an algorithm that worked. The group had code that did the job, but no algorithm written down.

What did Lamport mean by code versus an algorithm?
Leslie Lamport

Lamport says most programmers start by writing code, but he thinks in algorithms. An algorithm is more abstract than a program and can be implemented in any code. Since about 2000, much of his work has been persuading people who build concurrent systems to write an algorithm for the synchronizing core first. Code mixes many concerns unrelated to concurrency, which makes the synchronizing part hard to get right.

Source: 40:46–43:10 ↗
Why did the Paxos paper take about eight years to publish?
Leslie Lamport

Lamport says the referees found the paper acceptable but not terribly important, and he was in no hurry to publish. A new editor later decided to publish it, since it had been accepted but needed revision. Keith Marzullo wrote the interim update and a preface that kept the framing of an ancient system. Lamport says Butler Lampson recognized the algorithm's importance and promoted building systems with Paxos as state machines.

Source: 43:14–45:22 ↗
How was the Paxos paper presented, and who understood it?
Leslie Lamport

The host recalls Lamport dressing as an Indiana Jones-style archaeologist for the talk. Lamport says the lecture may have gone well, but almost nobody understood the algorithm's significance. Butler Lampson was the exception. Lamport says Lampson understood building systems and was one of the original people at Xerox PARC who built distributed personal computing.

Source: 45:24–47:32 ↗
Source: 38:17–40:43 ↗

QWhat did Lamport think of the Raft paper, which seems to solve the same problem as Paxos?

Leslie Lamport

Lamport says the Raft authors sent him a draft, and he replied to send it back with either an algorithm or a proof, though he does not recall which. He says he never read the later versions. Someone whose judgment he values read them and said Raft was basically the Paxos paper, with some of Paxos's unfinished tales filled in and described differently.

Lamport explains Paxos in two phases. The first phase elects a leader, and it can be done once for a whole run of decisions, as long as the leader stays the same. The second phase repeats for each decision. Engineers usually describe it in the opposite order, repeating the second phase until the leader fails. Starting fresh, Lamport says, the first phase's work could be built into the initial state.

Is Raft easier to understand than Paxos?
Leslie Lamport

Lamport says many people find Paxos hard, and he does not see why. He has explained it to some people in five minutes. The Raft authors taught Paxos to one class and Raft to another, and students found Raft easier. Lamport says a bug was later found and fixed in Raft, and he believes the version students found easier was the one with the bug.

For Lamport, understanding means being able to write a proof. For most people, he says, it is a warm, fuzzy feeling, and Raft gave them more of that feeling because it follows the order programmers already think in.

Source: 49:34–51:24 ↗
Source: 46:35–49:32 ↗

QWhat is the story behind LaTeX?

Leslie Lamport

Lamport says he was starting to write a book, and TeX was the basic typesetting system he had to use. He needed macros to make TeX do what he wanted, and he figured a little extra effort could make them usable by others. Before TeX he had used Scribe, which let authors describe a document's logical structure and left formatting to the system. Scribe did not format well, but Lamport liked the idea that the ideas matter more than the typesetting.

How did the book with Addison-Wesley come about?
Leslie Lamport

Lamport says Peter Gordon, an Addison-Wesley editor, convinced him to write a book. At the time, Lamport did not expect people would pay for a book about software. The publisher introduced him to a typographic designer whose work became the typography of the standard LaTeX styles. Lamport says he did most of the work in his spare time, over six to nine months.

Source: 53:10–54:16 ↗
Source: 51:46–53:07 ↗

QWhat did Lamport mean by 'thinking without writing'?

Leslie Lamport

Lamport says the remark was meant for people building computer systems. Write a description of an idea before trusting it. He recalls a maxim to write the instruction manual before the program. He did not follow that advice with LaTeX, but while writing the book he found some things hard to explain and changed them.

Why is writing good for thinking?
Leslie Lamport

Lamport says it is easy to fool yourself. When his algorithms grew complicated, his usual proof style broke down, because too many details had to be tracked. He devised a hierarchical proof, a sequence of steps where each step has its own proof, which can be a paragraph or a further sequence of steps. A step that does not follow from the stated steps shows the proof is wrong, even if the theorem is true.

When he presented this to roughly 20 mathematicians in a small seminar, their reaction was angry, and he thought they might physically attack him. He believes the fear was that they would have to write proofs for a computer, though he says the method needs only organization, not formalism. Writing a proof exposes steps the author left unstated. Lamport says thinking you know something you have not written down only feels like knowing it, and that is where errors enter.

Source: 55:41–59:55 ↗
Source: 54:40–55:39 ↗

QWhy did Lamport's career stay in industry rather than academia?

Leslie Lamport

Lamport says he started out programming and took jobs that led him into what is now called computer science. He did not realize until the mid-to-late 1970s that computer science was a field in its own right. At one point he had to choose between computer science and teaching math at a university. He chose computer science for fairly random reasons. Until about the mid-1980s he did not think computer science was something people needed a university to learn, and he did not think teaching it would be fun.

Source: 59:58–1:01:46 ↗

QDid Lamport feel like a failure for not finding a grand theory of concurrency?

Leslie Lamport

Lamport says many people doing this work looked for a Turing machine of concurrency, an abstraction that would capture concurrent computing. Nobody has found one, though some think they have. Petri nets were a big topic in the 1970s, and a community still works on them, but they were language-based, and Lamport was never interested in languages.

He now thinks the Turing machine of concurrency is the state machine, described only by a state and a next-state relation, with no commands. A Turing machine describes what is possible. A state machine can also describe things that are not possible.

Why are infinite values useful in state machines?
Leslie Lamport

Lamport says that when he describes an algorithm, he lets a variable take any integer, although a real program would use bounded integers. People often assume that because something is infinite, it is more complicated. Lamport says they have it backwards: infinity simplifies arithmetic, which is far messier on a finite set of integers. He says mathematics is the most powerful way to describe a state machine.

Source: 1:04:06–1:06:01 ↗
Why are programming languages the wrong tool for concurrency?
Leslie Lamport

Lamport says many programmers and computer scientists are hung up on languages, and they keep inventing new ones. A semantics for any of them would be given in terms of a state machine. Code has real advantages, mainly efficiency. For understanding, though, Lamport says you cannot beat mathematics, and language-based attempts to reason about concurrency are the wrong approach.

Source: 1:06:03–1:07:05 ↗
Source: 1:01:49–1:04:03 ↗

QHow can someone who does not consider himself smart achieve so much?

Leslie Lamport

Lamport says psychologists have observed that people who are good at something often do not notice it, because it seems simple to them. The reverse also holds: people who are bad at something tend to overrate themselves. He says the gift he has is not raw intelligence but abstraction. He realized only in the last ten or so years how much better he is at abstraction than most people.

Source: 1:07:48–1:09:01 ↗

QLooking back, what would Lamport tell himself just after college?

Leslie Lamport

Lamport says he learned early not to waste time on questions he does not have to answer. He does not dwell on what he should have done, because that is a question he does not have to answer.

Source: 1:09:05–1:09:22 ↗

Section 30 · interview

Making strong cryptography available to everyone

Martin Hellman recounts the invention and political resistance to public-key cryptography, then reflects on reconciliation and the broader risks he now studies.

QHow did you enter cryptography, and why was the government concerned?

Hellman encountered IBM’s unclassified cryptography work after his PhD in 1968. At MIT he began to see how his information-theory background might contribute. He initially pursued it in his own time, anticipating government concern but believing research itself was lawful.

A July 1977 letter from an NSA employee, sent privately to IEEE, alleged that publishing certain papers violated export rules. The issues cited repeatedly contained Hellman’s work. He describes the argument as treating cryptographic research as technical data about implements of war under the International Traffic in Arms Regulations.

Stanford’s general counsel believed that such a broad interpretation would be unconstitutional, but warned that this was a legal opinion that would require resolution in court. This section records a historical dispute and counsel’s response, not present legal guidance.

Did the warnings deter you?

He and Whitfield Diffie had already opposed DES’s fifty-six-bit key, arguing that exhaustive search could break it. They expected a cheap technical correction; after months of resistance, they concluded it was a political problem. Having invested in the work, Hellman chose to continue and describes his temperament as willing to argue rather than back down.

Source: 03:43–04:50 ↗
What could have gone wrong?

He believed imprisonment was possible and that his life might be at risk, perhaps from Soviet intelligence rather than necessarily from the NSA. He says stronger publicly available cryptography threatened intelligence services’ ability to read other countries’ traffic. These are his fears and interpretations; he does not describe an actual assassination attempt.

Source: 04:51–05:33 ↗
Source: 00:34–03:42 ↗

QWhat happened after Stanford’s counsel became involved?

Two papers were due at a Cornell symposium in October 1977, one with Ralph Merkle and another with a student whose name is not reliably established in the captions. Counsel advised Hellman to present because Stanford was more clearly positioned to defend a faculty member than a student.

The students initially wanted to speak, then accepted the arrangement after considering the risks. Hellman brought each student to the podium and publicly credited the work while taking legal responsibility for speaking. He believes the explanation earned them more recognition than an ordinary presentation would have.

Source: 05:35–07:26 ↗

QWhy pursue the field despite so much opposition?

Colleagues argued that the NSA had a vast budget and decades of experience, making new discovery unlikely. Hellman did not need to know more than a secret agency: even rediscovering a technique could matter if it became available for commercial use. He distinguishes the later British claims about prior privacy-related inventions from digital signatures, which he regards as an additional contribution of the open research. The priority assessment is his account of the history.

Source: 07:28–08:35 ↗

QHow did people encrypt before your public-key work?

He says much civilian traffic was simply unencrypted, while some banks and other businesses used weak encryption. Military use was different and had long been central to cryptography.

What about military communications?

Military secrecy provided one route toward thinking about trapdoors: a cipher might be secure for a general who knew hidden design information but insecure if an adversary captured it and used it. Hellman says this imagined trapdoor cipher was not something they successfully implemented, but the idea pointed toward public-key cryptography.

Source: 09:07–10:16 ↗
Source: 08:39–09:05 ↗

QHow does Enigma illustrate the relationship between encryption and computation?

He describes Enigma’s keyboard, electrical signals, rotors, and illuminated output letters, with rotor selection and arrangement contributing to the key. Encryption was a specialized form of computation built with the technology of its time.

In his telling, the Germans knew the system could in principle be broken but did not anticipate the Allies building machinery to do so rapidly. The lesson he draws is that advances in computation change the practical meaning of security. He also reflects on the injustice of Alan Turing’s treatment after the war. These are his historical explanations, condensed without treating the film he mentions as an independent source.

Source: 10:19–12:46 ↗

QWhat do you mean by arrows pointing toward public-key cryptography?

Trapdoor reasoning and one-way functions already expose an asymmetry: evaluating a function or checking a proposed solution can be easy while finding the input may be hard. Hellman relates this to the question of efficiently checking versus solving computational problems.

His examination analogy makes the intuition concrete. A professor can reveal a prepared answer and verify it in minutes even if students struggled to find it. In a stronger hypothetical version, the professor supplies a one-way function’s output; finding the input takes enormous effort, but evaluating the known input immediately verifies it. This is an explanatory analogy, not a proof of any specific function’s security.

Source: 12:47–14:52 ↗

QDid the NSA try to recruit you?

Yes, before the major results, representatives approached him at conferences about consulting. He would have liked to learn what they knew but insisted on independent publication. They would not permit that, so he declined classified consulting.

Much later, around 1995, he accepted access to classified information as part of the National Research Council’s CRISIS review of cryptography policy. The committee included security officials and privacy advocates and reached unanimous conclusions. He emphasizes that classified briefings filled in details without changing the committee’s fundamental judgments. He wanted to be able to address the argument that outsiders would think differently if they knew the secrets.

Did they offer enough compensation to draw you into classified work?

The discussion never reached compensation. By the time the confrontation developed, he felt committed. He admits that he did not dwell on possible imprisonment or death and was unsure how real the risks were. His experience felt more like gradually falling into a consequential conflict than choosing a fully understood heroic role.

Source: 17:47–18:50 ↗
Source: 14:55–17:45 ↗

QWhat were the crypto wars?

He divides the history into three conflicts. The first, in the late 1970s and early 1980s, concerned publication freedom and DES’s key length. His group estimated that exhaustive search was practical at a per-solution cost of roughly ten thousand dollars, even with the technology of the time; advancing computing would erase a modest estimation error.

The second concerned the 1990s Clipper Chip and key escrow: strong encryption would be permitted if authorities could obtain access through stored keys. He sees unresolved international problems about who holds keys for communications across jurisdictions. His committee invited the government to experiment and return with solutions, which he says did not happen.

The third, illustrated by the San Bernardino iPhone dispute, returned to exceptional access under a different name. He argues that a recovery capability could be demanded repeatedly or stolen, weakening the system more broadly. He would prefer legitimate access while excluding illegitimate access but does not see a way to reliably achieve that separation. These are his historical categories and policy views.

Source: 18:51–22:43 ↗

QWhy did the government favor a shorter DES key?

Hellman interprets the decision as preserving an intelligence agency’s ability to search the key space. His estimate used a large parallel collection of specialized chips to test keys rapidly; a sufficiently large machine might search the space in roughly a day.

The advantage was partly economic utilization. A state agency with many targets could keep expensive equipment busy, while a civilian interested in an occasional target would leave it mostly idle and incur a much higher effective cost. The crude “trapdoor” was a resource asymmetry rather than a secret mathematical shortcut. He acknowledges that the early estimate may have been optimistic.

Source: 22:46–24:58 ↗

QWhy need secrecy if you have nothing bad to hide?

Banking information and authenticated software updates provide ordinary reasons for security. He recognizes that harmful actors also benefit from strong encryption, but says it cannot be made available only to good people. His car analogy contrasts malicious and beneficial uses: restricting the technology to a classified monopoly would also withhold ambulances, ordinary travel, and other public benefits. The dilemma is a real tradeoff in his view, not a proof that misuse disappears.

Source: 25:00–26:20 ↗

QWhat is the story behind Diffie–Hellman–Merkle key exchange?

Diffie contacted Hellman in 1974 after traveling around the country to investigate cryptography. A planned short meeting lasted through the night and began a sustained collaboration. They developed public-key ideas while also responding to DES.

Independently, Berkeley student Ralph Merkle proposed a key-distribution idea as a course project. His professor preferred a more conventional option; Merkle left the course and continued alone. A journal then rejected his paper, partly criticizing the lack of prior references. Hellman emphasizes both the novelty and Merkle’s inexperience at writing a paper.

Hellman later helped revise the paper and recruited Merkle to Stanford with funded research-assistant work and tuition coverage. He stresses Merkle’s contribution and the difference between the whole public-key framework and the privacy/key-distribution portion. Delayed publication should not be confused with later conception.

Source: 26:22–30:42 ↗

QWas unclassified cryptography unusually poorly supported?

Yes. Hellman reiterates that colleagues thought the field irrational because intelligence agencies were so far ahead. He connects this to other breakthrough stories he has heard, where an initially dismissed research direction later won major recognition. His point is that good ideas can appear unreasonable before results; the anecdotes do not imply every rejected idea is good.

Source: 31:29–33:39 ↗

QWhat gave you confidence when everyone called the work foolish?

He traces some of his independence to childhood antisemitic bullying. Wanting to fit in, he adopted a defensive attitude of not wanting to be like others, and eventually came to value difference. As an adult, being called crazy could attract rather than repel him. Family examples reinforced his comfort with unconventional choices. This is a personal explanation of temperament, not a universal method for deciding which criticism to disregard.

Source: 33:43–35:21 ↗

QWhat problem guided the 1976 paper?

The original ambition was a theory of cryptography. An editor invited a paper, Hellman asked to include Diffie, and they developed drafts. In May 1976 Hellman found the key-exchange construction and presented it the following month; the editor urged its inclusion in the paper nominally assigned to the November issue. Hellman notes that the issue actually appeared in February 1977. Merkle’s earlier submission was delayed until 1978, an example of how editorial history can obscure intellectual chronology.

Source: 35:23–36:46 ↗

QHow do key exchange and digital signatures differ?

Key exchange lets two parties establish a secret across a channel an observer can hear. Merkle’s puzzles force the observer to solve far more puzzles than the communicating parties. Hellman then offers a strongbox analogy: one person adds a lock, the second adds another, the first removes their own, and the second finally opens it. The independent locks illustrate the importance of operations that commute.

For the mathematical construction, he describes modular exponentiation: applying the two private exponents in either order produces the same combined exponent. In a finite setting, inversion can be hard even though the forward operation is efficient. The analogy is an intuition for this shared-secret construction, not a literal statement of the protocol’s message count.

A signature instead allows public verification of an action only the secret-key holder can perform. He credits Diffie’s framework and RSA’s implementation. A phone may contain a public verification key without giving someone who extracts it the ability to sign a future software update. Confidentiality and authenticity are therefore separate purposes.

How do symmetric and asymmetric cryptography compare?

Asymmetric systems use a public and a secret key; conventional symmetric systems use the same secret for encryption and decryption. The older military model could deliver a shared key with a courier, but that arrangement does not scale naturally to a bank and all its internet customers.

Source: 41:25–42:09 ↗
Why do modern systems combine mechanisms?

Public-key operations are slower, so they can establish or transport a session key and then leave bulk communication to a faster symmetric cipher such as AES. Similarly, a software signature usually covers a hash rather than every byte through a slow public-key operation. Each mechanism supplies the property it handles efficiently.

Source: 42:11–43:03 ↗
Source: 36:47–41:16 ↗

QWhat happened in the patent dispute with RSA?

Hellman says he did not understand that patent claims, rather than merely the underlying ideas, define the protection. He believes better drafting could have covered RSA, but Stanford spent little on the original filing and assigned it to a law student. He says MIT’s side prevailed in the dispute between the institutions or their licensees.

He contrasts RSA’s large commercial outcome with the little he earned from the patents. Captions contain an inconsistent sentence about the money, so the summary retains the clear qualitative comparison without inventing a precise personal payout.

After years of resentment, he decided the fight was over and approached RSA’s leader to reconcile. He thinks a later award nomination may have come from Ron Rivest but is explicitly unsure. The value of friendship was his reason for reconciliation, not a tactic to obtain that nomination.

How did you become able to let go of resentment?

He credits lessons learned while repairing his marriage. He and his wife had developed a damaging pattern despite loving each other. Her search for help led them to a group addressing interpersonal and international conflict, whose ideas he initially resisted.

A crucial insight was the self-reinforcing cycle in dismissing someone: treating his wife’s ideas as crazy provoked reactions that he then treated as proof that she was crazy. Becoming willing to consider her ideas interrupted the cycle. He sees an analogous pattern between countries and connects that lesson to reconciling after the patent fight.

Source: 45:24–48:05 ↗
Source: 43:05–45:22 ↗

QWhy do similar discoveries arise independently at nearly the same time?

He jokingly imagines a muse whispering ideas that most people dismiss and a few pursue. More concretely, available computing power helped make public-key methods implementable; fifty years earlier, the same idea might have remained impractical. He does not claim a complete explanation of simultaneous invention, and leaves room for mystery in his personal outlook.

Source: 48:08–50:26 ↗

QHow did your work shift toward rethinking national security?

Hellman now focuses on reducing nuclear risk and fostering a more cooperative world. He gives a stark personal estimate about the risk a child faces over a lifetime. That estimate is his assessment in the interview, not an independently established probability.

He discusses a proposed bill identified as HR 3564 and says it would constrain some unilateral launch decisions while retaining an exception for launch on warning. He dislikes that exception because warning systems can err, but considers it part of making the proposal politically feasible. The bill number, sponsor count, and policy account describe his discussion at recording, not current legislative status.

What about AI as an existential threat?

He recounts disagreement among AI researchers and says he does not know who is right. He nevertheless believes cooperation is needed for other reasons and is concerned about AI entering nuclear command and control. Very short decision times make computer assistance likely in his view; the combination motivates caution and policy work.

Source: 51:05–53:15 ↗
Source: 50:29–53:00 ↗

QWhat do you remember about working among prominent Stanford researchers?

He offers affectionate anecdotes about colleagues’ unusual habits and about how Diffie’s proximity made collaboration easy. A more consequential story is his own doctoral uncertainty: shortly before a breakthrough, he considered leaving because he doubted his ability to contribute original knowledge.

Stanford encouraged him to spend time elsewhere before joining its faculty to avoid reproducing his advisor’s research. He initially saw that as a needless hurdle. IBM exposed him to Horst Feistel’s cryptography work, and MIT brought a paper connecting information theory with cryptography. Those experiences gave him a distinct direction on his return in 1971. What looked like a detour became central to the result.

Source: 53:18–57:30 ↗

QHow do you think about death?

At about eighty, after being asked to review an obituary draft, he feels he has had a good life and hopes for more time. His concerns are mainly for people he may leave behind and unfinished nuclear-risk work.

He compares humanity’s possible early destruction to infant mortality: eventual mortality does not make a premature end acceptable. He believes change must proceed through a feasible process rather than remain stuck in the present or demand an immediate leap to an ideal world. This is his ethical and personal framing of the problem.

Source: 57:31–59:39 ↗

QWhat advice would you give your newly graduated self?

He imagines an aspiring world-saver being told first to build a reputation and resources. That advice would look like a detour, but his own technical career later supplied influence and financial independence for broader work. He did not originally plan the sequence. His reflection is that an indirect path can equip a person for later contributions, rather than that fame and money should be everyone’s first goals.

Source: 59:40–1:00:39 ↗

PurposeWhat it enables in the interview

Symmetric encryptionCommunicate efficiently after the secret is established.

Section 31 · interview

Measure the architecture against the work it must do

David Patterson connects RISC, compilers, energy limits, and AI accelerators, then explains the personal habits behind a long research career.

QWhat was the RISC-versus-CISC debate, and why was it controversial?

Early microprocessor designers often borrowed instruction-set ideas from mainframes and minicomputers. The prevailing view favored increasingly sophisticated instructions that would bring machine vocabulary closer to high-level programming languages. Patterson and John Hennessy instead asked what instruction set would suit the emerging single-chip computer and let compilers bridge the abstraction gap.

Simpler instructions generally require more instructions per program, but each can run faster. He recalls measurements showing about thirty to forty percent more instructions yet four- to fivefold faster instruction execution, implying a substantial overall speedup. Those historical ratios describe the comparisons he discusses, not an automatic speedup for every modern RISC chip.

The debate was fierce partly because architects feared that lowering the instruction-set level harmed software. Patterson thinks intuition dominated architectural discussion before quantitative comparisons became common. Feature catalogues and philosophical arguments could not settle the actual engineering question.

Why did the gap between language and machine become a philosophical controversy?

Without agreed measurements, people argued qualitatively about the “right” level of abstraction. He wanted designs evaluated scientifically through numbers, rather than accepted because a more elaborate instruction sounded closer to software needs.

Source: 04:05–05:05 ↗
Source: 00:36–05:05 ↗

QDid either side win the RISC-versus-CISC war?

He rejects declaring CISC the winner from the PC era alone. Binary software distribution made x86 compatibility enormously valuable, creating a barrier to a different instruction set. That commercial persistence does not settle the underlying architectural comparison.

The Acorn team, influenced by Berkeley RISC work, designed a simpler processor. Apple’s Newton then highlighted its usefulness for energy-constrained devices, even though the device itself did not succeed commercially. Later mobile adoption made ARM extremely widespread. He cites hundreds of billions of ARM processors and a very large share of processor units, then points to Apple’s computer transition and hyperscalers’ ARM work. These figures and market judgments belong to his account at the time of recording.

RISC ideas also influenced competing implementations: modern x86 hardware translates its external instruction set into simpler internal operations. Paying that translation cost made business sense because it preserved the valuable software base. The external instruction-set label therefore conceals some internal convergence.

How could someone still conclude CISC won?

They may define computers as PCs and servers and end the story around 2000. Patterson thinks that boundary ignores the mobile and post-PC era.

Source: 08:12–08:41 ↗
Does energy efficiency matter only for mobile devices?

No. He considers everything energy constrained, including cloud computing. Billions of transistors allow designers to hide some compatibility overhead, but power and resource costs still matter.

Source: 08:43–09:43 ↗
Source: 05:08–09:43 ↗

QIs CISC ever the right engineering tradeoff?

Patterson explains the historical attraction through control design. Maurice Wilkes proposed storing sequences of control signals as microinstructions, making microprogramming a systematic alternative to ad hoc control logic. With the memory technology of the 1960s and 1970s, using a simple internal interpreter to implement a richer instruction set could be reasonable.

RISC reconsidered that layering as technology changed: could compilers target simpler operations directly instead of paying an interpretation step? He thinks a new instruction set today would rarely be designed to require a microcoded interpreter, although he leaves open small, unusual applications. This is an argument about designing a new architecture, distinct from the commercial need to preserve an existing one.

Source: 09:46–12:50 ↗

QHow does the compiler connect software and hardware in a RISC design?

Registers are a major example. They are much faster than memory, but early compilers lacked the algorithms and computing resources to allocate them well. C allowed programmers to provide register hints because the compiler could not always make the best choices.

Improving compiler algorithms supported simpler instruction sets. RISC designs also commonly provided more registers—he contrasts thirty-two with the eight or sixteen in some older designs—making allocation easier even before the compiler was perfect. Hardware and compiler design therefore reinforced each other.

Were complex instructions underused because compilers were deficient?

Architects often assumed that an elaborate operation would help a compiler without verifying that assumption with compiler writers. In some cases, separate simple instructions were faster than a dedicated procedure-entry instruction. The processor then carried complexity and microcode overhead for instructions compilers did not want. Patterson presents this as a mismatch between imagined software needs and observed use.

Source: 15:38–17:36 ↗
Source: 12:51–15:36 ↗

QDo GPUs and other processors also have instruction sets, and why did specialized architectures emerge?

He frames GPUs as domain-specific architectures that began with graphics. A graphics processor did not initially have to satisfy every operating-system and general-purpose computing requirement. Specialization let it use resources differently.

For decades, transistor growth and Dennard scaling together made faster general-purpose processors possible without proportionate power increases. Lower voltages offset the effect of additional transistors. Around 2005, he says this power-scaling relationship stopped working, forcing the move from one increasingly sophisticated core to multiple simpler cores. Programmers then had to parallelize work to exploit the available resources.

Around the 2010s, transistor scaling also slowed and general-purpose gains became less dramatic. Designers had already used the multicore approach, so a narrower domain offered another way to improve efficiency. Machine learning emerged at an opportune moment. He credits Google with recognizing demand and investing early in custom AI hardware, while explicitly acknowledging his own Google affiliation.

Source: 17:38–23:06 ↗

QWhat are the high-level differences among a CPU, GPU, and TPU?

A CPU remains general purpose, supporting operating systems, compilers, and diverse workloads through familiar cores. A GPU’s graphics heritage emphasized high memory performance and many hardware threads: when one operation waits for memory, the hardware can execute other work. Graphics also tolerates narrower floating-point formats than many scientific applications.

Cheap GPUs offered attractive single-precision computation per dollar. Before a suitable programming system existed, users sometimes reshaped other work into something resembling image generation. CUDA made the architecture more directly programmable with a C-like interface. Patterson sees both the programming environment and specialized libraries as central to expanding GPUs beyond graphics.

He describes AlexNet’s 2012 image-recognition result as a turning point: GPU computation enabled substantial exploration, the neural-network approach performed extremely well, and the field rapidly adopted both neural networks and GPUs.

Google’s clean-sheet TPU approach centered on matrix multiplication, rather than retaining a graphics mission. Predictable machine-learning memory access could be scheduled in software instead of relying on the same hardware-cache structures as a general-purpose CPU. He also discusses narrower arithmetic formats such as bfloat16, emphasizing range rather than high numerical precision. The interview moves across TPU developments, so these points should be read as a design lineage rather than a precise specification of one generation.

He reports large inference advantages in an early comparison—about thirtyfold over a contemporary GPU and eightyfold over a CPU—and sees the public TPU announcement as prompting broader investment. Those are historical comparisons in his account, not ratios that can be applied to today’s products.

Are these increasingly specialized levels of computing?

Yes, because the broad performance growth once supplied by scaling is unavailable. CPUs still serve the general-purpose tasks they suit; large investment is now directed toward AI accelerators. Designers must ask how their architecture fits that workload rather than assume one processor will efficiently serve everything.

Source: 30:48–32:10 ↗
Source: 23:08–30:46 ↗

QIs it controversial to say Moore’s law is slowing?

He distinguishes the original transistor-doubling rate from the broader claim that technology improves. Missing the doubling cadence does not mean all progress stops. For about fifty years, that cadence also coordinated industry investment, making it more than a description of isolated chip releases.

Improvement is now uneven. He says logic continues improving while SRAM changes much less, and memory density no longer advances at its old rate. Chiplets and packages containing multiple large dies can increase the transistor count in a product without restoring the same rate within a single die.

He disagrees with the claim that the old law simply continues, while recognizing why the phrase can be emotionally important to people who built their careers around sustaining it. His argument is to inspect component-level data and distinguish packaging progress from the original density trend.

Source: 32:12–35:40 ↗
Editorial synthesis
Architecture choices answer different requirements
ArchitecturePrimary design pressure in Patterson’s explanation
CPUGeneral-purpose compatibility and support for diverse software.
GPUMany threads, memory throughput, and graphics-derived parallel computation.
TPUDedicated matrix computation and software-managed machine-learning data movement.
Source: 23:08–30:46 ↗

QIs there a new law guiding AI-processor progress?

There is no equally simple underlying guideline, he says. Designers combine improved packaging, shorter communication distances, narrower arithmetic formats, and larger or faster matrix-multiplication structures. They must estimate each technology’s progress and assemble a system around those estimates.

He describes the TPU training architecture as remarkably stable across roughly a decade: matrix units, high-bandwidth memory, and a complementary vector unit remain recognizable while growing in size and speed. This stability is his praise for the original design, not a claim that nothing changed.

Source: 35:41–38:25 ↗

QWhat benchmark compares AI accelerators such as GPUs and TPUs?

Patterson helped with MLPerf, inspired by the earlier SPEC effort: competing companies benefit from agreeing on workloads instead of debating whichever benchmark best favors each product.

The result measures hardware together with compilers and especially tailored libraries. Nvidia’s large software engineering investment lets it optimize libraries for specific applications and new architectures. He regards that ecosystem as a major component of the CUDA moat, beyond the language itself.

This also limits what a startup can show. A good new architecture with a much smaller software team may compare poorly because it lacks equally tuned libraries. Google built its own software stack, using compilers heavily, while its deployment model historically focused on internal use or cloud access. Patterson therefore sees MLPerf as useful but not a neutral measure of hardware in isolation.

Source: 38:25–41:56 ↗

QWhat are the most useful lessons from your talks about having a bad career?

He began the inverted format by teaching graduate students how to give a bad talk, then extended it to research careers, centers, labs, and AI’s carbon footprint. For positive lessons, he points to his reflections on the first half-century of his career.

Personally, he prioritizes family, distinguishes happiness from wealth, and protects time for fun. A senior colleague’s regret about insufficient family time stayed with him. He describes choosing happiness when it conflicted with greater wealth and maintaining activities such as cycling, soccer, lifting, and time with family.

Professionally, he urges deliberate time for important work that is not urgent. Messages and fully packed calendars can consume the space needed for thought. He also learned to focus on finishing rather than accumulating starts: the textbook and department leadership each became his main project during their respective periods. Concentrating on a few substantial contributions gives them a better chance of becoming work one is proud of.

Source: 41:56–46:57 ↗

QWhy do people so often regret too little family time rather than too much?

He treats this as a question about what success means to a particular person. Reading Studs Terkel’s Working led him to think that people who helped other people often felt better about their careers than those whose artifacts had disappeared. A retired dean similarly emphasized the people rather than the projects.

Patterson believes relationships, work one enjoys, helping others, and a sense of something larger—possibly religion or contact with nature—matter for happiness. These are his reflections and interpretations of what he has read, not a complete psychological model supplied by this interview. His practical emphasis is on people one helps and works with.

Source: 46:57–50:00 ↗

QWhy do you consider courage important in a career?

He traces some personal confidence to wrestling as a smaller young student. Professionally, he believes safety does not eliminate failure, while a meaningful chance can make success possible. Courage also includes challenging arguments he believes are wrong.

He feels an intellectual responsibility to object when weak reasoning drives decisions, even from a company leader. Debate can improve ideas if participants share the goal of finding the best answer. He tempers this with an older colleague’s warning that enemies can endure longer than friendships: stand up when it matters, while being careful about unnecessary personal conflict.

Do you mean confronting technical errors?

Yes, along with weak political or organizational arguments. He wants a marketplace of ideas in which criticism strengthens the result. He extends the principle to public life, where he has written about issues he believes require correction. The point is a shared purpose and stronger ideas, rather than confrontation for its own sake.

Source: 52:29–54:01 ↗
Source: 50:02–52:27 ↗

QHow has optimism helped you?

Engineering has many ways to fail, so he finds a positive outlook useful. He illustrates his temperament through a teenage story: he interpreted an ambiguous response from his future wife optimistically, and their relationship continued into a marriage approaching six decades. It is an affectionate personal anecdote, not evidence that every uncertain answer should be interpreted favorably.

What helped your relationship last?

He reduces his advice to three sentences both partners must be willing to say: “I was wrong. You were right. I love you.” He emphasizes mutuality and sincerity rather than replacing the acknowledgment with an insult. The nine-word formulation is his personal advice about accepting fault and expressing care.

Source: 55:07–55:59 ↗
Source: 54:01–55:04 ↗

QWhat would you tell yourself at the beginning, or change if you could?

Arriving at Berkeley from graduate school initially brought impostor feelings. Eventually, expecting that tenure might not happen helped him focus on enjoying the work and maintaining family life. He thinks that attitude largely served him well after a stressful first year.

His major regret concerns leading the architecture research community during a period when young women were being harassed at conferences. He had assumed such behavior was too obviously wrong to occur among colleagues and was unaware of it. He wishes he had known and acted. The practical significance is the danger of equating one’s own expectations about decent behavior with what others actually experience.

Source: 55:59–58:07 ↗

Section 32 · interview

Operate, investigate, and stay grounded in how systems work

Marc Brooker connects customer needs, incident learning, database design, writing, and hands-on adaptation to the work of an influential engineer.

QHow do you find the problems that matter most?

Marc Brooker

Brooker recommends looking broadly rather than optimizing only the volume of one’s own code. Customers reveal work they find difficult, investments they are making, and operational chores they wish did not distract from their businesses. Technical trends supply another input: faster networks, storage, compute, multicore systems, and GPUs can make previously impractical designs possible. Changes in the wider world create openings too.

He gives a concrete collision of those inputs. While working with Lambda customers in 2020, he heard enthusiasm for serverless and containers but dissatisfaction with how operationally server-oriented relational databases fit those workloads. Moving to Aurora let him help address that mismatch. He also describes using an object store as a database durability foundation while adding architecture to supply latency and interfaces suited to online workloads. Customer needs and changes in technical economics together explained why the product could matter.

Source: 01:02–05:31 ↗

QWhy remain on call for so many years?

Marc Brooker

He sees on-call work and deep incident analysis as the source of much of his practical distributed-systems knowledge. Strong programming, mathematics, and computer-science foundations do not automatically teach how customers actually use a running system, how unexpected use changes its behavior, or how to make it resilient.

This is not praise for repeatedly closing identical tickets. Automate rote work. The valuable part is investigating unusual behavior, understanding it, improving the system, and sharing the lesson. He describes a broad weekly AWS meeting where engineers and leaders examine correction-of-error reports together and apply their lessons across services.

Leadership attention to operational reality helps guide product and architecture decisions. Repeated failures may expose a need for a common tool, library, service, or feature rather than another local patch. Brooker estimates having read between three and four thousand internal and industry postmortems over his career; even small lessons accumulate.

Source: 05:26–11:36 ↗

QWhat makes a good postmortem?

Marc Brooker

Begin by understanding what actually happened, rather than fitting the event to an existing bias. If that is impossible, the difficulty itself identifies missing observability, logging, metrics, or simulation capability. Then examine causes at several levels: the code defect, why testing missed it, why the testing approach or assumptions were inadequate, and which team or organizational decisions shaped those conditions.

A useful report must neither stop at the nearest defect nor dissolve into the vague conclusion that failures happen. It needs concrete actions at the relevant levels. Looking across reports can reveal whole classes of problems worth addressing with a shared mechanism.

While designing Aurora DSQL, the team studied recurring relational-database incidents. One pattern was a distributed client opening a transaction and then disappearing because of garbage collection, connectivity loss, or another pause while continuing to hold locks. The design question became how to prevent that whole failure class for customers, rather than only repair each incident.

Source: 11:33–16:56 ↗
Editorial synthesis
Source: 11:33–16:56 ↗

QHow can a database avoid trouble from a client that stops mid-transaction?

Marc Brooker

In the DSQL design he describes, reads use multiversion concurrency control rather than pessimistic locking. Rows have historical versions, so readers can read an appropriate version without preventing writers from updating it. Writes are accumulated locally in the query processor and checked optimistically at commit time.

This prevents a stalled reader from locking out writers and prevents uncommitted writing from blocking readers. Brooker corrects his own wording about writers: one writer does not hold a blocking lock over another, but conflicting changes can cause another transaction to fail its eventual commit check. That limitation follows from the required isolation semantics rather than the abandoned-client lock problem.

How much storage overhead does keeping old versions introduce?
Marc Brooker

He says it depends strongly on workload but is often smaller than expected. Updates tend to concentrate on a small portion of rows; an active row may acquire many versions while most data stays unchanged. In his experience it is unusual for an online workload’s version-retention storage overhead to exceed roughly ten percent. He does not present that figure as an unconditional sizing rule.

Source: 17:55–19:11 ↗
Source: 16:16–18:15 ↗

QWhy should a team with weak postmortem habits invest in them?

Marc Brooker

The choice is where to spend engineering time: improving the product or fighting the same fire repeatedly. A weak culture may lack a sufficiently clear focus on outcomes and customer experience. Standards need not be identical everywhere; durability-critical systems deserve especially high standards, while another product may deliberately accept more defects to optimize other goals. The important distinction is an intentional tradeoff.

Another failure mode is normalizing operational heroics. A team that stays up all night, tolerates constant pages, and fixes every emergency may feel admirable from inside, yet spend its strongest ownership and expertise on an expensive repeating break-fix cycle. The corrective move is to redirect that energy into understanding and removing causes. Preventing recurrence creates time for deeper product improvements.

Source: 18:56–23:45 ↗

QWhy is adding a cache sometimes a poor distributed-system design choice?

Marc Brooker

Caching exploits locality and can improve speed and scale. Its danger is the difference between modes: a warm cache containing the right data is fast, but an empty or unsuitable cache sends demand to a backend that may be unable to handle it. Overload can then prevent refilling the cache, leaving the system stably unhealthy instead of naturally recovering. Brooker calls that a metastable failure.

He gives two ways to reduce the mode change. DSQL’s storage tier holds a complete copy of the data, avoiding an empty-working-set recovery problem. Aurora continually tells potential failover targets what to cache so the new leader begins warm. Other options include a complete local materialized view for slow-changing data or a backend that provides the required scale directly.

He prefers avoiding caches where feasible but explicitly refuses to make that universal. The lesson is to understand recovery behavior and dependencies rather than apply “add a cache” as an automatic improvement.

How often do metastable failures occur in practice?
Marc Brooker

An individual service can run for years without one. Brooker nevertheless believes this mechanism underlies many of the industry’s most severe outages. When it occurs, recovery can be long and complicated and may require painfully stopping and restarting parts of the system. His claim is about the disproportionate importance of rare failure modes, not their being an everyday event.

Source: 27:51–29:46 ↗
Source: 23:47–28:04 ↗
