Source: 24:36–28:04 ↗

QHow do you expect AI to change software engineering?

Marc Brooker

Brooker begins with uncertainty: these are predictions. He believes software remains supply-constrained and that there is enormous room for more useful, personalized, better-fitting software. Falling development costs therefore excite him rather than implying all useful software has already been built.

He expects the economics of products, organizations, and careers to change, with success depending partly on adapting to and leading that change. He offers no settled timetable; the opportunity and the need to adapt are his central forecast.

Source: 29:24–32:50 ↗

QCan someone still succeed using older techniques instead of joining the new mainstream?

Marc Brooker

He describes three overlapping possibilities. Software craft can remain enjoyable as a hobby even when a method is no longer economically competitive, much as hand-tool joinery or retrocomputing can be worthwhile for pleasure. Older technologies can also support real careers in specialized niches because changing the real world is slow, shaped by policy, people, and organizational constraints.

His analogy is analog electronics: digital became dominant without eliminating valuable specialized work in areas such as radio and power. Nevertheless, he expects the main economic opportunity in software to move toward AI-assisted, agentic, specification-driven, and still-emerging practices that build at different cost and speed. He particularly sees interesting adoption problems where software meets the physical world. He would personally favor that new mainstream while recognizing the other paths.

Source: 31:55–37:39 ↗

QWhat should junior engineers emphasize when generating code becomes easier?

Marc Brooker

Find problems that matter and understand their context earlier: customers, the business, economics, and the surrounding system. Brooker expects activities once insulated from junior engineers to enter their careers sooner. A role centered exclusively on typing in an IDE for a full day may become harder to sustain.

He also sees opportunity for deep specialists. Scientific, technical, optimization, infrastructure, or database expertise helps a person ask the right questions. Less boilerplate can let that knowledge become useful software or a product with less friction. Understanding customers and developing depth are both valuable routes, not opposing stereotypes.

Source: 36:43–40:33 ↗

QWhat would you say to a new engineer frightened by those higher expectations?

Marc Brooker

He does not expect a new graduate to know everything immediately. Employers and early-career engineers both benefit from people succeeding, so organizations must build a supported learning path. First customer conversations can be scary; mentorship, feedback, guardrails, and progressively larger experiences make them learnable.

He compares this with other professions where much practical learning occurs on the job. What changes is the emphasis of the learning, not the fact that graduates need it. Leaders must rethink the career ladder rather than simply hire beginners and demand expert performance. He acknowledges uncertainty while remaining optimistic about the scale of opportunity.

Source: 40:35–44:21 ↗

QHow should senior engineers adapt?

Marc Brooker

Retain the value of accumulated judgment by returning to hands-on building. A person who influences design without practicing current development methods can become disconnected from what builders actually encounter. Brooker recommends curiosity, direct experience, and humility about how quickly the practice changes.

He argues that newer tools can make limited practitioner time more productive by reducing boilerplate, and that building reconnects engineers with the reasons they entered the field: learning technology and solving customers’ problems. In his conversations, active users offer concrete assessments of tools’ strengths, failures, and missing integrations; nonusers often have poor mental models. That is his observation rather than a categorical verdict on every skeptic.

He also sees the broader lesson in earlier AWS products. Engineers he admired could connect cloud strategy and economics with minute technical details. Grounded leadership helped them make enduring products. The gap between detached advice and implementation is not new, but he thinks fast-changing tools make it larger.

Source: 43:59–50:11 ↗

QWhy write so much as an engineer?

Marc Brooker

Writing lets expertise travel across both people and time. A product, individual mentorship, and talks all spread knowledge, but an old written explanation can still help a reader a decade later. He values writing as a multiplier rather than merely as a visibility activity.

It also sharpens the writer’s thought. Putting an idea into prose forces a depth and clarity that speech or slides may not. Brooker sometimes writes with no intention of publishing. He appreciates Leslie Lamport’s stronger case for formal mathematics while seeing prose as an accessible starting point. Sharing ideas, preserving them, and understanding them better are separate but compatible motives.

Source: 50:12–53:51 ↗

QWhat do you say to engineers who see documentation as busy work?

Marc Brooker

Ask what the writing is for and whether it operates at the right level of the problem. Brooker does not find every design notation useful; he criticizes UML as focusing on a semantic level that did not help his own work. A document can be valuable because it preserves a decision for future readers or helps reason through a difficult, hard-to-reverse design or API choice. Routine, reversible choices do not all warrant the same process.

For important designs, recording the rationale also distinguishes careful decisions from temporary guesses made without data. Future engineers can reconsider arbitrary choices with new evidence while taking more care to understand the reasoning behind deliberate ones. The amount of prior thought matters alongside the result. Writing for that purpose is a skill worth developing even if the activity is not naturally enjoyable.

Source: 53:52–57:54 ↗

QHow do you balance doing the work with discussing it?

Marc Brooker

He sees both extremes as failure modes. A deeply capable person who never communicates could have more impact by sharing and could miss important problems by staying inside an IDE. Someone who only talks could make their advice more relevant by returning to practice.

Brooker personally spends roughly seventy-five to eighty percent of his effort practicing and the remainder teaching or communicating. Strong colleagues vary from approximately ninety-ten to fifty-fifty; he offers these as observations rather than an optimal allocation formula. Dedicated communicators can have a different job, provided they remain curious and honest about what they do and do not know. During fast change, he would lean somewhat more toward practice without severing contact with the outside world.

Source: 57:57–1:02:34 ↗

QIs it better to be overrated or underrated?

Marc Brooker

For the long term, he would choose underrated. Being overrated may feel good but is difficult to sustain. Sports and crafts expose the gap between appearance and capability quickly; engineering can leave room for qualitative perceptions longer. The careers he admires are built on honesty about actual knowledge and skill, not on maintaining an inflated image. This complements his recommendation to communicate useful expertise rather than hide it.

Source: 1:02:36–1:04:30 ↗

QWhich AWS engineers do you admire, and why?

Marc Brooker

He highlights retired colleague Al Vermeulen, whose work included major contributions to S3 and database design. Brooker remembers debating fine points of Paxos with him around 2010 while also seeing him discuss executive-level cloud strategy and explain what the business should build. He admired the ability to move across those levels without losing depth.

More generally, he respects colleagues motivated by useful work and customer impact rather than celebrity. Breadth, detail, and purpose together form the example he wants to follow.

Source: 1:04:33–1:07:20 ↗

QWhat technical reading do you recommend?

Marc Brooker

He recommends Martin Kleppmann’s distributed-systems book and Hennessy and Patterson’s computer-architecture book. The captions contain an initial imprecise reference to the latter followed by his correction; the intended authors and subject are retained without reconstructing a full title. His comment about a forthcoming edition belongs to the interview’s time context.

For his own technical learning he reads many papers. He sometimes uses an AI summary to get oriented before reading the authors’ actual words; the summary is a bridge into the source. Old work also contains valuable insights. He describes Lambda traffic-management ideas drawing on Erlang’s much older work on telephone systems. Rapid industry change does not make foundational research obsolete.

Source: 1:07:20–1:09:37 ↗

QWhat advice would you give yourself when first joining AWS?

Marc Brooker

Be a little bolder about moving when learning and impact begin to taper. He loved his early teams in EC2 and EBS and was more hesitant to leave than he now thinks ideal. He made about four substantial organizational changes and suspects a few more might have been better, rather than recommending constant movement.

He would repeatedly ask what he is learning, whom he is learning from, and whether another environment would help him learn more quickly. Following curiosity has been both useful and enjoyable in his own career.

Source: 1:08:41–1:10:32 ↗

Engineering in the AI era

The guests disagree about speed, autonomy, and the future of programming. Their distinct arguments remain separate, with the assumptions and conditions that make each useful to examine.

Section 33 · interview

AI adoption should move with demonstrated capability

Casey Muratori frames his concern about generated software as a race between tool reliability and uncritical deployment.

QWas your warning that “vibecoding” could make software worse an accurate prediction?

Casey Muratori

Muratori immediately qualifies the warning: the bad outcome depends on a pattern that may not become dominant. His concern is people describing a desired product, generating it, and sending it into production without competent review. He distinguishes that from a trained engineer using AI while understanding and checking its output.

The resulting risk depends on two moving forces. One is how quickly AI becomes capable of making better decisions autonomously; the other is how widely it is adopted, by whom, and with how much scrutiny. If capabilities stay adequate for the uses people adopt, he would not expect a major deterioration. If adoption outruns the tools and the users’ ability to judge them, he expects trouble.

He explicitly says he does not know where the situation will be a year later. Although he is personally skeptical of AI, he hopes the tools improve because many people are already using them. In his account, freezing their capability at the current level would leave existing adoption in a worse position. These are conditional judgments in the interview, not a forecast supplied by this book.

Source: 00:00–04:09 ↗

QIs your criticism of corporate AI mandates that they push adoption ahead of capability?

Casey Muratori

Muratori says the joke about Shopify was partly a pun, but his substantive concern is organizational fear of being late. He thinks some companies act as if immediate adoption is compulsory before they have established whether the tools solve their actual problems or improve outcomes.

His proposed alternative is familiar technology evaluation: measure what a tool can do, test it against the organization’s problems, compare the workflow with the previous approach, and adopt when it demonstrates a net benefit. Dedicated teams can run aggressive experiments; that does not mean every team should be required to consume large amounts of AI capacity.

He ends by resisting a comforting story about the past. Software quality was already poor before the AI era, he says. AI can make particular things worse without being responsible for the industry’s preexisting failures. The criticism is therefore about how to improve the quality of the work, not about preserving an idealized earlier industry.

Source: 04:10–07:05 ↗
The two questions in Muratori’s argument
CapabilityAdoption
Can the tool reliably perform this work?Is it being used for tasks beyond that capability?
Can it make appropriate decisions without intervention?Who reviews the output, and how much do they understand?

Section 34 · interview

The percentage of code generated is less useful than the work humans still own

Anders Hejlsberg distinguishes growing code volume from the responsibility to understand a real system.

QWill AI soon write more than 90 percent of code?

Anders Hejlsberg

Hejlsberg asks what the percentage measures. Some generated applications already consist entirely of AI-written code, and generation itself greatly increases the total volume. A large share of that expanding denominator is different from a large share of high-quality, novel software. He is skeptical of treating those claims as equivalent.

He expects AI to do impressive things, but does not assume that increasing success on familiar patterns establishes that it can perform every kind of engineering work.

What is an example of code that does not fit the optimistic claim?
Anders Hejlsberg

He says his team tried using AI for their TypeScript compiler work and found it unable to reproduce that particular implementation. His explanation is that the unusual concepts and structure are not a typical match for learned patterns. He treats this as a limitation of the tools he tested, while acknowledging that they are improving. It is not a timeless claim about every future model or compiler.

Source: 00:58–02:30 ↗
Source: 00:00–00:56 ↗

QCould engineers stop reading the code or using an IDE?

Anders Hejlsberg

Hejlsberg worries about the point where prompting no longer fixes a bug or implements the next feature. Someone must then understand the system underneath. He also emphasizes responsibility for the application’s effects: the person or organization deploying it cannot treat AI as a substitute for understanding what they are vouching for. His hypothetical harm example illustrates that responsibility; it is not a legal determination made by this book.

Why does your view differ from the more sweeping claims made by some AI developers?
Anders Hejlsberg

He distinguishes admiration for AI from extrapolating its contribution to complete human irrelevance. Even if generation handles a larger percentage of code, people still need to connect the system to the business problem and the organization around it. That larger context is what a simple generation percentage leaves out.

Source: 03:36–04:25 ↗
Source: 02:32–03:34 ↗

QWill AI replace junior engineering work?

Anders Hejlsberg

He questions how senior engineers would be developed if junior participation disappeared entirely. He thinks the entry-level pyramid may narrow for some work and people may be expected to move toward supervision more quickly. The craft can shift from typing code toward reviewing agents’ work, but he still sees programmers as part of the process. These are his expectations in the interview rather than a current employment forecast.

Source: 04:27–06:05 ↗

QWould a future with less manual coding make the work less enjoyable for you?

Anders Hejlsberg

Hejlsberg still enjoys writing code after decades of doing it, but is happy to delegate parts he finds tedious, including testing-framework boilerplate. Reviewing other people’s code has often felt harder to him than writing his own. He hopes tools can make review more understandable and ergonomic by explaining changes rather than merely displaying file lists and diffs. The transition can change the craft without making every part equally attractive to every programmer.

Source: 06:05–07:11 ↗

Section 35 · interview

Use types and capabilities to make delegated work inspectable

Martin Odersky argues that generated implementation needs concise contracts and explicit limits on authority.

QHow might AI-generated code change programming-language design?

Martin Odersky

Odersky sees a control problem: a human asked to review a mountain of generated implementation can lose a practical understanding of what the system will do. He also worries about tools that can discover or exploit vulnerabilities. Programming languages are only part of the response, but he believes they can make the critical guarantees easier to inspect.

He expects attention to shift toward interfaces, types, requirements, and higher-level specifications. A precise type or interface can become a contract between a human and the code-generating system—something concise enough to review and strong enough to constrain the implementation. In his view, this requires closing escape hatches that undermine the claimed guarantees, rather than merely adding advisory annotations.

He also proposes capabilities: explicit, fine-grained authority over resources and effects. An agent should be given the particular read, write, or secret-access permissions it needs, so there are meaningful things it cannot do. He treats memory safety as a necessary starting point, while emphasizing that control over files, data, and secrets involves more than memory alone.

Odersky says Scala work in this direction was available experimentally in the context of the interview. He does not present it as a completed universal solution. He also hopes AI could help migrate existing software when the target design is clear. That is a proposed path toward safer systems, not evidence that a wholesale migration has already happened.

What would a capability guarantee look like in practice?
Martin Odersky

He gives a file-lifetime example. A program receives access to a file for a limited scope and should not keep using it after returning control to the environment. Without a constraint, it might save the file in a variable or hide access inside a returned closure or stream.

In the type-system approach he describes, a value that retains access to the file must expose that capability in its type. The environment can then require a returned type that holds no such capability. This makes retained access visible and gives the system a way to reject an escape. He relates the idea to ensuring that pointers do not outlive an arena and to controlling which secrets a component can access: the recurring question is what authority can remain beyond an allowed scope.

Source: 05:12–07:51 ↗
Source: 00:00–05:10 ↗

Section 36 · interview

Fast tools, cheap drafts, and expensive review

Charlie Marsh describes building Ruff, uv, and ty, then examines how agent use changes optimization, open-source participation, review, and the experience of founding Astral.

QWhy did you think Python developer tools could be better?

At a computational-biology company, Marsh was a software engineer serving scientists and machine-learning researchers. A small team needed leverage from type checking, linting, and package management as its code grew. Working across Python, Go, Rust, and web tools exposed a contrast: native JavaScript tooling was experimenting aggressively with performance, while much Python tooling remained implemented in Python. Ruff began as a concrete test of the hypothesis that Python tools could become much faster.

Did the proof of concept take only the nine days between two blog posts?

He had not noticed the dates were so close. After writing about type checking at scale, he chose a linter as the smaller experiment. A small core plus a useful subset of rules can deliver value immediately and grow iteratively alongside existing tools. A partly complete type checker or package manager is harder to make useful, although he explicitly qualifies that generalization. He wanted users to receive value quickly and establish a feedback loop.

Source: 04:07–06:03 ↗
Source: 00:45–04:01 ↗

QHow was the first public release received?

Hacker News and social attention brought initial users, but he sees that exposure as partly luck and neither necessary nor sufficient for success. He responded aggressively to issues, aiming to acknowledge, fix, and release within a day. When an influential potential user expressed interest, he asked what was needed for adoption and worked through those requirements.

He also takes developer marketing seriously. Excellent technical work can remain undiscovered if its purpose is unclear. A landing page, README, or article may have only seconds to convey why someone should care. He wants a skimmer to understand the main result without requiring the whole article, while still making every sentence accurate for the readers who do study it.

What was the concrete hook for Ruff?

A benchmark graph made the performance difference visible, paired with a simple compatibility-and-speed promise. He notes that benchmarks are imperfect; the hook should communicate a real advantage quickly rather than substitute attention for truth.

Source: 10:50–11:57 ↗
How do you balance a provocative headline with honesty?

He opposes misleading clickbait. The aim is communicating the most interesting true parts effectively. Lying can attract attention but destroys the basis for a useful relationship with users.

Source: 11:58–12:42 ↗
What about charts with a truncated axis?

He rejects deceptive chart presentation and then emphasizes the real benchmark difficulty: caches, project selection, and unrelated native builds can change the observed result. No single graph captures every situation. That does not remove the obligation to give users an honest sense of performance; he admits his own team may sometimes get the balance wrong.

Source: 12:44–14:34 ↗
Source: 06:04–10:51 ↗

QWhy choose Rust?

Initially, he candidly says, enthusiasm around Rust influenced him more than a sophisticated tradeoff analysis. In retrospect the choice suited the tools very well. Cargo’s common build, run, and test workflow reduced the barrier to entering unfamiliar projects. As a new systems programmer he could focus on meaningful language and implementation challenges rather than assembling a toolchain. He now also values safety and efficient execution, and expects Rust to grow, while recognizing useful ideas in Zig and successful work in Go.

Would you start a new project in C or C++?

Personally he usually would not unless an existing system, a specific technical need, or deep team familiarity justified it. He expects others to disagree and frames this as his preference. Rust’s memory safety has become more valuable to him than he understood at the beginning. The answer is not a claim that every project can ignore ecosystem constraints.

Source: 18:40–20:10 ↗
Source: 14:35–18:39 ↗

QWould AI make it worthwhile to rewrite your tools in another language?

He sees the rate of change in agent workflows as extraordinary: his own work shifted from editor-based changes toward prompting through Codex in a short period. He is interested in other teams testing large automated rewrites but would not currently plan one for Astral’s major tools.

Understanding the transformed code is one concern. Another is exchanging known problems for unknown ones. Even a good test suite approximates behavior, and users may rely on implementation details that were never formalized as an API. Passing tests can therefore push undiscovered incompatibilities onto users. For him, safe rollout and the responsibility to those users are more troubling than the models’ ability to produce a plausible translation.

His acceptable level of review varies by project. He describes an internal custom linter generated without reading all its code, where users are only his team and incorrect output is easy to notice. A widely used package manager deserves a different standard. He sees experimentation as valuable while remaining uncertain how much code understanding future agent-based work will require.

Is that simply the usual balance between change risk and verification?

The spectrum is familiar, but agents create an additional extreme where no human needed to read the code even to produce it. He observes repositories where both contributions and conversations appear agent-written and is glad people are testing new models of work, while not feeling ready to copy every approach.

Source: 26:45–28:40 ↗
Source: 20:12–26:44 ↗

QDo you block fully agent-generated contributions?

The projects have an AI policy intended to keep useful human contributions while filtering interactions that create more work than value. The team itself uses LLMs heavily. What matters is that a submitter understands what is being contributed and supplies insight, an actual reproducer, or information the maintainers can use. Pasting a generated answer to each maintainer question provides little value when maintainers can query a model themselves.

How can you enforce understanding?

He admits detection is imperfect. Excessive detail, gratuitous formatting, unnecessary links, or invented jargon can be clues, but undetectable useful material would not be excluded solely because a model helped. More deeply, open source historically invested in people whose learning compounded through feedback. If comments merely pass from maintainer to contributor’s agent, that human development may not occur. Cheap plausible PRs can impose long review sessions on technically difficult projects such as ty. He does not yet have a complete solution.

Source: 30:13–33:34 ↗
Source: 28:40–30:10 ↗

QWas the large rewrite discussed earlier reviewed by humans?

He does not think humans read significant portions, but explicitly bases that on his impression. He expects a forthcoming explanation of a phased process with validation steps, rather than assume it was one prompt. Those unverified impressions are recorded as such; the section does not declare the other project’s actual review practices.

Would you block a teammate’s rewrite even if the target language were agreed to be better?

At present, yes. His team still values deeply understanding its code, toolchain, and ecosystem. He acknowledges that his judgment could change and that the project’s consequences matter.

Source: 34:56–35:39 ↗
Source: 33:36–34:56 ↗

QHow much of the speed improvement came from Rust?

For early Ruff, changing implementation language was a large part. But multiple Rust designs can have very different performance, and subsequent improvements still matter. In uv, architecture contributes more because package management is dominated by network and filesystem work. An intentionally designed cache makes repeated installation cheap in time and storage. Native implementation supplies a useful baseline; algorithms, representations, I/O, and cache design determine much of the result. Python programs also benefit from better design.

Source: 35:39–39:11 ↗

QWhich technical work has been especially interesting?

He highlights a version representation designed by a teammate known as BurntSushi. Resolving Python projects creates and parses many version values; representing most common cases in one 64-bit integer reduced allocation and memory costs. He admires the implementation and measured results.

For ty, the larger architectural challenge is lazy, incremental analysis. Opening a file should not require checking the whole project, and editing it should recompute only dependent results. The system is built around queries using Salsa, also used by rust-analyzer. This requires accurate dependency tracking rather than merely making an individual checker faster.

What is hard about incrementality?

Changes have to flow through exactly the affected parts of the dependency graph. Large-project language servers must also manage memory, not just latency. He has used Codex to search for small improvements under constrained goals, as well as broader fixes for pathological cases. He enjoys being able to keep running such optimization experiments without calling the process autonomously self-optimizing.

Source: 42:57–44:51 ↗
Source: 40:06–42:56 ↗

QCould an agent invent the compact version representation?

Possibly with collaboration, but he would not expect that from a generic request for a moderate improvement. In his experience, models first make local changes around existing representations. A human can steer from profiling to allocation cost to asking whether the representation itself should change.

He retells another engineer’s example where a model greatly improved a deliberately poor renderer but still fell far short of a better first-principles design. The numerical anecdote is not an independently demonstrated benchmark here. His lesson is to ask how fast the system ought to be, rather than accept a large percentage gain from a bad starting point.

Why encourage your team to use agents despite those limits?

They build tools for engineers increasingly working with agents, so firsthand understanding of that experience matters. He believes he ships more, but teammates now scrutinize his PRs more closely because confidence in his handwritten work does not automatically transfer to generated work. He agrees with that feedback and has sometimes reread yesterday’s PR with disappointment. Agent use can lower the standard without its author noticing.

Source: 47:36–49:48 ↗
Source: 44:55–47:33 ↗

QWhat helps prevent plausible but substandard generated changes?

He wants more of the meaningful verification to be automated, while acknowledging that green checks do not yet make review unnecessary. ty runs performance and memory measurements and before-and-after diagnostics across ecosystem projects. These tools were needed even before agents, and now help assess the larger flow of changes.

Authors are expected to run agent review, maintain instructions and shared skills based on recurring errors, understand each changed line, and reread their own PR in the review interface. One recurring question was what an if-condition still protects when every test passes without it; he added a pass to look for obsolete conditions left after refactoring. These are practices being refined, not a guarantee against all unnecessary branches.

His initial fear was becoming more productive while losing the pleasure of programming. He feels better as tools improve and he discovers cheap experiments. An agent could move uv’s many test snapshots out of source files while he worked elsewhere. It did not provide the hoped-for general compile-speed benefit, but made snapshot-only iteration avoid recompilation. The value was answering a costly question quickly; production adoption still required work. Design thinking and fixing users’ problems remain sources of satisfaction beyond typing code.

Source: 49:50–58:31 ↗

QHow important is engineering experience when using agents?

He remains concerned about using the tools without substantial experience. The strongest engineers on his team are also effective at directing agents and correcting them. Some highly productive people use many tokens, but he explicitly does not infer causation or reward token consumption: such leaderboards can create bad incentives. Early-career learning is a difficult open question because a beginner may learn from an unreliable agent rather than supply the expertise that keeps it on track. His team is small and senior, so he acknowledges limited firsthand evidence about junior training.

Source: 58:31–1:02:19 ↗

QWhy turn Ruff into a company, and how did fundraising begin?

He left his previous job after a friend suggested founding together, initially explored overlapping ideas, and found himself spending spare time on developer tools that did not fit the friend’s interests. He started investor relationships before intending to raise, expecting to return months later with a clearer plan. Ruff’s growth and those conversations convinced him a company could exist sooner.

Potential investors helped articulate a roadmap and offered a psychologically useful exit: if he hated founding, he could stop and return the money. He doubts he would have done so but found the reduced pressure helpful. Starting felt less stressful than success later, when a team depended on him. He describes the process as unusually collaborative and fortunate, not a standard fundraising formula.

Why did you not announce later funding rounds?

He kept finding reasons to wait and did not consider the announcement the most important work while products and the business progressed. The planned announcement was overtaken by the acquisition described in this interview. He says the seed, Series A, and Series B were initiated by investors rather than active campaigns.

Source: 1:07:09–1:08:51 ↗
Did willingness to walk away give negotiating leverage?

He agrees that he had a strong position while declining to portray himself as an expert negotiator. He emphasizes aligned, supportive investors and little pressure beyond suggestions to grow more aggressively. That positive experience was fortunate; he recognizes other founders can have different relationships.

Source: 1:08:53–1:09:56 ↗
Source: 1:02:19–1:07:08 ↗

QHow does a company make money while its tools are free?

Astral launched a commercial private Python registry, described as a hosted counterpart to uv. Private artifacts and enterprise requirements created needs adjacent to the free tools. Integrating client and server helped address issues and improve speed. Existing open-source adoption supplied a funnel to a small set of high-quality customers. The plan was free tools plus paid complementary platform services, rather than charging for the tools themselves. In the acquisition context he hopes to release some platform work more widely, including prebuilt compatible packages for difficult GPU/PyTorch environments. These are his business history and intended next steps, not a verified present availability claim.

Source: 1:09:58–1:13:46 ↗

QWhat surprised you as an engineer becoming a first-time founder?

He distrusts universal startup advice because successful founders can give contradictory instructions and survivorship bias hides alternatives. Choose principles suited to the team and the life you want. Remote work let him hire a team he could not have assembled in one location, despite real benefits of meeting in person. Fundraising optimized for trustworthy partners, reasonable terms, and getting back to work. He did not force a cofounder relationship merely because it was recommended, though he later felt the absence of a peer sharing the burden.

How did you compensate for founding alone?

He leaned on his wife, consulted the early team, and built relationships with other founders. Each source of support has limits, including how much to place on family or employees. He also chose to work extensively himself without requiring everyone to do so: he wanted people to succeed during normal hours and be rewarded for useful performance. His advice is to make the actual culture honest and deliberate, rather than imitate a fashionable schedule.

Source: 1:14:50–1:17:54 ↗
Source: 1:13:48–1:14:50 ↗

QWhat book or learning resource influenced you?

He does not read much technical material and instead names a talk by Zig creator Andrew Kelley on data-oriented design. It changed how he looked at memory, allocation, and compiler design early in his systems-programming experience. He qualifies that his recollection is imperfect; the section preserves the influence without inventing the talk’s exact title or reproducing an unseen argument.

Source: 1:17:55–1:18:55 ↗

QWhat advice would you give yourself after graduation?

Trust decisions made for sound personal reasons, while remaining aware that hindsight can make a lucky path look inevitable. He worried that choosing Khan Academy cost him big-company experience and compensation; he now values the experience he actually wanted. He would not pretend to know how the alternative would have gone.

Could the broader ecosystem exposure have been essential?

He agrees and adds his earlier startup experience. That company did not achieve all its ambitious drug-discovery goals, which briefly made him question the years invested. Being an early employee taught him both how a company develops and technical lessons later used at Astral. In retrospect the experiences connected to building tools he loves. He recognizes that this reassuring account comes from a path that worked well, rather than proving every disappointment will produce the same payoff.

Section 37 · interview

Judea Pearl: Early AI, Causal Reasoning, and the Limits of LLMs

Judea Pearl traces the path from superconducting memory and early AI to causal reasoning, and argues that LLMs cannot reach causal understanding on their own.

Pearl's view: causal reasoning needs assumptions that probability cannot supply

In Pearl's view, causal reasoning needs explicit assumptions and a new algebra that probability alone cannot supply. Pearl traces the route from early computer-memory research and superconducting films to Bayesian networks, and then to a formal calculus of cause and effect. Pearl argues that LLMs draw on human-written summaries of causal knowledge rather than on raw data, so they cannot reach causal understanding on their own. Pearl says general intelligence would need causal AI that can intervene and reason counterfactually, and describes academia as dogmatic and slow to change.

Source: 00:18–1:26:24 ↗

QElectrical engineering and physics seem far from causal reasoning and AI. How did you get there?

Judea Pearl

Pearl grew up in the years before 1948, when high school teachers included academics who had fled Germany in the 1930s. Pearl says they taught science as a human story: who discovered what, when, and what the inventor did not know.

Pearl says students came away believing each of them could find a new proof of the Pythagorean theorem. Pearl calls that a useful illusion. It made the class assertive, and students made noise until a teacher slowed down to explain.

What is the advantage of learning science that way?
Judea Pearl

Pearl says it makes the student an actor in science rather than a passive observer. The student is puzzled too, and can follow the route the original discoverer took.

As a child, Pearl insisted that a square kilometer holds 1,000 dunams, while the class said a dunam was a square kilometer. The teacher later apologized to the class. Pearl took from it that insisting on one's own understanding is worth it, and links that stubbornness to the path into AI.

Source: 03:55–08:19 ↗
Source: 00:18–03:52 ↗

QWhat interested you in physics, and what made you passionate about it?

Judea Pearl

Pearl says physics lets a person predict results while sitting in a chair. Pearl admires Maxwell, who reasoned from a wave equation that the wave's speed matched light, and suggested light is an electromagnetic wave, without an experiment.

Pearl recalls waking one night convinced Maxwell was wrong, and being calmed by Pearl's wife. The next morning Pearl agreed Maxwell was right.

Do you have a favorite scientist of all time, and why?
Judea Pearl

Pearl says analytic geometry produced an almost physical excitement. Every geometric construction could be carried out in algebra, and Pearl found that transformation enormous.

Pearl found the same thrill in physics, where two languages describe one phenomenon from different perspectives, as with a field and a force.

Source: 11:17–13:23 ↗
Source: 10:07–11:15 ↗

QWhat was your early work on computer memory like?

Judea Pearl

Pearl worked mornings at RCA's laboratory in Princeton, New Jersey, while studying at Brooklyn Poly. Core memories were slow and clumsy, so Pearl's group aimed for superconducting memories and built 16-by-16-bit plates.

While studying persistent currents in thin superconducting films, Pearl found a new effect, now called the Pearl vortex. A current in such a film circulates indefinitely and can be read by flipping it, which makes a memory. The group never made it competitive with semiconductors.

Why did you not believe in the semiconductor direction at the time?
Judea Pearl

Pearl says the team doubted that a memory could be trusted to a battery, and was not impressed by early semiconductor results. The semiconductor groups beat the team.

Pearl adds that even then, researchers widely believed computers would one day emulate all human functions. For Pearl, the question was how and when, not whether.

Source: 18:05–19:38 ↗
Source: 13:26–18:04 ↗

QWhat did researchers expect about the timeline for human-level machine intelligence back then?

Judea Pearl

Pearl recalls early work on associative memory and pattern recognition, which excited researchers even on room-sized machines that ran on punch cards. Pearl says people were more optimistic than reality.

Pearl recalls a forecast in 1965 of about twenty years, which would have meant around 1985. Pearl says the field had not got anywhere close by then.

Are people more optimistic than reality today, or is this history repeating?
Judea Pearl

Pearl says it depends on who is asked. Some people are extremely optimistic. Pearl is not doubtful that AGI can be reached eventually, but doubts that LLM methods alone will get there.

Pearl calls LLMs a great surprise that also has clear limitations.

Source: 20:48–22:15 ↗
Source: 19:43–20:45 ↗

QWhat made the industry job frustrating, and why did you move to academia?

Judea Pearl

Pearl says the three years at Electronic Memories were frustrating. Pearl had to handle administrative problems, such as hiring and firing, and technical problems in chemistry, which Pearl did not know well.

Pearl's wife suggested academia. Academia then looked with reverence on people from industry, since major advances came from companies such as Bell Labs. Academia hired Pearl without an application or recommendations, which Pearl says was a good time to be hired.

Did Bell Labs disband its research group, and where did the frontier of research move?
Judea Pearl

Pearl says disbanding was part of it. The frontier of research moved to academia, where inference, logic and expert systems were developed. Pearl was hired at UCLA around 1969 or 1970, first through an engineering systems department and then into computer science.

Source: 25:06–26:46 ↗
Source: 22:19–24:14 ↗

QHow did your work move from computer memory toward AI at UCLA?

Judea Pearl

At UCLA, Pearl taught computer memory, then moved into pattern recognition and image compression using transforms that send fewer bits. That revived Pearl's old goal of understanding how the brain works and how computers might emulate it.

Pearl began teaching AI, which then meant game playing such as chess, checkers and puzzles like the eight puzzle. Pearl was drawn to chess because it captures what people do heuristically, and the interplay between formal analysis and gut feel about a position. Pearl links this to the fast and slow thinking framing, in which each mode feeds the other.

Source: 26:48–29:42 ↗

QHow do fast intuition and slow search interact in a chess program?

Judea Pearl

Pearl says a program can spend more time on the immediate static evaluation of a position, or search deeper. That is a trade-off. The program searches the game tree to a horizon, evaluates positions there, and backs the values up to choose the strongest move.

Pearl agrees that the intuition sits in the evaluation function.

Can the evaluation function itself improve through learning?
Judea Pearl

Pearl says yes. Samuel's checkers program used regression to set weights for features such as control of the center and material balance. Pearl calls this the first machine learning.

Source: 30:39–31:56 ↗
Were chess programs already superhuman at that time, and what did you prove about search?
Judea Pearl

Pearl says no, since beating a champion such as Kasparov by machine was still a dream. Pearl proved that alpha-beta pruning is optimal, in the sense that no method can inspect fewer positions at the search horizon. Pearl then grew tired of search.

Source: 31:58–33:20 ↗
Source: 29:43–30:37 ↗

QWhy did expert systems run into trouble?

Judea Pearl

Early medical expert systems encoded rules from doctors, such as the questions a doctor asks after seeing a fever. The hurdle was uncertainty, since real evidence is noisy.

Pearl later proved that these systems could not combine uncertainties well, because rules do not combine the way logical assertions do.

Source: 34:30–37:18 ↗

QWhy was probability considered impractical, and how did you make it workable?

Judea Pearl

Pearl says a probability model is a table with a number for every combination of events. Conditional probabilities need exponentially large tables and time, even for a small task such as judging malaria risk from travel and fever. Yet people reason fairly well, so Pearl asked what they rely on.

Pearl's answer is conditional independence: most facts are irrelevant to a given query, such as an uncle's eye color when diagnosing a disease. Bayesian networks encode those independencies in a graph, so relevance can be read from the graph instead of a full table.

Pearl calls the match between conditional independence and graph separation a philosophical revolution. Pearl developed a theory of graphoids with a Technion colleague in the 1970s to capture that shared logic.

Source: 37:21–43:10 ↗

QWhere does the graph come from, and is judgment an acceptable source?

Judea Pearl

Pearl says the input can come from data or from judgment. Judgment is acceptable when it is meaningful, condensed, and something a person is willing to defend. A few such judgments can buy a great deal of computation.

Pearl's example is that the sun does not respond to a rooster's crowing. Pearl says that claim is defensible without an experiment.

But what if your intuition is wrong?
Judea Pearl

Pearl agrees that this is part of the problem. A large language model's output is an average of countless internet judgments, over which it has no control. Pearl says there is wisdom in the crowd, and danger too, so trusted judges should count for more.

Pearl admits being wrong earlier. Pearl was sure probability captured human reasoning and protected against paradoxes, and came to see that this was mistaken. That led to causality.

Source: 45:23–46:51 ↗
Source: 44:01–45:13 ↗

QWhat showed you that probability alone was not enough?

Judea Pearl

Pearl says experts who encoded judgments as Bayesian networks always drew arrows from cause to effect, never the reverse, even when asked for the link between a symptom and a disease. The relation from disease to fever is stable in a way the reverse is not. Pearl calls this invariance.

In car troubleshooting, moving one component, such as a charger, to another spot changes one part of the model while the rest stays intact. That works only in the causal direction, and it led Pearl to think probability was insufficient.

Source: 46:55–49:41 ↗

QCan causation be programmed into a computer?

Judea Pearl

Pearl says humans handle causation well, but cannot separate their assumptions from their conclusions, since everyone shares the same assumptions. A robot needs them separated. Pearl argues that science has been bound to algebra since Galileo's time, and that the equality sign is symmetric.

That symmetry lets people ask questions both ways, such as how a beam breaks under a load or how to shape a beam for a load. It limits causal reasoning. Atmospheric pressure affects a barometer, not the reverse, yet a symmetric equation could suggest that adjusting the barometer changes the weather. Pearl argues algebra needs a notation for direction.

Source: 49:44–53:27 ↗

QHow does the new algebra handle cause and effect, and what is the causal ladder?

Judea Pearl

Pearl says the assignment operation in computing is not reversible. Putting that logic on top of algebra gives a causal calculus. The ladder has three rungs: association, intervention, and counterfactual explanation. A question on one rung needs assumptions from that rung or a higher one.

Association is ordinary statistics, such as how observed smoking relates to lifespan. Intervention asks what happens when someone is forced to act, which needs experiments or assumptions. Explanation asks what would have happened had the input differed, given what was observed. Pearl adds that even the first rung is hard with finite samples.

Where would you place LLMs in this causal hierarchy?
Judea Pearl

Pearl says LLMs do not look at raw data, such as patient records. They work from text written by doctors and researchers and summarized online, which already holds higher-rung information, so they do not break the ladder. Their answers carry the assumptions of those authors, and how LLMs summarize that material is a mystery no one has decoded.

Source: 59:34–1:02:22 ↗
Source: 53:30–59:33 ↗

QCould this approach lead to superhuman intelligence or AGI?

Judea Pearl

Pearl does not think so, not with this approach. A system would need an understanding of causality, so that it could learn without access to the internet. Pearl points to babies, who are born curious about controlling their environment. A baby plays with toys until it learns which ones make noise, and the restlessness settles once it understands cause and effect.

What if we built a baby robot that plays with toys, gathers data and feeds it into LLMs?
Judea Pearl

Pearl says that could produce some discovery, but it carries danger. A robot with that craving for control would treat people as part of its environment, and could turn them into pets or tools to satisfy its need.

Pearl compares human curiosity with that of monkeys, which are motivated by rewards such as bananas. Pearl says the wider need to feel in control shows in beliefs that sacrifices or better dinners can control outcomes.

Source: 1:04:11–1:08:48 ↗
Source: 1:02:24–1:04:08 ↗

QDo systems need human-like drives, such as a need for control, to reach AGI?

Judea Pearl

Pearl thinks so. Without such drives, autonomy would not appear, and autonomy is part of general intelligence. A text-only system might pass a Turing-style test, but Pearl says a real test should expose the system to raw data, not to internet articles.

Pearl describes an automated scientist that examines patient and smoking data and proposes experiments. Pearl thinks today's LLMs cannot do that without internet articles. AGI would combine LLM-style estimation from finite samples with causal AI that adds intervention and counterfactual reasoning.

What if a fleet of robots ran experiments, fed the data back into an LLM and repeated the cycle?
Judea Pearl

Pearl says that could help, but Pearl first wants to know how humans achieved this. Monkeys never invented Maxwell's equations. Pearl's hypothesis is that innate curiosity to control the environment is necessary, though Pearl is not sure it is sufficient.

Source: 1:11:10–1:13:12 ↗
Source: 1:08:49–1:11:08 ↗

QDo the major AI companies really believe LLMs will lead to AGI?

Judea Pearl

Pearl is not sure they do. Pearl says Hinton recently said the current approach is a dead end, and that there is no consensus on LLM capabilities. Pearl says people at some labs, perhaps Anthropic, expect results within three to five years.

Pearl criticizes anthropomorphic claims, such as that consciousness can now be programmed. Pearl says such claims need a definition of consciousness, a test, and proof that earlier limits have been overcome.

Source: 1:13:16–1:15:06 ↗

QIf an LLM fakes intelligence convincingly, should we treat it as intelligent?

Judea Pearl

Pearl says it depends on the test and the definition. Playing good chess already meets one definition. Under a stricter standard, Pearl says the Turing test has not yet been passed.

Pearl says faking is having it, because correct answers to causal queries would need memory that grows super-exponentially with the number of variables. LLMs skip that cost by drawing on text that people have written.

So the intelligence came from training data that intelligent people wrote?
Judea Pearl

Pearl agrees that this training data is very useful. Pearl says the first rung, estimating properties of a distribution from finite samples, is a very useful tool among the many that AGI would need.

Source: 1:16:46–1:17:53 ↗
Source: 1:15:08–1:16:44 ↗

QWhy study how people think rather than how machines might think differently?

Judea Pearl

Pearl says self-understanding is the main motive, and Pearl admits to being egotistic and lazy. Pearl raises the possibility that organic material limits human thought in ways silicon does not, and sees little reason to study biology, since silicon can capture most functions.

Pearl calls it a legitimate scientific question that others can pursue, and says Pearl is more interested in other questions.

Source: 1:17:56–1:20:00 ↗

QWhy is rebelliousness valuable in a scientific career?

Judea Pearl

Pearl says the academic community is among the most dogmatic, conservative and anti-progress institutions humans have invented. Cause-and-effect theory has struggled to reach statistics and economics, which Pearl sees as thinking like a century ago, and Pearl is disappointed by the forces of inertia there.

Pearl advises students to rebel against professors and not accept a professor's word as authority. Pearl recalls students who said Pearl knew nothing about AI, and Pearl later agreed that this pushed Pearl to study other aspects of the field.

Pearl says Pearl's own early work was dismissed as controversial because of dogmatism. Even very able statisticians, economists and philosophers, Pearl says, were held back by a few basic molds in their thinking.

Source: 1:20:02–1:23:44 ↗

QIf you could give your younger self advice at the start of your career, what would you say?

Judea Pearl

Pearl says Pearl might have learned more chemistry, but hated its memory demands. Every researcher must decide where to spend computational resources, and Pearl chose physics, engineering and mathematics over chemistry. Pearl admires people who master several fields.

Did you think physics and math were superior to chemistry because chemistry just requires memorization?
Judea Pearl

Pearl says yes, and that Pearl could not stand the memory demands. Physics and mathematics rest on a few basic axioms from which everything can be derived when needed. That is why Pearl is a strong advocate of world models, which derive answers instead of storing every question and answer.

Source: 1:25:38–1:26:24 ↗
Source: 1:25:02–1:25:36 ↗

Section 38 · interview

Leonardo de Moura: Lean, Formal Proofs, and the Future of Verified Software

De Moura explains how Lean checks proofs, why AI may make verification practical, and why hybrid human and AI work is expected rather than an end to handwritten math.

De Moura's view: AI makes machine-checked proofs practical, and people still write the specifications

De Moura argues that Lean is both a programming language and a platform for machine-checked proofs. Tests can show that bugs are present but not that they are absent, while a proof can cover every case. AI now writes and maintains many proofs, so verification becomes practical and people focus on specifications. The view expects hybrid workflows, in which people still write some proofs and set the goals, rather than an end to human work.

Source: 00:00–1:07:03 ↗

QWhat is Lean, and how can it show that a program has no bugs when testing cannot?

Leonardo de Moura

De Moura describes Lean as a programming language and a platform. Users write code, state properties of that code, and prove them. The proofs are machine-checkable, and independent checkers can verify them. The host frames this with Dijkstra's remark that testing shows the presence of bugs, not their absence.

How does Lean connect to software written in other languages?
Leonardo de Moura

De Moura separates two cases. Lean programs can be reasoned about directly, much like mathematical definitions. For other languages there are two routes. Shallow embedding translates a program into Lean, and a tool that maps Rust into Lean already exists. Deep embedding writes the other language's semantics in Lean, so a C program becomes a Lean data structure that can be reasoned about.

QYou worked on the Z3 SMT solver. What is it, and how does it differ from a SAT solver?

De Moura describes Z3 as a solver with background theories such as arithmetic and arrays, built for test-case generation and software verification. Z3 is fully automatic and push-button, while Lean is interactive, with automation that the user can guide. Z3 is not a programming language. It works more like a constraint solver, and can prove only simple things.

Leonardo de Moura

A Sudoku can be encoded as constraints, which Z3 solves almost at once. For a suspected security bug, a code path can be turned into constraints. Z3 then reports that the path is unsatisfiable, so it cannot run, or gives an input that reaches it. Properties with many universal quantifiers become undecidable, and the hand-coded heuristics often failed. Lean was started to prove the absence of bugs, a gap that Z3 did not fill well.

Bounded hardware problems, such as searching for a bug in the first ten steps, usually work well, because programs and hardware are correct for simple reasons. Non-trivial properties often time out. A colleague at Amazon named this proof instability, since changing the order of terms can break a proof. In Lean, the user controls the steps, so the proof stays stable.

De Moura admits to bias. Users value Lean's extensibility, since Lean is implemented in Lean. Users can add automation in the same file, and AI can write these extensions. Asked to isolate a problem in Lean, AI often writes a Lean meta-program to test its conjecture about the cause.

QWhat is the difference between dependent type theory and higher-order logic?

Leonardo de Moura

De Moura first chose higher-order logic because it was easier to implement. Jeremy convinced de Moura that serious mathematicians would want dependent type theory, which is more powerful for abstract objects. In it, types depend on values. A structure field can be a proof that x is greater than y, so the structure cannot be built without that evidence. A function can require a proof that y is not zero. Such proofs were once annoying to write, but AI can now synthesize them.

In higher-order logic, could you express the same things?
Leonardo de Moura

De Moura says no. Higher-order logic loses the dependencies. In Lean, a function can take a group and return a new group, treating the structure as a first-class object, which the guest says is a mess in higher-order logic. Mathematicians the guest has talked with agree. Listening to what a community needs matters if it is to be served.

Section 39 · interview

Michael Bolin: Meta Build Tools, OpenAI Codex, and Working with Agents

Michael Bolin traces a career from Google and Meta developer tooling to leading the open-source Codex repository at OpenAI, and explains how he works with coding agents and why he still advises engineers to learn the lower layers.

Bolin's view: follow the problems you care about, and keep your depth as the tools improve

Michael Bolin, introduced by the host as tech lead of the open-source Codex repository at OpenAI and a former distinguished engineer at Meta, uses the interview to walk through his career and his current way of working. His view is that the best projects start from dissatisfaction with something concrete, that careers go best when personal enjoyment overlaps with what an employer values, and that influence depends on how a point is made as much as on being right. On Codex, he describes a workflow in which models write most of the code while humans still own the security-critical parts, and he argues that engineers should keep digging into lower layers of abstraction, because the quality of the questions asked of an agent shapes the quality of the result.

Source: 00:00–1:19:09 ↗

QThe host found a dead link on Bolin's old website for something called Chickenfoot. What was it?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says it was his master's thesis project, a Firefox extension that put a small coding tool and read-eval-print loop in a browser sidebar. The goal was end-user programming for the web, with functions such as enter and click. A user could pass a string, and the tool would find the matching text box and fill it in.

Much of the work went into the heuristics underneath: for an instruction like entering a first name, the tool looked for those words in the page and chose the nearest text box. Bolin sees a similarity to what agents do today, except that agents now work in true natural language rather than a small JavaScript console.

So it parsed the page, and you could name a field in the console?
Michael Bolin

Bolin confirms. The tool relied on accessibility tags and the alt text of images, and it worked well. He says it was especially good on Craigslist, one of the simplest sites to automate. Friends of his built automated tasks with it and made real money from them.

Source: 02:17–02:44 ↗
Source: 00:44–02:16 ↗

QWhat drew Bolin to Google and to Google Calendar, and what was the culture like?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says he got online in the 1990s, when finding anything meant trying five search engines. A roommate pointed him to a newer search engine in March 2000, which struck him as better. He contrasts Yahoo's cluttered pages with Google's sparse, principled design, and he noticed that good people were taking jobs there.

In Bolin's account, Google understood the web better than Microsoft did at the time, since Microsoft had dismantled the Internet Explorer project while Google was web-forward. With the engineering quality and impact, it was the place he most wanted to go coming out of school.

What was the culture like, in terms of product versus infrastructure?
Michael Bolin

Bolin says founders keep a soft spot for whatever the company was first good at, which at Google meant information retrieval and infrastructure. Products such as Gmail were what drew him in, but they did not carry the same standing inside the company as search.

Calendar, he says, was mostly consumer-facing and was also sold to enterprises, though his team was not the one making the money. He compares the team to a call center.

Source: 04:05–05:02 ↗
Source: 02:45–04:05 ↗

QWhy did Bolin leave Google after four years, given that the departure read as bittersweet?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says the financial picture changed once the four-year mark passed. The deeper problem, he says, was a bad habit of working hard on things that mattered to him but not to Google. He lists Calendar, which was important, Google Tasks, a small feature with two to three orders of magnitude fewer users, and the JavaScript infrastructure and Closure toolset. He wrote the book on Closure out of motivation.

He is proud of that work, but says it was not the best career move, since others were being recognized while he was working hard on the wrong things. He calls it the harder-not-smarter mistake, and decided to look for a place where what excited him matched what the company cared about.

Source: 05:04–06:45 ↗

QHow did Bolin get involved in build tooling for Facebook's Android codebase?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says Facebook was planning a phone with HTC, forking Android, and this time the project was going to ship. An earlier attempt to put an HTML5 Facebook on phones had clearly not worked. Mobile would make or break the company, and a friend told him that to be a product person he should pick up Java or Objective-C rather than stay on JavaScript. He chose Java.

Unlike most projects, this one had a hard deadline, because a build had to go to HTC to be burned into phones. Part of the Android code had been inherited from a contractor and should have been thrown away, and the Ant-based build was so hard to modularize that the team had to hack it to support even four or five modules.

Facebook had a hackathon culture, so Bolin used one to build a new build system in the style of Google's. He says there was already a Python-based system in a similar mold, whereas his was in C++. His thinking was that either it would work and he would be happy as a developer, or he was not sure he would last at the company.

If you had not fixed this, would you have quit the company?
Michael Bolin

Bolin says he would at least have switched projects. He wanted a way to be happy coming in to write code every day. He credits colleagues for the fact that almost everyone told him this was a very bad idea, yet nobody said no. At Google, he felt, people said no more often. One senior Android engineer was the exception and backed him.

Bolin says he got something dramatically better, at least twice as fast, in a relatively short time. That turned heads, and the team went with his version.

QWhat gave Bolin the conviction that his build tool could beat the alternatives and become the default?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says his Java experience told him the existing process should not be that slow. Most of the pushback was that deviating from the standard meant risking being stuck if the standard improved a hundredfold, which he finds ironic at a company that built its own PHP virtual machine and language. He guesses the fear came from mobile timelines and a senior person apparently going off on a science project.

He also framed the work narrowly: only an Android build system, not a takeover of the company. He made it capable of supporting more but never pushed it. About a year later the iOS developers asked to use it, which he found heartening.

How did he influence people at a new company where he had no credibility?
Michael Bolin

Bolin says one prolific senior Android engineer, also ex-Google, advised him to do it fast before anyone cancelled the work, and promised support if it succeeded. That engineer welcomed a faster development cycle and was among the first to praise it.

Bolin also admits a mistake. Coming from Google, he thought of Facebook as a bunch of college kids and several times argued that Google did things a certain way. People told him they did not care, and he says they were mostly right: what worked at Google would not necessarily work there.

What was the technical reason it was so much faster?
Michael Bolin

Bolin says he sat down with the existing tool and asked what it was actually doing. It restarted from scratch whenever anything changed, which made incremental builds slow. He worked out what depended on what, including the complicated Android resources, so results from unchanged steps could be cached.

He adds that adding a module in the old setup took around 200 lines of XML build script that nobody understood, so nobody modularized. Buck made new modules simple, which produced more modules and more incremental builds. The host summarizes this as less redundant work.

QWhy did Bolin move on to IDE work, and how did his editor win out over a competing one?

Michael Bolin

After Buck, Bolin says, he spent a brief stint on iOS Messenger and still did not like it. The code came from an acquisition and still required hand-written reference counting, and Xcode did not feel right to him. Facebook always had the biggest app on both platforms, so it hit the scaling limits of mobile tools first, which he found interesting as a dev tools person because the problems had real business value.

Apple told the team that Xcode was struggling because the project was too big. That made it seem justifiable to build an editor as a nicer layer over the compiler tooling, especially as Facebook had moved from Git to Mercurial and Xcode would never handle its bespoke needs. He did not feel the same about Android, where IntelliJ had been made to work at scale.

Another team was building a web-based IDE on an abandoned Google open-source project written in Google Web Toolkit. Bolin tried to build credibility there, even speeding up their build, but concluded it made little sense for the React company not to build its tools on its own technology. As with Buck, he scoped his editor narrowly, to iOS only.

Why did leadership side with Bolin's editor when it had no users yet?
Michael Bolin

Bolin says the other team had existing users, perhaps a thousand. He gives two reasons for the outcome. One was his argument about the technology stack. The other was that his editor, which the captions render as "New Clyde", was a desktop application, and an Xcode replacement needed to talk to the simulator and plug-in phones. He also thinks the credibility earned with Buck made leadership willing to gamble on another of his projects.

QHow did Bolin react to the promotion to E8, described by the host as principal level in the industry?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says he was very excited. Having felt out of step with his employer at Google, he saw the promotion as validation that he was growing in more than technical skill: he was learning what it means to do work that is in line with the employer. That was as satisfying to him as the promotion itself.

QWhat are the pros and cons of open-sourcing the technology a company builds?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says companies have benefited so much from open source that, when something is not the secret sauce, sharing it feels right. He applies the same view to Codex. Even if no one adopts a tool, it serves as a reference for how something can be done, and in better cases it brings meaningful contributions. He recalls that Uber and Airbnb adopted Buck, as later companies hit the problems Facebook had met first.

On Google's internal Blaze, available externally as Bazel (the captions render it as "basil"), Bolin says Facebook was open source first and wondered whether that added pressure on Google, and he believes the Buck team got some unofficial credit from people who worked on Google's tool. He also sees open source as a recruiting signal that a company is at the leading edge of an area.

Is open-sourcing a bottoms-up engineer decision, or does leadership back it?
Michael Bolin

Bolin says it was bottoms-up in both of his cases. React and PyTorch are the big success stories where the value to the company is unquestionable, but he sees a longer tail of projects where managers get grumbly if engineers seem to do too much open source, depending on the economy. He says the work was not met with much resistance. It usually yields a conference talk or two and a blog post, and those posts pay dividends over time because they have a longer shelf life than people expect.

QAfter the promotion, what did Bolin do next, and what is the "hero quest"?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says he got a little over his skis by trying to help with web speed. Load time on facebook.com was poor and the architecture stale, and many colleagues had worked on web for a long time while he had been in mobile and dev tools. He and another engineer compiled V8 from source to see whether generating JavaScript differently would help. None of it panned out.

He concluded that different people suit different projects. He is better when a project involves writing a lot of code from the beginning, whereas this effort was about looking at data and talking to many people, which is not his strength.

What does hero quest mean?
Michael Bolin

Bolin calls it embarrassing, because it involves ego. Engineers say that if only someone would come in and cut this Gordian knot, and he assumed that since he knew JavaScript, he could be that person. He says he did not succeed, and that he has had to relearn the lesson at least once since.

He can do many things, but a smaller subset is what he genuinely enjoys, and he will be much more successful staying within that subset while trying to expand it over time. In his words, people do not all have to be the best at everything, and should accept and embrace that.

QHow did Bolin find the next senior-level problem, and why was the virtual file system worth building?

Michael Bolin

Bolin credits some luck. Small summits of engineers brainstormed what would bite the company later, and one concern was that the monorepo would keep growing until it hit scaling limits. A manager gathered a few strong engineers to build a virtual file system, and Bolin says that for quite a while he was the worst engineer on the project.

He explains the benefit for a monorepo. Most people need only a subset of its files, so with a virtual file system, cloning or updating to another commit does not write every file to disk, a cost that otherwise grows with the repository. When the operating system asks for a file, the system fetches its contents as if everything were laid out.

What was the part of the project Bolin thinks he was better at?
Michael Bolin

Bolin says the second part of the project was the one he was better at. Existing tools are used to reading every file, and ripgrep is one example. If a tool materializes all the files, the benefits of the virtual file system are lost, so the development flow and tools had to be redesigned around it. The host sums the idea up as lazy loading of a huge file system, and Bolin agrees.

Source: 30:25–31:31 ↗
What did Bolin build for file search, and how fast was it?
Michael Bolin

Editors normally find files by walking the whole file system, which would undo the benefits. Bolin and a colleague who now works on the Codex team built a service called Miles, as the captions give it. It ingested new commits from trunk on a schedule and tracked only the names of added and removed files. The colleague devised an index that supported fuzzy matching, such as typing only the capital letters of a camel-case name or misspelling it.

Bolin recalls the index handling over a million files in about 10 to 20 milliseconds, faster than Xcode or VS Code out of the box. It became a service used well beyond file search, and when he left he recalls around 30 servers spread around the world.

Source: 31:31–34:12 ↗
Was the index a trie, or something else?
Michael Bolin

Bolin says it was not. The design used two parallel arrays, one for the file names and one for an integer index. Each entry also carried a 64-bit mask with one bit per lowercase letter, capital letter, digit and a few symbols, set if that character appeared in the file name, so a search could skip many candidates immediately.

The parallel arrays suited CPU cache behavior, since memory is read linearly, and could easily be partitioned for parallelism. Bolin adds that it was not out of a textbook, and that he should write it up some day.

QWhat did Bolin learn about influence and conflict that delayed a promotion?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says most people at the E8 level and above do not write code. They spend their time on influence, writing the large document and getting teams on board. For a senior engineer who writes code, he says, reaching the expected impact means spending at least some time influencing others.

His problem was that he was so confident in his insights that he came down too hard. When Microsoft acquired GitHub, the editor he had built relied on GitHub technology, and he feared it would be replaced because VS Code would not let it stay a project. He says that turned out to be true. But he was anxious, pushed people, and did not account for people being happy with what they were doing and not wanting their cheese moved. He received a talking-to, and his promotion waited.

From the coaching that followed, Bolin says, he became more aware of what triggers him, including technical decisions, and tries to notice that and not act in the moment. If he is not in the best place to have the conversation, he might talk to the person's manager rather than charge in like a bull in a china shop.

He was right about the editor in hindsight but told to calm down. How does he feel about that?
Michael Bolin

Bolin says that about a year later he had conversations in which he asked to balance the ledger a little, and they worked it out. He agrees with the host that the learning was about how he went about it, not what he was right about.

QWhat drew Bolin from Meta to OpenAI?

Michael Bolin

Bolin interviewed at OpenAI at the end of 2023, after spending 2023 at Meta on developer tools built on language models, including a lighter in-house Copilot-style tool that the transcript names CodeCompose. Feedback often asked why it was not as good as GPT-4, and his answer was that the team was working with Llama 2. As an engineer rather than a researcher, he wanted to build the experiences with the best model.

He gives three more reasons. He respected the people moving to OpenAI and felt he could work with more senior people there. He told many people it felt like starting at Google in 2000, once the company had found its footing and product-market fit. And he wanted a large user base again: he went to Facebook hoping for consumer scale but ended up building developer tools for roughly 20,000 colleagues. Codex, he says, has what he recalls as over a million weekly users, growing almost vertically, against the 20,000 to 40,000 developers he could affect at Meta.

How does a research-led culture compare with an engineering-led one?
Michael Bolin

Bolin says it was certainly an adjustment, and that anyone coming from the big consumer tech companies who says otherwise is not being honest. He loves the harness work he does on Codex, but argues that if the model were not very good, nothing done on the harness would matter.

He values sitting next to the research team and working closely with it. Building the product with the people who build the model was another reason to leave Meta. He thinks that kind of co-development was possible at Meta only to a degree, and the impact was not the same.
