QWhat is the story of Codex's launch, and how did it come together after a rocky start?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says the Codex CLI launched in April 2025 as a one-more-thing moment at the end of a livestream, demoed live and open-sourced. It was good but rushed. Open source brought pull requests and, as he recalls, 10,000 to 20,000 stars within a week or two. The team, he says, was not staffed to drive it as needed.

A month later the company launched the cloud version, where Codex runs in a container and tasks can start from a phone. Bolin recalls about seven engineers and some researchers, a better-staffed effort. He thinks the long-term vision is correct but a bit ahead of its time: adoption was big at first but not as sticky as hoped, and by mid-summer local agents had the stronger product-market fit.

The team shifted over the summer, adding people to the CLI as GPT-5 approached. Bolin had prototyped a VS Code extension a couple of times and felt strongly that the terminal forces compromises that an editor does not. He describes August as a crazy month: GPT-5, a refreshed terminal interface with support for the open-weights model, and the extension. He treats that as the inflection behind today's growth.

Why does Bolin believe the long-term direction is remote and in the cloud?
Michael Bolin

Bolin says the users for whom the cloud version is sticky want automation, such as handing an agent every GitHub issue or Linear ticket that comes in on a private repository. He acknowledges costs and potential abuse, but that cannot all happen on a laptop.

He expects individuals may still spend more time with a local agent, but most agent compute time will be in the cloud once setup, which takes more work today, is done. The VS Code extension already has a button to move a conversation to the cloud, and he expects people to throw work over and bring it back when it is done.

QHow has Bolin's own AI workflow changed, and how much of his code does he write by hand?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says he is now a bigger user of the Codex app than he expected, after a period of living in the VS Code extension sidebar. He does look at the code. For true throwaway prototypes he will not, which he finds freeing, but for code that ships in Codex itself, which affects everyone else, he still reviews it.

He has developed a sense of when the model can handle a change without being babysat, so he writes a lot up front. He keeps four or five clones of the repository and likes the multitasking in the app, treating it as a game of how much throughput he can get. It can feel hectic, but he gets more done, and he almost feels bad writing code by hand.

What share of his code is written by hand versus by the model?
Michael Bolin

Bolin says the model writes about 80 to 90 percent. He gives debugging a test or a CI failure as an example of where he tells the model to add print statements and investigate, which he finds freeing.

Which work is in the remaining hand-written part, and which in the model's share?
Michael Bolin

Bolin says he asks himself each time whether to write something, and the answer is almost always no. The exceptions are lower-level work. The harness he works on is in Rust and does operating-system-specific things, and he spends much time on the sandboxing that upholds the security integrity of Codex, so that the model cannot go outside the bounds the user sets. He does more of that by hand because it must be correct and well tested. Sometimes he writes the groundwork and lets the model fill in the rest.

He also uses the model to split an oversized pull request into reviewable commits, which would once have taken much of his time.

Bolin likes the approach where the agent does several rounds of review until it is confident the change is worth a human's time, but people still look at everything before it lands. The team has an AGENTS.md file like others do, and humans still catch gaps, such as context that has not yet been written down.

He notes that people now use AI to write pull request summaries, and the summaries across the team are getting much better, covering the why and the what. Combined with the earlier Codex review, he says this helps the team get through a larger volume of review faster.

Michael Bolin

Bolin says he is not the most zealous about open source but sympathizes with it. If a tool runs on a user's machine, people care what it does, and in the domain of AI agents it matters that people can inspect it. The project also receives contributions and bug reports it would otherwise miss, and it shows the world how this is done. He has written one blog post about the agent loop and plans more, though time is the limit.

How does Codex find what tools and resources are available?
Michael Bolin

Bolin lists a few routes. The model, as trained, is fond of ripgrep and uses it well to find things. An AGENTS.md file or README can say which tools matter in a repository. When a user connects MCP servers, their tool definitions are injected at the start of the conversation, so that is not discovery by Codex but information placed in front of it. A large part remains the model doing the heavy lifting of finding things, which he confirms when the host asks.

QWhich technical books and other resources have helped Bolin educate himself across such varied projects?

Michael Bolin

Bolin first names a roughly thousand-page operating systems textbook from Addison-Wesley. He reached the virtual file system project having never written C, since his undergraduate work was theoretical. When colleagues said things he could not follow, he asked his manager what to read, was pointed to that book, and read it cover to cover, taking it to Hawaii.

He finds it both freeing and a little bananas how far engineers can get without knowing how computers work, because of the layers of abstraction. His advice is to actively go deeper through the layers. He saw others solve problems he could not because he did not know there was cruft between two layers that, if removed, could bring a tenfold improvement. He also recommends the O'Reilly Rust books as well written and thorough.

Outside books, he recommends capture-the-flag security competitions. They build an adversarial mindset and force breadth, like a computer decathlon, and are more fun as a game. One challenge led him to open GDB and reverse a tic-tac-toe game, which widened his toolkit.

What is a CTF, in practice?
Michael Bolin

Bolin describes a competition, usually in information security. In the Jeopardy style, a set of crafted challenges carries point values, with a fixed time limit, individually or in teams. Each challenge hides a flag, a secret piece of text that a solver can obtain only by reverse engineering or otherwise doing what the challenge intends, and submitting it proves the solve. He compares it to an escape room in a terminal.

Source: 1:03:12–1:04:31 ↗
With AI tools that handle tasks like GDB, what should people early in their careers learn?
Michael Bolin

Bolin says everyone is struggling to answer this and he has no great answer. He still comes back to forcing yourself through the layers of abstraction, because for now the questions asked of the agent affect the quality of what comes out. Without the right questions, he says, a person may not get the best engineering solution.

He expects this to change, perhaps with another layer removed, and says things seem to be happening faster than expected. Experienced people can lean on the taste they have built, but he has not pinned down what asking the right question means for someone starting out.

QHow does Bolin think about the very high expectations at senior-staff levels and above, and is it stressful?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says it was never not stressful. He sat in calibrations, discussing others' levels and impact and wanting to be fair, and he imagined someone doing the same for him. At E8, one is compared to a director who may have over a hundred people, and it is hard to match that impact.

Many senior engineers, he says, do it through a different form of people management, writing the right document and aligning people. They remain individual contributors because technical credibility makes their words land differently than a director's. Influencing 50 to 100 people that way is, in his words, director-level impact.

For those who mostly code, project choice matters, and it cannot be one that is merely fun. Bolin often decided not to write a fun feature himself and let someone else do it. On Codex he asks which code he personally should write to maximize impact, and if someone else could do it about 80 percent as well, he lets them. He looks for force multipliers such as the virtual file system, which he knew would unlock things later.

He also says senior managers do not get enough recognition for pairing the right senior engineer with the right project. Some senior engineers are excellent fixers and coders but not idea generators, and a manager can see that a hard project needs a person who would never have chosen it.

Source: 1:06:54–1:11:25 ↗

QA former colleague praised Bolin's ability to start projects. What advice does he have for engineers who want to build something from scratch?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says good projects often come from being a bit dissatisfied with something. He admits he often charged ahead without thinking about the best way to build it. His example is weather icons in Google Calendar: he mostly knew JavaScript, cobbled together the backend, and stored the weather data as a blob of XML. His tech lead asked why he had not discussed protocol buffers and binary formats. He had been so set on the feature that he never asked anyone whether there was a better way.

The host notes many people simply wait on a slow build. What gave Bolin the confidence he could make it better?
Michael Bolin

Bolin credits his time at Google. He never worked on the Blaze team or touched its code, but he knew a tool with that shape existed and was much better, which he calls an existence proof. Whether he could build it was still to be seen. He says prior art gives him confidence, and that he thinks of himself as a coding machine who can build a prototype and test the basic hypothesis that a way forward should exist. If you are determined, he says, you find a way. The host adds that people who see world-class infrastructure at big companies often go elsewhere and rebuild it.

Source: 1:13:09–1:14:39 ↗
Source: 1:11:27–1:12:54 ↗

QWhat advice does Bolin have for engineers who want to write better, given how clear his technical writing is?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says reading good writing is a start, since patterns get picked up consciously or not. He then stresses thinking at a high level about what he is trying to convey and what readers would really want to know, and outlining a lot up front. He asks whether the points follow linearly, and whether any jump from one point to the next is too big, such as something a reader could reasonably miss. He feels he has a reasonable sense of where such gaps arise, and says that for technical writing, anticipating them and adding the example the reader needs to make the jump matters a great deal.

Source: 1:14:41–1:16:03 ↗

QCan Bolin explain the three-step plan for impact from his career note?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says step one is figuring out what you really like to do. It is good to broaden that, but also to be honest with yourself, and he ties this to his hero quest, which failed because he was working on things he did not truly love. Step two is working out what is really valuable to your employer, and he says that at Google he did not do this well. He did work he was excited about, but it was not AdWords for Google. Step three is finding the intersection and leaning into it.

He says the more you can do that, the more successful you will be, but the intersection is not always there. If it is not, you may have to find somewhere else to make it happen.

Source: 1:16:03–1:17:05 ↗

QKnowing everything he knows now, what advice would Bolin give himself at the start of his career?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says he should have been open to learning more things sooner and been gentler with himself, as many beginners should. He observes that people have a soft spot for their first programming language, since it first let them do something, and that this is also a hazard. Having finally become productive, a person is tempted to hold on, not knowing how long the next foothold will take.

In his case he thinks he went too deep on JavaScript, and it took a long time before he wrote C++. Being more curious and flexible about project types and what he was willing to learn would have been the biggest shift. The host points out that Bolin's later stories, such as Objective-C and C++ for Miles, show deliberate effort to learn rather than openness, and suggests that Codex may lower the hurdle, for example by asking it to write something in Rust from JavaScript knowledge. Bolin agrees that it opens many doors.

Section 40 · interview

Sergey Levine: Robot Generalization, Data Flywheels, and Humanoid Timelines

Levine argues that humanoid progress depends on generalization, diverse data and a healthy ecosystem, and gives a rough timeline of single-digit years for structured deployments.

Levine's view: generalization and ecosystem health matter more than demos

Levine, speaking about work at Physical Intelligence, argues that humanoid robotics is still finding its fundamental technologies. It has not yet reached the predictable scaling stage that drove language models. Demos are informative, but they often hide how little generalization they show. Levine's central claim is that robots improve through diverse, autonomous experience inside a healthy ecosystem of data, hardware and manufacturing. The timeline Levine gives is single-digit years for structured deployments and a few years more for less structured ones, though Levine calls the forecast hard.

Source: 00:20–56:37 ↗

QWhere is humanoid robotics today, and how will the technology be deployed?

Sergey Levine

Levine says machine learning works at scale, but only if the right thing is scaled. Transformers mattered because they scaled better than the earlier LSTM designs, not because they were mathematically elegant. Technology moves in phases: first find a scalable design, then put industrial-scale effort into data and model size. Levine says robotics is not yet at the GPT-4-to-GPT-5 stage of that effort, so progress will not follow a predictable monthly curve. The puzzle pieces are falling into place, but the scaling coefficients are hard to forecast.

Source: 00:20–04:19 ↗

QWhat are the most astonishing emerging capabilities you have seen so far?

Sergey Levine

Levine recalls that in late 2024 a laundry policy pulled two shirts from the hamper at once. It set one aside, disentangled the pair and folded the other. Levine says nobody watching the evaluation expected that, and that it looked like common sense, even if training data may explain it.

Levine finds recent mistakes more revealing. In a kitchen evaluation, a robot that could not open the expected drawer put the utensils into the oven beside it. In a dishwashing test, the robot tracked cleaned plates on a scratch-pad memory. It dropped one, then moved its base so the dropped plate was out of view. Levine says these errors resemble a child's mistakes, and that the robot still needs to grow up.

Source: 04:20–07:01 ↗

QAmong Figure, Tesla and other humanoid efforts, has any achievement impressed you?

Sergey Levine

Levine says the most inspiring development is the takeoff of autonomous driving. Robotics is often criticized as always the technology of the future, like nuclear fusion, but people said the same about driving. Levine notes that a Waymo in San Francisco now takes riders with no driver. Levine says this is no accident in the mid-2020s, as large-scale machine learning pieces fit real physical systems. Driving and manipulation differ, but the example shows that learning-based technology can work in the physical world.

Source: 07:03–08:35 ↗

QIf a major AI lab such as Anthropic invested heavily in robotics, how would the industry change, and would competitors worry?

Sergey Levine

Levine says robotics is a less healthy ecosystem than computer vision or language. Those fields have freely available data, wide acceptance of learning, and fewer concerns about physical harm. Levine notes that robotics has not traditionally shared data, and that safety concerns there are not the same as a device causing physical harm.

Levine says more learning-based activity would shift thinking toward learned controllers and shared data. Levine is proud of the work at Physical Intelligence, but argues that it will take more than one company to change how everyone thinks about the field.

Source: 08:36–10:20 ↗

QChinese robotics demonstrations look impressive from outside. Are Chinese labs further along, and what is the lesson?

Sergey Levine

Levine says the useful lesson for US and European researchers is that robotics needs a healthy ecosystem across all its parts. That means strong researchers, open source, and healthy supply chains, manufacturing and hardware R&D, not only computer science and model building. Levine says the United States does some of these well and has let others slip.

Levine suggests studying strong results from labs anywhere, then investing across every facet. Levine disclaims business and investment expertise, so does not claim to know how to do this. Levine argues the field is holistic and cannot be outsourced one piece at a time.

As a robotics researcher in the US, what would most improve the field?
Sergey Levine

Levine says reliable, low-cost hardware is a big deal. Much research hardware now comes from China. Levine describes it as inexpensive, high quality and meeting the standards researchers generally need. Levine says it would be good to source that hardware domestically too, and does not think that is impossible.

Source: 12:27–13:14 ↗
Source: 10:20–12:24 ↗

QWill the first lab to reach scale pull ahead through a deployment flywheel, whether in the US or China?

Sergey Levine

Levine says there is much truth to the flywheel, but the lab must scale the right thing. The better framing is a positive feedback loop in which more deployed robots mean more model capability. A welding robot on a car assembly line may make many welds each month, yet that data alone is unlikely to produce anything more capable than a welding robot.

Levine argues that data is not a fungible commodity like oil or electricity. It has to be diverse, and is more like “an education program for your robot” than a commodity.

When do you first expect that flywheel to appear in the world?
Sergey Levine

Levine says the timing depends on how much structure developers accept. Unstructured home deployment brings diverse data at once, but the safety bar is high because people are present. More structured tasks face fewer safety issues and are more predictable, but each new data point carries less variety. Levine describes a trade-off between starting earlier on a smaller slope and starting later on a larger one.

Levine's sense is single-digit years rather than double-digit years. Structured tasks may arrive now or next year, and less structured ones a few more years out, but probably not a decade.

Source: 15:19–16:58 ↗
Source: 13:15–15:16 ↗

QCould you sketch milestones on a roadmap toward a robot in the home?

Sergey Levine

Levine warns that a demonstration often hides the level of generalization. Generalization is a property of many trials, not one. A mundane task with an unseen object in an untested room can be harder than a rehearsed backflip. So the roadmap centers on better generalization and on a mechanism that improves it with experience.

One milestone is a concrete system that improves through autonomous experience in a setting it was not trained for. It should reach practical robustness rather than capping out near 50 percent. Another is transferring common sense so a robot can recover from surprises. Levine uses the driver's instinct to slow down for a fire truck or traffic cones, even in an unfamiliar situation, as the example.

Source: 16:59–20:32 ↗

QAre you less interested in a narrow humanoid doing one assembly-line step, since that is not a step toward general intelligence?

Sergey Levine

Levine says narrow work is not uninteresting. The real world has leaky abstractions that make even narrow tasks more complex than they seem. Autonomous driving shows this. Early plans to use magnetic sensors along highways and transmitters in cars failed, because messy exceptions broke the system in the 1 percent of cases that matter. What worked was facing the mess in San Francisco.

Levine expects robotic manipulation to follow the same path. Leaving a fully structured factory means facing the full scope of the problem, even when most of the time the task looks straightforward. Levine adds that recovering from a spatula placed in an oven shows common sense can help a robot fix its own mistakes.

Source: 20:34–22:51 ↗

QDoes Figure's live-streamed package-sorting demo show generalization?

Sergey Levine

Levine thinks it does, and welcomes the creative ways people are making generalization visible, such as live demos and long time-lapses.

Levine describes Physical Intelligence's long-horizon runs. One robot assembled boxes at a chocolate factory over several days. Another made espresso drinks for 13 hours, cleaning up spilled grounds along the way. Levine jokes that the main downside was staff losing sleep to caffeine.

Did the robot clean up its spills by itself?
Sergey Levine

Not entirely. A person issued high-level prompts about every five minutes, including commands to clean the machine. Levine says that could be automated in principle, and the team is working on the high-level policy that issues those commands. Levine adds, with a laugh, that the robot also had to be told to clean up before the next drink.

Source: 24:29–25:15 ↗
Source: 22:51–24:27 ↗

QWhat is the best robot training data, what is the worst, and what are the trade-offs between simulated and physical interaction data?

Sergey Levine

Levine says data is easier for a model to absorb when it is grounded in physical understanding. A pilot learns in a flight simulator because they know it abstracts a real aircraft. A person watching someone cook can file away an add-salt step without copying every movement. Levine argues that a robot foundation model trained on lots of real embodied data may absorb other sources better.

That reverses a common instinct from LLMs, which is to start with internet video and add robot data on top. Levine says the evidence points the other way. A colleague and a Georgia Tech collaborator found that, with a small model and little robot data, human and robot experience stayed fully separate in the internal representations. With lots of robot data from many robots, features grouped by task instead. At full robot-data scale, the human and robot embeddings lined up perfectly, which Levine sees as a strong sign that a solid robot base absorbs other data well.

Source: 26:10–30:28 ↗

QDoes the base model need data from the exact robot it will run on, and can skills transfer between robots?

Sergey Levine

Levine says cross-embodiment models are a major focus, but deployment still generally needs data from the target robot. The better measure of generalization is how little experience a new robot needs to borrow skills from others. The model needs surprisingly little special machinery. There is no factorized representation for different morphologies. It outputs one large vector, padded with zeros when a robot has fewer degrees of freedom, and trains on all robots together.

Levine says transfer works best through the right intermediate representation. Text thinking carries high-level structure, such as opening a drawer before putting away silverware. Image thinking can carry low-level skill. The model dreamed up the next milestone as an image, which let a UR5 arm fold a shirt without any shirt-folding data for that arm. Imagining a folded shirt is easier than getting joint angles right.

So the model outputs an image of what its video sensor should see next?
Sergey Levine

Levine says it is like image editing, and video prediction could work too. The key is imagining progress on the task. Some planning is semantic and some is spatial, as when a rock climber pictures the arm reaching for the next hold.

Source: 34:00–34:58 ↗
Source: 30:29–33:58 ↗

QWhat would make you say single-digit years is coming, rather than a long tail with policy challenges?

Sergey Levine

Levine says a key difference is how thin the robot's software stack is. Training the foundation model is hard, because data must be gathered, curated and labelled. The software on the robot is very simple by comparison. Counted in lines of code, it is much smaller than a traditional autonomous vehicle stack, which started earlier with older technology and evolved over years.

Levine says safety is real and probably among the harder parts of the problem, but it is less of a hard stop. Dropping a fragile object is far less bad than a car hitting someone. Developers can pick tasks, environments and hardware where problems are milder. Levine argues that a simpler stack plus milder challenges make deployment easier, and that early deployment feeds a flywheel.

Source: 35:01–37:00 ↗

QIf humanoid robotics did not succeed in single-digit years, what would be the most likely reason?

Sergey Levine

Levine says it would come down to reliability. Robots need more robustness and generalization than people expect from LLMs and image tools. Those tools are interactive: a user can rephrase and iterate. A robot delivers its full value only when it acts autonomously, so needing someone to iterate on every task defeats the purpose. Demos can also mislead about how close a system is to practical robustness.

Levine believes in reinforcement learning that uses autonomous experience to fine-tune the last few percentage points, from about 95 to 100 percent, but says that is not yet solved. If progress takes longer, Levine says it would be because the bar is higher. Levine does not favor discarding foundation-model methods, since the puzzle pieces are good, but the methods need more work to cross the robustness threshold.

Source: 37:01–39:53 ↗

QIn LLMs everyone seems to do similar things. Is robotics the same, or are there hot-take architectures?

Sergey Levine

Levine says robotics is more varied than it looks. The dividing line is between embracing the foundation-model approach and building specialized vertical systems. The principle is that a general model trained on many problems beats a narrow specialist on one problem. Levine uses machine translation as the example: a general language model can outperform a dedicated translation system.

Levine says this is uncomfortable in robotics. A warehouse team may find it strange to collect data on putting away silverware in kitchens. Yet breadth of data builds generalizable skills that a well-built model can repurpose, even for warehouse edge cases. Levine says this cuts against the traditional approach of building vertically integrated robotic systems.

Source: 39:55–42:04 ↗

QIf AI companies become wildly successful, what safety and government concerns come up, and how would you handle them for a generalist robot model?

Sergey Levine

Levine says AI safety is not new. Stuart Russell, a colleague at UC Berkeley, was raising these issues more than a decade ago. Technology moves so fast that the important questions depend on how society reacts and which tools get adopted. Those are hard to anticipate. Levine has no fully satisfying answer. The approach is empirical: release systems, see what goes right and wrong in the real world, and adjust.

Levine argues that if computer-only AI already raises concerns, systems that can do everything people can physically do will raise strictly more. The risks are real, so the work is to keep watching and adjust.

Source: 42:05–44:24 ↗

QIf everything goes well and robots are very capable in ten years, is the north star the end of human labor?

Sergey Levine

Levine says it is a mistake to think of robots as mechanical people. Personal computing did not replace brains. Computers spread into desks, pockets, refrigerators and cars. Levine suggests physical actuation could appear in many everyday things, so people still do many tasks but get help with them.

Coding agents are a closer example. Levine says the endgame is unclear, but software engineers Levine has spoken with mostly find agents empowering rather than alarming, because they amplify how much work one person can do. Levine calls it a real job where AI adds leverage, though the outcome remains to be seen.

Source: 44:24–46:43 ↗

QAre there a few top papers that show the breakthroughs people should know about in humanoid robotics?

Sergey Levine

Levine offers a partly self-promoting pick: the ACT paper, which Levine also calls the ALOHA paper. Levine is a co-author, and says almost all the work was done by lead author Tony. The ideas were not new, but they were illustrated well. Low-cost hobbyist arms, which Levine says cost about $7,000 each, used a leader-follower teleoperation rig to collect data for very dexterous tasks. A fairly simple transformer-based model could perform many of them.

Levine says the insight is to put the right pieces together and trust what a simple robot can do with a good learning system. The code was open sourced and is the starter kit many people use. Levine recommends the paper to newcomers, because the details matter even if they need not be complicated.

Source: 46:44–49:33 ↗

QBoston Dynamics once had striking demonstrations and much mindshare, but you hear less about them now. Is there an industry shift behind that?

Sergey Levine

Levine says robotics is about building complex systems, from wiring and power sources to actuators and high-level planning. Classic Boston Dynamics results show sophisticated, carefully designed hardware, with traditional control by skilled engineers and less emphasis on decision making. That made sense when the physical body was the bottleneck. Now, Levine says, hardware is often good enough, and the big challenge is a decision loop that reacts intelligently to the environment.

Levine draws the line between controls and AI. Controls handle the robot's own body, such as a backflip on flat ground. AI must account for the world, such as picking up a coffee cup. Levine also says a hand-designed controller proves a skill is possible and often simple enough to learn, so the skill can be automated without controls engineers in the loop.

Source: 49:35–53:46 ↗

QKnowing what you know now, what would you tell yourself when you first entered the field?

Sergey Levine

Levine says the main change is recognizing that robotics needs broad prior knowledge. Levine once shared the common idea that robots should learn from scratch, as people do. The arm farm project at Google had many arms grasp millions of objects in a conference room. The arms learned to grasp, but that was a poor stepping stone to more complex skills.

Levine says language itself was not the point. Prior knowledge used as a scaffold is the point. Humans and monkeys absorb much of their knowledge through observation rather than language. Without prior knowledge, a robot faces a harder problem than humans do, like assembling flat-pack furniture without ever having seen any. Levine's advice to a younger self is to take prior knowledge more seriously, while still valuing learning from experience.

Source: 53:48–56:37 ↗

Section 41 · interview

Stay close to users, code, and the next useful capability

Boris Cherny traces growth through generalist product work, shared infrastructure, earned trust, corrective decisions, and building Claude Code for a changing model frontier.

QWhat work led to your senior-engineer promotion at Meta?

Boris Cherny

Cherny recalls a project connecting Messenger chats with Facebook groups, after several earlier attempts to bring the products closer. The product hypothesis was that interaction was moving from public social spaces toward more casual, real-time conversation. He picked up a PM’s idea, built an early version, then recruited a few engineers and design and data-science support as it showed promise.

The small team did work beyond coding. Without dedicated user research, they showed features to cafeteria workers and watched whether they could accomplish tasks without much prompting. He taught teammates the same method. The rough early experience still helped test whether the core idea worked.

He values that generalist approach at Anthropic too: engineers with product sense, design interest, and willingness to speak with users, plus other functions willing to code. His own background in small companies taught him to own the whole outcome. He says the initial half brought his promotion and the next half brought promotions for the rest of the early engineering team.

Source: 01:00–05:39 ↗

QWhat is latent demand, and why does it matter?

Boris Cherny

Cherny describes it as existing user intent expressed through a product not designed for that purpose. People were already buying and selling in Facebook groups; dedicated commerce groups and later Marketplace made that behavior easier. He cites observed proportions of group posts as an example of the signal, rather than as current measured usage.

He offers profile-view behavior as another hypothesized signal behind dating features. The broader principle is to notice what users are already trying to do, especially how they bend a flexible product, then reduce friction around that intent. His claim that a product cannot make people do something they do not already do is deliberately strong product philosophy, not a proven universal limit on innovation.

Source: 05:39–07:06 ↗

QHow do you work across organizations with very different cultures?

Boris Cherny

His Facebook product team prioritized rapid releases and engagement, while Messenger prioritized reliability and performance. The clash was built into goals, incentives, and organizational design, not just personalities. Messenger engineers had reason to fear changes that would damage the metrics they were responsible for.

He believes a version of the project failed partly because the benefit was much clearer for Facebook than for Messenger. Find a goal, hypothesis, or interest that both groups can genuinely share; simply expecting collaboration despite divergent rewards is weak.

What would you change if you could revisit that project?

He would seek an organizational arrangement with a closer common manager and better-aligned incentives, potentially bringing Messenger into the Facebook organization for the effort. He is describing a hindsight proposal, not a reorganization he carried out then.

Source: 09:08–09:42 ↗
Source: 07:06–09:08 ↗

QHow did side projects such as Undux affect your career?

Boris Cherny

He values curiosity outside one’s main assignment, even when the interest is not technical. Undux began because he found React state management unnecessarily difficult and wanted a simpler approach. A nonprofit used his early library; at Facebook he recognized that repeated support questions reflected the same problems he had encountered.

An initial announcement brought some users but did not by itself drive broad adoption. He grouped support complaints by team, contacted each team’s leadership, and gave many focused technical talks. Meeting users where their specific pain already existed worked better than expecting a general post to persuade everyone. He recalls it becoming widely used before newer tools replaced it.

Other side explorations included a TypeScript book and a meetup. The book consumed roughly a year and he does not lightly recommend that commitment, but it let him go deeply into the language. Meeting prominent JavaScript creators also made ambitious work feel more accessible: they were people building things, rather than an unreachable class of geniuses.

Did the state-management project help in performance review?

He thinks it appeared, but calls it a bonus rather than the work that alone earned the next level. Its larger value included learning, relationships, and useful experience with adoption.

Source: 13:10–13:25 ↗
Source: 09:42–14:44 ↗

QDid that language knowledge prove useful in later work?

Boris Cherny

He describes an unusual start to language exploration: a motorcycle accident injured both arms, making coding difficult. He experimented with languages requiring fewer keystrokes, including CoffeeScript and Haskell, then a colleague introduced him more deeply to Scala and functional programming.

Functional Programming in Scala is the technical book he says most changed his thinking. He recommends the way it teaches problem solving even to people who may never use Scala. The lasting idea is to think in types and pay attention to signatures as a guide to clean structure.

That habit transferred across Flow, Hack, Python, and TypeScript in his later jobs. He distinguishes the mental model from the particular syntax used at a given company.

Source: 14:45–17:04 ↗

QWhy do you think entering Meta underleveled was fortunate?

Boris Cherny

Lower expectations gave him space to explore and build things without immediately satisfying a larger set of project and people requirements. The host suggests that exceeding an initially lower bar can also create momentum and a strong first impression; Cherny agrees. He sees a downside to seeking a higher title at every move if it raises pressure before the person understands the new organization. This is his personal benefit from one circumstance, not a universal recommendation to accept lower compensation or responsibility.

Source: 17:05–18:56 ↗

QWhat work led to the staff-engineer promotion?

Boris Cherny

He wanted a better JavaScript-based web experience for Facebook groups, which still relied heavily on PHP with fragmented interactive state. Leadership initially resisted because supporting infrastructure was not ready. When the broader Facebook desktop rewrite, Comet, began, he offered groups as an early customer and helped argue that participating would let the team get ahead of required migration work.

The effort grew from an initial group of roughly a dozen engineers into a substantially larger migration. By helping build the platform rather than merely consume it, his product team could shape abstractions other teams would later use.

One example involved optimistic button updates and server responses arriving out of order. He built queuing around mutations to preserve consistent state. He recalls choosing a consistency tradeoff suited to the problem, and the shared work built relationships with the infrastructure team. His broader lesson is that product engineers can go a layer deeper into infrastructure and infrastructure engineers can talk to users.

What additional opportunities came from being early?

Besides shared infrastructure, the team helped define what product quality should mean on the new platform. Cherny wrote notes and gave talks about lessons others could reuse. Getting ahead of the migration gave the team a chance to set standards rather than only comply with them.

Source: 22:53–24:04 ↗
Source: 18:56–22:52 ↗

QHow many people would that migration require with contemporary coding agents?

Boris Cherny

Cherny revises the original scope to perhaps 20–30 engineers over about two years, then guesses that tools at the time of the interview might support roughly five engineers over six months. He imagines parallel agents building changes and using browser feedback to refine the interface. He explicitly warns that the estimate could change in three or six months, perhaps radically. These are speculative comparisons, not measured results from rerunning the same migration.

Source: 24:04–25:18 ↗

QWhy did you joke that VPs usually pick the middle of three options?

Boris Cherny

It was deliberately tongue-in-cheek. He thinks a distant decision maker wants evidence that the team explored options and tradeoffs, while also wanting to contribute a decision. A middle option can provide that. He qualifies the observation: some leaders investigate for themselves, and leaders differ in how much they trust teams. The “80%” framing is a joke from his story rather than a reliable statistic or a reason to manipulate every review.

Source: 25:20–26:39 ↗

QHow did reporting to a very senior manager affect your opportunities?

Boris Cherny

Cherny treats this as company-dependent. At Meta, access to leaders could help an engineer find scope and navigate an impact-focused review system. At Anthropic, he sees highly senior people reporting to line managers, so reporting level says less about authority or capability.

He also likes common titles because they make it easier to do useful work outside a narrow role. He describes Meta engineering titles and Anthropic’s broader member-of-technical-staff convention as supporting that culture.

Do common titles make it harder for another team to know how seriously to take you?

Yes, but he thinks the upside is stronger: people must earn trust rather than assume a prior title gives them authority in a new setting. Everyone deserves respect, yet authority over a particular decision still requires evidence and relationships. He recognizes the lost shorthand and considers it an acceptable tradeoff.

Source: 28:58–29:38 ↗
Source: 26:39–28:58 ↗

QHow did you scope work for hundreds of engineers?

Boris Cherny

Cherny recalls a large investment in Facebook groups as a community platform, leaving leaders to determine what newly allocated engineers would do. He produced many rough scoping documents with options and staffing estimates. In hindsight, he would have added people more gradually as specific products found fit: solving users’ problems is not made easier simply by distributing a huge allocation all at once.

A difficult groups-and-pages data-model problem stalled despite senior involvement. He brought technical leads into a short architecture exercise, split them into two groups, and gave both the same requirements. After a few hours, the designs overlapped substantially. Agreement showed where execution could begin; differences exposed risks to investigate with small technical spikes.

This let the team stop treating the whole problem as unknowable. The exercise created a concrete comparison without requiring one person to understand every detail in advance.

Did people accept the unusual design competition?

He scheduled it and made it appealing as an engineering problem. He thinks a leader sometimes needs to act to create a process through which consensus can form, while at other times acting without consensus would be wrong. Here the uncertain path made convening people useful.

Source: 33:29–34:19 ↗
Source: 29:39–33:28 ↗

QWhat helps a technical lead produce a quick scope?

Boris Cherny

Start at a high level and time-box the initial pass rather than disappear into unlimited detail. Cherny suggests roughly half an hour for a very rough view, or a few hours when code investigation is needed. Identify experts and show them a strawman instead of only asking open-ended questions; a concrete proposal makes feedback easier. He now sees coding agents as another way to explore relevant systems, but that is a tool-assisted extension of the same need to expose a reviewable first plan.

Source: 34:20–35:49 ↗

QWhat made the public-groups project a senior-staff-level challenge?

Boris Cherny

The visible change sounded simple: allow people to read, and in some cases comment in, public groups without first becoming approved members. The downstream changes were much harder. Following without reciprocal approval raised questions about how to represent membership, what admins needed, and how to handle more spam.

A senior engineer argued for separate data-model representations, and the team undertook a lengthy migration. Cherny also used a simple simulation of comment quality and spam to make moderation risk concrete, helping bring an integrity team into comment ranking. The work involved many experienced engineers whom he initially felt awkward directing because they shared his nominal level.

After auditing many call sites, he concluded the migration had mostly added branching without changing substantive logic. The old member field could support the needed behaviors. He pushed to reverse the migration, asking the senior engineer with the most context to help undo it. That engineer accepted the evidence and later supported Cherny’s leadership. The reversal was costly but reduced confusion for future developers.

His eventual judgment is that level does not reliably determine who has the best result. The achievement was not simply leading a large migration; it included recognizing when its premise was wrong and earning the trust to correct it.

Source: 35:49–41:10 ↗

QHow can a strong technical disagreement improve rather than damage a relationship?

Boris Cherny

Earn trust first. Cherny initially disagreed but committed to implementing the senior engineer’s decision, then developed evidence and showed technical judgment. A relationship in which both people know you will execute honestly makes later pushback easier to hear. His recommendation is to invest in that trust before assuming a correct argument alone will carry the disagreement.

Source: 41:13–42:02 ↗

QHow did you deal with imposter syndrome while leading strong peers?

Boris Cherny

He says not to assume that others at any level have everything figured out. His confidence did not arrive in one dramatic moment; it grew with experience. He regards some discomfort as a possible sign of stretching into unfamiliar work. This is encouragement grounded in his trajectory, not a complete technique that instantly removes anxiety.

Source: 42:03–42:42 ↗

QWhen should an engineer fill a product-management gap versus ask for more PM support?

Boris Cherny

Understand the decision maker’s tradeoffs before arguing for a preferred answer. A project may be hard to hire for, PMs may be needed on something more important, or an organization may have spare PM capacity that could sensibly be reassigned.

The same request therefore means different things in different settings. Think about what leadership values, what work your request displaces, and whether the proposed allocation helps them succeed. He does not give a universal rule that engineers should always absorb another function’s work.

Source: 42:43–45:04 ↗

QHow do you find useful engineering opportunities and give them to others?

Boris Cherny

He looks for repeated friction in his own coding and asks how to eliminate it. During review he kept a list of recurring comments with examples; once the same issue appeared repeatedly, he wrote a lint rule rather than continue to police it manually. Automation freed his own time and could improve work for many engineers.

He did basic validation on ideas, then connected engineers who wanted those opportunities. He thinks understanding their goals is better than simply ordering them to do a project. At Meta, better-engineering work helped an evaluation dimension many people struggled to demonstrate, so a useful project could meet both a system need and an engineer’s growth goal.

He also warns that prolonged distance from code weakens a technical leader’s intuition. Hands-on experience anchored the opportunities in actual constraints. His very large approximate count of people involved in side projects is a recollection, not a precise audit of his personal influence.

Source: 45:04–48:38 ↗

QWhat is a concrete way to source repeated, high-value side projects?

Boris Cherny

He gives large-data testing as an example. Ordinary tests did not cover a group with millions of members, a highly followed profile, or a very large event, so scale failures appeared only in production. Seeing the same pattern across products, he proposed infrastructure for creating and testing large objects; another engineer took it on and recruited help. The pattern is to notice recurring pain, check whether others share it, and build an abstraction that prevents a whole class of incidents.

Source: 48:39–50:44 ↗

QWhy did you move from Facebook groups to Instagram in Japan?

Boris Cherny

The move began with his partner’s dream job in rural Japan rather than a calculated promotion strategy. He tried several internal arrangements, but sponsorship or organizational rules blocked the earlier options. An engineer building the Instagram Tokyo office offered a workable path.

He joined despite having scarcely used Instagram, then came to value its emphasis on craft, human experience, and simplifying products as well as measuring them. The new setting taught him different habits from the Facebook organization he knew.

Source: 50:45–53:13 ↗

QWhat does “unshipping” mean?

Boris Cherny

Features compete for limited screen space and attention. Adding something useful to a small group can clutter the experience for the majority who do not use it. Cherny describes requiring a usage bar and deleting a feature that fails it, accepting that some users will be disappointed. His argument is about the opportunity cost of accumulated features, not that every low-usage feature lacks strategic value in every product.

Source: 53:14–54:18 ↗

QHow did you rebuild credibility in a new organization from far away?

Boris Cherny

Leaders and colleagues helped him connect with people working on code quality and technical debt, but he still had to earn trust. He spent early weeks meeting people, mapping goals and the organization, and writing code to understand the codebase.

The severe time-zone gap made meetings difficult, but unexpectedly restored time for coding after years of documents and conversations had left him unhappy. He says he still avoids standing one-on-ones. That made it possible to do work others wanted done but could not fit around their obligations.

He explored migrating parts of Instagram’s Python environment toward Hack and Meta’s infrastructure. He considered the original simple choice sensible at small scale but less suitable after years of product growth and a much larger engineering group. This is his contextual assessment; his praise of the alternative serving stack is not a universal language ranking.

He began with the people most likely to disagree, building personal trust before debating the migration. Supporters who had been reluctant to speak then joined the discussion. In a product-led organization, creating space for an engineering-led investment required those relationships as well as technical scope.

Source: 54:20–1:00:15 ↗

QWhen did you delegate the large migration, and how did you decide to trust another lead?

Boris Cherny

Cherny saw a colleague closer to the relevant organization as an excellent owner. He recommends delegating something you understand and care about so you can judge progress, rather than treating delegation as a way to dump disliked work. He cites High Output Management as an influence. Check more at first and less as evidence of reliability grows; with a proactive and technically strong lead, he needed little intervention. The handoff matched the project’s needs rather than preserving personal ownership for its own sake.

Source: 1:00:15–1:01:55 ↗

QWhat happened around the principal-engineer promotion?

Boris Cherny

His manager proposed putting him up for IC8, and he agreed. He had not been campaigning for it. He credits the manager’s willingness to notice readiness and advocate for people, with large modernization projects providing the context. He does not offer a detailed promotion packet or claim that a simple conversation alone caused the result.

Source: 1:01:55–1:02:28 ↗

QDid levels guide how you sought more impact and leverage?

Boris Cherny

Cherny sees levels as company tools for communicating expectations, comparing people in reviews, and planning costs. His own motivation was interesting problems, useful products, and making people’s experience better, rather than the next level itself.

He pitched ideas from his earliest weeks as IC4; several were rejected and one appeared in another form later. The point is a willingness to seek useful work without waiting for a higher title. His career happened to reward that approach, while he does not claim every company will do so automatically.

Source: 1:02:11–1:04:27 ↗

QWhy leave Meta for Anthropic?

Boris Cherny

Using an early ChatGPT product while living in Japan made AI feel like a field he had to work on. He was fascinated by the technology and by speculative possibilities he had encountered through science fiction. Conversations at Anthropic gave him a strong sense of shared interests and people thinking deeply about the same questions.

He also wanted to help make the technology develop safely. He describes becoming more conscious of risk after seeing new models and Anthropic’s investment in safety and alignment, including delayed releases. His examples of possible misuse and existential risk are his assessment, not independently established capability claims in this book.

The decision combined fascination, a cultural fit, and a mission. His metaphor of models as an alien life form conveys his excitement; it should not be mistaken for a factual claim about consciousness or biology.

Source: 1:04:27–1:08:47 ↗

QWhat felt different about Anthropic’s engineering culture?

Boris Cherny

He values a startup’s shorter distance between decisions and consequences: useful changes can seem obvious enough that less effort goes into persuading multiple layers. Mission is also personally powerful. He had felt it in Facebook groups’ community work, felt less of it in Instagram, and felt it strongly again at Anthropic. He acknowledges that geography or his own experience could have influenced the difference. He is describing what motivates him, not a ranking of how meaningful every employee’s work is.

Source: 1:08:47–1:10:14 ↗

QWhy did Claude Code catch on when other model-connected tools already existed?

Boris Cherny

Cherny contrasts the then-dominant coding autocomplete and Q&A model with a tool intended to act more broadly. His manager pushed him to build for capabilities expected about six months later rather than only what the current model could already do.

The product was initially weak and he used it for a small portion of his own coding. Later model improvements made the existing tool much more useful, matching the horizon the team had aimed for. He reports high fractions of agent-written code within his team and some others, plus a substantial increase in per-engineer productivity while Anthropic expanded.

Those usage and productivity numbers are internal claims made in the interview. The caption does not clearly establish the productivity metric, so the book does not convert them into an exact causal benchmark. His product lesson is to stay close enough to the model’s trajectory to serve near-future capabilities while avoiding a plan too far ahead to test.

Source: 1:10:14–1:12:54 ↗

QHow do you avoid accepting large amounts of poor or subtly flawed model-generated code?

Boris Cherny

Use the same quality bar for human and model code. If a change is poor, the team should refuse it and ask for improvement rather than lower expectations because an agent wrote it. Cherny thinks users can also ask for changes that are too large before learning to direct the tool well.

He chooses the method according to the work. Throwaway prototypes can be generated loosely. For maintainable product work, he usually aligns on a plan, inspects the implementation, and iterates with the model. Some core-loop details still matter enough to him that he writes them by hand.

He is enthusiastic about progress without saying the models are already excellent at every task. He sees substantial room to improve and warns that judgments about capability move quickly. That combination of optimism and retained review standards is more useful than treating generated volume as evidence of correctness.

Source: 1:12:55–1:16:32 ↗

QWhat do you think of Claude Code being used beyond software engineering?

Boris Cherny

He discovered a neighboring data scientist using it for SQL and analysis, then saw multiple sessions supporting data work, pipelines, and coding. He also reports salespeople connecting it with Salesforce and other sources. Those uses were not the original product intent. The examples return to latent demand: observe what users do with an adaptable tool rather than define its limits solely from the name.

Source: 1:16:32–1:17:21 ↗

QHow do you view competition with Codex, and what makes users stay?

Boris Cherny

He does not give a feature comparison because he says he does not personally use the competing tools and is unsure. The stickiness part of the host’s question therefore does not receive a definitive mechanism.

His management principle is to avoid letting competitors replace user problems as the product roadmap. Copying a visible feature is easier than discovering a better solution, but he wants the team focused on its own work, researchers’ needs, and users’ problems. He interprets more competitors partly as evidence of an important market, rather than only as a distraction to fear.

Source: 1:17:21–1:19:01 ↗

QHas not having a computer-science degree held you back?

Boris Cherny

He studied economics and left to build startups. He has not felt the missing CS degree blocked his own path and recommends learning programming through practical work, then adding theory as it becomes useful. His reasoning is that concepts are easier to connect to an actual product than to exercises without context. This is his experience and preference, not evidence that a degree never matters for a particular employer or technical field.

Source: 1:19:01–1:19:40 ↗

QWhat productivity advice would you give now?

Boris Cherny

His answer has changed with coding agents: learn to automate toil and coordinate several agents rather than depend only on faster manual typing. He describes a teammate using many parallel sessions and a task board to implement a feature over a weekend in a container. This is an anecdote about her workflow, not a verified effort comparison or a blanket recommendation to remove safeguards. Earlier his advice would have centered more on ordinary scheduling and focus habits.

Source: 1:19:41–1:21:00 ↗

QDo agents change the need for long coding focus blocks?

Boris Cherny

In his own work, somewhat. He still enjoys quiet coding time, including weekends, but can begin several tasks from a mobile or web interface in the morning and inspect them later at a computer. He sometimes merges after review, or brings a change locally to edit.

He sees this as making coding accessible in fragmented schedules, including for managers who have not recently written much code. He is describing a changing interaction pattern, not declaring concentration unnecessary for understanding or reviewing complex systems.

Source: 1:21:02–1:22:55 ↗

QWhat would you tell yourself at the start of your career?

Boris Cherny

Use and develop common sense. Organizational history and misaligned incentives can pull people away from what users and a business actually need. In startups as well as large companies, he would trust practical judgment, examine assumptions, and build toward the real market or user problem. The advice ties his generalist work, side projects, migrations, and product choices back to the same habit.

Source: 1:22:57–1:23:50 ↗
