Section 42 · interview

Thariq Shihipar: How Anthropic Builds, Harnesses, and Where Engineering Is Heading

Thariq Shihipar of the Claude Code team describes how Anthropic works with its models, from harnesses, loops and verification to writing, maintenance and career advice, and argues that taste, context and technical depth remain human.

Thariq's view: move up an abstraction level, but keep taste, context and technical depth

Thariq Shihipar, an engineer on the Claude Code team at Anthropic, argues that the most useful habit is to treat Claude as a thought partner and to work one level of abstraction above the code: build the system that builds the system. In Thariq's view, harnesses, verification, skills and context matter more as models improve, while taste, domain knowledge, clear intent and technical understanding stay with people. The host probes onboarding, autonomy, prompting, code maintenance, writing, career visibility and whether anyone should still learn to code. Product and model names follow the auto-generated captions and were not independently checked.

Source: 00:28–1:09:50 ↗

QIf an engineer joined from a less AI-focused company, what should they start doing to onboard onto the Claude Code team?

Thariq

Thariq's top tip, for people inside and outside Anthropic, is to treat Claude as a thought partner and give it the context it needs to work out next steps. Start from whether Claude can do the task, and if not, ask why not.

Thariq also recommends asking whether the work can move up an abstraction level: instead of building the product, build the system that builds it.

Does Claude replace the onboarding buddy completely?
Thariq

Thariq says teams still assign onboarding buddies, but for social and cultural reasons more than technical ones. Someone good at working with Claude can get most technical onboarding from it. A buddy still helps with how the team works, how to win buy-in, and simply having a friend at work.

Source: 01:52–02:52 ↗
Source: 00:28–01:51 ↗

QWhy is there such a big gap between how Anthropic staff talk about AI capability internally and how the outside world sees it?

Thariq

Thariq says Anthropic has a decent record of its claims proving true over a long enough time scale. Many engineers there are no longer in the IDE, and Thariq reports that some large enterprise customers say they have not typed a line of code in six months.

Anthropic treats it as part of its job to learn to work at a higher abstraction level, so a day spent failing to get Claude to do something autonomously is not wasted: it shows where Claude falls short.

Thariq says the calculation differs in an ordinary job where the task is to produce output. Automation is an investment that can fail, and a boss will not be happy with someone who spent the time on harness setup and shipped no code. The odds of payoff rise as models improve, but an individual still has to take the leap. Thariq calls the gap mostly cultural: Anthropic tries to live in the future and builds what it learns into the product and harness.

Source: 02:53–04:52 ↗

QWhat practices make a big difference at Anthropic that people rarely show on Twitter?

Thariq

Thariq points to using Claude Code for knowledge work. If you can describe a task as code-like steps, the model can carry them out. Thariq does personal accounting with Python scripts through Claude Code instead of Excel, and edits video with FFmpeg and rendering libraries.

In Thariq's view most knowledge work reduces to code and coding agents, and other people do this less than they could.

Source: 04:53–06:15 ↗

QHow important is the harness compared with the model?

Thariq

Thariq calls the harness super important and rejects the idea that better models make it unnecessary. As models improve, the harness has to become more complicated so the model can do more.

Thariq's example is auto mode, a classifier tied to the actions that would otherwise trigger a permission prompt. With earlier models, which Thariq names as Opus 4 and perhaps Opus 4.5, turns lasted a few minutes and pressing enter was tolerable. Now Claude can run for hours, so it must work safely and follow instructions. Thariq calls auto mode and sandboxing complicated software.

Longer runs also raise the question of how Claude reports eight hours of work. Anthropic uses artifacts for this, which Thariq treats as a form of prompting. Thariq calls harness engineering an unintuitive mix of science and art, and says pieces such as auto mode and workflows have become load-bearing.

Source: 06:18–08:55 ↗

QWhat share of changes at Anthropic is fully autonomous, compared with pairing with a model as a year ago?

Thariq

Thariq says it depends on what counts as autonomous and on the function. A designer might hand over a Figma file that Claude Code reads through a Figma MCP, but the designer has still done real work. Anthropic's goal is for Claude to handle the glue work, such as rewriting that file in React.

Thariq frames the question as: what is the unique work I must do today? The more time spent on that, the better. If the work only translates what someone else did, Thariq asks whether Claude can do it. Even a fully generated PR usually reflects decisions and context the person supplied.

How close are we to telling Claude "here is the ticket, don't tell me until you're done"?
Thariq

Thariq says it depends on the ticket. With a spec written precisely enough, Claude can probably do it. But a typical GitHub issue raises earlier questions: is it worth fixing, is it several requests combined, and does it fit a cohesive product vision.

In practice, Thariq says, people have not worked out what they want or the unknowns in the problem. Writing code used to surface those questions. Now people need new ways to find what they do not yet know, and chatting with Claude can help.

Thariq names a failure mode: tagging Claude with a one-sentence request and no context, disliking the result, and iterating forever instead of working out quickly what you actually want.

Source: 10:42–12:28 ↗
Source: 08:56–10:40 ↗

QAt Meta, intern projects were almost line-by-line specified. If Claude can handle that, what does an intern do at Anthropic?

Thariq

Thariq says there is a great deal of new work nobody has done before, such as evaluating new coding behaviors or measuring Claude's performance across millions of users and tasks with trade-offs, especially on the research side. Specs are harder to write and less existing experience applies.

Experience still helps with getting work done and learning, though Thariq notes interns also gain those skills at college. Internships are now less about writing React code. Fresh eyes help, and interns need to be more proactive and opportunistic than in a pipeline-style program.

Source: 12:30–14:48 ↗

QHow far away is computer and browser use from wide adoption?

Thariq

Thariq says the models have improved a lot and calls Opus 5 a really good computer use model. Edge cases remain: it cannot type a password for Thariq because the passwords are in a password manager, so it gets stuck.

Thariq expects APIs and MCPs to take over many uses of computers. Claude Tag, for example, rolls many things into APIs so Claude can work on a user's behalf without literally clicking through a virtual computer. Some tasks have no API and still need a browser.

Why does computer use feel so slow?
Thariq

Thariq says it is hard to make a small model very good at the task, because it needs much knowledge about how things fit together, and smart models are slower. Many people expected this sooner, and it has been harder than expected.

Thariq passes on someone else's remark that a computer is a state machine whose whole state you do not control. Add the wrong item to a DoorDash cart and you need a new flow to undo it, where you can err again. In code you control the state and can undo with git; in computer use, actions are harder to review or reverse.

Source: 16:24–17:40 ↗
Source: 14:51–16:21 ↗

QIf someone had infinite compute, what workflows would you tell them to run?

Thariq

Thariq says the difference is smaller than people think. Thariq uses a Max subscription on weekends and has almost never hit a five-hour limit. Much of Anthropic's heavy compute goes into probing model capabilities, such as testing math ability, rather than everyday work.

People can reproduce the practice by thinking at a higher level. Thariq's example is a funnel in which Claude drafts feedback for a user. Thariq monitors it and asks Claude for improvement ideas, annotates features with events Claude can access, and runs a morning loop to check which events fired and what changed. Thariq says this takes fairly modest compute.

More often Thariq sees people hit limits the opposite way: they start with a small task such as refactoring a function, then iterate through follow-on effects. Stating goals, letting Claude explore and write out a schema, and then letting it run would probably give the same output.

What is loop engineering, and would it hit limits on a Max plan?
Thariq

Thariq defines loop engineering as setting up a system that prompts Claude rather than prompting Claude directly. With Claude Tag this comes naturally: ask it to do something every day and that is a loop.

Around ten loops, for example to triage feedback and implement fixes, take real work on skills, triage quality and verification so changes land. At that level Anthropic has something monitoring issues the team could never have kept up with, which raises velocity. Thariq says full autonomy is possible in some cases but is a lot of work, and like hiring someone it has to be worth it.

Source: 20:45–22:46 ↗
Source: 17:42–20:43 ↗

QWhat is the next big shift that will spread across the industry?

Thariq

Thariq names Claude Tag first. In Thariq's description, Claude Code is good at implementing code, and Claude Tag covers the rest of the software life cycle: feedback, code review, babysitting, CI/CD and incidents. Thariq expects each part of the life cycle to become a routine or loop.

Thariq also expects generative interfaces. Artifacts will become a larger way to read and interact with Claude, and Thariq uses them for almost everything. If Claude Tag finishes work and produces a report, an artifact can make it readable on a phone.

What are artifacts, and how do people use them?
Thariq

Thariq describes an artifact as Claude uploading a web app for you to use. Artifacts can now call your MCP, for example to read, sort and tag your inbox, or show a coding plan with diagrams, file snippets and schemas.

As Claude does more jobs, Thariq says, text in and text out is not enough for everything, and Claude is getting better at building the right interface at the right time. Thariq encourages asking how you could interact differently, to learn, understand or stay in the loop. It is still early.

Source: 24:28–25:59 ↗
Source: 22:47–24:27 ↗

QDo engineers at Anthropic use different daily-driver models, or just the most intelligent one?

Thariq

Thariq says the aim is to get the most out of frontier models with well-shaped tasks and a good verification harness. For now there is not enough compute for everyone to run Fable at 100 percent of rate limits, but Thariq does not see choosing a model as a durable skill.

Today Thariq uses Fable for planning, brainstorming, finding unknowns, writing detailed specs and building verification aids such as schemas, and Opus 5 with workflows for implementation. Thariq expects people to think much less about model choice by next year.

Source: 26:01–27:36 ↗

QIs prompting a durable skill, given that each model has its own spiky intelligence?

Thariq

Thariq says prompting is more than the typed text. It includes skills, data and everything built up as context. When Anthropic staff write small prompts, they have spent a lot of time on the harness, verification and skills. Thariq thinks it stays valuable to improve at it.

Each model has quirks to learn and later unlearn. Citing a recent Anthropic post about removing 80 percent of Claude Code's system prompt, Thariq says one finding was to remove examples from tool descriptions. Examples used to be needed for good output, but now they mostly steer the model wrongly, because Claude is good at sticking to your intent.

So the skill being built is the skill to adapt. Thariq's first model was GPT-2, where getting JSON out was remarkable, and that experience still helps with prompting Fable 5.

Source: 27:38–30:54 ↗

QIs there any tribal knowledge or quirky tip for today's models?

Thariq

Thariq pushes back on advice like "just believe in yourself". Thariq reads Jared's post about the Riemann hypothesis as mostly giving the model permission to use compute, not encouragement. Thariq's habit is to say a problem is hard, that Claude may use sub agents and workflows, and that it should use its own judgment.

Thariq explains that models by default do what the average user wants: respond and start fast, and finish without spending a crazy amount of compute. To change that, nudge the model, for example "don't work yet, brainstorm with me", or invite it to use workflows. Overnight, Thariq may set the slash goal and let it run. The common thread is giving permission.

How did you prove that removing so much of the system prompt made things better?
Thariq

Thariq says Anthropic used user metrics, internal and external evals, and internal reports. Some changes are hard to catch: there is no eval for Claude finishing its work and telling the user to go to sleep.

The team removed lines, ran evals, watched reports and adjusted. Thariq says this was a full-time job for several people over a long period, so Anthropic published what it learned rather than recommending everyone repeat it.

Source: 32:57–34:15 ↗
Source: 30:56–32:56 ↗

QClaude Code is excellent on objective work but hit or miss on taste. How do you instill a style, for example in front end work?

Thariq

Thariq's method is to stay in the loop and give references, ideally with data. An HTML file beats a screenshot and a Figma file beats a raster image, because Claude can read a value such as a border radius from the Figma component and copy it. References in code are best.

For a non-designer, Thariq starts by admitting how much is unknown, including what good looks like. Ask Claude for help: say you lack design vocabulary, find reference sites, mark what you like and dislike, then ask for several mock-ups. Thariq prefers self-contained HTML mock-ups, then starts a new session to implement one.

Thariq argues that knowing what good output looks like will become more valuable. Thariq says Jared prompted the Riemann hypothesis work but could not tell whether it was correct until Lev, whom Thariq calls one of the world's best mathematicians, worked with it and asked follow-ups the Anthropic people could not follow. Domain knowledge is how you get good outputs; otherwise Claude might solve something and you would not know. The hardest part, Thariq says, is knowing when something is good enough and when to push harder.

Source: 35:02–38:58 ↗

QHow much glue writing, such as launch posts, updates and design docs, is now written by LLMs at Anthropic?

Thariq

Thariq's rule of thumb is that if you would be happy to show someone the prompt, you can send them the output. Often the prompt just collects context. Before each one-on-one, Thariq has Claude read Slack messages, GitHub messages and PRs and compile a report of what Thariq did. The manager lacks that context, and Thariq is comfortable with them knowing the prompt.

For data readouts, Thariq suggests showing you have read the result, for example with small edits or a sanity check of the numbers. For a pitch or new concept, people want to know you believe in it. Even if Claude's idea is excellent, Thariq would say that Claude generated it and that Thariq thinks it is great. What people dislike is feeling misled.

Some writing depends on individual words. Anthropic's internal essays arguing for a direction are generally human-written, and Thariq says having Claude write your essay is looked down on, because every word should be intentional.

So routine writing is AI-written but human-reviewed, and novel thinking stays human?
Thariq

Thariq agrees and adds that writing is a way of thinking, so if you need to think more about a readout, summarize it yourself. Gathering context is different: no one will hold it against you, and acknowledging the shortcut is good.

Source: 42:48–43:46 ↗
Source: 39:00–42:47 ↗

QIs there a "prompt blame", like git blame, that shows which prompt produced a change?

Thariq

Thariq says this is tough, because a prompt includes context and skills, so a basic-looking prompt may not be basic. Thariq treats a PR as no different from an artifact now, since Claude writes nearly all the code.

When Thariq sends a PR, Thariq usually attaches an artifact of every prompt sent to Claude, including failed approaches, so reviewers see what was considered. For a one-shot, Thariq says so and shares the prompt. Thariq wants to avoid sending a 10,000-line PR and being asked how much was read, so for large PRs Thariq shows the work as much as possible.

Source: 43:48–45:35 ↗

QWith AI generating so much code, what works for code ownership and maintenance?

Thariq

Thariq says to revisit what matters. Naming used to matter because it reflected how a team thought about an abstraction, but it matters less now, as do many stylistic things. A team should decide which opinions still matter.

On maintenance, Thariq stresses scaffolding: a verification harness and skills. Thariq's team uses the simplify skill a lot, but does not want the model to simplify by default before the work is correct, which wastes tokens.

Thariq wants a harness that gives real confidence Claude tests every part; a PR to Claude Code returns a recording of the feature in use. Thariq suggests about a hundred times more testing code than before: fixtures for everything, production data pulled to build mock databases on the fly, and Storybooks for front end.

The human part is deciding where the code base should go. Thariq's example is undo: in a single-player app it can stop working after four or five steps and few notice, while a multiplayer app needs composable operations. If you know your direction, put it in your skills. For Thariq, maintainability means having a vision of what the code base is good at.

Thariq expects every code base to face a moment of asking the model to rewrite all of it, for example in a faster language or as WebAssembly in the browser. Thariq says maintainability still matters but the mental model needs updating.

A friend leaves tech debt because the next model will refactor it. Is that sensible?
Thariq

Thariq says it is not completely wrong and depends on the case. It is the classic startup trade-off between refactoring and delivering customer value.

Thariq suggests thinking on shorter time scales and delivering value over the next month or two. If a project is meant to deliver value over six or twelve months, it may make sense to wait a little for the next model, while making the short-term delivery really good.

Source: 50:43–52:04 ↗
Source: 45:39–50:42 ↗

QFriends at big tech companies see more incidents as AI use rises. What has worked at Anthropic to prevent breakages at higher velocity?

Thariq

Thariq calls this a byproduct of moving faster and says Anthropic's uptime is not where it wants it either. Thariq notes that Anthropic is only around six years old and that no company has grown so fast, partly because Claude let it build more products faster.

Thariq's approach is to use Claude to improve uptime. The team asks what the dream testing and deployment environment would be: replaying requests across mock databases and fixtures, and chaos-testing everything.

Source: 52:04–53:24 ↗

QDoes everyone on your team have their own set of miscellaneous tools and scripts?

Thariq

Thariq says yes, and that it is partly the job. People sometimes build their own harnesses for a while to see if they are useful, and integrate them if they work.

Many have unique Claude Tag setups. Thariq has it manage calendar invites: anyone can tag Claude in a channel, and Thariq accepts what it puts on the calendar. Others use it for email, and Thariq has seen multi-Claude tmux setups showing around 50 Claude Code sessions.

Source: 53:26–55:20 ↗

QShould software engineers post on Twitter or X to build visibility?

Thariq

Thariq says to share your work externally as much as you can, though some employers do not allow it; side projects are an option. Before joining Anthropic, Thariq worked with different companies, built things, and wrote and talked about them. Thariq says this increased their "surface area of luck", and that the bar is much lower than people think.

Thariq says they give this advice to many people and almost none follow it, while everyone who did is in a job they are excited about or running their own company. The recipe: ignore your resume, choose an interesting project, work hard and lock in, then ship it and write about it. There will be reasons not to, but if the first attempt fails, do it again.

Twitter may not be the right place; Reddit or Hacker News might fit better. The goal is to find people who like what you do. People want high-quality content, which is a lot of work, and Thariq says there is no shortcut such as asking Claude to run your Twitter account. Engage authentically. Thariq compares it with going to the gym daily: simple, disciplined and easy to quit, and Thariq says they have not seen anyone who kept trying fail.

Can you give an example of expanding your luck surface area?
Thariq

Thariq describes how they got the job at Anthropic. Thariq did a fellowship at Good Fire, an interpretability AI company, doing applied research on using interpretability to make better products, and agreed up front that the goal was to share what Thariq built.

Thariq built an interpretability visualization and posted it. It got about 500 likes, which was big at the time. Several people saw it, some sent direct messages, and Thariq got an intro into a role at Anthropic. The project took about a month, and Thariq was paid for it.

Thariq says there is no shortcut: do interesting, novel work, work hard and be proud of it.

Source: 58:52–1:00:55 ↗
Source: 55:24–58:41 ↗

QBoris said coding is largely solved. Should people still learn to code?

Thariq

Thariq says being technical is really important: knowing how computers and programs work, what a back-end service or a cache is, what memory allocation is.

Thariq argues that only a great mathematician can tell whether someone really made progress on a hard open problem, and likewise only a great engineer can tell whether great software was built. To stay in the loop, reflect on your process and use Claude as a thought partner. Thariq cites Karpathy that learning should feel like effort: if Claude explains something and you only nod along, you have not learned it.

On "coding is solved", Thariq reads Boris as meaning that we no longer get stuck the old ways. Coding used to be high variance, with a bug taking a day or two weeks, and software projects rarely went well. Hiring someone to build software for a car dealership would almost certainly end in being scammed, not from malice but because software was so hard. Now coding can be used for things never done before. That is still a lot of work, but no longer a rare, difficult thing that mostly fails.

The host used to be shocked when software worked first try and now expects it. How should we read that shift?
Thariq

The host says the expectation has flipped: now the host is surprised when Claude's code does not work on the first attempt.

Thariq says humans get used to abundance quickly. Thariq cites an article about a modern apartment's wonders, such as music on demand suited to your mood, where once you would have hired a musician. Thariq believes more people are paid to make music now than ever and music reaches more people, and expects the same for software and math: given abundance, people want software in everything.

Source: 1:05:07–1:06:33 ↗
Does the earlier FFmpeg example suggest technical people still have an edge?
Thariq

The host notes that a non-technical person might not think to call FFmpeg to automate video editing.

Thariq agrees and says knowing how computers work matters. In Thariq's view the best CEOs tend to be technical, citing Zuckerberg and Elon. Thariq says they probably have not written code in a long time, but they understand systems and constraints.

Source: 1:06:36–1:07:40 ↗

QIf you could go back to when you entered the industry, what advice would you give yourself?

Thariq

Thariq describes it as two wolves. The first is to believe in yourself. When Thariq joined, it was rarer to believe in younger people, which Thariq links to the idea behind Y Combinator. Thariq suggests seeing yourself not as someone being trained but as someone who can do something incredible right away, and wishes they had done and shared bigger, bolder things.

The second is to learn from people. Young people tend to fail in one of two ways: not being bold enough, or being so bold that they never learn what others tried and why it failed. Everyone has a different failure mode. Thariq thinks they did not use mentors enough and had to relearn many things. Thariq adds that there is probably no universal advice, only things to think about when entering.

Part

Growing as an individual contributor

Career stories reveal how scope, technical ownership, visibility, and timing interact. These are particular experiences and organizational practices, rather than a universal promotion formula.

Section 43 · companion

Ambition, impact, and the limits of promotion checklists

A host and CTO debate how to make valuable work visible without reducing career growth to a transactional promotion checklist.

QShould an engineer organize a career around promotion or around developing useful behaviors and impact?

Guest

The guest strongly favors impact over title. In evaluating advancement, he wants to see important outcomes rather than an attempt to negotiate a checklist whose completion mechanically triggers promotion. A person can technically satisfy a stated activity while performing it in a way that adds little value; that leaves the underlying reason for advancement unmet.

He also acknowledges a personal reaction: repeated attempts to pin leadership down on rewards can feel transactional and annoying to him. That is his perspective as a leader, not a guarantee that all managers respond alike. His substantive argument is that genuine impact remains what should be recognized.

Source: 00:00–02:34 ↗

QHow should quieter engineers balance impact with making their work visible?

Guest

The host challenges a pure impact-first account: good engineers can be weak at communicating their results and may lose out when promotion decisions depend on people noticing. He distinguishes useful visibility from cynical self-promotion.

The guest agrees that visibility matters. Engineers need contact with people who understand important challenges, coordination with collaborators, and recognition of their capabilities so others can entrust them with bigger work. His distinction is the purpose and framing of the communication: making work understandable and coordinating it can lead to different behavior than trying to brag about oneself.

Updates should also recognize collaborators and thank the team. That makes the contribution legible without implying only the sender mattered, helps others feel valued, and supports the trust required for leadership. The host observes that two motives can produce superficially similar updates; the guest emphasizes how much the message centers the individual versus the work and other people.

Source: 02:34–06:34 ↗

QDoes the loud high performer often get promoted sooner than an equally strong quiet colleague?

Guest

The host argues that persistent lobbying can win extra attention even when both people have real impact. The guest says outcomes depend on organizational culture and that his own culture tries not to reward that behavior. He admits there are edge cases where lobbying earns consideration simply by keeping someone top of mind.

He does not advise abandoning ambition. He wants ambition expressed as a desire for greater impact: ask whether you are working on the most important problem, what you could learn, and where you could contribute more. A hardworking engineer can otherwise spend extraordinary effort on a low-priority task and still miss the outcome they sought.

Making those aspirations known and asking for opportunities are valuable conversations. What he opposes is reducing the relationship to contractual boxes followed by a demand for promotion. The debate therefore retains a real tension: the host worries about unequal recognition, while the guest prefers impact-centered visibility and managerial judgment to promotion bargaining. Neither establishes that recognition will always perfectly match contribution.

Source: 06:34–09:28 ↗

Section 44 · interview

Ask what the title is supposed to give you

Bryan Cantrill argues that promotion and financial goals need an underlying source of meaning, including a plan for life after success.

QShould an ambitious engineer focus on work or explicitly target promotions?

Cantrill offers a third path: first understand why the desired title matters. A distinguished-engineer label is an external marker; attaining it leaves the person facing the same question about meaning. He would help a mentee identify work that is important to them and supports continuing development.

He points to unhappy senior engineers and wealthy people to challenge the assumption that achievement necessarily supplies fulfillment. His provocative counseling jokes are condensed into that underlying concern, rather than presented as psychological diagnoses. He thinks meaningful motivation provides the fuel from which work and promotion can follow.

What if the actual goal is financial independence?

He asks what independence enables. If it means never needing to work for money, what would the person then choose to do? He wants that motivating activity identified now rather than assuming money itself answers the question.

Source: 02:21–03:14 ↗
What if the meaningful activity cannot support a living?

Then the person must balance it with a sustainable career. He recognizes the need to provide for oneself and a family, but objects to postponing all meaningful activity until an uncertain future financial milestone.

He recalls dot-com wealth existing on paper and then disappearing. The bust forced many people to rediscover why they were in technology apart from money. Some people who sold successfully faced a different problem: they no longer needed to work but still had to find purpose. Buying more houses or consuming more did not automatically answer it.

Source: 03:15–06:23 ↗
Source: 00:00–02:20 ↗

QWhy do some people reach financial independence and then feel lost?

A singular goal can organize life so completely that completion removes the structure. Cantrill says this can happen even after a meaningful engineering achievement: he anticipated a letdown after Oxide shipped its first rack because people had pulled toward that goal for so long. A financial milestone may create the same gap without having supplied meaningful work along the way. He does not endorse responding merely by escalating the amount one wants.

Source: 06:28–07:54 ↗

QWhat about someone who would be happy simply relaxing?

The host offers a real counterexample to the work-centered view. Cantrill responds with a story of an early Yahoo employee whose fortunate equity position made him wealthy despite limited interest in work. The employee’s responsibilities eventually narrowed considerably, and he still complained about the job.

The anecdote illustrates that unusual financial luck and dislike of work can coexist. Cantrill hopes the person found meaning elsewhere, but does not know that outcome. He does not actually establish that nobody can be content with leisure, so the host’s broader counterexample remains unresolved.

Source: 07:54–10:17 ↗

Section 45 · lesson

Choose a career you will still want after the promotion

A compilation of experienced engineers’ advice connects ambition with values, relationships, confidence, distinctive strengths, and useful judgment.

QBefore optimizing a career, how do you know the destination is worth reaching?

Guest 1

The first guest would spend more time clarifying values and what he actually wanted. A clear target made his early choices simple: he took roles that moved him toward development management. Once he reached that target and a high level comparatively young, however, he lacked a model for the decades of work still ahead and experienced a serious loss of purpose.

He warns against wanting only the attractive part of somebody else’s life. Wealth, title, age, circumstances, and daily work come together; admiring one feature does not mean you want the whole life. His lesson is to examine the destination before treating speed toward it as success.

He also remembers working until 11 p.m. while his fiancée was visiting, giving their relationship only a late dinner. They stayed together, but he regards that outcome as fortunate rather than proof that relationships tolerate unlimited strain. Some things recover from pressure; others break. Reaching the same senior level at 30 rather than 38 may matter less over a long life than maintaining a spouse relationship and family. Choose the tradeoff knowingly rather than assume everything else will wait.

Source: 00:43–05:33 ↗

QAre you pursuing your own goals or seeking other people’s approval?

Guest 2

Another guest reflects on a prescribed sequence of school, job, marriage, and achievement that encouraged comparison and validation from others. He would ask whether he wants the goal itself or is simply climbing a ladder placed in front of him. The person whose judgment he ultimately needs to satisfy is himself. He doubts his younger self would have absorbed that lesson immediately, which keeps the advice from sounding like an effortless mindset switch.

Source: 05:33–06:28 ↗

QWhat did imposter syndrome delay?

Guest 3

A third guest would trust his judgment sooner. Successful projects, good collaboration, and feedback eventually built confidence, but earlier anxiety kept him from trying some ideas because he feared rocking the boat. Several of those disruptive projects later worked well. He wishes he had tested them earlier and spent less time worrying, while grounding the eventual confidence in experience rather than claiming every first idea was right.

Source: 06:28–07:19 ↗

QWhat deserves the same intentional planning as a career?

Guest 4

Another guest would invest more in friendships, romantic relationships, and life outside work. The imbalance concerned attention and optimization as well as working hours: he planned career goals carefully but did not apply similar effort to the rest of life. Moving to Los Angeles and developing friendships outside the technology bubble changed that. His work continued to go well, while stronger mutual support, including friends willing to help him move, made life more fulfilling.

Source: 07:19–08:46 ↗

QHow can a combination of ordinary strengths become distinctive?

Guest 5

A guest who admired specialists in design and engineering worried that being only moderately strong across several areas would not work. His actual advantage was negotiating across those areas. He would focus less on being the best at a single discipline and more on the unusual combination he could bring.

He would also be braver about sharing ideas. His fear of public speaking at school contrasted sharply with his comfort pitching a product he cared about. Explaining material as a test of knowledge made him anxious; advocating for a change he wanted to create gave him a different purpose. Passion did not magically remove every challenge, but it changed what speaking meant to him.

Source: 08:46–10:49 ↗

QWhat would you keep and change about a career spent in fast-growing companies?

Guest 6

This guest would keep choosing growth. He compares his career ladder with an escalator: personal effort mattered, but the companies’ expansion also carried opportunities upward. He would change how late he recognized that jobs involve other humans. Expertise and correctness should be paired with relationships, friendship, and a reputation. Introversion need not prevent this; writing and online tools can build connections in a comfortable format. He recalls Amazon approaching him for a job as an example of the value of being known.

Source: 10:50–12:22 ↗

QWhat matters beyond being the person who writes requested code?

Dwayne

Addressing his younger self as Dwayne, this guest would ask how anyone knows that a requested implementation is the right thing to build. He would seek participation in those decisions, instead of defining his value only by what he can type. That wider role would have helped counter his early imposter syndrome and clarify that ideas and judgment can matter more than raw output.

Source: 12:24–13:15 ↗

QHow would you become more courageous without pretending embarrassment disappears?

Brian

Addressing himself as Brian, the next guest would be more courageous and less embarrassed by failure. He immediately qualifies the short advice as the beginning of a larger conversation about understanding feelings, not a command that makes them vanish. He thinks being more in touch with emotion, possibly through therapy, can help both the person and their relationships.

Is that easier said than done when embarrassment is something you simply feel?

Yes. He agrees and says the two-sentence advice would need deeper discussion of the feelings and how to understand them. He does not supply a complete technique for eliminating embarrassment.

Source: 13:24–13:56 ↗
Source: 13:15–13:56 ↗

QHow do you choose an environment that values your strengths?

Guest 9

Another guest says a strong front-end engineer can struggle on a back-end team, or a person who loves improving frameworks can receive poor results on a team focused on product delivery. Activity alone is insufficient: even hundreds of changes may not serve the team’s priorities. Recognize a persistent mismatch and seek a team and management chain that need what you are good at. The principle is fit between strengths and valued work, rather than simply doing more of a strength in any environment.

Source: 13:56–14:41 ↗

QWhat if a difficult technical area is intimidating?

Guest 10

The next guest encourages trying instead of treating others’ current ability as a permanent barrier. They may be better now, but sustained interest and continued effort can build competence. His framing is encouraging and informal: computers are learnable, and liking the work is a useful starting point.

Source: 14:43–15:03 ↗

QWhat should guide you when an organization’s inherited practices seem strange?

Guest 11

The final guest recommends common sense. Large companies can have misaligned incentives and processes retained mainly because they have always existed. Startups also need judgment about what markets and users actually want. He would trust and develop that practical judgment rather than assume organizational convention has already answered the problem.

Section 46 · interview

Discover performance gaps while you can still act

An Amazon principal engineer describes the limits of stack ranking and recommends explicit, early conversations about role expectations.

QHow many people does Amazon expect to manage out?

The guest declines to give an exact figure. Five or six percent appears as a hypothetical illustration, not a disclosed quota. In his account, guidance became more of a mandate in recent years, while a lack of backfills made repeated cuts more troubling.

He acknowledges the limits of his perspective as someone who considers himself a high performer: he has participated in decisions but cannot fully represent the experience of fearing dismissal. He stresses that performance conversations concern real people and emotionally consequential outcomes.

With ordinary backfilling, he could view some departures as an exit from a cultural mismatch. Without replacement, repeated cuts reach people who would previously have been considered strong enough. He was surprised by colleagues who lost their jobs and is particularly uneasy about applying percentages to very small management populations.

Does repeated stack ranking begin to remove people who are doing good work?

Yes, that is his concern. A repeated six-percent illustration applies to the remaining group each time; it is not simply three times six percent of the original population. As the group shrinks, people near the middle may be affected. The transcript does not supply enough data to infer a company-wide policy or actual cumulative rate.

Source: 03:34–05:06 ↗
Source: 00:00–05:06 ↗

QWhat happens in performance discussions, and how does a senior IC participate?

Senior engineers begin to be pulled in, and L7 or higher participants are regularly involved in his account. He describes lengthy meetings that can reduce people to metrics and feedback. He does not disclose the detailed process, but says it is not a simple linear algorithm. Time tends to concentrate on the edges of the distribution rather than allocate equal discussion to every person, partly because the population is too large.

Source: 05:06–06:04 ↗

QWhat advice would you give engineers near the performance boundary?

He dislikes treating a difficult fit as proof that the person is inherently a low performer. Passing a demanding interview already suggests considerable ability; the company’s expectations, culture, and the person’s assumptions may simply differ.

His advice is to identify the specific dimension on which expectations are not being met, then work toward solid performance before targeting exceptional ratings or promotion. Ask the manager directly what the expectations are and whether you meet them. If something is missing, agree early on a concrete improvement plan.

He views this as proactive growth rather than waiting for a formal performance-improvement process. The point is to discover actionable information while there is still time to respond. His estimate that few engineers explicitly ask about expectations is an impression, not a measured survey.

Should someone literally ask for a proactive PIP?

He would not use those words. The useful request is for clarity and a plan: what does the manager expect, is it happening, and what should change?

Source: 08:55–09:05 ↗
Isn’t meeting expectations obvious advice?

He thinks the missing step is often asking explicitly. Engineers may guess the standards rather than hear them from the manager. Even an uncomfortable answer that performance is falling short is better than remaining unaware.

Source: 09:06–10:27 ↗
Why seek bad news early?

A problem surfaced early in a career or review cycle gives someone a fighting chance to address it. Discovering the same issue shortly before a review leaves little room to act. He attributes the saying about early bad news being merely news to a colleague, without claiming certainty about its original source.

Source: 10:28–11:23 ↗
Source: 06:04–11:23 ↗
Editorial synthesis
Source: 08:13–11:23 ↗

Section 47 · companion

Senior scope grows in depth, breadth, and time horizon

Philip Su explains why the highest engineering levels require qualitative judgment and illustrates that scope through building Meta’s London engineering site.

QWhat distinguishes the work at E7, E8, and E9?

Philip Su

Philip Su begins with scope of influence: how large, valuable, or long-running an effort can someone reliably bring to completion? He offers approximate historical expectations, such as influencing roughly ten to fifteen people at senior/staff-adjacent levels and perhaps fifty at E7. He explicitly warns that his leveling information may be stale. These are illustrations from his experience, not a promotion standard for any company today.

Higher levels also differ qualitatively. An unusually deep specialist may solve problems that several less-senior engineers cannot substitute for. A broad generalist may integrate many kinds of work for a small or new team more effectively than separate hires. Headcount alone misses that distinction.

He recalls E9 being created after his initial E8 promotion and early decisions involving only a few very different candidates. Such a small and varied group makes a universal checklist implausible. At the top, informed judgment from peers and more-senior leaders matters: do they recognize work of that level, and why? He compares it to the qualitative recognition involved in academic seniority. The point is not that all evaluation is arbitrary, but that a list of tasks cannot fully represent exceptional and varied contributions.

Source: 00:00–05:37 ↗

QWhat if a strong E7 has no E8 or E9 nearby to learn from or assess them?

Philip Su

Su recognizes the problem both in small companies and in weaker teams inside huge organizations. Being the strongest local person can distort self-calibration or remove opportunities to observe better judgment. He recommends an environment where there is room to grow alongside strong colleagues, rather than treating being locally best as the only goal.

At very high levels, merely copying another senior person may not work because their archetype and strengths can differ from yours. He favors access to a coach who participates in the relevant promotion decisions and can give a qualitative assessment. That person can explain where the work remains short of the bar and help discuss what stronger work would look like. The desired input is specific feedback, not an assumption that proximity to a prestigious title automatically produces growth.

Source: 05:38–08:03 ↗

QWhat scope of work contributed to your own E9 promotion?

Philip Su

Su helped start Meta’s London engineering presence with twelve people and, over roughly four or five years, grow it to around four or five hundred. He describes managing the strategic and organizational transitions as the site expanded. A team of twelve could be run well by a capable engineering manager; several orders of magnitude of growth made problems more varied and answers less clear-cut.

One example was planning London internships and headcount based on anticipated visa constraints affecting future full-time arrivals in Menlo Park. He used data to recommend decisions roughly eighteen months before their consequences. Another was examining the site’s seniority distribution and whether engineers were developing at appropriate rates, rather than only checking each person’s nominal level.

The increased scope involved both breadth of people affected and the time horizon of judgment. He presents a collection of such decisions as the promotion story rather than naming one isolated code change or asserting that simply growing a site guarantees the same level.

Source: 08:04–10:36 ↗
Several ways for senior scope to grow
DimensionWhat Su emphasizes
BreadthCoordinate and influence a wider collection of people and decisions.
DepthSolve qualitative technical problems that adding less-senior engineers cannot reproduce.
IntegrationCombine many kinds of work where a strong generalist matters.
Time horizonUse evidence now to choose actions whose effects arrive much later.

Section 48 · lesson

Staff engineering begins with leadership beyond your own tasks

Peterman introduces staff engineering through scope, influence, and the individual-contributor career path.

A career branch, not an obligatory next promotion

Peterman describes a common progression from entry-level through mid-level to senior engineering. At many companies, senior can be a sustainable destination as well as a branching point: an engineer may continue on the individual-contributor ladder or move into management. He presents this as a broad framing, not a universal set of titles or a guarantee that every company organizes careers the same way.

Source: 00:00–00:41 ↗

Lead while remaining an individual contributor

In his framing, staff is the first individual-contributor level at which leadership is unavoidable. You can remain an engineer without becoming a people manager, but you must help other people and projects succeed. The promotion is difficult precisely because it is a change in scope and behavior, not merely recognition for writing more code.

Source: 00:43–01:31 ↗

Use engineering to extend your impact

He emphasizes the unusual scope of the engineering path: tools, systems, and methods can increase the effectiveness of both an individual and many other people. This creates a route to greater influence and compensation outside management. His comparison with other professions is an illustration of that idea, rather than a comprehensive claim about their career ladders.

Source: 01:33–02:14 ↗

Section 49 · interview

Adrien Friggeri: Data Tooling, Promotions, and Scope at Meta

Adrien Friggeri traces a path from a Facebook data science team through Instagram experiments, internal developer tools, and Clubhouse back to Meta, and explains how he built promotions and scope through impact and early agreement.

Adrien's view: impact and early agreement matter more than titles

Adrien Friggeri describes moving from a Facebook data science team to Instagram experiments, internal developer tools, Clubhouse, and back to Meta, where he worked on smart glasses. His view is that impact and early agreement with managers matter more than titles, and that sharing credit builds a career. He calls not joining Instagram's team one of his biggest career mistakes. Editorial framing: the interview runs in career order, and the host asks each question.

Source: 00:03–55:23 ↗

QWhat was the first team you joined, and why did you pick it?

Adrien Friggeri

Adrien says he was pre-allocated to a team then called data science, around 2011 or 2012, because of his PhD in social network analysis. Big data was emerging, and the team did early A/B testing at scale, measurement, and the data pipelines behind company counts. He joined a group of about 20 people, and the team joked that its work was mostly large-scale counting.

Did you see yourself as a data scientist or a software engineer?
Adrien Friggeri

His manager told him that software engineers have power at the company and should not box themselves into a narrow area. Adrien has always considered himself a software engineer, though his titles varied. Around 2014, product analytics roles were renamed data scientist, and the group grew from about 20 or 30 PhD data scientists to about 500, mostly doing product analytics. That caused an identity crisis, but he says impact mattered more than the title.

Source: 02:05–03:50 ↗
What was the difference between the old data science function and product analytics today?
Adrien Friggeri

Adrien says the earlier data scientists built the A/B testing tools and defined the algorithms and sampling methods. Today's data scientists mostly use those tools, which let the function scale.

His first project studied how rumors spread, meaning memes rather than fake news, with researchers including one who later became his manager. False rumors spread faster than true ones, and pointing out a falsehood did not really limit spread. The work took six to eight months and produced two or three papers, and it changed how much reshares were weighted in News Feed.

Source: 03:52–07:21 ↗
Source: 00:43–02:03 ↗

QWhat was the story behind your first senior-level promotion, at Instagram?

Adrien Friggeri

After the rumor work, Adrien met Instagram's co-founder and CTO. Facebook had acquired Instagram in September 2012, and the core team had about 30 people. Instagram had no personalization and no A/B testing. He started with the Explore tab, adding personalization, and needed a way to measure whether it worked. Product leaders said they had bigger priorities during Instagram's move from AWS to Facebook infrastructure.

He built the testing system anyway, with a product manager giving cover. He reused Facebook's system. Because Instagram ran on different infrastructure, he added a custom Facebook API endpoint, allowlisted to Instagram's app ID, to log exposures. He calls that hacky and probably expensive. He also added user hashing, connected the logs to the data warehouse, ran a server-side A/A test, and worked with mobile engineers on small experiments.

He says he did not know promotions existed. He was an IC4, and when his manager announced an IC5 promotion, he had to ask what the level meant. He then handed the A/B testing system to a newly created team that owned it.

Was reaching out to senior people and peers unusual early in your career?
Adrien Friggeri

Adrien says early Facebook was bottom-up: if you needed something you could not do alone, you found someone to help. In his first six months he joined about six hackathons, usually on Thursday evenings, working through the night on projects unrelated to his day job. He says that was the culture.

Source: 12:43–14:04 ↗
Source: 07:24–12:41 ↗

QWere there cultural differences between the early Instagram team and Facebook?

Adrien Friggeri

Adrien says he never officially joined the Instagram team. His data science group worked like consultants, embedding in other teams while his reporting line stayed the same, and he had two managers in his first few years. Instagram felt like a startup within a startup. Facebook had about 2,000 employees, and the core Instagram team of 30 to 40 people fit in one conference room, with a focus on design and craft over data.

What do you mean by your biggest career mistake, and where would your career be if you had joined Instagram?
Adrien Friggeri

He calls not joining Instagram one of his biggest career mistakes, but not a serious regret. His career might have grown faster, since colleagues who stayed reached senior levels sooner. He calls it a road not taken and says the counterfactual is hard to know.

Source: 15:43–16:33 ↗
Source: 14:05–15:42 ↗

QCan you tell the story behind your IC7, or senior staff, promotion?

Adrien Friggeri

Adrien worked on projects that brought data to non-data teams. One project to count users of a Facebook product needed machine learning and inference, but the tools were poor. He built a library to run data pipelines inside the machine learning framework. He says a pipeline that took about 300 lines in a standard system could take about 20 with the library. That convinced him to build tools that help others move faster.

Half the company used Jupyter and half used RStudio, and setup depended on outdated wikis. He proposed that everyone have a Jupyter instance, pitched a two-to-three-month trial to his manager, and built the first version of Bento. At first it was only a setup script. The vision was to connect it to company tools, so a user could open a browser, type Bento, and get a notebook with internal libraries ready.

Bento on demand later let users request a temporary instance instead of a shared dev server. Adrien helped lead the work and built the team by hiring people who were already building tools on their own time. He became a tech lead manager and was promoted to TLM2, which he says is equivalent to senior manager and to senior staff engineer in the industry.

Source: 16:35–22:05 ↗

QWhat is the step-by-step process for getting internal tooling from an idea to something everyone uses?

Adrien Friggeri

Adrien says Bento did not try to win adoption within existing workflows. The team targeted bootcamp, the onboarding program for new hires, and told everyone who worked with data that this was the way to set up. The company was growing fast, so many newcomers did not know the legacy systems, and others followed their peers onto the new tool.

The team also maintained legacy setups that had gone unmaintained. Doing that built trust with users.

Was the approach an easy sell because the company was growing, and did leadership support matter too?
Adrien Friggeri

Adrien summarizes the approach in two steps. First, use network effects to get a group of users through an easy path. Second, give value to people on legacy systems. Once trust was built, the team offered Bento features in place of a 25-step manual recipe. The host notes that developer tools usually need people to leave something they already use, but new hires in a growing company choose on a fresh slate, so the product may have been an easy sell.

Adrien also went to the head of analytics and another leader, said teams had real pain, and offered help. One leader said it was a good first step, but there were about 20 other things to fix. They agreed to take it one step at a time. Adrien then moved into the developer infrastructure organization to build a team focused on data developer tools, since no team then built tools for data science and machine learning.

Source: 23:55–25:55 ↗
Source: 22:07–23:53 ↗

QYou took on a performance risk to build something that could flop. Is that harder today, and how should someone take risks for bigger rewards?

Adrien Friggeri

Adrien says the stakes for underperforming are higher now, but the approach is the same. Align with your manager first, because people are judged against expectations. He told his manager he would step away from assigned work and asked for two or three months to explore the idea. He called it a calculated risk that the team agreed to.

He thinks doing your own project in secret is riskier, since you can show up after three months with a result nobody knew about. His advice is to overcommunicate and be ready to hear no. Later, when he tried to build consensus for other ideas, he was sometimes told no.

Source: 25:58–28:10 ↗

QWhat was the thinking behind moving into a tech lead manager role?

Adrien Friggeri

The team was building a product that had to scale, and it needed more people. Adrien could hire a manager with a different vision or try management himself. The move was driven by a wish to lead the team he had assembled, not by a plan to become a manager. The team needed a manager, and he became that manager.

Source: 28:12–29:00 ↗

QAfter reaching IC7, you left Meta to start your own company. What was the thinking, and how did it go?

Adrien Friggeri

Adrien had spent about seven years at the company, and he admits some hubris. He had built a platform used by about 60 percent of people doing data there, and he thought the outside world would need one too. He found he was not an entrepreneur at that time. He liked deep technical problems and had underestimated the work of rebuilding alone what a team of six had built over two years. He jokes that he took a sabbatical instead of starting a company.

What were the skill gaps between being a successful tech lead and being an entrepreneur?
Adrien Friggeri

An entrepreneur must delegate the hard parts. Adrien says that whenever something got interesting, he would have to hand it to someone else, leaving his own involvement superficial. He was not drawn to the work of getting people to use the product.

Source: 30:51–31:33 ↗
After the sabbatical, what led you back to Meta?
Adrien Friggeri

When the pandemic hit, Adrien was stuck in a small New York apartment. He bought a house in Denver and needed a stable job. He had several offers, but returned mainly to work with a director he admired, who had run an early Facebook open source program and was willing to hire him. The interview was behavioral, since he was returning.

Source: 31:35–32:50 ↗
Source: 29:03–30:49 ↗

QWhat did you do after returning to Meta, and why did you join Clubhouse?

Adrien Friggeri

Adrien returned in the summer of 2020 and spent about seven months on data infrastructure. A friend then connected him with a Clubhouse co-founder, as the app was growing fast. He was not serious at first, but the hype made it exciting. He joined when the company had about 10 or 11 people.

What did you contribute at Clubhouse?
Adrien Friggeri

He joined to help the data stack. There was no machine learning and no machine-learned feed ranking, and the notifications were spammy. He built the early analytics systems, including A/B testing so the team could measure its work, and introduced machine learning to filter notifications.

Source: 33:52–34:38 ↗
What was the internal culture like?
Adrien Friggeri

Adrien describes it as very hands-on, with eager, talented, self-driven engineers. Many came from Coinbase or Facebook, and they wanted to build an authentic social network.

Source: 34:39–35:07 ↗
Source: 32:51–33:51 ↗

QAfter Clubhouse, you went back to Meta a second time. Why?

Adrien Friggeri

Adrien had unfinished business at Meta and seriously considered an offer from Apple. He chose Meta for two reasons. A former manager, then the engineering director behind Ray-Ban Stories, wanted to work with him again. He had also never worked on a product or on hardware, and wanted to move beyond being the data person.

Was a referral through a trusted former manager the key to the role?
Adrien Friggeri

Not entirely. He had no interest in a tech lead role from the start, and returned as an IC7. After Ray-Ban Stories launched in September 2021, it had quality and growth problems, so he reviewed the growth data for about a year, which built trust with the organization. After a reorg at the end of 2022, he asked to move to the smart glasses project. He had no hardware experience, but argued that his product sense justified it.

Another engineer was the tech lead for the whole program. Over a couple of years, Adrien took on more scope and supervised the user experiences across that hardware line, which later included wearables.

Source: 36:19–38:50 ↗
Source: 35:09–36:07 ↗

QWere there growing pains in switching into the new domain?

Adrien Friggeri

Adrien says the organization was growing and maturing, so the pains reached him early. He struggled with the long lead times of hardware work, including validation and getting products into users' hands. It got easier once internal dogfooding started and feedback arrived.

Source: 38:51–39:41 ↗

QWhat advice do you have for ramping up in a completely different domain?

Adrien Friggeri

He starts with a social network exploration: talk to people and ask who else to talk to. Do not fear basic questions, since everyone knows a newcomer is new. He also gets hands-on. Although he never officially worked on firmware, he read the code and made a few changes. He then picks a hard problem he roughly knows how to solve, because he learns by doing.

Source: 39:43–40:48 ↗

QWhat scope got you promoted to IC8, principal engineer?

Adrien Friggeri

Adrien became responsible for all experiences on a device, across dozens of teams and about 35 product managers. Partner teams owned the operating system layer. His job was coordination, architecture, and hitting milestones. For a product such as Ray-Ban Meta, the experiences include on-device AI, music, photo capture, and the companion app.

IC5 surprised him. For IC6 he asked his manager to put him forward, and IC7 took a couple of review cycles. For IC8, his manager had never run that promotion, so they worked out the packet together, and Adrien wrote much of it. He built consensus with several vice presidents early, and asked a director for monthly check-ins on the gap to that level. Six months later, the director supported the promotion because he had been involved throughout.

Is identifying champions even more important for the highest-level promotions?
Adrien Friggeri

The host says champions matter most at the highest levels. Adrien agrees, but says the underlying impact still has to be there. Building consensus early keeps calibration from becoming a debate. His IC promotion took two cycles, and in the first, his manager socialized the idea without formally nominating him.

Source: 44:07–45:18 ↗
Source: 40:51–44:05 ↗

QWhen a role is limited to one person, such as the only tech lead for a program, how do you secure scope?

Adrien Friggeri

One engineer was the tech lead for the whole program. Adrien saw that much of the experience work could be handled by someone focused on it. He took it off the lead's plate so the lead could focus on the wider program, while the lead kept the systems work. The two built trust. After about a year, Adrien asked leadership to formally recognize the role, so he could describe it in one sentence.

He rejects the idea that taking scope is stealing. It is a problem only if you do not talk to the person. He asked the engineer first, who agreed, and he asked again later about a related area. Overcommunicating is the consistent theme.

Is giving up scope a win for the person who gives it away?
Adrien Friggeri

The host suggests that handing off scope can help a senior engineer grow into a bigger role. Adrien agrees, and says he has pushed junior engineers to take ownership, which helps them and lets him delegate more.

Source: 48:42–49:29 ↗
Source: 45:20–48:36 ↗

QYou have a skill set heavy in software engineering and data. What career experiences were possible only through that mix?

Adrien Friggeri

Adrien says he has always aimed to be well-rounded, with product and design sense as well as engineering and data. He calls himself a product hybrid, able to hold a deep product conversation and debug firmware the next day. He cites an author's view, attributed to Robert Heinlein, that a competent person should be able to do many things, and says he takes that to heart.

In wearables he built prototypes, designed his own circuit boards, and hacked together demos that were not production ready. He is not a hardware engineer, but those prototypes let him bring something concrete to product conversations.

Source: 49:32–51:39 ↗

QYour career has been a series of bumping into the right people. Do you have tips for maximizing luck with people opportunities?

Adrien Friggeri

Adrien says none of his work happened in a vacuum. Early on he had rough edges and strong opinions that did not help him, and he learned that people succeed together. He says trust and respect mean people show up when you need them, but you should not help others in order to get something back.

He also says do not be afraid to ask. For career changes, he never applied through a job website. He reached out to people he knew and asked for small favors, with an easy way to say no. People are busy, so silence is not a verdict. On luck, he says taking more shots increases the odds.

Source: 51:41–54:34 ↗

QIf you could go back to yourself right after graduating college in France, what advice would you give?

Adrien Friggeri

He would say to be a good person, invest in things that are fun, and invest in relationships with co-workers. Credit matters less than it seems, since everyone gets credit for something. He was very credit-driven early on. He would also tell himself to be patient, since he sometimes pushed for promotions before he was ready, and to stay curious and enjoy the work.

Source: 54:36–55:23 ↗

Section 50 · interview

Bryan Cantrill: Sun, Stack Ranking, Competing with AWS, Oxide, and Regrets

Bryan Cantrill, a former Sun distinguished engineer and co-founder of Oxide, argues that meaning, team and honest dealing with customers matter more than rank, titles or money.

Cantrill's view: meaning, team and trust last longer than rank, titles and money

Bryan Cantrill was a distinguished engineer at Sun Microsystems, later CTO at Joyent, and in 2019 co-founded Oxide. In this interview he argues that titles, ranks and financial independence are weak sources of meaning. In his account, the best periods of his career came from small teams doing work that looked too hard, and from companies that told their customers the truth. He supports this with his experience of Sun's rating and promotion rules, his objection to stack ranking, the Oracle takeover, competing with Amazon, and the founding of Oxide. The closing section reads back some of his old posts and asks about his regrets. All of it is Cantrill's own recollection and opinion. The host's questions set the order.

Source: 00:02–1:20:40 ↗

QWhat was the industry like when you started, and was there a FAANG equivalent?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says every era has a hot group of companies. In the 1960s, he notes, it was IBM and the group called the BUNCH: Burroughs, UNIVAC, NCR, Control Data and Honeywell. He graduated in 1996 and interviewed in 1995. On-campus recruiting was active, and Microsoft was dominant. He decided, as a point of principle, that he would not work there.

Why did you rule out Microsoft?
Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill grew up in the personal-computer era of the 1980s. DOS had no memory protection, so a misbehaving application could reboot the machine and an unsaved English paper was gone. At university, which he entered in 1992, he learned that the microprocessor offered memory protection that DOS did not use. He says Windows did not use it either, though he adds that Windows is complicated.

Then he met Unix on a workstation. At 18 he had a shell, an FTP session, a compile and a game download all running at once in separate windows. He found that mind-bending. Looking back, he says Microsoft was not really an operating system company. In his view its core strength was compilers. He says the Mac of that period was cleaner but also lacked memory protection, which he found unconscionable.

What was the abuse, in short?
Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill describes a pattern. Microsoft would announce that a promising company's application would become a feature of the operating system, and then the feature would not appear. He calls this vaporware and says Microsoft perfected it. He says Word was weak at first, improved over time, and displaced WordPerfect partly because Microsoft bundled it with the operating system.

He stresses that the anti-competitive behaviour was not only his opinion. He describes it as a judicial finding of fact. He adds that the company changed after the late-1990s antitrust case and as Gates reached middle age. He still would not have worked there.

QYour goodbye post said you did not particularly want to work for Sun. What changed your mind?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says the people he met in other Sun groups were fine but not energizing. He was used to being the youngest person in a group, but he wanted colleagues who shared his passion. Meeting Kevin Clark and Jeff Bonwick was, in his words, a bolt of lightning. Both were energized and saw the same potential for operating systems to be innovative. Both wanted to rip out broken code and replace it with beautiful code.

He remembers coming back from that trip certain that he would take an offer from Sun.

QWhat was the career ladder at Sun like?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill describes the ladder as member of technical staff, staff engineer, senior staff engineer and distinguished engineer. He thinks Sun may have originated these titles, though Xerox PARC is another possibility. He is not sure.

He tells a story about business cards. Early on he did not know his rank and assumed that an engineer on staff was a staff engineer. Colleagues soon told him that would be like claiming tenure. He was an MTS3. Most college hires started at MTS2, but he says he was an unusual hire. He had done kernel development at a company in Canada for two summers. After school in the Northeast and work in Canada, he wanted to come out to Silicon Valley.

Source: 08:15–10:09 ↗

QWhat stands out in your growth from MTS3 to distinguished engineer?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says he never focused on grade, rank or promotion. He would rather be underpromoted than overpromoted, and he did not want to do work performatively. He did what he judged most important: solving customers' problems and making the operating system what he believed it could be. Sun, he says, was accommodating of headstrong engineers. In 1996 he thought Sun was the only company still invested in its own operating system, and work on the Solaris kernel was energizing. Promotions simply happened along the way.

He also reports a plain finding about formal reviews: they never made him perform better. In his view a review measures performance, while it should be about feedback that helps everyone be the best they can. He found the annual cadence broken. His reviews looked like his own self-review with grammatical errors added. The highlights of his career were never promotions. They were a significant body of work, a hard bug, or working with someone on something they thought impossible.

He describes Sun's rating tiers as superlative, excellent and good, with a rough split he recalls as about 70, 20 and 10 percent. A superlative rating forced a promotion, and Sun did not want promotions faster than every 18 months. So managers gave apologetic reviews that rated clearly better work as merely excellent. Cantrill says he did not care. He was promoted to staff engineer, by his estimate around 2001, just as the dot-com crash hit. The company bonus, which depended on company performance, was zero from then on.

Cantrill calls the process for becoming a distinguished engineer regrettable and stupid, though he is not describing his own promotion. He says there were two routes. One was a vote by existing distinguished engineers, which he calls a political process and a country club, and a bad place for democracy. The other was an acqui-hire in which the acquired company's CTO arrived with the title. He says people could tell the homegrown ones from the acqui-hired ones.

His own case, as he understands it second-hand, was presented by Sun's CTO, Greg Papadopoulos, who had chartered the Fishworks group that built a storage product. Papadopoulos reportedly said he expected no one to vote against it, and the vote was unanimous. Cantrill says he is grateful and did not want to deal with the politics. He sees ranks as corrosive, and Oxide has none.

Source: 10:11–19:33 ↗

QIf an ambitious new graduate wants to become a distinguished engineer, should they focus on the work or ask their manager what the next level needs?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill would steer them to a third path. He would ask why they want the title, since reaching it does not give meaning, and he calls it a recipe for a midlife crisis. He would try to find what drives meaning for that person and what fuels them. His aim is to stop them depending on external validation. He would introduce them to miserable distinguished engineers, and to miserable wealthy people, to show that the title or the money cannot be the answer. In his view, once the person finds the real driver, the work and the promotions follow.

What if the mentee says they want financial independence?
Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill first asks what that means in such a well-paid field. He points out that anyone in San Francisco can buy an excellent six-dollar coffee. If it means never needing to work for money again, he asks, what then? If the meaningful thing does not pay, he says to balance it with a career. He thinks it is a mistake to plan to reach independence first and pursue meaning afterwards.

He draws on the dot-com boom and bust. Most people around him made money on paper and lost it. He argues the bust helped, because people who had come for the money left and the rest had to remember why they came. He knew people who made fortunes in the boom, were not much interested in tech, and struggled in the next decade, wondering what to do. One bought several houses and found them a pain. He says too many people work in the industry only to leave it. His advice is to go and do the thing you would do after leaving. His example was quitting a job at Meta to become a podcaster, and the host answers that they did just that.

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says the same problem appears in engineering even when the goal has meaning. He calls it postpartum engineering. When a team is focused on shipping something, shipping becomes the lens for everything. He feared this after Oxide shipped its first rack, when people who had pulled hard for a long time might ask what comes next. He adds that some people respond to the emptiness by chasing even more money. He names Larry Ellison as an example of a result people should not aspire to.

What about someone who is genuinely happy doing nothing?

Cantrill jokes that anyone with a billion dollars would simply do that every day. He then tells a story about one of the earliest Yahoo employees he knew. This person was hired as a web surfer to help curate Yahoo's directory of links, in the era before search engines. The person received an equity grant on joining, never got another, and made a fortune. Cantrill says the person was never promoted, complained that the job was awful, and by the end owned only one topic, snowboarding in Northern California. QSun's ratings had no bad tier. Why not, and what do you think of stack ranking?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says Sun did not use performance improvement plans or the rank-and-yank approach Intel was known for, which is stack ranking. He calls stack ranking organizational cancer, especially when a bottom percentage is terminated. In his view it rewards managers for keeping dead weight on their teams, so that someone always ranks last.

He says this happened at Sun anyway. Someone once took him aside and said that a weak colleague was in his interest, because that person always received a good rating, which left room for others to receive excellent or superlative ones. Cantrill calls this a set of perverse incentives. His main objection is that stack ranking teaches people their teammates are adversaries. He believes teams do extraordinary things, that everyone should want to serve the team, and that stack ranking works against that.

Sun's stock fell 98 percent. Was there no push for mass layoffs?
Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says the stock traded below the company's cash at one point. Sun resisted layoffs for a while, and Scott McNealy famously did not want to lay people off. Cantrill calls that a mistake and says McNealy waited too long. Once layoffs began, Cantrill recalls counting about 35 rounds over roughly eight years. Some were small, some large.

Employees could pull the staff directory programmatically from the internal organization tool. They ran a daily script they called the obits, which showed who had left. Some days it showed 1,500 or 3,000 people.

Source: 31:36–32:59 ↗
Was the company aware that you had that data?
Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says Sun's strength and weakness was that no one was truly in charge, so it would not have surprised him if people knew. He thinks Sun was a transparent company and that using the organization tool broke no policy. It was a way of knowing what was happening.

He adds that the whole industry was in the same position. He dates the dot-com collapse to the end of 2000, says September 11 made it worse, and says tech was basically dead for about five years. He places the founding of Y Combinator around 2006 and suggests it reflected a capital deficit, though he defers to Paul Graham on that. He calls the period bleak.
