QWhy was the Oracle acquisition of Sun so controversial?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says it was dramatic. He points to an SEC filing showing IBM and HP each trying to buy Sun and sabotage the other, partly to punish a competitor. Oracle then swept in. He does not see the acquisition itself as the controversial part. He sees Oracle as the issue. He says Oracle has little depth and compares it to an octopus that is good at feeding itself.

By contrast, he says Sun tried to do right by its customers and to solve hard technical problems with commercial relevance. It gave engineers great freedom and rewarded technical boldness. NFS, SPARC, Java, Solaris and the technologies he worked on all came from that passion and independence.

Cantrill says Sun often failed at business execution, so he hoped Oracle would bring that skill. He concluded he had overestimated Oracle. In his view Oracle focuses on its own profitability. It aims to gain something like a natural monopoly over its customers, suffocate competition and then raise the rent. He did not want to work for a company like that.

In your 2011 talk you got through a slide without crying and said Oracle screws customers and lies. What is the lying?
Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says Oracle has made many promises to customers that it does not keep and has not earned their trust. He says that if you ask customers whether they trust Oracle, the answer is no. He adds that the slide he nearly cried over was about Sun, not Oracle. It carried Scott McNealy's epitaph for Sun: “Kicked butt, had fun, didn't cheat, loved our customers, changed computing forever.” That still chokes him up because he says it was true. Oxide adopted it as its own mission.

QWere top engineers confiding in one another that they had to leave Sun?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says it was less like confiding and more like running from a burning building. Before the deal closed, some employees were not going to become Oracle employees and would be laid off with rich severance. He describes a line of people wanting to be on the list. He says he was not one of them. He says some people still resent colleagues who left that way. He was at the Fishworks group in San Francisco and was somewhat optimistic that the best of both companies could be combined. He quit after about 45 days because he could not work there in good conscience.

What did you see that made you leave so quickly?
Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says it was clear this was a very different company. After he decided to leave, he says, Oracle gave him several more reasons. The one he stresses is customer trust. Sun, for all its faults, had its customers' trust. They rooted for Sun to prevail because Sun was straight with them even when that did not serve its own interest. He says Oracle does not have that trust.

He realized he could not work for a company with such profound distrust. It eroded his sense of meaning. He felt ashamed to work at Oracle. At Sun he had sometimes felt embarrassed, but never ashamed.

How do you get yourself laid off?

Cantrill says there is no web form. You tell your manager to put you on the list, or you whisper around to learn what is going on. He says it was not about underperformance. It was about saying that Oracle had no interest in your work. Then, he jokes, if Oracle shows interest in what you do, you are upset.

QYou said Bezos is the apex predator of capitalism. What makes you say that?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill, whose company Joyent competed with AWS, says Amazon at its height was relentless in execution. He says it hit the mother lode, and not only by luck. It allowed S3 to be developed, built EC2, and realized it was onto cloud computing before anyone else. He calls the re:Invent conferences from about 2010 to 2015 relentless. Each one brought price cuts and many new services, which customers loved.

He adds that Amazon did not break out AWS revenue and declined to discuss it with analysts. Cantrill says this helped spread the idea that cloud was a terrible business, so people stayed out. Joyent ran a public cloud and knew the margins were great. He says Amazon is no longer what it was in those years. He is not sure when the last re:Invent price cut was, but it has been a while.

Why keep pressing instead of milking the market?
Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says Bezos is not merely a predator but an apex predator, and that is what made him so good. He pressed his advantage so no one could compete and no one wanted to enter the business. In Cantrill's view he did it the right way, by giving a great product at a reasonable price. Cantrill calls that a win-win and says it was essential for cloud-born companies in that era. He says it was very hard to compete with Amazon. Joyent had to find lanes where it could, and he calls the experience brutal given Amazon's extraordinary execution.

QWhat is the difference between VP of engineering and CTO?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill gave a talk at Joyent on this contrast, but he is not sure how much he buys the difference now. In both roles you are an engineering leader. He says a CTO is more outward-looking, spending a lot of time on the road with customers, and jokes that the title could stand for chief travel officer. A VP of engineering tends to focus more on the mechanics of an engineering organization.

He joined Joyent as VP of engineering because the company already had a CTO, and he says he did not particularly care about titles, as at Sun. When the founding CTO left, he did care that the company not hire externally for the role. He later became CTO.

Why not hire externally?
Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says an outside CTO was not what the company needed at that point. The company had removed its CEO and needed a terrific CEO, which he says it later got.

QWhat is the story behind starting your own company?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill knew he wanted to start a company with Steve, who had come up on the sales and go-to-market side. Cantrill had not spoken to Steve before joining Joyent, and found him amazing once they worked together. They both felt they would do whatever came next together. Their long walks in San Francisco produced, in Cantrill's words, one bad idea after another. They then tried to find ideas investors would fund, which were not ideas from their hearts. He recommends that others not do this, though he says it is understandable.

The turning point came when Cantrill went to look up a prominent venture capitalist's email address. He had known this person since early in the person's career and had lunch with him periodically. The last email, about 18 months earlier, had said he would fund anything Cantrill put in front of him. Cantrill told Steve to go big and do what was in their hearts: build the computer they wanted, a rack-scale machine. Cantrill says this was in their marrow, after 14 years at Sun for him, a decade at Dell for Steve, and a decade together at Joyent. They envisioned rack-scale design, their own boards and switch, and all the software. A catalyst was seeing Facebook's Tioga Pass at the Open Compute summit, which he likens to discovering Unix after living with DOS. He says the idea was contrarian, and contrarian ideas appeal to venture investors.

After talking to many investors, he went back to that same one. About 45 seconds into the pitch the investor said that if this was a computer company, he wanted nothing to do with it. Cantrill pointed to the old email, and the investor replied that it did not sound like him. Cantrill says he expected the refusal. In his view, an investor who has had big zeros in a similar area is no longer blind to the odds, and this one had two big zeros, one resembling Oxide. When the investor asked how he could help, Cantrill had a concrete request: an introduction to the founders of that failed company. He advises always having an answer to that question.

The founder explained what went wrong. Cantrill says the company built something smaller than a rack, which he compares to very early Nitro. It found one customer, a huge bank, that wanted it only for around six Active Directory servers. The company raised money and hired a large sales team, and the market was too small for the team. It was acquired, but Cantrill says the founder was left bitter and felt the investors had put in too much capital at the wrong time. That founder called Oxide a “suicide mission.” Cantrill says he wrote the phrase in a notebook and underlined it.

Source: 49:56–59:06 ↗

QWhen I think of rack-scale compute these days I think of racks of GPUs. Are you building that?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says Oxide set out in 2019, when GPGPUs existed but were not the focus. The focus was general-purpose compute, storage and networking. He says people kept asking about accelerators. Oxide wants to build systems from first principles, with transparency at the hardware and software interface, and to write the lowest layer of software. Cantrill calls the product hardware and software co-design. He says that does not work with Nvidia, a proprietary company that executes well and wants to own the whole stack.

As he sees it, there were two doors, compete with Nvidia or partner with it, and he wanted neither. He adds that competing is becoming more plausible. So Oxide focused on general-purpose CPUs. He finds it surprising that the GPU field is crowded and gory, while on the CPU side HP, Dell and similar vendors keep selling the same thing, leaving Oxide alone with a hardware and software product. Customers who own many GPUs also own many CPUs, he says, because AI and high-performance workloads attach a lot of general-purpose compute to the special-purpose compute. He thinks Oxide will build an accelerator at some point. He says he has been calling it 18 months away for a while, and that it is not in the foreseeable future.

QIn 1996, as a new graduate, you replied to a long technical post by David S. Miller with a personal jibe. What was the context, and what do you think now?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill puts it firmly in the regret column. He says he has few regrets in his career. He was about 22 and had no idea the post would last 30 years. He explains that the jibe referred to an obscure Saturday Night Live sketch in which William Shatner, at a Star Trek convention, tells fans to get a life. He says that does not make it better, and he is not defending it. It was a mistake.

Miller had plenty to say in reply. Cantrill says he wrote a longer post taking Miller's points apart one by one. He has never met or talked to Miller, whom he calls a very talented person. He recalls reading in a book about Linux that Miller said a Sun engineer had put him back in his place. If that is Miller's account, Cantrill says it is generous to him. He hopes both of them regret it a little, as young and excitable people. He calls it a life lesson.

Source: 1:02:38–1:06:55 ↗

QIn 2022 you tweeted that failure at a startup is almost always bad leadership, not the team. Does that apply to Sun, which ultimately failed?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill does not remember writing the tweet, though he likes it and cannot recall what he was responding to. On Sun, he rejects the premise. Sun was founded in 1983 and was acquired around 2008 to 2009, by his dating. It was a public company in the Fortune 200. Many children went to college because their parents worked there. He says it did not succeed to the scope of its own ambition, but he regards Sun as a success, not a failure.

Could different leadership have changed how Sun ended?
Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill thinks so. He lists several reasons Sun did not survive as an independent company. It had become strung out on the high margins of the dot-com boom and never fully got off them. It embraced x86 too late. The company became fractured, and the layoffs did not help. He thought Fishworks could have been an exemplar of the products an independent Sun might develop, but that would have required leadership strongly interested in that change, and Sun did not have it.

In hindsight, he says, it was probably time for a change. He compares it to a forest fire in a healthy forest, which is part of the life cycle and allows rebirth. He concludes that Sun had succeeded, had run its course, and had its time.

QIn 2022 you also wrote that Musk had no idea what he was doing at Twitter. Do you still agree?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says yes, and says he feels dirty being specific about it. He sees rampant bad behaviour on the platform. He credits Community Notes and describes nearly everything else as a tire fire.

What is the number one problem?
Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says it is the reason Oxide does not engage on Twitter. He says he cannot have an Oxide post sitting next to some of the posts he has seen, which include extreme racism, antisemitism and anti-Islam hatred. He rejects the free-speech defence. QYou have lived through several booms and busts. What advice do you have for people in today's market?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says booms and busts are endemic to the industry. His grandfather was a petroleum engineer, so he grew up hearing about plants and pipelines built and then shut down as oil prices moved. When he moved out here he thought software was immune. He says it is not. He sees the swings as partly endearing, because the industry gets ahead of itself both in optimism and in pessimism.

His advice is to be careful about listening to others and to be your own judge. In 1996 people told him operating systems were done, and he is glad he did not listen. People said you could not start a computer company in 2019, and he is glad Oxide ignored them. He says the same applies to software-as-a-service today. There is truth in the claim that LLM-assisted coding will squeeze such companies, but if your heart is in it, treat both the pessimism and the optimism with a grain of salt. Do not choose a field because it is hot. He finds the current LLMs amazing, but says the reason to go in should be intrinsic. He closes by borrowing Steve Jobs's line about putting a dent in the universe.

Source: 1:11:57–1:14:40 ↗

QAlmost everything in your career seems driven by fulfillment. Is there a time you would call the happiest?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says Oxide asks people when they have been happiest and why, for exactly this reason. For him it is not an era but moments, though he says he is pretty happy now. He recalls that a friend told him, during his walks with Steve, that he needed to answer why he wanted to start a company. It was not for financial return, which he says is not good life advice.

The answer was that his happiest moments came from working on a team where each person privately thought the task was too hard, and then everyone worked together, complimented one another and pulled it off. He had that feeling with the tracing work, at Fishworks, and a couple of times at Joyent, including the LX and Triton projects. Part of what drew him to Oxide's larger problem was the chance to attract such a team.

He says the organizational model for Oxide is a heist movie, with a safe cracker, a getaway driver and a demolitions expert, each skill arriving at the right moment. He and Steve share this team orientation, which he credits for how much Oxide has done with a small team.

QLooking back on your whole career, is there a top regret?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says he made an extraordinarily bad hire at Joyent, one he calls perhaps the worst hire in human history. He says the person had presented under an assumed name and had a serious criminal history, though he says that was not what made the person a bad employee. It was a bad experience, and also eye-opening, because he realized everything he had been doing about hiring was wrong.

After the situation was resolved, Joyent stripped hiring to the studs and rethought it from first principles. The result was a writing-intensive process that gets at intrinsic motivation, and it became the hiring process at Oxide. He says the extraordinary Oxide team is absolutely related to it, and he built it because he made the worst hire of all time. He says he needed that hire.

So you don't regret it?
Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says he does not regret it. He would not go back and remove it, because he thinks Oxide does not exist otherwise. He would have kept hiring naively, without rigor, and not selecting for values. He says he views many failures this way, as important and hard to remove. If he had a time machine, he says, he might remove the Usenet post, which he thinks would have no long-lasting consequences, but little else.

QIf you could go back to the start of your career, what advice would you give yourself?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill's answer is essentially not to mess anything up. He says he has been very lucky, in the right place at the right time many times, and that he trusted his gut when that was controversial. He would be scared to give his younger self advice, since he might tamper with a lucky career in which he worked with extraordinary colleagues. Section 51 · interview

Carey Nachenberg: From Symantec Fellow to Google X, Project Taste, and Imposter Syndrome

Nachenberg says that choosing impactful projects, focusing on other people's outcomes, communicating well and leaving jobs once learning stops mattered more to his career than raw intelligence, and that imposter syndrome held him back.

Impact, outcomes and communication outweigh raw intelligence

Nachenberg, a former Symantec fellow who later worked at Google X, Chronicle and Lyft and now teaches at UCLA, argues that career growth owes far more to project taste, focus on other people's outcomes, and communication than to raw intelligence. He traces his own rise at Symantec to choosing impactful projects nobody had assigned. He says imposter syndrome and a loss of confidence kept him in a comfortable job too long and later held him back at Google. The conversation ends with his views on how large language models (LLMs) change teaching, software engineering and product work, and with the advice he would give his younger self.

Source: 00:42–1:10:50 ↗

QCan you give the high-level story of your time at Symantec and how you grew to fellow?

Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg started in about 1992 as an intern at the Peter Norton Group, which Symantec later acquired. He thinks he was the first intern there and says the company had no desk for him, so he worked in the QA lab. By the time he left in 2016, he had gone from the most junior person to the most senior engineer at Symantec.

Did you set out to work in cyber security, or did it happen by chance?
Carey Nachenberg

By chance. Nachenberg first worked on a file-management utility, not security. In his third internship, Symantec bought an antivirus product and renamed it Norton Antivirus. The team that analyzed computer viruses needed an intern, and he was placed there with no experience.

Source: 02:43–03:21 ↗
Source: 01:27–02:42 ↗

QWhat did the career ladder look like at Symantec, and how did hiring work for someone as senior as you when you joined Google?

Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg says the levels tracked those at Google and Meta from junior engineer up to staff. They differed at the top, with distinguished engineer and fellow at Symantec. Google told him it could not hire a fellow without knowing how he would perform there. He was effectively downgraded to principal engineer, level 8, from what he says would have been about a level 10 and a vice president role at Symantec.

Was your hiring process tailored to your seniority?
Carey Nachenberg

Yes. Nachenberg did not apply. A former Symantec chief operating officer had moved into Google X, where a stealth project was starting, and invited him to talk to the team. He had a meet and greet with the founders in Venice, then about eight interviews in a day. He had an offer letter roughly six weeks later.

Source: 04:16–05:09 ↗
Did that loop include LeetCode-style coding, or was it mostly behavioral?
Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg does not recall any coding problems and thinks there was one design problem. Most questions were leadership-style: how he solved a hard problem, how he handles conflict, and where the field is going. Some sessions were effectively sales pitches about where Google X thought the world was heading. He believes the team already thought he was a good fit, so the day was mostly about going through the motions and selling him on the role.

Source: 05:10–06:26 ↗
Source: 03:21–04:14 ↗

QWhat do promotions at the highest levels look like?

Carey Nachenberg

At Symantec, Nachenberg says, promotions up to senior technical director were handled within the organization, provided a vice president or senior vice president agreed. Distinguished engineer and fellow went to a core group of technologists led by the chief technology officer. The group met quarterly, reviewed applications, and had candidates present their work. The aim was a consistent bar across the whole company, not division by division.

Was your promotion to fellow a big moment, or something you expected?
Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg skipped that process. After Symantec merged with Veritas, which already had a fellow role, the company needed to set the level. He was nominated without his knowledge, his portfolio was passed to the evaluators, and he was told he was a fellow.

QWhat set you apart from other engineers on the way to fellow?

Nachenberg credits impactful projects, not always the most technically difficult ones. He looked for gaps: things the company needed that no one was stepping up to do. Symantec in his early years was, in his words, the wild west, with no agile process and no engineers testing their own code. He was never handed a boxed-in project. Because he already knew the technology as an intern, he was told to work out what to do and do it, and he says he chose projects that landed, shipped and transferred into the product.

Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg says he looks for large business impact and for gaps. His example was polymorphic viruses, which mutated themselves into huge numbers of variants. Teams hand-wrote assembly to catch each variant, a process that took six months because the product shipped twice a year. New variants appeared the next day. He saw a need to respond faster, noted that such threats could not be found by searching for a string, and picked the problem. It became his master's thesis and then a product feature.

QCan you tell the story of Stuxnet, which you used in talks?

Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg calls Stuxnet unfathomable for its time: probably the first multiplatform malware discovered, reaching Windows machines and the controllers that ran centrifuge frequency converters. He recalls it used about six vulnerabilities, many of them unpatched zero-days. It hid itself on a USB drive, auto-launched, and hid its own logic on the controller. If someone downloaded the controller logic, it removed itself from the copy. If they uploaded updated logic, it reinserted itself.

Who do you think wrote it, and did you analyze the code?
Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg says it is fairly safe to say the Israeli and American governments, and he recalls coding styles that implicate both. He stresses he did not analyze Stuxnet himself. Early in his career he disassembled malware by hand, but later he built algorithms to detect it.

Did you write assembly at Symantec?
Carey Nachenberg

As an intern, yes, though most code was in C. The first antivirus engines were in assembly for speed. Nachenberg ported one to C after joining full time. It had less code and ran about five times faster, he says, because the original developers did not know algorithms. In his example, hash tables or binary search replace a linear scan over about 60,000 signatures, with no help from an optimizing compiler.

Nachenberg says it started as the stealth Project Lantern, with no fixed product. The team spent about six months deciding what to build, then built prototypes and an MVP. Before the product existed, they sat in customer security teams and watched where they struggled, which he found very useful.

The product, Backstory, treated security as a big-data problem. Firewalls, web proxies, DHCP and email systems produce huge logs. Nachenberg says a competing product forced customers to ingest a small fraction of that data and wait about 30 minutes per query. Chronicle ingested petabytes and indexed them, so an analyst could enter a file hash, IP address or file name and see affected devices and first and last infiltration in about two seconds. Nachenberg worked on the indexing.

Nachenberg says X aims to incubate viable businesses, give strong teams freedom and spin them out. Not at Symantec, where he could do what he liked. He thought about it at Google but concluded it would not help. QWhat project at Lyft were you most proud of?

Nachenberg says Lyft used the classic robotics architecture of hand-written decision algorithms with hand-tuned parameters, with neural networks used only for perception. He thought that was a dead end, citing conflicts such as switching from a lane-change routine to an avoidance routine, and parameters that interact in unpredictable ways. He says Tesla used the approach until recently.

He designed, with the team's old-school roboticists, an architecture that could host an end-to-end neural-network driver inside a safety layer. In his account the layer takes precedence, preventing collisions, stopping safely and following legal rules the network might miss. He guesses Waymo now uses end-to-end networks too, but says he does not know. He says the work was mostly influence, since he had no robotics degree and the roboticists resisted. They defined the approach together so that they could own it.

Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg says he lacks a good recipe and was not credited for this project; he says someone else took credit. He advises juniors to take notes when a project ends, recording accomplishments and metrics, which are hard to recall later. When writing a review, state what you did and its value without embellishing, and claim only your own parts, because committees notice overclaiming and it costs credibility. At senior levels it is harder, he says, because the work is soft power. He did not push his own credit so as not to alienate collaborators, and at review time he learned the team's manager was seen as having initiated the project. He says it still bothers him.

QHow did you become a lecturer at UCLA, and how do you make your lectures engaging?

Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg taught programming at Learning Tree around 1990 to 1991, including to DeVry staff. He also ran evening whiteboard sessions at UCLA as an undergraduate. Years later, a colleague at Symantec who lectured part time at UCLA told him to apply. Nachenberg assumed his lack of a PhD ruled him out. After months of silence, UCLA called in a panic when a lecturer dropped out, and he had two weeks to plan an undergraduate course. That was about 25 years ago.

For lectures, he designs for roughly the 30th to 50th percentile of the class, and uses himself, a slow learner, as the model. He asks what he would want to know on first meeting a topic, and what students are likely to be fuzzy on. He says he spends days with ChatGPT o3 simplifying concepts, then checks with Gemini and compares differences, because he finds good online material scarce and textbooks poor. He also wants students to enjoy class, so he adds humor, color and surprise.

Carey Nachenberg

Practice, says Nachenberg. He finds his own speaking declines within a year of not using it. He suggests giving a lunchroom talk about a project even when nothing requires it. People appreciate it, and you improve. He recalls giving his Stuxnet and malware talk privately inside X, after which colleagues said he was one of the smartest people they had met. He says people read good communication as intelligence, and it brings credit and opportunities.

QAre students cheating more with LLMs, and are they learning less?

Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg says last fall he allowed LLMs for autocomplete and simple, peripheral parts of projects. In retrospect he considers it a mistake, because students used them for much more than that. He saw large gaps between perfect project scores and poor exam results. He mentions a recent study on reduced brain connectivity when people use LLMs, but says he forgets the numbers. This fall he plans to allow LLMs for clarifying concepts, but not for projects.

He says plagiarism software compares every project with every other one, and LLM use shows up as shared word-for-word error messages, variable names and idioms. He adds that the latest models could probably earn about 95 percent on the projects, with poor code, because the course grades correctness, not code quality.

Source: 53:23–55:36 ↗

QShould people still get a software engineering degree as LLMs automate the work?

Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg says it depends on how the models develop, and he describes two scenarios. In the first, models stay very good but short of what he calls AGI programming: they solve tightly specified sub-problems and write tests, but need supervision on choices such as the algorithm used or a deep versus shallow copy. In that world, he says, software engineering stays a great field. Someone must read the code, understand the company's mission and standards, and decide what to fix. He thinks the ability to read and write code is valuable. He acknowledges that jobs are down now, probably partly because of LLMs.

In the second scenario, an AI could take on an L5-level project that takes weeks and do it correctly and securely. He says all bets are off in that world and the required skills differ.

What skills would matter in that second world?
Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg says engineers, or perhaps no longer engineers, would focus on what to build and why, not how. The best would deeply understand a customer's pains and how the customer measures success, then communicate those requirements clearly to an LLM. Clarification and outcome analysis would be the key skills. He expects big companies to remain, but thousands of smaller companies to serve niches such as pet sitters and doggy daycares, built by domain experts with these tools.

Source: 58:09–1:00:31 ↗
Is that essentially a product manager, with the LLM as the engineering team?
Carey Nachenberg

Yes, Nachenberg says, a competent product manager, though he says he has met very few. In his view competence means understanding customer outcomes and the metrics customers use, using methods such as jobs to be done or outcome-driven innovation. His own example is that he drools when brushing his teeth, and the mess is a metric by which he would judge a toothbrush. He says many product managers think in features and copy competitors instead of finding what customers struggle with, how often, and whether it matters. He also holds that empathy can be a repeatable process built on interviews and observation. He allows that there may be exceptions.

Source: 1:00:34–1:03:38 ↗
Source: 55:37–58:07 ↗

QLooking back, is there anything you regret or would change?

Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg says he should have left Symantec earlier. His rule is to stay while you are learning, building skills and feel free to fail occasionally. He lost that at Symantec, but stayed because he lacked confidence, not because the work interested him. He still values staying five or even ten years as long as you learn. Switching teams can keep a good reputation and institutional knowledge. Staying too long makes you stale and comfortable.

He also notes the cost of leaving. At Symantec he was widely known and appeared on TV and in major newspapers about Stuxnet. At Google nobody cared what he had done before, so he had to rebuild trust and reputation, which is stressful.

What about golden handcuffs, where you earn well but no longer learn?
Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg would never say to leave a good package. People need different amounts of money to feel safe, and people balance several things. Being comfortable and well paid for a while can be fine. But for someone who is solving for enjoyment and hard problems, he thinks too long in that state can become toxic.

Source: 1:06:36–1:07:13 ↗
Source: 1:03:39–1:06:36 ↗

QHow can someone find what they enjoy in software engineering?

Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg advises students to try many internships, though he acknowledges jobs are tough now and the market is cyclical. He found cyber security by chance, through three different internships. He says jobs that sound boring can turn out to contain interesting problems, good colleagues and interesting customers. His advice is not to wait for the perfect job, but to find a good manager, hard problems and room to learn, which might lead to a 25-year career.

Is the approach to search broadly first, then go deep?
Carey Nachenberg

Yes, Nachenberg says. But if a first-year internship is interesting and going well, he would stay with it. He calls the approach a greedy breadth search.

Source: 1:08:42–1:09:13 ↗
Source: 1:07:14–1:08:40 ↗

QIf you could advise yourself on graduating from UCLA, what would you say?

Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg says there is no single item. First, do not let fear of failure hold you back. You can probably do more than you think, and he says he might have had a richer career had he listened. Second, focus on outcomes: who will use the work, what they care about and how they measure success. Problems often need a small square piece, not a perfect round thing.

He says he once presented technology to senior leaders, who did not care how the algorithm worked. They wanted to know whether it was faster, by how much, and what it meant for revenue or headcount. Speak to their needs, not your own. Third, find a good manager who trusts you and gives you rope, since a manager can make or break your career and happiness. Fourth, learn to collaborate and not assume you are right and tell others they are wrong. He says he still struggles with this.

Source: 1:09:13–1:10:50 ↗

Section 52 · interview

Choose the staff role with its responsibilities in view

Ricky explains a fast Google promotion path built on ownership and measurable impact, while questioning whether faster advancement always improves daily life.

QWhat was the overall promotion and compensation timeline?

Ricky

Ricky joined Google as a new graduate in 2017 after an internship. He reports approximately $180,000 annual compensation plus a signing bonus, then promotion to L4 after a year and a half at about $250,000, L5 after another year and a half at roughly $350,000, and L6 three years later at roughly $500,000–$520,000. The amounts are retrospective figures from his own situation, including equity effects, rather than current compensation guarantees.

He credits a fortunate team match and considers reaching senior in three years faster than the typical path he observed. Staff took longer and involved a different kind of responsibility. The career story combines his deliberate work with opportunities he did not control.

Source: 00:43–02:30 ↗

QWhat happened in the junior-to-midlevel promotion process?

Ricky

In the review system Ricky describes, ratings arrived every six months. He first met expectations, then exceeded them, and received a still stronger rating alongside promotion. He believed his impact and independence matched the next level but worried that short tenure might count against him. His manager supported the attempt.

Who should initiate promotion discussions?
Ricky

He recommends employee initiative supported by an ongoing conversation with the manager. He regularly asked whether his current projects demonstrated the next level and aligned expectations about timing and scope. Managing upward made an accelerated path more deliberate; it was not a promotion that arrived without discussion.

Source: 03:12–04:30 ↗
Source: 02:22–03:56 ↗

QWhat behavior made the first promotion possible?

Ricky

Independence: finishing projects with less handholding and finding ways to unblock himself. This did not mean refusing to ask anyone for help. It meant learning enough to move the project without requiring the manager to solve every obstacle.

How did you become better at unblocking yourself?
Ricky

He deliberately asked questions despite fearing he would look incompetent. His alternative was worse: staying silent, learning nothing, and failing to deliver. Colleagues generally wanted him to succeed. Asking the knowledgeable engineer helped him learn to do the work himself.

They recommend a real attempt before asking, but not remaining motionless for half a day or longer. Repeatedly asking the same question or receiving the same code-review feedback without improvement is different from healthy learning. The desired pattern is increasing independence and fewer repeated mistakes over time.

Source: 04:49–07:05 ↗
Source: 04:19–04:49 ↗

QWhat changed when working toward senior?

Ricky

He became the owner and go-to person for a defined area, learning its code and delivering several impactful projects there. Ownership meant being able to answer questions and advance the area, not merely shipping more isolated changes.

Did you choose the area through an explicit promotion plan?
Ricky

At first he simply found a part of the advertising experience visually unappealing and interesting to improve. The improvements could also produce measurable impact. Repeated projects and exploration gradually made him the owner, rather than a manager initially assigning a complete senior-level charter.

Source: 07:34–08:46 ↗
Did you have to compete for that scope?
Ricky

His team allowed engineers to choose many of their own projects. He sought work with meaningful impact and enough challenge to extend his skills. He recognizes that managers may assign useful work too, but relying only on assignments would not necessarily supply the scope needed for his desired growth.

Source: 08:28–09:31 ↗
Source: 07:05–07:56 ↗

QHow did you recognize projects that were genuinely at the next level?

Ricky

He studied teammates’ successful senior promotions to understand the scope and complexity expected, generated comparable ideas, and asked his manager to calibrate them. Roughly a year before his promotion he proposed a roadmap and asked whether completing it would meet the bar.

This gave the manager something concrete to assess and made the growth plan explicit. The roadmap emerged after approximately six months of exploration following L4, rather than immediately on the day of that promotion.

When did you put that roadmap together?
Ricky

After the midlevel promotion he tried different projects and learned what interested him. He then wrote the one-year plan himself and sought managerial buy-in. Exploration preceded the more committed roadmap.

Source: 10:21–11:06 ↗
Source: 09:10–11:06 ↗

QWhat did you do when requested work did not advance that roadmap?

Ricky

He learned to say no to unrelated projects that consumed time without helping him grow. He distinguishes that from accountability: a bug he caused, or a bug within his owned area, still needed attention. A new request could also be worth accepting if its impact and scope were stronger than the existing plan.

How can someone say no without damaging the relationship?
Ricky

For an outside request he would bring the tradeoff to his manager and understand why it was assigned. For the manager’s own request he would ask whether it was required and explain the competing projects’ impact and growth value. This is a discussion of priorities, not a license to ignore obligations.

He believes managers should try to match important work with reports’ growth and interests. His own early record of finding and delivering projects earned trust, although the manager continued to guide which ideas were useful.

Source: 12:03–13:44 ↗
Source: 11:09–12:01 ↗

QHow did you learn which ideas would have impact?

Ricky

First define what the organization values. In his advertising area, revenue was a central metric, alongside whether the work helped users, advertisers, and publishers. Other teams might care about active users or product interactions. Running experiments exposed gaps where improvements could move the relevant outcome.

He found measurable results persuasive in arguments about project value. His emphatic statement that numbers settle the matter belongs to his experience in a revenue-measured area; it should not be treated as a claim that every engineering contribution is captured by one number.

Ricky

It felt more uncertain than the first promotion. Ricky believed he was ahead of the timing commonly observed around him and worried that the committee might want a longer record of next-level work. His manager supported submitting while setting realistic expectations that it could fail. It succeeded on the first attempt, which Ricky describes as fortunate.

Ricky

Yes. Handing project ideas to junior engineers made him anxious about whether experiments would succeed; some did not. He had to become comfortable with a portfolio of ideas rather than expect every one to work. A comparatively good success rate, mentoring, and positive influence on other people’s projects supported the case, while confidence developed through practice.

In the Google context he describes, senior engineers could stay at senior without an expectation to advance to staff. He is less sure about whether the same applies at midlevel. He frames staff as a choice to take on more responsibility rather than an obligatory badge of success.

At senior he knew and owned a space and delivered projects within it. Toward staff he challenged the boundaries of that space, questioned the established direction, and guided consequential decisions across teams and functions. Some changes required senior-leadership buy-in. Knowing an area became a platform for shaping where it should go, rather than only operating effectively inside it.

Reorganizations, poor fit, or a manager’s absence could have delayed otherwise good work. He separates the chance that an opportunity appears from being prepared to use it. Effort helped with the second; it did not fully control the first.

How much was ability and how much luck?
Ricky

He offers a rough fifty-fifty impression rather than a measured estimate. He feels confident he would eventually have reached senior with continued growth and effort, but another team might have required a move and a new ramp-up. His speed depended on the unusually good fit. Ryan notes that even a stronger engineer can struggle in an organization with repeated disruption.

Source: 33:30–35:08 ↗
Source: 32:12–33:39 ↗

QWhy stay at Google for seven years?

Ricky

He regularly reassessed whether he enjoyed the work and whether the team still offered what he wanted: growth, travel, and work that was sufficiently interesting. Staying was an active decision, not proof that he never considered alternatives. He also acknowledges survivorship bias: people without comparable growth or fit might have had good reasons to leave.

Ryan describes the accumulated advantage of staying in a healthy setting: relationships, code knowledge, and organizational context can expand from expertise in one area to many. That momentum can enable unusually fast growth, while changing employers can offer other benefits. They do not reduce the choice to a universal rule about job hopping.

Source: 35:11–37:55 ↗

QWhat advice would you give your new-graduate self?

Ricky

Trust his judgment more and try boundary-pushing ideas earlier. Anxiety made him postpone ideas he later pursued successfully. He believes earlier confidence could have reduced stress and enabled more experimentation, though he developed it gradually through results and good feedback.

Was the impostor feeling about technical ability?
Ricky

He worried that he had been hired for personality rather than ability because his interview and internship had not felt spectacular. At low levels he also lacked a way to judge his own performance. Repeated reassurance that he was doing fine did not answer his internal question of whether that meant barely passing or excelling. Successful projects and collaboration eventually supplied more convincing evidence.

Section 53 · interview

David Fowler: Microsoft Promotions, Permissionless Projects, and the Distinguished Engineer Path

Microsoft distinguished engineer David Fowler explains how building prototypes without permission, learning to delegate, and focusing on impact over cleverness carried him from intern to distinguished engineer.

Fowler's view: build things, scale through others, and let impact drive promotion

David Fowler, a Microsoft distinguished engineer, tells the host that his climb from intern to distinguished engineer came from building working prototypes without waiting for permission, then learning to scale through other people instead of through his own typing. In Fowler's account, impact matters more than cleverness at every level, mentors who are blunt about how promotion decisions get made are worth seeking out, and several habits that carry an engineer to senior can block the move beyond it. The talk also covers debugging, the culture change after Satya Nadella became CEO, and why Fowler stayed at one company. Everything below is Fowler's account of his own experience unless marked as an editorial note.

Source: 00:37–1:31:23 ↗

QHow does Microsoft's leveling system work, given that levels run upward from 59 with about two levels per title?

David Fowler

Fowler says he cannot explain why numbering starts at 59, and guesses the lower levels cover non-engineering roles. A college graduate typically starts at 59 or 60, depending on how many times they interned and how well they did. Fowler equates entry level with an SDE I at other companies.

A title maps to a band of about two levels, so a title does not reveal which level someone holds. Principal is the exception at three levels, and Fowler says that band is so broad that a new arrival from senior and a long-serving principal share a title. Above principal come the partner levels, which Fowler says have three bands, and then technical fellow.

Source: 00:37–03:14 ↗

QHow did you end up at Microsoft?

David Fowler

Fowler grew up in Barbados and left at 18 for Florida Tech, chosen partly because it held career fairs and was one flight from home. He started in computer engineering, decided after the first class that it was not for him because he wanted to code, and switched to computer science. He had been coding since about age ten, and was surprised that no one in the first Java class knew how to code.

Fowler and a close friend built games on nights and weekends. To stand out at their first career fair, they brought a laptop with a game demo. That produced about four internship offers. Fowler chose Microsoft over GE and smaller Florida firms, and the friend went to EA. After campus interviews and an in-person whiteboard round, he interned in 2006 and 2007, which he found eye-opening.

What was it like going to Bill Gates's house as an intern?
David Fowler

Fowler says every intern group traditionally ended the summer there, and he was in the last set to go. Interns had phones taken and were bused in from a church parking area. He was chatting when a rush of interns ran toward him, and Gates was standing behind him. Fowler shook Gates's hand and says they spoke once.

Source: 06:09–07:12 ↗
What did the Microsoft interview process look like in 2006?
David Fowler

Fowler says Microsoft was known for puzzle questions, citing the book How Would You Move Mount Fuji? and the manhole-cover question. His interview began with an easy coding question on paper, then a puzzle about making exactly four gallons from a three-gallon and a five-gallon jug. He had seen the film scene but could not recall the steps, and worked them out. The last question was how to count the gas stations in Florida. He asked whether it was a trick question, was told no, and saw no point. He thought it had gone badly but got a call back.

The host adds that LeetCode-style questions at least relate to the job, and recalls being asked to add two numbers in base negative two. Both agree interviewing has changed a lot, in some ways for the better and in some for the worse.

Source: 07:15–10:17 ↗
Source: 03:16–06:05 ↗

QWhat is the story behind NuGet, the .NET package manager?

David Fowler

Fowler says NuGet is now more than ten years old, and its impact today feels jarring compared with its start. The team was building a new web stack to compete with the LAMP stack, and Fowler did not question whether that made sense, because the leaders above him said to do it. Ruby on Rails and its gems had just arrived, and another group was looking at WordPress and Drupal, which also had packages. The consensus was that the platform needed a package manager so people could extend it.

The first version was an in-browser package manager in the style of WordPress. In a meeting with Scott Guthrie, whom Fowler describes as an EVP now, a product manager showed a PowerPoint mockup. Fowler and an architect had already built something and asked whether the team could start from there. That meeting formed the NuGet team: Fowler as first engineer, the architect David Ebbo, and Phil Haack. They also talked with people behind other open-source .NET package managers.

Source: 10:25–12:58 ↗

QWhat did your performance review look like after NuGet, for someone who was not yet a senior engineer?

David Fowler

Fowler's first promotion came about eight months after joining, before NuGet. Because he had interned twice, he arrived with a lot of Microsoft experience. Beyond assigned work, he read forums for feedback on Microsoft's products, built features to answer it, and showed the results to product managers, architects and the team. Looking back, he says those people became sponsors and positioned him to build NuGet.

Fowler calls himself a code-first, ask-questions-later person and says code is currency: a working sample beats a PowerPoint or a document. A director once told him he would send people to talk to David because David has energy.

Did the lasting impact of something like NuGet carry over into later reviews?
David Fowler

Fowler says the bigger promotions felt like accumulated history plus current success. Impact is officially meant to be for the year, and crossing a band boundary, such as to senior or to principal, takes more than moving within a band. He is unsure whether Microsoft has an official deferred-impact rule, but says it clearly mattered at the higher principal levels, where the question was whether he had shown repeated impact over ten years.

Source: 14:53–16:20 ↗
Source: 13:01–14:50 ↗

QHow did SignalR start?

David Fowler

Fowler says the name came from the era when web products dropped letters from their names. The project began on nights and weekends. Google Docs had just appeared, and Fowler was enthralled by smooth co-editing. He set out to build Google Docs for code, did not finish it, but learned about WebSockets, which he says had not shipped yet, and how to build that kind of app.

Damian Edwards, a product manager, was building a talk on long-running streaming apps in .NET. Fowler proposed building a library together. Microsoft allows moonlighting on projects outside official work, so the two worked until midnight and open-sourced it, and people started using it. Later a product manager said it should be made official.

Fowler calls it the first thing built from his own idea, after years of working on other people's ideas. He became a pseudo tech lead without ever being a manager, hired college graduates, and at one point led a team of about eight.

What pushed you to give up weekends and late nights for it?
David Fowler

Fowler had not seen anything like it. Google Docs was the first product of its kind to work that well, and Node.js with Socket.IO showed a new way to push data from server to client. The project hit limits deep in the core platform and taught him a lot about the networking stack. He says the volume of problems was like catnip.

Source: 19:12–20:27 ↗
Source: 16:22–19:11 ↗

QHow can others start projects like this within a large company, when the motivation comes entirely from them?

David Fowler

Fowler's one-sentence answer is that you can just do things, which people now call agency. He does not recommend spending every night and weekend on projects, but early on his goal was to get better at software engineering, and the way was to build everything possible: games, websites, many kinds of software.

The second habit was to find someone on the team whose career he wanted. Fowler attached himself to the architect David Ebbo, whose role spanned several areas and looked ahead, copied his behaviors, and for a while coded Ebbo's ideas, which turned into doing it independently. He then built prototypes and showed them to an advocate, the architect or the product manager, to ask whether they were useful. He says he would build a thousand things and maybe one would hit.

So agency at a big company came from energy, moonlighting and doing more than the assigned work?
David Fowler

Fowler agrees in part. Once an engineer builds a reputation for building things, more opportunities arrive and people ask for a take on new work. He cautions that this is not guaranteed, but in his case it was clearly true and continued after SignalR.

Source: 23:27–24:43 ↗
Is permissionless agency a way to bypass the credibility that permissioned opportunities require?
David Fowler

The host puts it that way, and the exchange adds that a stronger track record earns more room to be permissionless, because each success buys more latitude to fail. The host describes fast-growing engineers as trusted people management lets loose on risky projects, while an engineer struggling to meet expectations gets directed work and monitoring. Fowler agrees.

Source: 24:45–25:43 ↗
Source: 20:31–23:26 ↗

QWhat led to the promotion to principal?

David Fowler

Fowler recalls a boss who, when he reached senior, said promotions would slow. The jump to principal turned out to be large. Alongside SignalR, he built Kudu, an early Azure tool that let people push code and deploy an app instantly, as Heroku and AppHarbor did. A director then pulled him onto a new project that became the cross-platform .NET Core.

Fowler was senior, and he and another principal engineer were chosen as architects over about 30 engineers with free rein, which he calls amazing and terrifying. At first he tried to code review every change and was burnt out within a year, and had to learn to trust people and separate urgent from not urgent. He had his first child and was promoted to principal that same year.

How did you scale yourself out of necessity so you did not burn out as architect for so many engineers?
David Fowler

Fowler learned the first lessons on SignalR, a team of seven or eight including two new hires. Before that he never delegated to grow someone and assumed he could do the work faster himself. It flipped when he saw that investing in smart new hires would amplify impact even if early tasks took longer. He calls the senior-to-principal leap doing more through others than yourself, and the point where many engineers plateau because they prefer coding alone.

On .NET Core, where he says the team rebuilt the package manager, runtime and libraries from scratch, he stopped treating everything as equally urgent and let people fail. He says traits that get an engineer to senior, such as being a control freak or insisting on one way, hurt when scaling to a thousand engineers. The fix was to inspire others through one-on-ones and example, and to become outcome-focused.

Source: 28:53–32:23 ↗
Source: 25:44–28:49 ↗

QWhat does the architect role mean at Microsoft?

David Fowler

Fowler says it is a semi-official role open to the middle principal bands. When he joined, he saw a principal software architect and decided that was the role he wanted. He describes it as breadth over depth: overseeing the design of the whole system. Other archetypes at the top include a super coder who builds enormous amounts, deep specialists such as one of the leading garbage-collection experts working on the .NET collector, and people overseeing a hugely impactful product area.

As architect for ASP.NET Core, he oversaw the web framework, the web server and how packages shipped, vetting decisions that could last 20 years. He had not done this before and learned by shadowing mentors who had.

Source: 32:25–34:20 ↗

QAs a distinguished engineer, how has the share of your time spent writing code changed?

David Fowler

Fowler says the job may no longer reward daily coding, but selfishly he codes every day and currently sends many pull requests on a project involving Aspire. He does not want to be an architect who gives instructions without knowing the code and then disappears. He wants to be a peer on the team, facing the builds and the tests.

If you stopped coding and only led, would your performance review still look fine?
David Fowler

Fowler thinks so. A distinguished engineer is measured on organization-wide or company-wide impact, so part of the job is keeping the architecture sound, looking ahead, talking publicly, inspiring and mentoring. He gave four internal talks on using AI for software engineering, which began when someone asked after seeing him use it. He argues such talks matter because credible engineers explaining how they work persuade more than a boss giving orders.

Source: 35:45–37:08 ↗
Source: 34:24–35:41 ↗

QWhat is the story behind the promotion to distinguished engineer?

David Fowler

Fowler calls it the craziest promotion he has experienced. Distinguished engineer is the last level within partner, and it comes through an official process, not an annual review: a set of technical leaders peer-reviews the candidate. Guido van Rossum, who created Python, is at the same level, and Fowler describes maximum imposter syndrome. He also thought he was young for the role, though that did not count against him.

Fowler says earlier work carried it, because the role requires a body of work and a track record, not one good year. The email promoting him from principal to partner cited .NET Core, by then about seven years old, and he had acted as architect helping many teams adopt the new .NET internally. NuGet and SignalR counted as signals of how what he helped build affected the industry and the company. He says the fellows decide.

Were you involved in that process, or was it a surprise?
David Fowler

Fowler helped his leadership with content, supplying papers he had written and code contributions, and did nothing else. What affected him most was hearing other fellows say the promotion was well deserved and about time.

Source: 40:19–40:57 ↗
Do you worry about the lofty expectations of the level now that you have held it for a while?
David Fowler

At first Fowler called himself a baby DE. After roughly two and a half to three years he feels confident he can perform at the level. In his first review cycle he felt pressure to document all impact and tell his boss, because the level sits just below executive. He found a pattern of talking to bosses and staying visible, and feels less pressure now, though he adds that things could change.

Source: 40:59–42:41 ↗
Source: 37:10–40:17 ↗

QWhat does the final level, technical fellow, look like?

David Fowler

Fowler says people at that level are unicorns with different paths, so the useful move is to look for proxies for impact, not copy anyone. A fellow needs industry-wide impact. His examples: Anders Hejlsberg, whom people in his division idolize, made Turbo Pascal, Delphi, C# and TypeScript. Dave Cutler, who Fowler says built Windows NT, the Azure operating system and the Xbox hypervisor, is the only senior technical fellow, a title Fowler says is simply his own.

Fowler adds that Microsoft recently hired a fellow who invented RSS, and that a teammate was once an intern for Tim Berners-Lee and is on the HTTP specification. These are Fowler's own statements and were not checked against other sources.

Source: 42:44–44:45 ↗

QWere there unexpected perks of becoming a distinguished engineer?

David Fowler

Fowler says the best perk is an email alias called engineer that reaches every distinguished engineer at Microsoft. There is also an internal forum where they meet every couple of months. Access typically works through a sponsor, and when he became a partner he asked management for a mentor who was a fellow, reasoning that anyone wanting to become one should have fellows as mentors.

One was Jeffrey Snover, who invented PowerShell and, Fowler says, recently left Microsoft for Google. Fowler calls him one of his best mentors and a main sponsor, and he attended one of the technical leaders' forums as a result.

Source: 44:48–46:33 ↗

QWhat did that mentor say that made a difference?

David Fowler

Fowler says much career advice is vague, such as telling someone to do a super impactful project, whereas Snover was direct. He suggested going to the people who decide, including the CTOs, and asking what the role requires. Fowler found it jarring, since no one had told him to ask the source, but very helpful, because it showed him what he should and should not be doing.

A second mentor helped after Fowler received a feedback package from his manager and peers listing strengths, weaknesses and behavior under stress. His first reaction was to fix every weakness. The mentor said to amplify his strengths instead, because no one is promoted to these roles for being average. About five years ago this changed how Fowler works. He now builds teams around his gaps: he does not schedule meetings or run every shipping checklist, and makes sure someone who is good at that does. The host likens this to a power law, and Fowler agrees.

Source: 46:34–49:47 ↗

QWhich engineers do you look up to, and what makes them impressive?

David Fowler

Fowler's team includes about five other partner-level engineers with more than 20 years at the company, each excellent for a different reason: a garbage-collector expert, a super coder who he says is a true 10x engineer, someone who seems to know obscure details across C, compilers and the operating system, and others with a strong eye for what to build.

On the C# language design review team, Fowler sits with Hejlsberg, whose feedback he says never talks down and stays pragmatic, even though the code Hejlsberg commits looks like it is inventing theory no one has seen. Fowler also names Mark Russinovich, CTO of Azure, who still codes and recently emailed about a performance improvement he wrote. Fowler is inspired when senior engineers still code.

He warns about the meeting trap. After becoming partner, he sat in meetings all day and was sad. A mentor told him an individual contributor needs time to think and build, and to block at least eight hours a week. It took him a while to learn to decline meetings.

Source: 49:49–53:36 ↗

QIf you designed a university course on refactoring, what would its key concepts be?

David Fowler

Fowler says computer science is not software engineering. A first job involves a lot of time understanding what exists so the first change can be surgical and not break the build. He would put students in an artificially large codebase, changed every year so they cannot copy earlier work, and ask them to fix a bug and write a test. Working out where to put code, he argues, builds skills a LeetCode question or textbook exercise does not.

Each assignment could be a single fix. Fowler notes that many jobs are about tweaking existing software, and even someone working on Windows is unlikely to change the kernel unless building a new operating system.

Source: 53:40–56:15 ↗

QWhy do you say the high-leverage skill is debugging rather than writing new code, even though interviews focus on writing?

David Fowler

Early on, Fowler worked with platform engineers on the .NET team and watched them diagnose crashes, race conditions and threading issues. He concluded that shipping an app and handling crash reports and production problems calls for a second skill set, distinct from authoring code. He would like an interview that hands a candidate a crash dump, to see what they start doing, such as adding logs, rerunning, reasoning about race conditions or printing thread ids, not whether they solve it.

He tells of an early-Azure night at 1 a.m. when his CVP messaged asking if he was free, and he was added to a call of about a hundred engineers trying to work out why a very popular site was crashing. It turned out to be a concurrency problem in a dictionary. Fowler concludes that writing code is a small piece of an engineer's skill set.

What about the fixer archetype, who makes a one-line change after heavy investigation?
David Fowler

The host describes the fixer as someone who drops in and makes a one-line change that makes something two or three times better. Fowler says someone on his team does this: when a thread starts about a performance issue in a gRPC call, he adds that engineer, who returns a trace and solves it.

Source: 59:31–1:00:20 ↗
Source: 56:16–59:30 ↗

QWhat prompted your lukewarm take that the lower you sit on the technology stack, the fewer mistakes you are allowed to make?

David Fowler

Fowler works on the platform, and says changes there break services in ways that people higher up would find unheard of. Changing the order in which a method returns results, for example, can take down a company's website. He suspects the tweet followed a bug found during first-party adoption of .NET, where upgrading teams hit issues that shocked him, such as a method with about 400 arguments reaching a limit.

Source: 1:00:22–1:01:59 ↗

QYou tweeted that when promoted to senior you felt others were smarter and should have gone first. What did you take from that?

David Fowler

Fowler worried about being promoted early on a fast path. His team had four people from MIT and two from Carnegie Mellon, and he had gone to Florida Tech, so he worked through imposter syndrome by working very hard.

The promotion taught him that impact is not about being the smartest, but about whether the work is at the top of the business, as NuGet and SignalR were. He had always felt he needed to go deeper on some technology, and now asks whether that is for you or for your career. He says an engineer does not need to know how TCP/IP works to be promoted to senior. It helped him separate being smart from making impact.

Co-workers were happy for him, at least outwardly. When he asked about others who had risen fast, he was told everyone knew it would happen, and he adds that you never know which category you are in.

Source: 1:02:00–1:05:23 ↗

QOne of your big-company tips is to ask when the last reorg was before changing roles. What is the thinking behind that?

David Fowler

Fowler calls big companies machines and recalls hearing, perhaps tongue in cheek, that executives show motion through reorgs. A reorg is always coming or has just happened, so learn about the last one: who the leaders are, what triggered it and where the org is heading. Because Microsoft is so big, he says, every new org is effectively a new company. The tweet likely followed a mentee who had been reorged several times in a row, or something that happened to him.

Is this about reading what a reorg means for your future?
David Fowler

Yes. Fowler also relays advice he heard recently: when changing jobs, think about what you hate, not what you love, because the things you love will be easy. Someone who hates open offices should not join a company with open-plan seating.

Source: 1:07:36–1:08:24 ↗
Source: 1:05:26–1:07:35 ↗

QWhat has kept you at Microsoft for so long, since your internships?

David Fowler

Fowler describes himself as part of a millennial generation that broke from the boomer-parent habit of staying in one place forever, and says many job-hopping friends were paid well for it. His closest call came when he was senior and a boss who had left for pre-IPO Twitter asked him to interview there. He interviewed at Twitter and GitHub, got both offers, and stayed after much deliberation. The morning Twitter went public, he adds, brought instant depression that lasted about a week.

Microsoft's counteroffer was fine but not the main reason. An executive vice president told him he would be a distinguished engineer in five years, which Fowler says oversold it. What mattered more was that he had built something impactful and permissionless and had gained autonomy, and leaving meant starting over. People overlook the network and track record they have built, and the people matter as much as pay: not just good engineers but good people to work with.

He also stayed because he got to work on something new about every two years, by design, which kept him from feeling the need to go elsewhere.

If a mentee at Microsoft had a pre-IPO offer from a company like OpenAI, would you say stay or go?
David Fowler

Fowler would tell them to go. He recalls a mentee with an offer from another company who was not in a place to do their best work, and told that mentee to leave despite any counteroffer. He says that, in the same situation himself, he might have gone.

Source: 1:13:18–1:14:07 ↗
You tweeted that once in a career you should stay on a project long enough to see the long-term impact of your decisions. What prompted that?
David Fowler

Fowler's career had been to work on something and move on, still helping those who took over. .NET Core, at about ten years, is the longest he has worked on anything. Seeing the effects of decisions made in the first two years, good or bad, gave him a new perspective. He jokes that on a ten-year project every small issue you postponed becomes a big one, because somebody will hit all of it.

He is unsure twenty years on one project is good for career growth, but says it teaches you the implications of your choices and what you would fix in the next version. The host wonders what a chain of ever-higher jumps does for judgment if each project declines after the person leaves. Fowler does not fault either path and has done both. He cannot name the ingredients of a successful project, but can tell when he is on one, like a fine-tuned internal model built over experience.

Source: 1:14:09–1:17:14 ↗
Source: 1:08:25–1:13:16 ↗

QDid you notice the culture shifting internally when Satya Nadella became CEO?

David Fowler

Fowler says the shift was huge, but it is hard to see the jump from Steve Ballmer's era because he lived through it and it happened gradually. A big one was that, historically, two teams could work toward the same end state and one would win. Under Nadella the focus moved to collaboration over being first. He saw teams building solutions before knowing the problem, though not on his own team.

He describes changes in meetings, email and remote friendliness. He remembers being surprised by someone raising a hand in a Teams meeting, having grown up in a culture where you wait for a pause and talk. Earlier meetings were often a highest-paid-person's-opinion affair, where a loud senior person could stop others from feeling safe to speak. Early in his career he saw people shouting and wondered whether he would have to shout too. Now leaders model behavior such as inviting quiet people to share their views.

Collaboration also became part of reviews: engineers who avoided other teams' work, or cloned it, were marked down. The host summarizes this as a change driven by performance incentives and top-down messaging, and Fowler adds the behaviors leaders modeled. The host recalls the XKCD comic that draws Microsoft as people pointing guns at each other. Fowler says the real shift went from guns to ambivalence, with teams staying out of each other's way, and then to rewarded collaboration.

Source: 1:17:16–1:23:01 ↗

QLooking back, do you have major regrets people can learn from?

David Fowler

Fowler says no major ones, but early in his career he was very arrogant and lacked empathy, and the tone of old GitHub comments would show it. Building teams and influencing through others taught him patience and empathy. Being right is only one of many things, he says, and software engineering has many shades of gray. He has more self-awareness now, though it still creeps out occasionally.

He names as a possible regret that he did not take early opportunities at Twitter or Facebook, which would have paid a lot for a senior engineer. A smaller regret outside the career: a friend messaged him in 2008 about starting a Bitcoin company, and he dismissed the idea. The host jokes that the friend must now hold a lot of Bitcoin.

Source: 1:23:04–1:25:30 ↗

QWhat was your work-life balance like throughout your career?

David Fowler

Fowler used to say there was no balance, just working hard and playing hard. A comment he found useful recently is that balance is not about stopping at five o'clock but about what gives you energy and what drains it. He works a lot because programming is a passion as well as a job, and dials back now and then. Once he came back from vacation and began making games for fun, then took what he learned into work.

What drains him is meetings that feel purposeless. If he were in meetings all day and then went home to do the work he wanted to do, that would feel like burnout. He sees being paid to code as a privilege and plans to keep doing it until he can no longer.

Is intrinsic motivation the unfair advantage behind careers like yours?
David Fowler

The host says almost every very successful engineer seems to have it. Fowler agrees and recalls a talk by Andrej Karpathy about how much practice it takes to get good at anything (the captions garble the figure Fowler cited, so it is not reproduced here). Asked which book made him good, Fowler says he wrote and read a lot of code, and is not sure that is good advice but did not get good from a blog post.

His advice is to build everything: databases, distributed systems, games. He calls his GitHub a graveyard of projects, each of which taught a skill that only showed later. At 16 he tried to build a Street Fighter clone with art found online, purely to learn how a fighting game and key combos work. That need to understand how things work has lasted to this day.

Source: 1:27:28–1:29:51 ↗
Source: 1:25:32–1:27:26 ↗

QIf you could advise yourself when graduating college and entering the industry, what would you say?

David Fowler

Fowler's answer is to negotiate the salary. He did not know it was possible when he took his first job. A new graduate should get multiple offers and push the number up. Coming from Barbados and grateful for the most money he had seen, he was shocked to watch friends decline offers and say they would check Google or Facebook first. Having since sat on hiring committees for interns, he finds it impressive to watch a candidate bump up an offer well.
