Section 59 · panel

Getting to Staff Engineer at Big Tech: A Five-Person Panel on Scope, Relationships, and Promotion

Five engineers who reached staff level at Meta, Google, Activision, Netflix and Airbnb discuss the projects behind their promotions, how to find scope, and why relationships and communication matter as much as technical depth.

The panel's view: staff scope is found through problems and people, not through code alone

Rahul hosts four engineers (Lee, Ryan Peterman, Carly and Zach) and also answers as a panelist. Between them they have worked at staff level, or the equivalent, at Meta, Google, Activision, Netflix and Airbnb. Their shared view is that staff level changes the kind of work, not only its size. A staff engineer is expected to influence other people, to find problems that are worth the company's time, and to be known well enough that others can vouch for the result. They disagree on details, such as how much a staff engineer should still code, but they return again and again to three points: relationships, clear communication, and a direct read of the company's own promotion process. Everything below is the speakers' own experience and opinion, not company policy.

Source: 00:01–1:13:46 ↗
Levels discussed, as summarized by the host from a levels.fyi diagram
CompanySenior levelStaff-level equivalent
GoogleL5L6
Facebook / MetaE5E6
AmazonSDE IIINo staff title; the level after senior is principal
Source: 00:01–01:42 ↗
Panelists and the background each one stated
PanelistBackground as stated in the panel
LeeIn software engineering since 2004. At Amazon from 2012, first as an SDE II and later in people management. Then a staff-level IC role at Meta, which Lee says did not go well. About a year and a half before the panel, moved to Google as a staff engineer (chat, then Gmail notifications).
Ryan PetermanStaff engineer at Meta, working on Instagram. Graduated in 2017, spent about eight months at an Amazon satellite office, then joined Meta as a new graduate. Three promotions in about five years.
CarlyAt Activision. A senior manager who also holds an IC title equivalent to staff (lead engineer). Finished graduate school in 2017, started as a junior data scientist, joined Activision at senior level and took about two years to reach lead. Works in security.
ZachBegan in data engineering at Facebook in 2016. Then Netflix, where every engineer held the senior title. Then Airbnb, where Zach received the official staff title and stayed two years. Left about six months before the panel to create content full time.
Rahul (host)Runs Taro. About four and a half years at Meta, going from senior to staff. About two and a half years at Pinterest, where Rahul was rejected for promotion twice. Before that, a startup that Pinterest acquired.
Source: 00:52–06:01 ↗

Pace: promotion is not a race (Lee and Rahul)

Rahul says being rejected for promotion twice at Pinterest gave Rahul both the manager's and the candidate's view of the process. Lee says Lee failed three attempts at the senior SDE III level at Amazon, and also failed the first try to reach L6 as a manager. Lee reached the staff-equivalent level roughly 16 or 17 years into a career. Lee's point is that several panelists rose very quickly, by changing companies or succeeding fast inside one, but that is not the only path and a missed first senior promotion is not unusual.

Source: 05:18–06:58 ↗

QWhat project or projects got each panelist to staff level?

Zach moved up by changing companies. At Netflix every engineer held the senior title, but Zach felt the responsibilities were already staff-level, and Airbnb later hired Zach at staff. The project Zach credits is an asset inventory at Netflix. Netflix used microservices, which give each team ownership but also leave thousands of separate applications that could each hold their own vulnerabilities. Zach built a graph database describing applications, code bases, data sets and employees and how they connect to one another. The work took about two years.

Lee was also hired at staff level rather than promoted into it. Lee had managed people for about three years at Amazon before joining Meta. Lee says technical work alone was not enough. Some people point to a large, complex project they delivered alone, but staff-level readiness also depends on whether they planned the work, split it into parallel work streams, and reduced risk so the hardest part was not left until last. Lee's hardest technical project was a custom class loader that let an Android app use multiple executable files before Google supported that, so that Amazon's video app (now Prime Video) and its combined apps did not hit the method limit. Lee did not want engineers forced to write poor code to fit a technical limit.

Ryan Peterman describes a large efficiency project that made video processing at Instagram much cheaper, 94 percent cheaper for some basic encodings. Ryan says the project reached staff level because Ryan created the scope: Ryan found the problem, convinced people it was worth doing, got buy-in, and led execution. Ryan stepped in personally only on the riskiest components. Several engineers did most of the work while Ryan led and reviewed code. Ryan stresses that staff is one of the first levels where influencing others is a baseline expectation, because software is collaborative.

Carly says the step up is not just technical brilliance. It comes down to trust and to being a collaborator that others rely on. Carly points to a presentation of security findings to an executive leader and the CTO. Carly could explain technical work to people who did not want to sit in an engineering meeting, and received a job offer from a leader in that meeting. That became an internal move to staff. Carly says this is not a normal route. The wider lesson is to know your numbers, be ready to state your impact to technical and non-technical audiences, and work on large, cross-business problems that address a real pain point. The people who decide on promotion are often both kinds of audience.

Rahul names two projects at Meta. One was an internal tool that improved debugging of the product. Rahul measured that it saved thousands of engineering hours in a year, and other engineers could plug in their own debugging tools, which multiplied the impact. The other was re-architecting the product's calling architecture, moving it onto another team's set of APIs. Rahul's lesson is to think in terms of a portfolio of bets. A big-tech company has many things outside your control, so pair one main project with a smaller one you control, and switch when one is blocked. Two or three projects is realistic, not ten. Rahul adds that a company must also have enough business need for staff-level scope, so some people get promoted simply by moving to a company that needs their skills.

Is a staff promotion usually a sudden result of one project?

One panelist says no. A promotion packet is normally a track record covering several half-year review periods. By the time it reaches the promotion committee, people should already know the candidate's name and the candidate should have been doing near-staff or staff-level work for some time.

Source: 18:41–19:27 ↗
What kind of impact makes people notice a staff engineer?

Zach describes two directions of impact. Vertical impact is the direct effect on the business. Horizontal impact is helping a team move faster by improving how work gets done, not only what is built. Zach's Netflix example was a Groovy script that removed unused dependencies from the deployable file for pipelines. Zach estimates each deploy saved one to seven minutes, which at five or six deploys a day is about 30 minutes to an hour a day per engineer. Zach says the rest is adoption rather than technical excellence.

Another panelist adds a rough calculation: a 16 percent speedup across 66 people is the equivalent of a 10x engineer. The same panelist says that the very senior engineers they studied, three levels above staff, often make compounding improvements to tooling used by thousands of engineers.

Source: 19:29–22:33 ↗
Source: 07:00–18:38 ↗

QHow should a senior or staff engineer balance delegating work and doing it personally? (An attendee, Brian, asked, and Rahul rephrased the question.)

Zach recalls weekly conversations with an Airbnb manager about whether Zach was managing, delegating and coding enough. Zach loves to code Scala all day, and says that doing so has sometimes been to the team's detriment. Frank talks with a manager about how time is spent helped Zach see when more leadership was needed.

Lee says each person should know their own bias. An engineer who came from management may spend too much time on people and too little on reducing technical risk, while others lean the other way. The split does not need to be 50/50 each week. Lee also asks whether the engineer is leading from the front, finding the path and sending others down it, or from behind, pointing people in a direction. The answer varies by team: a team of peers differs from a team of new graduates. Lee says a manager's input helps here. A manager can point out that a 4 percent performance gain is good, but that no one knows which tools were used and nothing would be committed if the person were unavailable. In Lee's view how you do the work matters as much as what you do, and pairing with junior engineers helps them follow the threads.

Carly gives a manager's view, using Zach as an example. Carly would rather Zach had input into research, design and the roadmap of the big projects, so that someone with Zach's depth can quickly say what will break, and others do the deep implementation. Zach would step in when something is very complicated. Carly says the balance is hard to get right and is something to settle in talks with the manager.

Lee builds on this: one of the most powerful tools is asking the right question at the right time. A senior person who hears a team plan to re-architect something can say it is not the right focus and that it can sit behind a shim for now. Twenty minutes of that person's time can save two or three developer-years. Lee says that people's time should go where a design matters, because a missed hallway conversation can be costly.

How should a staff engineer decide what not to work on?

Zach tells of starting at Airbnb, when stakeholders were loud about certifying profitability numbers. As a newcomer Zach leaned on their requests. After about six months, Zach asked what difference certification would actually make, and the answer was essentially none, with roughly a one-day delay at most. Zach told the manager it was a case of diminishing returns, because the pipeline was too complicated to finish and the effort should move to higher-impact work. Another panelist notes that four people working on it for about four months likely cost the company a million dollars or more in salary alone, before counting what else they could have done.

A panelist adds that staff engineers must persuade, not just execute. Managers lean on staff engineers to identify what should and should not be worked on, which takes courage to tell stakeholders their project is being deprioritized. Explaining the reasoning is what keeps cross-functional partners' respect. Without it, the panelist says, mistrust builds first and resentment follows, and team dynamics can fall apart.

Source: 27:34–30:19 ↗
Is a staff engineer always less hands-on?

A panelist says no. It depends on the project and on the person's strengths. On a project with many senior people, staff may lead. Some very productive specialists, or people whose execution is worth four or five engineers, can have staff-level impact by doing most of the execution themselves. They are still expected to scale by sharing their knowledge. The panelist says not every staff engineer fits the tech-lead type: some are heads-down coders and some are domain specialists. Another panelist recalls that Meta had a "code machine" archetype for this kind of person.

Source: 30:20–32:02 ↗
Source: 21:45–27:31 ↗

QWhere does a staff engineer find, or make up, the scope?

Lee says that as you become better than your managers at your job, they can no longer see the landmines or the technical constraints on a project. Lee rejects the idea of making up scope to justify a promotion as a bad choice. The job is to identify what is hurting the team and holding it back, raise it, and convince others to fix it. Lee compares this to the question of whether calculus was invented or discovered. Lee says most scope is discovered: work that others fear, do not see, or do not think is valuable, and that you must persuade them will speed up the next three projects or enable something the product could not do before. It may be found by looking through code, or in product requirements where there is a gap.

Lee's own habit is to put a hand up when no one else will. Lee gives the example of an old, fragile system that no one wants to touch. Lee says that when someone suggests turning it off, it may turn out to generate hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue, so it is worth a gradual replacement such as the strangler fig pattern. Lee admits that this sometimes leaves a person stuck with something awful.

Rahul sums up that asking how to find scope to justify a promotion is already the wrong question. The right one is what the most burning problems are, and what is on the mind of the manager, director and other engineers, and whether you can build something that helps them. Rahul compares it to a startup: you start with the problem, not a solution. Knowing those problems takes relationship building and being embedded in the organization.

Source: 32:02–35:47 ↗

QHow deliberate were you about building relationships with mentees, tech leads, managers and directors who might speak for you at review time? (Rahul)

Carly calls it extremely intentional. Carly looks for people with a common problem or approach and teams up with them. Carly now has friends across business units, including people Carly seldom works with. Carly says that being remote full time makes this much harder than working in an office. Carly describes being an introverted extrovert and says people have to push against the urge not to message others, because no one will argue for you if no one knows you. Carly adds that someone working late and shown as online will not be noticed for that. People vouch for those they have seen deliver on time, on scope and on budget, and waiting to be rescued is the wrong approach.

Another panelist says that they were poor at happy hours, but their work was highly visible and they were promoted even during the pandemic. The key for them was to communicate the work: share the plan, get buy-in, and report the results. Writing and communication are strong tools, because in practice work does not market itself. A manager can be a cheerleader for only so long.

Lee says that being known was the difference between being stuck at L5 and being the person who pulled together Android engineers across Amazon, with data on when apps would run out of methods. People then send others to that person, and the person can point to the next step even when they lack the answer. Lee says human relationships are all there is. Lee worked remotely at Meta, never visited, and did not succeed. Lee had decent relationships but not the visibility, and so lacked help once things went wrong. Lee began asking one off-topic question a day on an Amazon team during the pandemic. Lee now does so in the chat rooms of two organizations at Google, and says people recognize Lee as the question person, which makes it easy to ask a product manager for help. Lee also suggests asking a manager whether anyone on the team needs a mentor, since even a no changes how they think of you, and sitting in on a product managers' event to understand their process and offer a developer's view. Lee says it may sound like politics, and sometimes it is, but it is part of the job. Lee, who describes being autistic with many social challenges, says Lee still has to do this to succeed.

Rahul offers a litmus test. If you asked a teammate what a person is known for, would they answer cohesively, such as saying that person is the expert on a system? If not, that is a bad sign.

Is telling people about your work just self-promotion? (Sean, an attendee, asked what happened to modesty.)

Rahul says do not frame it as bragging. Frame it as telling teammates how the work benefits them. Rahul's debugging tool at Meta made it faster to debug issues, and Rahul pitched it as a way to ease the work, help the product, and even help their performance reviews. Rahul's reframing is to give a call to action: here is how you can get plugged in.

Other panelists agree that sharing knowledge is mutual. Explaining what you tried, what failed and what worked, or building a lower-level framework others can reuse, makes the work more useful and spares others from learning the hard way. A panelist notes that big-tech engineers are often curious and open, and so they want to hear it. Lunch-and-learns and demos, such as a short screen share of a browser extension, can change how others work. The panelists draw the line between bragging and teaching there.

Source: 45:50–49:40 ↗
Source: 35:49–45:50 ↗

QWhat heuristics improve the chance of promotion to staff, for example the choice of team, its size, or infrastructure versus product work? (Rahul)

One panelist advises talking to someone above staff, such as a senior staff or principal engineer, asking what they would fix if they had the time, and doing that. A principal who supports your document goes a long way. The same panelist says to write the promotion document now, not when it feels ready. Show it to the people who review promotions and ask why they would reject it, then work on those gaps. Otherwise a promotion project might turn out not to be the right one, and that is the candidate's own fault. If the feedback is that you have never led anyone, the next project needs to show leadership rather than more code. Not understanding the process, the panelist says, leaves the outcome to luck.

Another panelist says they favor work on churn and finance-related problems at each company, because that is where the pain in the business is.

Zach puts the relationship with your manager first: without it, even a star will struggle. For data engineers, Zach says the data sets must be ones many other pipelines read from, such as master data. A data set made only for a visualization is not staff-level. A staff analytics engineer may instead own the whole chain from logging to data set to visualization and perhaps a model.

Another panelist describes three common rubric dimensions. One is the size of the work stream, such as the number of engineers and the duration. A second is complexity: could someone a level below solve it, or does it need domain knowledge such as distributed systems or AI? The third is impact: does it span several teams or reach significant business goals? This panelist says leverage comes from building things that other engineers build on, which biases toward infrastructure and tooling teams. Leading a very large product initiative is limited to a few places, and someone must grant permission, so those chances are fewer and harder to compete for.

Is the preference for infrastructure a fair measure of staff-level work?

Lee calls the focus on infrastructure and backend a legacy bias. Companies understood what top-level work on backend systems for billions of users looks like, but not what a principal front-end engineer does. Lee says people were advised to switch to a backend team to get promoted, which Lee considers wrong, though it has been real.

Zach adds that data engineering was new in 2016, and Facebook had only one staff data engineer at the time and now has dozens.

Rahul says the bias is not strictly front end versus back end. Engineers who build client-side infrastructure, such as an Android build system or a framework for client and server requests, also count. The key is that other engineers use what you build, and that is usually one layer below the people building the user-facing product.

Source: 56:12–59:06 ↗
Source: 49:42–56:59 ↗

QAudience question: once you are at staff level, how do you keep exceeding expectations?

One panelist says behaviors at staff and above are similar: influencing through others, growing people around you, and taking on the largest problems. What changes is that the initiatives are a step bigger. To exceed, find something larger in scope, such as influencing two larger organizations instead of one group of about 50, or building infrastructure for hundreds of engineers instead of dozens.

Zach, who says they received an exceeds rating at staff level at Airbnb for 2020, describes two parts. One was delivering the main "big rock" project, which for Zach was refining pricing and availability metrics. The other was design work on longer-term questions, such as a document on best practices for moving data from the data lake back into the Airbnb app, with feedback from principal engineers on edge cases. Zach says that missing the first means not meeting expectations at all, and doing both is what moves a person toward the senior staff level.

Source: 59:09–1:01:34 ↗

QAudience question (Alan): what resources help with technical communication and finding mentorship?

Rahul says the core skill is knowing your audience. At Meta, Rahul checked who belonged to an internal Workplace group before posting an update: engineers, leadership, or a cross-functional mix. Rahul then adjusted the depth, avoiding both too much detail and too little. Before a stand-up or meeting, find out who will be there and how much they know and care. Rahul has no book or video to suggest, and says the way to build empathy for different audiences is relationship building, which gives a sense of the personas you address.

Zach adds that posting on LinkedIn almost every day while at Airbnb taught Zach to say dense information concisely, because the platform rewards short posts. Zach recommends that skill for growth.

Source: 1:01:35–1:04:42 ↗

QAudience question (sesh): should a senior engineer become a tech lead first on the way to staff?

Ryan Peterman sees tech lead as a set of behaviors that can occur at any level, not as a level between senior and staff. Senior engineers on some teams lead smaller projects. Ryan suggests checking the company's own leveling system.

Another panelist cautions that if the missing pieces are leadership and visibility, being a tech lead may give more chances to practice them. But it is not necessarily a stepping stone, and doing the behaviors well does not guarantee a path to staff. A further panelist says the expected behaviors at each level should be written down at the company. Use that with your manager to see where you exceed and where you fall short, and ask for the documentation if you do not have it, because otherwise you can only guess.

Source: 1:04:45–1:06:22 ↗

QAudience question (Sam): how can a data engineer show backend work to a manager who is not their day-to-day lead?

Zach says that if there is no shiny front-end piece, part of the answer is to work with the data scientist or analyst who builds the visualization on top of your data. The other part is to show downstream impact. Zach says a data set can be sold as improving one of three kinds of decision: an executive's strategic decision, a data scientist's or analyst's product decision, or a machine-learning algorithm's automated decision. Zach's pricing and availability data sets at Airbnb fed Smart Pricing, an algorithm that sets prices for listings, which had a large effect on the business.

Zach adds that data engineers can also cite optimization numbers, such as a pipeline running 30 or 40 percent faster. At Airbnb, Zach cut the size of the pricing and availability data sets by 90 percent, so the company could use data 10 times smaller. Zach admits that data engineering can fall into the shadows because it lacks the show-it-off quality of a front end or a SQL query. Where the gain is only visibility, Zach suggests building a story around it.

Source: 1:06:24–1:09:32 ↗

Rahul's closing takeaway

Rahul's view is that the vast majority of engineers aiming for staff or senior roles, which Rahul puts at 99 percent, lack the skills of relationship building and talking to people. In Rahul's opinion, the task is less about the code than about working out what the problems are, who is hitting them, and how to solve them. The figure is Rahul's own estimate.

Source: 1:13:02–1:13:46 ↗

Section 60 · panel

Getting to Staff: Scope, Promotion Timing, and Visibility at Big Tech

Five panelists on reaching staff argue that high-scope work, early and explicit promotion conversations, willingness to take feedback, and visibility matter more than title alone.

The panel's view: scope, early asking, and visibility shape the path to staff

Editorial summary of the panel's shared view: the opening framing treats staff as the first level where an individual contributor must lead without managing people. Progression runs from tasks to features to projects, and then to several projects or a whole product. The panelists argue that reaching that level depends on choosing work with real scope and visible impact, asking for promotion early and explicitly, and then acting on feedback. They also say title opens doors without settling scope, that managers differ in how much they control promotion, and that infrastructure and product teams offer different routes. Several points are offered as personal experience rather than general rules.

Source: 00:00–49:27 ↗

QHow do you tell which problems are worth solving, when a staff promotion needs enough scope?

Zach describes a move at Netflix from an automated threat-detection project, which looked too ambitious, to a shared graph database that other teams could use in many cases. The shift brought more pay, more respect, and a larger leadership role.

Zach adds that scope is not the only test. Risky projects that may never pan out also waste time. Senior engineers can judge how much impact a project will have before investing in it, so a small request to them may sit in a backlog.

How do you build the judgment to see which work will matter?

Ryan says the main method is to read the incentives of the organization. Most teams publish plans with metric targets, so a person can compare an idea with a team goal and judge whether it is large enough.

Ryan also worked on an ads project outside Ryan's own team, which no one assigned, because the revenue opportunity looked large. The work had clear impact and was linked to a senior promotion.

Source: 04:44–06:23 ↗
Source: 02:18–04:42 ↗

QFor Carly and Lee: how explicit should someone be about wanting to reach staff, and how much should they tell a manager?

Carly manages staff engineers and says people raise promotion in different ways. In Carly's experience, about half of the requests to move to staff came from people who were not yet ready. The other half came from people who were ready long before they asked. Carly sees two groups: people who ask readily, sometimes before they are ready, and people who wait until readiness is proved, often a year past it.

Carly suggests reflecting honestly on readiness without setting the bar so high that a reserved person holds back.

Lee says promotions often trail performance at large tech companies, so a person who never raises the question may not know what is missing. Lee suggests stating the goal directly: a wish to grow on the technical track rather than into management. Ask what is missing, build a plan, and write down the evidence, so the manager has the material when the person is ready. Lee notes that not everyone wants a promotion, and some people prefer their current level.

Should a manager wait to be asked, or raise a promotion first?

Carly says both happen. Carly has raised promotions with people who did not ask, when Carly judged them ready. With a large team, year-end reviews are the main time to reflect, but Carly prefers that people speak up between reviews when they feel ready or are clearly above the bar. Carly calls waiting a passive approach and sees little downside to asking too early.

Source: 10:22–12:05 ↗
What should someone do if their manager says they are not ready?

Carly says to listen. Feedback usually points to a blind spot the person cannot see, and a well-meaning manager is not trying to block a ready person. Carly also treats the response to feedback as part of readiness. A staff engineer must take feedback from leaders and teams, act on it, and reflect on it without turning combative.

Another panelist describes a first attempt to promote them into a manager role at Amazon that did not go through. The panelist asked which objections were raised and what evidence would answer each one, then tracked those gaps. The promotion came later, and the panelist says the change was the response to feedback, not one more project.

Source: 12:07–14:39 ↗
What if you disagree with the feedback?

A panelist says that if you disagree and think the feedback is wrong, you can test it by interviewing elsewhere, because the market gives its own view of readiness. The panelist has been promoted internally only once, from junior to mid-level, and got later promotions by changing companies. Some feedback is unreasonable, the panelist says, but learning to take feedback still matters, and leaving is one valid option rather than a required one.

Source: 14:41–16:12 ↗
How should someone phrase a request for promotion?

A panelist says framing matters. A new hire who asks for a promotion right away is unlikely to get support. A better frame is to name a first goal, such as ramping up and having impact, and ask for a check-in in about three months to plan the path. A manager is likely to agree, because the request then shows both interest in promotion and sound priorities.

Another panelist says asking early and explicitly is worth doing, even when it feels uncomfortable. At each level, that panelist asked what it would take to reach the next one, and the manager was glad to help because the team gained impact. Once a promotion looked likely, the panelist also asked about the level after that.

Source: 16:14–17:45 ↗
Source: 06:24–10:20 ↗

QDoes a high performer have leverage with a manager?

A panelist says strong performers have leverage inside a company, because a manager wants to keep someone who solves the team's problems. Asking for growth from that position is more likely to get a receptive response than asking from a less central role.

The same panelist names the limits. A manager cannot promote someone on request, because processes and other decision-makers are involved. A manager can still steer projects toward the gaps named in a promotion plan. If the current team cannot offer that work, the honest options are to move to another team or look outside.

Source: 17:47–19:17 ↗

QHow much control does a manager have over promotion at each level?

Zach says that at Airbnb, managers decided promotions up to senior, while promotion from senior to staff and above went through a committee. Zach describes Amazon before it used committees for promotion, where decisions moved up the management chain through skip-level managers and directors above the senior level, not only the direct manager.

How does the process change at the highest levels?

A panelist says that from junior to mid-level, the direct manager's view is usually decisive, so alignment with the manager matters most there. At the highest levels, sign-off from VPs and other senior leaders is needed, and the manager becomes more of a messenger for the committee. That is why it helps to ask early, so the manager can collect the committee's feedback sooner.

Source: 20:16–21:01 ↗
Source: 19:19–20:13 ↗

QHow should someone judge which team is the best place to earn a staff promotion?

A panelist offers a rough test. At a company with many products, a team that works on the core product usually has more visibility than a team on a side product. The panelist jokes that working on a smaller app such as Garage Band is unlikely to lead to a promotion, while the flagship product gives visibility almost for free.

Another panelist says a team with less visibility can still make progress. Find the team that owns a weak spot, show them the problem in their code, and offer to help or pair with them. Fixing a real problem with that team makes a person a strong partner, which is different from a small cosmetic change.

A third panelist says caring about the work matters as much as its impact. During a Google interview, that panelist was offered an ads role and said it did not interest them. Work a person cares about gets their best effort, and that makes it easier to advocate for the product to others.

Source: 21:03–24:28 ↗

QDo product or infrastructure teams offer a clearer route to staff?

Ryan says staff-level opportunities are more common on infrastructure teams. Ryan's view is that product engineers usually reach high impact past senior by leading large projects, and there are few such seats. Infrastructure work has leverage built in, because foundational technology helps many teams move faster, which creates more roles. Ryan says Ryan's own infrastructure team is quite senior compared with others.

Does the same leverage show up in data and engineering roles?

Zach follows up with experience in both kinds of role. At Netflix, Zach was a staff-level tech lead on an infrastructure team building a graph database. At Airbnb, Zach was a tech lead on pricing and availability, which was closer to product. Zach says data engineering shows the difference most clearly. The more a person changes how other engineers do their work, rather than building one pipeline, the more leverage they have.

Source: 25:34–26:21 ↗
Does infrastructure work lead to promotion on its own?

A panelist agrees with Ryan's point and adds that changing how other engineers work, such as saving each engineer a few minutes a day, scales across hundreds of engineers. Then the panelist frames it differently. Infrastructure work often spans several teams and can have built-in impact, but the question is what impact is actually available, whether managers in that area know how to promote people, and who sees the work. If only the most senior person on a team sees it, the work may not support a promotion. Infrastructure teams offer more chances, but the team setup still matters, and product work is not ruled out.

Source: 26:23–28:07 ↗
Source: 24:32–25:32 ↗

QHow do remote or hybrid engineers compete with colleagues who sit close to the manager?

A panelist says the main answer is documentation, communication, and proof. Written evidence of impact lets the manager and others see the work without relying on physical proximity. The panelist has worked only in fully remote settings, so the hybrid case is an extrapolation.

Source: 28:08–29:32 ↗

QDid staff promotion require unusually long hours?

Panelists give mixed accounts. One says the project that led to promotion took more than 40 hours a week. Zach recalls about 50 to 55 hours, including the Netflix graph-database build. Another panelist says 50 to 60 hours was common but still left time for sleep. A further panelist notes that some people are promoted while working 40 hours.

Panelists who moved into management say hours mattered less. One says that as a manager, the panelist did not exceed 40 hours a week, and that multiplying other people's output shows impact in fewer hours than personal delivery. Another plans by goal rather than hours, working around 60 hours one week and around 30 the next.

Source: 29:35–31:11 ↗

QDo inflated startup titles lead to down-leveling at big tech?

A panelist says down-leveling happens when a candidate does not meet the level the company expects. The panelist does not think it can be avoided, except by being stronger or interviewing better. Startup titles are often inflated, so the panelist advises comparing the scope of the work with what each company expects at each level, rather than targeting a title.

Another panelist says title matters less than pay and meaningful work. That panelist moved from a mid-level role at a startup to a junior role at Facebook, for about an 80 percent pay increase, and calls that a good trade.

Source: 31:13–33:41 ↗

QSeniority opens doors, but bigger projects tend to come after promotion. How do you break that cycle?

A panelist says seniority helps but matters less than internal brand. The person a manager or director thinks of first for a hard problem usually gets the work, and level often tracks that trust. Being known as someone who gets things done brings opportunities even without a senior title.

Another panelist says title is one way through the door, not the only way. A person can be trusted with larger scope than their title suggests if a manager or senior sponsor vouches for them, and their own actions build that trust. A director-level sponsor can push for the scope, but the person still has to go find it.

Source: 33:44–35:45 ↗

QHow do you get visibility without feeling that you are self-promoting?

A panelist says visibility is necessary to move up, even when it feels awkward or the person is reserved. Visibility does not mean posting about every win. It can come from giving tech talks after a major launch, running a talk series that brings others in, or answering questions on an internal forum. The key is that the people who speak for you know what you do.

Another panelist adds that an internal brand comes from being approachable and helping teammates get unblocked. A promotion case usually needs peer feedback from three or four co-workers who can vouch for the person. Reaching across disciplines, such as product managers and data scientists, strengthens that case, because a person who wins over only one group is still not moving up.

Source: 39:33–42:01 ↗

QWhat was the main reason to seek promotion: money, title, or work-life balance?

One panelist says the main reason was the kind of work. Senior and principal engineers at Amazon were doing influence-heavy work, such as mentoring people, helping engineers grow, and shaping decisions above their own team. The panelist wanted that work. Pay was welcome, but it was not the main draw.

Does moving up change pay in a meaningful way?

A panelist says pay at big tech does not rise evenly with level. The jump from senior to staff is usually much larger than the jumps before it, and more of total pay shifts into stock. Money gives optionality, but stock adds risk. Another panelist recalls a grant worth about $1.5 million on paper that was worth roughly $600,000 six months later, after the share price fell. That panelist also says stock outcomes vary across companies and years.

Source: 42:46–44:20 ↗
Does a well-known employer still help after you leave?

A panelist says pedigree matters because people pattern-match. A name-brand company, such as a staff role at a large tech employer, can set a floor on a later job or a startup. The panelist acknowledges that pattern-matching can also work against people, including on race and gender, and calls that obviously bad. The benefit still mattered to the panelist's own job hopping.

Source: 44:21–45:58 ↗
Source: 42:04–42:44 ↗

QHow many people does a staff engineer typically affect?

A panelist thinks about the number of people affected rather than team size. A senior engineer should affect at least their own team and the scope of the senior manager above them. The panel's rough estimates are about 20 to 30 engineers at senior, up to 50 to 60 at staff, and into the hundreds at principal, which can mean a VP's organization.

Another panelist recalls an Airbnb marketplace organization of about 75 engineers, with around five staff engineers within it.

Source: 46:00–47:02 ↗

QHow does office politics affect advancement, and what should people do about it?

A panelist says politics is mostly about people. Some colleagues are difficult, and some use relationships to get ahead in harmful ways. The panelist does not expect a person to change or remove those colleagues, so the better move is to raise your own standing. If the environment is truly toxic, the right answer may be a different place.

The same panelist adds that when people talk about politics, they often mean difficulty communicating with executives or with another team. That gap can be fixed, and fixing it is part of the job.

How can someone who is right but blunt get their ideas heard?

A panelist says a manager once told them they were right on most points, but that the way they said things was too blunt for people to hear. The panelist learned to ask questions instead of declaring an idea wrong, to ask whether a design would hold at a larger scale, and to point to an earlier system that had failed in a similar way. The panelist says being heard matters more than being right, and that the questions a person asks can be a sign of intelligence.

Source: 47:55–49:27 ↗
Source: 47:04–47:52 ↗

Section 61 · interview

James Cowling: Dropbox Storage, Simple Systems, and Engineering Careers in the AI Era

James Cowling, former most senior engineer at Dropbox and now CTO of Convex, argues that simple systems, clear purpose, and daily mental effort matter more than complexity, promotion chasing, or AI hype.

Cowling's view: the best engineering comes from understanding why

James Cowling, introduced as formerly the most senior engineer at Dropbox and now CTO of Convex, argues that good engineering starts from a deep understanding of why something is being built. From that he draws several connected claims. Simple systems are harder to design than complex ones. Teams should be organised around the problem they solve, not the system they own. Leaders should explain purpose instead of relying on authority. Engineers grow by owning consequences and by struggling with hard problems before asking an AI tool. The conversation moves from his distributed-systems PhD, through the Dropbox storage system and its move off S3, to tech leadership, careers in the AI era, and his work at Convex. Everything below is Cowling's own account, opinion or estimate.

Source: 00:12–2:00:34 ↗

QWhat problem was the Granola research solving, and what else was in Cowling's graduate work?

James Cowling

Cowling says his career has followed two threads. One is abstractions: building simple models for complex problems, which he treats as a hard design exercise in how to design APIs. The other is large-scale transactional systems. He calls transactions one of the most incredible abstractions ever invented, because they let engineers manage what he considers probably the hardest problem in computer science, concurrency.

Granola, his PhD work, was an algorithm for coordinating distributed transactions, in particular what he called one-shot transactions. Code is sent to the server to run a set of reads and writes on several nodes, and the system must commit them atomically across shards. His master's thesis was on Byzantine fault tolerance. His best-known graduate paper, Viewstamped Replication Revisited, redefined a protocol that predates Paxos. Cowling regards Paxos, Raft and Viewstamped Replication as basically the same idea. Granola appeared slightly before Spanner, so it earned a citation in the Spanner paper, but attention then moved to Spanner.

How does Granola avoid the cost of voting for consensus?
James Cowling

Cowling says people often think about performance as raw horsepower, such as disk and network speed, but nobody has meaningfully faster disks than anyone else. What matters at scale is eliminating points of coordination, so that parallel throughput is not reduced to serial throughput.

In Granola, an independent transaction is one where the participants run pure functions over independent state, so each reaches the same result alone. They only need to agree on the serial order: each proposes a timestamp and the maximum is chosen. Most of the paper is about exchanging those timestamps efficiently. The alternative he wanted to avoid is two-phase commit with two-phase locking, which he says is slow because it blocks systems during the transaction, and risky because a node depends on another node returning.

QHow did Cowling build and test a distributed system as a PhD student at MIT?

Cowling says this was early in the days of AWS. His group had a rack of servers in its office, and academics could also use PlanetLab, a communal set of nodes that was a free-for-all with continual problems. For a long time he slept next to his desk and woke at odd hours to check whether PlanetLab was free so he could start a benchmark.

He says this was near the point where Google, with affection, ruined systems research. Before then the value of a paper was the idea. Papers then began to arrive from Google, Amazon and others describing whole systems, and program committees began to expect realistic benchmarks that graduate students could not produce. Cowling argues this obscured ideas, and cites the old paper on leases, which introduced the time-based lock, as a pure idea paper. He sees much systems research as now industrial, and academia as a great place for impractical work but unable to compete on pragmatism.

They cannot read a book or ask ChatGPT, and must learn to think through uncertainty. QWhat is multi-homing, and what problem does it solve?

James Cowling

Cowling defines multi-homing as keeping data in two locations, or homes, and separates primary-secondary replication from active-active multi-homing (compared in the table below). He describes Dropbox's block storage as truly multi-region, so that a whole region such as Ashburn, Virginia could go down with zero downtime and the data still safe.

He says multi-homing appeals to many engineers but is not right for most companies, because the speed of light is fixed. He estimates a synchronous write across US regions adds around 60 milliseconds to the commit path, which most applications cannot tolerate. When teams ask him about active-active, he normally says not to. If US East is down for a day the company is down, which is a shame, but avoiding the complexity lets a team move faster and build a better product. He sees multi-region availability as making sense for a company like Dropbox, with several exabytes and hundreds of millions of customers.

How many replicas would Dropbox keep of a single document?
James Cowling

Cowling says it is many. Dropbox advertised at least 12 nines of durability, and the internal model put it around 24 nines, which by the model means the universe would end before data is lost. This is his recollection, not a checked figure.

The method is erasure coding, which combines blocks with an encoding scheme and spreads fragments across locations. At that scale, he says, placement considers racks and rows on different power feeds and different eras and makers of hard drives, because they can fail together. A file might be spread over around 27 fragments, which does not mean 27 times the storage. Dropbox used a custom encoding matrix and fed in variables such as disk cost and network bandwidth cost, since the choice is between more copies and fast re-replication after a failure. He says the complexity was abstracted into one part of the system and did not leak elsewhere.

Source: 16:26–18:51 ↗
If a document is split over many machines, how do you avoid waiting on a slow one?
James Cowling

Cowling says erasure coding is actually faster. In a simplified example that is not Dropbox's scheme, if a file can be rebuilt from six of nine fragments, the system asks all nine and returns the data once the first six answer. In practice Dropbox also kept a copy on a single disk for fast access and served data from a region near the user.

He then argues against saving money by leaving the cloud. Almost certainly you cannot, he says, unless your needs are small or fixed or you invest very heavily. Beating Amazon on storage efficiency requires supply chain, capacity and data center teams negotiating with disk makers to push disks to 90 to 95 percent full. He calls the Dropbox effort a ballpark billion-dollar project and, as far as he knows, then the largest data migration in history. In his view the cloud is an incredible innovation and most people should focus on their applications.

QSince most people should not run their own storage, why did Dropbox migrate away from S3?

Cowling says leaving S3 was a long-held company desire, from before he joined in 2012. The motive was strategic: to control the company's destiny. Dropbox was then in the file sync and share category, and owning the file system was valuable. He says the project saved a huge amount of money, before the company went public, but was very hard and would be difficult to emulate without a huge investment.

He also sees an organisational benefit in hard problems. They attract engineers who like them, and those engineers rotate to other parts of the system once the problem is solved. After the very small storage team shipped, a colleague named Jamie redesigned the sync protocol and desktop client, and Cowling worked on the file system and distributed databases. His caution is that such a system is like having a baby: you cannot build it and be done, because you must keep investing.

James Cowling

Cowling says Amazon was not particularly aware for a long time, though data center people noticed Dropbox buying a lot of space. Dropbox already had heavily discounted rates, but at some point Amazon could not match its cost efficiency, because the new system really was more efficient at launch. He gives two reasons: Dropbox used new shingled magnetic recording disks, probably the first at scale, and it understood its own workloads tightly, whereas S3 must be designed for everybody. He would not recommend another company do this now, but it made sense for Dropbox then.

What is an example of workload knowledge letting Dropbox do what S3 could not?
James Cowling

Cowling says a newly uploaded file is accessed quickly, for example when shared or previewed, and access then decays. So Dropbox ran two clusters. One was temporary storage that was cheap to read and write but inefficient to store in. Data landed there first and was moved in bulk in the background to a colder, more static system that used more efficient algorithms and could go down for writes without harm. That separated the live write path from the long-term read path.

He adds a hardware example: estimating the amps each rack's circuit breaker needed from access patterns, and sometimes getting it slightly wrong, so that a bad batch of disks caused extra re-replication and a hot rack. He says this level of tuning only makes sense at multi-exabyte, million-drive scale.

QWhy did the storage system move from Go to Rust?

James Cowling

Cowling says the prototype was in Python, which he defends as decent for IO but poor for concurrency and memory management and hard to refactor. Because the system had to be correct, the team moved to Go, before Go was generally available. Go suits concurrency and proxies.

At around a million nodes, he says, the team itemised every cost, even sheet metal, and wanted nearly all spending to go on disks. A big problem was how much memory nodes used and how unpredictable it was under the Go runtime. In a storage system an out-of-memory restart looks like a disk failure and triggers re-replication, so a batch of them can cascade. He recalls a band, possibly De La Soul though he is unsure, releasing an album on Dropbox. A load spike on a few files made machines run out of memory, and reconstructing from replicas turned one fire hose of load into roughly seven. That is congestion collapse, and he calls designing against it one of the hardest parts of Magic Pocket, the storage system.

The team switched the storage nodes to Rust, before Rust was generally available, which he calls risky. It also dropped the file system and addressed disks directly using draft specifications from the disk makers. Congestion collapse stopped, reliability improved, and spending shifted almost entirely to disks.

Was there a postmortem for the cascading failure?
James Cowling

Cowling says none was needed, because the problem was evident as it happened when he was paged at night. He treats it as an argument for the cloud: you cannot cheaply swap memory chips in every machine of a hardware fleet that cost hundreds of millions.

He recalls a week when two trucks delivering racks both crashed, costing what he thinks was around six weeks of capacity. It was like a laptop disk filling, across a million disks, and customers could not be told to go away. The lesson was to plan buffers and design out congestion collapse and memory spikes. He also describes FMEA, a spreadsheet of every bad thing that could happen and how bad it would be, a kind of pre-mortem, and says he likes the moments where the rubber hits the road and no one can help.

Source: 32:17–34:59 ↗
At Instagram we had DEFCON knobs that degrade a system gracefully. Did Dropbox have something like that?
James Cowling

Cowling says never for durability, which was absolutely non-negotiable. There were knobs for background processes, CPU and memory, so a load spike could be met by turning off background work and test load. The team also built a system called trampoline: if capacity got too close to a threshold, data was written to S3, possibly around 30 petabytes in the worst case, and moved back later. That saved money because capacity could run closer to the edge. It rarely happened outside tests, but he found the escape hatch reassuring.

QHow do you coordinate such a large migration without breaking the system while it runs?

James Cowling

Cowling says the first builders were a handful of engineers, perhaps three to six. His first answer is to keep things simple, with cleanly abstracted systems whose failure modes are understandable and which are decoupled. He adds that in his view agents are not good at building simple systems, so simplicity is still a human domain for now.

His second answer is thick validation. During the move off S3 the team did a dark launch, double-writing data to both systems. The founders required six months with no incidents, downtime or data loss before any data could be deleted from S3. Partway through, a bug slipped through several layers of release process into production. Nothing bad happened, but Cowling told the VP the clock would reset, at a cost he describes as double-digit millions. The VP thanked him and said they trusted him. Cowling says people were almost proud, since he was acting on the company's principle of putting user safety first.

Once validators were running around the clock, the team migrated as fast as it could, peaking at about 764 gigabits per second between Amazon and Dropbox. He received a slightly nasty email from someone at Amazon about doing so many reads and so few writes, and did not reply. He stresses that AWS was a great partner and Dropbox still uses it, but says the episode probably strained the relationship.

You mentioned simplicity. Is there a concrete example?
James Cowling

Cowling describes the map from each block to the disks that hold it. Dropbox used a cluster of about a thousand MySQL nodes indexed by block ID. New hires from academia or elsewhere called it unsophisticated and suggested a Patricia trie or a distributed hash table. He says that optimises for the wrong thing. With one big table, services can walk it constantly and check that every block is where it should be; a complex structure is much harder to validate. Design should be for validation and understanding, because what matters is what you do when a system does not work.

He argues that engineers who want to look like intellectual problem solvers drift toward complexity, whereas simple systems are far harder to design. The best compliment is for people to call a design the obvious way, as they say of Convex, though it was not obvious when no one else was doing it. Simplicity scales over years as well as queries per second: a simple system can absorb new features and changed requirements for five years, while a complex over-optimised one cannot. He warns that, especially with LLM-assisted design, something working does not make it maintainable or understandable.

QEngineers I know have had promotions rejected because their work was not complex enough. What do you make of incentives that reward complexity?

Cowling says it nearly angers him and is partly why he started his own company. His ideal is to be appreciated for solving the problem. He uses a farming analogy: there was no incentive to make milking a cow complicated, because the reward was milk. A startup works the same way. At a large company, with many layers, people build alternative incentives such as green checks on an OKR plan, and he finds it maddening when people chase artificial goals. He accepts some people have no choice, but says working where you are appreciated for problem solving makes you a much better engineer.

From interviewing, he says some engineers at big companies, with Google as his example, describe building a system but cannot say why or how it is used, only that a VP asked. He calls this a caricature, and says it allows competent engineering but the best engineering comes from a deep understanding of why. At Convex everything exists for a reason; you should not build a fancy load balancer unless needed, though he notes the team now does need one.

To cynical juniors he says to fight the system a little. His happiest times were spent dedicating himself to a cause and trusting that promotion would follow, or he would go elsewhere. He suggests finding a team that wants to do good work, which he calls being true to yourself, not selling out.

While building the system it was called the Magic Pocket team, after a silly code name. As soon as it shipped, he renamed it the storage team, which took real work across emails, channels and repositories.

His argument was that the storage team's job is to meet the organisation's storage needs, not to advocate for Magic Pocket. If moving back to S3 were better, the storage team should be the one to say so. When staff-plus engineers he mentored complained about an inefficiency, he asked whether it should be solved right now, and if so what lower priority work should stop. Often nothing was lower priority, and then, he says, you accept it. He sums it up as you break it, you bought it. Shutting a product meant redirecting it, not causing problems, and he credits his success to ownership: instead of complaining he wanted to fix things. Cowling picks the second without hesitation. He notes it is easy for an older person to say this.

He says that for a long time Dropbox had no proper level system, and he believes that as tech lead he earned the least on his team, which he knew as a technical manager. It worked out. He would take working with the best people over 20 percent more money. There is no shame in a regular job, he says, but anyone maximising career growth should maximise skills, and he believes talent correlates with pay and growth. He compares leaving early to leaving a basketball game before the end. If the job is bad, he says, leave it.

Cowling says they become people managers who see the job as keeping a team happy, coordinating it or handling day-to-day issues, but are not organisational leaders pushing the team toward excellence or shaping technical strategy. QTech workers can be anti-authoritarian. How does a tech lead keep credibility?

Cowling says command-and-control companies, where a manager just tells people what to do, are typically not excellent. To get engineers who feel personally responsible for good decisions, they must believe in what the team is doing. As founder and CTO of Convex he cannot just tell someone to do something; they might because they like him, but they would ask why. He spends time explaining where the market is trending and where the product has gaps.

He describes a hierarchy of values, then why, then what, then how. Engineers often debate the how, but he says most organisational conflict comes from well-meaning people who disagree on why: one team thinks the priority is more features to grow, another thinks it is reliability. He wants everyone to have 100 percent alignment on why, and then trusts the team.

At Dropbox one of his jobs was resolving cases where one team called another an idiot. In his telling the other team was not, and once he learned their motivations they chose to do the project, not out of fear. A tech lead has little authority, he says, and leading by authority produces a culture where people do as they are told and good ideas do not arise.

Meta technically has no titles. Is Convex run the same way?
James Cowling

Cowling says Convex is very flat but has tech lead roles. He does not fully buy that everyone is just a software engineer; at a company where everyone is a member of technical staff, people still notice when the most senior person comes to their desk. What matters is a culture where no one acts only because a senior person said so. Reputation counts, and an experienced person's explanation probably holds wisdom, but even the most senior should win hearts and minds. A principal engineer who orders a database deleted without saying why is not empowering, he says; one who offers to talk through where the product is trending is.

His mentoring helps people become more spiky in the area that makes them special, and works on the personal side: understanding people and the why.

QHas any career advice you would give changed in the last five years because of agentic tools?

Cowling says his own view has not changed much but the industry's has changed dramatically. He says demand for senior engineers in Silicon Valley is incredible, while it is getting harder for juniors to succeed and grow. In his view LLMs cannot do everything: architecture, simplicity and design remain human work, despite what is said on Twitter, and the labs are desperately hiring senior engineers. Junior tasks are becoming commoditised, which worries him.

He describes wisdom as facts put into practice and then synthesised. People say learning is easier now because ChatGPT can explain two-phase commit or snapshot isolation versus serializability, but he says growth requires wisdom, which comes from synthesis. He remains bullish on young people, and Convex hires hungry juniors. His advice is to train your mind and to ignore claims that knowing less engineering will be an advantage, which he calls ludicrous. Engineering is an intellectual discipline for breaking problems into building blocks, and that takes experience, like lifting weights: light weights, or letting a robot lift the heavy ones, does not make you grow.

He would never tell someone not to use a coding agent, but warns of a passivity trap. Spend time in the intellectual wilderness of struggling with a problem: think of a solution first, then check with an LLM. He says it is getting harder to resist reaching for help, and compares this to his own difficulty reading books after a day of watching videos.

Cowling replies that agents are currently not good at many parts of engineering, such as designing distributed-systems protocols or managing a three-million-line code base, and that the labs are still aggressively hiring engineers. He doubts human ingenuity will stop mattering.

He poses a thought experiment. If AGI arrives in a year, one person has given up on problem solving and just runs 17 coding agents accepting whatever Claude says, while another still wants to understand and think hard. Who is better placed? Engineering, he says, is a way of improving your mental processes. He still does whiteboard coding interviews, and says Anthropic does too; candidates are getting worse at coding, but he knows no better way to evaluate problem solving. He compares it to proving already-proven theorems in a maths degree, where the act improves your mind. Coding and engineering are different, he adds, so he sees a promising role for people in engineering even if not in coding.

Quitting because AGI is coming, and being wrong, means getting off the ride. He calls this a cool time for engineering, hates talk that AI leaves humans no role, and wishes his peers would drop the doomer narrative. Convex was started to make it easier to build cool things, not to eliminate jobs.

QWhy did you leave Dropbox to build Convex, and what is Convex?

James Cowling

Cowling says Dropbox is a great place, but after eight years, and a while as its most senior engineer, he wanted to grow and do his own thing. He left amicably.

He started Convex before the agentic era, on the view that the main differentiator in a large project is the quality of its abstractions, design and architecture. He thinks the hardest challenge in engineering is distributed state management: storing state reliably and reasoning about it while others modify it concurrently. In his description, Convex is a transactional database whose transactions are written in TypeScript and run as serializable stored procedures, with automatic reactivity so the client sees a consistent view of the server. It is designed to be composable, so application developers can build complex full-stack applications.

Agentic development then helped, he says, because what humans find hard, agents find hard too: large code bases, action at a distance, race conditions across services, and keeping architecture simple over time. Almost everyone using Convex has a coding agent building the front end but needs a back end at a higher level of abstraction than AWS or hosted Postgres.

Is Convex a layer of abstraction on top of primitives like AWS?
James Cowling

Cowling says yes, and ties it to making problems go away. He mentions that he watched the host's interview with Barbara Liskov, his grad school advisor, with whom he worked on abstraction and clean designs that minimise complexity. He calls AWS and Postgres fine tools, though he says none of the mainstream databases is that great, but says they do not make problems go away. Convex aims to let developers avoid reasoning about state management, concurrency, scheduling, transactions, polling, data sync and type safety.

He sees engineering history as the abstraction floor rising, from punch cards to operating systems, C, higher-level languages and the cloud. Most people never think about how S3 is implemented, which he calls a successful abstraction. He believes the world is overdue for another one level up, and that people using agents mostly do not want to own a Postgres instance or choose between Kafka and RabbitMQ.

Source: 1:39:55–1:42:09 ↗
What are you most excited about behind the scenes at Convex?
James Cowling

Cowling calls Convex a new operating system in some respects, with primitives such as queries, mutations, actions and subscriptions, running on its own distributed database that tracks read and write ranges. As workloads grow larger and more performance-sensitive, the team is building a lower-level API for efficient background processes and singletons, with fork-like primitives, which he expects to speed up components such as the workflow system.

He says he still finds Convex very hard and struggles every day. Designing the new API is a problem ChatGPT cannot answer well, because it is innovation. He finds it stressful, tiring and exciting, and encourages engineers to look for work on the edge of liking it and finding it tough.

Source: 1:42:11–1:44:15 ↗
What does fork mean in a distributed system?
James Cowling

Cowling says live traffic is bound by user interactions, so Convex rarely has scale problems there. The harder scaling is background workloads, such as someone kicking off a million jobs, and scheduling. Many of these would be efficient with a background singleton process.

His simple example is a voting system where each vote is a row and a tally is needed. A table scan, the obvious Postgres approach, does not scale. A better design is a background job that adds up new votes and keeps a tally, sleeping on a condition variable when there are none. Most users will never know such primitives exist, he says, but they enable high-performance scheduling and background aggregation.

Source: 1:44:16–1:46:05 ↗
Source: 1:37:21–1:39:54 ↗

QWhat was the most technically stimulating work of your career?

James Cowling

Cowling says some of grad school was stimulating, such as formally modelling consensus protocols and reasoning through them on weekend calls with Barbara Liskov. What he found most stimulating, though, was working on a very large storage system with a team when things were going wrong, where the rubber hits the road. At Convex, he says, that happens daily, for instance when a background compaction process runs into trouble and may need partitioning.

He feels most stimulated when a clear constraint is in front of him. He admits he does not know the definition of engineering, but offers his own: engineering is science with constraints, solving problems under resource limits. He is not interested in constraint-free environments, which he calls art, and the more visceral the constraints, the more fun. He says he has always placed himself on the hardest team owning the hardest problem.

Source: 1:46:06–1:48:07 ↗

QHow did you become a consultant on the TV show Silicon Valley?

James Cowling

Cowling says he had nothing to do with season one. After the show was picked up, the writers had a storyline that reached a compression algorithm and did not know what came next, so they needed a compression expert. He says that ostensibly meant him, though he thinks he was more a storage expert. The writers came to his office and talked, and he became heavily involved in story ideas.

He says the show cares about technical accuracy more than people would expect, down to what a rack and a wall diagram should look like when characters build a data center at home. Mike Judge, who wrote the show and is also known for Beavis and Butt-Head and Office Space, started as a software engineer, Cowling says, and he thinks at Lockheed. The writers collected real stories from many tech companies, and the characters are based on real people and archetypes, which is why some people find it too accurate to watch.

Are there Easter eggs, and was the work paid?
James Cowling

Cowling does not think he can name them, but some stories echo early Dropbox, such as ideas being copied by other companies and meetings that turned out to be a competitor gathering information. On pay, he had to be paid because of a Hollywood union rule, though he would have preferred not to because it complicated his visa. He now has a green card, and says he earned a grand total of $400.

Source: 1:51:05–1:52:13 ↗
Source: 1:48:10–1:51:03 ↗

QLooking back, is there a regret others can learn from?

James Cowling

Cowling says he underinvested in his personal life. He could have left grad school three or four years in and learned as much, or joined Dropbox two or three years earlier and earned more. He says he does not regret missed chances to co-found companies that might have become worth billions. The cost was a lot of sacrifice: on call his whole career, a laptop almost every day, many skipped dinners, parties and events. People in his life have suffered as a result, though they love him and accept his passion.

He says everyone has to decide how hard to drive their career, because there is a real trade-off. Looking back he would take more vacations and have a more balanced life. He cautions against hustle culture, including 996 hours and performative photos of a laptop in a bar. He says he probably works more than 996 himself, but not as a checkbox, only because he wants to do the work. His summary is to focus on solving problems, work hard and be passionate.

Your career shows long hours, on call and fires. How do you wind down?
James Cowling

Cowling says he winds down by building things in a little workshop at home. He repeats that the cool thing is doing important work that people use, not working long hours or boasting about running a coding agent all night.

Source: 1:54:55–1:55:53 ↗
Source: 1:52:16–1:54:53 ↗

QDo you have a best technical book recommendation?

James Cowling

Cowling admits he has read almost no technical books. In academia he read a lot of papers. He says reading is great but should be balanced with practice, and that most of his learning has come from doing, since nothing develops an engineer like facing a real problem.

Source: 1:55:54–1:56:34 ↗

QIf you could give your younger self one piece of advice, what would it be?

James Cowling

Cowling would say it will be okay and not to sweat the small stuff so much, while noting that this is hard for him, since his engineering brand is caring about details and he admires the designer Dieter Rams. He says to ignore stories of 22-year-old billionaires, which he calls not repeatable, not normal and not that healthy. He has been an engineer for several decades and is still learning.

He sees a modern feeling that you must max out your growth in the next three months before AGI arrives, and says that is impossible. You do not need to run 17 agents at once. His advice is to orient your career around learning every day, getting better at what you do, and trying to solve things in the simplest way.

On Twitter I see the idea of a permanent underclass if you do not make it in time for AGI. How do you respond?
James Cowling

Cowling does not want to be unsympathetic to people in financial difficulty, but calls the attitude not instructive, since there is little to do with it except feel bad. When someone replies that you can get really good at Claude, he says it is not very hard to use. He forgets which model is latest because it does not matter, and gives the example of Ralph, a loop technique that was the biggest thing on Twitter for about a month and that he no longer hears about.

He calls much of this noise, like tech tabloids, comparable to reading about Beyoncé but as a nerd; you are not growing by it. You can miss a new coding agent and, if it matters next year, just use it. He has not seen a hard skill in using Claude Code or similar tools for someone good at engineering. His closing advice is to watch out for tech tabloidism and keep building real things, and he jokes that people should ignore him on Twitter too.
