Section 62 · interview

Joakim Recht: Uber Distinguished Engineer on Promotions, Influence, and Engineering Regrets

Joakim Recht recounts building Uber's stateful-platform effort into a distinguished-engineer career and argues that scope, trust and hands-on code, not promotion tactics, drive influence.

Scope follows the work, and trust follows hands-on code

Joakim Recht, who reached distinguished engineer at Uber, argues that promotion and influence follow the real scope of the work, and that scope grows when an engineer removes waste for more and more people. In Recht's view, that requires staying hands-on: writing code regularly, leading by example, and earning the trust of the people one wants to influence, rather than delegating upward and directing from documents. Recht says promotion committees are unavoidably imperfect, that organisational politics is mostly noise to stay away from, and that top-down decisions engineers did not believe in were what finally pushed Recht to leave Uber for a startup. Recht also gives a candid account of engineering choices at Uber that did not scale. Everything below is Recht's own account and opinion; the host's questions set the order.

Source: 00:51–1:25:48 ↗

QWhat was the initial problem you were solving, and what is the story behind the project that eventually got you promoted to distinguished engineer?

Joakim Recht

Recht says that soon after joining Uber, the Denmark office was asked to build a new data store, because Uber's single large Postgres instance, with many replicas, was projected to run out of capacity. The office built an object store called Schemaless, based on sharded MySQL, and Recht's job was mostly to manage, operate, monitor and scale those MySQL shards. The early setup was bare-metal machines configured with Puppet, so every master promotion or replacement meant hand-editing Puppet and hoping for the best, which got harder as the system grew.

Containerization was still new, and Kubernetes had only just reached its first alpha, when Recht began asking why the databases should not run in Docker. That would allow different MySQL versions side by side and let several databases share one host. A sharded MySQL setup, Recht says, needed at least nine physical servers per database, which was expensive and badly utilised. The second idea, then uncommon, was to declare a goal state instead of running procedural steps: say that you want a database made of nine clusters of three nodes each, and let a system make it so. Recht describes this as GitOps plus an orchestration and monitoring layer, because plain GitOps is a one-way push with no feedback. Built first for Schemaless, it made scaling, monitoring and operations much better.

The next step was to do the same for every database type. At the time each technology had its own team doing bare-metal work, host management, provisioning and decommissioning with its own toolchain, which Recht calls wasteful. That became the Odin effort: one platform able to operate an entire stateful fleet. Recht says it took a long time, partly to persuade teams that had built their own tooling and partly to make it work with technologies never designed for containers, such as HDFS and Kafka, where host names are baked in and moving data around is hard. The scope grew from the team's own databases to the company's stateful workloads. Recalling numbers loosely, Recht says it ended up with around 120,000 physical servers and around half a million databases, operated by a team of roughly twenty, while separate database teams kept the Cassandra and MySQL expertise. Fleet tasks that normally take heavy manual effort, such as a one-click kernel upgrade, became routine.

Was the main motivation capacity savings and engineering time, with fragmented machines wasting capacity?
Joakim Recht

Recht agrees with the host's summary and adds a third benefit, consistency. Availability should be the same everywhere, and problems such as a failing disk should be discovered by shared tooling once, rather than every team inventing its own way to check that servers work.

Source: 08:06–08:52 ↗
Source: 00:51–08:03 ↗

QYou did not have a grand plan to manage all of Uber's stateful workloads, so how did you convince people to start running databases in Docker?

Joakim Recht

Recht credits the freedom of early Uber, which also came with a cost: at one point someone counted around 52 different database technologies in use. Because few people had to approve it, adopting the approach for Recht's own team was easy. The harder part came when the team realised it should be done for everything.

Recht says they deliberately did not try to convince everyone at once. They would start with what the Denmark office owned, then move to teams owned by friends in other departments, then to increasingly resistant groups. They also knew the platform would not be ready on day one anyway. Recht prefers not to force anything on anybody, and would rather build something, make sure it works, and let sceptics see it running elsewhere. Recht says this incremental approach helped a lot and also took a very long time.

What was the main pushback from other teams, and how did you answer it?
Joakim Recht

The most common objection, Recht says, was that a team already had something that worked, so a replacement was waste. Recht calls that a local view rather than a company-wide one, since the aim was to improve stateful workloads in general, not one team's setup.

Recht concedes the cost. Uber lacked a full software-defined network, so a new host means a new host name and a random port, and logical moves are not possible. That makes some storage technologies very hard, and teams had to rebuild working tooling under a different paradigm. Recht says the payoff was real and often free. One example is NUMA, aligning memory with the CPUs a database process runs on, which matters for data-heavy workloads and for scheduling. A shared platform can handle that, whereas a single team seldom gets around to it. The more of these benefits the platform accumulated, Recht says, the more people came around.

Source: 11:13–13:45 ↗
Source: 08:53–11:12 ↗

QWas this a bottom-up effort, and when did leadership get involved?

Joakim Recht

Recht says the effort could only go so far from below. Uber's stateful side was split in two: the online databases (MySQL, Postgres, Cassandra and similar) and the data stack (HDFS, Kafka, Pinot and similar), which sat in a completely different org whose management chains met only at the CEO. The data-stack side initially said the idea sounded nice but they did not care.

Over time more support built up the management chain, and eventually leadership declared Odin the future and said teams would no longer be allowed to run their own servers. Recht says the mandate helped adoption, because stragglers always exist however good the product is, and full alignment is hard to reach alone.

Source: 13:46–15:29 ↗

QFor people interested in the career side, how did your career grow at each step of this?

Joakim Recht

Recht describes a self-admittedly naive hope that promotion is not always fair, but pretty fair, and tied to the scope of the work and the number of people affected by it, not through direct authority. Odin followed a natural expansion: first inside the team, then the local org, then the wider platform, then beyond. Running a project of that scope to success, Recht says, produces a series of promotions that happen almost automatically, and it drags the whole team along.

Recht acknowledges some luck: one project lasted a very long time, whereas many people are shuffled around or see projects cancelled, which makes it harder, though not impossible, to show expanding scope. Recht's promotions tracked the work. Background work came first, then the first version of the platform, which Recht thinks earned a promotion. Expansion to standard MySQL and Cassandra then led, Recht believes, to principal engineer (title names changed along the way). Handing the project to the team so Recht could do other things led to distinguished. Recht says that progression was never the reason for doing the work.

What are the typical ways to have your work influence more and more engineers?
Joakim Recht

Recht names a personal driver: a dislike of doing the same thing many times. Replacing a database host by hand a few times makes it something to automate or abstract away. The same question then extends from one's own waste to the waste of the team and of others, and Recht says that is where scope expansion comes from. Recht jokingly refers to this as the lazy engineer idea. The drawback is the depth-first rabbit hole: a task needs a tool, the tool needs a better build system, and so on, which can badly sidetrack the real work. Recht sees natural leverage in it, because tooling lets software act on one's behalf and help others.

On scaling oneself and being a force multiplier, Recht prefers helping others work better and faster, ideally by removing their problem entirely, over mentoring or pushing designs down. The question Recht asks is what people could do if they no longer had to do that thing.

Source: 19:05–22:37 ↗
Source: 15:30–19:04 ↗

QYou said promotions are typically fair, based on the impact of the work. What does it mean when you say they are sometimes not?

Joakim Recht

Recht has sat on promotion committees for a long time and says the format changed a great deal. The first one covered all of platform engineering. Managers, VPs, senior directors and senior engineers sat in a room for a day to go through every engineer, with Recht guessing the number was somewhere in the hundreds, with no preparation or written material. Each manager said how good each person was and, unsurprisingly, thought everyone should be promoted, so a point system was improvised. In that setup, Recht says, outcomes depended on how well the manager could present the case: a weak manager meant a weak case, though a good manager could also be attached to weak work. Recht links this unfairness partly to Uber's early culture problems.

Structure improved, but Recht says objective judgment is impossible. An engineer may depend on another team that never delivers, or a nearly finished project may be cancelled by management for reasons that are not the engineer's fault. A committee must then choose between promoting on code that nobody used and denying someone who did good work, trading fairness against motivation. Some engineers also feel treated unfairly because they excelled compared with a weak team, or lived on an island and had not realised other groups were much stronger. Recht recalls Uber moving from Python and JavaScript to Go when nobody knew Go, and committees judging some groups' output as simply not good enough.

Recht says that feels unfair to people who were not prepared for what they entered. That is why Recht wrote a guide to what it means to be a software engineer at Uber, which Recht expects differs from Meta or Google. The title, something like beating the promo committee, was just catchy. Recht regrets that people prepare packets and collect peer feedback without correction along the way, only to be turned down.

The guide is less about promo packets and more about becoming a stronger engineer. What was in it?
Joakim Recht

Recht says its core was good engineering practice, and above all this claim: "If you're not writing code, you're not a software engineer." Recht applies this at every level. The amount may vary, but code should be written regularly, ideally every day. Recht advises against overthinking it or assuming that higher levels need more advanced code, and says they have never seen anyone who keeps writing code fail to grow along with it.

Secondary advice was to write good code, write good commit messages, review code, and make code easy to review. Recht says this craft is rarely taught in college, which is mostly theory, and is learned by watching others, though AI can help now. Engineers also need to articulate their work, for example in design documents. Recht's second philosophy is that running code beats perfect code. Aiming to handle every case before committing can mean a month of work with no feedback, possibly on the wrong track.

Source: 29:08–33:09 ↗
Source: 22:39–29:06 ↗

QCommon advice is to scale yourself by delegating and becoming a tech lead who stops writing code. What is your view?

Joakim Recht

Recht does not subscribe to that idea at all, and sees it often. Part of it is taste: Recht has always liked writing code and says they would probably still do it without a job. But Recht also gives reasons. If an engineer stops writing code, the system keeps evolving and the engineer loses touch with it. Designs grow more idealistic and detached from reality, and when they are handed off, the implementers wonder who the person with the whiteboard and documents is, because the real problems are different.

Recht defines scaling oneself as enabling as many people as possible to work efficiently, not cloning oneself, which rarely works. That is easier when people trust you, know that you understand their pain points, know your suggestions usually work, and know you listen. As people rotate in and out, a leader who is not hands-on loses touch with both people and system. Recht says the result can be hostility, with people not saying so to the leader's face. Recht personally dislikes being told what to do by someone without skin in the game, while staying open to input, and promises to stay out of others' work in return.

Why don't engineers trust management, even when a VP says the same thing an engineer does?
Joakim Recht

Recht says top-down direction from people who do not know the team creates mistrust and sometimes plain hostility. In the worst case, people say it is a good idea and then simply do none of it, which Recht calls the most annoying outcome. Recht traces the distrust to a feeling that the speaker does not really know what is going on. The idea might be right, but without a connection to the speaker it is hard to take at face value.

Recht is unsure whether this is human nature or personal, and suspects it may be partly Danish, since there is little structure there, but says authority alone does not take one all the way in the Bay Area either. When people say yes but do not believe it, they do not take ownership, and the project may get done but not well. Recht says earning real belief takes more effort than people would like.

Source: 38:42–41:22 ↗
Source: 33:10–38:40 ↗

QYou had to influence many people to scale your project across Uber. How do you influence other engineers and avoid that situation?

Joakim Recht

Recht says someone somewhere will never be convinced, and 100 percent is not the goal. Recht believes in leading by example: if you say what will be built, you help build it and take on much of the pain. The higher the level, the more one is told to concentrate on the hard things only the senior person can do, but Recht says there are very few of those. Recht argues that the person who had the idea tends to keep the interesting parts, such as new algorithms or the fun work, whereas most of the time the hard work should be delegated down, to people who can barely manage it, with support to keep them on track. The senior engineer keeps the boring work, since at that level there is nothing left to prove.

Recht says taking the grind earns a lot of credit and lets others grow much faster, because a challenged team works and grows faster. Leading by example mostly means writing code, plus improving documentation or fixing odd bugs, which usually brings little glory. Recht is a strong believer in it.

That is the opposite of the usual advice to take the hardest, most impressive parts and push the easy work to others. What are the downsides of your approach?
Joakim Recht

Recht does not list downsides. Instead, Recht argues that easy work often hides problems. Looking at why a team has so many bugs can lead to bad reviews or bad testing, and the easy task can grow into something non-trivial that really did need a senior person.

To engineers who ask how to find the right project to get promoted or grow scope, Recht gives the same advice: forget that and write some code that works, however small. Each time, ask whether the work is the right thing, because building a system often creates work for other people, who then have more systems to manage and configure. Consider the net result and how to improve it. Recht's philosophy is that scope then comes by itself, and engineers who worry about finding the right scope should relax and focus on providing value. In most cases it works, Recht says, and where it does not, that is back to the fairness problem, but Recht considers it by far the most successful route.

Source: 44:46–48:01 ↗
Source: 41:25–44:43 ↗

QAs you advanced, did your role become more political?

Joakim Recht

Recht first asks what political means, then describes what changed. There is more talking and more fighting, because one must promote ideas and, perhaps worse, listen to everyone else's. There is also more exposure to reality. As a junior engineer it seems someone has a grand plan and everything is under control. Later, Recht says, one realises nobody is in control, and decisions can rest on a vision from the shower or on a conversation with another person who does not know either, and that becomes the strategy. Recht finds this scary for a rational engineer, says it is not for everybody, and did not like it at all.

Recht's coping approach was to abstract from it and do their own thing. Recht has seen many people get sucked into weeks of planning. Because Recht does not need others to tell them how to do things, they do not tell others either. Recht was never a career planner and has a strong aversion to projects that look like dead ends, which Recht left to others, saying no a lot, perhaps too much in some people's view. That works only if one's own work is significant enough to fill one's scope. Recht also has low patience for talking about doing something for days and ending with a vague plan for next year.

Some people avoid promotion to avoid that stuff. Do you regret reaching such a high level and having to deal with politics?
Joakim Recht

Recht says there were 'if only' moments, but that it depends on how well one resists pressure, how confident one is in oneself, and how much one cares about other people's opinions. Caring a lot makes it hard.

Recht credits the remote setup. The Denmark office worked with San Francisco teams, so its days were uninterrupted and meetings came in the evening, pulling people in for only a couple of hours a day. Nobody could grab them in a hallway to join a discussion. Recht says the physical and time-zone distance helped a lot.

Source: 52:44–54:43 ↗
Source: 48:02–52:42 ↗

QYou said the best outcome is when the other person thinks the idea is theirs. What do you mean?

Joakim Recht

Recht says it does not happen often, but those are the best days: overhearing someone argue with conviction, months later, an idea that Recht had put forward and that they had not liked, without crediting Recht. The Odin resistance is an example. A team that had to rebuild tooling it already had could initially see only the cost, and later came to see the benefits without being forced.

Recht may have nudged a few times, or the environment may have changed the person a little. Recht describes the feeling not as being proved right but as pride that those people are now on the right track, reached without force.

Source: 54:44–56:59 ↗

QYou reportedly pick mentees outside your own org and disperse them to increase your influence. How do you pick mentees?

Joakim Recht

Recht says mentoring sounds appealing but is very inefficient as a way to scale, because it is one person talking to one other person. Recht therefore aimed mainly at a network and at two-way conversations, in which the other person also shares something. Mentoring inside one's own team raises the question of who is actually learning what, and close-range advice can be given informally in group settings.

With people further away there is more work and also more benefit. Recht can learn what they do, give input on their work, and plant seeds. Recht has seen people who complained about getting bad projects start to think another way of working might be possible, which can rub off inside their teams and eventually the wider org. That is why Recht prefers mentees who are not very close.

How can a promising mentee signal potential and set up mentoring naturally?
Joakim Recht

Recht would not open with a request for mentoring, which can sound like a large responsibility. Better to ask for help with something specific, or to talk about a design or product, and go from there. Cold outreach works most of the time, though Recht did not receive many such requests. Recht also suggests showing up at talks and asking questions, which Recht reads as a good signal of interest.

Recht thinks a mentor should not disqualify someone who does not know what to say, since needing mentoring is the point. Willingness to learn can be gauged in a 10 to 15 minute chat. Recht prefers mentoring to be informal, and disliked the various mentoring programmes Uber tried, because what people need is individual and does not suit a plan or schedule. It is also fine to say the mentoring has run its course.

Source: 59:55–1:03:23 ↗
Source: 57:01–59:54 ↗

QWhy did you leave Uber?

Joakim Recht

Recht says it is not a nice story, because they were actually happy there. Joining in 2014, Recht found a crazy-paced, very hot company, with people arriving from Google, Netflix and Amazon, and felt imposter syndrome as someone from small tech. Recht hit the ground running and expected to be gone after three or four years. But the newcomers were not much better, Recht says, and they changed jobs often, which makes long projects hard to sustain. Despite a performance and promotion culture that felt unnatural for a Danish workplace, it was fun. The Denmark office had outsized influence and senior engineers almost from the start, most of them grown internally. Recht says it produced two distinguished engineers out of about 70 people in a company of roughly 4,500 engineers, and the work was the kind others only read about in blog posts.

Then management changed, and with it the engineering culture. Recht's local manager, who was also the site lead, left, then the office's first distinguished engineer, then many people in the US. Management became more top-down. Earlier, especially in platform engineering, engineers took part in design decisions, and even when they did not get their way, they understood the reasoning and could stand behind it. Recht gives the cloud move as an example. Uber had been running on-premises, with benefits and downsides, and the decision to move was based on price. Recht says no engineer believed it would be cheaper and that it was not true on its own; it became cheaper only because platform costs had to be cut by almost 50 percent, which Recht says could also have been done on-premises.

Recht says this top-down style drained senior engineers. Staying would have meant working in an environment where Recht could not stand behind decisions. A peer or manager suggested staying, doing their own thing and taking the money, but Recht felt they could not witness what others were going through. Having tried to change how things were done without effect, Recht concluded that Uber no longer needed engineers at that level. Recht calls it a sad, self-inflicted loss of good people, many of whom have gone to Databricks.

Source: 1:03:25–1:10:46 ↗

QWhy a startup rather than Databricks or another big company?

Joakim Recht

Recht gives two reasons. Databricks had a local office and wanted to build much the same infrastructure Recht had already built once, and Recht wanted some change. The second reason is that being a senior hire is scary. In a new place one has no personal reputation, only whatever reputation comes from outside. Recht has often seen senior people arrive to fix something they fixed elsewhere and find that it never transfers cleanly. They meet resistance, and some colleagues cheer when they fail. Some companies ease them in, but there is still much catching up and proving to do.

Recht did not want a natural move to another large company to do the same work. If a move was happening anyway, Recht reasoned, it might as well be drastic, the opposite end from 4,500 engineers. Recht notes the other options remain open, including Databricks, or even Uber, which Recht does not want, so going all in on a startup made sense.

How has the startup compared with your expectations?
Joakim Recht

Recht says it has been interesting and a lot of fun. It is an AI enterprise automation startup that builds a great deal every day in a space nobody has been in before, which keeps Recht on the edge. Recht likes building a whole product instead of only infrastructure, which Recht loves but says leaves one disconnected from reality. Fundraising and the worry of running out of money are stressful. It has been harder than expected, but for now still worth it, though not financially so far, and Recht hopes eventually.

Source: 1:14:03–1:15:15 ↗
Source: 1:10:48–1:14:01 ↗

QWhat is the biggest engineering mistake you saw at Uber that was only obvious in hindsight?

Joakim Recht

Recht says many choices did not scale, but were right when made, and Recht is not sure they would do it differently. The 50-odd databases came out of a philosophy of letting builders build and not letting anyone block them. Ten years in that is an insane strategy that will kill you, Recht says, but early on there is no need for structure because nobody knows what will succeed. The hard part is knowing when to expand and when to contract. Recht says Uber should have been better at the transition from full freedom to more structure, though Recht has not reflected much on how.

Recht's main illustration is distributed tracing. After Jaeger was built, there was a mandate to enable tracing across thousands of microservices that nobody could fully understand. Recht guesses a first email went out in 2015 saying all teams must implement it, with a deadline three months later. The same message followed, and the push dragged on until perhaps 2017 or 2018, after which the emails stopped without it ever really getting done. Recht says this inability to drive global change made many projects hard, and calls it an engineering culture problem and a major source of waste.

Recht adds one concrete example, while acknowledging that someone may be angry about it. A team proposed a software networking stack, in which service traffic would go through an ingress and be routed across a software network, implemented in Node. Recht recalls a platform tech talk around 2016 and thinking the plan was insane, but Recht was not yet senior and assumed the senior people knew what they were doing. Recht says they did not, and the decision caused a lot of pain and many years of untangling.

Source: 1:15:18–1:20:13 ↗

QWhat was it like to experience Uber's cultural backlash around 2017?

Joakim Recht

Recht says Denmark and Silicon Valley differ a lot, and found the news bewildering, having assumed everyone was just coding and having fun. The distance was a help. With a nine-hour time difference the office's days stayed quiet and it could keep executing while people left or were fired and board members and the CEO were pushed out.

Recht's impression of Uber's culture was that performance reviews, promotions and even salary negotiation were all about the individual and not the team, which Recht finds baffling. The Denmark office never fully adopted that mindset, so for them the change was smaller. Recht cites scandals they could not understand, such as misuse of someone's private data and a board member's remark about women on the board during a company-wide livestream after a harassment scandal. Recht had mixed feelings, glad of the distance but sometimes watching with popcorn. On visits to US offices before 2017, Recht found it odd to be offered whiskey on a Tuesday afternoon.

Source: 1:20:15–1:24:33 ↗

QKnowing what you know now, what advice would you give yourself at the start of your career?

Joakim Recht

Recht says to try things and not be afraid because something looks hard or because others seem much better. They might be better, but one can get there; it is not rocket science, just computers, and anyone who likes computers is well off if they keep going. Recht advises letting curiosity lead, and not assuming that the current work is the best available, because something better probably exists or soon will. Do not discard it just because the present work is fun. Recht admits it is hard to tell what is better than what one has, so sometimes one simply has to take a chance.

Source: 1:24:35–1:25:48 ↗

Section 63 · interview

John White: Promotion Culture, Meta Teams, and Career Regrets

John White describes how promotion incentives shaped Meta's AI infrastructure and monetization teams, why he treats team culture as a choice, and what he regrets most.

John White's view: promotion incentives, not only pay, steer what engineers build and how teams work

In John White's view, big-tech promotion systems reward a visible career story more than the work itself. He says that in Meta's AI infrastructure and monetization groups, promotion goals pushed teams to ship projects many people expected to fail, and to build systems tightly coupled to other systems, because a rollout that touched many systems helped with promotion. He argues that engineers still have real agency to choose a healthier team, even though that choice can mean slower promotion and lower pay. Editorially, the rest of the conversation covers his early years on experimentation tools, the cost of treating industry as a fallback, statistics and A/B testing rigor, and his regrets.

Source: 00:03–42:45 ↗

QIs John still bullish on Meta and MSL after working there from the inside?

John White

John says he is very bullish on Meta as a company, now as a stockholder rather than an employee. He is much less bullish about being an employee who holds little equity, which he says describes most people, since most staff are paid mostly in cash.

He says working at Meta is less enjoyable than before, even though the business is run very well for the bottom line. He keeps investing in the company and expects to continue. He describes being an employee there as a more stressful time than before.

What makes being an employee harder now?
John White

John says the labor market for engineers has shifted across Silicon Valley. Employers once made large sacrifices to keep scarce engineers. Outside a small set of AI researchers at frontier labs, he says, most employers now see engineers as oversupplied, and some worry that AI makes the surplus worse.

So employers spend less on pay, perks, and staff voice. John says this is a general pattern, not unique to Meta, and it makes being an employee rougher overall.

Source: 02:03–03:42 ↗
Could weaker employee leverage also shape reorganization decisions?
John White

John agrees. Earlier Meta did many things that were bad for the business but made sense for keeping talent, and the company is doing less of that now. He says the fear of layoffs is the biggest emotional stressor for most people, more than perks such as food. After layoffs, people who had complained about losing perks became more tolerant of losing them.

He says MSL feels more stressful than some other frontier labs because layoffs seem possible there. The captions make his comparison with OpenAI and Anthropic hard to follow, so it is not restated here.

Source: 03:44–05:23 ↗
Source: 00:46–02:02 ↗

QDid the promise of career growth change as a retention tool at Meta?

John White

John says many Meta divisions stopped talking about pay, purpose, and enjoying the work as reasons to stay. People instead said the only reason to do anything was a clear story about a promotion. When he moved from data infrastructure into AI infrastructure, he found almost no one whose first goal was not promotion.

Monetization was the strongest case. It hired people out of AI infrastructure with detailed plans for getting promoted. John says that worked for promotions but wrecked many teams, including several he later managed and had to repair. People on those teams agreed the work was bad and unlikely to succeed, yet shipped it to meet their promotion bar.

He says this made good software decisions almost impossible, and that the skills that would help careers most became separate from promotions. When the market turned against employees, managers told people to fear layoffs more than they hoped for promotions. He does not think that was a good cultural fix, though he sees it as an attempt to undo earlier damage.

Did you see people keep playing the promotion game even when they saw unusual behavior?
John White

John says unless a VP is ready to fix the culture and shut it down, people have to play along. He calls not playing the game irrational, because one person cannot unilaterally disarm. He says the culture was dominant in AI infrastructure and monetization, was bad for nearly everyone, and left people in a demoralizing rat race.

Source: 09:46–10:30 ↗
What could someone do about a culture like this?
John White

John says people have a lot of agency in choosing their team's culture. Meta had many teams without the promotion-first culture, PyTorch among them, where people worked for the love of the craft. Inside the system you still have to follow its rules, but you are not forced to stay in that machine. Not everyone would meet the bar for those teams, but many could.

He chose stable teams that would improve over time and keep a healthy culture, even though that meant slower promotion. He says he is torn. If the goal were lifetime earnings, fast-promoting and fast-firing teams might be economically rational. For him, enjoying the craft mattered more, and he was willing to accept about 20 percent less compensation to work somewhere he was prouder of.

Source: 10:32–14:28 ↗
Did outsiders see PyTorch engineers as under-leveled?
John White

John says outsiders often believed PyTorch held a higher bar for promotion, which made it easier to convince others that PyTorch engineers were ready for higher levels. In hiring conversations, candidates sometimes asked whether PyTorch was under-leveled. John would say they might be, or that PyTorch held the right levels and the candidate had to decide whether to take a chance on them. He says PyTorch also trained people who became remarkably good.

Source: 14:30–15:14 ↗
Source: 05:25–09:24 ↗

QHow was your early time at Facebook on the experimentation tools, before the promotion pressure?

John White

John says his first two years at Meta were some of his happiest, though also among the most frightening. He had asked for six months of leave to work on Julia, a language he was a core contributor to. While he was away, the manager who hired him left, and the team he had joined split into core data science and data science infrastructure.

He wanted to join core data science but worked closely with data science infrastructure, which owned the experimentation tools. He says that work was the most valuable thing he did as an individual contributor, and that people who know him from Meta remember him for it. Core data science was turbulent, with reorganizations, new managers, and churn.

A few months in, a paper from a research-leaning group that John was affiliated with became a major PR problem for Meta. John remembers it as something like 'Emotional Contagion in Social Networks'. He tried to prevent the problem but lacked the authority. The author later apologized to the company in a Q&A. John found himself in meetings with the head of legal, and his team faced the possibility of being disbanded. He calls it a formative experience, though the fallout faded.

Over the following years he became one of the main developers of Deltoid, its third iteration. When most senior engineers left within about six months, he became the only person who remembered how the system worked. At about IC5, he became a de facto tech lead and drove the vision for the A/B testing tools for years. He calls it some of the most fulfilling work he did at Meta.

What was Deltoid, in short?
John White

John confirms that Deltoid is an A/B testing framework, where users are assigned to one code path or another and the team measures downstream effects. He says the Statsig product he knows looks almost identical to Deltoid in interface and features. He says he should have built a Deltoid-style startup years earlier, but lacked the wisdom to. He is not sure of Statsig's current state.

Source: 19:51–21:00 ↗
Source: 15:15–19:49 ↗

QWhat is Julia, and what was the data science language war about?

John White

John says he may have made Julia part of that war more than it needed to be. He argues that programming languages are products in zero-sum competition, and that saying otherwise misleads people. Julia's pitch was high-level code that reads like Python or MATLAB and still runs fast. MIT mathematicians designed it to replace MATLAB, so it targeted that market more than data science, though John helped push it toward data science.

His example is a distance-matrix function. The underlying C code is a set of plain loops, and a naive translation into R keeps the same loops, yet R runs far slower. John estimates 1,000 to 10,000 times slower than C. He was frustrated that many Python and R users treated speed as both impossible and unimportant. Julia rejected that view. John was a heavy R user and was disappointed by how often R fought him.

John says Julia has become less fashionable but is still doing well, and he believes it is among the top 25 languages by users. He thinks it is probably the only community still fighting that fight, even though he does not think it has won.

What is the intuition behind R being about 10,000 times slower when the code looks similar to C?
John White

John says slow code usually does work it does not need to do. R pays a heavy overhead because it allows dynamic behavior that may never be used. In R, the brace used to mark a block can be redefined, so you must check whether it has changed. John says he may be misremembering whether it is braces or parentheses. Each such check can cost hundreds to thousands of machine cycles, while adding two 64-bit integers takes one.

R is also lazily evaluated, so function arguments become promise objects. John recalls a paper by two students and a senior professor, Jan Vitek, on the design of R. It found that most promises could have been evaluated eagerly, perhaps 70 to 90 percent, though he is not sure of the figure. Python's inspect module can also change the symbol table, so names cannot be trusted without checking. Fast languages have many guarantees, and R has very few.

Source: 26:15–29:23 ↗
Source: 22:09–25:42 ↗

QWhy did John find it frustrating that grad students and postdocs see industry as a safe fallback?

John White

John says what frustrated him most was that many PhD students wanted to be professors or postdocs, and treated industry as the fallback if they failed out. In interviews, some candidates clearly did not want to be there and saw the interview as a failure, which is not a good sign for an employer.

He also says many academics assumed industry jobs would be easy, as if smart people stayed in academia and weaker people went to industry. One candidate, effectively a computer science professor, could not pass values between functions in code. They printed values in a REPL, read them, and retyped them by hand. John says that method would not work for production code, and that the belief hurts students across the academic system.

Source: 29:24–31:46 ↗

QWhy does John hold such strong views on statistics, and which books does he recommend?

John White

John says he loves statistics but calls it one of the craziest fields. It sells the idea that statistical methods work in real life, yet much of the work is pure mathematics about idealized settings. In pure math, a proof only has to be internally consistent. In applied fields such as software, it is enough that the code runs. He says statistics reasons mathematically and then makes practical claims, and that is where opinions come in.

He says some statisticians hold themselves to a very high bar, while others call a claim true because they said so. His top recommendation is Larry Wasserman, whose books he calls the embodiment of intense honesty. Wasserman states what is assumed and what is implied, and avoids claims that are not true. John says no book has been better for learning statistics. He also recommends a book he recalls as something like Introduction to Agnostic Statistics, by an author the captions render as 'Peter Eranell'. He calls that author hyper-rigorous, and says the book is a little less math-heavy than Wasserman's, which suits social scientists and practitioners.

Do people in industry approve launches on a green bar without checking the statistics underneath?
John White

John agrees and gives an example from the Deltoid 3 launch. Deltoid 1 was still the default. A reviewer blocked the launch because a holdout that had been a statistically significant win was no longer significant under Deltoid 3, and the reviewer read that as a regression. John replied that it might be a regression, or it might be the truth, and that nobody knew which. The reviewer wanted to wait until the half ended and goals were met. John argued that a result that close to the line is not a real win, since mild code changes could flip it.

John calls it a dangerous culture to treat results that barely cross or miss the significance line as clear wins or failures. He describes a team he managed that shipped code to hit a goal, although it planned to delete the code a day into the next half. He asked why they were shipping it, and they said they could not miss their goals. He argued that goals should not reward shipping code that will be deleted right away. He convinced them not to ship, since as the manager he decided ratings.

John says weak statistical understanding feeds other odd evaluation habits, and the two together become especially dangerous.

Source: 35:07–37:59 ↗
Source: 31:48–35:04 ↗

QDo you have a regret that others could learn from?

John White

John says he has a stock answer, because he is asked often. For his first several years, his skip-level manager, Javi, ran office hours. John's manager, Danny, kept suggesting that someone should go. John did not go, because he felt he had nothing valuable to say to Javi.

Later, as John ran office hours for a larger organization, he wished people would come, and he realized Javi had felt the same way. John says he missed a valuable opportunity and made things worse for Javi as well. He calls it a decision made out of fear that harmed both parties.

His advice for junior engineers is to go when a leader says they want to hear from people. Directors and above are far removed from the work, and John says he sometimes had managers managing managers. Bring a concrete idea rather than asking how to get promoted, he says. Leaders welcome that, and many people are afraid to do it, which makes everyone worse off.

Source: 38:02–41:02 ↗

QIf you could go back to the start of your career and give yourself advice, what would you say?

John White

John says he holds strong opinions but can be more self-conscious than he should. His advice is to believe that bigger work is possible, and that with high discipline it is. From high school through college, he says, he too often cast doubt on what he could do. He calls that the biggest set of mistakes he has made: not being ambitious enough, or not believing a problem was tractable.

He also says people over-convince themselves of others' greatness and under-convince themselves of what they can achieve. That combination makes them take fewer risks than they could. Until he worked with many people who succeeded, he says, he did not see how often those people were not much better. They just tried, and others did not. For a 20-year-old version of himself, that is the main lesson he would give.

Source: 41:05–42:38 ↗

Section 64 · interview

Let the problem choose the role

Ilya Grigorik traces a founder, manager, and principal-engineer career built around curiosity, self-sufficient teams, and a versatile combination of skills.

QWhy are Waterloo’s co-op students so effective?

Grigorik credits alternating academic terms with work terms, rather than treating industry experience as an optional interruption after years of study. Roughly six placements offer repeated experiments with industry, company size, role, and working environment.

A short placement can disprove a preconceived preference without the resume stigma of repeatedly leaving permanent jobs. Someone who imagined Wall Street may discover the city, people, or work do not suit them. Repeated choices build a better model of personal fit.

The applied work also puts theoretical tools in context. An engineer must solve a real problem under constraints and recognize when a theoretically sophisticated optimization does not matter—for example, when the array has only ten items. He would like more universities to adopt that repeated learning loop.

Source: 00:41–04:34 ↗

QWhy found PostRank after graduation?

He initially planned graduate school partly because he did not know what to do. During the summer, he explored a product idea: links could signal useful content, but comments, likes, and other social interactions could add signals in the newer web. PostRank aggregated those interactions to rank posts.

His launch brought both demand and implementation problems. He recalls several sleepless days because the servers struggled, admitting that poor code contributed. Publicity led to investor conversations.

Facing the graduate-school start, he noticed that the courses most appealing to him concerned entrepreneurship. He could study those ideas academically or learn while already speaking with investors. He postponed the program, closed funding, and never returned to complete the degree. The choice was an experiment connected to a real opportunity, rather than a predetermined founder identity.

Source: 04:36–08:39 ↗

QHow did Google’s acquisition conversation begin?

After a conference presentation, a Google Analytics product leader approached the team and invited a conversation. The discussion was friendly and exploratory, beginning with understanding the product and asking whether they could work together. Grigorik later understood that Google’s response to Facebook and its social initiatives created demand for relevant talent and infrastructure. Analytics could use their experience to understand social engagement, making a mutually useful connection.

How did Google decide levels and compensation for an acquired team?

The team, including Grigorik, underwent full interview panels in an accelerated group process. Google evaluated engineering quality and level rather than assume acquisition alone established those. Deal negotiations also had distinct layers: people, customers, product, and intellectual property.

Source: 11:18–12:34 ↗
Was an acquisition payment simply a large signing bonus?

Not necessarily. Different deals acquire different combinations of assets and people. PostRank supplied useful intellectual property, but its product largely had to be rebuilt within Google Analytics. Moving from tens of thousands of accounts to internet-scale pipelines changed the engineering economics: even a small field addition could imply enormous storage. He remembers learning from reliability engineers to scrutinize such changes.

Source: 12:11–14:03 ↗
Source: 08:41–11:15 ↗

QWhat was your role in Google Analytics, and why leave a director trajectory?

He joined as an engineering manager because he had been founder and CTO. He remained committed to the original aim of helping publishers understand engagement and spent about a year rebuilding the stack. With the team on a sound trajectory, he considered another direction.

A VP offered a clear path toward director, but Google’s technical environment drew his curiosity. Internal documents showed work far ahead of published papers, and engineers sometimes lacked time rather than permission to share the advances. He became interested in contributing to a broader web ecosystem.

The Make the Web Fast group worked across cellular systems, protocols, proxies, and the fundamental question of measuring speed. Grigorik chose a lateral move into IC work even though he might be downleveled and reset the conventional management path. He valued more self-direction, fascinating problems, and collaborators he admired.

Were curiosity and control of your time the actual tradeoff?

Yes. He says a manager’s calendar largely serves other people’s needs. He wanted another mode in which he could direct more of his own work toward research or projects where his skills were especially useful. He acknowledges substantial uncertainty in making the choice.

Source: 19:58–20:35 ↗
Source: 14:05–19:56 ↗

QWhy later return to management in developer relations?

He regards movement between IC and manager as an underappreciated pattern among senior engineers. A person may first discover a path alone, then realize that building the full solution requires a team. His analogy distinguishes cutting a trail from constructing a highway.

His performance work moved into browser standards and metrics. Once those metrics existed, the bottleneck became adoption across analytics vendors and open-source projects. One person could not do all that outreach. A developer-relations team could accelerate adoption that otherwise might take several years.

He therefore returned to recruiting and organizing people in service of the problem. The management move was a means of carrying work through a new stage, not a permanent declaration that people management was the only kind of growth.

Is a tour of duty about whichever role best serves the mission?

Yes, while not every problem must become his personal mission. Often success means helping a team reach the point where it can execute without him. Continuing dependence suggests he has not sufficiently strengthened it. If he commits to lead for a period, he still needs a succession plan: finish the problem or establish a self-sufficient trajectory, then step back and find the next problem as an IC.

Source: 24:33–27:03 ↗
Source: 20:35–24:32 ↗

QWhat does principal-to-distinguished growth at Shopify require?

He does not supply a checklist or name one promotion project. A principal engineer must identify useful work amid ambiguity. He expects someone entering an unfamiliar area to learn the landscape, build partnerships, understand leaders’ problems, and determine where their skills apply.

For distinguished work, he emphasizes a demonstrated range across technical layers and business requirements. Someone must understand low-level constraints, reconstruct the actual problem, and connect it to what product and business partners need.

The execution mode also changes with the situation. A frontier problem requires rapid experiments that reveal unknowns; a long-lived platform API requires slow consideration of consequences for the ecosystem. In either case, exploration must lead to a recommendation and useful execution. He compares the role’s ambiguity with a VP receiving difficult problems that lower layers could not solve.

Why aim to be the only person rather than the best?

He respects deep specialists but considers a portfolio more resilient if demand changes. Modest design, sales, support, hosting, security, and engineering skills can combine into a useful capability that otherwise requires a team. When a specialist arrives, he can hand over one part and focus elsewhere.

Cross-functional learning also lets him translate among marketing, PR, engineering, and business partners. He recalls intensive marketing reading to learn their vocabulary. His rapid-learning percentages are personal heuristics; they are not demonstrated learning rates for every domain.

The senior person need not know the most. His responsibility can be finding experts and helping them navigate the difficult space between platform possibilities and business requirements. Knowing how to find answers and facilitate decisions is different from memorizing every API.

Source: 31:20–36:34 ↗
Source: 27:03–31:20 ↗

QDoes a broad skill intersection make a generalist distinctive?

He agrees. A person with sufficient knowledge of several relevant areas can combine them for an unusual problem and change their contribution as circumstances change. Management experience is another available tool: even as an IC, he can coach, give feedback, and partner effectively with managers. His probability-language analogy expresses uniqueness; the interview does not establish an independence-based mathematical model for career success.

Should an IC try management, and is returning a demotion?

He suggests team leadership as a way to explore and management itself if it suits the person. He wants organizations to permit movement in both directions without penalty. Senior managers can value what they learned while still remembering an earlier technical role as their happiest period. Returning to that kind of work can be a new challenge rather than a failure.

Source: 38:26–40:07 ↗
Source: 36:37–38:24 ↗

QWhat regrets should others learn from?

Do not let success raise the threshold for trying so high that it stops learning. His early writing and code now seem embarrassing, but publishing them generated feedback and encouragement that made improvement possible.

A larger audience creates an expectation of exceptional output. That can suppress ordinary observations and experiments that would once have been shared freely. He continues to struggle with that filter and encourages the courage to be mistaken or disliked without claiming to know everything.

How do you enter an unfamiliar domain when people expect a distinguished engineer to know the answers?

Set expectations explicitly. He arrives to help and learn, asks foundational questions, and explains that he needs to build a model quickly. Curiosity can otherwise sound like an attack. Acknowledging both what others know and what he can contribute makes the exchange collaborative: they supply domain expertise while he can remove obstacles or connect ideas.

Source: 42:49–45:03 ↗
Source: 40:09–42:49 ↗

QWhat author or book influenced your career?

He recommends Sir Ken Robinson’s books and talks about education, creativity, and finding one’s element. The philosophy resonates with the co-op discussion: allow people to discover their strengths and combine skills rather than fit a rigid age-based factory model. He recognizes that implementing such an education system is difficult; his endorsement concerns its direction rather than a ready-made policy.

Source: 45:06–46:59 ↗

QWhat would you tell yourself at the beginning?

Value the ability to combine skills rather than feel inferior because friends excel more deeply in individual areas. Early uncertainty about his own broad but uneven competence eventually gave way to recognizing its usefulness.

He would also be braver and filter himself less. Public speaking once terrified him; pitching a product he cared about felt entirely different from performing knowledge for a class. Passion changed how he engaged. He could not have predicted that communication would later become a large part of his job.

Source: 47:00–49:33 ↗

Section 65 · interview

Life after the next promotion stops being the goal

Philip Su examines career limits, the emotional cost of stepping down, and the need for meaning beyond status and financial security.

QWhat did you think when you reached distinguished engineer—did you want another promotion?

Early in his career, Su assumed that promotions would continue every few years and did not consider an eventual end. By level seven, he recognized that higher roles require more scope and that the business must actually need that scope. An organization might limit partner-level positions for budgetary and organizational reasons, irrespective of an individual’s ambition.

When Facebook first introduced level nine, the initial promotees seemed extraordinarily accomplished and universally recognized. He did not consider going further realistic. His recollection challenges the idea that every promotion simply starts another predictable step upward: roles narrow, opportunity matters, and people encounter limits.

Source: 00:45–03:17 ↗

QWhat kept you growing through staff and beyond?

For much of his Microsoft career, levels provided a substitute for the grades and tests he had enjoyed at school. Professional work offered few clear numerical indicators, so promotion felt like an achievement score. He actively pursued that score into his early thirties.

Beyond level seven, he became unsure whether he would enjoy the changing work or meet its expectations. His later promotions to eight and nine were consequences of work he found interesting, rather than explicit targets. Facebook was then small and mission-focused; he says he did not even know levels existed there until his manager told him he had been promoted.

Source: 03:17–05:37 ↗

QWhat changed your view of promotion?

The reward became less uncomplicated. A promotion brought expectations he was no longer certain he could fulfill. Staying at a level where he already enjoyed the work began to feel comfortable, and he recognized that it might be his final level.

He recalls immediately asking how to reach eight after a mentor promoted him to seven. The mentor asked whether they could spend one meeting celebrating. Years later, Su realized that this respected, more experienced mentor was himself at the same level. He now sees his earlier response as insufficiently humble: doing excellent work at an existing level is already a substantial accomplishment.

What calmed the intense desire for more?

He thinks age may contribute, while explicitly valuing young people’s ambition. A more concrete factor was the changing job. Up to about IC6, the work often felt like a larger version of coding, refactoring, and longer-term engineering projects.

For a generalist beyond that point, advancement increasingly means setting team direction, judging whether a product is worth building, and resolving conflicts between organizations. More meetings come with the work on either the IC or management path. He became less enthusiastic about those future changes. He acknowledges rare engineers whose exceptional coding ability supports another path.

Source: 08:33–11:35 ↗
Source: 05:39–08:31 ↗

QBefore seeking a demotion, did you ever ask not to be promoted beyond IC7?

Not when moving from seven to eight: that promotion surprised him, and the smaller Facebook of that period still involved relatively little organizational overhead. Later, the Seattle office alone had grown from a handful of desks to more than two thousand people. Senior roles in a much larger organization contained more coordination and less direct technical work.

He distinguishes enjoyable people work—welcoming colleagues and creating collaborations—from politics, unhappy colleagues, and constructive feedback. He felt effective leading Facebook London but much less effective at some of the latter responsibilities. Even a senior IC without direct reports is expected to improve people around them, so opting out of management does not remove interpersonal demands.

How did moving from IC9 to IC7 feel?

It was difficult despite choosing it. Rising had felt like progress; being at the top mixed remarkable opportunities with exhausting expectations. He felt a continuing spotlight on whether the company was receiving value from a highly paid senior employee.

Watching people formerly below his level rise above him brought wistfulness rather than a wish to limit their success. He remembered being capable of that work and wondered whether he could do it again. His Beowulf analogy expresses the desire to deliver one last great performance, while accepting that this may no longer be right for him.

Source: 14:30–17:32 ↗
Source: 11:36–14:30 ↗

QWhat changed that made the higher level harder to sustain?

His environment changed. In a small company, his generalist range was useful: for Facebook video calling, he wrote code, negotiated partner contracts, dealt with testing arrangements, and spoke to the press. A large company assigns those tasks to specialized functions. He thinks senior domain experts fit that setting better, while his own strengths became less relevant.

One later team spent an entire half fixing bugs in an internal tool. He was willing to help, but it was not work in which he felt especially distinguished. Meanwhile, he tired of the pressure to meet senior expectations. Earlier, being the weakest person on a team could feel exciting because he was catching up; later it felt like a recurring risk rather than a desirable challenge.

Was that pressure mostly impostor syndrome, given your promotions?

He allows that some may have been, but considers much of it an honest assessment of fit. At IC4 he could imagine doing many IC5 jobs with time. At IC7 he could see peers doing work he did not believe he could do. Higher-level business roles also become more specific: the organization needs a particular combination of technical and other strengths, and his own shape did not match many of them.

Source: 20:26–22:06 ↗
Source: 17:34–20:26 ↗

QWhy did you work extreme hours after you stopped pursuing promotions?

Shipping the first Facebook video-calling version brought a strong sense of mission. During six weeks in Menlo Park, he describes moving almost directly between work and sleep and losing about ten pounds. He was not seeking a level; he enjoyed seeing users benefit from fixes and believed easier video calling would matter.

The tiny team created a sense of responsibility to colleagues who were working equally hard. Direct contact with user problems and a meaningful product supplied motivation that the promotion score had previously supplied. His recollection explains his choice; it is not presented as a prescription for everyone’s hours.

Source: 22:06–24:12 ↗

QLooking back, was working so hard worth it?

Su understands why successful, wealthy people telling younger people to slow down can sound unpersuasive. Some tradeoffs become clearer only after living them. For his personality, very senior roles with broad people-oriented pressure became a poor long-term fit.

He also recognizes what the career bought him: enough savings to spend two years building his own software. He does not reject the earlier work outright. His regret is that he pushed without understanding the exchange he was making. Greater awareness could have connected present effort to future freedom and made competing priorities explicit.

Source: 24:13–26:21 ↗

QIs advice useless if people only understand it after experience?

He distinguishes ignoring advice from never having heard it. Advice provides a reference point: when the consequence arrives, someone can recognize it and act sooner. It can also cause a person to pause at a later decision even if they do not follow it immediately.

His small example is buying an expensive, highly recommended pen once he felt financially secure. It was slippery and rolled away; he preferred a cheap familiar pen. The disappointment made advice about consumption and happiness concrete. He uses the story to show delayed understanding, not to claim every expensive purchase disappoints.

Source: 26:22–28:48 ↗

QAfter financial security, what provides meaning outside the earnings treadmill?

He distinguishes personalities that remain content with prolonged leisure from his own need for goals. A week on a beach feels wonderful; an extended stay starts to feel purposeless. His analogy of an animal endlessly triggering pleasure expresses why pleasure alone does not constitute fulfillment for him.

He imagines that the saving phase of financial independence could be more satisfying than retirement for someone like him: it gives a measurable goal and repeated evidence of progress. He says he never adopted the movement himself. Periods without work exposed his difficulty answering what he should do next. This is self-description, not a judgment that others’ retirement preferences are wrong.

Source: 29:45–33:13 ↗

QWould you have been happier with slower promotions spread across your whole career?

He initially thinks spreading the rewards out might have helped, then acknowledges the dilemma. Six promotions over a forty-two-year career would imply seven years per step, which he would have found painfully slow at the beginning. Faster early growth leaves very long intervals later, or decades with no promotion.

The arithmetic is illustrative rather than a proposed career plan. It reveals that promotion cannot remain the sole source of motivation for an entire career. He also wonders whether a late reward has the same appeal as an earlier one, using a sports-car purchase as an analogy. He remains torn rather than endorsing deliberate slow advancement.

Source: 33:13–36:10 ↗

QHave you found meaning without an immediate career goal?

For him, regular social contact is essential. Work supplies a recurring shared place and schedule. After quitting Facebook for six months, he expected coffee with former colleagues to fill that gap, but they were busy working.

His best period between jobs came when two former colleagues were also available. They skied on weekdays and spent time together regularly. He uses an imaginative comparison with leisure-class social life to express the difference: free time is more satisfying when others can share it. Whether employed or not, he now considers a reliable social setting central to happiness.

Source: 36:10–38:28 ↗

QWhich book helped you think about life and career choices?

He recommends Four Thousand Weeks because viewing a life as a finite number of weeks made time more precious and clarified his need to examine values. The recommendation is his account of what helped him, with no claim that it answers every reader’s situation.

What practical question did it help you ask?

Visualize your largest current goal, then imagine you have achieved it and ask what happens the next day. A satisfying answer suggests something durable beyond the goal itself. Su did not have that answer and compares the resulting difficulty to athletes who reach the peak without building another identity or set of skills. He encourages planning for the day after success.

Source: 38:34–40:13 ↗
Source: 38:28–40:13 ↗

QIf you could begin again, what would you change?

He would change periods when he made himself maximally available to the employer and minimally available to friends and family. Some work he justified as helping the family also meant he was rarely present with them.

Interestingly, he does not single out the intense video-calling launch as the main regret. His family moved to California with him, and he remembers that arrangement as making the period more acceptable even with very little daily time together. Other periods involved routine absence without that shared context.

Would prioritizing family have reduced your career success?

Possibly, and he considers the exchange worthwhile. He does not know the counterfactual: breaks can improve performance when fatigue creates errors, so shorter hours might sometimes have helped him professionally.

He also rejects an unconditional promise that forty hours produces the same results as longer work. All else equal, he expects sustained additional effort to affect results and rewards. His conclusion is therefore candid about costs: he suspects greater family availability could have affected his career, and would still accept that tradeoff.
