Section 66 · interview

Michael Novati: Early Facebook, the Coding Machine, and Reaching Senior Staff

Michael Novati, an early Facebook engineer who rose to senior staff, argues that output was constant over a career and that taste, trust, and feedback loops are what moved him up.

Novati's view: output gets an engineer started, but judgment, trust, and feedback loops carry the career

Michael Novati joined Facebook as an intern in 2009, when the company had roughly 200 engineers, and later reached senior staff (IC7). In this interview Novati argues that raw coding output was already high in the first week and barely changed over the career. What moved Novati up the ladder was accumulated taste and judgment, built through repeated feedback, plus the credibility to make wide-reaching changes safely. The host, who is not named in the captions, also asks about early Facebook culture, stories about Mark Zuckerberg, whether LLMs threaten the coding-machine archetype, and why Novati left Meta. Everything below is Novati's account and opinion unless marked as an editorial note.

Source: 00:00–1:25:39 ↗

QWhat was the story behind joining Facebook as an intern, and why that company when it was small?

Michael Novati

Novati started as an intern in May 2009, between undergrad and grad school. A PhD in human-computer interaction at the University of Washington was already planned, with housing and a research assistantship lined up. Novati wanted work experience at a top company doing interesting product work, and applied online only to Facebook and Google. Getting interviews was not hard then, Novati says, and seems harder now.

The Facebook fit was close to accidental. Novati happened to interview with an engineer building internal collaboration tools: diff review, tasks, and discussion. That was the kind of "social network for work" Novati most wanted to build. After doing well on the LeetCode-style questions, Novati joined that engineer's team, with that engineer as manager. Novati calls it the stars aligning.

How big was the company then in terms of engineers?
Michael Novati

About 220, Novati says, with a caveat. Production engineers were not classified as software engineers at the time, so the exact count depends on how the line is drawn. Roughly 200 is the safe figure.

Source: 02:31–02:48 ↗
Source: 00:26–02:30 ↗

QWhat drew Novati so strongly to Meta's culture?

Michael Novati

Novati names a technical pull and a social one. On day one, following the setup instructions, the dev environment ran Apache and PHP locally against a MySQL database, much like a side project, only with a larger federated database behind it. Novati says it felt like home and in tune with how the company built things.

Socially, Facebook was a product everyone had heard of and had opinions on. Novati could get plenty of feedback about what people liked and disliked, and found it motivating to build something people cared about. Novati adds that the company went through ups and downs, even during the tenure.

Source: 02:49–04:15 ↗

QMany engineers who joined then were put off by PHP. Did Novati feel the same?

Michael Novati

Novati gives a split answer: yes and no. Meta now mainly uses Hack, a derivative of PHP, and the path there took stages. The first was a compiler that turned PHP into faster code. There was also a debate about rewriting the whole codebase in Java or Python, and the company chose to optimize and customize the language instead. Novati recalls type-related changes, described as "loose typing", among the early additions.

Off-the-shelf PHP carried a stigma at the time. Novati's reading of Facebook's approach was to make the language better than any other could be for this company, by customizing it at the language level so it was easier for engineers and faster. The host adds a view of their own, that PHP gets more criticism than it deserves and that Hack is a much better experience.

Source: 04:16–05:50 ↗

QWhat does Novati think of "move fast and break things," now that the culture has changed?

Michael Novati

Novati describes having been "the move fast and break things person" at the time and still likes the framing. In Novati's reading, the "break things" half was partly an outside perception, and Facebook did not want to tell the public that people were recklessly breaking everything. The original spirit was breaking norms: first-principles thinking, trying things from scratch, not following trends for their own sake. It was not meant as causing havoc.

Novati still thinks it would be a fine motto today. At a larger, more mature company, though, even the smallest bug can cost millions or tens of millions of dollars, so Novati can see why the company dropped it.

Source: 05:52–08:28 ↗

QDid the culture change over the years, given that Novati started when there were about 200 engineers?

Michael Novati

Novati describes an extremely engineer-driven culture. Designers and product managers had to win engineers over, because work an engineer would not build did not get built. Nearly all internal tools were written in-house and used by employees, which set an engineering-first tone that Novati loved.

Novati sees the 2012 IPO as a turning point. The stock fell afterward because people asked how Facebook would make money, a question that had barely come up in the first three years. As the company grew, Novati developed a more mature view: ad optimization, cost savings, and efficient infrastructure became more important. Early on, senior engineers argued out designs head-to-head, largely independent of management. By the end, VPs of two teams more often negotiated and the result percolated down.

Source: 07:39–10:23 ↗

QWhat was the mood at the IPO? Ecstatic, or scared by the stock drop?

Michael Novati

Not scared, Novati says. It was celebratory but grounded. Zuckerberg was good, early on, at keeping things humble and not chasing press or perception. Novati describes the IPO as a rational way to raise funding rather than a party, yet still something that pulled employees together. Nasdaq brought the bell button to campus and a stage was set up. Novati says there was a story about how it was wired up and suggests asking internally.

Zuckerberg's parents stood right beside Novati in the crowd, with tears in their eyes, and Novati later told Zuckerberg about it. Novati found the moment impactful. Financially, nothing changed at first, because the stock vested about six months after the IPO.

What was it like when the stock vested after it had fallen?
Michael Novati

Novati remembers the day clearly. About 20 colleagues were at a movie theater when phones went off all at once with notices that vested stock had been deposited. The IPO changed little in behavior over the short term. Over a longer horizon, Novati says, people could afford houses and children in the expensive Bay Area.

Source: 12:22–13:13 ↗
Source: 10:25–12:21 ↗

QDid Novati hold the stock, or diversify as soon as it vested?

Michael Novati

Novati held the IPO-era shares and still has all of them. At some later point, Novati says, vested shares were sold as they vested in order to diversify; the timing is not remembered. Novati was grateful for classes, taught by veterans of the Google and Yahoo IPOs, on managing finances and stock-based compensation. Having grown up in Canada, Novati had not deeply understood stock pay and found the lessons on risk "infinitely helpful".

Was Novati sweating when Meta stock fell to around 90?
Michael Novati

A little, Novati says. Holdings were diversified enough that retirement was not at stake. The host notes the price had been around 150 to 180 when the host joined in 2018.

Novati draws a lesson for people comparing offers, from watching stock swings. Novati knows people who joined during the dip and saw their stock rise nearly sixfold in about three years (Novati's own estimate). Candidates often compare offers in today's dollars and agonize over single-digit percentage gaps. Novati calls it reasonable to care, but stresses that the numbers are estimates and that stock prices, acquisitions, and scandals are outside anyone's control. Novati advises prioritizing the company where the candidate will fit and perform well, because performance is more within one's control and is rewarded over time. The host adds that early in a career, a single promotion can mean about 40 percent more pay.

Source: 14:32–16:50 ↗
Source: 13:16–14:29 ↗

QWhat was the internal newsletter that made Novati well known, and why start it?

Michael Novati

It was called "the weekly Novati", a weekly post on the Notes product, Facebook's blogging feature. Notes had no owner when Novati joined in 2009, so Novati improved it at hackathons, adding rich text to what had been plain text. The change was an 11,000-line diff, so large that Novati had to organize an in-person meeting to review it. Novati also used the product constantly, as part of Facebook's dogfooding habit.

A few slightly controversial posts about product building drew traction, so Novati posted more regularly, often off the cuff. Facebook was adamant about staying on the Menlo Park campus, while startups such as Stripe and Uber in San Francisco were drawing employees away. Novati wrote repeatedly about it, including a post proposing a South San Francisco office, and that office later opened.

Would Novati recommend an internal newsletter like that today?
Michael Novati

Overall, Novati says, no. There was no strategic reason to write it. It came from Facebook's value of being open and transparent: Novati wanted to strip away pleasantries and look at products honestly, for example admitting when a product grew through luck and not substance. Novati contrasts this with startups and boot camps that treat a little traction as proof they built something great. The posts had nothing to do with performance reviews or influence.

The cost was friction. Novati once openly called out that engineers with titles such as network engineer or data engineer could not move between teams as easily as software engineers. Novati did not realize it was a sore point behind the scenes, and executives said the post did not help and that they now had damage control to do. Novati's lesson is that an off-the-cuff style has consequences, though Novati still tries to be direct and open on Reddit and LinkedIn.

Source: 18:56–22:11 ↗
Did HR ever ask Novati to take posts down?
Michael Novati

Nothing took the form of a takedown order, Novati says, but HR did give feedback. One post covered which companies were poaching Facebook engineers, and Uber was then offering very large stock grants. HR pointed out it might unintentionally encourage people to explore other jobs. Novati had not thought of that and says such off-the-cuff posts may not have been worth the friction.

Concerned, Novati messaged Zuckerberg directly. Zuckerberg was fine with it and encouraged Novati to keep posting.

Source: 22:13–23:34 ↗
Could Novati really message Zuckerberg directly and get a reply?
Michael Novati

Yes. Facebook was small when Novati joined, and Novati dealt regularly with the executives. When leaving, Novati messaged each executive one-on-one, including Chris Cox, and says they replied with thanks. Novati felt a relationship with all of them, formed from interacting genuinely while the company was small, and got to know Zuckerberg best, partly outside work. Novati has not spoken with many of them in the past couple of years as Facebook has grown.

Source: 23:35–24:26 ↗
Source: 16:01–18:55 ↗

QDid Zuckerberg still write code when Novati joined, and did Novati ever see a diff from him?

Michael Novati

Novati worked with Zuckerberg on a 2009 hackathon project built on Zuckerberg's idea that anyone should be able to react to any post with any emoji. Novati was skeptical but thought it feasible. Novati and another engineer got a version working, but the code was so bad it never shipped. Zuckerberg did not give up, and when reactions launched later under a product manager, Novati thought it was done properly and so much better than Zuckerberg's code.

Novati also tells a story from a 2010 lockdown, when Facebook worried a rival product (the captions say only "plus") might dent its user base and pushed to ship features fast. At a company-wide Q&A, Novati bet Zuckerberg would not commit code by the end of lockdown, and offered to stop riding a Ripstik around the office if he did. Zuckerberg committed it, and Novati was banned from riding. Roughly 2012, Novati adds, the head of HR emailed the five most prominent riders for feedback on a draft email banning Ripstiks, a classic way to win over opponents.

When Novati first arrived, could you see the founders' names in the codebase history?
Michael Novati

Occasionally, yes. In company lore, the earliest engineers were not known for the best-quality code, but they wrote fast and did the job. Later a wave of more experienced engineers arrived, including some poached from Microsoft, and began laying down structure and framework. Others wrote the core abstractions that became the foundation for the product infrastructure team, which Novati says existed for a very long time. Their names were all over the codebase, including Evan Priestley's, and they were Novati's role models when Novati wanted to become the coding machine who writes a lot of code.

Source: 28:30–29:48 ↗
Source: 24:26–28:28 ↗

QWhich engineers impressed Novati most, and why?

Michael Novati

The product infrastructure team, which built PHP abstractions that evolved into today's React framework. Novati watched the framework go up brick by brick and saw those engineers as a different type, a specialty that was not Novati's. The person most like Novati was Evan Priestley, who Novati says was the top committer before Novati. Priestley wrote the internal code-review suite essentially alone, and it was later forked and open sourced (the captions render its name unclearly).

Would Novati choose Priestley or four regular senior engineers for a new product team?
Michael Novati

Priestley. Novati then qualifies it as context-dependent. Being called a coding machine is not magic: it comes from hard work, from holding a lot of code in memory, and from attention to the littlest details. Novati says that on Oculus firmware, productivity would be slow at first. In a comfortable codebase where everyone has ramped up, Novati would pick the coding machine. For something truly new, a more diverse group may bring more flexibility and creativity. A coding machine, Novati says, makes things happen that people thought impossible.

Source: 31:45–33:26 ↗
Can Novati give an example a team of seven senior engineers would not have finished?
Michael Novati

Novati's canonical example is a framework called Preparables. A component had a data-fetching function and a rendering function, so all data could be fetched in parallel before rendering. It was later replaced by async/await and more modern approaches. Thousands of classes used it, and Novati manually and relentlessly refactored every one away, roughly three to six thousand by Novati's estimate, until the parent class was gone. It took several months and was a solo effort.

A second project removed every direct PHP endpoint hit on the server in favor of the routing framework. Neither was the company's top priority, Novati says, and without personal drive they would have consumed resources better spent on new products. One person doing them made all engineers' lives easier by removing legacy frameworks.

Source: 33:28–36:19 ↗
Source: 29:50–31:42 ↗

QWill LLMs kill the coding machine archetype, given that a large refactor like that sounds doable by an LLM?

Michael Novati

Novati did the Facebook work in Vim, with an in-house indexed code search tool and a class-name tab-completion plugin, and was very productive. Modern editors would have made Novati more so. Novati sees LLM tools as the next step, like going from Vim to VS Code: they make refactors and changes faster. Agentic flows are emerging with some success cases but are not mainstream.

In Novati's view, most engineers still use AI tools much less than those at the leading edge. If everyone used them the way leaders do, the industry would already have changed massively, coding machines included. How agentic flows will affect coding machines and everyone else, Novati says, is undecided.

What is the biggest difference between the old Vim workflow and working with LLMs?
Michael Novati

Novati works in a roughly 500,000-line codebase and still knows most of its structure, so multi-file agentic flows are used only occasionally. The main use is speeding up code Novati already knows how to write. For something like a 100-line page component, Novati makes a real-time call about whether typing it or prompting it is faster, and builds up prompting intuition prompt by prompt.

Novati says the product workflow is similar to six months earlier but code output is about five times higher (Novati's own estimate). There is no fixed endgame, Novati adds, since each new model or command-line tool brings new intuitions.

Source: 39:00–41:19 ↗
How would Novati feel if coding became a hobby and programming was no longer driven by humans?
Michael Novati

Novati thinks it is a cool future. Clocked honestly, much engineering time is copy-paste, searching, and staring at the screen. Without that, engineers could focus on the fun parts: creative product work, and for Novati the joy of cleaning up code and merging unrelated things into one concept. Novati offers Sergey Brin dropping into whatever he wants to work on as a model.

Novati also finds it scary for the profession, because it raises the question of what being a software engineer means: writing code, designing data models, systems work, or gluing things together. For the near term, Novati is more confident that experienced engineers with strong taste become more productive and that building that experience gets harder for newcomers.

Beyond that, if AI writes and maintains its own code, Novati expects it will not look like today's code. It might manage services behind contractual APIs, in code no one reads. Novati expects the change to come step by step, not as an overnight dystopia, and says people should try to make that world as good as possible and not push back.

Source: 41:20–45:04 ↗
Source: 36:20–38:58 ↗

QWhat impressed Novati about the React-framework engineers, whose archetype differed from Novati's?

Michael Novati

Novati files them under the specialist archetype: people very good at one stack. Another example is an engineer who was one of perhaps ten people in the world who deeply understood email protocols, including the practical side of spam and routing. Novati likes a sports-team analogy: on a baseball team every player can play most positions reasonably, yet you want distinct roles and mutual respect for each player's place. Novati respects those engineers and sees the team as exceptional when it has different kinds of players.

Was it that they solved problems others could not?
Michael Novati

Yes, Novati says, and their abstractions were especially impactful because every engineer used them daily. Novati's own cleanup work also eased everyone's life, so there was some similarity. Their frameworks cut the mental overhead of tasks such as fetching data. Novati notes that an elegant, fast, easy-to-use API is very hard to design, and that making things simpler can be more work than writing a lot of code.

Source: 46:30–47:27 ↗
Source: 45:06–46:29 ↗

QNovati has said about 30 percent of time went to the team and 70 percent to self-directed projects. How does that work?

Michael Novati

Novati frames it as being a senior engineer on a team of about ten while spending more than half the time on codebase-wide initiatives: cleanups, refactors, a new framework, one-off help, and emergencies. The 30 percent was a share of mental focus, not a slice of the eight-hour day. Novati was on the team all day, reviewing code, bouncing ideas off junior engineers, mentoring them toward promotion, and writing features the team had queued. Novati also joined product meetings and assessed feasibility of what product managers proposed. The volume of code from team work was that of a senior engineer.

How did Novati manage the relationship with the manager, given that most bandwidth went elsewhere?
Michael Novati

Novati often, though not always, reported to more junior managers and acted almost as a peer who helped them manage the team. The skip-level manager usually did the performance reviews, and Novati effectively reported to that skip unofficially. Novati met a VP monthly for the whole org and the skip every two weeks. On the org chart Novati reported to a frontline manager, but in practice Novati was a dotted-line resource for senior people, "a weapon of the org" that went wherever needed.

Source: 49:40–50:59 ↗
Source: 47:30–49:38 ↗

QHow did Novati transition into IC7, solving the hardest problems for the whole org?

Michael Novati

Novati says output was already at coding-machine level from day one. What improved was taste and judgment. As an example, there were two forks of the task tool on the same data source, one fast and streamlined, one bloated with features and slow. In a week or less, Novati merged them into one with the speed of the first and the features of the second. Novati told no one, posted to the whole company that the tools were merged, and says this could not be done now.

Everyone congratulated Novati, but the lesson was that surprising hundreds of users with changed URLs was not the best way. Novati had not understood the consequences for teams. Over many large changes, some too fast and some buggy, Novati kept the same speed while improving judgment: how much to change at once, what other people will feel, and which spots are sensitive. That accumulation of judgment and taste is what crosses the line into IC7, Novati says. Advice on building it depends on context: talk to a manager, then a skip-level manager, then a very senior engineer in a similar org.

So high productivity and initiative let Novati take on extra work and become known for it?
Michael Novati

Yes, Novati says, but judgment and taste matter more than the code. They extend to the push process. Facebook had no continuous integration then. If something broke in production, the pushing team had to ship a fix, and an engineer who broke too much lost its trust, which would hurt a coding machine. Novati built that relationship, and more than once said a change needed to land and that if it broke the site Novati would resign. Novati had burned credibility before, so had to be very sure of the fix. An engineer who simply writes a lot of code, without years of built-up trust, could not get away with it.

Source: 54:31–56:28 ↗
Would Novati have resigned if it had broken again?
Michael Novati

Novati thinks so. The statement puts so much pressure on Novati, perhaps a personality trait, that Novati triple-checks every line and thinks through every odd case.

Source: 56:30–56:54 ↗
Source: 51:00–54:30 ↗

QWhat do taste and judgment mean for a software engineer?

Michael Novati

Novati likens taste to the patina on a cast-iron pan, built up in layers of history. Some people have stronger instincts early, perhaps from upbringing or from experience outside code such as dancing or sports. In general it takes experience. Novati's second image is a speed skater: you cannot read a book, put on skates, and be fastest. It takes years of feeling the ice at different temperatures and the difference between a skate used once and twice.

Novati sees too many people early in their careers trying to jump ahead, like entering the Olympics before building that feel. That is okay, Novati says, and nothing is wrong with them. The advice is to put in practice and reps, get feedback, iterate, and have the grit to keep going; without feedback, practice does not improve skill.

Is taste about how to design software, or about which problems are worth solving?
Michael Novati

Both, for different people, Novati says. A product manager's taste is mostly about what to build, built by shipping many things and watching some fail. Novati says the exceptional ones have shipped mostly things that failed or were mediocre, and learned at each step (a loose, unmeasured claim). For an engineer, Novati says, taste applies to the code itself and to strategies for moving fast.

Source: 59:16–1:01:04 ↗
Source: 56:55–59:14 ↗

QNovati was touching everyone's code. Did other teams give feedback, and how was it handled?

Michael Novati

Yes. In one case Novati refactored an old framework in the live version of a team's tool while that team was building a newer tool and carefully maintaining backward compatibility. They had many diffs in flight, and the refactor caused merge conflicts. They wanted it reverted. Novati had not paid attention to that, and the lesson is to be careful where teams are mid-migration on complex, longer-term work.

Did anyone object that Novati added something without owning its maintenance?
Michael Novati

That never came up, Novati says. The philosophy then, which Novati reports Kent Beck also described recently, was that every line you write you are responsible for. If you are willing to be woken at 3 a.m. to fix your code, you can skip tests. If you want to work nine to five, write more tests so the code is stable while you are away.

Novati did not refactor and forget. Sometimes two years later an automatic bug would be assigned because Novati had touched the code last, and Novati fixed it as now Novati's. Novati had no territorial conflicts and did not step on people's product judgment. Novati compares it to surgery, learned the hard way through early over-aggressiveness: finding the line between disrupting people's day-to-day work and still getting the cleanup done.

Source: 1:01:47–1:04:18 ↗
Source: 1:00:06–1:01:46 ↗

QAs engineers get more senior they are pulled into more meetings. How did Novati protect focus time?

Michael Novati

Novati minimized meetings. When calendar invites arrived without context, Novati asked what they were for and pushed back on many. Novati skipped standups unless relevant, for example during a crunch to ship within a month, and did not attend ones that were social chitchat. Novati was strict about time and chose teams deliberately, valuing managers who understood that their job is to help reports perform exceptionally. Novati's managers protected Novati from unnecessary meetings so impact could be highest.

Novati admits being too arrogant at times. Novati recalls walking out of a meeting or two after deciding it was no longer useful, and now regrets it, feeling bad for whoever ran the meeting.

Did HR ever ask Novati to be nicer?
Michael Novati

No, Novati says, because it was not a table-flipping situation. Novati had good relationships with the product managers, who liked that Novati built and fixed things fast, including bugs that were not Novati's. Meta's product managers want things moving fast and watch every pixel. They would often give Novati permission to leave when a meeting no longer needed Novati. Novati describes the attitude as cutthroat about not spending time in meetings when Novati could be coding.

Source: 1:06:39–1:07:55 ↗
Source: 1:03:27–1:06:35 ↗

QHow did Novati develop the skill of picking problems that mattered, so the code was more impactful?

Michael Novati

Novati says first that Novati is not great at it and is still poor at prioritizing. Novati tended to pick things where Novati could already see the answer, so the only question was how fast the code could be typed. That is also why LLMs help Novati so much: the idea is in Novati's head and the tool gets it out faster.

Novati calls this one of the things that probably held back the career. When a manager asked for task A, and Novati could not see the answer, Novati did B through H instead. That earns a passing grade and is appreciated, but if A really mattered, the company's overall impact would likely have been higher had Novati done it. Novati frames it as a weakness, limited by what Novati can figure out how to do.

So the priority list was whatever Novati could crank out instantly, not full business value?
Michael Novati

Novati agrees and adds that if you crank out enough, it adds up and can have huge impact, but it is a different way of thinking about work.

QWhat did the IC7-plus engineers have in common?

Michael Novati

Novati says there was a common bar regardless of archetype, whether coding machine, specialist, or fixer. Everyone showed extremely strong diligence and conscientiousness, and was sharp. Novati cites a straight-A school record and a sense of being fairly smart, yet acknowledges that many in the group are probably smarter. In a room, a newly proposed protocol would not get an hour-long presentation; people would ask sharp follow-up questions at once. Attention to detail was very high.

For Novati these are personality traits, such as using obsessive tendencies productively on every detail of the product. Others reached them through 25 years of experience. In conversations with junior colleagues, Novati says, context is often missing, follow-ups are less sharp and take longer, and projects are usually smaller in scope.

Source: 1:10:20–1:12:55 ↗

QWhat are the top tips for landing code fast, for someone who wants to absorb the coding-machine skill?

Michael Novati

Novati's step one is to do something, anything. Many people who ask for advice think too much and do too little. Step two, which Novati calls critical, is to get feedback from respected people with experience, taste, and judgment, act on it, and repeat. Novati once thought a manager hated Novati because the manager spent all day reviewing a flood of fast, problem-filled code and kept asking for style conventions to be followed. Novati says that annoyance is the loop working: get the gears turning, take the feedback, iterate. It compounds quickly.

Novati names three mistakes. The first is not turning the gears at all. The second is getting feedback from the wrong people, such as a boot-camp graduate taking feedback from a peer only slightly ahead, which lacks the experience and taste one wants to learn. The third, which Novati made often, is treating feedback as judgment or approval and not as information. The host summarizes it as shortening the cycle time, getting good feedback, and internalizing it.

For someone already productive, what advice takes things to the next level?
Michael Novati

Be more ambitious. Take on something that pushes beyond the normal scope. Novati says this is specific to Meta, where impact is judged by breadth and scope, so a coding machine in a department needs to push beyond it. The advice Novati gives, despite saying Novati is poor at accepting leaders' prioritization, is to reach out to senior people in other areas. Novati had many one-on-ones with the senior leadership, such as a 15-minute chat with Chris Cox, and says a credible but stuck coding machine can use such talks to find wider-scoped projects.

QWhy did Novati leave Meta, and what was the career thinking?

Novati says Meta got big fast. Around three-quarters of the way through the tenure, the feeling faded that the company had Novati's back completely and Novati had the company's, a feeling Novati admits was a bit culty. It started to feel like a business relationship, and that was the first sign Novati was open to leaving.

Vesting logistics sharpened it. Some years had longer grants and overlapping vesting cycles, and Novati expected take-home pay to drop about 80 percent over a period (Novati's own figure; details withheld). After the previous performance cycle, Novati told the manager that Novati would leave in three months, did a farewell tour on a Messenger-for-kids project, and slowly ramped down, taking things home from the desk. Novati describes being either all-in or not, says that all-in feeling broke as Meta grew, and wanted to put the dedication elsewhere.

Source: 1:18:41–1:20:42 ↗

QAt the highest levels of performance, how much is talent and how much is hard work and growth?

Michael Novati

Talent exists, Novati says, shaped by biology, upbringing, and opportunity, and some of it is undiscovered. Someone who feels untalented may simply not have found it yet, or may be talented at something that is not their day job. Novati says this is the mission behind the current work of helping people find the most impactful work they can do, since not everyone had the chance to explore. Novati believes everyone is better than most at something, and finding it is a big piece of high performance.

Hard work, in contrast, is within your control. A friend of Novati's makes the point that talent and luck are outside your control and effort is not. If you are good at your job and like it, Novati says, you can outwork similar people and will probably be recognized for it.

QWhat percent of Novati's career growth is luck?

Novati says 50/50. Coming from Canada, Novati's first day at Facebook was a surprise: Novati took a laptop and left onboarding, and was called back because Novati had not collected a phone. Facebook handed over a phone and accessories as if rolling out a red carpet, and Novati wondered what it all was. Staying in Canada would probably have gone well, Novati says, but without the same acceleration.

The luck was landing at Facebook when Novati did: a perfect fit for Novati's personality then, aligned values, and code that matched what Novati could handle. Novati has seen people without the same drive who got the luck and are doing well, and says either factor can work out. Novati says both applied here.

Source: 1:23:01–1:24:26 ↗

QWhat advice would Novati give to a just-graduated self?

Michael Novati

Novati sees many people, including those preparing for interviews, seeking approval: a green check mark, a perfect grade. Novati was that person, wanting an A+ without really knowing what was being learned. Because of that, Novati treated feedback as a grade to judge by and not as input for improving, and pressured toward 100 percent next time instead of toward improvement.

The advice to ambitious people who want perfect scores is to reflect on feedback and push past the comfort zone, instead of treating feedback as judgment.

Section 67 · interview

Mozilla Firefox CTO: Chrome vs Firefox, Distinguished Engineers, and the AI Browser Wars

Bobby Holly traces Firefox's fight with Chrome and Google, explains how Mozilla defines distinguished-engineer impact, and argues for impact over titles and for keeping the web open as AI arrives.

Holly's view: pursue impact, not titles, and keep the web open and independent

Bobby Holly, who grew from a Mozilla intern into the CTO of Firefox, argues that engineers should chase the biggest problems and real impact rather than titles, and that the web's open, multi-vendor character is worth defending against Chrome's dominance and the rush to put AI into browsers. The conversation runs from Holly's start in Mozilla's volunteer-heavy open-source culture, through the browser wars with Google, security crises, the Rust and Servo bet and the Quantum CSS launch, to Holly's views on promotions, distinguished engineers, writing, and the future of the browser. Every claim, estimate and recollection below is Holly's own. The host is not named in the transcript.

Source: 00:00–1:34:54 ↗

QBefore joining Firefox you interned at Nvidia. Why did you pick Mozilla over Nvidia?

Bobby Holly

Holly describes the Nvidia internship as a good, standard one: orientation, a desk, a basic starter project and check-ins every few hours. Mozilla was quite different. On the first day Holly's manager, the director of platform who ran Gecko, was extremely laid-back and, asked what to work on, said to get on IRC and Bugzilla and start figuring something out.

Holly says that reflected how Mozilla worked. It had grown as an open-source project partly by accident, with almost no support, so newcomers had to work out for themselves how to download the code, build it and file bugs. That selected for highly motivated people, and management's job was to nurture the culture, get the right people together and get out of the way. Holly found it disorienting at first and then inspired by the people, some paid and some not, who had started out in college dorm rooms trying to make their browser crash less.

A long-time hero was Boris Sabarski, whom Holly says became one of Mozilla's first distinguished engineers. Holly describes a codebase of probably about 10 million lines inherited from Netscape and largely unowned, of which Boris owned perhaps half and was the person of last resort. For years Holly met him only on IRC, where he was in about five other channels at once.

How does this fit the timeline of Chrome and the browser wars? Was this before Chrome?
Bobby Holly

Holly says it was before Chrome and gives a short history. In the 1990s Internet Explorer beat Netscape, largely because Microsoft bundled it free with Windows and pushed hard on distribution. Netscape open-sourced its code and created the Mozilla Foundation, while Microsoft put the browser in maintenance mode because a cross-platform web did not fit its strategy. Contributors such as Boris kept improving the Netscape code, adding pop-up blocking and tabs, until a few relatively junior people built a stripped-down browser that became Firefox and, Holly says, took off like wildfire.

Google was closely aligned, Holly says, because a search company benefits when the web is useful. When Holly started in June 2008, interns had badges to eat at Google, Google's default-search deal made Mozilla financially sustainable, and Google engineers worked on Firefox. Soon after, Google announced Chrome, and Mozilla staff were told it was still friendly and aimed at Internet Explorer. By 2009, Holly recalls, a New York Times article described group hugs between Mozilla and Google as getting tricky, as Google's business interest in controlling the user's journey created tension.

Source: 05:07–10:54 ↗
Source: 01:05–05:05 ↗

QHow did things move from Google badges and free food to full competition, in your own experience?

Bobby Holly

Holly does not think any individual at Google decided to go after Mozilla. It was the way organizations work, and collaboration with many Google engineers continued. Two things happened at once. First, Google ramped up its push for Chrome share. Holly says this was probably aimed at Internet Explorer, with Mozilla as collateral damage, and estimates Google spent hundreds of millions of dollars a year on advertising and distribution, reaching into the billions if promotion on google.com is counted.

Holly cites Jonathan Nightingale, then a Firefox vice president, who later described a 'year of 100 oopses': each time Google did something that hurt Firefox, such as putting a banner on google.com telling Firefox users to download Chrome, it was framed as unintentional. Holly believes that was true at the organizational level, but that individual incentives rewarded it, since a fix weeks later still left the metrics won.

Second, Holly says Firefox had legitimately fallen behind. Chrome arrived with a multiprocess architecture, a more robust plug-in architecture for Adobe Flash, and a very fast JavaScript engine. Mozilla also made an ambitious early-2010s bet on a web-based mobile operating system, Firefox OS, because Android and iOS looked potentially hostile. It drew surprising industry interest but did not work, and it competed for resources with keeping Firefox competitive. Firefox's extension model was a further drag: extensions could modify almost anything and depended on undocumented internals, so nearly any change risked breaking one.

Why did people spend so much time working for free on a project like this?
Bobby Holly

Holly says there were few major open-source projects then, so Mozilla offered a chance to have meaningful impact. Boris got involved because, as Holly tells it, his options for browsing from an MIT dorm were a remote Internet Explorer 5 session or a Netscape build that kept crashing, so he set out to fix it for himself and found the codebase a vast intellectual challenge.

The biggest factor, in Holly's view, was the mission: the web should be open, interoperable and controlled by no single company, and the internet should be a global public resource. Holly argues that was not a given for anyone who grew up in the 1990s with Microsoft dominant. Mozilla was not only advocating but building a browser that gave users pop-up blocking, ad blocking and tabs, and Holly says that inspired many people.

Source: 16:28–19:00 ↗
Source: 10:56–16:26 ↗

QOnce you got there, which projects were most interesting or shaped your career, and what stories come from the early days?

Bobby Holly

Holly started as an intern on the front end of a new mobile browser for Nokia devices, then worked on the graphics engine and image rendering library. Because so much code was unowned, fixing one thing quickly led to hearing that Holly now owned it. Holly gravitated to the hardest and gnarliest parts, especially after Chrome launched with the V8 JIT-compiled JavaScript engine. Shipping Firefox's own JIT was delayed by months for Firefox 4 because of the tangled bindings between the JavaScript engine and the DOM, and Holly dived into that code at the manager's advice.

That code carried much of the browser's security enforcement, isolating websites from each other and from the browser's own JavaScript front end. Holly says it was imperfect and became a cat-and-mouse game with outside security researchers, in which a clever trick could climb the prototype chain into the address bar and tab code. After Firefox 4 improved the architecture, Holly worried that some categories of attack had no robust fix, only band-aids, and launched a cross-functional effort of at least a year, jokingly called Slaughterhouse, to remove the Chrome object wrappers. Mozilla paid small bounties for confidential Bugzilla reports, though the black market paid more.

Holly's main story involves a zero-day exploit in the wild. While disassembling it, Holly realized it was written by a researcher Mozilla worked with and, without thinking hard, emailed an accusation of double-crossing. The researcher concluded his own devices were deeply compromised and went off the grid. About an hour later Mozilla learned the real cause: a threat actor had compromised Bugzilla. Weeks later the researcher phoned from a bowling alley in upstate New York where he was hiding, and Mozilla explained and helped him recover. Slaughterhouse had just wrapped, and of roughly 45 exfiltrated bugs by Holly's recollection, all but two were already fixed. Holly's lesson is to get ahead of security and architecture, because sometimes you do not have time to fix things when you need to.

How did you know that researcher wrote that exploit?
Bobby Holly

Holly says people have particular styles, and these were handwritten logic attacks, for example binding a function to an API and sending a call around the event loop twice, so the fingerprints were visible. Holly separates these from memory-safety vulnerabilities, which were less artisanal and more often produced by fuzzing tools. Because the codebase was C++, a memory hazard could mean a web page takes over the computer, and Holly says this motivated Mozilla's investment in Rust.

Source: 27:00–28:25 ↗
How does a Firefox compromise take over the computer? Wouldn't the operating system shield it?
Bobby Holly

Not at the time, Holly says. Windows applications largely ran with system privileges, and researchers proved a compromise by launching the Windows calculator. Chrome helped raise the baseline, and today's browsers use defense in depth, including in-process and operating-system sandboxing. But Holly says this was bolted on over time on Windows, unlike iOS, which was designed around application sandboxing, so securing browsers there remains an ongoing challenge.

Source: 28:28–30:26 ↗
Did you ever work out how Bugzilla was compromised?
Bobby Holly

Holly is about 85 percent sure it was a leaked employee credential, before Bugzilla, a tool dating to the 1990s, had two-factor authentication.

Source: 30:27–30:44 ↗
Source: 19:17–26:58 ↗

QHow does the organization prioritize security when there were also big investments in performance?

Bobby Holly

Holly says security is easy to neglect for short-term reasons, and some products may reasonably do so, but a long-lived browser cannot. At Mozilla it is a cultural obligation to protect users that predates management structure or company objectives, and it produces bottom-up energy and pride. Holly puts Chrome's security organization at 70 or more people; Mozilla has nothing close, so security is a shared responsibility. Slaughterhouse was not a top-down edict, Holly says. Holly owned the code and felt it had to be right.

Holly is proud that Firefox has won the Pwn2Own award for fastest to patch, on the order of 24 hours, for the last two years. That relies on people in time zones around the world working without any management instruction to stay up late, simply because they care. Holly notes that every browser gets compromised in that competition.

You mentioned no performance reviews and a scrappy bottom-up culture. How does that kind of culture work?
Bobby Holly

Before there was much management, Holly says, it was uneven. It generally worked because the caliber of people was high, but if the owner of some code did a poor job, everyone lived with it. Ownership was treated as close to final, and Mozilla's module system and governance were insulated against executive power. Holly thinks parts of that culture are worth preserving and describes the leadership question as how to keep what makes the technical culture great while addressing its shortcomings.

Source: 33:19–34:40 ↗
Source: 31:00–33:17 ↗

QHow did Mozilla adopt Rust, and how does it solve the memory-safety problem?

Bobby Holly

Holly says that in the early 2010s Firefox had real structural issues. Many could be solved by hard but incremental work: a multiprocess architecture, an extension architecture without tendrils into undocumented interfaces, and native video playback to escape Flash. Two issues were different. One was memory safety, because in a C++ codebase a large share of mistakes compromise the browser and, without sandboxing, the computer.

The other was parallelism. Core counts were rising while browsers stayed largely single-threaded, but multithreaded C++ produced hard nondeterministic bugs that could also become exploitable. Holly says both problems were rooted in deficiencies of C++, which every browser used. Firefox had just taken on the world in 2010, so Mozilla began sponsoring internal research into a new language with compile-time guarantees of no memory-safety issues and no race conditions, to be followed by a new browser engine. Rust co-evolved with Servo, a test bed meant to be memory safe and, more importantly, parallel, so that Mozilla could close the gap with Chrome and leapfrog it through safe concurrency.

Source: 34:42–38:14 ↗

QWhat was Mozilla's strategy to compete with Chrome, given its performance and distribution advantages?

Bobby Holly

Holly calls it multifaceted. The first part was recognition. Holly says there was early denial about the value of Chrome's architectural advantages. Chrome had a method JIT while Firefox had a tracing JIT that Mozilla expected to be better and was not. When Chrome shipped a multiprocess architecture, the first reaction Holly heard was good luck doing that on Mac, and then Chrome did it. On video, Chrome had a better Flash plug-in architecture and was early with native playback, so YouTube was stable there while Firefox crashed constantly, which Holly says was Adobe's fault and not fixable by Mozilla. So Mozilla had to close many hard, discrete gaps, but closing the gap was not enough. It had to do something better, and Rust and Servo were the strategy for that.

How did the Servo effort go? Was it successful, given that Google's distribution eventually dominated?
Bobby Holly

Holly says Servo and Rust had captured something real. Servo was an incomplete prototype but had features never done before, including a multithreaded CSS engine. The problem was scale: about a dozen people on Rust and Servo against hundreds of Chromium engineers, with most of Mozilla's effort still on Gecko. A competitive engine is years of accumulated work, so Servo had more to catch up on every year, and Holly found it hard to believe it would ever match a production engine.

Around 2014 to 2015 Mozilla concluded it needed a fully refreshed Firefox, including the parallel CSS engine uplifted from Servo, a project Holly personally led and calls the highlight of the career. Hooking a Rust CSS engine to the C++ DOM had no tooling, so the team built it. Holly recalls rendering time on Amazon.com improving by on the order of 25 percent, and says the engine, being parallel, is still the fastest on the market. Firefox was performance-competitive again, and Holly's lesson is that coordinated technical effort and the right bets can win.

Source: 40:24–43:30 ↗
Source: 38:15–40:23 ↗

QWhere were you in your career at that point, and how did it grow as you worked on these projects?

Bobby Holly

Holly says early Mozilla had a choose-your-own-title culture, and Holly chose 'negative entropy' for the complex codebase. By Firefox Quantum, Mozilla had a more standard ladder. Holly had reached senior staff during Quantum CSS, and after launch Holly and the engineer who led the other half of Quantum were promoted to principal engineer, a level held by probably fewer than five people at the time by Holly's estimate.

Holly's long-term dream was to be like Boris Sabarski, one of Mozilla's three distinguished engineers, and the route was to be prolific across as many parts of the code as possible: WebRender, mobile, multiprocess, layout. Holly's manager, who ran engineering, asked Holly to spend one day a week not opening a terminal and to think about impact more broadly than direct code. Holly was shocked and says it was not a natural way to work.

Do you have a way of thinking about which contributions are more impactful than others?
Bobby Holly

Holly says it was a guided search for the biggest problem on offer, which changed over time: DOM bindings and security, then media playback to solve the YouTube problem, multiprocess, the Rust-based CSS engine, WebRender, and then mobile. Holly's model was to jump into the most pressing area, learn its code and work with its leaders, not always typing the code but reviewing, setting direction and setting priorities. The host summarizes this as prolific but aimed at the organization's biggest problems, and Holly agrees.

Source: 46:39–47:52 ↗
Source: 43:50–46:26 ↗

QIn the industry I hear two approaches to growth: focus on the promotion first, or build skills and behaviors and let the promotion follow. Which is better?

Bobby Holly

Holly has strong opinions and says to focus on impact, not title. That is what Holly looks for when deciding whom to advance. Someone having that level of impact does not need to sell themselves the way promo hacking implies, which means pinning down a management chain on exactly what must be done to earn a promotion.

Speaking frankly, Holly finds that annoying, comparing it to a child asking for a reward in exchange for doing what was asked. Holly also sees a substantive problem. A person focused on impact will achieve things, whereas a person focused on boxes someone else presented may technically satisfy a stated condition in a box-checking way that misses the point. Impact is what should be recognized and rewarded.

Softer-spoken engineers often do great work but market it poorly. Brag documents and sharing wins seem a reasonable balance. How do you weigh the two framings?
Bobby Holly

Holly says similar activities can be framed several ways, and the framing shapes how they are carried out and what they achieve. Visibility is a basic fact of impact: you need to be connected to people who understand the biggest challenges, coordinate with them, and make sure they know what you can do so they can put you in a position to do more. But Holly says trying to brag and trying to communicate, coordinate and create visibility for important work lead to very different outcomes.

Source: 50:27–53:02 ↗
The wording of an update can be subtle, and the same post can come from different incentives. Can people tell?
Bobby Holly

Holly says much depends on how much the update is about you versus the work, the team and other people. Everyone knows the sender likely had a significant hand in the work, so an important part of any update is giving visibility to others and thanking the team. Holly sees that as part of leadership: being a humble leader who creates recognition for other people's contributions.

Source: 53:03–54:51 ↗
Doesn't the squeaky wheel get the grease? A loud high performer who lobbies for promotion is often rewarded before a quiet, solid one.
Bobby Holly

Holly says it depends on the organization and its technical culture, and Mozilla tries hard not to reward that. The message is not to avoid ambition but to frame it as the impact you want, not the status you want. Holly allows that in edge cases people lobbying for themselves get a little more consideration because they are top of mind.

The conversations Holly likes best are about how to grow and have more impact, such as whether you are working on the most important thing. Holly calls it the saddest outcome when someone works very hard on something not important enough to give the impact they want. Pinning leaders down on which boxes to check is, Holly says, extremely annoying, and you do not want leadership to find you annoying.

Source: 55:17–57:13 ↗
Source: 48:34–50:26 ↗

QYou were focused on impact and had distinguished engineers as role models. What did the growth look like next?

Bobby Holly

Holly kept working on the hardest challenge in the browser and moving from team to team, assuming that Boris Sabarski's level of impact would eventually mean becoming a distinguished engineer. Then the CTO at the time sat Holly down. The existing distinguished engineers had held the title since about 2010 and no new ones had been made since. The CTO said Mozilla would make new ones for the first time in almost a decade and that Holly would not be among them.

Holly was a little surprised, since Holly thought anyone would say that, though perhaps not at Boris's level, Holly knew the Firefox code better than almost anyone. The CTO explained that this was the traditional Mozilla model and that he now wanted something oriented around industry impact.

The definition of impact shifted while you were working toward distinguished engineer. What was your thinking about the new criteria?
Bobby Holly

Holly found it inspiring, though some people worried Holly would be upset. Holly compares it to doing a new Pilates move and discovering a muscle you did not know you had and that is extremely weak. What defines a distinguished engineer, Holly says, depends on what matters to the organization. Early on, Mozilla's make-or-break problem was managing a sprawling codebase with few people, which called for a prolific contributor and enabler. At some companies the title means building a billion-dollar business, but Mozilla is about changing the world, so its criteria focus there.

Holly says Holly probably still has not reached the industry impact of some of Mozilla's other distinguished engineers, and that the eventual promotion was a hybrid of the old and new definitions. But understanding that model of impact was profound and shaped where Holly directed effort.

Source: 59:04–1:00:54 ↗
Source: 57:14–58:56 ↗

QWhat does distinguished-engineer-level impact look like? Can you describe some people who have done impressive work?

Bobby Holly

Holly describes three engineers promoted at the time as archetypes of world-changing impact for an individual contributor at Mozilla.

The first is Martin Thompson, still at Mozilla, whom Holly calls an international standards extraordinaire. His name is in the author line of protocols such as HTTP/2, QUIC and web push, and Holly says he was heavily involved in WebRTC and geolocation, adding that Holly is not familiar with every credit. This was core design work, not editorial formatting. By designing new protocols that were faster, giving the industry a business reason to adopt them, while leaking less metadata and having fewer security issues, he increased the privacy and security of the internet.

The second is Luke Wagner, whom Holly considers the person most single-handedly responsible for WebAssembly. Running non-JavaScript code such as AutoCAD in browsers had relied on plugins, which Holly calls awful for security and user experience. A side project from another engineer compiled C++ to naive JavaScript, which worked but was very slow. Wagner, then a lead engineer on the SpiderMonkey JavaScript engine, wanted it viable, and the idea became having the tool emit a restricted subset of JavaScript the engine could detect, verify and run more natively. That started a flywheel of compiled native experiences in browsers and then momentum for a real bytecode format, WebAssembly, which is native-speed, sandboxed and portable. Google was pushing a plugin-like alternative, Native Client, so Wagner handled the technical and political pieces to forge a browser consensus.

The third is Tim Terbury, the codec lead. Native video playback was blocked because the dominant format, H.264, was heavily patent-encumbered, which an open-source browser could not ship. Mozilla spent years developing royalty-free codecs. Terbury's team built the Opus audio codec and then a video codec called Daala, which was incorporated into AV1, now an industry standard from the Alliance for Open Media. Holly says that powers video today and that the vision for truly unencumbered codecs came from Terbury.

The value these engineers created is huge, with WebAssembly making a company like Figma possible, but the value is captured elsewhere. Does that bother people at Mozilla?
Bobby Holly

Holly says Mozilla has no shareholders and is not trying to make gobs of money. Its mission is an internet that is open and accessible to all. Holly grants it is convenient for big tech companies to have a royalty-free codec, but notes they could pay. Mozilla's angle is to build formats that empower everybody and create economic value, even though some capture more than others.

Holly adds that Mozilla wants to keep existing, which means thinking about revenue, and a lot of its revenue comes from Google, one of the dominant advertising players. Mozilla would like to change that, but it is hard and not where its heart is, so Holly describes a real tension about how much to focus on business versus impact.

Source: 1:08:31–1:11:02 ↗
Source: 1:00:56–1:08:29 ↗

QWhat advice would you give someone who wants to become a distinguished engineer?

Bobby Holly

Holly's answer is writing, which anyone can work on at any level. Holly says Mozilla, including Holly personally, did not have much developed capability here, and that writing is one of the most powerful skills. Holly points to an internal memo, now public, called 'writing things down', which argues that writing matters both for the artifact, which helps coordination, wide review and feedback, and for the process, since writing is thinking, refining and articulating ideas. Holly calls clarity of thinking one of the most important things and says you only get it by forcing yourself to write your ideas down.

As timely advice, Holly says not to use an LLM to produce text you put your name on. It is fairly easy to tell, and more importantly you lose the thinking that writing forces.

Do you have tips on how to write well?
Bobby Holly

Holly says a document should be no longer than what you have to say. When you run out of things to say, you either refine your ideas or you are done, because fluff is never useful and padded documents are among Holly's least favorite things. Focus on substance over rhetoric. Holly rejects the idea that non-native English speakers cannot write as well as others: there is a baseline of articulation to work on, but good writing is not flowery words. It is clarity of thought, which is relatively easy to express once you have it, if you practice.

Source: 1:12:53–1:14:16 ↗
Source: 1:11:04–1:12:49 ↗

QAs CTO of Firefox, what do you expect from the new browser wars, with AI browsers and AI being added to existing browsers?

Bobby Holly

Holly says the new AI browsers announced each month are not browsers as Holly thinks of them. They are different front ends, window dressing and monetization keys on top of Chrome, because much of what powers a browser is the engine, and engines are extremely hard to build and have been disappearing. Holly says Firefox, built on Gecko, is the only independent browser with no dependency on someone else's engine. Safari is vertically integrated with WebKit, and Chrome, Opera, Perplexity and Edge all use Chromium. Holly argues these companies are not trying to evolve the web platform but to control the consumer touchpoint in the coming AI world.

Holly's view is that AI is coming to consumer technology 'like water running downhill' and will not be stopped, but where it ends up can still be steered, and many parties want to capture it. Holly says Chrome is making an aggressive play to control the AI stack, both in the browser, with what Holly describes as thousands of Gemini integrations, and in the web platform, through proprietary APIs Mozilla does not support that let websites use an LLM inside the browser. Site authors like this because they can offload inference costs. But there is no way to specify an LLM or give it deterministic, interoperable behavior, so these calls are fundamentally unspecified, and as owner of the dominant browser Google has the market power to get websites to tune their usage to what Gemini expects.

Holly says Mozilla is not building a foundation model and has no horse in the race. It wants the space to stay open, users to choose which AI systems they use, and the web to remain relevant. Holly sees a real risk that the web becomes a backend detail used by retrieval behind a ChatGPT query or by an agent. Much would be lost, Holly argues, because the web gives users agency: it is reinterpretable content the browser can modify as the user chooses, as ad blockers show, it is safe to open a link from an untrusted source, and no one company controls it. Holly calls this multistakeholder structure a historical accident that matches Mozilla's vision, and wants AI's changes not to sacrifice it.

Many AI browsers and Opera are built on Chromium. What would happen if Firefox were built on Chromium, and what is the advantage of its own engine?
Bobby Holly

Holly says it is a lot of work and Mozilla likes hard things, but the advantage is a seat at the table when web standards are decided. Engines have dropped off because from a bottom-line view an engine is a giant cost center. Mozilla keeps going because it is driven by impact. Holly pictures a world with Apple running WebKit and Google in charge of everything else: both capable, but entrenched in their own interests and not getting along, and bilateral entrenchment can prevent progress, as in mobile. Despite a smaller share, Mozilla brings a fresh perspective and can tilt the conversation back toward the user and the web.

Holly's example is performance. Historically each vendor designed a benchmark suited to its own engine and the others dismissed it as cooked. A couple of years ago an initiative called Speedometer 3 aimed to produce a shared benchmark representative of the web. Holly says a bilateral Google and Apple effort would predictably go nowhere, and that Mozilla's involvement kept everyone focused on making engines faster together. By Holly's account Firefox and Chrome have each doubled their score, and in Firefox the measured effect on real-world page load and time to first paint was about 30 percent, so Holly judges it reasonable to say the benchmark made the web 30 percent faster, which would not have happened without Mozilla in the room.

Source: 1:20:58–1:26:53 ↗
Source: 1:14:18–1:20:57 ↗

QYou were an IC through and through for most of your time at Mozilla. Is there a technical decision you wish you had changed in hindsight?

Bobby Holly

Holly points to a case where the technical outcome was good but the process was not worth it: WebRender, the graphics backend in Servo. While working on Quantum CSS, Holly was excited about uplifting more of Servo's rendering pipeline and advocated heavily that the graphics team replace its rendering and rasterization pipeline with Servo's. Holly says this was not based on technical expertise in that area but on a vibes judgment about where things were going, and the vibes were infectious. Holly was not strictly a decision-maker, but the view caught on with management.

Many engineers on the graphics team had strong doubts that it was ready or that it was too risky. When they raised concerns, Holly recalls, an engineering leader replied that C++ is not the future. Holly says enthusiasm for a risky direction over the concerns of the people who knew the area best was toxic, and several of the most senior and impactful graphics engineers left. The rest rallied, and WebRender became a major, expensive, many-year project. Holly stresses that the result is a fantastic, performant and safe engine and that Holly is proud of the team. But pushing it on a team that was not ready or aligned had collateral damage that Holly regrets.

Source: 1:26:06–1:29:09 ↗

QIs there a top book that made an impact on your career?

Bobby Holly

Holly says Holly is an avid reader who does not read many books, and that the ideas that most shaped Holly's thinking come from books Holly has not actually read. Holly consumes content widely and sees reading a whole book as a depth-first approach. That works for many people, but it is not the only way.

As examples, Holly read only a three-page review of Good Strategy, Bad Strategy, and says it stuck as a crisp account of what is wrong with many strategy documents. Holly also cites Turn the Ship Around, unread, on empowering teams, and Clayton Christensen's The Innovator's Dilemma as a powerful analysis of how the industry works. Holly values Ben Thompson's writing on tech but urges people to look beyond tech, for example to geopolitics and national security writing by people who think about what goes well and badly on a battlefield. Holly says those ideas rhyme with big-tech competition and with how to manage and motivate teams.

Source: 1:29:11–1:32:06 ↗

QIf you could give yourself advice when you had just entered the industry, what would it be?

Bobby Holly

Holly's answer is to be humble. Holly says the younger attitude was not strictly about self but about engineering, that engineers were the center of the universe. Over time Holly realized that many other things matter, and that when you start at an organization you do not understand why certain processes and functions exist, such as a legal team. Moving into leadership, Holly developed appreciation and empathy for the different players in the organization and industry, recognizing that everyone has a point of view and a place they are coming from, and that working to understand where people are coming from is how to make progress.

Source: 1:32:09–1:33:27 ↗

QDo you have any last words for the audience?

Bobby Holly

Holly's main message is that the web matters and underpins much of what we do, even though for many it is invisible and taken for granted, like water from the tap or the semiconductor supply chain. Holly warns it could easily backslide into unilateral big-tech control over people's experiences, and that losing focus because it has been good for so long would be a tragedy. Holly encourages people to think about what they gain from an open and free web and to do their best to keep it open.

Holly's practical request is that people building websites make sure they work in all browsers and avoid the lazy path of building something that works only in Google Chrome, which Holly calls the first step back to where things stood 25 years ago.

Source: 1:33:36–1:34:54 ↗
