Neetcode: Google vs Amazon, Interviews, and Quitting Big Tech

Neetcode describes a short Amazon stint, a move into full-time content creation, and the view that enjoyment and sustained practice matter more than raw LeetCode talent.

A practical view of interview preparation

Neetcode describes a short first job at Amazon, a move into full-time content creation, and the view that enjoyment and sustained practice matter more than raw talent in interview performance. Much of the conversation tests the common belief that passing big-tech interviews requires solving the hardest LeetCode problems.

Source: 00:00–34:40 ↗

QWhat happened after the first full-time job offer at Amazon, and why did Neetcode leave so quickly?

Neetcode

The Amazon role came soon after college, around age 22. Neetcode had expected a hard environment but found the culture a shock. The team had about five new grads who joined in the same month, and several burnt-out mid-level and senior engineers. Neetcode says the team was unfriendly and that most people left within about a year.

Neetcode says the decision to quit after a couple of months was a poor one, made without a backup plan or savings, though it worked out. Neetcode would not recommend it to most people.

What did you see at Amazon that made you want to quit so quickly?
Neetcode

Neetcode separates intense high-performing teams, where people compete and still root for each other, from cutthroat teams where people do not. The Amazon team felt like the second kind. Icebreakers were cold, and nobody seemed to be rooting for anyone else.

Neetcode stresses the limit of that judgment. Neetcode was there for only a short time and cannot say whether people tried to harm each other.

Source: 01:54–03:17 ↗
What gave you the confidence to quit so quickly?
Neetcode

Neetcode calls the decision uncharacteristic. Shortly before starting at Amazon, Neetcode had been broke and felt on top of the world. Within the first day, the manager signalled that the team was burnt out, and the situation seemed to get worse steadily.

Source: 03:19–04:04 ↗
Source: 00:37–01:54 ↗

QDid the Amazon job require LeetCode-style interviews?

Neetcode

Neetcode says the LeetCode questions were surprisingly easy, close to variations of the two-sum problem. The leadership principles interview was the harder filter. Neetcode admits giving answers that matched the company's picture of a high-agency, risk-taking employee, although Neetcode is naturally risk-averse and careful about mistakes.

Neetcode says the real work at Amazon asked for much higher initiative than expected, and adjusting to that took time.

Did a recruiter's logic-puzzle assessment resemble the Amazon screen?
Neetcode

The host recalls a group logic-puzzle test with multiple-choice pattern questions. Neetcode says a similar online test was part of the process, though only one section of it.

Source: 05:16–05:58 ↗
Source: 04:08–05:14 ↗

QCould Neetcode solve the hardest LeetCode problems today?

Neetcode

Probably not. Neetcode says Neetcode was never especially strong at LeetCode. The skill spectrum is compressed on LeetCode, so strong and very strong solvers look similar to most observers. Codeforces, by contrast, spreads skill over a wider distribution.

Neetcode still knows the core patterns and could usually say what the solution would be. Writing it by hand under time pressure would be harder, since few people hand-type code now.

What percent of LeetCode medium problems could Neetcode solve now?
Neetcode

Neetcode would be curious to try, and would not solve all of them. For most mediums, Neetcode could explain the pattern or the answer.

The host notes that an impromptu whiteboard session with hard problems was recorded separately and not included in this conversation.

Source: 07:22–08:03 ↗
Source: 06:01–07:21 ↗

QWhere does someone who passes interviews fall on the LeetCode and Codeforces skill scale?

Neetcode

Neetcode says the answer is wide. Passing an interview requires competence and some luck in being asked a problem the candidate already knows. Neetcode does not think there is one average candidate, and believes the average is lower than many people think.

Neetcode estimates that solving about a third of LeetCode mediums gives a good chance of passing an interview. A college competition illustrated the spread. One strong teammate solved three of 13 hard problems, while the Caltech team solved all 13.

Does a competitive programmer's skill transfer to complexity theory?
Neetcode

The host suggests that competitive programming sits above LeetCode. Neetcode answers that practice transfers less than people expect. Training for one format does not guarantee performance in another, and communication can suffer in a real interview.

Neetcode also says making videos consumed much of the time that might have gone into improving problem-solving, so the videos were a partial distraction.

Source: 11:22–13:10 ↗
Source: 08:09–11:12 ↗

QWhat share of LeetCode performance comes from memorization rather than derivation?

Neetcode

Neetcode guesses at least 90 percent is memorization, and considers that acceptable given how much material interview preparation covers. Neetcode notes that pure memorization is not enough. Candidates still need enough understanding to choose between approaches, such as depth-first or breadth-first search.

Source: 13:13–14:23 ↗

QIs LeetCode an accurate measure of intelligence?

Neetcode

Neetcode says definitely not. Tests such as the SAT correlate with other traits, but LeetCode measures a narrow subset of skill. A dog could not solve these problems, which shows they are not general intelligence.

Neetcode believes the main bottleneck is sustained enjoyment, passion, and work ethic. Neetcode did not do anything exceptional. Neetcode kept making LeetCode videos when most people would not have been willing to put in the time.

Source: 14:25–16:17 ↗

QWhat kept Neetcode making LeetCode videos for so long?

Neetcode

Neetcode says school computer science classes often stopped just as topics became interesting, leaving Neetcode wanting to go ten times deeper. LeetCode videos felt productive, even though views were modest and income was not expected.

Neetcode continued out of stubbornness, enjoyment, and a belief that the videos helped people.

Source: 15:40–17:22 ↗

QCan anyone become good at LeetCode?

Neetcode

Neetcode believes most programmers who enjoy programming could reach that level. Many people feel they are not smart enough, and many give up along the way because they find the grind unpleasant or prefer other routes, such as networking into a job. Neetcode regards that choice as reasonable.

Should some people simply give up on LeetCode?
Neetcode

Neetcode says Neetcode does not recommend giving up. The video came from frustration with a dismissive attitude toward effort, and Neetcode believes people can do more than they think.

Neetcode says about 95 percent of people who clicked on the video liked it, and many said they needed the message. One viewer preparing for a Microsoft internship interview said the video helped them lock in for the next few weeks.

Source: 18:29–20:11 ↗
Source: 17:23–18:27 ↗

QWas the 'give up' video the frustrated response of a disappointed teacher?

Neetcode

Neetcode accepts that description and says it would not make sense to teach people while telling them to quit. Neetcode says the wording was not the nicest. The worst part, in Neetcode's view, was calling one question dumb. The remark was not personal, and Neetcode did not call anyone unintelligent.

Source: 20:12–20:58 ↗

QWere you worried about how the rant video would be received before posting it?

Neetcode

Neetcode watched it a couple of times before posting and was unsure whether to send it. The rant was not planned. Looking back, Neetcode says it ran through five tangents, and a version designed to go viral would have been tighter.

Source: 21:00–21:52 ↗

QHow did the video career lead to the Google job?

Neetcode

Neetcode hoped that someone would eventually arrange an interview and that Neetcode would do well in it. It took almost a year. The offer came from Google, which Neetcode says felt like a dream job. The interview felt manageable thanks to heavy preparation.

Google's team was friendly and the work technical, but it was sometimes boring and process-heavy. Neetcode felt that the chance to go full-time on the channel and algorithms would not last, so Neetcode left, though Neetcode says it could have been done sooner.

Source: 22:40–24:10 ↗

QWhich companies ask the hardest LeetCode questions?

Neetcode

Neetcode says the AI labs, including OpenAI and Anthropic, ask demanding questions that do not follow the traditional LeetCode format. Neetcode attributes difficulty mostly to supply and demand: how many people apply and how many roles are open. Neetcode believes smaller companies are often harder.

How do OpenAI and Anthropic run their coding interviews?
Neetcode

Neetcode has heard mixed reports. Knowledge of data structures and algorithms still helps. Interviews may include parts of an algorithm, several files, or an open problem to reason through rather than a classic LeetCode task.

Neetcode's understanding is that the Anthropic interview does not allow AI assistance, and that the most recent OpenAI candidate Neetcode spoke with reported the same. Neetcode says some candidates mention AI access, and finds the formats unpredictable.

Source: 25:26–26:23 ↗
Source: 24:55–25:23 ↗

QWere you nervous about showing your face on the channel?

Neetcode

Neetcode was faceless for the first three years of the channel and began showing a face about three years ago. Being recognized created chances to meet viewers and other creators. Neetcode says part of Neetcode liked the faceless version because it allowed a private, introverted life, but Neetcode has no regrets.

Source: 26:25–27:50 ↗

QHow has quitting Google to work full-time gone?

Neetcode

Neetcode says it was easier because Neetcode enjoyed the work. Building a site, making videos, and studying algorithms all fit. Neetcode says people who dislike their jobs but do not know what else they want have a harder time.

Neetcode reports no regrets, and says quitting is not for everyone. Neetcode does not buy into the idea that everyone should leave a job for a side business.

Does Neetcode miss Google?
Neetcode

Neetcode misses the free food and, more, the culture of a large company. Running Neetcode's own channel made it possible to hire people and shape a culture, which Neetcode enjoyed. Neetcode describes the work as problem solving rather than culture building, and says the management load has been more than expected.

Source: 28:51–29:36 ↗
What did Neetcode dislike most about Google?
Neetcode

Neetcode found the company very slow. Urgency and speed did not seem to matter, which is pleasant for work-life balance but frustrating for ambitious people who want projects shipped or promotions. Neetcode says Google placed processes and engineers' feelings ahead of customer impact, the opposite of Amazon in that respect.

Source: 29:38–30:57 ↗
Source: 27:23–28:49 ↗

QWhat is the top technical book recommendation for software engineers?

Neetcode

Neetcode recommends Designing Data-Intensive Applications. Neetcode acknowledges that many readers do not retain the details, but says the book changes how readers think about systems. Neetcode finds parallels to LeetCode problems in almost every chapter and says the book is not for everyone.

Source: 30:23–32:57 ↗

QIf Neetcode could advise a younger self just after college, what would it be?

Neetcode

Neetcode would focus more on what they enjoy. Neetcode chose a job that was expected to be reasonably enjoyable and assumed any technical role would do. Neetcode learned web development because it seemed popular, but found it boring. A less common field such as operating systems or databases would have suited Neetcode better.

Neetcode says the same is true of LeetCode. It seems hard to some people, but Neetcode found it easy because Neetcode enjoyed it. The advice is to try to enjoy the work at least a little.

Nimit Sohoni: Quant Finance vs AI Research, PhDs, and Startup Careers

Nimit Sohoni compares quant finance and AI research careers, explains when a PhD helps, and describes working at Cartesia, a voice AI startup.

Nimit Sohoni's view: fundamentals and problem taste matter more than credentials

The host introduces Nimit Sohoni as a Stanford PhD and former Citadel quant who now works at Cartesia, a voice AI company. In Nimit's view, a PhD opens doors in both AI research and quant finance but is not required. Strong math and computer science fundamentals carry across both fields. The skill a PhD really builds is research taste: picking problems that matter and can be solved. Nimit says quant work usually offers better work-life balance than AI research, while quant pay is opaque and firms are more secretive. The conversation ends with advice for technical people moving into AI research: build fundamentals, read widely, and show evidence of the skill through school or a startup.

Source: 00:56–58:14 ↗

QWhich career opportunities are hard to reach without a PhD?

Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says few opportunities are closed to people without a PhD, but a PhD makes some much easier. Academia requires one. Industry AI research and quantitative finance are the two areas where Nimit has seen a PhD open doors. Nimit adds that industry research in computer science and math is increasingly converging on AI.

Does a PhD help at the first filter, or later in the hiring process?
Nimit Sohoni

Both, according to Nimit. An interview is easier to get when a candidate has differentiated themselves, and a PhD can do that. Applying to a top AI firm without the usual school, internship, or connection signals is harder but still possible.

A PhD also builds a skill set that helps later on. Learning on the job, without a PhD, is another route that works for many people.

Source: 01:52–03:37 ↗
Would the role itself change with a PhD versus without one?
Nimit Sohoni

Yes. Engineering-heavy AI work, such as training or evaluation infrastructure and data processing, does not need a PhD. More speculative architecture design can benefit from one, because a PhD gives time to explore directions that may not pay off soon.

A PhD is not necessary for someone whose only goal is to become an AI researcher. For someone still exploring and looking for problems that interest them, Nimit says a PhD can be a good way to do that.

Source: 03:39–05:22 ↗
Source: 00:56–01:50 ↗

QWhat skill set does a PhD develop?

Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says the main skill is finding the right problems, which Nimit puts at about 90 percent of research. A researcher must find a problem that is interesting and meaningful, sometimes persuade others it matters, and scope it so it is tractable. Execution was Nimit's strength before the PhD. Research taste and problem selection were the big lessons, and they come from immersion in the field, through reading enough papers and talking with enough people.

What tips help a researcher find the right problems?
Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says the main habit is keeping up with the literature by reading as many papers as possible. Full reading is not needed. Skimming abstracts shows what people are thinking about.

Nimit also recommends working up gradually. Early on, a researcher should attack small sub-problems, such as extending a method to a special case. As they mature, they can take on bigger problems and new ideas. Skipping these steps is generally inadvisable.

Source: 06:14–07:52 ↗
Source: 04:32–06:11 ↗

QWhere do you get your feed of hot research papers?

Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says X is the main source, with talking to co-workers as a second. Nimit curates the feed so it is mostly machine learning papers.

To start, Nimit followed people from Stanford, professors whose papers Nimit had read, and prominent researchers at large labs. When a followed account shares an interesting paper, Nimit follows the authors tagged in it, so the list grew on its own.

Source: 07:52–09:12 ↗

QWhere were you in your career, and why did you become a quant?

Nimit Sohoni

Nimit joined Citadel Securities after the PhD, having interned there just before graduating. By then Nimit had spent four to five years in AI research. Nimit had considered three careers that fit an interest in math and computation: machine learning research, quantitative finance, and quantum computing, which Nimit had no experience in.

Friends who had interned at Citadel Securities and other quant firms said they enjoyed it, and Nimit was curious. Nimit liked the work. It felt refreshing after a PhD that Nimit describes as a grind that can cause burnout, because the problems and environment were new.

Source: 09:13–10:58 ↗

QIs the work culture at quant firms as intense as its reputation suggests?

Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says the reputation is real in some places but varies by team and firm. Nimit personally had a good work-life balance as a quant.

Nimit links this partly to trading hours. US traders work around US market hours, plus a little time before and after, and the office culture follows that schedule. People cluster their work around those hours and rarely take work home, even though the work could be done at any time.

Source: 10:58–11:49 ↗

QHow would you describe quant work day to day?

Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says it depends on the team, the sector, and the firm. A hedge fund and a market maker can have very different problems, and front-office and back-office quants do different jobs. Some quants focus on alpha, meaning they generate and backtest trading strategies and put them into practice. Others focus on monetizing strategies or on risk, building metrics that reduce risk without cutting profit. Some do data analysis on large sets of historical trade data.

Nimit says a strong math background is the common thread across these roles.

How does math play a concrete role in the day-to-day work?
Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says stochastic calculus is the backbone of finance and comes up almost everywhere. Other areas include numerical optimization, numerical interpolation, and numerical linear algebra. Nimit says more firms are going deep into machine learning, and some have set up research arms doing LLM-type work.

Nimit says quants keep finding new fields of math to apply, partly for fun. Still, stochastic calculus is the most unifying part, which Nimit calls finance 101 math.

Source: 13:20–15:01 ↗
Source: 11:49–13:17 ↗

QHow do quants and software engineers collaborate?

Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says it depends on the company. At Jane Street, the number of people called quants is small, and traders are technical and implement much of their own work. At Citadel, which Nimit calls more quant-forward, quants may be roughly equal in number to the technical staff. Roles overlap a lot across quants, software engineers, and traders.

At some firms, quants design strategies and hand them to engineers to build. At others, one person may do both, because the person who can implement something best understands its reasons and edge cases. Nimit did a lot of coding, mostly in C++ and some Python.

Source: 15:03–16:37 ↗

QHow do finance and tech compare across these roles?

Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says the skill set is quite similar. Math and computer science were Nimit's main interests, and the goal was a job that used both. Nimit knew nothing about finance before joining Citadel Securities but read a few recommended textbooks, and technical skill carried the rest. Nimit says AI research works the same way: strong fundamentals let a person pick up the rest.

Nimit says the transition was not rough in either direction. Culture differs, such as San Francisco versus New York, and so do hours. Nimit says quant offers better work-life balance than AI, because AI is very competitive and many places gain an edge by outworking rivals.

Source: 16:37–18:13 ↗

QHow are compensation and bonuses structured at quant firms?

Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says quant pay has no standard levels like tech companies use. Pay depends on how the firm and the team did that year, how a person's strategies performed if they work on alpha, and seniority or tenure. Nimit says quant firms are secretive, so how these factors combine is opaque. Alpha roles can be very bonus-driven and riskier, while back-office roles tend to be more predictable.

Nimit says multimillion-dollar pay is real for some people, but for the median case pay is still very good, not outlandish.

What about NDAs, non-competes, and garden leave?
Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says finance firms take confidentiality very seriously. What surprised Nimit, compared with tech, was how tight-lipped people are even within one firm. Teams may have rules on what they can share, and some people stay quiet to protect their alpha.

A non-compete bars a person from working for a competitor for a set period after leaving. The firm usually sets the length. Nimit says it can be zero, up to about two years, and rarely three, with six months to two years as the norm. During that period, called garden leave, the person is paid to not work. It keeps ideas from reaching competitors, and by the time it ends, a strategy may no longer matter.

Source: 20:36–23:44 ↗
Does that secrecy push colleagues to be hostile to one another?
Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says the incentive exists. Many people are reluctant, or forbidden, to discuss what they do, and some will not name their sector. Some firms run pods, where each pod is responsible for its own profit and loss and the firm takes a cut.

Pods can end up working on similar ideas without knowing it, since they do not share information. Nimit says the logic is uncorrelated returns. If pods shared ideas, they could converge on similar trades, so one error could wipe out a whole team. Independent work carries less risk.

Source: 23:45–24:54 ↗
Source: 18:13–20:34 ↗

QWhat sets the top 1 percent of AI researchers and quants apart?

Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says there are several paths. Raw technical skill, intuition, and execution speed all matter. So does playing the political game, which can help people rise. Quant is harder to game because performance is easier to measure. A strong alpha quant who makes the firm a lot of money is clearly recognized.

In AI, the measure is harder to read. A seminal paper or a real breakthrough, such as a much better model, plays the same role. Nimit adds that being in the right place at the right time matters in both fields.

Source: 24:55–26:28 ↗

QWhat are the top quant firms, and why?

Nimit Sohoni

Nimit calls RenTech the gold standard, depending on who you ask, and says its returns over 20 to 30 years are remarkable. Nimit names Jane Street, Citadel, Jump Trading, and Hudson River as other well-regarded firms with strong technical talent and returns. Having one on a resume can help with later quant roles.

Nimit also points to smaller, more secretive firms with excellent returns, naming TGS, in Southern California, plus XTX and Radix as newer firms in that group.

Source: 26:30–28:08 ↗

QAre there any interesting stories from working in quant finance?

Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says firms take the rules seriously. Quants face trading restrictions and must get trades pre-approved. Nimit describes stories of people who shared stock tips in group chats and split the profits. That is illegal, and those caught can be fired, sued, or even jailed.

Did you see colleagues disappear suddenly?
Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says that does happen. Trading on group tips is one of the things firms cover in training. Non-compete disputes can also lead to accusations that someone took strategies to a rival.

Nimit describes job security in quant as an inverse parabola rather than a U shape. Senior quants become expensive, so even a good one can stop being worth the cost, while earlier-career quants cost less. Quant culture is up-or-out and trims low performers. Alpha roles are easy to judge by profit, and trading roles are easy to monitor, so the pressure can be brutal.

Source: 28:54–31:15 ↗
Source: 28:08–28:54 ↗

QWhy did you leave Citadel to join Cartesia?

Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says joining Citadel Securities was partly a chance to learn a new domain and finance, and Nimit became more financially literate. By the time Nimit left, growth had started to level off. Nimit had also seen AI take off, having graduated just before ChatGPT came out.

Nimit knew the Cartesia founders from the Stanford PhD and had great respect for their research. A small startup offered growth, a return to AI, and a chance to shape the company and culture as an early employee. Nimit describes this as a different risk profile: after the PhD, Nimit was more risk-averse, but by then had some stability.

Source: 31:15–32:41 ↗

QWhat problem is Cartesia solving?

Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says Cartesia is a voice AI company whose mission is to build the next generation of voice AI and a platform for it. The flagship product is text to speech. Cartesia also offers speech to text and voice agents. Nimit says voice AI is one of the fastest-growing areas of AI, used in call centers, entertainment, and companion products.

Why does Cartesia focus on voice?
Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says voice is a useful test bed for research ideas. Cartesia has a research arm on longer-term problems such as long context, multimodality, continual learning, memory, and test-time compute. The broader goal is real-time systems that are truly intelligent, that people can interact with, and that learn from experience, such as an always-on personal assistant.

Source: 34:14–35:02 ↗
Source: 32:44–34:12 ↗

QWho are the top competitors in voice AI?

Nimit Sohoni

Nimit names Eleven Labs as the main competitor, a very similar company that Nimit says had about an 18-month head start. Nimit once used Eleven Labs for fun videos, long before Cartesia existed. Nimit says Cartesia stands out for low latency, because a pause between turns of a conversation breaks the illusion of talking to a person.

Nimit also describes the usual voice agent pipeline of speech to text, then a language model, then text to speech. Nimit says this loses information and adds delay, so Cartesia is working toward more end-to-end systems.

What would it look like if Cartesia completely beat Eleven Labs?
Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says Cartesia already wins on latency and cost. A full win would need quality on many dimensions: following the transcript exactly, which is hard with special characters and repetitions; naturalness; speed; voice cloning; accent localization; and control over emotion. Nimit says Cartesia leads in some areas, trails in others, and wants to lead in as many as possible.

Nimit says switching costs exist in AI, especially with large enterprise customers, though a startup can move faster. If a provider is conclusively better in every way, Nimit says it becomes hard to argue against switching.

Source: 36:58–39:11 ↗
Source: 35:04–36:56 ↗

QWhat is the main difference between an AI startup and a big lab?

Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says big labs have strong resources, compute, and many researchers. The flip side is that they can be averse to out-of-the-box ideas, prone to groupthink, and less willing to take risks, because failed experiments are expensive. Startups can be more nimble and explore strategically, challenging orthodoxy. That is what drew Nimit to Cartesia.

Nimit credits co-founder Albert Gu with showing, through Mamba, that the common belief that scale alone solves sequence modeling was wrong. Nimit says the work showed real gains in efficiency and quality from state space models, and from hybrids that mix them with transformer layers.

Can you give a quick primer on state space models versus transformers?
Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says the main challenge of transformers is memory at inference time. Transformers store a representation of every token in a key-value cache, so memory grows linearly with sequence length. For very long sequences, this becomes costly in compute and memory.

State space models compress the past into a state of fixed size, so the cost of each step does not grow with sequence length. Nimit cites co-founder Albert Gu's analogy: a state space model is like a brain with a fixed-size state, while a transformer is more like a database that can recall anything in context. Nimit sees the two as complementary.

Source: 41:41–44:15 ↗
Is the compressed state lossy, and what are the trade-offs?
Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says there are trade-offs. On recall-heavy or fact-based tasks, pure state space models can lag transformers, because transformers can do exact in-context recall. On other tasks, state space models can scale as well as or better than transformers, even on a fixed parameter budget.

Nimit says the best of both worlds is often a hybrid that interleaves state space and transformer layers in some ratio. NVIDIA has released work like this, and some recent model families use the same approach. Nimit thinks hybrids are the likely direction for text.

For audio, Nimit says compression is a useful built-in assumption, since each audio frame carries little information. Nimit says state space models improved quality and inference speed in Cartesia's audio work.

Source: 45:54–48:42 ↗
So lossiness is an asset when the data is redundant?
Nimit Sohoni

Nimit agrees. Text is densely informational, so each token matters, while audio frames are redundant. Nimit says architecture and data are closely linked, so an architecture cannot be chosen apart from its modality. Co-designing architecture around modality is one of the core research problems that drives Cartesia's work.

Source: 48:44–49:41 ↗
Source: 39:13–41:41 ↗

QWhich works better, a company focused on product or one focused on research?

Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says a company should have both. Nimit is skeptical of startups that focus on core research without a clear path to a product. Big labs have more resources, and a company must eventually deliver large returns, so that bet can be all or nothing.

Nimit also sees risk in product-only companies built on other people's models. Many wrapper companies were made obsolete when base models improved enough to do the same work with little scaffolding. Being at the intersection is valuable. A real product shows the issues firsthand, and that drives fixes at the model level, so the company keeps control over its models.

Nimit says Cartesia is first and foremost a product company, and believes building the best products requires solving some fundamental research problems.

Source: 49:41–52:17 ↗

QWhat advice do you have for a technical person who wants to move into AI research? A host says a software engineer friend worries that software engineering may fade within ten years.

Nimit Sohoni

Nimit's philosophy is to build technical skills as much as possible. Once fundamentals are good enough, opportunities tend to come to you. Nimit advises getting as good as possible at coding and AI, reading many papers, and building math skills and intuition, which Nimit has optimized for since undergrad.

Nimit says switching teams or companies can be the only route at a big company, where people can get siloed. Some companies handle moves better, and Nimit has seen engineers move into research. A qualification such as a master's in AI can help with a lateral change.

So there are two common paths: more education, or a startup where you mold yourself into a research role?
Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says that is roughly right, but even at a startup, a person needs some evidence of the skill, whether grown organically or gained in school. A track record on a resume makes it easier to get a foot in the door. Cartesia has seen people make that switch, because a small company means everyone knows everyone and can judge a change of career from working together.

Source: 53:55–56:17 ↗
Source: 52:17–54:43 ↗

QWhat is your biggest regret looking back on your career?

Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says they often overthink things and have spent time regretting past decisions that did not matter in the end. Nimit now tries to learn from that and not sweat the small stuff. Minor setbacks happen, and beating oneself up is not a productive use of time.

Source: 56:17–57:08 ↗

QIf you could give your younger self advice on entering the industry, what would it be?

Nimit Sohoni

Nimit says to focus on building deep technical skills and not to waste time on trivial work or spread too thin. Focus on the skills you want to use in your day job, get good at them, and spend most of your work time there.

Nimit calls this a simple recipe that is very hard to follow, since it takes discipline, much like exercise and healthy eating.

Source: 57:08–57:45 ↗

Section 70 · interview

Philip Su: Meta Levels, Management vs IC, and Choosing Your Career Goal

Philip Su, a former Microsoft, Facebook and OpenAI engineer, reflects on rapid promotion, moving between management and individual contributor tracks, how senior levels are judged, and why wanting the right goal matters more than reaching it fast.

Philip Su's view: grow fast if you must, but choose the goal on purpose

Philip Su is introduced by the host as one of the few engineers promoted to distinguished engineer (IC9) at Meta. Philip's view is that fast career growth rests on luck, talent and hard work, and that hard work buys speed at a real cost to health and relationships. The larger lesson Philip draws from a career at Microsoft, Facebook, a Gates-funded nonprofit and OpenAI is to decide what you actually want before sprinting toward it. The conversation covers moving between management and individual contributor tracks, a deliberate drop from E9 to E7, how seniority levels are judged, building Facebook's London engineering site, why Philip left Facebook and later joined OpenAI, how Philip learned to write, and whether to specialize or stay a generalist. Levels, headcounts and company history are Philip's recollections, and Philip flags several as dated.

Source: 00:00–1:20:39 ↗

QWhat does Philip credit for the fast climb through Microsoft's ladder?

Philip Su

Philip names several causes. One was working with very good managers and teammates. The Microsoft tablet PC team had about 20 people, and three of them were distinguished engineers, which Philip calls very rare at Microsoft. Philip learned a great deal quickly from them.

Another cause was very long hours. In the first year Philip kept a sleeping bag in the office and often slept there. Philip set a 3 a.m. alarm to follow what Philip describes as Da Vinci's idea of sleeping in two four-hour blocks, coding between them.

Philip sums up fast growth as luck, talent and hard work. Luck means being in the right place at the right time, for example being at Stanford when Sergey and Larry were there. Talent matters because Philip rejects the idea that anyone can become anything: Philip will never be a great basketball player, and a weak public speaker can become passable but not a Cicero. Hard work matters because someone who outworks equally talented and equally lucky people will get further. Philip adds that Philip does not recommend this to everyone.

If the goal is growth at all costs, were those hours actually optimal?
Philip Su

Philip says the work week is often defended by pointing to Henry Ford's finding that each added hour is less productive. Philip agrees that output per hour falls as one stays up too long, but says that for many people the curve runs a long way before an added hour becomes negative. In Philip's view, working 50 or 60 hours probably gets more done in total, though each extra hour is less effective.

Philip adds a second consideration with a surgeon analogy. Philip heard from a surgeon that the quickest way to gain surgical experience is to log many surgery hours, so a long residency may pack six years of exposure into four. Nobody wants a surgeon in the 34th hour, Philip says, but a surgeon with wide experience is valuable. Philip would not recommend the crazy hours Philip worked early on, yet they gave Philip far more experience than a typical junior Microsoft hire. There are diminishing returns, but still returns, so a person who truly puts career above all, including relationships, should work more. Philip says Philip's own work life was out of balance for years.

Source: 03:23–06:47 ↗
Source: 00:56–03:21 ↗

QWhy did Philip become a manager, and why did the role keep changing?

Philip Su

Philip says the promotion to the Microsoft equivalent of E7 came as a manager, after which Philip also worked as an individual contributor at that level. Early on Philip was very ambitious and came from a culture, as an ethnically Chinese person, in which managers were more respected and advanced further. Philip now calls the belief that management was the next growth step somewhat misguided.

Over a career Philip has moved between managing and individual contribution at least six times. Philip loves being an individual contributor but is often asked to manage, for example as a temporary manager.

Did Philip step in on poorly managed teams, or did managers ask Philip for help?
Philip Su

Philip says both happened. Philip's order of preference is individual contributor first, then manager of a team that lacks a better manager, and left to their own devices Philip would rather not manage people. Philip would rather manage a team that is poorly managed than leave it that way.

Philip also says that four separate times a former manager of Philip's asked to report to Philip.

Source: 07:46–08:40 ↗
How does a manager come to report to someone they used to manage under?
Philip Su

Philip says each case differed. Sometimes the manager reported to Philip on the same team. Sometimes the manager asked, years later, to join Philip's team after both had moved on. In one same-team case the manager wanted to become an individual contributor while Philip, a strong individual contributor, wanted to manage, so it was almost a swap in place. In most cases Philip joined a team elsewhere and a former manager who liked working with Philip was happy to work for Philip there.

Philip suggests part of the reason is having learned from great managers. After chasing management early in the career, Philip stopped looking for management roles as actively as for individual contributor ones.

Source: 08:42–10:23 ↗
Source: 06:48–07:43 ↗

QHow should someone decide between staying an individual contributor and becoming a manager?

Philip Su

Philip is open to new experiences and generally advocates trying management if you think you might like it or be good at it, with a few caveats.

The first caveat is not to walk through a one-way door by accident. Philip has gone back to being an individual contributor roughly six times, but says many people cannot. They become managers of managers, drift far from the code, and are then unwilling to take a lower-level job or unable to meet an individual contributor's expectations at their old level. Philip kept the door open both ways by diving into code even while managing teams.

The second caveat is that people tend to think only about themselves when they want to manage. Philip's test is that you are ready to lead when your team would have elected you: "Would you want to work for you?" If the answer is not a solid yes, there is something to improve. Philip notes that nobody can truly make you lead, because teams can slow-roll or sandbag work, so people have to want to work for you. Philip expects that once those improvements are made, people will ask you to manage.

Source: 10:26–13:07 ↗

QDid Philip lose progress by switching between the two tracks?

Philip Su

Philip says yes, intentionally and willingly. When Philip moved from site director of Facebook London to an individual contributor on Oculus, Philip was eventually releveled from E9 to E7. Philip bought into that and says it was necessary, because the skills shown as a site director differed from those needed to be a good coder on Oculus.

Many people cannot accept such a step, Philip says, either for ego reasons or because lifestyles grow to fill whatever compensation people earn. Those who will not change their lifestyle paint themselves into a corner with fewer and fewer jobs they can take.

Philip also says timing matters. One or two years into a career, a lateral move such as junior software developer to junior product manager is easy, and many people will coach you. Around the senior E5 range, moving from E5 software developer to E5 product manager is very difficult, unless the engineering work already involved product management. At more senior levels the skills converge again, so the shape is a diamond. An effective E8 individual contributor, in Philip's description, has a technical vision, understands infrastructure weak points, plans staged migrations, coaches well and understands business strategy. Philip concludes that the middle of a career is where changing tracks is hardest.

Does the diamond come back for deep specialists, for example in AI?
Philip Su

Philip agrees that for some archetypes it does not come back. Someone who goes very deep, for instance on SQL query optimization, may not need to develop the other skills that go with leading teams, and may not transition well into management.

Source: 16:36–17:33 ↗
Source: 13:10–16:34 ↗

QHow did Philip handle the move down from E9 to E7?

Philip Su

Philip had worried about this when first promoted from E8 to E9 as London site director. Philip told the Facebook CTO of the day (captioned "Shrep") that, because Philip liked being an individual contributor, Philip doubted the performance level could be kept when moving back to coding. The CTO replied that they should worry when it happened and not withhold a promotion because of a possible future return to coding.

Back in code, Philip understood the E9 expectations were out of reach. Being moved back to E7, the level Philip joined at about eight years earlier, felt great. Philip says it is far better to perform well at a level than to barely tread water at one where you feel imposter syndrome and doubt you will stay qualified. Philip also did not want pay above what Philip deserved relative to teammates.

Philip says few people make so large a change, and it demands a particular ego. Philip went from running a site of perhaps 400 or 500 people to reporting to a manager who reported to a manager. Philip also had to avoid voicing opinions about running the site, and avoid using outsized influence from the past, so the new leaders could succeed.

Source: 17:35–20:05 ↗

QWhat do engineers at E7, E8 and E9 typically do?

Philip Su

Philip caveats that Philip's information is coarse and probably stale, since it comes from working at Meta starting about 15 years earlier. In general, levels reflect scope of influence: how big, long or valuable a project one can single-handedly guarantee. An intern might guarantee a small feature. A senior developer at E5 or E6 should deliver the work of about 10 to 15 people. At E7, Philip would expect regular influence over about 50 people, driving technical direction for a team that size, being consulted by product and engineering managers, and personally delivering about six months of work with no check-ins. A director might influence about a hundred people.

On the individual contributor side, Philip says large scope comes in different forms. Some people are narrow but deep in a way others cannot match, and four E6s cannot replace them. Others are broad generalists, especially valuable for new teams and startups, where three E6s cannot outperform one great generalist E8.

Philip stresses that the qualitative difference matters most and cannot be captured in an HR bullet list. People at those levels excel for different reasons, and someone more senior must judge them. When Philip was first promoted to E8, E9 did not exist. Philip says the company later had to invent such levels for individual contributors like John Carmack. Philip recalls, if memory serves, that when the first E9 promotions were discussed the company had several thousand people and was considering three engineers, each a different archetype. Philip compares this to becoming a professor, where there is no formula and it comes down to whether other E8s think you are an E8.

What if an excellent E7 has no E8s or E9s nearby to give qualitative input?
Philip Su

Philip says this happens often at small companies or on weak teams. When Philip worked at Microsoft it had about 140,000 people, and Philip believes it was about 240,000 before the layoffs. In a company that size there are always weak teams, where someone may feel awesome only because peers are weak. That leads to overleveling or to having nobody to learn from. Philip uses a real-estate analogy: you do not want to be the most expensive house on the block, with no room to grow, nor the worst, so find a block where you are the middle house.

At the highest levels, Philip says, good role models are hard to find and each excels differently, so a model may not match your strengths. More useful is a coach who has a say in promotions and can say you are qualitatively far from where you need to be. Then you can discuss what to do about it.

Source: 26:50–29:14 ↗
Source: 20:08–26:48 ↗

QWhat project or scope earned Philip the E9 promotion?

Philip Su

Philip brought 12 people to start the engineering portion of Meta's London office and, over roughly four or five years, grew it to about 400 or 500. A good level-six engineering manager could run 12 engineers, Philip says, but with each order of magnitude of growth the problems get harder and the solutions turn gray. The promotion rested on handling a wider variety of things and more strategic decisions.

One example: in one of Philip's last meetings as site lead, Philip argued to people in Menlo Park about how many interns to hire and how much headcount London should have that summer. The argument rested on math about expected H-1B volume 18 months ahead, for full-time offers moving to Menlo Park. Earlier, as an E8, Philip was the first of Meta's sites to look at the seniority pyramid and ask whether people were growing at a commensurate pace. Philip describes these as decisions that grow in scope, by breadth of people affected or by how far ahead one must think.

Source: 29:17–31:59 ↗

QWhat made the London site's engineering culture strong?

Philip Su

Philip names two helps. First, before London Philip had been the second person hired in Meta Seattle, the company's first office outside its Palo Alto headquarters, and saw it grow from four desks to 120, including mistakes in how it grew. Second, before starting London, Philip interviewed site directors from other companies. One was the former site director of Google London, David Singleton, whom Philip says later became Stripe's CTO.

Singleton told Philip that Google had experimented with landing teams, the group sent to bootstrap a site's culture, and concluded the team should commit for at least two years. Philip contrasts this with companies that send a team for three or six months and then leave the site on its own. Philip thinks that is a mistake, because culture is hard to hold while new people are about as numerous as those who have been around more than three months. The CTO wanted enough engineers for two full interview loops, about 10 to 12 people.

Philip interviewed nearly 50 volunteers from the company, plus some of their peers and their managers, to choose 12 who would carry the culture. Each was asked to bring a project to lead, and the group included exceptional individual contributors who were happy to do whatever the site needed. Philip says Philip was lucky in the choices and credits learning from people who had done it before.

Was the two-year commitment tied to pay or a contract?
Philip Su

Philip says no. Pay stayed what it had been and nobody signed anything. Philip had a serious conversation saying Philip wanted only people committed to at least two years, so those who could not commit opted out. One or two had to return sooner for understandable reasons, and Philip supported them.

Far more stayed longer than expected. Philip believes about four of the original team are still in London 15 years later. Philip says they did not join planning to settle there. They loved London and the office.

Source: 34:31–36:57 ↗
Source: 32:01–34:29 ↗

QDoes Philip have favorite stories from working with Zuck and Bos?

Philip Su

Philip's first manager at Facebook was Bos, who later became CTO, and during the London years Philip's manager was the then-CTO captioned as "Shrep." Both gave great advice and guidance. Philip spoke one-on-one with Zuck only a few times, so Philip's insight is limited, but Philip says Zuck felt genuine in how he led.

What impressed Philip most about both Zuck and Bos was their willingness and ability to grow. Philip joined at 33, when the company's median age was 27, and was the oldest person in the Seattle office for the first seven months, so most of the people Philip worked for were younger. People who had worked with either for years could say exactly how they had grown. Philip saw both as open to coaching, probably seeking it, and making a deliberate effort to improve.

Philip's small example is Zuck's AMAs. Within about two years of Philip joining, Philip says, they had improved a lot. Philip is pretty sure someone coached Zuck on how to hold his head, because early on his natural pose had the head tilted slightly upward, and over the years he deliberately corrected it to face the crowd straight on.

Source: 37:00–38:59 ↗

QWhich high-profile individual contributor impressed Philip most?

Philip Su

Philip mentions John Carmack, whom Philip calls legendary but worked with only indirectly through Oculus. Beyond being very prolific, Philip says, Carmack could drop into a codebase after about six months away and give concrete advice. On Philip's small product, Oculus 360 Photos, Carmack tried it one day unprompted. He had insights about distortion at the corners of photos while turning and performance ideas that nobody on the team had thought of.

Philip worked more with Scott Renfro, who came to London for a six-month rotation. Peer feedback on him was consistently glowing: even for a dumb mistake, his code review comments were sensitive and never shamed anyone, and peers wrote that he took time out of his day to make them better. Philip calls him a force multiplier for his teams, and says he later led huge infrastructure-wide changes at Meta, with Philip pretty sure GDPR was among them. For Philip he is a clear case of seniority well earned, because he could guarantee a huge scope of work personally and also lift every team he joined.

Source: 39:02–41:39 ↗

QWhy did Philip buy the whole company coffee for a day?

Philip Su

The host remembers it as a day of free coffee for everyone and puts the cost at over $23,000. Philip did not state a figure in this answer. Philip says the idea began several years into the Facebook years. After the company moved to its Menlo Park campus, a coffee shop opened in Hacker Square, and one Christmas Philip bought everyone a coffee for a day. Philip found the joy infectious, and the chief executive of the coffee chain wrote to say its staff had never seen anything like it.

When Philip left, Philip wanted to give something back. Philip stresses luck. People forget, Philip says, that when Philip joined, the talk was that Friendster might return, that Google+ would roll over Facebook, and that Facebook would never make money on mobile. Philip had left Microsoft after 12 years, in which Philip says the stock rose about 15 percent, and had low expectations. The Facebook outcome was, in Philip's words, "a brick of money" that came from luck, not design. Philip says Philip gave all IPO proceeds to charity because they felt undeserved, citing luck in being born when an interest in computer science pays and in emigrating to America. Philip then coordinated with coffee shops at the major Facebook sites, around five, by calling the owners, and says it was fun and rewarding.

Source: 41:42–45:51 ↗

QWhy did Philip leave Facebook when things were going so well?

Philip Su

Philip says the biggest concern in 2018 was the rising income gap in America. Philip wanted to start a B Corp to bridge it. Philip was already telling co-workers that technical unemployment was coming, before the term was common, because Philip was convinced robots would replace people and society needed to adapt quickly. Most co-workers disagreed. Philip also felt Facebook had grown to where it would be more than fine without Philip.

Judging Philip's own usefulness at the same level as on joining, Philip felt more useful as an individual contributor when Facebook was small. Philip joined as the second person hired in Seattle, when Facebook had about 500 engineers globally. Philip and two other engineers shipped the whole video calling feature in about six months, and Philip also helped negotiate the Skype contract and hire and manage the testing contractors. Eight years later, with thousands of engineers, Philip thought a generalist was much less useful than specialists. Philip felt like a generic coder contributing nothing exceptional.

Do small companies generally value generalists more, with specialists favored at the largest companies?
Philip Su

Philip says that is Philip's intuition. Every small company can use at least one specialist in its domain. The bigger force, in Philip's view, is quantization. A large company can hire a full-time communications person, but a small one cannot hire someone for three hours a week, so it asks a product manager who communicates well to cover it for a while.

Generalists can be fractionalized across many roles. Once a company is large enough that each fraction of work needs one or more people full-time, a generalist wastes energy because perhaps 15 percent of their skills apply to the job.

Source: 47:36–49:15 ↗
Source: 45:53–47:34 ↗

QWhat brought Philip back into industry, and why OpenAI?

Philip Su

After Facebook, Philip started a local nonprofit in Seattle, captioned "Outere," building free software for global health. A Gates Foundation grant funded it, and Philip says the software was deployed in Nigeria, Kenya and South Africa to assist rapid malaria testing. Philip then took an unemployed break and used GitHub Copilot in VS Code, trying and failing to persuade friends to pay for AI tools.

When AI took off, around the ChatGPT 3.5 or 4 period, Philip saw a huge transition point. Philip felt Philip had missed two while at Microsoft, the dot-com wave and mobile, both of which Microsoft largely missed, and had been lucky to catch the social network wave. Philip increasingly believed AI could be as big as or bigger than the internet. Philip reasons that humans might be the first species to create something smarter than itself, which might even answer the Fermi question.

Philip says Philip applied only to OpenAI because of a Facebook lesson: join the market leader or nobody at all. A leader can afford to fail at a few things and take brave, big shots. A follower such as Google+ has to match all of the leader's checkboxes and add one differentiator, circles in that case, and its timeline is set by the leader. Philip loves the craziness a leader can afford. The plan was to join OpenAI or keep writing software independently.

Source: 49:17–53:53 ↗

QHow did OpenAI compare with Facebook?

Philip Su

Philip first notes that the stages differ: Facebook had about 500 engineers when Philip joined and OpenAI about 120. With that caveat, Philip calls OpenAI the highest talent density of any group of engineers Philip has worked with. Moving from Microsoft to Facebook was a big jump in the average quality of colleagues, and Philip felt OpenAI was a notch above that.

Was it technical ability that stood out, or something else?
Philip Su

Philip says the technical capabilities were exceptional. The difference Philip names is product focus. Facebook focused heavily on what the product is and why people use it, Philip says, because beyond a network effect and a product people loved it had little magic sauce. In the early ChatGPT days, with no viable competitors, a lousy product could still be used. Philip recalls that a year or two earlier a server error appeared in about every fourth conversation thread.

Philip expects OpenAI to get increasingly better at product. As competition heats up, Philip says, success will come from research shipped in compelling products, not from pure research.

Source: 53:56–55:40 ↗
Source: 53:02–53:53 ↗

QHow did Philip develop such strong writing?

Philip Su

Philip says Philip was a bad writer through college because Philip did not respect communication. Coming from a culture that prized getting A's, Philip viewed the hard sciences as real and history and English as a waste of time, with no right answers, and so did not invest in soft skills.

At Microsoft, in spare time, Philip reread classics hated in high school. Philip names Hemingway and The Great Gatsby, saw them differently as an older reader, and developed a love of language. Philip cites Virginia Woolf for the idea that to write well you need to read well, and names David Foster Wallace, Alice Munro's short stories and Pilgrim at Tinker Creek as writing that shows what language can do. Philip then came to see writing as a skill as valuable as a hard science skill, and started working at it.

Beyond reading well, Philip says, it takes a willingness to rewrite several times and to leave material on the cutting-room floor, and many of Philip's well-known posts were rewritten repeatedly. Philip also notes clever rhetorical moves in other people's Substacks and tries to remember them. Above all, Philip says, the change came from no longer disrespecting the skill and seeing it as essential even for scientists and technical people.

Was the non-chronological essay structure planned, and did an editor help?
Philip Su

Philip says the structure came from a moment of inspiration about how to tell that story compellingly. Philip says chronological order is usually the most compelling because it makes sense. Some stories work better out of order, Philip says, because a different, threaded arc in a person's life becomes visible, and Philip felt that way about this one.

Philip had no editor for those pieces. Philip did hire a professional editor, captioned Rebecca Ambrose, for a podcast miniseries, wanting the words well structured and expecting a professional to do better, and learned a great deal. Philip says nothing posted professionally was ever edited by another person, though Philip did receive feedback in the podcast case.

Source: 58:59–1:01:32 ↗
Source: 55:43–58:56 ↗

QHow did the Great Post Explorer side project come about?

Philip Su

Philip wrote the tool inside Facebook to rank and surface the most commented-on or most reacted-to posts of all time on the company's internal network. Philip had benefited from serendipitously finding great things written by people who came before, and wished they were cataloged and crowdsourced by category so they could be browsed.

Philip's underlying point is that posts fade with time, and in Philip's opinion the value of a post is often temporal, but for some posts it is not, much as some podcasts are evergreen and others cover current news. The tool aimed to help people discover timeless posts. The host recalls it was still live about two years earlier. Philip is not sure what happened to it.

Source: 1:01:35–1:02:47 ↗

QIs software engineering like athletics, with a performance peak and then decay?

Philip Su

Philip thinks engineers can keep getting more valuable over time. Everyone's growth curve is asymptotic and everyone has a different final level, so growth slows near it. As with work hours beyond 50 or 60, though, each increment can still be growth, so one need not flatline.

Philip's image is that when young, Philip outran everybody but ran serpentine, and experience means jogging in a straight line. An experienced person senses when things are not heading the right way and either avoids that work or persuades the team to stop early, saving a team's worth of time. Philip's example is a friend at Microsoft whose organization's vice president met weekly to triage bugs for shipping. Philip told the friend that this meant the project was nowhere near shipping on time. Philip says people also learn what is worth investing in.

Philip also values having everyone run in the same direction even if it is three degrees off the ideal. As a young person Philip held the idealistic view that there was one right direction. Philip now thinks a team pulling together at roughly 98 percent correct will get further than half the team pulling perfectly while the other half argues, and links this to Amazon's "disagree and commit." Philip concedes some things decline: Philip lacks the stamina of age 24, and if woken at 3 a.m. today would code slowly, whereas at 23 it was no problem. Philip hopes that while some things weaken, others strengthen.

Source: 1:02:51–1:07:01 ↗

QHow did Philip win respect as a very young manager?

Philip Su

Philip says it was difficult, because Philip lacked humility and was overly ambitious. Philip says Philip would not have worked for Philip's own 24-year-old self. Philip became a manager because Philip was one of the team's strongest engineers, and the team figured it was better to keep a good engineer happy by letting Philip manage.

In that first year, at 24, Philip had to fire a 40-year-old. Philip calls it exceptionally difficult, made harder by awareness of how junior Philip was. Philip says the person deserved it for missing expectations but was two levels above Philip's own level, and Philip says Philip was too immature to know how to manage someone more experienced.

Philip says Philip was a pretty bad manager at first but obsessed with growth: Philip collected mentors, asked for feedback and read nonfiction about managing teams and hard conversations. Philip says Philip made huge mistakes even in the last year of managing. The biggest weakness Philip names is giving feedback. Philip pulls punches, hates confrontation and downplays how serious the feedback is, so people miss the point. Philip says Philip has gone from very bad to passable and does not expect to become excellent. A strength is motivating action, since Philip joins only teams Philip believes in, and Philip's passion and vision excite people.

Source: 1:07:03–1:10:20 ↗

QShould someone early in their career become a specialist or a generalist?

Philip Su

Philip calls this tricky and dependent on how well a person knows themselves. A chess prodigy who is clearly gifted by eight or nine should specialize. Most people lack that certainty, and Philip would caution against binding too early to a specialty.

Philip names three dangers. First, how can you know you are a specialist rather than a generalist without having been a generalist? Second, an idiot-savant risk. Philip's example is the mathematician Erdős, who Philip says did not know as an adult how to cut his own grapefruit, so his mother cut it, although he published a great deal. Third, the specialty may disappear, especially in the age of AI. Philip compares a specialist in a fading technology to a COBOL expert hoping for another Y2K. Philip would encourage someone starting at 22 or 23 to dabble in a few things before committing hard.

Source: 1:10:23–1:12:59 ↗

QIf Philip could advise a younger self at the start of the career, what would the advice be?

Philip Su

Philip first cites Roy Disney, that decisions are easy when your values are clear. Philip's decisions were often hard because Philip lacked clear values, so Philip would tell a younger self to spend more time on what Philip actually wanted before committing.

Philip also says Philip was "the dog that caught the car." On joining Microsoft, Philip was convinced the goal was dev manager, and for about eight years took any job that moved closer, which made decisions easy. When Philip reached the level, which Philip places at around age 30 though the captions are unclear, and saw that E7 might be a terminal level, Philip had no mental model for what came next. Philip likens it to a child actor who peaked early and faces decades of work. Philip says this led to a period of serious depression after losing a sense of purpose. The second caution is to be sure you want what you want: people love Warren Buffett's billions, Philip says, but would they want them in their late 90s?

Philip adds that some things bend and some break. While Philip kept sleeping bags in the office, a fiancee visited from Maryland, and Philip saw her only each evening at 11 p.m., when work ended, for a late Denny's dinner. Philip says Philip is lucky that she is now Philip's wife, and says listeners usually guess the story ends with the engagement ring being returned. Philip recognizes now that Philip was bending something to an extreme that most things would not survive.

For anyone who cares only about career and wants the fastest route, Philip says first be sure that is what you want, and then be sure you are comfortable with other things breaking. Philip would tell the younger self that reaching E7 at 30 rather than 38 makes no difference in the long arc, since there are still about 30 years of work after 38. The real question, Philip says, is how fast you want to reach a terminal level versus keeping healthy relationships with a spouse and children.

Would the younger Philip have accepted that advice?
Philip Su

Philip says no. Advice feels good to give, but Philip says about 90 percent of the time you have to be ready to receive it for it to matter, and Philip was nowhere near that level of maturity. Philip compares it to being told that money does not buy happiness: everybody thinks they are the exception, but an unhappy person is still unhappy ten years later with more to spend.

Source: 1:18:09–1:18:54 ↗
Source: 1:13:02–1:18:06 ↗

QIs there a closing idea Philip wants the audience to consider?

Philip Su

Philip says Philip remains concerned about technical unemployment. Philip says the change from technology will be massive and will come sooner than people expect. Philip thinks Americans need to work out how to help the average person through it, and that very bad things can happen if society is not helped to adapt. Philip links this to Philip's earlier worries about automation and the rising income gap.

Source: 1:18:58–1:20:31 ↗
