Rahul Pandey: Startup to Pinterest, Meta Staff, TLM, and Founding Taro

Rahul Pandey traces a path from a Stanford spin-out to Pinterest, Meta staff engineer, tech lead manager and startup founder, arguing that credentials, mentors, clear stories and relationships compound while luck can be partly manufactured.

Rahul Pandey's view: use credentials to take bets, build things, and let relationships compound

Rahul Pandey is a software engineer who went from a Stanford spin-out startup to Pinterest, then to Meta, where he reached staff level (IC6) and later a tech-lead-manager (TLM) role, before leaving to co-found Taro. He walks the host, Ryan, through that path in order. In Rahul's account, early credentials made risk cheap, and promotions came from mentorship, self-built tooling, clearly framed stories and trust built over time. Management and founding suit people who enjoy helping others and hold strong opinions. Much of the outcome, he says, was luck, which can be partly manufactured by staying curious about people and sharing work. Everything below is Rahul's recollection and opinion unless marked as Ryan's.

Source: 00:55–1:09:55 ↗
Career stages (editorial summary of Rahul's account)
StageRole or levelWhat Rahul says drove it
Stanford spin-out startupEarly employee, new gradTook a bet on a professor's startup while holding multiple big-tech offers; acquired by Pinterest within about eight months of formation.
PinterestL3, then L4 after two rejections and an appealMoved from recommendation systems to Android; a staff-level mentor and pair programming; a promotion packet that needed clearer framing.
Meta (Portal)Hired at IC5, then IC6Led a migration of Portal's calling infrastructure back onto Messenger's, plus a self-started debug tool for Portal engineers.
Meta (TLM)Tech lead managerA hybrid role Rahul found taxing and unsustainable long term; he switched teams, then left.
TaroCo-founderLeft with a trusted co-founder, financial runway and an audience built through tutorials and webinars; went through Y Combinator.
Source: 00:55–50:54 ↗

QWhy did Rahul join a very small startup straight out of Stanford?

Rahul Pandey

Rahul stayed a fifth year at Stanford, finishing an undergraduate and a master's degree, partly because he felt he had made no faculty connections. He worked as a research assistant in the lab of a rising-star professor, who later spun the lab's work out into a company. Rahul notes that Stanford is generous about letting faculty start companies.

He had offers from Google, Microsoft and Meta, and he knew he could be one of 10,000 or 20,000 engineers in big tech. The startup offered mutual trust with the professor and a distinctly Silicon Valley story: great if it went well, a good story if not. Aside from the two founders (the professor and an industry veteran), Rahul counts himself as roughly employee number two. Ryan adds that so early in a career there was little responsibility to lose.

How did Rahul think about the risk compared with a safer big-tech job?
Rahul Pandey

Rahul gives two reasons. First, he sees most early career moves as two-way doors: try it, learn, and go to big tech later if needed. Second, he would probably not have taken the risk without prior approval from big tech. After a 2013 Facebook internship he received five offers (Google, Facebook, Microsoft, Twitter and Square), which with Stanford on his resume he calls an insurance policy.

Without it, he says, he would have thought twice and taken a stable job first, so that his second job would be easier to land.

Source: 03:15–05:24 ↗
Source: 00:55–03:12 ↗

QWas the startup's acquisition a strong outcome, or closer to an acqui-hire?

Rahul Pandey

Closer to an acqui-hire, Rahul says. He calls "acquisition" one of the most overloaded terms in Silicon Valley. At one end is a deal such as WhatsApp's sale to Facebook in 2014, which Rahul puts at 19 billion dollars. At the other end is a failed company whose sale is called an acquisition to protect the founders' dignity. His startup sat in the middle, nearer the failure end, though he hesitates to call it a failure.

He describes it as an opportunistic bet. The company had interesting, fairly academic intellectual property but no clear route to revenue or a product. Pinterest, already a hot company with 100 million users, offered to pair that technology with its product-market fit. The startup ended within about eight months of formation. Rahul says the package was somewhat higher than a normal Pinterest new grad's, not life-changing money.

He adds that storytelling is powerful: the story of an enterprising 22-year-old taking a bet on a startup has given him a lot of mileage. When mentoring, he says that if two options are close, the one with more unique people, opportunities and stories is a good one to pick.

Source: 04:44–07:52 ↗

QWould Rahul recommend the same startup choice to a new grad today?

Rahul Pandey

It depends, Rahul says, and he treats his own case as the exception. It made sense for him because he already had social proof (Stanford and a Facebook internship). The founder was also, in his view, among the best in the world on recommendation systems and big data, so he could learn from watching that person. With those conditions he would encourage a risky bet.

For the typical new grad, with a decent school and a degree but trouble finding a first job, he recommends the biggest reputable brand available, such as Amazon or Google. He argues that credibility accrues there and sets up whatever comes next, and that the standard path is standard for a reason.

Ryan agrees. In Ryan's view, a big-brand job gives an instant step change in credibility, and one or two years at big tech to build engineering fundamentals while collecting that stamp is one of the highest expected-value moves.

Source: 07:54–10:55 ↗

QWhat was it like to be acquired by Pinterest?

Rahul Pandey

Rahul says he was happy in the end, but the process was chaotic and stressful. The two founders had 20 years or more of experience and were better informed. One day the team was told that Pinterest would acquire the company and interview everyone, with a full round the following Monday, only a couple of days away.

Rahul had been out of interview prep for almost a year, and he stresses that interview prep is a different skill from engineering work. Pinterest took the whole team straight to a final round: five or six interviews in one day. Rahul was borderline and was called back to the San Francisco office for two more interviews, which he says he did well, and then he got the offer.

The stakes were real, he says. A Tech Crunch article announced the deal, and the company was only about eight months old, so nothing had vested; failing would have meant no equity upside. After the on-site he messaged old recruiters at other big-tech companies as a backup, though he still wanted to join Pinterest with the people he knew.

Was the Pinterest interview loop a standard algorithm loop?
Rahul Pandey

Rahul says it was standard: LeetCode-style coding, questions about his startup projects, and one behavioral interview. Ryan notes that failing it would have made for a much weaker story.

Source: 14:06–14:52 ↗
Source: 10:57–14:04 ↗

QHow was Rahul leveled at Pinterest, and how did he choose a team?

Rahul Pandey

Pinterest had just created a leveling system, borrowed from Google and Facebook. Rahul came in at L3, the entry level (L4 is mid-level and L5 senior). He moved away from recommendation systems and data engineering into mobile, which he calls a career reset. It meant a longer ramp-up and, later, a rejected promotion.

Pinterest let new hires choose a team through "base camp," a two-to-three-week version of Facebook's boot camp. Rahul decided against backend work. He wanted to be close to the product and able to build things end to end, including side projects, and liked the idea of an app in the Android store that his Android-using family could try. His startup had no mobile team, so he saw Pinterest as a chance to learn Android professionally with strong people and benefit twice, at work and on the side.

Did Rahul learn what he wanted to learn on the Android team?
Rahul Pandey

Yes, though the first months were rough. A strong staff-level engineer joined a couple of months after Rahul, and the mentorship was a huge pivot. But Rahul says he had not yet learned how to learn. The Android app already had hundreds of thousands of lines of code. He read documentation and code but wrote little of his own, and he links that slow ramp-up to his first failed promotion.

What changed, he says, was being surrounded by good people, especially an L6 engineer from Facebook who started pair programming with him. Being accountable to a team that would judge his work was a fire under him. With mentorship and enough time in the role, it eventually clicked.

Source: 17:41–19:47 ↗
What matters most when picking a team?
Rahul Pandey

Rahul names two things. The first is the people, because what he learns is dominated by who he interacts with. The second is how important the team is to the company. In 2015 Pinterest's big initiative was international growth, and Android dominates outside the US, so he expected the company to put smart people and money behind it. His view is that working adjacent to an area of high growth means seeing some of that growth yourself.

Ryan relates this to the idea that a rising tide lifts all boats. Ryan has seen people go from new grad to director in five years by working on the company's most important problem and delivering, since career growth tends to track impact.

Source: 19:50–21:25 ↗
Source: 14:54–17:39 ↗

QHow did Rahul eventually get promoted after the failed promotion at Pinterest?

Rahul Pandey

Rahul calls it a difficult journey. The first rejection came about a year after he joined. He thinks the feedback was fair: he had done Android professionally for only about nine months and had not shipped much. He tried again six months later and was rejected again, which he found truly demoralizing. He had arrived through an acqui-hire expecting to be among the best engineers, and two rejections for the same promotion were a real setback.

Pinterest had an appeal process, and Rahul worked with his manager to use it. The appeal succeeded. The anonymous committee had read one project in his packet, described as 16 months of work, as a lack of urgency. Rahul says that was not true. His manager clarified and advocated for him. His lesson is to be clear about what a document says, because readers may interpret it differently, and to have promotion and one-on-one documents reviewed by experienced people.

Ryan notes that a long project can instead signal larger scope. Rahul agrees that context decides: align with the manager on the narrative and collect feedback from tech leads, because 16 months can look impressive, or count against you if it was a minor experiment others expect to take three months. His conclusion is not to assume how others will judge you. Software engineering is a social endeavor, so learn your evaluators' view of your growth areas before a review.

What helped Rahul build skills quickly from L3 to L4?
Rahul Pandey

Rahul credits a lesson from the mentor: be willing to work outside the main codebase. Building the Android app and deploying it to a phone sometimes took two to five minutes, so debugging was slow. The mentor showed Rahul how to create a small separate Android app, copy over themes, and iterate in that sandbox with a much faster loop.

Making a new app had seemed like a big, ambiguous task, but it was easy and raised his speed. It also removed his fear of breaking things and copy-pasting code, which helped with side projects. He calls this the biggest mindset shift behind the L3 to L4 promotion. Ryan agrees that a fast iteration loop matters when promotion rests on contributing more code.

Source: 25:30–27:50 ↗
Source: 21:28–25:28 ↗

QWhy did Rahul leave Pinterest for Meta in mid-2017?

Rahul Pandey

Rahul gives three reasons: Meta was a much bigger company with a stronger engineering brand, it paid more, and he did not see a clear path to rapid growth at Pinterest. He wanted to see whether he could get a meaningful bump in level or compensation.

He thinks job hopping works better early in a career than later. As people move up, he says, impact comes mostly through influence. A staff or principal engineer rarely writes enough code to justify the role; they build frameworks, tools and systems that make other developers productive, which takes years of relationships and trust. Early on, showing you can write high-quality production code may be enough to be hired higher.

Ryan's experience matches. Ryan's move from senior to staff was unusually quick because of long relationships on one team, while peers who switched companies quickly had fewer such ties.

Was another prestigious name on the resume the real reason?
Rahul Pandey

Partly, Rahul says. He admits some ego in wanting a brand everyone had heard of, since far more people knew Facebook than Pinterest. But he agrees it was not the main factor: he already had Facebook and other known names on his resume. The main reason was a sense that he could grow his career much faster at Facebook.

Source: 29:34–31:03 ↗
Source: 27:53–29:31 ↗

QWhat cultural and technical differences did Rahul notice between Pinterest and Meta?

Rahul Pandey

Culturally, Rahul found them similar, since Pinterest's culture was shaped by ex-Facebook and ex-Google people. He describes Facebook as the authentic version, "on steroids." At Pinterest, every change needed at least two reviewers, and Herald rules added blocking reviewers automatically. At Facebook one accept was usually enough to land code, which shocked him.

He also found people more direct at Facebook. At Pinterest, he says, a common criticism was that the company was too nice: people avoided hard feedback or prioritization, so projects and people who should not have stayed lingered. At Facebook people more readily said a project made no sense and should be cut, and he perceived a more aggressive performance-improvement-plan culture.

Was learning Meta's custom stack difficult?
Rahul Pandey

On paper the stacks were similar: Android with Java, and no Kotlin yet. Facebook's scale meant many workarounds and a custom build system, Buck, which Rahul found easy. The harder part was that he joined Portal, then called Building 8, a hardware team. Its software was a forked Android with about 30 custom Android apps on a custom operating system, so its build system and tooling differed even from the rest of Facebook. It took him roughly four or five months to understand it.

Ryan explains that Portal is a standalone video-calling device. Rahul adds that the team first used an Android tablet, later flashing custom hardware with their own OS. Building all 30 apps would take three or four hours, so each engineer built only their own app, in Rahul's case the calling app.

Source: 32:34–34:59 ↗
What did the debug tool Rahul built for Portal achieve?
Rahul Pandey

Because the Portal workflow was so unusual, Rahul came to understand how it differed from other engineers' and built a debug tool for people on Portal. He says hundreds of engineers in the Portal org or nearby orgs used it daily or weekly, and estimates it saved hundreds of hours of engineering time each month. Ryan says this sounds like IC6-level impact.

Source: 35:02–35:45 ↗
Source: 30:20–32:32 ↗

QWas Rahul hired at IC5, and did he have to do anything special for that jump?

Rahul Pandey

Rahul was hired at IC5 (senior), so the move from Pinterest was effectively a promotion. He did nothing special, he says; the level was Meta's proposal after interviews in which he felt he had solved nearly every problem.

He also came from a position of strength: a couple of pending offers, a Facebook internship, time at a respectable company, and a hot market for Android developers, all of which made Meta want to give him a compelling offer.

Source: 35:48–36:38 ↗

QWhat work led to the promotion from senior to staff (IC6)?

Rahul Pandey

Rahul worked on Portal. Facebook already had a mature cross-platform video-calling infrastructure inside Messenger. Portal's first step was to fork Messenger and go its own way as an experiment. Once Portal had hundreds of thousands of daily users, the team needed to return to the normal infrastructure, because the Messenger RTC team kept improving it. Rahul's main project was migrating Portal's core infrastructure back to Messenger's, keeping Portal's custom features and adopting the new capabilities RTC offered.

He calls it cross-functional work with a lot of bureaucracy, involving the Messenger team, Portal leadership and product managers. Some people can rely on one big project at staff level, he says, but a portfolio worked well for him. The second project was the debug tool, purely engineering-driven and built for himself and his teammates. Together, he says, the two made a clear promotion case.

Was Rahul intentional about reaching IC6?
Rahul Pandey

Rahul says how the promotion conversation is phrased matters. In his first year at Facebook the goal was to do well. Later, as a manager, he learned that a new hire who immediately asks for help getting promoted is a turn-off. He also felt imposter syndrome from joining at a fairly high level, so he focused on meeting or exceeding IC5 expectations first.

After about a year, with some trust built and good work landed, he had a clear conversation with his manager about growing on the IC ladder. Since he enjoyed talking to and mentoring people, they also discussed management. They agreed, and Rahul thinks it was the right call, that he should climb the IC ladder first and try management later.

Source: 38:14–40:29 ↗
Did Rahul create the scope for the shared-infrastructure project, or was it assigned?
Rahul Pandey

Neither, exactly. Rahul says it was obvious that someone had to do it, and both the RTC team and the Portal team wanted it. The open question was who would be point person. With long tenure, seniority and a relationship with the Messenger RTC team, he was a natural fit, and he says it was clear to everyone that he was one of the best people, perhaps the best, to take it on.

Source: 40:31–41:53 ↗
Source: 36:41–38:11 ↗

QWhy did Rahul move from IC6 to tech lead manager (TLM)?

Rahul Pandey

Rahul says his current company is about helping people, and he sees good managers as people with a real desire to help others grow. As a byproduct, he says, they can have large impact, since managers are usually senior and respected. He also had context and relationships, so the move felt natural: a growing team needed someone to give feedback and keep people on high-impact work, and he had already expressed interest.

What concrete steps should someone take if they want to try management?
Rahul Pandey

Rahul starts with a question: do you enjoy helping and working with people? If you dread one-on-ones, he says, you will struggle, because management is mostly one-on-ones and reacting to pings, so a manager cannot guard their time. He suggests testing this by actually holding one-on-ones and leading meetings now.

His second point is having opinions: about the quality of the team's work, and about how the team and organization should change as priorities shift. He thinks the best managers have a strong point of view and bend the organization toward it. Ryan suggests tech-leadership and direction-setting work is a good simulation, and Rahul agrees: very senior ICs must also articulate and sell clear opinions about what the team should do over the next six months or year. Someone who would rather just execute and write code is not a good fit for management.

Source: 42:34–45:36 ↗
What surprised Rahul about management, and what did he learn about the TLM role?
Rahul Pandey

Rahul found the TLM role tougher and more taxing than expected. Straddling IC and management work meant that at the end of a day he asked what he had actually achieved, since his time went to meetings, one-on-ones and roadmapping.

He thinks TLM is fine as a transitional role while deciding between full-time management and full-time IC, but not sustainable long term. It is unclear whether you are judged on code or on people leadership. He switched teams afterward. Ryan, who also became a TLM, asked many TLMs beforehand and says every one advised against staying long term, because the role makes you a jack of all trades and master of none.

Source: 45:40–48:03 ↗
Source: 41:54–43:17 ↗

QWhy did Rahul leave Meta to start his own company?

Rahul Pandey

Rahul says the idea of starting a company had been in his mind since around 2016; it was a question of when. He lists three reasons it felt right at Meta. The biggest was a co-founder he trusted, enjoyed working with, and whose timeline matched his. Second, he felt he had reached a satisfying level, or in a more negative framing had plateaued, with a harder path to director. Third, pay, promotions and stock growth meant he did not need to work for a few years.

He also had a signal: Android tutorials he had published on YouTube since 2019. He enjoyed teaching and working with developers and wanted to see whether he could build on it.

Where did Rahul find his co-founder?
Rahul Pandey

The co-founder is Alex. They worked together on Portal in 2017, when Alex was on the same team for a few months, and stayed in touch after Alex moved to Instagram. Before COVID they met weekly in person at Facebook. After COVID began they talked almost every other day about ideas to try together.

Source: 49:34–50:15 ↗
Had they built anything before quitting?
Rahul Pandey

Nothing was built. They had committed to each other to work on it for at least six months or a year, and they knew the broad domain, career growth. For roughly six months before quitting they did community building and research, running free webinars on career growth during COVID. Rahul says one drew around 800 people, partly because people wanted social interaction at home. They planned to look for funding or build something after quitting.

Source: 50:17–50:54 ↗
Source: 48:04–49:32 ↗

QIs Y Combinator the best way for a big-tech employee to start a company?

Rahul Pandey

It depends, Rahul says, because "start a company" is as overloaded a term as acquisition. It might mean utility Android apps, small apps earning about 5,000 dollars a month, or a billion-dollar company. For those aiming at the largest outcomes, YC makes sense as a funding vehicle, depending on one's network.

A first-time founder without much of a network should find YC a no-brainer, he says: credibility, money and accountability. A repeat founder, or someone who already knows top-tier VC firms, can argue that YC is not worth it.

Source: 50:55–52:24 ↗

QWhat are the biggest differences between running a startup and working in big tech?

Rahul Pandey

Rahul names structure and accountability first. At a three-person company there is no boss and no deadline, whereas Facebook or Pinterest has a cadence of quarterly releases and launches. The founders try to manufacture urgency. He finds this both empowering and scary, because without urgency a team could spend five years twiddling its thumbs.

The second difference is ambiguity about what to build. Taro began as a developer tool, perhaps for reviewing or writing code. The team found the community angle more powerful, which led to courses and then to a fairly robust course platform. He says big-tech engineers often lack product-management skills such as talking to users, iterating on feedback and reading data, and a tiny company has no data scientist or user researcher next to you.

Source: 52:25–54:30 ↗

QAt what point does it make sense to start a company?

Rahul Pandey

Rahul says it depends on how you define success. In his view, climbing to director or higher at Meta gives an amazing life, in the top 0.1 percent of people in the world. But more control and autonomy plus an outlier outcome, meaning a small chance of a huge result, is hard inside big tech. He doubts Meta will grow five or ten times in value in five years, while admitting he could be wrong.

His rule of thumb is to go for a bigger swing once you have stability: big-tech credibility and finances. The other ingredient is a co-founder you get along with, which he compares to a marriage. Timing is the other trap: some people wait for the dream co-founder who is never on the same timeline, because of bonuses or vesting, children, or marriage. Aligned timelines and commitment on how long to run the startup matter as much as the person.

Ryan adds a friend who left Meta to start a company and said they would regret reaching the end of a standard big-tech career without a story worth telling.

Rahul Pandey

Rahul names three. The first was meeting the mentor at Pinterest: pair programming, learning by osmosis, and discovering he was empowered to change his environment. The second was at Meta, leading the migration and building the debug tool, which was the first time in big tech he felt he created value, from an idea of his own that people chose to adopt. Before that he often felt like a worker bee carrying out work passed down from above. He says this helped give him the confidence to start a company.

The third, less relevant to a big-tech audience, was the two or three months of Y Combinator: weekly group check-ins brought intense pressure, since underperformers were effectively shamed, and he learned a lot.

His main candidate is the 2014 startup. He does not exactly regret it, since he learned a lot and has a good story. But he suspects the choice was somewhat ego-driven: he did not want to be one of many people in big tech and wanted something unique. He doubts he had enough engineering maturity for it and says he floundered a bit at the startup and at first at Pinterest. A more structured environment might have been the better bet.

Otherwise he has few regrets and feels lucky. He says he was rejected from jobs he would have taken, at companies that he says "completely exploded" a year later, and he counts that as luck. QHow much of Rahul's career growth was luck?

Rahul Pandey

Rahul says he feels he has "failed my way into success" and that a lot of it was luck, in the opportunities and people he came across. He adds that luck can be manufactured by being curious about the people and opportunities around you. Finding his co-founder, the 2014 startup and the Facebook opportunities all came from keeping in touch: asking what someone is up to, what they like about a new job, or offering help on a project.

He says the debug tool came from talking to people about their workflows, and many job hops came from knowing what respected people were doing. He sees this as a repeatable process, not luck. He also describes posting on social media as deliberate: people who see helpful content think of you for opportunities.

Ryan notes that some people call this maximizing your luck surface area, and says internal writing and reaching out give the same visibility at a company. Ryan suggests that credibility from such sharing probably helped Rahul get the shared-infrastructure project that led to staff.

How can someone network without it feeling manufactured?
Rahul Pandey

Rahul hesitates to call what he does networking. He points to two ingredients: genuine curiosity about what the other person is doing, and thoughtfulness about what he shares. Rather than only asking questions or for mentorship, he says one of the best ways to build a relationship is to share something he has worked on that may interest the other person.

In his words, showcasing what you are up to creates gravity: people are drawn to you for your opinion, so it becomes a two-way street. If you always ask and it is never reciprocated, the other person may simply not be interested, or you may need to become more interesting.

Ryan recalls that networking felt artificial as a new grad, but side projects such as writing content and building a keyboard make conversations natural.

QWhat advice would Rahul give his college-graduate self?

Rahul Pandey

Rahul wishes he had realized much earlier that there are no gatekeepers: you need no permission to learn a technology or try something new. He cites his own recent projects, such as extensions for a Mac app launcher, as the kind of work he means.

In his view, feeling empowered to do something unique based on what you care about, rather than what peers, instructors or managers expect, is how you get an outlier outcome. He wishes he had cultivated creative interests earlier and set aside time for them deliberately.

Ryan observes that Rahul took more initiative later. Rahul agrees: YouTube tutorials, published Android apps and webinars with 800 people felt like a blindfold lifting. His advice is not to wait until you are ready to start a company, publish an app or teach, but to do it now. He was passive early on, waiting to get better and smarter, and wishes he had adopted that mindset in middle or high school.

Section 72 · interview

Rapid growth, broader learning, and the costs of chasing the next rung

Evan King and Ryan Peterman compare fast staff-engineer paths, showing how initiative and support create growth and why a successful ladder can still leave gaps.

QDid fast career growth require starting programming as a child?

Evan King and Ryan Peterman

Evan encountered computer science in a high-school AP course near Seattle. Classmates with Microsoft-employed parents seemed far ahead of him, and the subject initially threatened his identity as a straight-A student. He worked hard enough to succeed but did not enter college determined to study computer science. In an introductory engineering course, his small head start suddenly made him feel capable relative to beginners. Enjoyment followed that experience of competence.

Ryan had no AP computer-science course and did not know what the field was until UCLA. He entered engineering undeclared, chose electrical engineering because he liked computers and games, and switched to computer science and engineering in his junior year when he understood its employment path better. Overlap in the degree requirements allowed him to reuse earlier coursework. Neither presents his later progression as evidence of childhood programming genius.

Source: 01:23–04:24 ↗

QWhy start a college hacking club, and what did it teach?

Evan King and Ryan Peterman

Evan played Division I soccer at Cornell until his junior year. The training, early workouts, and weekend travel consumed time, yet he knew he intended to become a software engineer rather than a professional player. Quitting created room for building things. After participating in capture-the-flag competitions with teams found online, he recruited locally with flyers, assembled founding officers, and grew a core competition team of roughly 25 people; some weekly teaching sessions attracted as many as 200.

The club combined technical practice, friendships, and teaching. Evan remembers peers who were stronger technically than he was, and he learned by building sophisticated projects with them. Ryan connects organizing, recruiting, communicating, and aligning people with the work of senior engineers. A leadership role can have lasting value beyond improving an application, especially when the activity itself is enjoyable.

What made your own side projects useful?
Evan King and Ryan Peterman

Ryan built a Raspberry Pi service to indicate whether his engineering club’s lab was open. Because an officer had to be present, the service watched the lab Wi-Fi for known officer-device MAC addresses and let students query a Slack bot for current presence. It solved a real problem and gave him a concrete interview story.

They recommend noticing problems nearby and writing software that people actually use. A project chosen from a generic list may still provide practice, but without users it resembles another class assignment and misses the learning involved in taking a useful solution all the way through delivery.

Source: 07:11–09:28 ↗

QDid competitive hacking make the hiring interviews easy?

Evan King and Ryan Peterman

Evan found algorithm interviewing difficult at first and spent many hours practising with classmates. His successful Meta campus interview included a hard problem whose trick he had skimmed the previous evening. He believes that lucky encounter mattered materially: without it, the rest of this career path might never have happened.

Ryan also struggled despite spending most of his Bloomberg internship’s spare time practising. His assigned project took only a small part of the summer, but intensive preparation did not prevent him from failing his later onsite algorithm interviews. He finished with a Bloomberg return offer and an Amazon offer obtained through an unusual campus logic-test format. He chose Amazon partly to remain on the West Coast.

Evan recalls badly misreading a Palantir interview: being released early was described as compatible with either exceptional success or failure, so he waited confidently for an offer and was devastated by rejection. Their comparison of then-prestigious employers—Palantir, Quora, Jane Street, and other finance firms—is a recollection of their college hiring environment, not a current ranking. The larger point is that preparation, expectations, and luck all influence entry opportunities.

Content integrity offered machine-learning problems, a mission he found meaningful, and colleagues he related to. He joined a terrorism-content team being established in Seattle, initially with a manager shared across teams and a part-time technical lead.

Ryan selected Instagram infrastructure with much less understanding of the long-term tradeoffs than he has now. At Zillow, after finishing his rental-team work, he turned posters about locking unattended computers into a playful internal security game. Colleagues could record an unattended machine, and leaderboards and graphs encouraged participation. Spending time with security colleagues eventually led to attending Defcon with them, despite security being outside his team’s charter.

He describes a similar pattern at Meta: completing the requested implementation created time to improve it and explore adjacent ideas. He frames this as pursuing useful, interesting work rather than merely doing extra work for its own sake.

QHow did you finish assigned engineering work fast enough to explore more?

Evan King and Ryan Peterman

Evan initially resists claiming a simple secret, because the reputation for speed feels more grand than his conscious process. Ryan describes deep familiarity with a code area, a practiced editing-and-review workflow, and enough repetitions to know exactly where a requested change belongs. At one coding-heavy period he remembers submitting about ten diffs a day. He also worked very long days and acknowledges that adding working time is one way to create an extra budget for growth.

Evan kept searchable notes whenever he solved a problem so he would not have to solve it from scratch twice. He also became comfortable investigating a blockage for roughly an hour, finding the person who knew the area, asking a focused question, writing down the answer, and continuing. Ryan emphasizes that a well-timed question can save days of blind searching, dwarfing small editor optimizations.

Both highlight code search as a lasting skill. In a large monorepo, someone has usually solved a similar problem already. Guessing likely function or variable names, finding the analogous implementation, and understanding the surrounding context accelerates junior execution and later work on ambiguous cross-system problems.

They distinguish the experience of being absorbed in enjoyable work from forcing long hours on work one hates. Ryan enjoyed the novelty and growing fluency; Evan stresses that advice about extra hours becomes dangerous when detached from that motivation. The time-budget explanation describes their experience, not a claim that everyone should work those hours.

QWhat was the anchor story behind the staff promotion?

Evan King

Evan’s progression took one half year for the first promotion, two halves for senior, and three for staff. During the last stage he led graphic-violence engineering when the Christchurch mosque attack was livestreamed and copies circulated. He describes an emergency response involving integrity leadership and policy colleagues, repeated overnight work, model training, and changes to detection and content-matching systems. He emphasizes the victims and families rather than treating the atrocity as a career opportunity.

The response exposed underinvestment in detecting catastrophic events on live video, which differed from screening existing photos and recordings. The company formed realtime integrity around Evan and a product manager and asked them to determine staffing, scope, and a roadmap. Early progress was slow because the events were rare: training on the handful of known cases risked overfitting, and waiting for another tragedy was an unacceptable way to assess the system.

His golden-set-recall project curated past examples and built an evaluation environment that replayed videos and comments through real production infrastructure while isolating them from users. It tested the complete path rather than only a model. Evan reports that the initial measured recall for the better-represented suicide examples was roughly nine percent.

Looking closely at misses revealed a neglected signal: viewers’ comments often showed they understood the danger before image and audio models did. Adding temporal comment signals raised recall to roughly fifty to fifty-five percent in his recollection, created more detected training examples, and enabled further improvements. He says recall eventually reached the mid-nineties by the time he left, but the staff promotion came earlier, when evaluation and substantial initial improvement had been established. These are his retrospective figures, with some uncertainty in the precise intermediate numbers.

How large did the new team become?
Evan King and Ryan Peterman

At promotion time Evan remembers approximately four or five engineers. Realtime integrity later reached roughly twelve to fourteen before splitting into two teams of eight near his departure. Increased investment followed demonstrated progress and sustained attention from senior leadership; the original project was not assumed successful from day one.

He does not know the exact decision maker. At the time he felt he had advocated strongly for the new team after the incident. His own initiative and leadership mattered, but he deliberately corrects a purely self-created-opportunity version of the story.

QWhich behavior mattered most in the staff story?

Evan King and Ryan Peterman

Evan points to trying the simple, obvious solution and keeping the whole problem in view. His multidisciplinary team crossed infrastructure and modeling boundaries, but technically sophisticated researchers could become absorbed in improving the model itself. With less investment in that particular expertise, he focused on what would move the actual detection number. Comments seemed obvious only after the team had been concentrating on pixels, audio, and complex temporal modeling.

Ryan describes a similar Instagram compute-efficiency project. He explored video-processing efficiency before pandemic usage made capacity critical. After brainstorming with strong engineers, the best improvement was a comparatively trivial removal of redundant work. He values the ratio of useful impact to time, complexity, and maintenance burden: a simple change with a large effect can beat an elaborate year-long project.

They praise the Meta culture they experienced for rewarding realized impact rather than merely implementation difficulty. The practical skill is to identify the important constraint, find what actually improves it, and drive the work even when the solution lacks technical glamour. Their descriptions of reward systems are personal observations of that context.

QWhat did startups teach that your Meta role had not?

Evan King and Ryan Peterman

Leaving humbled Evan. His rapid promotions and broad team leadership had given him confidence, but he discovered large practical gaps. At Meta, he could change a narrow component and rely on an enormous surrounding organization to deploy it to billions of users. In the startup he had to learn these pieces while delivering. He now feels more able to enter an unfamiliar situation and work out what is needed. Ryan mentions a counterview from another engineer: startup setup work can feel technically routine compared with deep specialist problems inside a large company. They therefore distinguish breadth from depth rather than asserting that all startups teach more in every way.

Evan thinks learning broad foundations first could make later specialized optimization more meaningful, while hesitating to recommend that order as the best career strategy. He also wishes he had used his time at Meta to investigate abstractions he consumed every day and read the engineering explanations that were available around him. Evan King

Evan realizes that saying he did not work much at Meta understates informal work. He usually arrived around eight or eight-thirty and left around five-thirty or six, then sometimes checked experiments, made tweaks at home, or woke to see whether a model-training run had completed. It exceeded an ordinary forty-hour week, although he also left early for weekly snowboarding and usually did not treat weekends as compulsory work.

The first startup was much more demanding. He was both learning foundations and supporting a fast-paced realtime analytics product where failures mattered financially to users. Days could run from morning until midnight or two, and he carried a laptop even to a friend’s birthday because an incident might fall to him alone. Hello Interview later became steadier; he still worked more than at Meta but could attend social events without carrying the laptop. The business’s incident profile changed the experience as much as the startup label did.

How does that fit with your advice about work-life balance?
Evan King and Ryan Peterman

Near the end of Meta, Evan had considered two broad ways to live: make work a central source of passion and fulfillment, or do a strong bounded workday that financially supports interests and relationships elsewhere. He thought he might adopt the latter after another promotion. Founding instead returned him to a passionate work-centered period. He admits the apparent contradiction and sees the quieter option as a possibility later rather than claiming he had already achieved it.

Source: 1:47:28–1:49:01 ↗
Source: 1:44:28–1:47:26 ↗

QWhat is your biggest career regret?

Evan King

He wishes he had slowed down to understand why things worked. Iterating until a metric improved or a system functioned could produce immediate impact without building a durable explanation. The same shortcut appeared during early startup pressure: once something worked, he moved on.

As the company stabilized, he could finish required work with time left over and use that margin for reading engineering explanations and investigating underlying libraries and platforms. He sees a tension in an impact-oriented culture: it can reward shipping and moving on even when understanding the abstraction underneath would improve the engineer’s long-term foundation. He would keep the useful drive for impact while adding that inquiry.

Source: 1:48:55–1:52:06 ↗

QWhat would you tell yourself when graduating?

Evan King

Invest in friendships, romantic relationships, and life outside work with some of the deliberateness given to career goals. Evan had roadmaps and frequent checks for professional growth but applied much less effort to broader life. Moving to Los Angeles and making more friends outside the technology bubble helped him value mutual investment and everyday support.

He now finds those relationships a major source of fulfillment alongside continuing work. This is not only an hours-allocation lesson: even when there was time, he had not recognized what deserved deliberate attention.

Would you accept slower promotion in exchange for stronger relationships?
Evan King and Ryan Peterman

Given a strict choice, yes: he would prioritize relationships. But he rejects the premise that he actually had to choose. He believes he had enough time to build both and simply did not invest enough in relationships or understand their importance yet.

Source: 1:53:12–1:54:37 ↗
Source: 1:51:43–1:54:37 ↗

A final nuance about interview preparation

During the closing promotion, Ryan mentions a roommate who was initially overconfident in system-design interviewing because he already designed systems at work. The useful lesson is that an interview is a particular format that may require targeted practice; professional seniority alone does not ensure performance. The service endorsement itself is omitted.

Source: 1:56:16–1:57:10 ↗

Section 73 · interview

Retired Engineering Director: Netflix Culture, Hiring, Meta Leadership, and Work-Life Balance

A retired engineering director who worked at Netflix and Facebook recounts how Netflix culture scaled, how he hired engineers, what he learned leading at Meta, and why a 2004 illness changed his view of work.

David's view: judgment, trust, and balance matter more than heroics and long hours

The host introduces David as a retired engineering director who worked at both Netflix and Facebook, and the conversation follows his 36-year career. In David's view, strong engineering organizations depend on three things: colleagues who are good to work with, a fair and objective way to record who did what, and a pace that leaves people a life outside work. He argues that engineering judgment matters more than LeetCode speed, that a new leader must earn trust before changing a team that already works, and that a serious illness in 2004 turned him against 24/7 work culture. Everything below is David's opinion or recollection from an auto-generated transcript, and several names and figures are unverified.

Source: 00:40–1:17:19 ↗

QHow did Netflix differ from the other companies David had worked at?

David

David says every earlier employer, from IBM through several smaller companies, tolerated prima donnas: very smart people who were hard to work with, who yelled at colleagues and customers, and who could not admit mistakes. He describes one 1990s engineer treated as indispensable, with a cubicle packed with junk, who avoided other people and fixed problems overnight while managers did not understand his work. When he quit, the company survived, and the rest of the team came to understand the area he had guarded.

At Netflix, David says, nobody was like that. The culture deck said the company did not hire brilliant jerks and would let go anyone difficult or unapproachable, however smart. David calls this revolutionary in the early 2000s and notes that the large tech companies he knows now work the same way.

His interview with Patty McCord, then chief people officer, who approved every hire at that small company, surprised him. David says she told him Netflix did not value 24/7 work and that he should impress the company with what he could do in an eight-hour day. David later watched a manager say he could not keep working around the clock. McCord thanked the manager, then told him not to do it again and to set up his team so that he did not have to. David calls that unthinkable in 2008 or 2009 and says he learned more about leading and collaborating from McCord than, he thinks, even from Reed Hastings.

David gives his own example. During early, unstable attempts at continuous deployment, a strong engineer remarked that David must enjoy having weekends off, because the systems would fail if the team stopped working. David told him in a one-on-one to take a vacation and said he did not care if things broke. The engineer took a week off, others rested too, and David says the team then stabilised the system quickly with its own approach.

David ends with Hastings. According to David, Hastings saw DVDs by mail as a stepping stone to streaming, which is why the company is not called DVDsbymail.com. Hastings was not a video expert but built a team of strong leaders and engineers to solve the problem.

Source: 00:40–07:59 ↗

QHow did the Netflix culture change as the company grew?

David

David first says the culture memo is aspirational. When people asked whether Netflix really worked that way, he answered that it described what the company aspired to be.

He then describes what failed to scale. Netflix credited the team, not individuals. When the company shipped on the PlayStation 3, David says, Sony's DVD division asked Netflix to stop because it had not designed the console for this, and Netflix carried on. Afterwards nobody named the foundational engineers; the credit went to Netflix. That worked when the company was small. As it took on many products, individual contributions got lost, and if engineers are not credited, he says, leaders collect the credit.

Netflix also had no engineering levels. Everyone was an engineer or a senior software engineer, and a business card could carry any title except manager, director, VP or chief. That suited an all-senior team. As it hired more juniors, David argues, teams contain strong, good and weak engineers, and without an objective way to tell them apart and reward wins, the best people leave. By the late 2010s he was arguing for levels. He assumes they have since been added, but he has been away for six years.

David adds that McCord interviewed almost every early hire and Hastings met a few new hires at a time, which could not continue as the company grew. When he left, he felt the memo suited a very small, aggressive, engineering-focused company.

What is the culture memo?
David

David describes a deck of roughly 15 slides, released around 2007 or 2008 by his recollection. Its ideas included no brilliant jerks, very smart people, inspiring people to sail the seas rather than telling them how to build a ship, top-of-market pay, and a "keeper test" under which the company fires aggressively. David calls it revolutionary at the time. In his reading it was about freedom and responsibility: hire excellent people, explain why the work matters, give context, and trust them to execute without micromanagement.

He adds that the talent was not limited to engineers. His HR partners challenged his hire and no-hire decisions, and he says he learned how to build a team from them.

Source: 08:28–10:17 ↗
If everyone was at the same level, how did Netflix pay people differently?
David

David says Netflix generally did not hire new graduates, though he found ways around that. Pay followed a concept of personal top of market, and the memo encouraged people to interview elsewhere. His own starting salary in 2007 was $175,000, which he calls solid for then. If Google had offered him $200,000 a year later, he says, his manager would have had to match it or let him go. Leaders therefore had to track offers and market rates.

David says this became unsustainable. An engineer matched to a double-pay offer could, three years later, earn three times as much as a peer doing similar work, with no performance review or context to explain the gap. In another case, five candidates Netflix had made offers to each received Facebook offers about 1.2 times higher, the memo said to match, and without leveling nobody could justify it. He argued with his leadership using year-over-year spreadsheets and believes Netflix fixed this after he left, since a large company needs pay ranges.

Source: 14:32–18:53 ↗
Source: 08:01–14:31 ↗

QHow does David identify really strong software engineers in hiring?

David

David says his hiring succeeded all the way up to Meta. Large companies such as Meta, Google, Amazon and Microsoft need structure and consistent standards, so they use a formal interview system. At smaller companies, when he made the hire or no-hire decision himself, he, three team members and HR interviewed each candidate.

He tells of a late-1990s candidate who had built driverless-train software. David was the last interviewer, and his 45-minute slot ran to 90 minutes, with two whiteboards covered in state transitions. He says her grasp of a complex system of interacting parts was among the best he had seen. Others gave her coding questions and she did fine, but the panel was lukewarm and his boss pushed back. David argued that the team was struggling to integrate disparate systems and needed her. They hired her, and he says she excelled. He claims his hiring record at small companies was close to perfect.

David knows his next view is controversial: he does not love LeetCode. He says it shows how fast someone can write code for a problem practiced many times. He accepts that at the volume Meta and Google hire, they have little alternative.

His alternative is an engineering foundation: understanding complex systems, strong technical intuition, and sound decisions without enough data. He has seen engineers from other fields do very well in software. He has also seen people who aced LeetCode and rehearsed system-design questions such as Google type-ahead get hired and then produce poor engineering, which he saw in their review packets. He believes this foundation is largely innate, like musical talent, and says he can help someone improve their software but cannot teach them to make good decisions.

His second story is about a project partner in graduate classes at San Jose State, taken in his 50s just before he joined Meta. She was finishing a master's in civil engineering, worked in wastewater treatment, and wanted to move into software. David was impressed by her analytical mind and command of statistics and wanted Netflix to hire her. Her take-home video-software task took three weeks and had rookie mistakes, so to help close the deal David suggested she teach the team something. She spent two hours at a whiteboard on wastewater treatment, and halfway through David realized he was watching a very complex state machine. A manager asked what sewage had to do with software but hired her, and later told David at a Meta event that she was doing very well. David says that when you see a brilliant engineering mind, LeetCode speed or building a scalable type-ahead does not matter, because those can be learned quickly.

David accepts that this approach does not scale at Meta or Google, where legal and policy problems would break it, so they set a bar and a level. His level advice is to take a lower offer: someone who was a 6 elsewhere and is offered a 5 at Meta should accept it and execute at the higher level, because bonuses, multipliers and refresh stock follow. An over-leveled hire who struggles has no clean fix. His rule is that when in doubt, go low and earn the quick promotion.

How do you spot that fundamental engineering skill? Is there a question you ask?
David

David says to interview the person, not the process. The wastewater candidate showed mastery of a hard engineering problem and explained it to engineers who knew nothing about it, until those who understood saw a finite state machine. He argues that many engineering systems, such as engines and other mechanical systems, reduce to states and transitions, though structural engineering differs.

Netflix would have hired her at a junior level, such as data analyst. As a full software engineer against the usual expectations she would have failed. A smaller company, he says, is flexible enough to hire and build up such a person.

Source: 29:16–30:51 ↗
Source: 18:55–29:15 ↗

QWho was the strongest engineer David worked with, and what made that person strong?

David

David names Giannis, though he usually avoids names. The captions garble the surname, so it is omitted here. They met in 2000 at InterVideo. Giannis had left the industry to teach signal processing in Greece, and in summer 2010 David brought him in during a break to help with ideas about parallel encoding. David says that work led to content-based encoding, which the whole industry now uses, and to an early patent.

Giannis later joined Netflix and, David says, took the idea further, in what the captions render as "convex all encoding", probably convex hull. David says it delivers the highest quality for a given bandwidth and is now the model at both Netflix and Meta. Giannis also built a cost-benefit model for codec evaluation. David sees his strength as forcing academic rigor into practice: decisions rest on tests across 10,000, a million or a billion videos, not on what two compressed videos suggest in theory.

Source: 30:52–32:59 ↗

QHow did David come to be recruited to Meta?

David

David says the early Netflix culture deck advised interviewing often to learn your market value. When Facebook contacted him in late 2017, as he recalls, he had not interviewed in about ten years. He went in, in his own words, a bit full of himself, citing how Netflix had built the highest-scale encoding platform. One interviewer told him Facebook could not solve its video scale problem with CPUs. David was floored, later thanked him, and realized he had understood video too narrowly. He got an offer and turned it down because he was not ready.

Soon after, Giannis told David about a Facebook offer and the custom chip (ASIC) work he would do. David saw a passion in him that he had not seen for a while. He thinks Netflix's culture, not built around individual contributions, may not have rewarded Giannis, and that the problems may not have seemed big enough to him. David says he did not try to talk Giannis out of it: as his boss he did not want to lose him, but as his friend he could not argue against it. David had been interviewing mainly to exercise his interview skills, but in the end he came to see Facebook's video work as a very hard problem. His team was solid and a successor was ready, so in 2019 he left Netflix, and Facebook offered him a job quickly.

At Netflix his encoding team had grown from one person to about 55, and trust grew with it. At Meta he took over a video processing team of 55 to 60 who did not know him. In an early meeting he talked about what needed work. A team member told him in a one-on-one that he had been there two weeks and was already telling the team what to do. David concluded he needed to stop talking and build trust, a skill he had never had to develop.

His lesson is that leadership is about relationships. If a team is broken, the leader's job is to fix it. If it is already executing well, the job is first not to break it and second to help it move forward, and he had jumped to the second step. David calls the saddest thing about Meta that it was his last job. He believes he would now be a much better organizational and engineering leader but no longer wants that responsibility, and he says he learned the most about engineering leadership there.

Concretely, what does building trust look like for a senior leader joining an existing team?
David

David says it meant slowing down and spending a lot of time in one-on-ones, asking questions, taking notes, and learning the system, the roles and the people. In a technical role, he says, a leader must understand why the team does what it does.

His first decision came when the team needed a manager. Many told him to promote an existing manager, but he did not know them and refused to decide just because it looked politically right. After taking time with them, he concluded an existing manager was the right choice. That manager had felt the role was his, so the relationship was difficult at first. David told him he was sorry for the delay but had needed to understand first, and that he was now confident in him. By the time the manager left Meta, David says, he no longer assumed the worst.

Looking back, David thinks his investment was still too small. He would tell his boss that for the first six months he was in school and that critical decisions would be made together.

Source: 41:30–45:24 ↗
Source: 33:02–41:28 ↗

QWhat was David's favorite work or project at Meta?

David

David first names bringing Netflix-level quality to Meta's scale, which he says succeeded. He then turns to COVID. He joined in late July 2019, and by March 2020 everyone was working from home. Meta planned for New Year's Eve from the summer because video traffic spiked for 24 hours. By April 2020, David says, every day looked like New Year's Eve in uploads, streams and live video. Systems that had never run at that sustained load were slowly bleeding out, with race conditions among the problems. He says the prime minister of India was addressing the country on Facebook Live, and he was terrified by the weight of it. The team worked from home, found the problems and resolved the race conditions. After about a month the systems and metrics held, and David says he was proud of that.

He also describes how his view of the company's value changed. He had first seen Facebook through a US-centric lens as a social app. He came to see what 3.5 billion customers means. By David's rough comparison, Netflix's roughly 300 million subscribers are the wealthiest 5 percent of the world by income, while Meta reaches the wealthiest 50 percent. He calls wealthy a loaded term, since at the bottom people live on about $68 a day. He says Instagram, WhatsApp and Facebook are a lifeblood for small shops across India, and an Uber driver from Somalia in Seattle told him WhatsApp kept his scattered family in touch.

David says US debate about social media focuses on harms such as fake news and overlooks how much the products improve lives elsewhere. He believes the company changed lives by giving people a business, a platform to share and earn from video, and a way to stay close to family, and that it feels good to be part of that in a small way.

Source: 45:26–50:51 ↗

QHow did work-life balance change across David's career?

David

David says that in the late 1990s he worked hard for a visionary executive because the team was trying to catch up, not because anyone demanded it. At InterVideo, a startup, the expectation was 24/7. He arrived around 10:30 in the morning and left around 10 at night, sometimes at 2 or 3 in the morning, often seven days a week, chasing deals to lift the stock price after the IPO.

In January 2004 he fell ill on a Sunday and kept getting worse. On the Friday his wife took him to the emergency room, where, he says, a doctor said it was colon cancer, with a blockage that could kill quickly. He was in hospital for about three weeks with two surgeries and chemotherapy. It was stage three with lymph node spread, and he puts his five-year survival prognosis at about 25 percent. His children were two, four and seven, and he says the youngest barely knew him.

In hospital he decided that his way of working was wrong. He told his boss he still wanted the job but could not work that way, and he says that if a company threatens to fire you for not being there late, the best thing you can do is leave. He believes InterVideo used hours to cover for poor leadership. He calls work-life balance something thrust upon him, and he was determined never to be a leader who expects people to kill themselves for a job. Hearing at Netflix that the company did not value 24/7 work was a shock.

His advice is not to wait for cancer or a heart attack. Bake balance in early, take vacation, and leave the company alone for a week. If it cannot survive seven days without you, David says, that is its problem.

David says high-performance companies such as Meta and Netflix are often misunderstood. He recalls a Meta poster of a rocking horse that read, in effect, do not mistake motion for progress. He suggests agreeing with your boss on the most important work and telling the boss which tasks you will not do; if one matters, someone else must do it or priorities must change. Crunch time will come at big tech companies, but it should be the exception, planned in advance, such as a push in May and June followed by a vacation. He says balance is achievable even at Netflix or Meta, if the manager gives clear context.

Source: 50:52–59:03 ↗

QWhich job taught David the most, and why?

David

David says his last four jobs each contributed. The first turned him into a high-performance software engineer, performing by problems solved, not hours worked. The second gave him a video foundation. Netflix, he says, was zero to one, and there he learned leadership, hiring and firing, context setting and cross-functional work, which he brought to Meta.

What he lacked on arrival at Meta was an objective process for planning, reviews and performance. He calls the PSC performance cycle both his most dreaded and his favorite time of year. In his account, everyone writes a self-review, the manager builds a packet with feedback tied to goals, and managers then defend their engineers in calibration meetings. Each manager thinks their team is the best, David says, so the aim is to persuade with data about who deserves what level and who did what on a project. He valued getting each engineer's impact on paper. He says departing employees keep every performance package they were ever given.

David had heard horror stories about the performance cycle but found it mattered once inside. His greatest joy, he says, was giving a direct report a top rating, and he also valued helping people who were below expectations recover. He adds that he used to think he understood scale from books on sharding and microservices, but in his view those authors do not know scale at Meta's level. The most valuable thing he would bring to a new job is a system for objective planning, review and performance.

Source: 59:04–1:04:07 ↗

QIs there a top book that influenced David's career?

David

David chooses a late-1990s book he names as 12 Secrets to Microsoft Success; the title comes from auto-generated captions and was not checked. He says it described radical thinking at Microsoft. One idea was betting the company, which he says he saw at Netflix, Amazon and Meta when a big opportunity is worth risking the company on without going all-in. Another was good failure: in a healthy company, projects and people will fail, and what counts is how you fail, what you learn and whether the bet was reasonable and managed early.

As he recalls the book, Microsoft was the first company to say publicly that it aimed to hire the top 5 percent of software engineers, and it coined the term dogfooding. When the NT server was failing badly in the mid-1990s, he says, Bill Gates made the whole company move to it, which put the bugs in front of everyone and got them fixed. After rapid growth Gates also imposed a company-wide hiring freeze because people were working on things that did not matter, such as Microsoft Bob. Executives were forced to kill projects, and David says the bottom 20 percent were cut, which he thinks should have happened anyway.

David says Microsoft set early models for modern engineering leadership, and others borrowed from it. Before the 2022 crash he thought the hiring rate did not add up. During COVID everyone accelerated hiring and nobody slowed. He believes that had big-tech leaders read the book, they would have seen in late 2021 that hiring was out of control.

Source: 1:04:09–1:09:49 ↗

QIs there anything David regrets that others could learn from?

David

David says his first six years out of school were wasted at very large failing companies. He names Hughes, spun off from General Motors, and an IBM division sold to Siemens, both of which failed. He had a good salary and an easy job, thought only about the moment, and did not think about growth. He does not mean being ambitious about a vice-president title in ten years, just thinking about growth.

For software engineers in particular, he says, everything learned will be obsolete in about five years. When he joined Meta, the bootcamp and the whole development environment had been replaced; he had been proficient as a director, but when he later went to an individual-contributor role he found everything had changed. His way of staying successful, David says, is to keep pushing toward the edge and keep learning new engineering skills.

Source: 1:09:52–1:11:37 ↗

QWhat advice would David give himself at the start of his career?

David

First, work on hard problems. David says that if the job is not difficult, you are not growing. Once a role flatlines, he says, an engineer at a company like Meta, where moving internally is easy, should find another hard problem. Hard problems are what move engineers forward.

Second, company size does not matter, but everyone should work at a small company or startup at some point, ideally while young. He cautions against being too taken with the technology and says to work for visionary leaders who can also execute, since vision without execution goes nowhere. He cites Zuckerberg and Hastings as visionary, and says Hastings was one in 1999, when Netflix had four people. Leaders should make you dream of sailing the seas, not just cut lumber for a ship.

Third, plan for work-life balance deliberately from the first job. Work and life are in tension, he says, but the best engineering comes from people who love the work and also enjoy time off.

Fourth, start financial planning on day one, because as technical people succeed they earn more and, without a plan, will not know where it goes. David recommends a deliberate plan for spending and for short- and long-term savings, small regular contributions in your 20s, and no extended credit or debt. He says that by the early 40s this will not usually allow retirement unless you were lucky, as with an early job at Facebook or Netflix, but it can give financial independence, so you could take a lower-paying job. In his view a 401(k) alone and Social Security will not be enough for those who start late. He knows many engineers in their 50s who earned well but have no plan, and says a good engineer employed for 30 to 35 years has no reason not to retire comfortably. He says elsewhere that he is not a financial planner, so this is one person's opinion.

Source: 1:11:39–1:17:19 ↗
