Section 74 · panel

Ryan and Ricky: Internships, Promotions, and Big Tech vs Startups

Ryan and Ricky argue that visible work, frequent questions, and clear writing shape early careers as much as coding skill, and they compare big tech with startups.

The speakers' view: visible work, questions, and writing shape early careers

Ryan and Ricky, who both studied at UCLA, share what they wish they had known before graduating. Ryan manages interns at Meta, and Ricky works on ads at Google. Their central view is that early career progress depends on visible impact, frequent questions, and clear writing, more than on coding skill or luck alone. They also explain engineering levels, how interns are judged, how to earn a promotion, and how to weigh big tech against startups. The talk then covers money, job changes, and AI's effect on entry-level work. These are the speakers' own views and experience, not general rules.

Source: 00:01–47:56 ↗

QWhat do the engineering levels mean, from junior to staff?

Ricky

Ricky explains that junior engineers write and ship code with a fair amount of help. Mid-level engineers work more independently but still need help at times. Senior is often a stopping point, with few people expected to go further. Staff engineers set a team's direction and lead engineers at other levels. Ricky estimates that moving from junior to mid-level takes about two to four years, and mid-level to senior a similar time.

Ricky says some companies use an up-or-out policy, where people who do not reach the next level leave, and that Google is less aggressive about this. Ricky estimates, without exact data, that 90 percent or more of people reach these levels. The speakers say the levels site is fairly accurate, except that equity pay moves with the stock price.

Source: 01:41–05:45 ↗

QHow do interns succeed, and how are they judged?

The speakers say interns are judged on three things. The first is productivity: how much of the assigned project they finish, ideally in half the internship. The second is quality, shown by fewer rounds of code review by the end. The third is communication, including proposing improvements or a new project after finishing the first one. A strong intern does all three.

What was Ricky's own internship like?
Ricky

Ricky's junior-year internship at Google produced only about 800 lines of code, which felt low. Halfway through, Ricky had about 300 lines, while a UCLA friend on the same program had about 11,000. Ricky spent much of the time learning the codebase and wrote a detailed design doc comparing several approaches. That work showed productivity, and Ricky received a return offer.

Source: 07:29–09:47 ↗
Source: 05:47–07:27 ↗

QHow did you get promoted so quickly to staff engineer in your 20s?

Ricky

Ricky says each level expects a different kind of work. Many projects at the current level do not earn the next promotion. One project at the next level, which clearly shows readiness, counts for more. Managers often describe these expectations as behaviors. Ricky and Ryan focused on projects that would move them up, not on busy work that would not.

Ricky also says that, after each promotion, Ricky asked the manager what the next level required and then took on that kind of work. The manager explained which skills to build, and Ricky credits this for the fast promotions.

Source: 09:50–11:20 ↗

QIs career success mostly luck?

Ryan

Ryan says luck is a big part of it, but people can raise their own luck through initiative. After about eight months at Amazon, Ryan felt stuck and could not see the path to the next level. Ryan applied to many companies and received offers from every company interviewed with except one. That led to Meta.

Is luck mostly opportunity, or can preparation change the outcome?

Ryan adds that grinding LeetCode problems and applying widely raised the odds, and that personal agency matters. Ricky frames luck as two parts: the opportunity itself, and being prepared when it comes. Without preparation, a good chance can pass by. Ricky adds that Ryan's move away from Amazon created more opportunities.

Source: 12:26–13:08 ↗
Source: 11:22–12:24 ↗

QWhat one piece of advice would the speakers give?

Ricky

Ricky says the main advice is to ask a lot of questions, at work and during an internship. Ricky once told a mentee to keep asking, and at the end of the internship the mentee said Ricky had not really meant it. Ricky says the biggest difference between people who succeed quickly and those who do not is how fast they start asking questions, learning, and unblocking themselves. Fear of looking foolish holds many people back.

What separates strong interns from weak ones?
Ryan

Ryan has had five interns at Meta. The strong ones had the nerve to propose improvements and ask questions, even though Ryan was the senior person. Some suggestions were wrong, but many were right. The weaker interns were quieter, and Ryan could not tell how they were progressing. Time passed with little progress, and such interns often did not get return offers.

Source: 15:24–16:11 ↗
Source: 13:09–15:22 ↗

QAre the best engineers the smartest students in the class?

The speakers say no. Strong engineers need solid technical skill and soft skills, such as persuading and influencing others. Work is a large group project, and disagreements are common. Telling a colleague that their idea is bad does not win them over. Naming the other person's frustration, acknowledging their view, and proposing a middle ground makes it more likely that the work ships. The speakers say these skills matter about as much as coding.

Source: 16:13–17:49 ↗

QHow much of the job is actually code?

One speaker says code is a smaller part of the job than new graduates expect. Writing is a large part of it. A design doc comes before the code, a change needs a written description, and a finished project needs a write-up of its results. The speaker says this writing is how a person influences others, so people skills often decide how far an engineer goes.

Source: 17:52–19:30 ↗

QDo experienced engineers still get imposter syndrome?

Ricky

Ricky says imposter syndrome is very common, and that most people feel it. Ricky felt it on joining Google, after passing the interviews and the internship, and found the other engineers very strong. Even after promotions, Ricky wondered whether the company had made a mistake. Ricky copes by learning as much as possible and doing the best job possible, on the view that even being fired would leave something learned. Ricky says the feeling still returns in waves.

Did praise at work reduce the stress?
Ricky

Ricky describes being an anxious person who was always stressed about work. A manager once told Ricky to calm down. Ricky was not sure whether the praise meant a passing grade or a strong one. Talking through expectations with the manager helped, and the stress eased somewhat.

Source: 21:02–21:48 ↗
Source: 19:32–21:01 ↗

QHow do you advocate for yourself at work?

Ryan

Ryan says good work is required but not enough, because people decide promotions and they must know about the work. The last few percent of effort is to tell people about it. That can mean writing about a result, presenting it in a meeting, or telling a manager that a milestone is done early and the next task is ready. Ryan says a clear post about strong results makes a return offer hard to refuse. Ryan says this step is often skipped, especially by introverted people.

Is visibility a separate skill from doing the work?
Ricky

Ricky says visibility can come from a manager, a product manager, or teammates, as well as from the person's own writing. Ricky compares unseen work to a tree falling in a forest that nobody sees, and says people cannot promote work they do not know about.

Source: 23:41–24:21 ↗
Source: 21:50–23:10 ↗

QShould new graduates choose big tech or a startup?

Ryan

The room was polled first. Most audience members chose big tech. Those who chose startups cited first-mover upside and a larger share of impact at a smaller company. Ryan says big tech brings brand value, so a resume from a known company is an easier hire. Ryan describes Amazon as the lowest tier of the big companies at the time, yet recruiter messages arrived in large numbers after joining it.

Ryan frames the choice as a trade-off between high expected value and high variance. Big tech usually gives a better average outcome on a steady path, but rarely produces very large wealth. A startup can boom or fail. Someone who joins early and the company grows can rise quickly, which big tech rarely allows.

Why did Ricky choose big tech over startup offers?
Ricky

Ricky had offers from both startups and big tech, and chose big tech for work-life balance. Ricky's startup friends work very hard, and the results have varied. Ricky says big tech teaches established practices with less variance, while a startup's role can change a lot. Ricky recommends big tech, at least for the first few years, to build prestige and a base.

Source: 28:06–30:37 ↗
Source: 24:22–28:03 ↗

QHow do managers measure impact?

The speakers define impact as the concrete, measurable results of the work, such as revenue, cost, speed, or user growth. The measure depends on the team. On an ads team it may be money. On infrastructure it may be the cost or latency of a database. On a growth team it may be daily active users or sign-ups at key steps. Engineers should learn the measure from their team and manager, because that is how their work is rewarded.

The speakers also say one small change that improves a key number can matter more than ten thousand lines of typo fixes. Their example is a one-line change that gives a 20 percent gain on something that matters.

Source: 30:40–32:25 ↗

QDo you need an MBA for engineering management?

Ryan says no, and Ryan is a manager without one. Ryan describes a graph from a company that gathers LinkedIn data, covering a few thousand directors and above. Pay with and without an MBA looked comparable, and pay without one was slightly lower. Ryan describes this as research done with a company, not a published study.

Did family expectations about an MBA affect Ricky?
Ricky

Ricky's mother believed Ricky would not succeed without an MBA, and pushed for a top school. She has become more relaxed since Ricky reached staff engineer, and now reads about careers and thinks the path is good.

Source: 33:20–34:12 ↗
Source: 32:27–33:18 ↗

QWhat was college recruiting like?

Ricky

Ricky says it was hard. Ricky describes a 15-minute coding challenge from Yelp, written in C++ on the merge step of a merge sort. The code looked right, but it kept crashing with a segmentation fault that Ricky could not explain, and Ricky was rejected. Ricky emailed the recruiter, insisted the code was correct, and asked for an engineer to check it. The engineer said the code looked correct. Ricky got another challenge, passed it, and reached the interview round. Ricky's lesson is that it is worth pushing back and advocating for yourself during recruiting.

Source: 34:15–35:08 ↗

QIs the first job the hardest to land?

Ryan says yes. The first role is the hardest, new grads have to be scrappy, and later offers get easier. Taking less desirable companies can build experience. Ricky says Ricky's first role was at a little-known company that Ricky no longer lists on the resume, but it made the next application look stronger and opened the door to better companies.

Source: 35:10–36:00 ↗

QHow do you make as much money as possible?

Ryan says it depends on the goal. For very large wealth, the usual path is a few years in big tech, then a company of one's own, or an early join at a company that grows fast. Ryan says that for a good life, with money for the things you want and for vacations, big tech and good work are enough.

Ricky says reaching that level of wealth would take the two speakers decades of promotions, plus a rising market. Ricky says that, for a good life, big tech and a solid job are enough. Ricky had no real idea about money in college.

Source: 36:01–38:33 ↗

QIs work the most important part of life?

Ricky

Ricky says work is not everything. Looking back at their 20s, Ricky's happiest memories were time with friends and trips, not working or getting promoted. Ricky says people should work hard and also build a life beyond work. Someone whose whole identity is their job can struggle after a layoff, while a person with other interests can handle it more easily.

Can work-life balance be framed as diminishing returns?

One speaker describes diminishing returns: each extra effort in one area gives smaller gains, so a person who wants the most out of life should look for areas where returns are still growing. The speaker says this favors spreading effort across several parts of life.

Source: 39:25–40:16 ↗
Source: 38:36–39:22 ↗

QWhat are your goals now, and did you push for promotion?

Ricky

Ricky says Ricky was not very career-driven at first. Ricky and Ryan were roommates and still are. Ryan would ask whether they could aim for promotion faster than the usual timeline. Ricky had seen data on how long each level took, and Ryan's push made Ricky test whether a faster path was possible.

Ricky says Ricky put in the effort, was promoted faster than average, and did not give up other interests to do it.

Source: 40:18–41:49 ↗

QShould people change jobs every two or three years for pay or promotion?

Ricky says the answer depends on the case. Ricky has stayed on the same team under the same manager at Google, while still looking at other teams. Ricky notes survivorship bias, because people who left may have had a worse time. Ricky suggests asking every six months whether you still want to be there, whether the opportunities still fit, and whether the team and manager support you.

Ryan says the common advice to job hop for promotion is more nuanced. Early in a career, job hopping can be the fastest route, because momentum matters less than reaching the next level. At senior levels it can backfire. Ryan says companies usually do not hire outside candidates straight into E7 or L7, and promotion there depends on credibility and a track record that frequent moves do not build. Ryan's advice is to job hop aggressively early and to be more deliberate later.

Can leaving a company help someone come back at a higher level?
Ryan

Ryan says this is rare. Ryan has seen a person leave a company, join a startup, and come back to Meta at a higher level. Ryan says a person who leaves a clear ladder is harder to place, so a return can leave room for a higher offer, but few cases work this way.

Source: 45:15–46:05 ↗
Source: 41:52–45:13 ↗

QWill AI reduce entry-level software engineering jobs?

The speakers say it is hard to predict five to ten years ahead. In the short term, they expect AI to change things less than many fear. They note that engineers already use many non-AI tools that write code, and that this did not scare anyone. They see AI as a tool that empowers engineers. Their advice is not to change majors only because of job fears.

What might entry-level work look like in five to ten years?

One speaker says entry-level engineers may write less code, because AI will do more of it. They will still need to tell the AI what to build and check that the result is correct. The speaker expects AI to remain a tool, and people will still be needed to build it.

Section 75 · interview

Ryan Olsen: Instagram Stories, Fast Promotions, and Small Teams

Ryan Olsen traces a path from a failed Facebook interview to leading iOS on Instagram Stories, rapid promotions, a tech lead director role and a startup, arguing for small teams, strong designers and building for people.

Olsen's view: go small, build for people, and bet on yourself

Ryan Olsen, a former Instagram principal engineer (IC8) who now co-founded the company behind the social app Retro, argues from his own career that small teams with full ownership move fastest, that product engineers multiply their impact by pairing with a strong designer and building their own ideas, and that promotions are an incentive system rather than a pure measure of output. The host walks him through a failed Facebook interview, a Flipboard internship, the White Out redesign, Instagram Stories, IGTV, IG Labs, a stint as tech lead director, and the move to a startup. Editorial note: every claim below is Olsen's recollection or opinion, and the captions are auto-generated, so some names are normalized.

Source: 00:48–1:33:10 ↗

QIn 2011 Olsen interviewed at Facebook and failed. What was that experience like?

Ryan Olsen

Olsen says he badly wanted Facebook and was extremely nervous. The interviewer turned a laptop toward him to code on, and Olsen says his hands shook so hard the keys audibly rattled, which started a feedback loop of pounding heart and worsening nerves.

The question was an "engram buckets" problem, as the captions render it, with a simple dictionary-based solution. The solution did not come to him and he wrote a horrendous triple-nested loop. The interviewer cut the session short and said he would not make it at Facebook, which Olsen calls a knife to the heart. He says he would never end an interview early as an interviewer. He adds that the question was later banned at Facebook.

Olsen was down for a while, then bounced back, had a good career at Facebook, and feels he proved the interviewer wrong. He never learned the interviewer's name.

The host says this shows how broken the interview process is, since a high performer failed it. Does Olsen agree?
Ryan Olsen

Olsen says he has always struggled with LeetCode-style interviews and wanted to change them at Facebook, but the process there is a machine spread across a big company. He enjoys that at his own company he does not have to do things he disagrees with.

Source: 02:50–03:38 ↗
Source: 00:48–02:48 ↗

QAfter the failed Facebook interview, how did Olsen end up as an intern at Flipboard, and what was that like?

Ryan Olsen

A couple of months later Olsen interviewed with Amazon by phone, felt far more comfortable, and received an exploding offer: a call on Friday, an answer due Monday. He was prepared to accept, but an investor friend who had offered to connect him with startups told him not to take it yet. That Sunday the friend emailed an introduction to a Flipboard co-founder named Evan.

Olsen did not want another interview call but is glad he answered. By his account, Evan had worked at Apple on the core of iOS, wrote the UIViewController class, and taught the Stanford course CS 193P, which was on iTunes and was how Olsen learned iOS. Flipboard suddenly looked more interesting than Amazon.

That summer Flipboard had about 50 people and roughly four interns. Olsen describes an extremely high density of talent, including people who had written iOS frameworks at Apple. An intern beside him had written Apple's push notifications framework and told stories about a clock-app time zone bug that left alarms silent around New Year. Olsen says he learned a great deal about iOS and building product.

Dylan Field, who founded Figma, ended his internship midway through the summer and founded it then. Olsen questioned whether to return and finish his last year of school and is ultimately glad he did, though it felt like a moment he might miss.

Source: 03:39–08:08 ↗

QDylan Field of Figma and Devon Finzer, a later OpenSea founder, were both interns. Did Olsen notice traits that foreshadowed their success?

Ryan Olsen

Olsen says both were plainly determined to start companies, unlike his university classmates, whose highest aspiration was a job at big tech. There was a lot of talk about ideas.

On Figma's early days, he says the founders had one real insight: WebGL was a new technology that would enable new things on the web, and Dylan's co-founder was a skilled early WebGL engineer. They went through iterations not aimed at designers, including, as Dylan once described it, a meme generator app for about a week. Olsen's view is that it took time to find the use case and customer, but they stuck to the belief that the technology would change things.

Source: 08:08–10:05 ↗

QWhile at Flipboard, Olsen built a successful open-source project, with first commits in 2014. What is the story behind it?

Ryan Olsen

During the internship Olsen built internal debugging tools for Flipboard's iOS app. It was his first deep work in Objective-C, and he liked that the language is compiled but has a runtime exposing classes, methods, state and properties while the app runs. The first version, called FLTweaker internally, inspected and tweaked app state on demand.

He kept iterating on it on nights and weekends while the three-to-five-person iOS team built Flipboard. Colleagues found it useful for seeing network requests and the file system. Everyone agreed to open-source it, and it became, in his words, one of the more popular iOS debugging tools, used at Facebook and Instagram. He has been a less active maintainer since a couple of years into Instagram, and an engineer named Tanner took it over.

The host asks whether open-sourcing the tool had an unexpected effect on Olsen's career.
Ryan Olsen

Olsen says it did in some ways, though less than he hoped. At his Instagram interview none of his interviewers wanted to look at the released code; they wanted a phone-number-sorting problem, which he found frustrating. But a Facebook iOS engineer outside the interview loop, who Olsen says may have created the original Xcode project for the Facebook app, got him to interview after seeing the tool and advocated for him in candidate review.

Having been very nervous in the internship interview, Olsen took a prescribed beta blocker for the full-time interview. He describes it as blocking adrenaline, so the pounding heart and sweaty palms never start a spiral, and says performers such as comedians use it too. Editorial note: this is one person's account, not medical advice.

The loop was still LeetCode-style, which he does not do well at, with a few strong-hire results and probably a few no-hires. He joined at IC4, one level above a new grad, and believes he was underleveled partly because of that loop.

Source: 12:51–16:12 ↗
The host asks whether the beta blocker removed the nerves entirely or only helped a little.
Ryan Olsen

Olsen has used them only a handful of times. He says they pretty much removed the physical effects, though a person can still be in their own head about what they are saying.

Source: 16:14–16:37 ↗
Source: 10:06–12:29 ↗

QWhat was the Instagram iOS team like when Olsen joined, and what did he do first?

Ryan Olsen

About ten iOS engineers worked on Instagram when Olsen arrived. As the story was told to him, the team had been about twenty before an internal war over the codebase. The manager, Scott Goodson, had built Async Display Kit for Facebook's Paper app; some engineers backed it, others wanted vanilla iOS. Olsen says the factions fought until nobody won and many left, so few engineers had been there more than six months to a year, and there was low-hanging fruit.

His first move was profiling cold start with Xcode's time profiler. The startup path did work for the profile tab that most people never open, and deferring it cut cold start by about 20 percent. Next, AFNetworking was built with assertions on and so crashed the app on benign failures such as a network error. A one-line change to block assertions cut the crash rate by 80 percent, he says.

That earned him the axe, a weekly award for outsized impact open to any function, in the form of a large physical axe carried around for a week.

Where did the axe tradition come from?
Ryan Olsen

Olsen's account is that a men's magazine asked the founders for a holiday gift guide, they listed a bespoke axe, and an investor read it and sent them a huge one. Facebook security disliked a weapon in the office, so it was mounted on a plaque.

Later in his time there the tradition was ended deliberately, apparently because people felt excluded by a weapon being passed around. Olsen was sad, since the founders were gone and it felt like early Instagram culture being swept under the rug.

Source: 20:48–21:59 ↗
Source: 16:37–20:46 ↗

QWhat was the story behind White Out, the big Instagram redesign?

Ryan Olsen

A couple of months after joining, Olsen heard that a new app icon, which became very controversial, was coming with a visual refresh. He told his manager he had to work on it and says he maneuvered himself onto the project. He spent two or three months in a conference-room war room with the main designer, passing the phone back and forth screen by screen.

They built a new color palette and icons to put the focus on photos and videos and take the color out of the chrome, which at the time was dark blue and black. Olsen says it is basically how Instagram looks today.

Was it a gated launch or all at once?
Ryan Olsen

Olsen says A/B testing was new at Instagram, and the CTO and co-founder, Mike Krieger, told him not to bother and just to build and ship. Having seen long-lived branches go badly, such as direct messaging, Olsen put the redesign, which touched every surface, behind a feature flag and kept merging, using semantic colors so code said "icon color" and a function switched between old and new design.

That opened up testing, with a 2 percent holdout on the old design. The night before launch, with the app submitted and champagne ready, someone on Facebook's executive team demanded A/B tests up front because a Facebook redesign had gone badly. Olsen backed things out and resubmitted around 1 a.m.; it tested well, but the delay crushed the planned launch.

His takeaway is that testing is valuable, including for onboarding at his startup, but for high-level product direction he prefers a strong opinion over letting data alone decide. Too much experimentation risks incrementalism: easy 1 percent wins but never a 50 percent jump.

Source: 24:06–28:14 ↗
The host notes the other risk: that the product taste is off and people hate the change. How did that play out?
Ryan Olsen

Olsen says the redesign felt right internally and was fine, but the icon was more controversial and people hated it at launch. He stopped looking at Twitter after what was meant to be a celebratory day. He attributes this to change being hard, people feeling ownership of their home screens, and a more bleeding-edge flat-and-gradient look in an era of skeuomorphic icons.

The data nonetheless showed the icon change materially raised daily app opens, and he says he has seen icon visibility affect opens with Retro too.

Source: 28:16–30:18 ↗
The host links this to Thomas Dimson's work on ranked versus chronological feeds, where public perception differed from usage. Was Olsen persuaded by ranking?
Ryan Olsen

Olsen says ranking shipped around the same time and he was skeptical at first. What changed his mind was that people with the ranked feed shared more themselves, partly because ranking showed them friends more often. He adds that the story may differ today. That fit the mission he liked, capturing and sharing the world's moments, so more creation looked like a good sign.

Source: 30:21–32:27 ↗
Source: 22:02–24:05 ↗

QThe host notes that Olsen credited finding an amazing designer. How did he find one, and what makes a designer great?

Ryan Olsen

Olsen says he has tried to be the engineer that top designers want to work with. At companies like this, designers' work can flow through you, and a product engineer's impact is multiplied by building a good working relationship with a strong designer.

Why a designer rather than a very senior engineer?
Ryan Olsen

Olsen distinguishes roles. For product engineers building user-facing features, the best pairing is a designer. In an infrastructure role the analogy is a super-senior engineer with great ideas, and being the engineer they want to work with.

Source: 33:11–34:07 ↗
Source: 32:29–33:10 ↗

QWhite Out was in 2016, the same year Olsen helped build Stories. What is the story of building Stories?

Ryan Olsen

After the redesign, Olsen's team moved to New York and he declined to relocate, so he joined Search and Explore. Within weeks a friend who led the creation team and the project that became Stories quit, and his manager said it was an important effort and a good opportunity. Olsen believed in it because Instagram felt, in some ways, like it was dying: everyday sharing among normal people was evaporating, replaced by creators and influencers, with some going to Snapchat's ephemeral format. The task was to make normal people comfortable sharing on Instagram again.

One of his first moves as iOS lead was to cut the team substantially. The project had churned through directions that did not feel good, and there was too little real work for the people on it. The core was Olsen and one other iOS engineer, plus help from other iOS engineers, two Android engineers, and only half the time of someone from infrastructure. Full ownership meant no stepping on toes and faster decisions. His summary: to go fast, go small.

They built it in two to three months. Olsen says he worked 16 to 18 hour days, seven days a week, driving home to San Francisco at 1 or 2 a.m. rather than sleeping in the office, which he now calls silly. It was intense but fun, the team bonded, and the product manager is now his co-founder. They felt like the underdog against Snapchat.

What did the Instagram version do better than Snapchat?
Ryan Olsen

Olsen says Instagram had an unfair advantage: people already had their friends there but lacked the right outlet to share with them. Once that existed, the outflow of everyday sharing to Snapchat stopped. He gives Snapchat full credit for the container, a 24-hour, full-screen, immersive format, but says Instagram added touches such as tapping left to go back.

He also built hold-to-pause after using an early autoplaying build that moved too fast and instinctively pressing his thumb to stop it. His advice to engineers he mentors is that product engineers can build their own ideas, so they should build and put them in front of people.

Source: 39:51–42:07 ↗
The host asks about the 16 to 18 hour days. Did he ever feel a person could not survive that?
Ryan Olsen

Olsen says it probably was not 16 to 18 every day, but it was a lot, and he sacrificed other parts of life. A serious rock climber who had competed in World Cups on the US team, he effectively gave that up. It was a unique chance to build something going to hundreds of millions of people, and he loved seeing someone on the Caltrain using a feature he had built a week earlier. He calls the pace unsustainable but says it can make sense in stints.

Olsen thinks Stories was better executed than the efforts at Facebook and Messenger, partly from the team's care. He feared it would crash and burn and was surprised when people called it polished. Delivering on a tight timeline with that craft, he says, helped him get onto the most interesting projects afterward.

Source: 42:09–45:19 ↗
Source: 34:08–39:49 ↗

QOlsen went from IC4 to IC6 in two consecutive halves. What happened?

Ryan Olsen

Olsen says the promotion cycle was in July while Stories shipped in early August, so calibrations took place mid-crunch. He believes managers were cautious, and he felt fairly confident he had been underleveled when hired, having not known much about levels. His Android counterpart, Will Bailey, who he says was tech lead for Stories and an IC8, got him into meetings with Mike and Kevin and set an example of a successful product engineer. Seeing IC4 beside IC8 on similar roles opened his eyes to leveling.

He told his manager, Eddie, a director to whom he reported directly because of the project, that he had been misleveled and should go from four to six that cycle. Olsen credits him with not brushing it off: he checked with HR, who said it had been done twice in company history and both people left quickly. Olsen says he mainly wanted to seed the idea that his correct level was higher. He got IC5 for White Out and infrastructure work, then IC6 for Stories.

His broader point is that levels and promotions are an incentive system. He thinks there is a real effort to make them fair, but promotions can be delayed so two do not come in quick succession, because it is a carrot dangled in front of people.

The host asks how strong performance gave Olsen the freedom to choose projects.
Ryan Olsen

Olsen says it showed that if he is put on a project he will do well, so when a new effort starts the company picks people who did well on earlier ones. He calls himself lucky, with good execution setting him up for later chances. When the host notes that Threads reused this model of pulling proven people into a small team, Olsen agrees it is a fun environment.

Source: 48:51–50:08 ↗
Source: 45:21–48:48 ↗

QThe next promotion, to IC7, came through IGTV. What was that project?

Ryan Olsen

Olsen says IGTV began with Kevin, the CEO, and a designer, Ian, who unveiled a vision for longer-form, mobile-native vertical video at an end-of-year all-hands. Olsen wanted to work on it. He says recent antitrust litigation against Facebook shows tensions between the two companies then; his team was told for a while not to work on it, and he sees it as roughly the end of the founders' time.

The team was small: Olsen, Will Bailey and Thomas Dimson as iOS, Android and server leads, each with one or two others per platform. The product no longer exists and did not do well. Olsen thinks it held part of the future, since vertical video is now central, but it tried to put YouTube-style long-form content in a vertical format and people were not producing high-quality long-form vertical video.

The team tried AI techniques to reformat landscape video for vertical, on which Olsen holds a patent, but creators were horrified. Pushing creators to make original vertical long-form never produced the inventory, and Olsen sees some hubris in assuming Instagram could change what creators make. He believes it informed what shipped as Reels.

Source: 50:09–53:26 ↗

QThe host asks what the antitrust angle is that Olsen mentioned.

Ryan Olsen

Olsen says internal communications made public through the antitrust suit, in which he understands the Justice Department is trying to unwind the Instagram acquisition, made some confusing events less confusing. His reading is that Instagram, small when acquired, grew into a peer of Facebook and the new popular kid. Stories was received better than Facebook's Stories, creating tension between the leaderships and concern that Instagram would cannibalize Facebook, which he says guided some strategy decisions.

The host recalls confusion at the time about cross-sharing from Facebook to Instagram being turned off and says Mark Zuckerberg's internal memo explains it. Olsen says he read the same material.

How might Mark Zuckerberg view it today?
Ryan Olsen

Olsen wonders, since the communications suggest an understandable emotional attachment to Facebook, which Zuckerberg created, while Instagram was less his own thing. Olsen's own view is that the best outcome for a company owning both is to let them compete and improve each other, since stifling competition makes it likelier an outsider builds something better. He adds that he is armchair CEOing about someone running a multi-trillion-dollar company.

Source: 56:03–57:27 ↗
Source: 53:42–56:01 ↗

Editorial note

The antitrust and Facebook-Instagram tensions in these two rounds are Olsen's and the host's readings of public litigation material and their own recollections. Olsen hedges (he thinks the Justice Department is the plaintiff), and this section does not verify them.

Source: 53:42–57:27 ↗

QWhat is the story behind IG Labs, and how did it lead to the IC8 promotion?

Ryan Olsen

After IGTV, Olsen says he spent time in what Thomas Dimson calls the impact desert and was close to leaving. Reels was the new effort, and although his manager worked on it, he was fairly sure he did not want to work on passive video consumption.

Culture was changing too: the founders had left, new leadership came from Facebook, and old Instagram culture felt pushed out. Olsen pitched the new head of engineering on bringing back small teams, attention to craft and a wider scope, arguing the brand could support things beyond the existing app, such as location, maps and places ideas.

He started the group with a designer, Vivian Wong, at first just the two of them, as a Delta Force-style small, high-talent-density team for initiatives that did not fit cleanly into the org. By his account Instagram had grown so large that projects outside its structure were underinvested. The group tried many things, and much of it never shipped. He points to collaborative posts, with multiple authors on one post, as a lasting result and another of his patents. The group could also be pulled onto a major new initiative, which he says ended up being Threads.

QOlsen tried the rare tech lead director role. What was his thinking, and how did it go?

Ryan Olsen

Olsen says the role was rare at Facebook. It happened mostly because he had started the group, and it made more sense for him to manage the people than for his manager over Reels, who was less connected to their work. He was already representing them in calibrations, so the role was a formal recognition.

He says Facebook keeps individual contributors and management separate, and he disagrees. He cites Tesla as more flexible, with ICs often having reports and managers expected to be competent technical contributors. He holds what he calls a controversial opinion that senior engineers should code, citing Nassim Taleb's skin in the game: a senior IC who codes will not hand off an architecture as someone else's problem, and a manager close to day-to-day work operates better.

He also found an upside to a visible title. Facebook levels are private, which he likes for engineering debates because nobody can pull rank. In cross-functional work, such as shipping collaborative posts across many teams' PMs, a higher title gave a better baseline of credibility, since in a huge company you keep re-establishing reputation. He supported at least a public senior designation.

The host says people warn that doing two jobs means you drown and neither career flourishes. What does Olsen say?
Ryan Olsen

Olsen says the criticism is probably correct. He was not optimizing for career and never intended to stay long: on Facebook's sentiment survey asking how long you plan to stay, he never put more than one year. He had no aspiration to reach IC9, which freed him to do what suited the team, and he knew he would not be fired for performance.

He also saw the cost firsthand: he believes his ratings were lower than they would have been as an IC, since he was exceeding as an IC but only meeting as a manager.

Source: 1:06:32–1:08:18 ↗
Source: 1:01:47–1:06:49 ↗

QWhat made Olsen leave Instagram and start Retro?

Ryan Olsen

In his last months at Instagram, Olsen talked with Nathan, now his co-founder, with whom he had built Stories. Nathan had gone to the Facebook side, started Facebook Dating, then worked on virtual reality. The close friends talked at a bar about building products and structuring a company differently, and about wanting to be in the driver's seat, but timing never aligned until both were ready. An investor friend and mentor, the one who connected him to Flipboard, told him it was time to bet on himself.

Olsen says the goal is a world-class product studio where great builders do the best work of their lives, making products people feel good after using, and also a successful business. Retro is the first product, not the reason the company exists.

Retro is a friends-focused social app. Olsen contrasts it with traditional social media, which he calls brain rot or entertainment. He says Instagram today shows him few people he knows and pulls him into short-form video that hijacks his attention. Retro is for staying up to date with people you know and looking back at your own photos. He says almost half of daily users post, much higher than he saw at Instagram, and that it became popular in Taiwan once it hit critical mass there. Editorial note: these usage claims are self-reported.

Source: 1:08:19–1:13:18 ↗

QWhat design philosophy did Retro take, and is it harder to grow when the app is less addictive?

Ryan Olsen

Olsen says a key decision was no ad-based business model. He does not think ads are evil, but ads combined with an algorithmic feed are a little evil because the incentives are misaligned: the app wants more of your time than you intended.

Growth is a real challenge. There are no creators; friending is mutual and private, with a limit of 250 friends, so no one can build an audience. He says Instagram grew partly through creators financially motivated to spread it, a path Retro lacks. He points to BeReal as a friends-only network that grew through a viral notification. His view is that growing a friends-only network is possible but harder, as is the business model, and the team is open about that. He frames it as an opinionated stance: some say to build what people want, but Retro bets that something better should exist as an option.

He says Retro coexists with Instagram; he still opens Instagram but gets sucked in less, and it has helped him break a phone habit.

How does Retro make money without ads?
Ryan Olsen

Olsen says a small share of users take a premium subscription covering features that cost more to provide, such as video, since storage and bandwidth cost more than for photos. Posting video requires it, but he says the free version is good, and 93 percent of what people share on Retro is photos.

Source: 1:17:19–1:18:10 ↗
Source: 1:13:57–1:17:16 ↗

QAcross learning, satisfaction and compensation, how has working on his own company compared with big tech?

Ryan Olsen

Olsen says compensation is quite a bit worse. He and Nathan pay themselves less than the employees and hold more ownership, which he thinks is right, accepting delayed pay in exchange for possible equity upside. Building a company was always what he wanted, and he was somewhat surprised to end up in big tech.

He says his time on interesting work is much higher now. In his later Instagram years he spent much of his work convincing layers above him that something should ship. He thinks more people worked on the app than needed to, which created gatekeeping over whether a team could ship and political wrangling about making someone feel an idea was theirs. He now spends none of his time on that; his only meeting is a daily one-hour standup, leaving nearly the whole day to build. His summary is that satisfaction and learning are higher and compensation lower.

Source: 1:18:29–1:21:32 ↗

QWould the company be better off if half the people were laid off?

Ryan Olsen

Olsen says yes. His team used to discuss a Thanos-style thought experiment in which half the company vanishes at random, and they often felt things would go better. He acknowledges that at Instagram's scale a 0.1 percent improvement can be worth hundreds of millions of dollars, but thinks the cost of each added person is underappreciated.

He cites organizational overhead of stakeholders, meetings and coordination, and the weight of more code. Just before leaving, a tool showed him spending more than four hours a day waiting for the app to build, because tooling had not kept up with how fast people wrote code. With a thousand engineers that slows everyone, though it is not noticeable per added person. When the team was ten and the app small, things were far easier, and he says White Out would be a massive project at Instagram today.

The host raises Twitter's post-layoff experience as a case study. How does Olsen see it?
Ryan Olsen

Olsen says projections were that Twitter would fall over entirely after the cuts. His experience of it is somewhat buggy, but it keeps running, and he says he saw that its economics improved and it is now profitable, whereas it lost money through most of its history. Editorial note: these are Olsen's impressions, not verified figures.

Source: 1:24:20–1:25:08 ↗
Source: 1:21:32–1:24:19 ↗

QWhat stories show what made the founders and other colleagues exceptional?

Ryan Olsen

Olsen calls Mike Krieger something of a hero and says much of his thinking about engineering leadership came from him, including a simple-thing-first approach and attention to detail and craft. He describes a lead-from-the-front style in which Krieger never put himself above the team and jumped in wherever help was needed. At the end of Stories, a friend Olsen had borrowed from another Facebook team to build the drawing tools was pulled back partway through. Krieger said he would finish it, coded the neon brush, worked the same insane hours, and was up at 2 a.m. reviewing Olsen's diffs. Olsen says that informs how he leads teams.

Of Will Bailey, Olsen describes a strong product vision. During the dark days when Stories was spinning in circles, Bailey wrote a document outlining how the product should work, which Olsen later saw as essentially the five-year roadmap. He was an example of how a product-focused engineer can succeed and influence product direction, which Olsen says was valued more at Instagram than at Facebook, where he recalls bootcamp talk that juniors go to product teams and seniors to infrastructure.

He calls Thomas Dimson probably the smartest person he has met, and not in a savant way, since Dimson has social skills and understands people. Dimson started ranking at Instagram, with infrastructure skill but a product mindset. Olsen says he is interested in technology only as a means to create things for people, and sees Bailey and Dimson as similarly human-oriented, thinking about psychology and how products make people feel.

Source: 1:25:10–1:31:28 ↗

QIf Olsen could advise himself just after graduating, what would he say?

Ryan Olsen

Olsen says to invest in the tools of your time to build things for people. A new grad is not stuck as an iOS person or any one technology, so can pick up the latest tools. He believes that with the new AI tools new grads will probably be more skilled than senior engineers, who did not learn them natively.

He saw this with iOS: senior engineers were writing Java and the back end, and he stood out because iOS was the first thing he learned and he was eager and hungry. His advice is to learn the tools of your time, get good at them, and make good things for people. He says it is probably scary because it is hard to know how it will play out, and demand for junior engineers seems to be falling because of AI tools. But he believes anyone who gets very good at those tools will have roles.

Source: 1:30:22–1:33:10 ↗

Section 76 · interview

Steve Huynh: Amazon Promotions, Layoffs, and Interview Packaging

Steve Huynh explains how a non-CS path led into Amazon, why behavioral fit shapes big-tech interview levels, and how promotion and managed-out cycles work.

Steve's view: big-tech interviews judge fit, and promotion depends on early, explicit feedback

Steve Huynh's view is that a big-tech interview is mainly a test of fit. Coding and system design rounds work as a pass or fail filter, and behavioral answers shape the level a candidate is offered. Steve applies the same idea to careers: ask directly what the expectations are, raise bad news early, and close gaps in a promotion packet rather than repeating strengths. Steve credits Amazon's customer focus and writing culture as real strengths, and says its managed-out cycles are hard to watch and have become more of a mandate. These are Steve's own views and experience, not verified facts. Editorial note: the host is not named in the transcript, so the host appears only as the host.

Source: 00:55–1:18:40 ↗

QHow did someone with a liberal arts degree and no computer science major get into Amazon?

Steve Huynh

Steve says the liberal arts label is somewhat misleading. Both parents were electrical engineers, and a family computer was always around. Steve programmed from a young age, took the high school AP computer science exams, and built a Tetris clone.

In college Steve earned a liberal arts degree, a minor in math and applied math, and some computer science courses. After graduating, Steve wanted to be a writer, but a writing professor said there was no job called writer. Steve went back to the programming skills from high school instead. Steve agrees that an English major alone would not stand out to a recruiter.

Source: 00:55–03:41 ↗

QHow did Steve get the first job at Amazon?

Steve Huynh

Steve says it came through networking. A high school AP computer science classmate had earned a degree and worked as an Amazon software developer. The team needed support engineers, and the classmate helped Steve get an interview for a contract role.

Steve says the support work involved scripts and maintaining systems, so the coding interview was not a worry. Steve was a green badge contractor, Amazon's term for a temp, for about nine months before moving to a full-time blue badge role.

Did a referral matter more than skills in getting hired?
Steve Huynh

Steve says both matter. Opportunity arrives unevenly, so a referral from a friend or relative can open a door. Preparation is the part a person controls. Steve says the two have to meet, because an opening is wasted without the skills to fill it.

Source: 05:29–06:18 ↗
Source: 03:43–05:27 ↗

QWas it harder to break into tech before interview prep became a large industry?

Steve Huynh

Steve says yes. There were no widely shared lists of LeetCode questions when Steve was trying to get in, so a non-traditional candidate had a harder time than today. Steve does not say that getting in is easy now.

As a support engineer who wanted to be a software developer, Steve collected interview questions from colleagues and asked them not to give the answers. Steve worked each problem in an IDE and wrote custom test cases, which Steve calls the old-fashioned way.

Is interview prep a competition in which a candidate must beat the other candidates?
Steve Huynh

Steve says yes and no. Demand for software developers is skewed toward senior roles, with little demand for junior engineers. Steve sees the competition at the selection stage, when recruiters screen candidates, not in the interview itself.

Steve says a candidate can stand out before the interview, through a contact at the company or by going deep in one area.

Source: 07:59–08:56 ↗
Source: 06:19–07:57 ↗

QWhy is most interview prep advice poor?

Steve Huynh

Steve says most interview prep is not optimized. Candidates focus heavily on coding and, lately, on system design. Steve says prep turns the interview into a test. That view is partly right, since a candidate who cannot code or design a system is unlikely to be hired, but Steve says the focus is too narrow.

What would a better balance of interview prep look like?
Steve Huynh

Steve says an interview is more like a date than an SAT, because both sides are deciding whether they want to work together. Prep sources present it as a test because a test is easier to sell.

Steve suggests spending less time on coding and system design and more on behavioral work. A rough split Steve offers is 40 percent coding, 40 percent system design, and 20 percent behavioral. Steve treats the figures as an illustration, not a rule.

Source: 09:59–10:55 ↗
Source: 08:58–09:56 ↗

QHow much does the behavioral part of an interview count compared with coding and system design?

Steve Huynh

Steve says coding and system design work like the small and big blinds in poker. They are required to play, but they do not decide the hand. The behavioral round decides the hand. Steve was a bar raiser trainer and trained thousands of Amazon interviewers. Steve says the functional rounds are pass or no pass.

Steve says Amazon will say no to candidates with poor behavioral answers, even when coding and system design are strong. That does not mean the candidate lacks experience. Interviewers can often see early that a candidate will not fit the company. Once a candidate passes, the behavioral answers shape the level.

How can a candidate avoid being down-leveled because of weak behavioral answers?
Steve Huynh

Steve recommends packaging: presenting one's experience as a clear story about what one has done, how one operates, and what one is about. The story does not have to be entertaining, but it should be efficient and honest.

Steve says the core question of an interview is whether the interviewer wants to work with the candidate. Good behavioral answers help the interviewer answer that. Candidates should not misrepresent themselves, but should put their best foot forward.

Source: 12:55–14:24 ↗
What does a packaged answer sound like?
Steve Huynh

Steve gives an improvised example for a tell-me-about-yourself question: a focus on backend distributed systems, a love of customer-facing products, a sports interest, and experience building teams and improving engineering culture. Steve says many candidates rush through this question.

Steve says stories betray level. A story about an entry-level task sounds junior when the candidate is aiming for a senior role, and that mismatch can lead to being down-leveled.

Source: 14:25–16:13 ↗
Source: 10:59–12:52 ↗

QCan someone's level be judged in a short conversation?

Steve Huynh

The host suggests a blind test: talk to someone for five minutes and guess their level. Steve says Steve is fairly confident in judging level this way. A junior engineer usually shows it in how they carry themselves and what they talk about.

Steve says judging whether a strong senior engineer could pass as a principal would be harder. Steve believes Steve is well calibrated on level overall.

Source: 16:16–17:54 ↗

QHow can someone stand out before the interview, for example when seeking a referral?

Steve Huynh

Steve says a direct, genuine message to someone on a team with an opening can work. Steve suggests saying you noticed their team has openings, and asking what their day-to-day work is like. The message should not look like spam, an automated DM, or AI-written text.

Steve cites a poll Steve ran in a Discord community. About 90 percent of respondents said they would engage with a genuine message like that, and would refer the sender if asked. Steve presents this as informal, not as evidence.

Steve says real networking means making a connection and offering value. Newcomers who are willing to pick up a useful skill are also more attractive to big tech.

Source: 17:57–19:45 ↗

QShould a learner go deep or broad, and which language should they pick?

Steve Huynh

Steve says most people should go deep rather than broad. Jumping between a React tutorial, Rust, and PyTorch creates no cohesion. Steve suggests starting with a framework or language the learner already knows and going as deep as possible.

Asked for a top language for 2025, Steve jokes that English is the top language. Steve says the high-leverage skill is communicating and packaging one's experience. Steve says languages come and go, and that Steve's own Perl expertise is no longer useful.

Steve says curiosity should guide the choice. Java is not going away, so becoming an expert in it is a fine choice even if it is not glamorous.

What does going deep look like in practice?
Steve Huynh

Steve gives the example of asking what a Java virtual machine does, what a garbage collector does, and what tuning one means. Steve notes that tuning garbage collection can backfire, but looking under the hood is something no one can stop a learner from doing.

Source: 21:42–22:31 ↗
Source: 19:48–21:38 ↗

QWill AI take over junior engineering work? Meta's chief executive, called Zuck in the conversation, recently suggested AI could produce mid-level engineer code within the year.

Steve Huynh

Steve says CEOs make predictions that tend to undershoot on timing and overshoot on ability, but that the vision is real. Steve reads the hedged wording about mid-level AI engineers later this year as a sign the rollout is further away than the words suggest. Steve says leaders' jobs are to move the goalposts a little past where things are.

Steve agrees that AI should take on some tasks. Steve compares it with older tools: code generation, Lombok annotations that remove getters and setters, and IDE refactoring. Steve calls AI help an amplifier.

Can AI take a non-coder from idea to working product, and does that scale?
Steve Huynh

Steve says AI can take a non-coder from zero to one very easily. Steve mentions app-building products that go from start to finish, but doubts they would handle an app that does not work as intended or must scale to a very large user base.

Steve believes an engineer can become much more productive with AI help today, moving from a 1x to a 10x engineer. Steve does not see a jump from zero to a 10x engineer happening later this year.

Source: 25:20–26:20 ↗
Source: 22:34–25:17 ↗

QHow did Steve move from support engineer to SDE1, SDE2, and SDE3?

Steve Huynh

Steve says the path from support engineer to SDE3 took about three and a half years. At SDE1, the focus is independence: understanding where one's work fits in the development life cycle and taking tasks all the way through, so that the team trusts the person without hand-holding.

Does independence mean never asking for help?
Steve Huynh

Steve says no. Self-contained is not the same as independent. Steve says the real skill is knowing how to unblock oneself, and being comfortable asking questions and raising issues when stuck.

Steve warns that hiding problems becomes a performance issue. A two-week task reported as on track until the Thursday before it is due is more serious than a task that is merely slow.

Source: 27:34–29:20 ↗
What changes at SDE2?
Steve Huynh

Steve says the key word at SDE2 is ownership. An SDE2 takes an active part in the development life cycle and acts as a steward of the team's codebase, cleaning up tech debt instead of leaving a mess. Steve likes the image of not littering, and sometimes picking up trash.

Steve says each step up is an argument for more scope. An SDE2 works at team level, understands the codebase's strengths and weaknesses, suggests where it should go, and takes on-call shifts. Steve calls this a meat-and-potatoes role, and says it is what a person needs to show to move from SDE2 to SDE3.

Source: 28:25–30:18 ↗
Source: 26:22–27:32 ↗

QCan an SDE2 stay at that level for a whole career, or is it a terminal level at Amazon?

Steve Huynh

Steve says this is debated at Amazon. Steve sees the SDE2 band as wide, and says many senior engineers at other companies would sit at the upper end of SDE2 at Amazon. Steve says SDE2 could be a terminal level, but Steve does not advise treating it as one.

Is there an up-or-out policy?
Steve Huynh

Steve says SDE1 is clearly up or out. Staying more than about two years brings progressively stronger guidance to move on, though it is not a fixed 24- or 36-month rule. Steve calls it a feel thing.

For SDE2, Steve says the answer depends on upper management and on the individual's manager. A manager who sees an SDE2 as overdue for promotion could make staying very hard. The conversation notes that many people worry Meta could become more like Amazon, which is known for intense performance management.

Source: 31:19–33:06 ↗
Source: 30:20–31:16 ↗

QHow many people is Amazon expected to cut each year?

Steve Huynh

Steve will not give an exact number. Steve uses five or six percent as an example. For an organization, that figure used to be a soft recommendation to manage out part of the team over a year. In the past couple of years, Steve says it has become much more of a mandate.

Steve says the pressure grew when backfills were paused. Until recently, Amazon did not backfill many roles, so people felt chased from behind, and Steve does not think that was healthy. As a self-described high performer, Steve says it is hard to speak to what it feels like to fear losing a job.

Is managing out the low end of the curve a relief or a problem?
Steve Huynh

Steve uses a group of 20 people as an example. In normal years, people on the low end of the curve are often not thriving in Amazon's culture. Steve says removing them can feel like a relief, a blessing in disguise, because it ends a poor fit.

Steve is uncomfortable when cuts reach people in the middle of the curve, who would be fine in other years. Repeated cuts of about six percent, with no backfill, push out people who are doing well.

Source: 34:54–37:45 ↗
Source: 33:09–34:52 ↗

QHow do senior engineers take part in the meetings where people are discussed for being managed out?

Steve Huynh

Steve says engineers are pulled into these discussions from senior engineer level, and definitely from L7 and above. The meetings can run three days, with people in a room discussing colleagues through measurable results and other people's feedback. Steve says some recent cuts of middle managers surprised Steve, since a 6 percent target makes little sense for a group of four or eight people.

Steve says the process is not linear. In a perfect world, each person would get equal time, but the discussion tends to focus on the edges, the strongest and the weakest. Steve sees this as a matter of the numbers, not a verdict on the decision makers, and says the process strips out some humanity. Steve says it is not a favorite time of year.

Source: 37:47–39:37 ↗

QIs Meta showing the same intensity as Amazon?

Steve Huynh

Steve says Meta appears to be on a hiring spree, and that a figure of about 5 percent of low performers has been floated around. Steve has a sense that people affected are not having a good time, but thinks most people at Meta are fine.

Steve says that with a large population, someone is always struggling. Meta's inflow of hires is far larger than its outflow, so Steve would not be too worried.

Source: 39:39–40:53 ↗

QWhat protects someone who is meeting expectations during a cut cycle?

Steve Huynh

Steve says solidly meeting expectations is the main protection. Steve does not think a 5 percent stack ranking should remove people who meet expectations, and Steve dislikes the label low performer. Steve describes it as a mismatch between a person and the culture around them, not a judgment of ability.

Steve says offers at Meta are hard to get, so the people in that process are not weak. Steve advises people labeled as low performers to find the specific dimension they are judged on, rather than trying to become high performers in general.

What should someone do first when judged to be below expectations?
Steve Huynh

Steve says to crawl before walking and running. Find out exactly what the judgment is about, then check with the manager whether expectations are being met. If they are not, propose a preemptive plan to get back to the median. Steve would avoid the phrase PIP, for performance improvement plan, when asking for one.

Source: 42:50–43:41 ↗
Should employees ask managers directly what the expectations are, and when should they report bad news?
Steve Huynh

Steve says most people never ask this. Steve estimates that about 25 percent of software developers have explicitly asked their manager about expectations. Steve recommends asking directly what the expectations are, then asking whether one is meeting them.

Steve credits a friend with the saying that early bad news is just news, while late bad news is terrible news. Steve advises surfacing problems early in the review cycle, not in the month before a review, so there is time to fix them.

Source: 43:44–46:34 ↗
Source: 40:55–42:49 ↗

QHow did Steve get principal-level scope at Amazon?

Steve Huynh

Steve says a reorg moved Steve into Prime Video after a team Steve cared about, the Amazon Tickets team, was spun down and its developers scattered. Steve chose a Prime Video team focused on delivering live sports, then saw a large catalog project that principal engineers knew needed doing. Steve decided to take it on and stay on the team.

Steve says the work fell in the gaps between principal areas, such as playback, clients, or catalog. It needed an end-to-end solution, and the other principals were busy with their own areas. The host adds that delivering such work gives principal engineers context to champion the candidate in a promotion packet.

Source: 46:37–49:25 ↗

QWhat usually blocks someone from going from senior to principal at Amazon?

Steve Huynh

Steve says Amazon effectively skips a level, and that a staff level could be inserted between senior and principal. Steve says the jump from senior to principal is two levels, so the criteria roughly double. Influencing multiple teams makes it hard to show that in one year.

Steve sees a common failure. People think they are ready, push for promotion, get rejected, and go back to their strengths. Closing the feedback takes a long time, and many give up. Steve knows people who left Amazon and now work at senior staff or principal levels elsewhere, but could not make the jump there.

How can someone get a low performance rating while doing principal-level work?
Steve Huynh

Steve says performance and promotion are decoupled. Reviews run yearly, with a smaller check every six months, and promotion can happen quarterly or every six months. Steve describes an anti-pattern: a senior engineer who stops doing senior work and focuses only on principal-level work.

Steve says senior engineers must code. Principals also code, but less, and they do cross-functional work such as sponsoring projects, acting as a backstop, or evangelizing an initiative across several dev teams. Steve recalls a promotion review that said Steve acted like a TPM, and Steve took offense.

Source: 52:23–54:32 ↗
What feedback did Steve get on coding, and why?
Steve Huynh

Steve says the review said to code more. Steve had checked in a lot of code, but in one six-month stretch Steve coded less, and the review looked only at the code delivered in that period. Steve says that gave no credit for time served.

Steve says on-call history was also raised, though Steve had been on call for years, including about four years in a row. Steve also says Steve reached senior in 2012 and principal in 2020, after the promotion process changed three times in four years.

Source: 54:35–56:15 ↗
Source: 49:25–52:21 ↗

QWhat did Steve learn from becoming an expert in the promotion process?

Steve Huynh

Steve says Steve did not get promoted through ability alone. Steve became an expert in the process of getting promoted, and thinks that skill is useful. Steve had not produced enough tangible evidence for the packet, and needed a manager's support. Steve says the process changed three times in four years.

Steve's first lesson is to start early. Many people wait until a big project lands, but the project landing is often not what a rejection is about. Steve advises submitting the packet early to get real feedback on the gaps.

Steve's second lesson concerns strengths. A packet gives some credit for strengths, but reviewers focus on the delta. Steve advises prioritizing weaknesses and gaps, and keeping strengths from regressing, the way a cook tends one pot of risotto while the other pans rest.

Source: 56:17–59:51 ↗

QWhat are Steve's favorite parts of Amazon's culture?

Steve Huynh

Steve says the biggest part is customer obsession. From interns to VPs, people were expected to put the customer first. Steve says working backward from the customer is the right North Star. Optimizing for short-term profit or for competitors can backfire, and Steve credits Jeff Bezos with the idea that long-term profit and customers are the same thing.

Steve calls the writing culture a superpower, and credits a writing background with making a six-page document easier to write. Meetings often begin with about 30 minutes of reading the document, followed by discussion. Steve says writing is learnable and need not be a focus before joining.

What does Steve dislike about the culture?
Steve Huynh

Steve says the inside joke among friends was frugality. Anything cheap or poor, such as the lack of free food or weak hardware, got the label. Steve says free food is a perk and its absence does not mean a company is bad, but frugality can go too far.

Steve recalls begging and pleading for a laptop with enough memory so the fan did not overheat while building code. Steve says a company hiring tens of thousands of developers should give them working computers, and recalls monitors being taken after intern season.

Source: 1:03:39–1:05:24 ↗
Source: 59:52–1:02:40 ↗

QWhat made a good manager stand out, given the many managers Steve had?

Steve Huynh

Steve says the count was more than 17, closer to the 20s. Steve says the best managers were personal, but Steve resonated with managers who reasoned from principles. Those managers treated the leadership principles as axioms, so decisions followed from them and had implications.

Steve says the best managers held firm on customer obsession and on thinking ahead. They would accept a short-term hack if it fit a future-facing choice. Steve found managers focused only on near-term delivery harder to work with. Steve also notes that some people who complain about micromanagers really need things broken down.

Who were the worst managers, and what made them bad?
Steve Huynh

Steve does not name names. Steve says the worst managers were a mix of style mismatch and a sense that the hiring and promotion processes should have filtered them out. A manager who is caring and engaged for one person may be a poor fit for another.

Steve says it was sometimes hard to see how some managers had reached their roles.

Source: 1:06:39–1:09:19 ↗
Source: 1:05:27–1:06:55 ↗

QWhy did Steve stay at Amazon for 18 years?

Steve Huynh

Steve says Amazon's size allowed many careers inside one company. Steve worked on the first Kindle, on a precursor to Prime Video, back on Prime Video, and in payments. Steve says it did not feel like one team for 18 years.

Did Steve consider leaving, and what is the advice on job hopping?
Steve Huynh

Steve says Steve considered leaving several times. Early in a career, job hopping makes sense to raise total pay, and Steve says that advice works until about the senior level.

Steve says distinguished, principal, and staff engineers at the top usually stayed on the same team, on the same problem, for at least three years and often about five. Steve's rule of thumb for a fast climb is to job hop every two years until about mid-level, then put down roots.

Source: 1:10:22–1:12:10 ↗
Why did Steve choose to put down roots?
Steve Huynh

Steve says staying made sense without a computer science background. There was a lot to learn in large amounts of code, wikis, and internal videos. Steve felt Steve could grow the way Steve wanted by staying.

Source: 1:12:13–1:13:00 ↗
Source: 1:09:20–1:10:19 ↗

QWhat is Steve's biggest career regret?

Steve Huynh

Steve says the regret is not noticing a bad situation or team and making a clear decision about it. The default is to stay put, and deferring a decision turns into staying by default. Steve's advice is to weigh the considerations and then make the choice explicit.

Source: 1:15:48–1:16:44 ↗

QWhat would Steve tell a younger self who had just finished college?

Steve Huynh

Steve says Steve would warn against people pleasing. Steve describes a culture of tracks, such as school, then job, then marriage, and a sense of being ahead or behind. Steve also sought validation after each achievement, and doubts a younger self would have listened.

Steve says the person to please is oneself. Steve asks whether a person is doing what they want or what someone else expects, and whether they are climbing the ladder to reach the top or because it was put in front of them.

Section 77 · interview

Zach Wilson: Job Hopping to Staff at Airbnb, Interviews, and Internal Brand

Zach Wilson recounts a rapid climb from junior data engineer to staff at Airbnb, arguing that interviews and impact stories outpaced promotions, and counts the cost of long hours.

Interviews and impact stories move a career faster than waiting for a promotion

Zach Wilson describes a path from junior data engineer at Facebook (called Meta by the host) to staff data engineer at Airbnb by age 26. Zach's central argument is that the interview is the highest-leverage part of a career. Two of the level jumps came from changing companies, and in each case the tool was a clear impact story, not hours worked. Zach also lists the costs: roughly 60-hour weeks, a staff-type role taken before the matching behaviors were in place, and a Netflix reorganization that ended in a mental health break. The host adds that companies hold back promotions when someone has impact but not yet the behaviors. Pay figures and company details are Zach's recollection and are not verified.

Source: 00:56–1:05:52 ↗

QHow did Zach get started in the industry?

Zach Wilson

Zach began at several startups as a data analyst. A plan to become a math professor faded because it meant a lot of school for modest pay. An early job at Think Big Analytics taught Hadoop when it was new, about ten years before the recording, and Zach credits that experience as the main reason Facebook later wanted to hire.

Zach held four jobs in two years. On graduating, Zach was unsure whether to be a mobile engineer, a math professor or a data scientist, and tried several roles before settling on data engineering. With a dual major in computer science and applied math and only math tutoring on the resume, Zach still got four or five interviews and calls this luck.

How did the Facebook offer come about, and why did Zach turn down a counter-offer?
Zach Wilson

After a year in Utah, Zach moved to Washington, DC, to try something new. Six or seven months later a Facebook recruiter reached out on LinkedIn, a site Zach says has been critical since the Think Big job in 2015. Zach had been rejected twice by Google for mobile roles, so the approach felt almost as if Facebook were applying to Zach.

The DC employer countered. Zach recalls about 180 from Facebook against about 200 from the DC company, with units not stated. Zach declined because a request for a 20 percent raise two months earlier had been refused for lack of budget. Money that appears only when someone is leaving, Zach reasoned, signals that growth there would be painful.

Source: 03:02–05:11 ↗
Source: 00:56–03:00 ↗

QWhat was boot camp like, and how did Zach choose a team?

Zach Wilson

Moving to Silicon Valley also put Zach closer to family in Utah, which had felt distant from DC. Zach says the first month of boot camp felt like Disneyland more than a job. The onboarding sold the company's values, such as moving fast and being bold, and felt like college because no deadlines applied yet.

Zach interviewed for three teams: ads, growth and community support. Ads pitched making Facebook millions through data, community support pitched preventing bad content, and growth pitched having fun. Zach joined core growth and notifications, partly on that pitch and partly because of an entrepreneurial manager who is still a close friend.

Source: 05:14–07:28 ↗

QDid Zach understand the career ladder on joining?

Zach Wilson

No. Zach did not know what L3, L4 and L5 meant and did not realize the hire was at L3. Zach had two years of big-data pipeline work at startups, yet new Stanford graduates with no experience were paid the same, and Zach found that unfair. Zach concluded the hire was at the wrong level and worked hard to reach the next level, which took about seven months.

Zach says this taught that how someone interviews is the highest-leverage part of a career, more important than the impact made in the role.

What did Zach do to earn the L3 to L4 promotion?
Zach Wilson

Zach could tell early that things were going well: work was clearly tasked out, energy was high and a lot of code shipped. Notifications had a waterfall framework for tracking conversion, click and delivery rates, and Zach found it poor. Fixing it meant XHP and React work, not SQL and Python, so Zach learned both. Zach says the manager took this as proof of someone who solves problems outside the job description, and nobody had asked for it.

Doing only the assigned tasks, Zach says, earns a meets-all rating at L3, so Zach looked for where the impact was.

Source: 09:11–10:32 ↗
Was the promotion expected?
Zach Wilson

It came as a surprise. The half lasted five months for Zach because the start date was late July. Zach thinks the company recognized the mis-leveling and skipped the usual steps. The host adds that a promotion within one half usually signals a hiring miss that the company fixes quickly.

Zach contrasts this with Utah, where promotion follows tenure, not impact. In Utah, Zach had thought a software engineer would top out near 200k at about age 35. Facebook offered about that figure at the start, with a route toward a million, and Zach says companies reward business impact because the value created exceeds the pay.

After boot camp, Zach ramped up to roughly 50 to 60 hours a week, usually arriving around 9:30 and leaving near 8 pm, because breakfast, lunch and dinner were all provided. Zach jokes that free meals left a basic life skill, cooking, unlearned.

QAfter L4, why did the next promotion, to L5, not happen?

Zach wanted L5 within a year and felt confident while the first manager was in place. That manager left the next summer. The team reported to the director for a while and then to a new manager from Netflix, so Zach had three managers in one year. None had the full context, and Zach had to restate past work again and again. Zach says this disrupted the plan, and that trust takes time to build. Zach says good managers extend trust by default, while others demand proof first.

Zach earned a greatly-exceeds rating in the first half as an L4 and again in the next. The feedback was that Zach was not yet operating as a senior engineer. Zach was taking on too much work, and leadership doubted that delivery at L5 level was sustainable.

The host says a promotion must be sustainable, and a leader may wonder whether someone working long hours can keep it up. Did that match what Zach learned?
Zach Wilson

Zach says it did, and calls it one of the most important lessons from Facebook. Hours worked do not necessarily drive promotion. Extra hours can cover a skill gap, but they do not give leadership confidence that someone is ready for the next level.

The host agrees that promotion committees look for behaviors, meaning the ability to take on more leadership, and not simply extra hours. The host notes this can leave a hard worker bitter.

Promotions at Facebook usually landed around March, and after learning there would be none, Zach decided it was time to take the story to market. Facebook had rated Zach as greatly exceeding expectations, which made it a strong story.

Zach points out that an interviewer does not see hours worked, only what was done, and gets a different vantage point on impact without much of the negative data from the current job. After the notification machine-learning optimizations and other technical work, Zach was sure a senior role was available at any big tech company by describing that work in detail.
