Zach credits luck: the Netflix hiring manager was the former Facebook manager, who had already seen the work and trusted it. Zach says this is why building a network matters.

Zach separates personal brand, such as LinkedIn posts or videos, from internal brand, meaning how colleagues know a person. Zach says a strong internal brand was what worked here, built by working hard with that manager.

QWhat was Zach's plan at Netflix, and how did promotions and reviews work there?

Zach Wilson

At 24, Zach pictured becoming a principal engineer (L7 or L8) by 30, doing deep technical work, and judged that data engineering would not get there. The Netflix work was real-time security threat detection, which Zach calls cutting-edge and hard.

Netflix had no promotions in the Meta sense. Managers gave a quarterly color: green meant fine, yellow meant pick it up, and red meant imminent firing. Once a year came a pay discussion based on what other companies would offer, not on past work, and a manager could adjust pay at any time.

Zach did not mind the lack of levels. Zach expected high pay and still had much to learn from the manager. Zach says to think about the story of impact at every company and to tell it in an exciting way.

Zach tends to leave jobs about every two years, so Zach has to be satisfied with the story first. At Airbnb, Zach felt an urge to quit early but realized there was no good story yet and stayed six more months. A story is a fully delivered package of impact that can be sold: if hired, here is what will be delivered in two years.

What was the Facebook story that Zach sold to Netflix?
Zach Wilson

Zach names three items. The first was a reachability metric for notifications, a counterweight to spam that tracked who was turning off settings and proved more complex than expected. The second was the first growth dashboard that covered WhatsApp, Instagram, Messenger and Facebook in one chart. The third was the pipeline behind Facebook's notification-selection machine-learning algorithm, which Zach made 90 percent cheaper, or ten times more efficient, using sorted merge bucket joins.

It caused so much stress that Zach took a month-long mental health break. Zach agrees that the Netflix case shows the problem the delay is meant to prevent. Zach says content creation has helped with the last one, which means presenting an idea so others will back it.

At earlier levels an engineer simply delivers the assigned work and solves the hard problem. At staff level, Zach says, the new behavior is deciding which problem to solve, which Zach found overwhelming at Netflix.

Zach Wilson

By December 2020, Zach had played a lot of video games and felt unfulfilled and depressed. Zach's girlfriend at the time asked what Zach was doing with life, and they broke up. With no job, no partner and a dog to support, Zach decided to take another swing at interviewing.

Zach also started making content on LinkedIn that month, having told Netflix colleagues in March that they would see Zach again as a famous person. Zach regrets not starting during the pandemic, when growth was easier. Zach interviewed at Meta, Google and Airbnb, for software engineering at the first two and data engineering at Airbnb, and received offers from all three.

Zach Wilson

Google and Facebook both offered senior roles. Zach recalls about 400 to 415 from Facebook and a lower Google figure that the captions cut off, similar to what Netflix had paid years earlier. Airbnb offered, by Zach's account, more than $100,000 above that, which made the choice easy even though the offers were not really competing.

Zach also liked how Airbnb does data engineering. The work was about 95 percent Scala and 5 percent Python, with no SQL, and the pipelines had to match online pricing and availability systems. Zach says this blend of pipelines, integrations and optimization was what Zach had wanted at Netflix.

QIf Zach started again as an IC3, what would Zach change?

Zach Wilson

Zach would be more open to other perspectives. In the first years Zach focused on becoming the most technical person, and now thinks that matters mostly up to senior engineer. After that, technical skill helps only marginally and other skills are needed.

Zach did not start building soft skills until Netflix, when things were on fire and the skills were urgently needed. Developing them earlier at Facebook, in lower-risk situations where failure felt smaller, would have given better balance and probably faster growth.

Zach also says not to eat dinner at work. Zach calls it a scam: in Zach's view, Facebook and Google offer it to keep people at the office longer. Zach would have used those hours for the gym, since fitness started only in 2018, and for other parts of life.

Zach adds that health matters: earning $20 million while stressed and dying at 50 is not a good life, and health, wealth and happiness each matter differently at different times.

Part

Leadership, influence, and organization

Technical work happens inside relationships and organizations. These sections examine decision-making, management, corporate politics, and the ways good intent can create unexpected effects.

Section 78 · companion

Escalation, corroboration, and credible alternatives

Ethan Evans explains why leaders can resist evidence of a weak manager and how careful, truthful framing can make a difficult career conversation easier to hear.

QHave reports escalated problems with their managers to you, and why might a skip-level leader resist acting?

Ethan Evans

Ethan Evans says such escalations were common. He describes an uncomfortable incentive: accepting one report’s account can create three problems for the skip-level leader—deciding what to do about the manager, replacing and training someone if necessary, and covering the work in between. Dismissing the report as oversensitive instead makes the problem easier to delegate back to the manager. Evans presents this as a possible subconscious bias, not a defense of ignoring a valid concern.

He recounts discovering a leader’s poor treatment of women only after several reports accumulated and he spoke with affected colleagues. A lone earlier report might not have moved him, a failure he describes candidly. Multiple independently supported accounts changed his understanding. He therefore recommends corroboration when colleagues are willing to provide it; the speaker’s “mutiny” metaphor concerns workplace escalation and should not obscure the seriousness of the example.

Should a high-performing IC compare observations with colleagues before escalating?
Ethan Evans

If possible, yes. It first checks whether the problem is a broader pattern or a working-style mismatch. A colleague who works well with the manager may offer a useful adjustment; colleagues seeing the same problem may corroborate it. Shared dissatisfaction is not enough unless they are also willing to speak.

Evans proposes telling the skip-level leader that named colleagues are willing to share similar examples and asking the leader to speak with them. He thinks many leaders will do that, while explicitly refusing to guarantee it. The host flags the difference between casual complaints and formal escalation, including the possibility of retaliation or being wrong.

Source: 03:04–05:21 ↗
Source: 00:00–03:03 ↗

QCould you seek a move for business reasons instead of organizing an escalation?

Ethan Evans

Evans separates two approaches. If there is a genuinely plausible case that another role would make the engineer equally or more valuable to the organization, lead with that case and do not introduce the manager complaint. If the real need is incompatible working relationships, explain that blame-free and think several moves ahead about the choices the leader actually has.

He describes his own move at Amazon. His leader wanted to keep him in the current role, but Evans had another available role outside that leader’s organization as well as a preferred role inside it. Explaining that remaining where he was had ceased to be an available choice changed the decision from “keep him here or move him internally” to “keep him in the organization or lose him.” After weeks of resistance, the internal move happened quickly. The story depends on having real alternatives, not on inventing an outside offer.

Source: 04:35–08:06 ↗

QHow did you communicate those alternatives without sounding threatening?

Ethan Evans

He framed the situation in terms the leader would recognize. Both were vice presidents, and the alternative offer came from a senior vice president. Evans explained that he needed to answer and that once he gave his word, he would have to honor it—as the leader himself would. That let the leader understand the constraint without a blunt demand.

Evans recommends preparing the key phrase before a predictable conversation rather than improvising under pressure. The facts and commitment should remain true; careful framing changes how the other person receives them. Delivery matters too. The same statement about needing to consider one’s career can sound hostile or calm and understandable depending on tone and body language.

He acknowledges that some engineers dislike workplace politics. His argument is that leaders still have emotions, stress, and defensiveness, so understanding the human interaction helps a person communicate an honest need more effectively. He does not claim he has fully figured out how to teach the skill.

Were there three different roles involved?
Ethan Evans

Yes: the current role, the role he wanted inside the same organization, and another available role elsewhere. The host characterizes the alternative as leverage. Evans agrees with the underlying structure while emphasizing that he did not explicitly issue a threat; he stated the true consequence of accepting another offer and giving his word.

Source: 09:35–10:24 ↗
Source: 08:07–12:34 ↗

Section 79 · interview

Managing managers changes the consequences of small actions

A Meta senior manager explains why wider organizational scope requires new interaction habits.

QWhat skill gaps appear when a first-line manager steps into a manager-of-managers role?

Meta senior manager

The guest emphasizes learning how to add value to the managers who report to you. A more senior role changes which interventions help and which undermine the organization. He illustrates this with a skip-level meeting in which a newly promoted leader asks leading questions about an employee’s manager. The employee may start relying on the senior leader instead, while the manager feels bypassed and weakened.

The important failure is not simply having the meeting. It is overlooking how questions and judgments propagate through a management chain. Small actions become magnified across multiple relationships. The guest says these subtleties are often learned through observation and practice, not only from reading about management.

He expects some mistakes during the transition, just as new managers make mistakes when moving from individual contribution. A promotion decision should therefore consider the support around the person: whether their own leader can help them recognize and repair problems. Strategy and organizational design also matter, but early interaction errors can cause damage before those longer-term responsibilities become the main issue.

Source: 00:00–03:10 ↗

QHow do individual-contributor and management growth compare, and are they meritocratic?

Meta senior manager

He says that evaluation becomes more opaque at high levels in either path. In calibration discussions, a person may be associated with a valuable initiative without having been instrumental in its success. The same attribution problem applies to managers. A short review period can make it difficult to separate a persuasive account from a clearly demonstrated contribution.

Longer observation can clarify the picture: a leader who repeatedly produces good outcomes over several years is easier to assess than someone in one half-year cycle. He thinks some senior IC and first-line-management work is more visible to an outside observer, while higher-level work often requires access to the internal details and leadership chain.

He does not offer a simple verdict that one ladder is fair and the other unfair. His concern is insufficient evidence and accountability when the relevant impact is hard to trace. The resulting frustration is real for employees with limited visibility, and a desire for fairness does not automatically create the data needed to judge it.

Source: 03:12–05:49 ↗

Section 80 · interview

Principal work begins by defining the problem

Ilya Grigorik describes senior technical agency, versatility across execution styles, and the resilience of a broad skill portfolio.

QWhat distinguishes principal and distinguished engineering?

Grigorik resists a fixed checklist for principal engineers. At that level, defining useful work is part of the job. He expects someone entering an unfamiliar organization to understand its landscape, locate problems, form relationships with directors and other partners, and determine where their skills can help. His seven-day reconnaissance analogy emphasizes agency rather than a literal universal deadline.

Distinguished work adds evidence of dynamic range. Technically, someone must be able to reconstruct constraints from low-level implementation while also understanding business requirements and translating them into useful changes. Equally important is choosing an execution style that matches the problem.

At a frontier, rapid experiments reveal what is unknown: act, observe, adjust, and repeat. A platform API with consequences for a partner ecosystem years later needs slower, more deliberate analysis. Even there, divergent exploration must converge into an actionable recommendation. He compares distinguished expectations to a VP’s responsibility for difficult, irregular problems that lower layers could not resolve.

His broader career philosophy is to become the only person able to combine a useful portfolio of skills, rather than always compete to be the best at one specialty. He respects specialists, but thinks broad combinations can be more resilient when a field, company, or market changes.

Source: 00:00–09:57 ↗

QDoes “be the only” mean combining multiple skills to handle ambiguous situations?

Yes. He illustrates it with his own ability to combine modest design, sales, support, hosting, security, and engineering skills to create something useful without assembling a large team. When a true specialist joins, he can hand over that component and redirect his attention.

Learning enough of another domain to understand its language can make cross-functional work possible. He recalls reading many marketing books to converse with marketing colleagues, while writing experience helped with PR. His estimates about acquiring a high fraction of competence quickly express a heuristic rather than a measured universal learning curve.

The senior person need not be the most knowledgeable. Grigorik’s role can be to understand platform fundamentals and business needs, identify the people who know the implementation details, and help them navigate the decision. Pattern recognition, knowing where to find answers, and facilitating the right expertise are different from memorizing every API.

Management experience provides another usable skill: an IC can temporarily coach or give feedback with an understanding of managers’ concerns. The portfolio matters because it lets someone change how they contribute as the problem changes.

Should ICs try management, and can they return?

He encourages a team-lead role as a way to learn, and management itself if it suits the person. He rejects treating the transition as one-way or viewing a return to IC work as a demotion. Managers sometimes remember being happiest before taking the next role, even while valuing what management taught them. Organizations should let people carry those skills across roles without penalty.

Source: 11:29–13:12 ↗
Source: 09:57–11:27 ↗
Editorial synthesis
Different uncertainty requires a different execution style
SituationUseful mode
New product or frontier with unknown constraintsRun quick experiments, observe results, and redirect.
Platform decision with lasting ecosystem effectsExplore consequences deliberately, then converge on a recommendation.

Section 81 · interview

Scope quickly enough to learn, and concretely enough to get feedback

Boris Cherny recalls planning a rapidly expanding organization and using parallel designs to expose risk.

QHow can one person scope projects for hundreds of engineers?

Boris Cherny

Cherny describes a period when Facebook Groups grew from roughly 150–200 people to roughly 600–800 as leadership invested in a communities strategy. Executive support created resources quickly, and technical leads then had to decide what those engineers would actually build. He repeatedly produced rough scoping documents that compared several technical options and matched an approximate team size to the selected approach.

In hindsight, he would have added fewer people at first. He thinks the important work was solving people’s problems and finding product fit, then gradually increasing investment. Headcount could not create that learning all at once. The distinction is between an executive’s capacity to fund a priority and the product team’s need to discover a good direction.

For a particularly large migration merging group and page data models, the problem spanned product, integrity, advertising, and data layers. Rather than wait indefinitely for a decision, Cherny gathered technical leads, divided them into two teams, and gave both the same requirements and roughly three hours to design a solution. The independently produced designs were about 80 percent alike. Their shared core offered a direction for execution; the differences made the uncertainty visible and suggested targeted technical spikes.

Source: 00:00–03:42 ↗

QHow did people react to the internal design competition?

Boris Cherny

Cherny says it was an unusual idea and he largely acted by scheduling the session. The unclear path required action, but because he did not already know the answer, it also required gathering people to build agreement. He treats leadership as balancing those two modes: sometimes a leader must create the conditions for a decision instead of first obtaining consensus on every part of the process.

Source: 03:44–04:34 ↗

QWhat advice would you give a technical lead who needs to scope work quickly?

Boris Cherny

His main warning is spending too long in details. Start at a high level and time-box a rough plan—he suggests about 30 minutes for an initial pass, or a couple of hours when the code needs investigation. Scoping cannot eliminate every detail before work begins.

Find the experts and present a straw-man design rather than only asking an open-ended question. A concrete proposal gives them something to correct. He also says the AI tools available in his interview context could help explore a codebase and identify systems involved, a task that previously demanded more manual investigation. That tool example is part of his account, not a requirement to adopt a particular product.

Source: 04:34–05:44 ↗
Editorial synthesis

Section 82 · interview

Understand the incentives behind a performance plan

Ethan Evans explains how a target can force neglected performance conversations while also biasing managers toward departure.

QWhat do you think of stack ranking, attrition targets, and performance improvement plans?

Ethan Evans

Evans describes an Amazon attrition-target system from his management experience: a list of people whose departure was considered unregretted, with pressure to reach an annual proportion through improvement, resignation, or termination. His quoted percentages vary by period and are historical recollections, not verified current policy.

He says that when Amazon experimentally removed the target, managers stopped having difficult conversations with struggling performers, and the goal returned. Managers may avoid acting when a person is well liked, especially in a large organization where the immediate cost is not obvious to them. The target forced attention to a real problem.

The other side is distortion. A quota can put someone on a list who still had a plausible chance of success. Once a manager has mentally decided a person should leave, confirmation bias can make the improvement plan psychologically unrealistic. Evans believes many plans therefore function more as a route to departure than an open-minded attempt to improve.

He reports unsuccessful experiences coaching roughly half a dozen people on Amazon PIPs and similar outcomes among people who did not use his coaching. He now urges people in that situation to prepare for another job rather than rely on reversal. That is a strong warning based on his cases, not a measured universal failure rate.

Even a manager starting with good intentions may face pressure from HR and leadership to count an exit, or to name another person if the first improves. Evans’s broader diagnosis is that companies often fail to train managers for early, useful performance conversations, then depend on a distorted late-stage process.

Source: 00:00–04:58 ↗

QWhat prevents a manager from presenting an employee unfairly to HR?

Ethan Evans

Evans distinguishes removing one employee from repeatedly driving people out. A pattern of high turnover can eventually expose a manager, but one case may remain difficult to challenge. The manager usually has higher status and can frame the issue for HR before the employee realizes that a dispute is developing.

He illustrates narrative ambiguity with code reviews. The same large number of reviews can be described as improving everyone’s code and developing the team, or as nitpicking others while contributing little original implementation. Counts do not by themselves determine which interpretation is accurate.

He says he has not personally used this power to target someone unfairly, and notes that keeping capable partners serves a manager’s goals. His concern is the vulnerability to a vindictive manager or a genuinely different view of what constitutes useful work. HR hearing a familiar denial of poor performance may not easily distinguish a legitimate complaint.

His practical conclusion is to repair the relationship where possible or find a different manager, rather than assume HR will necessarily rescue the employee. This is his description of a power imbalance, not approval of retaliation or a claim that every organization lacks checks.

Source: 05:00–09:29 ↗

Section 83 · interview

Brendan Burns: Kubernetes Strategy, Open Source, and Convincing Management

Burns explains how Kubernetes was pitched inside Google, why it was open sourced and governed independently, and what the team learned about scale and career choices.

Burns's view: a running prototype persuades more than a strategy document

Burns describes Kubernetes as a prototype built by Burns, Craig, and Joe that then had to be argued for inside Google. In Burns's view, a running system persuades more than a strategy document. Open source was the realistic route once other companies were building similar tools, and written governance kept any single company from controlling the roadmap. Editorial framing: the rounds follow the interview order, from business case to build, architecture, governance, scale and career.

Source: 00:37–1:06:16 ↗

QWhat would Burns have told Google's leadership about the impact of building Kubernetes for the industry?

Brendan Burns

Burns says the hardest early task was persuading people inside Google, though the team was clear on the goal. Burns gave three arguments. The first drew on MapReduce and the big data wave. Google had written the original white paper, but Hadoop re-implemented the ideas as an open source project, and Google got no credit.

The second argument was about containers. Burns says reliable software needs systems that act like autopilots for applications. The third was open source, which Burns calls the most interesting part. People accepted that the system should be built, then asked why it should not stay on Google's own platform.

Why would it not work to keep Kubernetes only on Google's platform?
Brendan Burns

Burns says many people were on other clouds or on premises, and an exclusive product would shut them out. They would build an alternative. Burns compares this with Linux, which won because it could run anywhere. Most people were not on the leading platform, and Google Cloud was not the leader.

Burns's answer is to build for everyone, and make the system strongest on Google's platform. Burns also says that if nearly everything else was open, a closed project would need to be so differentiated that people wanted it anyway.

Source: 03:47–05:24 ↗
Was the idea to take market share from AWS, so developers would migrate to GCP?
Brendan Burns

Burns describes AWS as dominant and first, and GCP as up and coming. Burns agrees the aim was attention, but adds that copying an existing model, such as virtual machines, is hard to sell. Creating a new field where Google was the thought leader gave it a voice, even among people who did not use its platform.

Burns says the strategy did not fully work, because GCP was still third. Burns would not call it a failure. Kubernetes consolidated across the cloud market and is now a utility everywhere.

Source: 05:26–07:09 ↗
Did leadership understand the visibility benefits when they agreed to the project?
Brendan Burns

Burns says the team explicitly wanted to be front and center in thought leadership. That value is hard to quantify. The effort was cheap, with about eight or nine engineers.

Burns calls the separate Kubernetes brand a blessing and a curse. It gave the team freedom to fail without damaging Google Cloud's reputation. Moving to the Linux Foundation let companies such as Red Hat, Azure, and AWS bet on it with confidence. Burns calls the structure an insurance policy, and says it made the team more agile than startups such as Docker.

Source: 07:12–09:24 ↗
Source: 00:37–03:46 ↗

QThe earliest version was you and two others hacking something together. What did the first demo do?

Brendan Burns

Burns says it was almost a demo of what happens when existing open source tools are joined together. A basic control tool deployed a container across several machines. Requests to one endpoint reached different replicas, a killed instance came back, and a basic upgrade worked. Burns says that was about it.

How long did the initial MVP take to build?
Brendan Burns

Burns says a little under a week, roughly four or five days, since Burns does not work weekends.

Source: 10:21–10:34 ↗
Did you drop existing work to build it, since it was extra?
Brendan Burns

Burns says the other work was not dropped outright, but there was room to slack on it for a short stretch. The MVP was hacked together with every shortcut available. Much of it came from other open source projects, joined with glue code.

Source: 10:35–11:42 ↗
Source: 09:26–10:20 ↗

QMany engineers think they cannot build something like this beside their existing responsibilities. What advice would you give?

Brendan Burns

Burns gives two answers. The first is advice Burns has given everyone who worked for Burns: hide about 10 percent of your effort from management. Everyone has slack, and as an organization grows, that 10 percent can do more. Burns says many influential ideas came from it. The aim is to let people make local decisions without asking permission up the chain.

Burns warns that some ideas will fail, and the failures waste time. Still, one success may separate exceeding expectations from meeting them. A person has to accept betting on several ideas. Burns says this is not everyone's path.

Burns's second answer is that the time has to come from somewhere. Burns asks what people give up, since most have 10 to 20 hours a week outside work, spent on games, streaming, or YouTube. Burns says the returns were exponential: two times the time for a year could bring 20 times the impact.

Burns also found the work addictive. Once users filed issues on GitHub, Burns wanted to keep closing them, and kept going until falling asleep at the laptop. Burns was not thinking about a career payoff.

Source: 11:43–16:12 ↗

QIt seems it took a while to get leadership buy-in. How did that happen?

Brendan Burns

Burns says it took a solid six months to go from a very hacky prototype to something a team could use. Many early hires had built similar systems, so the project felt like a clean-room chance to rebuild with better ideas. Burns says that is rare for an engineer.

There were no users yet, so the team did not have to fix bugs for a paying customer. The people involved had long thought about what the system could look like, and could now build it.

Source: 16:13–17:30 ↗

QWhat does hiding 10 percent of effort from management look like in practice?

Brendan Burns

Burns says a person should always have a side project that nobody assigned but that matters. The host compares this to Google's 20 percent time, and Burns agrees the idea is similar.

Burns says hide is meant literally: do not ask permission at first. A project may need a couple of months before it can be shown. Burns says a running system is far more persuasive than a document or slide deck. The manager then decides whether the built idea is good, not whether to spend time on it.

What if nobody cares when you launch, or it is not as good as you hoped?
Brendan Burns

Burns says that is the flip side. Some time will be wasted, possibly including a promotion that did not come because the work was not the breakthrough the person expected. Burns says this is a risk, like a startup. A person should enter thinking the idea is good, worth trying, and acceptable to fail.

Source: 19:51–21:18 ↗
Do senior engineers need to take that kind of risk to be promoted?
Brendan Burns

The host says senior engineers who ask how to get promoted are often told to find the project, since the work has become too ambiguous to hand over. Burns agrees this becomes a necessity at higher levels, where people must come up with good ideas, not only execute them.

Burns says the project helped Burns's own career. Credit for an idea you create entirely is obvious, while credit for a bigger project or someone else's idea is harder to attribute. Burns calls it a roll of the dice, and says timing matters too.

Source: 21:20–23:25 ↗
Source: 17:33–19:49 ↗

QBorg looked like a competitive advantage for Google. How did you convince people it was acceptable to share part of it?

Brendan Burns

Burns says people who leave Google are not wiped like the characters in Men in Black. The team also talked to Facebook, Twitter, and other scale-out companies building similar systems, so the technology was not really a secret. Mesos was similar, so an open source option was coming.

Burns says the team reframed the choice. The question was not whether an open source version would exist, but whether Google wanted to influence it or see someone else control it. A proprietary option was not viable.

Source: 23:33–25:27 ↗

QWith no customers yet, how did you decide the minimum feature set before launch?

Brendan Burns

Burns says the team of three had complementary skills. Craig was a strong product and business lead, Joe was strong in API design, and Burns could write prototypes quickly. The team drew on the pain of deploying onto traditional infrastructure and on immutable infrastructure ideas that Netflix was discussing.

Burns says there were no customers yet, but there would be. Burns describes Kubernetes as a coalescing of ideas already circulating in the industry, given an anchor point and a clear expression.

Did you write most of the initial code yourself?
Brendan Burns

Burns estimates the high 80s percent, or more, of the original code was Burns's, though Burns is not sure of the exact figure. Burns is now about fifth on the overall GitHub commit list, after being first for a long time.

Source: 27:23–27:54 ↗
Source: 25:28–27:20 ↗

QAfter writing so much of the code, which part of the system was hardest to build?

Brendan Burns

Burns says the hardest part was the early decision to make the system loosely coupled. Many independent control loops act across the system. That helps resiliency, but when something goes wrong, roughly 15 processes must be pieced together from many logs, and early logging and events were inconsistent.

Burns says problems that reproduce easily are simple to fix, since you add logs and run again. Transient race conditions are much harder. The team was also learning Go, with gotchas picked up on the fly.

Was there something controlling everything, such as leader election? What did you use?
Brendan Burns

Burns says the team relied almost entirely on etcd. It was an open source key-value store that CoreOS had written, now part of Kubernetes, and it implements the Raft consensus protocol. Paxos is hard to implement and not many people understand it. Raft is provably correct and much easier to implement.

Burns says etcd does not do leader election directly, but it gives enough building blocks. Burns also pushed hard for a rule that all access goes through an API server, so nothing wrote to disk directly.

Source: 30:19–32:45 ↗
What is the main benefit of routing everything through the API server?
Brendan Burns

Burns says components can restart and come back working, without worrying about corruption or schema changes. Apart from etcd, they are effectively stateless, so the system was easier to make stable. The downside is loose coupling, which made debugging harder.

Burns frames it as state machines versus control loops. A state machine is easy to debug but hard to make reliable, because an unexpected state may have no clear next step. Burns says the system was designed to be stable but hard to debug. Control loops drive the current state toward a desired state, from wherever they wake up. The host recognizes this as PID control, and Burns agrees.

Source: 32:48–35:03 ↗
Source: 27:55–30:17 ↗

QKubernetes is declarative rather than imperative. What are the pros and cons of that design?

Brendan Burns

Burns says the approach was part of the wider infrastructure-as-code movement. The benefit is clarity. A list of steps records actions but not the objective, while a declaration writes down the goal, such as a reliable website, and asks the system to reach it. That record lets the system self-heal after a failure or restart.

Burns says a declaration also allows code review and unit tests. The main downside is complexity, including a YAML learning curve. Burns says there is now enough educational material, and generative AI helps. Burns's view is that the upsides are large and the downsides small.

Does declaring the outcome also let you optimize under the hood?
Brendan Burns

The host suggests so, and Burns agrees it makes machine failures easier to handle. People do not say run this on that machine. They say they want three replicas somewhere, so if a machine fails, the workload moves.

Source: 37:45–38:46 ↗
Source: 35:04–37:43 ↗

QHow did you get companies such as Red Hat, with OpenShift, to bet on Kubernetes?

Brendan Burns

Burns says many early partners were building a platform or a reliable web service anyway. For them, building the same layer together beat building it alone, because their value was not in that layer.

Burns says partners had to be equals. Taking a dependency also means depending on someone's roadmap, so the team offered a seat at the design table. Later, networking and storage providers joined, because their users were moving to Kubernetes.

Source: 38:47–41:05 ↗

QHow did you keep Google from dominating the roadmap, when Google started and largely funded the project?

Brendan Burns

Burns says independence was critical to adoption. The first step was a foundation. About a year in, the team donated all of Kubernetes to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, under the Linux Foundation, because partners cannot easily collaborate when one company holds the trademarks.

The second step came later. The project had no written governance for its first few years, which Burns calls a mistake. In 2016 the team wrote rules so that no single company could take control, with a distributed, democratic model rather than a benevolent dictator. The host says contributors would not join without good governance, and Burns agrees.

Do you mean a constitution? Did you write it yourselves, or did lawyers?
Brendan Burns

Burns says the team wrote it. About seven or eight people met in a couple of intense sessions, looked at other communities, and codified loose arrangements that already existed informally. They also created a steering committee, which had never existed before.

Burns says the group was called the bootstrap committee. Its members were respected leaders who did not fight with each other. Burns credits Sarah Novotny, the community leader at the time, with bringing them together.

Source: 44:02–46:06 ↗
Source: 41:06–44:00 ↗

QWhat share of contributions comes from the community, and what share from the main companies?

Brendan Burns

Burns does not have Kubernetes numbers. From general open source experience, core contributors make up roughly 80 to 90 percent of the work, and less than 10 percent comes from other people. Companies such as Microsoft commit to upstream teams, but for many users, technology is a means to an end.

Burns says it is hard to justify putting 10 percent of staff into upstream work at a bank or retailer, especially when leaders did not grow up in open source. Legal teams also block some contributions, because they fear liability for bugs. Burns says that worry does not hold water, and the Linux Foundation can supply case law, but it can still be enough to stop a contribution.

Would someone actually be sued for adding a bug?
Brendan Burns

Burns says the chain of logic is easy to imagine, such as an open source JPEG library in a smoke detector causing a fire. Burns does not think it holds, since many open source licenses include indemnification language. Burns says a developer in a non-tech company may not be able to argue with legal, so the contribution fades away.

Source: 48:17–50:00 ↗
Source: 46:07–48:15 ↗

QHow has Kubernetes adjusted to AI training, which runs in huge bursts, and to inference, which needs low latency?

Brendan Burns

Burns says Kubernetes could not handle much more than about 100 nodes early on. The team optimized the core systems and reduced noisy APIs. etcd can be the main bottleneck at scale, so running etcd well is central. Burns compares this to any large database: the team ran the system, saw where it broke, fixed it, and repeated.

Burns says cloud users changed the shape of demand. On AKS a cluster appears in about two minutes, so many users run hundreds or thousands of smaller clusters. The team had to invest, with Azure, in managing clusters consistently. Burns jokes that containers were meant to end snowflake servers, and now clusters are the snowflakes.

Is there an upper bound? If load rose tenfold, would Kubernetes break?
Brendan Burns

Burns says the storage layer is the limit. Most other parts scale out horizontally. At ten times the load, the team may have to make etcd scale or replace it with something similar that can run at larger scale. Burns sees nothing inherent in the design that prevents this.

Burns cites a familiar saying: every time you change an order of magnitude, the problem moves. Burns expects people to keep pushing scale, because motivation drives the work, as long as the design does not block it.

Source: 53:22–55:29 ↗
Source: 50:01–53:20 ↗

QYou have a PhD in robotics, and many people advise against PhDs. What is your view?

Brendan Burns

Burns says it is among the top questions Burns gets. In one story, a college classmate went into start-ups and industry, and ended up at the same level as Burns, who had done a PhD. Burns says it probably does not matter much either way.

Burns also says the PhD was fun, and taught writing and presenting ideas that industry did not. That helped in the six-month argument for open sourcing the project. Burns later taught CS 101 for a couple of years, which helped explain Kubernetes to newcomers.

Burns's summary: the degree probably does not matter, but Burns learned useful skills and had fun.

What is the top question you get asked?
Brendan Burns

Burns says the most common question is how to know what to learn. Burns does not care which field someone learns, only that they are learning. Find something you are excited about, because you will then put in the effort instead of watching YouTube. Systems engineers are still needed.

Burns says there was never a career plan. Burns chased things that seemed useful or fun. A plan suits some people, but things that look like mistakes can become critical lessons. As long as you are learning, you are probably fine.

Source: 58:24–1:00:21 ↗
Source: 55:31–58:14 ↗

QBurns has said the inevitable trajectory of software is death. How could Kubernetes end?

Brendan Burns

Burns still stands by it. The point is not to cling to software that is dying, and to be willing to throw code away. Burns says Kubernetes's own original code has been rewritten several times. An ending would likely be something that achieves similar things more easily, with less complexity.

Burns expects some technologies to become hidden. A reliable natural-language interface could make a web service easier to request than writing YAML. Burns notes that Kubernetes sits on Linux, and Linux on a processor, and people may focus so much on AI that they forget the layers beneath.

Burns would be surprised if Kubernetes was still running in 100 years, though computing has not existed long enough to be sure. Six years ago Burns would have doubted x86 was going away on servers. Now GPUs do much of the processing, and ARM64 matters on servers for energy reasons. Burns compares predictions with self-driving cars, which were five years away for about 15 years.

Source: 1:00:23–1:04:14 ↗

QIs there a book that most affected your career?

Brendan Burns

Burns says the biggest early influence was the Gang of Four book on design patterns, from the late 1990s or mid-1990s. The host names it as Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software, and Burns agrees. Later, Leadership on the Line mattered as Burns became a large organization leader, and The Five Dysfunctions of Teams is good for how teams operate, though Burns is unsure of that title.

So engineers should read the first book, and managers the other two?
Brendan Burns

The host sums it up that way, and Burns says that is about right, though a career evolves and a person may read both.

Source: 1:05:07–1:05:29 ↗
Source: 1:04:16–1:05:04 ↗

QIf you could go back to just after college and give yourself advice, what would you say?

Brendan Burns

Burns says keep better notes. There is a strong MBA thesis or book in the Kubernetes journey, but Burns does not have enough notes to write it.

The host jokes that an LLM could parse the code. Burns says notes and code are not the main gap. Burns misses the partner discussions and interpersonal work, which Burns remembers only in part.

Source: 1:05:29–1:06:16 ↗

Section 84 · interview

Choose career moves for the capabilities they build

An engineering leader traces a research-to-CTO path and explains why directing managers, earning trust, and adapting to company growth required new skills.

QWhy did you move from research to Facebook?

After five years in a PhD program and three at IBM Research, the guest questioned a mixed research-and-engineering career. He considered academia, quantitative finance, and software engineering, then chose engineering because he wanted to build products affecting many people.

He also wanted engineering to have central status. In his view, finance treated it as supporting another function, while a fast-growing company like Facebook offered both engineering priority and broad impact. These are his reasons for choosing among the opportunities available around 2009, not a general ranking of those professions.

Source: 00:41–03:23 ↗

QHow did the director opportunity at Square arise?

He corrects the host’s premise: he joined Square with a director offer rather than receiving an internal promotion from frontline manager. The team grew from approximately twenty-five to more than fifty people in about a year. Building machine-learning and data infrastructure teams exposed him to a new job: directing through managers rather than directly managing engineers.

Source: 03:23–05:07 ↗

QWhat was the biggest skill gap in moving from manager to director?

At Facebook he had become a manager after being an IC, so knowing the team’s technical details gave him authority. At a new company, his reports had longer tenure and knew more than he did. He could no longer justify the extra leadership layer by being the most informed person in the room.

He thinks he performed poorly during roughly the first half-year. Reflection led him toward strategic direction, cross-department resource coordination, and the organization’s hardest problems. The job was to guide an organization toward a better future, rather than reproduce the frontline managers’ work.

Another turning point was understanding what each manager wanted from him. He tried to identify missing capabilities and help them grow toward the next level. That reframed him as someone adding value to their careers.

How did you handle managers who hoped to receive the role you were hired into?

He recognized the natural disappointment and tried to demonstrate that his arrival could help their prospects rather than block them. Building trust came first, followed by concrete help with growth and obstacles they could not remove alone. He credits The Five Dysfunctions of a Team with emphasizing trust as the foundation beneath other team behavior.

Source: 09:16–11:29 ↗
Source: 05:09–09:16 ↗

QIs changing companies the best way to move up management levels?

He does not think so; former Facebook colleagues reached very senior roles by staying. His own moves followed a different goal: eventually becoming CTO of an AI company. The intended outcome revealed gaps in infrastructure, frontend work, products, and how an industry business operates.

At Snapchat he could lead data or camera. He deliberately chose camera despite a data and machine-learning background, learning iOS and Android work and spending about two months on iOS study. The product role forced collaboration with product managers and designers that he might not have gained by staying in a familiar backend specialty.

He recalls those first two years as especially happy because he was expanding his knowledge every day. The lesson is to choose an opportunity for the capability it supplies, rather than infer that any external title increase is a sound strategy.

Source: 11:31–15:31 ↗

QHow much must an engineering leader know the team’s details?

Facebook’s bootcamp impressed him: even a newly hired VP fixed bugs and submitted code alongside other hires. He adopted the belief that engineering leadership should remain technical. He still writes and reviews code, mentioning several pull requests a week, and wants enough detail to make sound strategic judgments rather than speak without understanding.

How do you balance technical depth with higher-leverage leadership work?

At the start of a week, he identifies the three most important outcomes and concentrates there. Sometimes learning implementation detail is one of those outcomes; other weeks it is not. Recalibrating priorities toward his broader goal matters more than repeating the same activity or simply adding hours. Time is finite, so the key is allocation.

Source: 17:03–18:52 ↗
Source: 15:31–17:03 ↗

QHow did Los Angeles differ from Silicon Valley?

Snapchat itself felt surprisingly similar to Facebook’s fast-moving culture, partly because early employees came from established technology centers. The wider city offered a more varied social environment than the technology-heavy conversations he remembered from the Bay Area. Neighbors in unrelated professions helped him consider users outside technology and AI circles. A captioned neighbor’s job title is uncertain, so it is not specified here.

Source: 18:52–20:53 ↗

QWhat drove your organization’s growth to about 250 engineers?

He relates the team’s growth to Snapchat’s overall expansion from approximately one hundred employees to three thousand in two years, while crediting recruiting and interviewer effort. Rapid growth was also painful: a culture that works for one hundred people differs from one for three thousand. He likens each doubling to building a new company. Leaders need to adapt instead of insisting that an earlier organizational answer remain right indefinitely.

Source: 20:54–22:42 ↗

QWhat did you learn from working with Evan Spiegel?

He recalls an unusually high product-quality bar, down to pixel-level issues in demos. His team learned to bring a genuinely polished demonstration, and he compares that attention with the familiar image of Steve Jobs.

He also describes a leader who valued personal relationships and kept promises. One story is Spiegel telling another leader not to fire the first fifteen engineers because of their founding contribution. Another is returning to the small house associated with Snapchat’s beginnings for board meetings. These are the guest’s accounts of leadership and loyalty, not a recommended universal employment rule.

Source: 22:43–24:58 ↗

QHow were you recruited into later leadership roles?

He says opportunities came inbound through recruiters or personal connections rather than an active search. He preferred people he knew because companies inevitably face both good and difficult periods. He wanted partners he could trust and think with through downturns. Building a professional network early made those later opportunities possible, though his personal inbound experience should not be assumed for every candidate.

Source: 24:59–27:23 ↗

QHow do you compare leadership offers when company size and titles differ?

He does not primarily rank valuation or reporting headcount. In fact, he says he would welcome fewer direct reports. The central test is whether the work brings him closer to the product-building outcome he wants.

Titles belong to a company’s structure and can lose significance when someone leaves. He would rather be known for making a useful product than for holding a senior label. He imagines a very small team building an extremely valuable company, but presents that as an aspiration and prediction rather than an established requirement.

When hiring for his startup, he wants candidates both to believe a large outcome is possible and understand that its probability may be very low. The small probability is a candid framing of startup risk, not a measured forecast.

Why tell candidates that the chance of success is low?

He wants people to choose the challenge consciously so normal difficulties do not immediately overturn their expectations. Transparency helps identify the subset of engineers who want the journey, rather than persuade everyone. His battlefield analogy emphasizes preparation for uncertainty and shared commitment.

Source: 31:26–32:15 ↗
Source: 27:23–31:26 ↗

QWhat are the benefits and costs of using a personal north star instead of money or level?

He sees no universally right criterion. His research colleagues could have successful conventional careers. His own test is future regret: if, fifteen years later, he would regret never trying an AI company, he would rather try now. The goal aligns with his motivation, but he acknowledges that it can create a less conventional path.

Source: 32:15–34:16 ↗

QWhat do you regret or wish you had changed?

If he had known he would choose software engineering, he might not have taken the PhD route, though it taught him valuable things. He cannot predict ten years of change—and says even the next few months of AI are uncertain—so he emphasizes adaptability rather than wishing for perfect foresight. Difficult transitions from research to engineering or manager to director can be periods of adjustment, not proof of permanent failure.

Source: 34:16–36:00 ↗

QHow much management growth is situational rather than controllable?

Management roles are constrained by the organization’s needs and structure, which depend on company strategy. He increasingly accepts that he cannot control much of the timing. Doing excellent work in the current role is within his control; promotion is a later signal shaped by other conditions.

He criticizes treating the next level’s bullet points as a contract guaranteeing promotion once checked. That makes happiness dependent on an outcome the person cannot fully command. His alternative is impact now and movement toward work one wants over the long term, while remaining open to later opportunities or founding a company.

Source: 36:00–38:30 ↗

QWhat would you tell yourself just after your PhD?

Conventional wisdom need not decide a unique person’s path. He recalls choosing Carnegie Mellon over more broadly prestigious alternatives because of computer science, and leaving research for a small Facebook when few research peers would have done so. An unfamiliar route is less comfortable, but he believes independent thinking can reveal opportunities others miss. The advice follows from his goals rather than asserting that every unconventional choice wins.

Source: 38:30–39:58 ↗

QWhat is your current company trying to build?

The guest describes HeyGen as a human-centered video-generation platform aimed at everyday content professionals such as marketers and salespeople, rather than only film production. He emphasizes quality, consistency, controllability, and communicating across languages. His ambition is to make visual storytelling possible without a camera. These are the founder-side product claims and aspirations given in the interview, retained as context for the AI-company goal.

Source: 39:58–41:52 ↗

Section 85 · interview

Lead the project while preserving room to build

Jake Bolam describes large infrastructure migrations, accessible technical leadership, protected focus time, and a deliberately risk-sensitive review style.

QWhat was your path from joining Meta to principal engineer?

Bolam joined at IC6 in Facebook Groups during early pandemic remote onboarding. With election work limiting teammates’ availability, he had a slow start. His manager helped represent that context in reviews. He later moved to Instagram Web, closer to the UI and React work he had intended to do, and could contribute immediately.

Was your performance at risk during the slow onboarding?

He remembers a satisfactory rather than exceptional rating and thinks his manager’s explanation of the slow onboarding mattered. He does not claim that every slow ramp is automatically protected.

Source: 01:50–02:20 ↗
What was your background before Meta?

He began with frontend work but repeatedly moved into frontend and then backend infrastructure. He hoped a large company would let him specialize in product UI; the same pattern recurred. Experience made infrastructure easier for him to influence, and the larger server platform offered a greater impact surface.

Source: 02:50–04:45 ↗
Source: 00:48–02:50 ↗

QWhy did your managers offer you leadership across several teams?

He had already told them he wanted career growth and had led several teams before Meta. The organization needed coordination during a stack migration, and a strong first month demonstrated readiness. He was offered an opportunity to stretch from one team to multiple teams; he still had to deliver the project rather than treat the assignment itself as a promotion.

Source: 04:45–06:30 ↗

QWhat do IC7 and IC8 scope mean in your kind of work?

In his lens, IC6 often leads one team and IC7 works across teams or a broader area; IC8 extends the reach further. The significance of the problem also matters. Framework work affecting thousands of engineers can have substantial scope even without a corresponding reporting structure. He explicitly recognizes another path through deep specialists whose small code changes produce very large savings. These are examples, not fixed team-size rules.

Source: 06:30–08:40 ↗

QDid you deliberately choose a leadership archetype?

Not especially. He tries to do what the project needs while leaning on strengths in communication, coordination, and creating a team people enjoy working with. He wants others to succeed and thinks that can compound across a long project. He does not usually think in the host’s “force multiplier” label.

Why not management?

He has tried short management stints but wants the option to write a large amount of code when needed. He also prefers having managers who can check his occasional careless remarks. His preference combines the technical work he enjoys with awareness of interpersonal responsibilities.

Source: 09:50–10:18 ↗
Source: 08:42–09:50 ↗

QWhy remain available to colleagues despite senior responsibilities?

Accessibility reveals ideas and problems that might otherwise remain invisible and helps people move forward. He may have to defer a meeting when overloaded, but tries to find a route to help.

How do you decide whom to give time?

He tries to ignore levels, including for interns. Genuine questions and acting on advice encourage further investment. When he lacks time, he may defer or connect someone to a better-informed colleague. This is an attempt to balance access with limited capacity.

Source: 11:22–13:00 ↗
What makes a good question?

Be sincere about what you want to understand rather than script an impressive interaction. A real question makes it easier to identify the right person, including someone else with more time or expertise.

Source: 13:00–13:49 ↗
Source: 10:18–11:38 ↗

QWhat work drove the IC7 and IC8 promotions?

For IC7, a migration originally thought to take roughly two years achieved most of its work in about six months. That freed most resources for other work, including ads on Instagram Web. He credits the team rather than claim individual ownership of the speedup.

For IC8, leadership trusted him with the much harder move of Instagram’s backend into the main Meta stack. Many engineers initially saw no reason to leave a familiar, effective environment. Instead of beginning with a demanded migration, the team improved developer experience between the stacks, then added missing Instagram capabilities to the destination.

Over several years, crossing the boundary became easier, more surfaces moved for their own benefit, and demand shifted toward completing the migration. Major surface and traffic milestones demonstrated scope before the entire program was finished. He describes approximately one hundred fifty involved teams and meaningful performance or development improvements, while leaving exact credit and promotion decisions to their broader context.

How did a two-year migration become a six-month effort?

They cut scope, changed the strategy, and developed team momentum. Moving pages in larger batches rather than one at a time created difficult initial integration work but then allowed compounding progress. The team played to individual strengths and became convinced it could move sooner.

Source: 14:37–15:37 ↗
How did you make the team excited?

He cannot fully explain an organic process or take all the credit. He brought energy, colleagues reinforced one another, and people enjoyed shared progress. Finishing earlier benefited the whole team and enabled valuable subsequent work.

Source: 15:37–16:37 ↗
Source: 13:49–20:55 ↗

QHow did you keep developers satisfied during the infrastructure change?

A server-champions group connected representatives from across the organization, with product engineers making up most of the participants. That kept infrastructure grounded in everyday development. A continuing feedback channel often revealed trouble within hours, earlier than broad complaint groups where issues had to become severe before someone posted. Metrics complemented, rather than replaced, those relationships.

Source: 20:55–22:44 ↗

QHow did your work hours change as responsibility increased?

Hours fluctuate with excitement and the project: he sometimes works sixty or seventy hours, then deliberately returns toward forty or less during another period. He wants a life beyond work and attributes recent balance to systems developed across his career. The pattern is personal, not an assertion that a particular average guarantees principal-level impact.

Which systems protect that time?

He reserves roughly half the week for focus, avoids morning meetings because mornings suit him, aims for no meetings on Wednesdays and Fridays, and groups one-on-ones on Monday afternoons. Tuesday and Thursday afternoons can then hold project discussions. Exceptions occur; the value is a protected default, not rigid adherence.

Source: 23:54–24:55 ↗
What changes during a concentrated coding period?

He cancels many meetings for a few weeks once work has momentum and people know the plan. His projects may have necessary workstream meetings without layers of central recurring syncs. Lead coordination happens when needed through direct conversations or broader forums, and he remains reachable for urgent questions.

Source: 24:55–27:17 ↗
Do you also review code during those periods?

Yes. He checks pending reviews before his own coding and revisits them frequently because waiting for approval can block another engineer. Review is part of moving the project forward, rather than an interruption to personal output.

Source: 27:17–28:16 ↗
Source: 22:44–23:54 ↗

QHow do you decide the depth of a code review?

He scales effort to risk. Core architecture, live production changes, and system-wide decisions receive thorough attention. A gated, isolated leaf component can receive a much lighter review because its failure or rewrite is contained. He still looks for conspicuous hazards. He calls this controversial and acknowledges that it differs from many colleagues’ expectations.

What if someone actually wants a deeper review?

Authors can flag that in the summary or return an approved change for more scrutiny. Their signal can correct his assessment of risk or indicate a desired design discussion. The approach also depends on team trust; new colleagues do not immediately receive the same assumptions.

Source: 30:42–32:10 ↗
Why ask how to accept rather than how to reject?

He wants to identify real blockers rather than require code to match his personal style. Experienced engineers can recognize multiple workable forms. His unusual extension is to approve with a clear warning even when a fix is mandatory, trusting known colleagues to correct it before landing. He says that has not caused the feared production failure in his experience, while asking unfamiliar authors to return when ready. This is an attributed team practice, not a recommendation to treat known defects as safe.

Source: 32:10–33:50 ↗
Source: 28:18–30:42 ↗

QHow do you judge whether you are moving too quickly?

He uses production feedback and metrics to adjust. If a rollout is healthy and brings little negative signal, he may increase exposure faster than conventional increments; if problems appear, he pulls back. The host and Bolam agree that some risk accompanies speed, while daily breakage suggests too much. The transcript does not establish that absence of complaints proves absence of harm; it records the signal-based judgment he describes.

Source: 33:50–35:33 ↗

QDo you use AI?

He uses ChatGPT often outside work and internal tools at Meta. He sees them as useful tools with mistakes and caveats, and thinks engineers should learn to use available capabilities. The calculator analogy expresses enthusiasm about adoption rather than a claim that model outputs are equally reliable.

Source: 35:33–36:14 ↗

QWhat is a tech lead responsible for?

The project’s success, in his view. Usually the most useful action is aligning people and ensuring they contribute in the right direction, but the lead may need to write code or debug a problem no one else can resolve. He gives an example of spending weeks tracing an elusive bug. The role is flexible contribution to the outcome rather than a single activity.

What mistake do new technical leaders make?

They can become absorbed in daily operations and lose sight of the goal, especially when the surrounding direction changes. The lead must notice and redirect the team rather than continue executing an obsolete plan.

Source: 36:57–37:46 ↗
Source: 36:14–36:57 ↗

QHow do you balance coding with wider leadership?

He usually writes some code weekly to stay in the complete toolchain, often taking a task he can finish far faster than someone else. Focus blocks help. But he may stop coding for weeks when reviews, resource planning, or another activity offers greater value. The aim is useful allocation, not preserving a coding quota.

How do you learn what is worth your time?

Experience helps. An earlier heuristic was to seek work he believed important that nobody else would do. He now recognizes that neglected work can also be neglected because it is unwise, so the judgment still needs scrutiny. He also reserves time for useful contributions that may not appear in performance-review credit, including helping colleagues and maintaining technical contact.

Source: 39:10–42:12 ↗
Source: 37:46–39:10 ↗

QWhat is your note-taking system?

A separate VS Code window contains plain-text files in one large folder, named for people, projects, and priorities. He navigates by fast filename search, adds dates and times through shortcuts, and writes frequent notes because memory is unreliable. He avoids elaborate filing. Links between files provide connections; a graph view is interesting but not central. The archive includes work and personal thoughts accumulated for years.

Do you maintain an achievement diary for reviews?

Not consistently. He did so for one year but usually reconstructs achievements later, acknowledging the cost of spending a day on that reconstruction. His existing notes serve current thinking more than daily credit accounting. The host suggests launch posts as another record because they already need to be written, and Bolam likes that idea.

Source: 44:40–45:55 ↗
Source: 42:12–47:00 ↗

QWhat advice would you give a new graduate version of yourself?

Go where your strengths are valued. Someone good at frontend, debugging, or frameworks can be ineffective in a role whose leaders need a different contribution. A poor review does not automatically mean those strengths are worthless; recognizing the mismatch and moving can change both performance and enjoyment. He also advises being kind, simple, and able to enjoy work as oneself.

What is the cost of bringing an informal personality to work?

He sometimes says something unwise. He tries to acknowledge it and apologize promptly, while relying on an established reputation for good intent. He does not treat authenticity as permission for extreme or harmful remarks.

Source: 49:21–50:02 ↗
Source: 47:00–49:21 ↗

Section 86 · interview

Make growth explicit, adapt your coaching, and remove friction

Laurent connects candid career alignment, fair evaluation, sustainable team leadership, and whole-problem ownership across Airbnb, Instagram, and Stripe.

QWhy did you choose to join Airbnb?

Laurent

Laurent had worked at Apple and Meta and decided developer productivity was the area he cared about: making engineers more effective at writing software. Moving to San Francisco turned his existing commute into roughly ninety minutes each way, which prompted a search. Airbnb combined people he liked, an office he could walk to, and a developer-infrastructure organization early enough to offer substantial work to shape.

He joined as one of two test-infrastructure engineers just as the broader effort was becoming multiple teams. The choice combined everyday quality of life with a technical opportunity; it was not a purely title-driven move.

Source: 00:44–02:43 ↗

QWhy transition from test-infrastructure IC work into management?

Laurent

One manager was responsible for several teams and more than fifteen people, leaving limited time for development and support. Laurent had already begun doing some of that work as tech lead. As his team grew toward six to eight engineers, many early in their careers, he thought a dedicated manager could support them better and improve delivery of the large project.

He pitched the need to his manager and offered to try the role with help. He began with two reports and later managed the whole team. His rationale was an organizational problem he could help solve, rather than management as the automatic reward for technical seniority.

Did managing former peers create uncomfortable power dynamics?
Laurent

Yes, so they addressed them openly. A colleague used the first one-to-one to test his judgment: recruiting had said an employee missed an assigned interview, so what would the new manager do? Laurent said he would first ask what had happened and establish the facts. The colleague considered that a pass; immediately punishing the employee would ignore possibilities such as a mistaken name or inaccurate email.

The anecdote illustrates hearing all sides before acting. Formal authority does not eliminate the need to investigate or earn trust with people who were previously peers.

Source: 03:55–05:38 ↗
How many managers would fail that test?
Laurent

He does not supply a percentage. Instead he criticizes treating management as one fixed style—tough, hands-off, or micromanaging. A directive approach may help a team of beginners and fail with experienced engineers. Good management requires adapting to the people and situation.

Source: 05:38–06:33 ↗
Source: 02:13–04:37 ↗

QHow did management change your experience of boredom at work?

Laurent

He treats boredom as a signal to examine what is wrong rather than simply tolerate it. Becoming a manager initially supplied intense learning: hiring levels, reviews, promotions, then building relationships and planning reports’ growth. Later he used his optimization instincts to improve the team’s working conditions.

He built a calendar tool to reduce fragmentation across his own and reports’ schedules. He also surveyed every team process in detail—meetings, planning, code review, and ways of working—to improve team health. The survey showed that everyone thought the long stand-up was useful for someone else, while no one actually benefited much from it. Changing that and other processes improved engagement and enabled more work with less time.

After a three-week wedding trip, he returned to find the team had planned the next quarter and assignments using the process they had established. That successful independence also left him bored. The next possible step was managing managers, but he did not feel ready and missed coding, shipping, and seeing the effect in production. He returned to IC work. The story frames a well-functioning team as success even when its manager then wants a different challenge.

Source: 06:33–11:51 ↗

QDid learning management make you a better IC afterward?

Laurent

Yes. Understanding reviews, career framing, progression, and promotion helped him navigate his own work, while coaching and difficult-conversation skills improved his leadership of others. He continued developing those abilities after returning to IC work. The benefit was a new set of skills rather than merely privileged knowledge of a committee.

Source: 11:36–12:57 ↗

QIs pitching the organizational value a good way to move into management?

Laurent

He broadens the lesson to alignment with a manager. People often hesitate to say they want promotion, expertise, or another kind of growth, then present a year’s activity at review time and hope for the desired result. He prefers an ongoing conversation that gives both employee and manager the chance to shape the work.

As a manager he used a “surprise factor” exercise: before delivering the review, each person wrote the expected rating and promotion result, and they compared that with his own written assessment. Agreement was the desired outcome. He got close to full agreement without reaching it. The purpose was reducing uncertainty and demonstrating whether communication during the year had been effective.

Can a positive review surprise also reveal a problem?
Laurent

Yes. Someone doing excellent work without knowing it may be unnecessarily cautious. A manager should have coached that person toward greater confidence and productive risk-taking earlier rather than leave them anxious until an unexpected promotion. Positive surprises, like negative ones, can reveal missed communication.

Source: 15:04–15:53 ↗
Source: 12:37–15:01 ↗

QWhen should ICs try management, and what are the tradeoffs?

Laurent

Laurent found the experience invaluable and encourages people who are considering it to try. It is a different job, so direct experience can reveal both useful skills and whether the role fits. Even a poor outcome can teach something about one’s preferences and limitations.

He recommends starting with an intern while warning that one intern is a highly biased sample. Interns often need more direction and inspire strong personal attachment, unlike a group of experienced ICs. He recalls emotionally difficult intern calibrations because mentors strongly wanted their own intern to succeed and confused a return offer with proof of good management. A manager can do a good job even when the correct decision is no return offer. He helped run calibration sessions to make that distinction clearer and the process less frightening.

Source: 15:31–18:53 ↗

QWere your own promotions and reviews free of surprises?

Laurent

He first says he was often surprised, then clarifies that the surprises were ratings rather than promotions. He sees that as evidence he had not understood the system and its values well enough. In one transition, he expected his technical leadership to support a staff promotion but switched into management near the end of the cycle.

The rating came back as meets expectations because he had spent too little time in the new role. He found that frustrating and redirected his effort toward reaching the next management level. He now thinks he should have explicitly asked beforehand how the timing of a role change would affect review and promotion.

Did the role change reset your progression?
Laurent

He does not give a universal reset rule. Companies, organizations, and even local teams can develop informal calibration rules about tenure, role transitions, or unusually fast promotions. Some later become codified and communicated; others remain unstated until someone asks.

As a manager he challenged rules he found demotivating or inconsistent with the intended values and tried to explain calibration transparently to ICs. His bar was that an employee unexpectedly observing the meeting should be proud of the work, not feel that unfair decisions were being plotted. Because he sees management as representing company interests, strong value alignment was necessary for him to defend the decisions sincerely.

Source: 21:17–23:46 ↗
Source: 18:38–21:38 ↗

QHow can a manager or IC successfully challenge an established rule?

Laurent

He starts by examining the biases a process may introduce and what makes employee evaluation fair. Gather evidence, understand the reason behind the rule, and make a case. The history may reveal a useful constraint you did not see—or an old precedent that no longer fits.

He generally prefers initial one-to-one conversations to a public confrontation in calibration. In front of a group, people can interpret disagreement as a threat to reputation and become defensive. Understanding those human dynamics improves the chance of changing the process rather than just winning an argument.

What if a senior leader proposes penalizing people for a low count of code changes?
Laurent

He would first clarify what the penalty and metric actually mean. Different contributions make lines of code or pull-request counts a poor general measure of engineering output. At Stripe, concerns about that kind of measurement motivated a more useful inquiry into the journey of a code change: thinking, writing, CI, review, iteration, and merge.

Time spent in different stages can reveal organizational friction. If one area takes twice as long to land changes, investigate why—perhaps a poor codebase or inefficient process. He explicitly rejects equating fast shipping with high productivity or slow shipping with low value. The metric is a diagnostic signal that helps remove obstacles, while a manager must assess the complete contribution, including noncoding work.

Source: 26:29–30:00 ↗
Source: 23:50–26:42 ↗

QWhat stood out about Airbnb’s engineering culture?

Laurent

He found it harder to explain why low-level infrastructure mattered in a designer-led company, but that different professional perspective also produced useful ideas. During a period of reliability problems, the company drew on people with emergency-response backgrounds to improve crisis management.

He admired the rigor and practices that resulted and took some to later jobs. His positive example is the willingness to ask which other field already handles a similar kind of problem well, rather than assuming all incident-management expertise must originate inside software engineering.

Source: 29:51–31:48 ↗

He could identify dozens of possible improvements during a code change, then group related problems, rank them, and address the valuable ones. The goal is not merely collect annoyances.
