Section 87 · interview

Navigate power without confusing it with merit

Ethan Evans examines credit, scope, promotion, social leverage, management failures, and the ethical limits of treating a career as a competitive game.

QHow do you receive credit when collaborators compete for visibility?

Ethan Evans

Evans argues that recognition depends partly on who tells the story. Communicate a real accomplishment promptly, name collaborators, and state your own contribution clearly. If somebody else announces first, add a useful comment about the specific problem you solved rather than hoping that silence will be interpreted as modest excellence.

He also observes that later career narratives are often less contested than immediate credit allocation. His own shorthand about being an early engineer on the product that became Prime Video illustrates how an accomplishment’s public description can outlast detailed memories of everyone involved. He treats this as a practical feature of recognition, not proof that colleagues’ contributions cease to matter.

What if a product manager or engineering manager handles all upward reporting?

First ask the person to highlight the team and specific contributions. They may be concentrating on news rather than withholding recognition deliberately. Evans once prompted his vice president to send a congratulations message after the first Amazon video launch, and the message arrived soon afterward.

If that fails, supplement the announcement with useful technical context. He compares this with sports commentary: another person can announce what happened while you explain how it happened and what it means. A follow-up note can describe readiness to scale, limitations, or necessary future investment while making the engineering contribution visible.

Source: 04:41–07:46 ↗
Source: 02:03–04:41 ↗

QDoes encouraging visibility reward noise instead of impact?

Ethan Evans

He agrees that an organization in which everyone talks without adding value is unhealthy. His proposed response is to raise the quality of one’s own contribution, rather than opt out of communicating. Tell leadership something it needs to know, such as whether a launch is ready for growth or will require additional investment if successful.

Evans directs the strongest part of his argument toward people who remain quiet because they dislike self-promotion. He says that refusing to participate does not create a fairer assessment system; it can leave useful work unseen. This is a pragmatic argument for useful visibility, and the host’s concern about excessive political behavior remains a real limitation.

Source: 07:46–11:25 ↗

QShould you be as loud and outspoken as possible?

Ethan Evans

No. Evans distinguishes making the strongest defensible claim from becoming a boastful person who claims falsely. He favors simple accomplishment language that an audience can remember, while accepting that simplification may irritate people who prefer a more exact label.

His example is calling himself the first engineer on Prime Video even though his work began on Amazon’s video product before the Prime name existed. A colleague disputed the naming, rather than whether Evans had done the underlying work. Evans is comfortable with that boundary; the discussion exposes a contested judgment about how much simplification is acceptable, not a rule that every embellished statement is harmless.

How do you find a defensible place in that gray area?

He says soft skills depend on context and audience, so binary thinking is often inadequate. Explain an accomplishment in a way the audience can understand, and remain able to back it up. Multiple descriptions can be true: first engineer, first manager, or the person who hired the team that built a product.

He uses jointly held patents to illustrate ambiguity about credit: formal inventor lists may not match each participant’s sense of who originated an idea. The transcript varies between approximate patent totals, so the useful point is the ambiguity of shared credit rather than a verified exact count.

Source: 13:42–16:09 ↗
For the fastest growth, how far toward the strongest claim should someone go?

Evans recommends claiming more until the claim becomes hard to defend or damages reputation. His target is chronic underclaiming: people expecting someone to inspect all their work and award a precise, academically graded result. He believes workplace evaluation instead depends heavily on relationships, descriptions, visibility, and memory.

His classroom analogy is deliberately bleak: the manager remembers a person and estimates their score rather than regrading every answer months later. This is his account of organizational behavior, not evidence that technical quality is irrelevant or every manager evaluates this way.

Source: 16:11–19:17 ↗
Source: 11:26–13:34 ↗

QHow can a naturally quiet engineer make work visible?

Ethan Evans

Writing can substitute for speaking in meetings: email, internal posts, Slack messages, white papers, and technical talks all expose work to an audience. Another person can also help publicize it. The central requirement is that the work should not remain in isolation.

A shared component used widely can create its own reputation. Evans recalls Amazon’s interview-tracking system being called the Matt Round Tool, or MRT; he knew of its author through the widely used tool despite never meeting him. Even this supposedly silent route needed distribution and a recognizable association with its creator.

Source: 19:18–21:31 ↗

QIf you find a valuable new opportunity, how do you secure the chance to lead it?

Ethan Evans

Make three cases together: the idea is valuable, you can execute it, and you can make time for it. A manager needs trust in your ability and a credible plan to hand off, document, or automate existing obligations. Originating the idea gives you a useful lead because you have thought about it most, but it does not erase a weak track record or another critical assignment.

Explicitly express enthusiasm for building it. Otherwise leadership may hear only an idea and assign it to someone else. Evans also recommends making disappointment visible when an opportunity is taken away rather than responding as though every allocation is equally acceptable.

He candidly describes a managerial temptation to appease demanding employees while postponing help for easygoing ones. He says a manager may intend to come back to the quieter person but never do so. His advice to be somewhat difficult to disappoint addresses that pattern, while acknowledging that it is an unfair practical tradeoff rather than an ideal of leadership.

Source: 21:32–27:31 ↗

QWould you prefer an entire team of ambitious stars or steady role players?

Ethan Evans

Evans prefers a mix. A high-growth business can sometimes supply enough attractive projects for many highly ambitious people; with flat headcount and constrained opportunities, those people may compete destructively with one another and the manager.

Only easygoing role players can produce a calm team without enough pressure for change. He values some people who question constraints and push ideas, while too many people simultaneously pushing in different directions can create chaos. The best composition depends on the business’s supply of useful scope.

Source: 27:31–29:35 ↗

QHow do you handle peers who want to take part in your attractive project?

Ethan Evans

His first move is to challenge scarcity thinking. Other engineers’ excitement can make the project larger, faster, or more valuable, with its originator coordinating contributions. Try to create a shared win before treating every interested colleague as a threat.

If protecting ownership is necessary, being further along in a prototype or waiting until responsibility is clear can help. Offering other worthwhile ideas may give peers useful opportunities without displacing yours. He also describes handing off existing work to free capacity, but explicitly warns that appearing to dump unattractive work on named colleagues can create enemies.

Evans stresses understanding motives, satisfaction, fears, and emotions. His poker analogy separates competing skillfully within accepted rules from cheating, such as secretly seeing another player’s cards. He believes a person can understand the social game and win without dishonest manipulation. Some examples, including challenging a peer to demonstrate commitment through weekend work, are described as social tactics rather than presented as obligations every teammate should accept.

Source: 29:35–36:18 ↗

QHow do you protect yourself from unwanted work that somebody else wants to hand off?

Ethan Evans

Evans recommends establishing valuable initiatives before a handoff arrives. If people already know what important work you are driving, there is a credible reason not to load you with somebody else’s maintenance. Once you are only defending against a specific assignment, he considers you behind in the negotiation.

If somebody calls the work easy, ask why they cannot automate or solve it. Be clear about capacity and about the cost of replacing your other work. He uses an aggressive animal analogy to make the point that people sometimes give assignments to the person least likely to object. That observation explains his advice to set boundaries, although it does not make offloading work onto a quieter colleague a fair result.

He also proposes constructive bargaining. Acknowledge that unattractive work needs doing, complete a bounded amount of it, and ask for a better opportunity afterward. Volunteering in advance for a maintenance sprint can show that you are on the manager’s side while creating a specific exchange, rather than silently accumulating an indefinite backlog.

Can you refuse your manager without appearing unhelpful?

Constant refusal can make you a poor team member, he says. His preferred combination is useful work, a cooperative response to unavoidable assignments, and an explicit expectation about what comes next. Tell the manager that you will finish this work but want a more challenging assignment afterward, then return to that expectation if the pattern continues. The skill is communicating disappointment without becoming a jerk.

QHow do you win a promotion when only one slot is available?

Ethan Evans

First ask whether the competition is realistically winnable. If several qualified and more senior people are already waiting for a single role, leaving for a growing organization may be better than trying indefinitely to jump the queue. Evans will not promise that every constrained situation can be solved.

Where there is a path, state your interest and ask what circumstances would make you the manager’s first choice. This invites concrete criteria instead of mind-reading. He then emphasizes being the person the leader can depend on during difficult problems or crises. Ask what keeps the leader awake or which of their biggest problems is worst, and help solve it.

He is explicit about cost: crises may fall outside convenient working hours, and becoming exceptionally dependable can require sacrifice. He has answered how to compete for the role, not how to guarantee it with no additional effort. The advice concerns making a real contribution valuable to the leader, rather than only expressing eagerness.

Could asking for the manager’s worst problem seem like obvious flattery?

Yes, if it arrives abruptly without a relationship. He suggests building gradually from solid work to useful help, then discussions of growth, special challenges, and a role as a trusted partner in difficult situations. Personalities differ, so the wording must fit the person. The objective is a mutually useful working relationship, not an immediate offer to do anything in exchange for a promotion.

Source: 48:17–52:14 ↗
Did you really tell people to “promote themselves”?

Evans says he used that framing to ask for demonstrated work and an explicit growth agreement. He wanted a strong, senior team and was willing to defend the resulting salary cost upward. In his view, rewarding performance is part of building a successful organization.

He also admits a failure: early at Amazon, he made a promotion agreement, missed a process window he had not understood, and the engineer left angrily. He believes that departure was justified. Later commitments sometimes took longer than intended, but he says he followed through. This admission qualifies any suggestion that an employee alone controls a promised promotion.

Source: 52:14–55:40 ↗
Source: 44:06–48:15 ↗

QWhat if your manager will not talk explicitly about promotion?

Ethan Evans

Evans first considers whether a different manager would be more compatible with your ambition. If changing is impractical, study what this manager actually rewards. Look at several promotions, talk to those people about the work and conversations that preceded them, and learn the manager’s language for growth rather than assuming everyone negotiates as directly as Evans.

If no one progresses, or the manager’s choices have no workable pattern, there may be no usable process to follow. Accepting a slow and uncertain system or moving elsewhere may be the real choice.

He suggests using AI to examine a manager’s communication and propose an approach that fits their style. His confidence about personality inference is his opinion, not a validated assessment presented by the interview. He distinguishes adapting communication from manipulation, while predicting that persuasive manipulation and AI countermeasures will become more important.

QHow do you handle a promotion carrot that remains vague?

Ethan Evans

First separate legitimate uncertainty from avoidance. A manager may need a committee, skip-level approval, or another decision maker and cannot guarantee their response. Ask what it would take for the manager to become an enthusiastic advocate, rather than demand a promise about the final result. Evans’s own VP sponsor committed to put his reputation behind the attempt but could not guarantee Jeff Bezos’s approval.

A manager may also be uncertain whether the work will be strong enough, or reluctant to specify a checklist that ignores new requirements. Acknowledge those limits while explaining the practical effect of having no visible target or timing. Ask what success would look like, how to measure progress, who has succeeded, and how you are supposed to work toward an unknown destination.

For a manager who simply strings people along, compare your experience with others’ outcomes. If people do receive opportunities, investigate what differentiates them. If nobody gets anything, Evans recommends leaving that manager or changing the leverage in the relationship. His suggestion to use negotiation questions is aimed at eliciting clarity; it does not create a guaranteed promotion where no real opportunity exists.

Source: 1:00:20–1:06:29 ↗

QWhat if your manager’s lack of advancement is blocking yours?

Ethan Evans

If the manager wants to grow, consider a shared plan: help them achieve a goal that creates room for both careers. Evans says he enlisted strong reports in arrangements where their promotions and his reinforced one another. Ask about their goals rather than assume stagnation means indifference.

If the manager does not want to advance, ask whether they can help you find an opportunity elsewhere. Some less aggressive leaders are strongly motivated to support people and may be willing to do that. If they need to keep you, explain that your career matters, that you would prefer to grow in the team, and that you will need to consider alternatives if a path cannot be created.

Evans proposes explaining an authentic season of urgency, such as plans for family or caregiving. The host challenges the gray area when future plans are uncertain. Evans defends expressing feelings and possibilities but says not to lie. The defensible substance is to explain a real priority and preference, then let the manager respond; the transcript does not establish a right to invent a personal obligation.

He also distinguishes normal ambition from implausible demands. A new graduate insisting on becoming a VP in two years needs a reality check. A manager who rejects ambition entirely may simply be a poor fit for this audience, while a hard-driving manager can create a different problem by demanding too much.

Source: 1:06:30–1:15:40 ↗

QDid your own reports use these political tactics on you?

Ethan Evans

Evans recalls a few very smooth negotiators, but most people were direct, perhaps because he openly discussed growth. He says he also encountered dishonest claims and removed people who made them. He distinguishes these cases from legitimate ambition.

Some strong reports wanted roles he could not offer quickly enough. He supported departures when another company had a substantially better opportunity, including a move to a large role at Samsung. Even an ambitious and supportive manager can run out of available scope.

He is frustrated by unspoken, passive-aggressive dissatisfaction because it prevents either fixing the problem or honestly discussing its limits. At the same time, he recognizes that some employees are in a life stage where they want to do their job and be left alone. That choice can coexist with a team of climbers, although he warns that such employees may receive less desirable work.

QHow can a manager remove someone for lying when the normal process requires evidence?

Ethan Evans

Evans says provable dishonesty may support a direct termination, but suspicion without decisive evidence is a different case. His broader, disturbing claim is that a manager in good standing has many informal ways to drive one employee out: unattractive assignments, discouraging advancement, critical reviews, excessive scrutiny, or a pattern of demands that makes continued employment unpleasant.

He illustrates how seemingly defensible work allocation can conceal punitive intent, and how a powerful manager can frame the situation for HR before the employee complains. These examples explain an abuse mechanism; they do not establish that such behavior is fair, lawful, or a sound management practice. Evans acknowledges that an innocent person could be harmed and relies on decent managers’ desire to retain good people as the usual restraint.

His stated distinction is between getting rid of someone he considers dishonest or damaging and targeting a good employee. That distinction depends heavily on the manager’s judgment, which is precisely the vulnerability the host presses.

What if the employee simply has a style the manager dislikes?

Evans’s gentler alternative is an honest compatibility discussion and help finding another team or company where the person can thrive. He has encouraged such transitions and thinks a mutually frustrating relationship may improve for both parties when it ends.

He then admits that hierarchy favors the manager if the employee refuses to move and becomes too costly to work with. He does not claim that this is wholly justified. His explanation is that the manager is accountable for the whole team and is subject to similar pressures from leadership above. The passage reveals the limits of relying on personal compatibility as protection.

Source: 1:18:43–1:24:41 ↗

QCan an employee successfully challenge an unjust manager through HR?

Ethan Evans

Evans thinks framing and timing matter: a manager may already have described the employee as a performance problem. An employee should instead bring factual behaviors and their effect on productive work, rather than lead with a demand that the manager be fired. Independent corroboration, an established performance record, and specific documented misconduct can make an uphill case stronger.

He says he has removed managers after multiple employee accounts accumulated and matched his own observations. He also thinks leaders often protect managers they personally like, even while employees leave. In one coaching case, a leader had tried for 18 months to improve a manager whose people kept quitting. Evans challenged the leader to consider what they would recommend if the same story involved somebody they did not like.

The practical limitation is institutional inertia. He believes leaving is often easier than persuading a hierarchy to remove a manager who has a good relationship upward. His numerical language about odds and first-mover advantage is rhetorical, not measured probability or a guarantee about any particular HR process.

Source: 1:28:53–1:35:14 ↗

QHow do performance and being liked affect power at work?

Ethan Evans

Evans describes poor performance combined with broad dislike as easiest to act on. A mediocre but widely liked colleague is harder to remove: no single disaster supplies an obvious reason, and others defend the person’s helpfulness and warmth. In his view, relationships therefore change the practical consequences of similar performance records.

He reconciles likability with boundaries by recommending ordinary friendliness and selective, modest pushback when an assignment or decision matters. Humor can communicate that a repeated pattern is unacceptable without creating a confrontation. His playful “tokens” example frames a limited amount of unpleasant work as something he will accept, then asks whether the manager wants to use part of that allowance now.

The token framing is an illustrative negotiation tactic, not a formal employment limit. Its purpose is to make a cost and expectation visible while remaining cooperative.

Source: 1:35:16–1:39:24 ↗

QFor job security, is being liked more important than performance?

Ethan Evans

He says the answer depends on context. Decisions can include considerations beyond output. A leader might defend a likable person by arguing that their presence will help morale and cooperation after a difficult event. Evans recounts a layoff discussion that used family circumstances, which he labels improper; the book treats this as his recollection rather than verified legal guidance.

A technically indispensable but unpleasant engineer can also be retained, yet the team may be actively trying to transfer that knowledge so it no longer depends on them. He calls that dependency a fragile form of protection. The aspiration is to be capable and decent, not necessarily unusually charming.

He adds that managers can feel insecure about their technical ability. Publicly humiliating a manager may threaten both ego and authority. People then rationalize retaliatory choices as serving a greater good. This is his account of a social failure mode, not a justification for retaliation or an instruction to avoid all technical disagreement.

QHow do you defend against peers undermining you while competing for a promotion?

Ethan Evans

If the behavior is already visible, discuss the pattern with leadership before a specific accusation defines you. Evans suggests asking to be judged on actual contributions and given a chance to demonstrate them, while declining to join a campaign of mutual attacks. He thinks this makes later disparagement easier for a manager to recognize.

If the accusation has already landed, ask calmly what the manager has heard and what evidence would give them a full picture. He recommends reflective questions, including mirroring a few words, to draw out information rather than immediately become defensive. Then make the work verifiable and agree on better future visibility.

He also describes supporting colleagues whose contributions are unfairly dismissed, which may help them notice a pattern of undermining. That can be constructive when it means accurately affirming work; his language about traps and planting doubt also shows how quickly defensive politics can become another political campaign. He returns to an important exit option: teams full of this behavior are not the only teams available.

QIf everyone uses political tactics expertly, does the best strategy change?

Ethan Evans

Evans first rejects the premise that workplace relationships must be adversarial. Honest credit sharing, growing people, better business performance, and rising equity value can produce shared gains. The darker cases in the interview are failure scenarios, not his ideal organization.

In the hypothetical where everybody maneuvers expertly against everybody else, he expects the advantage to cancel out. His practical advice is to find an environment where your particular combination of skills creates a clearer edge. For his own coaching business, he combines public speaking, career knowledge, and social-media experience; he does not need to be the best individual practitioner of each to have a distinctive intersection.

He compares being a star on a less prestigious team with being a bench player on a championship team. Status, compensation, learning, and preferred competition can point to different valid choices.

But if someone stays at the expert table, how does play change?

Simple bluffs and shortcuts stop working, mistakes are noticed, and behavior becomes more cautious. He thinks the person must rely on stronger execution rather than easy moves against inexperienced competitors.

Source: 1:54:23–1:55:09 ↗
Source: 1:50:38–1:54:21 ↗

QDid you build an empire as an Amazon VP?

Ethan Evans

In hindsight, Evans says yes, though he often told himself that more people would let him execute more useful ideas. He recalls an Amazon Appstore staffing request that Jeff Bezos rejected because the proposed buckets were large and their purposes vague. After two weak answers, Bezos asked for a new plan with small groups of two or three people and exact responsibilities, then reviewed it line by line. Evans thinks Bezos was right: the team had imagined possibilities instead of doing the allocation work.

Later he tied expansion to concrete businesses, customers, and results. He describes negotiating staged releases of hiring capacity and proving that he could recruit good people into each tranche. The important difference was making resources produce value, rather than simply asking for a large team.

Merch by Amazon illustrates a pivot. His team tried printing merchandise for game developers as a way to attract apps to Amazon’s store. That original theory failed: merchandise was not important enough to change developers’ platform choices. T-shirt printing nevertheless found demand for slogans, events, and other designs, and became a separate business. Evans reports a very large later revenue scale, but that is his interview claim, not independently verified current financial information.

He also moved people from failed projects onto promising ones before leadership could reclaim them. He admits that colleagues might regard his tactics as slippery and that he rationalizes them by pointing to results. The interview preserves both the value he believes he created and the resource competition he participated in.

Did leadership ever claw back headcount, and how did you prevent it?

Amazon grew through much of his tenure, so he saw relatively few pure reductions. He stayed ahead of review by reassigning resources to useful work and filling authorized positions quickly. He describes an allocation system where more positions could be opened than ultimately funded, making early successful hiring an advantage when the gate later closed.

He sometimes argued that other teams’ unfilled allocations could support his faster hiring. This was deliberate competition for a finite resource, even if his teams delivered value. He also prioritized visible releases and iteration, admitting that some releases may have been too raw. The growth context and the quality tradeoff matter; this is not a general instruction that every team should hire or ship as fast as possible.

Source: 2:03:44–2:07:33 ↗
Source: 1:55:11–2:04:15 ↗

QHow should people prepare for uncertain AI effects on technical careers?

Ethan Evans

Evans offers predictions, not a crystal ball. He expects winners, losers, eliminated jobs, changed jobs, and new roles. He favors flexible learning and human skills alongside practical familiarity with AI tools. He worries that specializing only in operating a tool may preserve a role briefly while the work itself is automated away.

He also considers the opposing possibility: easier production can expand demand, just as tools have done in some other industries. People experimenting with software may eventually need engineers to make it reliable. He does not know which effect will dominate.

His central recommendation is to watch where value moves. More code or more features is not necessarily what customers need. Choosing what to build, what to omit, what to release, and how to explain it may become more prized. He would rather occupy a position requiring judgment and taste than depend entirely on manual operation of the tools. His claims about where AI is strongest or weakest describe his expectations at interview time.

Source: 2:07:33–2:12:00 ↗

QIs flattening the management hierarchy a permanent change or a cycle?

Ethan Evans

Evans sees pressure to remove layers as cyclical, especially when a company wants to keep headcount flat. He doubts that new tools remove the human need to organize, centralize, and communicate work. AI might let a manager oversee more people, but greater output can also generate more decisions and coordination needs.

He cautions against generalizing from exceptional leaders with many exceptionally senior direct reports to ordinary first-line management. A team of highly independent senior leaders is a different problem from a manager trying to scale from ten engineers to a hundred. His reference to a very long history of administration supports his intuition rhetorically; the transcript’s ancient-history details are not established here as verified historical facts.

Source: 2:12:03–2:15:19 ↗

QHow can you reduce layoff risk and explain a layoff without negative optics?

Ethan Evans

For explaining it, state the organizational fact briefly and truthfully, then turn toward what you can contribute next. If an entire organization closed, say that; do not imply a whole-organization event if it did not happen. Evans believes large-company layoffs have become common enough that such an explanation carries less stigma than it once did.

For prevention, he first admits that some layoffs cannot be avoided. He has seen leaders try to place key people elsewhere when an organization shuts down. Strong ratings, recognizable accomplishments, needed unique expertise, and visibility to leaders above the immediate manager can help someone be considered for those moves.

The pattern remains a combination of valuable work and relationships. He does not promise that either technical indispensability or executive familiarity guarantees protection when a business is eliminated.

Source: 2:15:19–2:19:04 ↗

QWhat is executive presence, and how do you develop it?

Ethan Evans

Evans defines it partly through what other people do: do they respect you in a room and seek your judgment even outside your direct work? He also cites a framework combining gravitas, communication, and appearance, with a roughly 60/30/10 weighting. That numerical framework is his reported reference, not an independently validated formula in this book.

He distinguishes expertise from the signals of authority. Confidence, decisiveness, controlled pace, pauses, body language, composure, and specificity can make somebody appear credible. He also points to unfair social biases involving physical appearance and identity; he describes those as biases people respond to, not as desirable standards.

His own failure mode is sounding more certain than his knowledge justifies. His wife has sometimes withheld a correct objection because he sounded so confident. He deliberately invents a precise “62%” statistic during the conversation to show how confidence and specificity can make nonsense sound convincing. That number is a demonstration of fabrication and must not be reused as evidence.

He says no single superficial trait is necessary. A strong record can create respect without theatrical speaking. The examples contrast a quiet, established expert with leaders who consciously control stage presence; they are his interpretations of public figures.

Why do you call Elon Musk’s speaking showmanship when it seems less polished than Steve Jobs’s?

Evans sees Musk’s particular strength as communicating conviction in extraordinary goals and invoking a record of previously doubted achievements. That can make speculative ideas seem plausible even without a polished delivery. Evans explicitly leaves room for disagreement about whether a given promise is visionary or fantasy. The point is how conviction and track record interact, not that every claim is true or inevitable.

Source: 2:27:25–2:29:23 ↗
Source: 2:19:04–2:27:20 ↗

QHow do you build relationships at work organically?

Ethan Evans

Find something you enjoy, know reasonably well, and can share. Turn it into a class, talk, tool, recording, useful service, or advice. Giving something valued creates a common interest and a reason for future conversation without demanding that you become an expert at approaching strangers in a room.

Evans taught managers how to hire quickly and well, then expanded his teaching and online advice. Another Amazon employee arranged bulk ski tickets and resold them at a discount internally. That person benefited from something he enjoyed while building hundreds of connections with other skiers.

The expertise need not be extraordinary or even technical. Shared interest makes conversation easier, and sustained useful interaction can deepen into a relationship. Engineers can do the same with a technology they understand better than the average colleague.

Source: 2:29:26–2:33:28 ↗

QHow can you form an organic relationship with a powerful decision maker?

Ethan Evans

Evans starts with value you already provide. A useful tool, class, or service may interest a VP directly, or may matter because many of their employees benefit from it. A modest note explaining that usage can open a conversation without pretending to share a personal interest you do not have.

A network can also supply an introduction through someone who already knows the person. He recounts seeking help to transport medical supplies for Ukrainian refugees to Poland; a contact connected him to the chair of United’s board, and the bags traveled without the expected fee. The outcome was far beyond what he had originally needed.

His explanation is that a well-placed, easy favor can let the intermediary contribute to something worthwhile and feel good about helping. A network is therefore useful for needs that cannot be anticipated when the first relationship forms. He does not reduce every helper’s motivation to self-interest; he acknowledges the legitimate desire to help.

Source: 2:33:29–2:39:32 ↗

QHow did you respond when people approached you with an obvious networking motive?

Ethan Evans

He was often explicit about his limited time. For someone asking for regular mentoring, he sometimes offered one meeting and challenged them to bring an interesting idea or information he did not know. If the meeting created value and maintained his interest, they could have another.

Evans presents this as a more useful opening than a blanket refusal. Some people used the opportunity well; others did not return. His direct, transactional style suited him but is not assumed to be every senior leader’s preference.

Source: 2:39:33–2:40:59 ↗

QHow do you discover what someone wants when they do not explain incentives directly?

Ethan Evans

He gives four methods: ask, listen, triangulate, and observe. Listen to the problems and goals mentioned in meetings; ask people who work with the leader what they have heard; and examine where the leader puts time, money, hiring, and attention. Actions can clarify priorities that general statements obscure.

Then move toward something the person values and make that contribution visible through an appropriate route. That may be a report, a mutual contact, a hallway conversation, or a direct question. The style must fit the relationship.

Evans regards explicit value-for-growth agreements as fair when the opportunity is open to everyone, but recognizes that some people prefer implicit arrangements and tolerate less direct language. Building trust can eventually make a private conversation clearer even when the person remains indirect in public. Until then, more ambiguity may be unavoidable.

Source: 2:41:01–2:44:30 ↗
Four ways Evans identifies another person’s priorities
MethodWhat to look forLimit
AskTheir stated goals and problemsSome people will answer indirectly
ListenRecurring topics in meetings and all-handsPublic messages may not reveal everything
TriangulateWhat trusted colleagues and direct reports have heardThese remain other people’s interpretations
ObserveWhere time, money, hiring, and attention goInfer cautiously from a pattern, not one event
Source: 2:41:01–2:44:00 ↗

QWhen somebody disappears suddenly from a company, what may be happening behind the scenes?

Ethan Evans

Evans says abrupt departures can concern conduct or risk rather than an ordinary performance process: harassment, racism, theft, disclosure of confidential information, or similarly serious events. He recalls employees being removed after leaking internal material to reporters and leaving a trace in company systems.

He gives two unusual examples to distinguish intent and consequence. A game artist brought a real gun collection to the office as visual reference for weapons; leadership considered it thoughtless rather than threatening and sent him home with an instruction never to repeat it. In another case, a cleaner’s alarming harassment of a female employee led to removal and, in Evans’s account, an order barring contact.

The stories show why colleagues may see only the sudden absence while managers know a confidential conduct incident. They do not let an observer infer the cause of any particular unexplained departure, nor establish that every sudden exit involved wrongdoing.

Source: 2:44:30–2:50:28 ↗

QDid you ever have to harm somebody else to get ahead?

Ethan Evans

He is reluctant to claim an unqualified no because people rationalize their own behavior. He remembers competing and trying to come out ahead, but does not recall deliberately targeting someone for destruction.

The case he feels worst about happened in his first week at Amazon. He was offered a choice between a customer-facing video product and ingestion infrastructure supporting video, music, and books. He chose the product without knowing that another incoming manager had apparently been promised it. That person arrived the next week and received infrastructure instead, an outcome Evans believes was bad for him.

Even if told about the conflict, Evans says he would have advocated for the job that fit his experience and interest. He distinguishes wanting an opportunity from intending injury, while admitting that the other person still bore a lasting cost. Lack of malicious intent does not erase that result.

Source: 2:50:28–2:53:26 ↗

QWhat do you say to people who find the whole political game morally distasteful?

Ethan Evans

Evans shares the wish for a world in which merit, intentions, and contributions receive fair recognition. His defense is that people must navigate today’s limited resources and biases while trying to improve them. He believes transparency, honoring agreements, and coaching people through existing discrimination can help without endorsing the discrimination itself.

To make the moral conflict concrete, he recounts helping fund a bribe that, in his account, enabled a Ukrainian friend’s husband to leave military service after two years. He recognizes that somebody else may have borne a cost and says he does not know whether that consequence occurred. The story is his personal claim and moral justification; its legality, details, and effects are not verified by this transcript.

He is comfortable with the decision because it helped someone he knew, while admitting that it can be condemned from other moral positions. The example makes his approach more complicated than simply being helpful: he accepts partiality and uncertain external costs. The host’s ethical discomfort remains part of the discussion rather than being resolved by an editor’s endorsement.

Source: 2:53:26–2:59:03 ↗

QWhich books do you recommend on people, negotiation, and power?

Ethan Evans

His first recommendation is Leadership and Self-Deception by the Arbinger Institute. He takes from it the distinction between seeing people as humans with concerns and treating them as obstacles or interfaces whose buttons you press to obtain a result. The former can make cooperation warmer and less manipulative.

He recommends Chris Voss’s Never Split the Difference for negotiation and understanding motivation. He also reluctantly recommends The 48 Laws of Power as a catalog of darker tactics. He says awareness may help readers recognize manipulation, while acknowledging that the same material can be used to become manipulative.

Source: 2:59:04–3:00:53 ↗

QIf you were trying to reach VP as quickly as possible today, what would you do?

Ethan Evans

Evans would not assume that his Amazon path is repeatable in a company growing much more slowly. He reports that Amazon expanded dramatically during his tenure, creating opportunities that he thinks are less available in the setting discussed. His suggested hypothetical is to learn intensely for roughly 18–24 months, develop externally valued expertise such as AWS knowledge, then seek a high-growth company where that expertise solves an important adoption problem.

He would deliver value, make growth goals explicit, learn management, decision making, psychology, and organization, and take some large risks. He argues that high-visibility wins can accelerate advancement, while admitting that failures and multiple company moves may be part of the path. His language about leaving the “smoking ruins” of failures exposes a real cost of optimizing solely for career speed; it is not a guarantee that repeated risk-taking succeeds.

He thinks early engineering-level growth may still be possible inside a mature company, but higher-level advancement increasingly requires an available business case. A skill that makes you one among thousands inside a large company can make you uniquely valuable elsewhere. His employee counts and salary comparison are illustrative approximations, and his recommendation reflects the interview’s market view rather than a verified present-day forecast.

Source: 3:00:57–3:06:38 ↗

Section 88 · interview

Pair ambition with relationships and procedural knowledge

Ethan Evans traces a rise from abrasive startup leader to Amazon VP while exposing the gap between output, recognition, business value, and managerial power.

QWhat did your career look like before Amazon?

Ethan Evans

Evans wanted to work in computing as home computers emerged. Apple’s reply to a letter about employment helped shape his choice of university; he attended Carnegie Mellon and later completed a master’s degree at Purdue. His early jobs were a sequence of small companies connected loosely by networking, search, network management, advertising, and audio streaming, with a brief detour into entertainment lighting.

Amazon eventually recruited him partly because streaming-audio experience fit its planned video work. Most of the startups after his first struggled or failed around the dot-com era. He describes being made redundant twice, with his confrontational behavior contributing. Becoming an Amazon VP was not his initial life plan; the path evolved.

Source: 01:00–03:33 ↗

QWhy did you initially choose startups over established companies?

Ethan Evans

The first choice was driven mainly by friends and an apparently attractive opportunity, not a carefully reasoned comparison of company sizes. Friends joined a local company founded by professors and introduced him to stock options. An earlier-joining roommate did especially well; Evans joined later but earned enough for a house down payment. Only afterward did he learn to make more intentional career decisions. The story illustrates why a successful early choice need not have begun as a sophisticated strategy.

Source: 03:35–05:01 ↗

QDid you see the layoffs coming, and what part did abrasiveness play?

Ethan Evans

No, despite warnings. His first manager had already noticed combative problem-solving, and Evans once proudly framed being a “loose cannon” as being aimed at people who were wrong. Technical ability and energetic execution still carried him into startup leadership, but peer conflict became increasingly costly.

In one company, a product leader warned that the planned scope could not be delivered with available time and resources. Evans now thinks the warning was correct; at the time he treated it as disloyalty to the mission. During downsizing, he offered to leave for another startup, and the CEO accepted. He suspects removing conflict made that easier.

In the next company, he argued with a sales leader who promised capabilities that did not exist. Evans still sees the truthfulness problem, but recognizes that the company was fighting for survival. He was the only person in the resulting “layoff,” so he regards it as being fired to remove contention. After the second experience, he finally investigated his own recurring role in the pattern and changed how he dealt with disagreement: more questions and listening, less escalation.

Source: 05:02–08:52 ↗

QWas early aggression useful, or would interpersonal skill have made it better?

Ethan Evans

Evans thinks energy combined with good interpersonal skill would have been better. He still favors having an opinion and advocating for it; pure compliance is not his model of leadership. The difference is how one argues. His earlier version raised his voice and dismissed ideas as stupid. A more skillful version can be persistently challenging without being abrasive or hostile. Being right often let him get away with the poor version, but did not make it the best version.

Source: 08:53–10:18 ↗

QHow can a leader avoid being removed through politics behind their back?

Ethan Evans

He says excessive confrontation can cause people to stop debating with you and start discussing you with others. The first defense is to leave enough room for honest disagreement that people do not feel a private campaign is the only route.

The second is a wider set of trusted relationships. Evans lacked allies who would tell him when another peer raised a concern; instead those people agreed that he was a problem. Technical correctness cannot replace relationships and the feeling people have while working together. He acknowledges that organizations sometimes choose a less technically good solution because it feels easier to support.

Source: 10:18–12:15 ↗

QWhat finally made you take interpersonal skill seriously?

Ethan Evans

The second departure, followed by difficulty finding another job after the dot-com crash and September 11, forced reflection. An interviewer challenged the story that he had been so valuable yet could not be retained. Evans concluded the missing capability was not coding or driving projects, but working well with people. He studied motivation, questions, and the psychology of work, then became interested in how to lead and inspire rather than only state answers. The painful feedback became a sustained learning interest.

Source: 12:17–14:10 ↗

QWhy was moving across the country to Amazon worth the risk?

Ethan Evans

While at a search company partnered with Barnes & Noble, Evans had investigated why that retailer was losing online to Amazon. Seeing Amazon through a competitor gave him a concrete appreciation of its capabilities, which he could discuss when Amazon’s recruiter approached him.

He was also tired of startups struggling with funding and product-market fit. Amazon was public and not yet profitable, but its scale looked stable compared with firms of dozens or hundreds of people. The decision combined admiration for the business with a desire for a different risk profile; it was not a bet on the million-person company Amazon later became.

Source: 14:10–16:00 ↗

QWhat did promotions to director and then VP actually require?

Ethan Evans

For director, Evans describes the ability to lead a business or major effort with only high-level goals. In his case an outsized event mattered: he pursued a video partnership with TiVo despite leadership’s advice against it, explicitly giving the senior leader a chance to order him not to proceed. It worked, and his promotion narrative emphasized that the partnership would not have happened without him.

He also made his career priority clear to his VP, who was preparing to leave. Evans politely explained that if Amazon did not value his growth as much as he did, he would need to consider that. The timing created retention pressure because both leaders leaving would damage the project. He sees both demonstrated judgment and explicit advocacy as central.

He admits a troubling managerial tradeoff: when two people were similarly qualified, the one pushing for advancement and threatening to leave sometimes got priority over the patient team player. He describes practical retention pressure rather than defending it as ideal fairness.

The successful project was a genuine risk. An ordinary result might have left him where he was, while a disaster after ignoring advice could have hurt him. He would take more calculated risk in retrospect, but his outcome does not erase the possible downside.

VP involved a longer process of building stakeholder support and trust with a stable manager. He worked on a partnership in which he would solve important problems and his manager would advocate for recognition. After roughly two and a half years, the VP agreed to stake his reputation on the attempt, without guaranteeing the final decision. A reorganization soon afterward highlights how favorable timing mattered alongside effort.

Source: 16:02–26:14 ↗

QWhat went wrong when you promised a strong engineer a promotion early at Amazon?

Ethan Evans

A young engineer agreed to help ship the first version of the product in return for support moving from the entry engineering level to the next one. Evans agreed in good faith but assumed promotion worked as it had in startups. He was preoccupied with launch problems and did not know Amazon had fixed review cycles. The window passed.

He explicitly owns the error. The engineer was not responsible for the manager’s ignorance, yet the engineer bore the career cost. Evans recommends that employees learn the process anyway: check whether the manager knows it, identify deadlines, and ask about concrete documents and dates. A new manager may sincerely intend to help while lacking the necessary procedural knowledge.

The engineer left and had a successful career elsewhere. Evans regrets the lost time but stresses that a year’s setback need not define a career lasting decades. The appropriate lesson is both managerial accountability and employee awareness of the process, rather than blaming the employee for a broken promise.

Source: 26:14–29:13 ↗

QWhy leave an 800-person organization for the Twitch integration role?

Ethan Evans

Amazon used a VP as an integration liaison after acquisitions, while leaving the acquired company’s CEO in charge. Evans sought that position after Amazon bought Twitch because it would test influence without authority. He would advise the CEO rather than command him, with no team of his own.

He had learned to run a large global organization with formal authority. Now he had to work with a younger, newly wealthy founder serving an audience and business culture different from his own. He gave up the large team to learn that challenge and enjoyed both the partnership and learning to stream on Twitch.

Source: 29:14–31:15 ↗

QWhat gaps did you see in a young founder running a rapidly scaling company?

Ethan Evans

Evans recalls Twitch treating continuing losses as normal because venture funding had always been available, and initially assuming Amazon’s money made profitability less urgent. His leadership wanted profitability, so a core challenge was establishing that the objective mattered at all.

He also saw the difficulty of loyalty to early employees whose skills did not scale with the organization. Bringing in a more experienced leader above a friend, or changing their role, required hard conversations and sometimes led to angry departures. He notes that the founder might describe the gaps differently; this is Evans’s view of the learning process.

Source: 31:17–33:45 ↗

QHow did Jeff Bezos and Andy Jassy differ as leaders in your experience?

Ethan Evans

Evans reports dozens of meetings with each and emphasizes founder status as a major difference. He recalls a budget discussion in which Bezos answered a warning about limited cash by asking how much there was, because he might want to spend it. Evans interprets that as the founder claiming the authority to take extraordinary bets with the company he created.

He describes Jassy as a more conventional executive who must partner with other leaders and operate within board and founder expectations. Both demanded a great deal.

His personal fit differed too. He felt Bezos’s questioning was followed by enthusiasm and a sense of shared commitment, while Jassy’s questioning felt more like scrutiny followed by personal accountability. Evans explicitly says other executives could have experienced the opposite. This is a comparison of his working relationships, not a universal ranking of either person.

Source: 33:47–36:49 ↗

QWhat happens to a VP’s review when a business initiative fails?

Ethan Evans

Evans distinguishes meeting near-term goals from achieving the business vision. Prime Gaming could ship features and meet some financial targets without making Amazon the major gaming force its founder imagined. He says he received strong VP ratings even while some businesses did not deliver that larger ambition.

He recalls expecting to hit all his Appstore goals while considering them ultimately unimportant. His broader criticism is that large organizations can let products persist because nobody wants to admit failure or close them, while nobody knows how to make them major successes. His comments about later shutdowns and possible future gaming outcomes are interview-time claims and speculation.

Why not change the goals to match the vision?

Because the goals that determine pay and review create a different incentive from the goals the company ideally needs. Competing with a preinstalled app store from a sideloaded position was important but not something Evans knew how to achieve, so he resisted being measured on it. He candidly admits wanting achievable evaluation goals while the business needed a much harder outcome. An ambitious vision is not automatically a workable plan.

Source: 39:24–41:21 ↗
Source: 36:53–39:22 ↗
Three different measures of success
MeasureWhat it asksRisk Evans identifies
Project deliveryDid the team ship the agreed work?Visible activity can look like success
Performance reviewDid the leader meet negotiated goals?Goals may favor what is achievable
Business visionDid the initiative create the strategic result?The organization may keep meeting goals without progressing toward it
Source: 36:53–41:21 ↗

QWhat do stack ranking and performance plans get right and wrong?

Ethan Evans

Evans describes a historical Amazon attrition goal that pushed managers to deal with weak performance. When it was removed experimentally, he says managers avoided hard conversations, particularly with well-liked people, so the goal returned. He gives varying annual proportions as recollections of the system, not current verified policy.

The problem is that a quota can turn a support process into a departure process. By the time a manager writes a PIP, they may already have decided the employee should leave. Confirmation bias and pressure from HR or leadership to record an exit can work against genuine recovery. Taking one employee off the list may create pressure to identify another.

He reports that the people who asked him for help on Amazon PIPs were later fired, as were several who did not use his coaching. He now urges people to prepare for another role. His strong warning comes from personal cases rather than a controlled success-rate study.

His diagnosis is that companies often do not train managers to address issues early or conduct useful difficult conversations. A formal plan arrives late and under distorted incentives, even when the manager initially believes they intend to help.

Source: 41:21–46:09 ↗

QWhat prevents a manager from framing a report unfairly?

Ethan Evans

Evans distinguishes a pattern of removing many employees, which can become visible through turnover, from one targeted case, which may be hard to challenge. The manager has status and can establish the performance narrative before the employee complains.

The same review count can support opposite narratives: a strong engineer improving everyone’s work or a person nitpicking while producing little original code. Neither count alone answers the value question. The manager may be malicious or may honestly evaluate the work differently.

He says he has not personally targeted an employee this way, and recognizes that good managers benefit from capable partners. The danger concerns a vindictive leader with power over the narrative. His practical advice is to improve the relationship if possible or find another manager, rather than assume HR will automatically rescue the employee. This is an account of a vulnerability, not an endorsement of unfair treatment.

Source: 46:12–50:43 ↗

QWhat advice would you give yourself at the start of your career?

Ethan Evans

Keep preferring growth. He compares his career ladder to an escalator because fast-growing businesses created upward movement alongside his own effort. The scale change he reports at Amazon supplied opportunities that personal drive alone could not create.

Learn sooner that work is done with humans. Expertise and being right should be paired with friendships, trust, and being known. An introvert can use writing and online tools rather than force a single extroverted style. Amazon approached him, and he sees a strong reputation as part of what makes that kind of opportunity possible.

Source: 50:44–52:23 ↗
