Section 89 · interview

Seek better answers, then design incentives around them

Brian Attwell connects intensive early learning with prioritization, truth-seeking, management responsibility, and a critique of ladders that reward scope alone.

QWhat most explains your rapid rise to senior staff at Uber?

Brian Attwell

Attwell credits the combination of a growing engineering organization, strong people to learn from, and a culture he experienced as meritocratic. Growth supplied many problems, though he acknowledges that a company does not need growth to have useful work. He also regards caring about the team as essential to sustained success.

His intentional choice was unusually intense work. He believes learning compounds and that managers assign valuable work after seeing evidence of capability, so he created time to develop that evidence himself. Early in his career, he expected to have more discretionary time than later. His claimed relationship between effort and growth is his judgment, not a demonstrated universal formula.

Source: 01:29–03:34 ↗

QWas the extreme effort worth it when you look back?

Brian Attwell

For him, yes. He recalls being told during an internship that he might die, then recovering after a medication problem was discovered. What he regretted in that moment was not having built the things he still wanted to build. That personal experience conflicts with the familiar maxim that nobody wishes for more work at the end of life.

He also compares a painful period of teamwork with a hard-won sports match: the effort was difficult, but the shared outcome could make it memorable and enjoyable. He admits he overdid it at times. This is an unusually strong personal preference, not a claim that everyone should make the same tradeoff.

Source: 03:34–05:04 ↗

QHow do you notice that you are working too much?

Brian Attwell

He watches for reduced patience and irritability rather than relying chiefly on an hours limit. After weeks without a day off, his partner may notice he is becoming grumpy. That signal matters especially in management, where patience affects other people.

His earlier warning system was much worse. He recalls collapsing on the way home from Uber with chest pain and being unable to move for about 15 minutes. He later consulted a doctor and reports being told that anxiety and excessive work were involved. He uses the story to acknowledge that he should have cut back sooner.

He compares sustained effort with athletic training that still needs recovery. The account is a personal recollection of a serious event; it does not establish a medical diagnosis or a safe workload for another person.

Source: 05:04–06:44 ↗

QWhat concrete work helped you grow as an engineer?

Brian Attwell

On a team addressing mobile maintainability during Uber’s expansion, he and a colleague, Yi, were among the most junior engineers. They listened to experienced colleagues debate options and noticed that eliminating bad approaches was easier than choosing the best remaining one.

After ordinary project work, they prototyped competing approaches using representative failures from postmortems. In one example, Attwell tested alternatives including RxJava on Android while Yi explored iOS, and they reviewed one another’s work. Working examples changed the team’s choice from an initial preference to an approach the experiments supported.

Their early hit rate was poor: many searches stopped at the edge of their knowledge, and the company would not necessarily have funded that exploratory time. After months of practice, they became better at finding useful questions and were increasingly invited into major decisions rather than overhearing them. Their influence later spread across a much larger mobile organization.

Attwell reports working roughly 90–100 hours a week, including weekends, with physical discomfort and headaches. He calls that the route he used to achieve an unusually young senior-staff promotion and makes a strong claim about its necessity. The book preserves it as his view; the episode does not establish that such hours are the only path, or that they are sustainable or appropriate for everyone.

Source: 06:44–10:14 ↗

QHow much of that trajectory was luck?

Brian Attwell

He separates frequent actions from infrequent decisions. Doing many small things well repeatedly gives less room for chance than choosing a company once every few years. He chose Uber intentionally, but recognizes that the choice could have gone wrong.

He thinks his effort and mindset would probably have served him well inside that particular merit-oriented setting. Joining an organization that did not value the same contributions could have delayed growth. He explicitly rejects a fully deterministic mapping from personal effort to career outcome.

Source: 10:14–11:33 ↗

QWhat signals made Uber attractive, and how would you evaluate another company?

Brian Attwell

He would examine the quality of engineers and the hiring process that brings them in. He favors difficult, job-relevant tasks requiring reasoning about conflicting requirements, rapid assimilation of new material, and tradeoffs, rather than only recalling practiced solutions.

His example is reading a complex postmortem and debating what it reveals about the team or architecture. He believes designing good interviews for many distinct roles requires substantial leadership effort and ongoing experimentation. Assertions about tests and intelligence reflect his hiring philosophy, not independent scientific validation in the episode.

Source: 11:33–13:27 ↗

QHow would you test the reasoning ability you are looking for?

Brian Attwell

Attwell prefers tasks that require keeping multiple ideas and constraints in mind while remaining relevant to the job. An applied programming problem with conflicting requirements or a postmortem whose details challenge one another can reveal more than practiced recall.

He is also considering formal intelligence screening, especially to reduce the time spent on unsuccessful PM interviews. He describes such tests as a screening aid rather than a complete ranking of already strong candidates. His statements about their trainability, predictive value, and AI’s limitations are attributed claims and are not established as research findings by this transcript.

Does greater intelligence imply better job performance?

He believes it contributes, but says strong technology companies have already selected a comparatively capable pool, so it explains less variation within a team than across an unrestricted population. He still wants applied experience and relevant skill, and acknowledges that no interview process perfectly predicts later performance.

Source: 14:26–15:45 ↗
Source: 13:27–16:29 ↗

QWhy are product managers harder to interview than engineers?

Brian Attwell

He sees the role as less consistently defined, more varied across disciplines, and lacking the same established educational and interview traditions. His organization asked several CEOs what excellent PM work looks like, wrote its own definition, and designed a process around it because there was little it wanted to borrow unchanged. He again frames intelligence screening as a possible early filter, while leaving later interviews to distinguish good from exceptional applied performance.

Source: 16:29–18:09 ↗

QBeyond being smart, how do you choose the best use of your time?

Brian Attwell

Attwell agrees that other skills need conscious development, especially prioritization. He considers the value of an initiative over a fixed period, how much his involvement changes its chance of success, and the time it will require. He is trying to maximize incremental expected value per hour.

The company’s top priority may already be well staffed by the time a junior engineer hears about it. A less prominent but still valuable initiative may have a larger gap that the engineer can fill. Working on the most important project and making the largest personal contribution are therefore different questions.

What does success “with and without you” add to ordinary benefit divided by cost?

It asks what your presence changes. Early in a career, look for important work that will otherwise remain unstaffed. Later, match distinctive skills with a real problem where they can improve the outcome. These estimates are fuzzy; he explicitly rejects pretending to have several significant figures of precision.

Source: 19:58–20:51 ↗
Source: 18:09–19:58 ↗

QHow can an engineer learn to estimate business value?

Brian Attwell

Ask why a metric or quarterly goal matters. A model-recall target might be intended to reduce churn, which in turn relates to revenue. Use one-on-ones to understand why leaders choose or cancel projects. If the company has an initiatives sheet with estimated value or a reason each project matters, study that column: it exposes other people’s reasoning and helps build intuition. He expects this to be learned, since most new engineers have little business background.

Source: 20:51–22:28 ↗

QWhy did you eventually become a manager?

Brian Attwell

He delayed the move despite several managers recommending it. At his later company, a strong group of engineers already treated him as a technical leader, so he enjoyed directing work without the full obligations of formal management. When his boss said the group needed either him or a newly hired manager, he accepted because he wanted to protect a team and technical vision he cared about.

He initially did the job poorly, hiding in coding instead of handling management fundamentals. A new teammate once asked after three months whether Attwell was actually his manager. He took that as evidence of neglect, improved those skills, and afterward saw the organization reporting to him grow rapidly. The story does not make technical leadership an automatic substitute for people management.

Source: 22:28–24:58 ↗

QWhy did more organizations keep moving under you?

Brian Attwell

He begins with a belief that even a strong team may have major room to improve. Rather than preserve every inherited practice, he invites people to question assumptions, including his own. Suspicions about a long-standing process are useful starting points for discovering waste.

An integrations team maintained about 1,200 connections intended to gather restaurant-industry information. Each had once seemed a good investment, but maintenance had accumulated without a fresh comparison of value. A colleague questioned how all of them could still be equally important. The team spent days estimating their value distribution, stopped supporting a low-value subset, reduced pages, and improved support for the important remainder.

He describes the overall product as improving even though it now supported fewer integrations. Reclaimed time also enabled new work. The example shows how subtraction can create capacity when the useful outcome is broader than the count of supported items.

Source: 24:58–27:51 ↗

QHow do you handle the people conversations when scope moves between leaders?

Brian Attwell

Attwell says these conversations need empathy and honesty. A capable person may nevertheless not be delivering what a particular role now requires, or may need a smaller scope. Explain the needed work, identify the gap, and recognize what the person still does well or contributed previously. His description favors clear expectations over hiding the reason for an organizational change.

Source: 27:51–28:32 ↗

QHow can incentives keep managers from clinging to scope?

Brian Attwell

He regards an automatic link between promotion and organization size as a poor design because it encourages empire building. His company originally borrowed a ladder resembling Uber’s, then attempted to improve it. Travis Kalanick challenged the revision as still too focused on scope and insufficiently insightful.

Attwell and a colleague then invested months in understanding other systems’ weaknesses. His core concern is that scope captures one kind of complexity while rewarding position and political maneuvering more than useful ability.

Source: 28:32–30:39 ↗

QWhat changed in the redesigned leveling system?

Brian Attwell

They began with roughly a thousand examples of people differentiating themselves through real work, grouped those into about 250 attributes, and used an analysis he calls principal-component analysis to arrive at twelve skill dimensions. He describes compensation as rising with demonstrated skill and impact along those dimensions rather than primarily with position.

The emphasis shifts from influencing teams as a status marker to having sound ideas, including successfully questioning foundational assumptions. Communication remains a separate competency with examples of good work. He wants people to improve capabilities that generally help the company even if they are also trying to earn advancement.

Where did the initial examples come from?

He spoke with engineers, read books, and reviewed years of quarterly calibration notes. He wanted examples he knew had actually occurred, so the upper levels would not become an imaginary standard that nobody could attain.

Source: 32:04–33:00 ↗
How do you assess good communication?

Give a verbal description and concrete examples, then compare a person’s actual artifact with them. This can support a more grounded conversation than relying only on social proof, although it does not remove judgment.

Source: 33:34–34:13 ↗
Can a manager still bias the examples or exaggerate performance?

Yes. The framework changes what people posture about rather than abolishing politics. He thinks striving to look good at truth-seeking or communication is still more useful than merely collecting scope. Leadership must also spot-check calibration and act on deliberate misrepresentation; he presents this as substantial continuing work, not a solved measurement problem.

Source: 34:13–35:39 ↗
Source: 30:39–33:57 ↗

QIs it especially difficult to remove an underperformer whom everyone likes?

Brian Attwell

Attwell disagrees with treating this as an insurmountable problem. A frontline manager may feel attached and see the social bonds, but hardworking colleagues may also resent covering for the person. He expects a difficult immediate response can give way to a happier team afterward. This is his view of the tradeoff; the episode does not show a particular termination or prove that this outcome always follows.

Source: 35:39–36:25 ↗

QHow do you provide evidence of truth-seeking?

Brian Attwell

Look for useful discoveries that challenge accepted practice: an important problem in plain sight that nobody recognized, or a justified departure from an industry norm because the team’s constraints differ. A novel opinion by itself is not enough; there needs to be value and reasoning behind the divergence.

He admits subjectivity remains and managers must be calibrated on examples. Existing technology-company ladders are not wholly broken, and he expects changes at the margin rather than completely different results. The distinction he wants is somewhat more attention to the leading behaviors that produce good results, rather than rewarding only an already-achieved position or outcome.

Source: 36:25–38:52 ↗

QCould excellent work still be rewarded when its project gets deprioritized?

Brian Attwell

Yes, in his system. If a person did excellent work and leadership cancels the project for a reason unrelated to that work, the person’s contribution can still be evaluated. He places responsibility for late cancellation partly on leaders. At the highest levels, he expects greater business judgment about whether a project should exist, so that qualification changes how the case is assessed.

Source: 38:52–39:23 ↗

QWhy do some large companies fail to reward their highest performers strongly?

Brian Attwell

Attwell thinks they can sometimes retain people anyway, especially when appreciating equity already makes compensation feel good. He objects to using past investment gains as a reason to reduce future reward and says his company tried to avoid that. He favors designing processes around fairness for long-term organizational benefit. These are his judgments about incentives, not a verified description of every large company’s pay policy.

Source: 39:23–40:27 ↗

QWhat did starting at Google teach you?

Brian Attwell

It left him skeptical of how well large technology companies are managed. He recalls a teammate he thought did little work, yet a manager and director emphasized that the person was pleasant and liked. Attwell complained, and the person eventually moved elsewhere, though he cannot prove his complaints caused the move.

He thinks leadership should at least have had a serious performance conversation. The anecdote is his perspective on one situation, not an evaluation that the reader can independently verify.

Source: 40:27–42:02 ↗

QWhy might a large company avoid that hard conversation?

Brian Attwell

Attwell argues that individual-team performance can be weakly connected to a large company’s near-term results, letting managers prioritize convenience over difficult improvement. Raising standards takes energy; asking less of people often creates little resistance. He expects standards to drift downward unless leaders deliberately counter the trend or a crisis forces change.

He also reports that several Google managers told him of a past strategy to retain smart people even when they were not productive, partly to keep them from competitors. He explicitly says he did not see this in writing and cannot prove it existed. That uncertainty is central; the anecdote should not become an established corporate policy.

Do you see merit in retaining talent mainly to keep it from competitors?

No. He doubts a company can monopolize intelligence because there are many capable people. His answer concerns the strategy as he understands it, even though the alleged policy remains unverified.

Source: 43:20–43:53 ↗
Source: 42:02–43:53 ↗

QWhat is the thesis behind the company you are working on now?

Brian Attwell

Attwell describes a goal of making fresh prepared food inexpensive enough that people can choose to reclaim the time spent cooking. He sees large avoidable costs in food labor, logistics, property, and ordering systems, and believes a sufficiently integrated approach can reduce them.

He reports restaurant robotics reducing labor cost, a lunch-logistics network lowering meal cost, lower-cost real estate, and the Otter software platform improving orders. The percentage reductions, order share, and trillion-dollar opportunity are company claims he makes in the interview, not independently verified market facts.

Some products are early while others have many customers. His prediction that robotics will eventually do much more of this work expresses the company’s ambition. The useful mechanism is coordinating several cost reductions across a supply chain rather than assuming one app alone makes prepared food affordable.

Source: 43:53–46:36 ↗

QWhy does the company keep such a low public profile?

Brian Attwell

He says conventional publicity can help fundraising, hiring, and a founder’s reputation. In their case, Kalanick already had wealth, funding access, and a strong network, so those benefits were smaller. Attwell sees costs in leadership distraction, negative coverage, and alerting competitors to the company’s plans.

He recounts public launches attracting many competitors and favors quiet execution at the parent-company level. This is a strategy suited to their circumstances, not a universal case against distribution or brand building.

How do you distribute products while remaining quiet?

Much of the business is B2B, and individual products such as Picnic and Otter still have names, advertising, and sales activity. The company speaks less about its central organization, rather than never promoting products. Recruiting is harder, which is part of why he is willing to appear on the podcast.

Source: 49:21–50:18 ↗
Source: 46:36–49:21 ↗

QWhat is your biggest career regret?

Brian Attwell

He distinguishes mistakes he lacked the knowledge to avoid from choices where he knew better and stayed silent. As a young Apple intern, he had a chance to show Steve Jobs a prototype improving phone usability in sunlight. While his mentor pitched its product potential, Attwell minimized it as a small amount of code. Jobs left, and the mentor explained that the team had lost a chance to win support.

Attwell does not dwell on that as a regret because an inexperienced teenager did not know how to pitch product value. He treated it as something to learn. The cases he regrets involve recognizing midway that a decision was wrong but failing to tell people because the conversation was uncomfortable.

He cannot share a concrete private example without affecting others, so he offers a hypothetical instead: tell the team that your earlier judgment was wrong and give them the chance to reconsider. Even if they do not change direction, colleagues deserve the information. He thinks you owe them the benefit of believing they might listen.

Source: 50:18–54:20 ↗

QWhat is it like working directly with Travis Kalanick?

Brian Attwell

Beyond the familiar intensity, Attwell sees a patient teaching side. At a senior-engineering offsite, Kalanick taught backgammon and coached people in water skiing between work sessions. Attwell describes enjoying that patience, including with less athletic teammates. This personal story adds a different dimension without claiming it represents everyone’s experience of the founder.

Source: 54:20–55:10 ↗

QShould someone choose an early-stage company largely because of its founder?

Brian Attwell

He thinks that can make sense because a founder with substantial control shapes composition, culture, and standards. A strong person can multiply the company’s effectiveness, while the wrong leader can do the opposite. The advice is to assess that influence carefully rather than treat founder reputation alone as a guarantee.

Source: 55:10–55:59 ↗

QWhat advice had the greatest impact on your career?

Brian Attwell

A high-school computing teacher repeatedly told him to figure things out himself. Attwell never knew whether that was deliberate teaching or simply the teacher not knowing the answer, but it helped him accept self-directed learning. He believes most professional learning requires that habit: keep moving beyond the area in which you are already comfortable.

Source: 55:59–56:51 ↗

QWhich books would you recommend?

Brian Attwell

He does not identify one transformative title. Instead he suggests studying interview-preparation material for an adjacent discipline: system design for a front-end engineer, or product-management material for a back-end or machine-learning engineer. Such books provide broad introductory vocabulary and exercises that can make ideas stick, improve conversations with other roles, and establish a foundation for deeper learning. He is recommending a use of the genre, not claiming interview tricks create expertise.

Source: 56:51–58:09 ↗

QWhat would you tell yourself when first entering the industry?

Brian Attwell

Be more courageous and less embarrassed about failure. He immediately qualifies that as an opening for a larger discussion of understanding emotions, possibly including therapy, rather than a command that makes embarrassment vanish. He thinks greater emotional awareness can help both the person and their relationships.

Is that easier said than done?

Yes. He agrees that embarrassment is felt and that the short advice needs a deeper conversation about one’s feelings and how to understand them.

Section 90 · interview

Stefan Mai: Manager Career Growth, Performance Systems, and Amazon vs Meta

Stefan Mai, a former Meta senior manager and earlier Amazon engineer and manager, describes the manager transition, promotion politics, rating buckets and PIPs, and the cultural differences between Amazon and Meta.

Stefan Mai's view: management is trade-offs, and small behaviors and incentives decide outcomes

Stefan Mai, who worked as an engineer and manager at Amazon and later reached senior manager (M2) at Meta, argues that managing well depends on small human behaviors: listening, telling a team its own story of winning, and understanding the personal incentives behind organizational politics. He also holds that no leadership style is best in the abstract, because what works depends on the stage and culture of the company. The host draws out his Amazon years, his move to Meta, promotions, rating buckets and PIPs, how AI is changing interviews, and his reflections on job hopping, writing and agency.

Source: 00:00–1:31:24 ↗

QWhat did you work on at Amazon, and how did you get there?

Stefan Mai

Stefan describes himself as an engineer who paid little attention to school and wanted to build. His early work was scattered across consulting and startups, and he felt he had not found technical depth. In 2012 Amazon offered work on hard problems at scale, and he took it despite the company's reputation for grinding engineers down. He joined the early advertising group, on a team building self-service advertising for vendors.

In his first week, he says, his manager gathered the team at about six in the evening and committed everyone to nights and weekends to ship by October, a death march of six to eight months. Stefan leaned in, though he says he would likely refuse today. The episode shaped his early development and his thinking about leading teams, and he calls it emblematic of the negative side of many people's Amazon experience.

Did you choose advertising, or were you placed there?
Stefan Mai

Amazon was not recruiting generally then. Candidates were approached for a specific organization, and Stefan's recruiter covered only advertising. He chose among several teams there, picking the one with the most growth, which he considers a good career choice because it was the start of Amazon's ad business.

Source: 04:16–05:03 ↗
Was the work always a grind, or only the early death march?
Stefan Mai

The death march was not standard across his tenure. Stefan says the average was working hard, as any big-tech job demands, more so for the ambitious. Fifty to sixty hours a week was fairly common, though not always nights and weekends.

Source: 05:04–05:44 ↗
Source: 01:34–04:14 ↗

QAre there notable stories from your growth into a software development manager at Amazon?

Stefan Mai

Stefan says his ownership meant he was often the de facto tech lead and effectively acted as the team's manager, because his boss had no time for the niceties managers normally provide. The title lagged what he felt he was doing, so he pushed for it.

He believes he got it prematurely. People feel ready, he says, without realizing how far they have to go. Most new managers make many early mistakes, and the support structure around them largely decides how they fare. His first year was uncomfortable and he was failing in ways he did not fully see. Around 18 months in he began to get a knack for it.

What early mistakes made it premature?
Stefan Mai

Stefan calls management a soft discipline with few output metrics, in which part of the job is telling the story of your contribution and of how you leveled people up. The soft skills were what he lacked. He had not learned each person's goals, and did not know how to get people to open up about what mattered most, so he could not tailor support or assignments to the individual. He calls that an elementary mistake.

Source: 07:32–08:53 ↗
Do you have tips for new managers on getting people to reveal their goals?
Stefan Mai

Stefan says a new manager's position is tricky because the team knew them as a peer, and the new power dynamic corrodes those bonds. A manager needs to learn about career objectives and what in the current work drags on the person, not just whether a friend is having a good week.

His first advice is active listening, which engineers can take a while to learn: show interest, reflect back what was said so the person feels heard, and ask questions that show curiosity. Engineers often talk almost like APIs, he says, and most people are not like that. He adds that early on he ran one-on-ones as a transactional laundry list and thought opening small talk was wasted time. He now sees its value.

Source: 08:56–11:23 ↗
Source: 05:46–07:30 ↗

QDo you have tips for improving storytelling?

Stefan Mai

Stefan calls storytelling a bedrock skill and says part of it is practice. People tell stories all the time without attending to them: recalling details is a story, and so is the motivation you give yourself to get out of bed. His first trick is to notice those moments and ask what story he is telling himself today, since one version helps you get up and another does not. Once you can critique your own stories, you can practice telling them better.

He says it came naturally to him as a manager. Every few months he looked back over what the team had accomplished and painted it clearly so people could feel proud, for example that they started as a team of two with a poor on-call, fixed it, and used the freed bandwidth to deliver.

Stefan's claim is that a team that feels it is winning, with the manager defining what winning means, gets much else downstream: people avoid zero-sum thinking and bickering, and feel excited about their work. Without that story, such problems fester.

Source: 11:25–15:02 ↗

QWhat was your manager doing, and how did you get to do the manager's role before having the title?

Stefan Mai

Stefan's manager was a senior manager expected to manage other managers but did not want to hire other SDMs, or wanted to delay as long as possible. Stefan's impression was that this was a way of keeping control of the product, which the manager loved: working with design and refining it for market. Stefan finds it debatable that this was the best use of the manager's time. Tasks a manager traditionally owns, such as checking progress, understanding careers and mentoring, fell by the wayside.

Was the sentiment in that org negative?
Stefan Mai

Stefan says a lot of people were pretty upset about the situation, and that he would not say things were particularly good.

Source: 16:00–16:20 ↗
Source: 15:05–15:58 ↗

QAt the end of your Amazon stint, what made you leave and join Meta?

Stefan Mai

Stefan first stresses that Amazon is a special and worthwhile place, undoubtedly successful and with a strong engineering discipline. His reasons for leaving built up after a considerable time there.

First, succeeding at Amazon involves assimilating into a distinctive leadership style the company called its peculiar ways. He came to feel that makes you a good Amazonian, not necessarily a good engineering leader, and he worried he was not growing. Second, Amazon keeps compensation more even, at some cost. He recalls a promotion or very high rating with no change to his compensation, explained by stock appreciation, which he found frustrating since it applied to the whole team.

Third, when a Facebook recruiter reached out, he was not a fan of the product but admired the engineering culture. The team was in integrity, working on child safety and preventing terrorism. At Amazon, his supply chain and ML work moved profitability, which had some effect on people but not the same qualitative impact. The first two reasons made him look, and this one tilted him into the move.

Which parts of Amazon's peculiar ways suit Amazon but not engineering leadership in general?
Stefan Mai

Stefan begins by saying all leadership is trade-offs and no style is best. Amazon's approach grew out of a company that long ran on low margins and operational leanness. Each management layer gets involved in detail in the layers beneath it, so even as a line manager he was expected to know what everyone on the team was doing at any moment.

The benefit is discipline: things do not just happen, and people track metrics closely. The cost is stifled creativity, which he did not see until he left. In his view it limits Amazon's ability to pursue new products while making it very effective in growth stages where the goal is to move revenue or cost by one percent.

He uses Kent Beck's explore, expand, extract framework. In explore, as at a seed-stage company, upside is asymmetric and moving fast matters. In extract, the best case is a one or two percent gain against a looming catastrophic risk, so risk aversion fits. Stefan finds Amazon's culture leans toward the later stages, partly because of how it has grown.

Source: 19:07–22:49 ↗
Source: 16:22–19:05 ↗

QHow was the move into ML work and forecasting? Was it challenging?

Stefan Mai

Stefan says it always is. Ordinary software projects are close to binary, working or not. ML is shades of gray, and people commonly carry bugs in a training pipeline for years without noticing, then fix them for marginally better performance. The work is scientific and experiment-driven, which was unfamiliar to him.

To make the move he read many books, entered Kaggle competitions, and built models on the side. Pivoting into AI is far more popular now, he notes, but many people treat it as a study session about learning the 101. The 101 matters, he says, but effectiveness also depends on judgment and instinct, which develop only by building and practicing.

So the key was building intuition, not just learning the fundamentals?
Stefan Mai

Stefan says for him the key was Kaggle plus finding ways to work ML into his existing role. Many things are non-obvious until you practice them.

Source: 25:00–25:31 ↗
What motivated the move into ML?
Stefan Mai

Stefan always found ML interesting. Having coded from an early age by instructing computers step by step, he found it seductive that a program could be implied from data. Much of what mattered societally then, such as news-feed ranking, recommendations and Amazon's supply chain, was ML. In supply chain, machinery predicting truck arrivals, vendor inventory and customer demand combined to produce something forgettable, an item arriving at the door, and he finds the complexity behind that beautiful.

Source: 25:34–27:13 ↗
Source: 22:50–24:59 ↗

QWhat was the story behind your promotion from frontline manager to senior manager?

Stefan Mai

Stefan was promoted about three and a half years into Meta, after roughly seven managers in that period. That turbulence held him back, and he suggests part of his promotion story is how to handle organizational shifts while keeping momentum.

On joining he wanted to be useful quickly, so he joined the on-call and wrote code, which built trust with his engineers and peer teams. That cannot be sustained, so he shifted to recruiting, where he says he had a blank check from his director. How people perceive a manager is a headwind or a tailwind, he says, and being pigeonholed can be devastating because people struggle to update their view of what someone will become.

Once his team's effectiveness was shown, he was given an additional manager. Leading a leader, he says, is yes and no the same as leading engineers: a far smaller shift than becoming a manager, but treating it as identical fails quickly, and for many it ends in mutiny. In manager stacks there is an unstated competition, since if the org is not growing, leaf-node managers can advance by taking the place of those they report to. His promotion came when his org reached about 30 to 40 people. By then he sat in calibrations alongside other M2s, and it was hard to deny he was doing the job.

How does that mutiny surface in practice?
Stefan Mai

Stefan says the easiest place to see it is skip-level meetings, where managers gripe that their manager is not helping, does not understand their career, or changes priorities too much. Some grumbling is about real problems, and some is a way to improve a manager's standing relative to their own boss.

He recounts a talk with his director about two teams in different organizations with overlapping responsibilities. Stefan saw a scientific experiment: let them run side by side and see who wins. The director called that naive, because the teams would find ways to undercut each other unrelated to their goal, and the friction would dwarf any gain. Stefan says the director was right. Most people have good intent, he adds, but want to move and grow in ways not always aligned with the organization, and a senior leader's job is to line those up.

Source: 31:29–34:17 ↗
Is there a secret chess, with personal career motives behind the business ones?
Stefan Mai

Stefan would not call it secret, because it is fairly obvious. Few people's main objective is to make Facebook more valuable. Their goals are varied: money, positions or influence, interesting problems, working with certain people.

His examples, around an interesting project, are to pair up and form a coalition, cookie-lick by being first to put a name on it, announce it in a post so it is hard to pull someone away, or show others are not capable. Being aware of that dimension is, in his view, key to being a senior leader of any large organization.

Source: 34:19–36:47 ↗
Is this zero-sum behavior more common in shrinking or stagnant orgs, with growth bringing abundance?
Stefan Mai

Stefan agrees. The zero-sum mentality usually appears when winning slows: the org stops growing, success is less obvious, and people redefine it. A leader's job is to equip the team to win, and focus on performance is among the most fundamental, with many other problems downstream. He adds that different leadership styles fit different stages. Early Facebook leaders were talented engineering leaders who rode a wave of growth, and whether the same people do best during a plateau is, he says, an open question.

Source: 36:51–38:26 ↗
So the mutiny is a manager telling their skip-level boss that you are thrashing things?
Stefan Mai

Stefan says it looks like any disgruntled team: people make noise because they are unhappy, and the implicit goal is a change, most obviously of people. He adds that seniority reduces control over outcomes. A senior leader whose manager underperforms cannot do that job for them without the manager hating it and leaving. The higher you go, the more impact on direct reports shrinks and the more action becomes binary. There are fewer levers to turn things around.

Source: 38:27–40:32 ↗
Source: 27:16–31:27 ↗

QAre managers harder to lay off than ICs?

Stefan Mai

Stefan says moving managers is inherently painful because the blast radius is larger. Whether removal is hard depends on whether the person is load-bearing: someone with a tight team and deep domain knowledge, whose cross-functional partners are not pulling their weight, is very hard to move out. If the team sees little value and partners complain, removal can even be invigorating.

On layoffs, he does not think managers are less likely to be cut. Most companies target a ratio of managers to ICs, so after cutting many ICs they need fewer managers. Companies also do span-of-control reductions, which he believes Amazon did recently, and managers go first. He does not think it is easier or harder for a comparably leveled IC.

Source: 40:34–42:52 ↗

QWhat leadership is most effective in a very small company versus a very big one?

Stefan Mai

Stefan says small companies need inspirational executors. Work is all hands on deck, and people want to work for someone impressive who could do their job and step in. As companies scale this gets harder, and those same people often lack the organizational aptitude needed. In big companies, he says, focus is a precious commodity. Go-getters who run at an opportunity without aligning or moving information up and down the chart get in the way and siphon energy from core initiatives.

He contrasts how Amazon and Meta scaled. Amazon built concrete API-like boundaries between teams, each owning two or three metrics, so leaders could assemble dependable pieces into a tall stack. The cost was value lost in organizational seams and slow response to change. Facebook's org was malleable: engineers moved between projects, assignments were weak, and code was communally owned. Its leaders needed soft alignment skills, knowing people's strengths and how to move and inspire them.

Stefan adds a caveat: a company cannot be staffed only with organizationally savvy people, since it turns negative-sum, with sharks fighting each other. As an example he offers OpenAI, noting he has not worked there and is relying on its hiring process and conversations with people inside. Its interviews favor technical achievements over organizational skill. It has plenty of politics, he says, but in its early phase it needs technical achievers to attract talent. As orgs grow there is entropy, and a need for people who can navigate it.

Source: 42:55–49:48 ↗

QIf a typical M1 were dropped into an M2 role, what would be the biggest skill gaps?

Stefan Mai

Stefan says the main gap is credibly adding value to the people who report to you. Managers of managers have fewer ways to interact with teams, and a straight M1 struggles to recognize those limits and where to use the important ones.

His illustration is a new M1 who sets up skip-levels and asks an indirect report, Jan, leading questions about whether her manager, Jim, is doing the job. Jim confronts the M1 a week later, and Jan says the M1 has insights Jim lacked. The M1 has disintermediated Jim, demotivated Jan and created new problems. Small acts by a senior leader have magnification effects, he says, and you learn them by observing or by having a good model of how things propagate.

Such mistakes are the easy way for a new M1 to fail, and he says leadership expects them, as with a first-time manager. Strategy and org design mistakes come later, but small behavioral ones in the first weeks can sink you.

Source: 49:49–53:44 ↗

QHow do IC and management growth paths compare, and are both meritocratic?

Stefan Mai

Stefan says at high levels everything becomes opaque and fuzzy. In calibrations he found it hard to stomach very senior ICs talking a big game without visible evidence, since it was unclear whether they were merely around valuable initiatives or instrumental in driving them. The same goes for managers: attribution is hard. Over a long run, such as four years of continued success in a role, it is undeniable, but on a half-to-half basis it is dubious.

For ICs at the sixes and maybe sevens, an outside observer can tell more easily, and an M1's team and deliverables allow a decent read. Further up, someone outside the leadership chain cannot see as clearly, and Stefan sees some unaccountability in much of management, comparable to judging a company's leadership team in the stock market. At some level, he says, it is difficult to have the data. The host summarized this as early promotions being easiest to verify and later ones more open to optics and narratives, and Stefan said that was a good summary.

Source: 53:46–56:22 ↗

QWhat cultural differences stand out between Meta and Amazon?

Stefan Mai

Stefan says Amazon is disciplined, a major strength, and he would expect more structured design reviews there. He thinks Meta engineers were on average a bit stronger but less disciplined, so reviews were fuzzier. Amazon was more predictable, partly because the business moves slower and partly because you can rely on other teams to meet SLAs. At Meta you might have to make the change yourself because the owner now works on photos. Many who move from Amazon to Meta find the unstructured environment paralyzing.

At Meta, the main positive he saw was openness and collaboration: engineers on his team worked with orgs across the company, such as a researcher in Paris, often without him setting it up. He also liked Meta's focus on empowering people. Amazon is process-oriented: when something fails, it adds a mechanism to prevent a repeat, whereas at Meta someone is more likely to say they learned the lesson. That has downsides, he says, and many of Facebook's privacy issues reflect an inability to do the process work Amazon does well. In ML, he was surprised by how hard data access was at Amazon, with teams building their own data lakes, while Meta had one shared warehouse.

Stefan prefers Meta's approach, especially for leadership, but missed some things from Amazon. For some people, he thinks Amazon is the better fit, since they would like it more than Meta's chaotic execution.

Source: 56:24–1:00:23 ↗

QHow do the performance systems at Meta and Amazon compare?

Stefan Mai

Stefan says they are pretty close. There is a public process in which ratings are set and given to reports, and a more private process, usually limited to higher levels, to decide where to invest: a top-tier designation at Amazon, additional or discretionary equity at Meta. The aim is to find the linchpins the company wants to keep. Whichever company, people must believe the process rewards performance.

He once tracked the time spent on Meta's review cycle (PSC) and estimated the cost at about $15,000 per engineer. The tempting reaction is that this is wasteful, but he says that misses the forest for the trees: the integrity of the review process is the whole ballgame, and if people do not believe it produces outcomes for them, they will not perform.

One difference he saw is that Meta was willing to go to bat for the upper quintile. Amazon, partly from frugality and partly from fairness, did less of this. In his org some engineers received about twice as much compensation as peers through extra equity, because they were seen as very important and going places. At Amazon that is uncommon, and the company tends to find a way to pull it back.

How do conversations about discretionary equity or top tier work?
Stefan Mai

Stefan says VPs and directors usually drive it, and how much they involve managers varies. Being asked who deserves it is a sign of trust. The question is who has trajectory, the rocket ship, even after a stellar but not exceptional half. At Amazon he recalls growth and replaceability, meaning whether the person's leaving would break the organization, as the two dimensions. Those positions can be lucrative, since companies tighten golden handcuffs when the org depends on someone.

Source: 1:03:34–1:05:23 ↗
Source: 1:00:25–1:03:19 ↗

QDid you experience low-performer quotas, and how do they work?

Stefan Mai

Stefan says every company of scale has them. In Meta's PSC process a merely good half gets written up as world-shaking, and assessments inflate in a way that cannot be true on average. Companies therefore target a distribution and, to keep performance high, must let some people go. Managers dislike this, Stefan included, but if a team does not act on a low performer, the team suffers because it no longer seems fair.

He says the share placed in the lower bucket varies, typically seven to 15 percent and sometimes up to 20, called needs improvement at Amazon and, per the captions, meets some or meets most at Meta. Some in that bucket are expected not to make the cut, and that is when PIPs start. Managers fight to keep people out, mostly to save face.

The worst scenario, he says, is telling a team how hard they have worked, then being told by your director that someone must be in the low bucket, and having to tell that person their work was not acceptable. A better case is a manager who messages a lower-quartile outcome early, so nobody is surprised.

Do PIPs work, or are they a formality to create a paper trail? Do they differ between companies?
Stefan Mai

Stefan says people can definitely get out of a PIP. It is first and foremost a legal paper trail, but to keep that credible people must be able to get through it. HR usually moderates, and its appetite to advocate for the employee varies.

At Amazon, while he was there, HR mainly wanted managers to check the boxes, and he calls it a pretty savage culture. Expectations are set, and the employee either turns it around or is gone, with managers holding a lot of discretion. Since most managers dislike firing, a manager may genuinely be rooting for the employee, though whether their hands are tied is up to some other power.

At Meta, he says, HR wanted every avenue exhausted before letting someone go. This is probably not true of modern Meta, but it was several years back, partly to protect its reputation as an employer. Stefan says this sounds cold, but companies have to reward performance, so terminations are part of the picture. They should be handled fairly and sensitively, but they have to happen or the company will not last long.

Source: 1:08:56–1:11:48 ↗
Source: 1:05:25–1:08:56 ↗

QWith AI cheating tools and LLM assistants, how much does cheating come up in interview prep?

Stefan Mai

Stefan says incentives in interview prep are mostly aligned, so cheating at mock interviews makes little sense, yet it has happened a few times. A coach reported a candidate talking to a friend in the background. His guess is that candidates may be testing their setup.

Remote interviews have always been somewhat cheatable, he says, and current tools make it worse. Recruiting teams over-rely on mechanisms that probably are not fully effective, such as checking browser focus or copy-paste activity, which catch only the least sophisticated. He expects interviews to change because software engineering is changing, with some companies allowing AI in assignments or choosing questions AI routinely gets wrong. He is more optimistic about evolving assessments than about anti-cheat measures.

He adds that companies are ruthless about performance now, so someone who cheats into a job may find it does not pan out. He has no formal accounting, but says plenty of people find themselves on the rough side of a review shortly afterward.

Algo interviews seem easier to cheat on than system design. Do you see a shift?
Stefan Mai

Stefan says companies are leaning more into design interviews, including lower-level design: classes, coupling and interactions between subsystems. In an AI-coded world, he says, the quality of design is load-bearing, and good abstractions matter more.

He has not seen any acute departure from coding interviews. People have predicted the demise of LeetCode for ages, but it serves a useful purpose for companies. Interviewing is very painful, but he thinks calling it broken goes too far, and it is premature to assume coding rounds will go away in the short to mid term.

Source: 1:15:02–1:16:51 ↗
Source: 1:11:50–1:15:01 ↗

QIf someone were set on passing OpenAI or Anthropic interviews, what is the optimal game plan?

Stefan Mai

Stefan says it varies, but those companies look for depth. OpenAI was notorious for asking the same questions in basically every interview, and he does not know why. Going deep on the functional areas they tended to ask about was an effective preparation strategy. That is not memorizing solutions, since interviewers are cleverer than that, but knowing roughly the areas gives a step up.

Behavioral and retrospective interviews matter a lot there, he says, because the companies want to see whether candidates have walked the walk. Because that is hard to judge yourself, he suggests asking a friend how you came across. He repeats his point about leaning toward technical accomplishments, not how you massaged the organization. For many people, he says, the crowning achievement of a big-tech staff career is seven docs, six teams aligned and five lines of code. That work was hard, but these companies do not value it the same way.

Source: 1:16:52–1:18:30 ↗

QWhat are your thoughts on job hopping, given you stayed in roles for around four years?

Stefan Mai

Stefan says that for ambitious people at lower levels, moving usually has advantages, because growth tends to come when you are uncomfortable in a new environment and must generalize your skills. He has not subscribed to it himself, since his motivation is going deep: after about two years he reaches the point where he can make an impact, which he finds most rewarding.

At higher levels, he says, frequent moves are a bad sign, because it is hard to get deep enough to build relationships and understand the domain. As a hiring manager he would second-guess a senior person moving every 18 months or two years, since he would invest a year ramping them up and then see them leave. For a mid-level hire that is a decent tenure, but for staff level he would hesitate. Early on, moving makes sense; as you get more senior, it pays to find places to put down roots.

The host suggests credibility compounds like a snowball inside one org, which is why hopping helps less later. Does that fit?
Stefan Mai

Stefan adds a trap: the snowball can become a shackle. Some very senior engineers become known for the system they created, and however hard they try to move in new directions, everyone knows them for that thing and they are stuck. He suggests asking yourself how comfortable you are. If you are not challenged, even at a senior level, it may be time to move. Otherwise the snowball works in your favor.

Source: 1:21:01–1:22:34 ↗
Source: 1:18:33–1:20:59 ↗

QLooking across your career, when did you grow the most, and why?

Stefan Mai

Stefan says mostly at transitions, when he is in a new space learning and applying at once, which stress-tests his skills and shows what is durable and what was fake. Moving to Facebook stretched him, from a leadership perspective, in unexpected ways amid a lot of stress in the company. The pivot into an ML-focused role left him feeling he had a lot to prove, which brought external pressure he appreciated.

Other growth happens over smaller spans. A lot of his effectiveness as an IC and manager comes from writing well, which he largely learned at Amazon. He says some of Amazon's writing culture is a waste of time, with people nitpicking trivia, but the company encourages good writing, which means good thinking at some level.

What is your top tip for an IC or EM who needs to improve their writing?
Stefan Mai

Stefan's main tip is to learn to be a critic first. Work out what you like and dislike in writing: read a doc, notice what hits you, scan it to see whether you get the big picture in seconds, and look for imprecision or conclusions that are not well supported.

When he first wrote docs at Amazon he got a lot of negative feedback while thinking they were great. He cites Amazon's PR FAQ exercise, a press release followed by frequently asked questions: fast-forward to the end and get the reader excited about what will be delivered, and if you cannot sell it there, it probably was not worth doing. Many PR FAQs open with a single pane of glass, which excites nobody, whereas people respond to something like a 50 percent reduction in time spent. Admitting your own writing is boring to anyone not knee-deep in it is, he says, the first step to good writing. The host summarized this as honing your taste as a reader first, and Stefan added: then practice.

Source: 1:24:22–1:26:21 ↗
Source: 1:22:36–1:24:21 ↗

QWhat motivates you now, having left for a startup after so much success at Meta?

Stefan Mai

Stefan says he likes interesting problems, ones he can tell his kids about and that set the stage for the future. The relentless march up the ladder is secondary for him now. Money matters because it powers everything, he says, but he realized he might be near the cap of what he could achieve in the ranks and asked what came next.

His method is to ask that question and then work backwards: if you want that thing, why not now, and what is keeping you? For more than a decade his answer was that he wanted to start a business, and he gave himself excuses. Eventually he told himself he was lying to himself. That was the impetus to leave big tech and build a business, and asking what he is really after remains his animating force.

Source: 1:26:22–1:28:09 ↗

QIf you could advise yourself just after college, what would you say?

Stefan Mai

Stefan says he could have been better about finding mentorship. He did much of it alone, and asking someone like himself three questions might have saved months of toil.

He also points to written plans: taking stock of where he was, deciding where he wanted to go, and building a checklist. He still has an old plan in his Dropbox for getting into ML. Such plans paid incredible dividends that he still under-emphasizes. Most people lack the agency to decide where they want to go and then take it, but the world is very malleable to such plans.

He recalls that shortly after becoming a senior manager he told his boss and director a long list of things he would get done, many of which he did not know how to do. The director later told him that this was the moment he knew Stefan would succeed in the role. Lack of agency holds many people back and is hard to instill, Stefan says, but forcing yourself to write a plan for what you really want has a huge gradient on your ability to grow.

Source: 1:28:12–1:30:17 ↗

Section 91 · interview

Support people, stay close to the product, and make tradeoffs explicit

Fiona Fung reflects on management, mentorship, product feedback, and the choices that took her from Microsoft to Meta and Anthropic.

Fiona Fung’s account connects three habits: make the partnership with people explicit, experience the product yourself, and treat culture as something people enact. The examples span developer tools, Marketplace, VR, and her early experience with Claude Code. Her comparisons describe those teams at the times she worked on them; they are observations from a career, rather than permanent descriptions of entire companies.

Source: 00:03–00:18 ↗

QHow do you balance an important project against team health?

Fiona Fung

First establish whether the situation really warrants an exceptional push. Fung remembers Marketplace lockdowns or war rooms that concentrated people on an urgent objective. That focus could be valuable, but it had a real cost to morale. Leadership should discuss the tradeoff deliberately with the team, rather than allowing the cost to remain implicit.

One war room had a growth target as its exit condition. The team initially imagined that a few fixes might achieve it, but the effort continued much longer than expected. In hindsight, she would have assessed the likely duration more realistically, discussed the effect on team health, and explained the journey and expected length up front. A measurable target alone did not make the sustained intensity manageable.

How long did that war room last?

It felt like at least two months. There were physical rooms in Menlo Park and Seattle, and at one point the team launched 75 experiments at once. The contrast with a week-long launch push is central to the lesson: the team did not understand the duration when it entered the arrangement.

Source: 02:25–03:04 ↗
Source: 00:34–02:24 ↗
Editorial synthesis
Source: 00:49–03:04 ↗

QWhat changes when you become a manager of managers?

Fiona Fung

The relationship becomes a partnership between people who each bring management skills as well as technical skills. When she first supported managers, including a TypeScript manager she considered an exceptional compiler engineer, she asked what each person did well and how they could divide responsibility. Supporting another manager creates more opportunities to complement strengths.

Delegation also needs a balance of trust and verification. If delegation removes too much contact with the project, the supporting leader can lose touch. She asks managers for fast feedback and transparency about both successes and problems. The useful conversation is the one that exposes where help is needed; a reassuring report that everything is fine can conceal the very issue the partnership should solve.

Source: 03:05–05:30 ↗

QHow can a mentor make the relationship useful?

Fiona Fung

Begin by asking the mentee what they want from the relationship and what success would look like after three or six months. An explicit goal gives both people a way to use their time effectively.

Also distinguish mentoring from coaching. In her description, mentoring combines listening with advice drawn from experience. Coaching acts more like a mirror, helping the other person discover answers within themselves. Clarifying which mode the person wants can change how the conversation should work.

Should the mentee or mentor drive the relationship?

The most effective relationships she has seen start with goals set by the mentee. The mentor contributes experience, advice, and resources, but the person seeking mentorship should state what they hope to gain.

Source: 06:23–06:54 ↗
Source: 05:32–06:21 ↗
Two modes of helping someone grow
ModeWhat the helper contributesUseful starting question
MentoringListening, experience, advice, and resources.What do you want to gain over the next few months?
CoachingA mirror that helps the person find their own answers.What do you need to understand or discover for yourself?
Source: 05:40–06:54 ↗

QWhat should an individual contributor do with one-on-one time?

Fiona Fung

Put routine status reporting into an asynchronous channel. Fung uses messages or a shared, living one-on-one document where either person can add updates.

Use the live conversation for topics that benefit from interaction: something the person wants to learn, a deeper discussion of their work, or a product question worth exploring together. The point is to reserve the scarce meeting time for conversation, while making the operational updates available separately.

Source: 06:55–07:41 ↗

QWhy did you leave Microsoft for Facebook?

Fiona Fung

She had friends enjoying Facebook, but repeatedly wanted to finish the work in front of her at Microsoft. Her final project there involved JavaScript and TypeScript, and she cared about helping the team deliver TypeScript 1.0. A former Visual Studio colleague, who became her first Facebook manager, contacted her in late 2014 about building a product around buying and selling in groups. She joined in 2015.

The commerce mission mattered for three reasons. Used goods could make a meaningful affordability difference for people with tighter budgets. Reuse could give existing goods a second, third, or fourth life. A selling platform could help a local business begin without first needing a physical store. Marketplace also represented a new kind of connection for her: meeting new people, rather than only reconnecting with people she already knew.

After eleven and a half years at Microsoft, she also wanted to test and broaden her engineering ability outside an ecosystem in which she had become comfortable. The move combined a mission she cared about with a chance to learn beyond familiar tools and practices.

Source: 07:41–10:58 ↗

QWhat stood out about the difference between Microsoft and Facebook?

Fiona Fung

Both offered talented colleagues who cared about their work. The clearest difference in her example was speed: early Marketplace shipped weekly updates, while the Visual Studio work she remembered used roughly four-week sprints. Even those four-week sprints had once felt short compared with earlier development cycles.

Facebook also felt much smaller at the time. She appreciated the expectation that a problem was everyone’s responsibility, regardless of role. Her example is a willingness to lean in and help, rather than to treat an issue as belonging exclusively to someone else.

Source: 10:59–12:12 ↗

QWhy is using your own product so valuable?

Fiona Fung

Her first job involved using Visual Studio to build Visual Studio, so daily product use was built into the work. It gave her empathy for users and a feel for the product’s condition. She carried that habit into Marketplace, keeping items to sell so that she could experience the workflow herself. Meeting users also made the effect of the work tangible and motivating.

On VR and related device teams, she used Quest devices and early Ray-Ban products. For a manager who rarely gets to write code, using the product can be a way to experience what the team is building and to contribute directly. She describes reproducing a difficult floor-height bug at home and collecting logs as a small piece of maker time.

Peterman adds that a leader’s report can bring attention to a bug that was already known but had lost urgency. Fung emphasizes another effect: team members notice when a leader uses and cares about their product, and that can build rapport.

Source: 12:14–15:34 ↗

QHow do you make frequent product use sustainable?

Fiona Fung

Integrate the product into something you enjoy. She used VR for exercise, watching movies, and knitting while watching. Enjoyable everyday use creates repeated exposure without making the activity feel like a chore.

At the time of the interview, building Claude Code with Claude Code made that feedback loop part of her day job and let her ship production software again. She also mentions continuing to submit Meta product feedback after leaving.

Leaders can add structured product sessions. On her last VR team, she and her product and design partners tried nearly ready features together on Fridays and gave fast feedback. That complements daily use with a regular opportunity to inspect what is approaching release.

Source: 15:37–17:26 ↗

QHow can an engineering leader work well with product management?

Fiona Fung

Start with the shared objective of the leadership group and the strengths each person brings. Because there will be more work than people, agree explicitly on who owns which pieces and divide the work accordingly.

Using the product also improved her partnership with product managers. Their one-on-ones could become substantive product conversations grounded in something they had actually experienced. The discussion links partnership and product knowledge: an engineering leader has more to contribute when they stay close to what customers use.

Source: 17:28–18:31 ↗

QWhat does kindness contribute to an engineering organization?

Fiona Fung

She connects the principle to the pandemic, when device teams were trying to ship Quest 2 and develop Ray-Ban products without normal access to offices, labs, and colocated specialists. People were doing difficult work while also coping with pressures at home.

A personal example made the principle vivid. Her grandmother was in a Canadian care facility that she could not visit. Staff could arrange only limited FaceTime calls, and a rare available slot conflicted with a one-on-one she had promised to attend. The person she supported readily accepted a last-minute cancellation. What may have felt like a small accommodation to him had a large effect on her.

The lesson is that a colleague’s private circumstances are often invisible. Kindness is a practical way to work with people whose full situation you do not know, while the team is trying to accomplish difficult things together.

Source: 18:32–21:25 ↗

QWhy did you choose Anthropic?

Fiona Fung

She was happy working on VR and Horizon OS at Meta and was not conducting a broad search for a new job. The choice she describes was essentially joining Anthropic or staying in a role she already enjoyed.

Using an internal AI tool to build useful work tools showed her that AI was already changing her own workflow. Conversations with Anthropic employees then drew her to their mission orientation, emphasis on safety, and sense of shared responsibility. She likens that attraction to the mission that had drawn her to Marketplace. These are her reasons for the move and impressions of the organization at that time.

Source: 21:26–23:12 ↗

QDid Facebook’s culture change as it grew?

Fiona Fung

Yes. She treats culture as a living thing expressed through actions, rather than a statement on a wall. Growth changed the company, although she still saw strong commitment to the mission within teams such as VR.

When new employees asked which team would give them the most impact, she also asked what they were passionate about. That question restored a dimension that could disappear in a comparison focused only on career impact.

How should someone choose between greater impact and work they care more about?

Have an honest conversation with yourself about what motivates you. Impact, learning, and working with good people can matter in different proportions to different people; she does not prescribe one universal winner.

Share those priorities with your manager. When supporting someone new, she asks what they want from the partnership, what has worked or failed before, and what is important to them. An explicit discussion is more useful than either person guessing the other’s priorities.

Source: 24:36–25:43 ↗
Source: 23:13–24:35 ↗

QWhat stood out during your first two months at Anthropic?

Fiona Fung

She saw the mission and responsibility toward society expressed in onboarding, which made it feel more substantial than an interview slogan.

The speed of the Claude Code team also stood out, even compared with the Marketplace period she remembered as fast. Broad internal use supplied a rapid cycle: build an idea, launch internally, get feedback from employees, release publicly, and keep learning. Her concern as the team grew was preserving that agility and speed.

Source: 25:45–27:21 ↗
Editorial synthesis
Source: 25:55–27:21 ↗

QWhat feedback most changed your career?

Fiona Fung

It was feedback on how she received feedback. Her instinct as an engineer was to debug the situation immediately: ask questions, replay what happened, and determine how to improve. Someone pointed out that giving constructive feedback was already uncomfortable, and her questions could make the person feel they had to justify it.

She changed the first conversation to listening and learning. Questions could wait until another day, after she had reflected. The distinction is about timing and the experience of the person raising the issue: a sincere wish to understand can still feel like a demand to defend the feedback if it arrives too quickly.

Source: 27:23–28:43 ↗

QWhat would you tell yourself at the beginning of your career?

Fiona Fung

Enjoy the experience while it is happening. Work and life move quickly, and the moments that later feel like the good old days are also the moments you are living now.

Source: 28:44–29:08 ↗
