Section 92 · interview

The best technology still needs a route to users

James Everingham connects browser competition, engineering leadership, relationships, and his current thesis about managing corporate AI agents.

QHow did being dismissed from college lead to a university job?

At eighteen, Everingham neglected classes while obsessively programming. Penn State’s library computing staff independently found and used his uploaded software, discovered he was local, and recruited him to migrate work from mainframes to PCs. One part of the university dismissed him as a student while another hired him. He remembers having to explain the unusual good-and-bad news to his mother.

Was the result positive for you?

Very. As staff, he could take computer-science courses free, including advanced classes, without following a complete degree program. He received substantial education without the credential. Continued donations or payments for his shared software then led him to leave and start a business at about twenty.

Source: 02:54–04:04 ↗
What did distributing software mean before modern repositories?

People dialed bulletin-board systems with modems, waited for a free connection, and downloaded files slowly. Some systems used a single home computer and phone line; networks exchanged messages by calling each other at night. He uses “shareware” and related terms rather than a precise modern licensing category.

Source: 04:04–05:41 ↗
Source: 00:51–02:54 ↗

QHow did authorities find your teenage phone-system hacking?

He says they traced his number and also found his name on software he was proud to distribute. His mother answered when the FBI arrived and asked him to stop. He remembers that she did not understand the computer work and worried about its effect on school.

What did the software do?

It reproduced operator-control signaling on older telephone infrastructure, enabling actions such as unauthorized calls or listening. The detailed tone and key sequences are not needed to understand the career anecdote. The episode shows both his technical curiosity and his youthful lack of judgment.

Source: 06:18–07:12 ↗
Source: 05:41–07:57 ↗

QWhy did you join Netscape?

Borland recruited him after seeing developer tools he had distributed. Its programming tools had been central to his learning, and the job brought him to California. Relationships there, especially a close colleague, later brought him to Netscape.

He hoped an internet startup would avoid Microsoft’s competition, which was already damaging Borland. That judgment proved wrong: Netscape became an even more direct target. He still regards the relationships formed in those companies as lasting assets; some colleagues have accompanied him through five or six later companies.

Source: 07:57–10:49 ↗

QWhat does useful networking look like for an engineer?

Ask questions, show curiosity about others’ work, offer help, and participate in discussions. He credits a colleague’s advice to seek mentorship by being useful rather than opening with a request to be mentored. Avoid burning bridges: the people beside you may occupy very different roles twenty years later. He views lasting working relationships as the foundation, rather than networking as a schedule of transactional coffee meetings.

Source: 10:49–13:10 ↗

QWhy did Netscape scale and go public so quickly?

He describes a chaotic expansion from about one hundred fifty employees to over three thousand in roughly a year, with unfamiliar new colleagues appearing even after a brief absence. He remembers an era when a compelling internet story could attract public capital with fewer procedural barriers. His broader account contrasts dot-com enthusiasm with later expectations for credible revenue and growth. A recalled calendar date is uncertain and omitted rather than turned into publication history.

Source: 13:10–15:55 ↗

QWhen did you realize Netscape would compete directly with Microsoft?

Very quickly. Microsoft viewed web applications as a threat to its operating-system and packaged-software model. Everingham’s engineering assumption was that a superior browser would win. The important competition instead became distribution: Microsoft bundled a free browser, and defaults mattered more once quality was similar.

Netscape’s initial browser-selling business suffered. His lesson is that technical superiority alone does not establish a viable competitive position, especially against a company controlling a major distribution channel.

How did the team react?

Engineers felt validated that their mission mattered, but also stressed and discouraged when the competitor gave away what they sold. Netscape’s default landing page supplied traffic, so the company developed web services and monetization to help replace revenue. The response had to be invented while the threat was unfolding.

Source: 17:48–18:42 ↗
Source: 15:55–17:48 ↗

QDo you remember the Internet Explorer logo prank at Netscape?

Yes. He remembers a large logo placed on the office lawn and treats it as friendly rivalry alongside serious competition. Engineers moved between companies, and he later worked closely with one of the people involved, sharing stories from opposing sides of the browser contest. The precise office location is inconsistent with the host’s account, so no location is asserted.

Source: 18:42–20:46 ↗

QWhy give Netscape’s browser source code away?

The company was badly out-resourced and wanted to change the contest by inviting the wider developer community to help. He regards the resulting open-source effort and Firefox as a meaningful continuation. Releasing the code was itself difficult: the team removed restricted cryptographic components and reviewed embarrassing internal names and comments before publication.

Why not simply search for inappropriate words?

Some problematic references were unusual phrases or variable names rather than a predictable list of terms. He recalls reviewing printed code because a simple known-word search would not discover every issue.

Source: 22:15–23:05 ↗
What did it mean that SSL was treated as a munition?

He describes historical export restrictions on cryptographic technology and the concern that public encryption could frustrate authorities or be used by adversaries. This is his account of the restrictions during that release effort, not a statement of present legal requirements.

Source: 23:08–24:04 ↗
Source: 20:46–23:05 ↗

QWhat career lesson did the browser war teach you?

Understand what the competition actually turns on: technology, data, distribution, or another advantage. Choosing an employer invests time and often concentrates financial exposure through equity, so he thinks engineers should examine the business as well as the code. He frames this as a career decision-making lens, rather than individualized investment advice.

Source: 24:04–25:38 ↗

QHow did you become Instagram’s head of engineering?

He spent six and a half years on Luminate, a product he likens to shopping functionality for publishers, without finding the desired success. A sale to Yahoo, a board relationship, and a prior Instagram acquisition conversation later connected him to Instagram. Although he had verbally accepted another opportunity, meeting the team clarified his enthusiasm: he actually used and cared about Instagram. He credits network, timing, and relevant image-product experience, including lessons from a company that had not become a breakout success.

Can founding a startup let someone return to big tech at a much higher level?

It can, but a company still needs evidence that the person can do the job. His own move from a small startup into a much larger Yahoo organization relied on previous experience leading substantial teams at Netscape and Tellme. Founding alone did not substitute for demonstrated leadership capability.

Source: 27:54–29:14 ↗
Source: 25:38–27:54 ↗

QWhy reduce the initial Instagram Stories team?

A competitive threat does not always call for more people. He wanted a small group of highly capable, proactive engineers with clear ownership and few dependencies. With the founders closely involved, the team could get a product working quickly, then integrate and scale it. Larger teams can create federated components and dependencies that slow the same work. He connects the roughly three-month effort to Instagram’s principle of doing the simplest thing first to test a thesis before committing the whole company.

Source: 29:15–32:55 ↗

QHow did the CTO and head-of-engineering roles differ?

Mike Krieger wanted to focus on technology and coding, while Everingham took responsibility for people and execution as engineering approached one hundred employees. They published job descriptions and decision-routing examples to prevent conflicting expectations. Technology experiments and roadmap questions went to the CTO; headcount, hiring, structure, and reviews went to the engineering head. He often finds companies asking for a CTO when the actual difficulties concern engineering management.

Source: 32:55–35:32 ↗

QWhat else did Instagram teach you?

He initially expected familiar communication failures around one hundred engineers but found the team functioning well longer than expected. Problems appeared later, around one hundred fifty to two hundred. He attributes the delay to talented people maintaining a great deal of shared context. He also values builders being power users of their product; an intern’s quick hackathon project became a highly engaging feature. These examples explain his appreciation of the team rather than define universal organization-size thresholds.

Source: 35:32–37:17 ↗

QWhy leave Instagram for the Libra/Novi initiative?

David Marcus described the mission privately and invited him to lead engineering. Everingham initially found the proposal implausible, then became absorbed in the possible impact: safer, cheaper money movement and financial inclusion. His product partner had a similar change of mind. They joined because the mission appealed, despite affection for their existing jobs.

How did the project go?

He says the intended project never shipped. Political and regulatory resistance forced repeated architectural changes over years, and he believes continued opposition remained even after substantial compliance work. He wishes they might have launched first, but that is a retrospective opinion. When both he and Marcus wanted to leave, their shared mission led them to start another company together.

Source: 39:44–42:02 ↗
Source: 37:18–39:44 ↗

QWhy move from crypto infrastructure back toward AI and developer tools?

He considers himself skeptical of much crypto enthusiasm but sees value in its money-movement base layer. After building a team and preparing a successor, he felt a burdensome commute and limited immediate additional value justified stepping back. Meta then offered developer infrastructure, reconnecting him to the developer-tools focus of his first decade. AI made that role exciting: a large, senior organization could explore ambitious productivity improvements.

What observation led you to found Guild?

An internal agent platform became highly sought after by developers, consuming major server capacity as demand spread. Agents performed tool-driven work beyond code generation. He saw a chance to apply the lessons from tens of thousands of internal developers to a much broader market.

Source: 45:29–46:19 ↗
Source: 42:02–45:29 ↗

QWhat gives you confidence in an intensely competitive AI market?

He carefully distinguishes drive from certainty. He believes companies need an agent-control layer regardless of which model wins: permissions, observation, budget limits, circuit breakers, and centralized execution. He criticizes products aimed at gaps he expects models to close, while acknowledging constant attention to competitors.

He imagines many agents operating internal workflows. A duplicate-issue agent illustrates a narrow task separate from coding; other agents might work across product, design, or HR. Those agents need different permissions, just as employees do. He argues for predictable infrastructure boundaries around nondeterministic model behavior.

A customer’s runaway token spending illustrates why scattered laptop execution is difficult to manage. These examples support his product thesis; forecasts about the market and claims about competitors remain his opinions.

Source: 46:19–51:11 ↗

QWhat do you think of management that stays deeply in every detail?

Different environments call for different tools. His normal style is to support capable people, focus them on outcomes, remove obstacles, ask questions, and let them create the solution. He has temporarily intervened more closely with failing teams, then stepped back. He worries that permanent micromanagement drives talented people away, but does not claim enough knowledge to judge every public leader’s circumstances. Management detail is one intervention rather than his only mode.

Source: 51:11–54:45 ↗

QWhat regrets or lessons would you share?

He is happy with where the path led but wishes he had appreciated that time eventually becomes the scarce resource. Years of unproductive struggle are costly; doing work one loves and having good days matter. He also recommends going where capable people and mentors are, which helped him almost by accident. His tactical retirement-saving suggestion is to begin early; it is retained as his personal reflection, without making a current financial recommendation for every reader.

Source: 54:45–56:27 ↗

QWhat would you tell yourself at the beginning?

Speak up even when afraid of appearing uninformed, ask more questions, and build relationships. He also wishes he had deliberately moved earlier to a place offering the opportunities and resources relevant to his field. Being recruited to California changed his career; he compares waiting in Pennsylvania to an actor not considering Hollywood. This is his own geographic experience rather than a claim that everyone must make the same move.

Section 93 · interview

Great engineering connects theory to decisions at real scale

A former Netflix director describes an exceptional colleague and how a job interview changed his view of video systems.

QWhat made the strongest engineer you worked with exceptional?

Former Netflix engineering director

The director singles out a colleague who moved between academic signal processing and practical video engineering. Their work on parallel and content-based encoding later expanded into convex-hull encoding, which the guest describes as a way to obtain the best video quality for a given bandwidth constraint. His praise is grounded in work they did together at several companies.

He highlights a cost-benefit model for codec evaluation that connected energy expenditure with compression efficiency. The distinctive strength was not academic brilliance in isolation: it was bringing theory into a form that supported operational choices. A result on two videos was less useful than understanding what happened across very large collections. The guest uses tests across thousands, millions, or billions of videos to emphasize the difference in scale.

Source: 00:00–02:18 ↗

QHow did you come to work at Meta?

Former Netflix engineering director

An earlier Netflix practice encouraged employees to interview periodically to understand their market value. The director initially interviewed with Facebook without intending to move. He felt confident because of the large video platform his team had built, but an interviewer challenged the assumption that familiar CPU-based solutions could handle Facebook’s video volume. He says this exposed how narrow his understanding had been. He received an offer and initially declined it.

Later, the exceptional colleague described the problems and opportunities in his own Facebook offer with a renewed enthusiasm. The director recognized that the colleague wanted harder work and more visible recognition of individual contribution. He distinguishes recognition from celebrity: even an executive explicitly acknowledging good work can matter. His account contrasts the cultures he experienced without claiming that every Netflix employee lacked recognition.

As the colleague’s boss, he did not want to lose him; as a friend, he supported the opportunity. The director’s own team was doing well and had a successor ready. When he eventually left Netflix in 2019, Facebook contacted him, required another interview because the earlier process was too old, and made an offer he accepted. The story shows how interviewing for practice can reveal a genuinely compelling problem, even before a person decides to change employers.

Source: 02:18–06:03 ↗

Section 94 · coaching

Reasoning through hard interview problems without perfect recall

A live whiteboard exercise preserves the useful partial reasoning, clarifications, and remaining gaps in three familiar algorithm problems.

QHow would you find the minimum insertions, deletions, or replacements needed to convert one string into another?

Neetcode

Neetcode recognizes edit distance and begins with recursion rather than claiming to remember every detail. Matching characters let the comparison advance without an edit. A mismatch creates three possible actions—insert, delete, or replace—and exploring those choices supplies a recursive starting point that can be memoized.

He then sketches a two-dimensional dynamic-programming grid, with dimensions corresponding to the strings and expected O(n × m) time. The exchange does not finish the transition formula, boundary cases, or implementation. He briefly says “maximum” while describing possible recursive results despite the prompt asking for a minimum; the correct-looking direction should not be mistaken for a fully checked recurrence.

What does one cell of the grid represent?
Neetcode

He works toward the edit distance between prefixes of the two words, with later cells derived from previously solved subproblems. The host clarifies that interpretation, and Neetcode agrees. He admits that mapping each edit action to a neighboring cell is the part requiring more careful thought and would usually start writing code to make it precise.

He says deriving the DP from the recursive solution is easier than jumping straight to the grid. A concrete example can show why different actions are needed, but this verbal sketch stops before completing all cases. The host’s diagnosis is that the candidate is going in the right direction and still needs time for case analysis.

Source: 02:49–05:47 ↗
Source: 00:00–02:46 ↗

QHow would you find the median of two sorted arrays?

Neetcode

He knows binary search is associated with the problem but does not remember the elimination rule. He constructs an example with overlapping values and duplicates and talks about time management: elaborate diagrams might help reasoning but consume limited interview time.

A brief exchange corrects the task from finding a target to finding the median. With nine total elements in his example, he knows the fifth ordered element is the goal. He tests whether part of one array can safely be eliminated and recognizes that comparisons must involve both arrays. He then considers comparing the arrays’ medians and flags odd/even and off-by-one complications.

The segment ends with a partial reconstruction, not a complete algorithm or correctness argument. He says it has been about five years since making his solution video and uses the struggle to show how first-principles reasoning can get him closer without instant recall. The host moves on rather than supplying a finished solution.

Source: 05:12–10:29 ↗

QHow would you count placements of n queens on an n-by-n board with no mutual attacks?

Neetcode

He proposes backtracking over placements and skipping moves already attacked by another queen. Sets or similar hash structures can record occupied rows and columns. The challenge is identifying diagonal membership without scanning the board.

He derives one diagonal key by noting that increasing a row while decreasing a column keeps their sum constant. After some hesitation he derives the other direction from the row-column difference. With row, column, and both diagonal keys, a tentative placement can be checked through quick membership lookups before recursing.

The host accepts the overall direction. Neetcode does not provide code, a complete enumeration scheme, or a verified time complexity; he notes that the search tree is large and probably exponential, even though each membership lookup is constant time. His belief that the approach is optimal is not proved in the exchange.

Are the diagonal keys just a way to test quickly whether a diagonal is occupied?
Neetcode

Yes. Neetcode confirms that the goal is a key-based membership lookup, then completes the distinction between constant sums on one diagonal direction and constant differences on the other. The clarification helps him finish the reasoning he had been reconstructing.

Source: 13:53–14:54 ↗
Source: 10:27–15:43 ↗

Section 95 · interview

Austin McDonald: Behavioral Interviews, Downleveling, and How Hiring Committees Decide

Austin McDonald, a former Meta hiring committee member, explains how leveling and hiring decisions are made and why scope-focused behavioral stories decide outcomes for senior engineers.

Senior hiring turns on scope shown in behavioral stories (Austin McDonald's view)

Austin McDonald, introduced by the host as a former Meta hiring committee member who led mobile hiring across the company, argues that for senior engineers the behavioral interview, and even the first recruiter conversation, is where level is decided. A candidate who wants to avoid being downleveled should know the company's rubric, choose the highest-scope stories that still fit the question, show technical, organizational and business depth, and treat every contact (recruiter, hiring manager, closing questions) as evaluative. The second half moves to interviewer dynamics, story structure, and Austin's own reflections on regret, scope and fear. Everything about Meta's process is Austin's account of their own time there and may differ at other companies or today.

Source: 00:49–1:41:33 ↗

QWhat actually happens in a hiring committee, and who touches a candidate between first contact and the final decision?

Austin McDonald

Austin says that when a senior packet reached the committee, the first thing Austin read was the behavioral interview. Austin wanted to see the scope the engineer had operated at, their level of influence, insight and communication, and the size of the organization they had worked in. Committees are made up of engineers and influential engineering managers, recruited by a chair such as Austin, and work with recruiting on two decisions: hire or not, and level. Austin describes a company-wide committee that mostly does a gut check against a cross-company bar, and says that at Meta a final committee of engineering directors makes the hiring and leveling call.

The path starts with a sourcer, an entry-level recruiting job whose task is to find candidates or process referrals. The sourcer looks at the job description, years of experience and past companies. The phone screen that follows is often a coding interview, and sometimes a multiple-choice technical quiz used as a pre-filter. A clearly strong phone screen goes straight to on-site scheduling. A borderline one comes to the hiring committee for the first time, which decides whether to add a follow-up, move the person on, or pass for now.

The committee is also consulted for specialized candidates, for example a low-level C++ mobile engineer who needs a fitting system design interview, and for the choice between senior and staff. That choice changes the loop. At Meta, Austin says, staff candidates get two system design interviews, so no one could be hired at staff without them, and principal and distinguished loops add further behavioral interviews. After the on-site, the committee decides hire, level and follow-ups. Behavioral interviews generate most follow-ups, because Austin considers them among the hardest to give and to read. Committee members sometimes go with the recruiter to the directors to argue for taking a chance on someone whose packet is weak in one area but strong in a trait the company needs.

How is a candidate's starting level first decided?
Austin McDonald

Austin says the early call rests on years of experience and previous title: a staff engineer at Google will likely be brought in as staff at Meta. Many companies, Meta included, do not publish levels, so a LinkedIn profile rarely shows level, which is why years of experience carry so much weight.

Source: 06:45–07:34 ↗
What happens to a high-titled candidate from outside big tech?
Austin McDonald

Austin says sourcers and recruiters know that titles inflate in parts of the industry. A manager of 50 or 75 people at a business-oriented company might be downleveled to a team of eight or ten engineers at Meta, and individual contributors are treated the same way. Calling oneself a principal engineer on LinkedIn does not draw principal-level outreach, because different companies attach different expectations to the same level. Austin adds that a consistent industry-wide scale would be nice, but it does not exist.

Source: 07:36–08:53 ↗
Could someone get through by inflating a title on a resume?
Austin McDonald

The host posed this as a hypothetical about an unethical candidate. Austin says the first phone screen at staff and above is also a scope check: some coding, some system design, and a walk through a large shipped project. Lying convincingly is hard, because interviewers sense whether the story is true and follow-up questions expose gaps. Austin says coaching clients who recite AI-generated stories start giving vague, inconsistent answers once asked about the technology.

Austin concedes that anyone can be fooled by a good enough liar, but the on-site interviewers for staff and principal candidates are very senior and highly calibrated, so a liar would have to lie repeatedly and convincingly. Austin jokes that someone able to do that might be good enough for the job, and says that in a career of hiring thousands of people, Austin has not heard of a hire later found to have invented their background.

Source: 08:54–12:17 ↗
Source: 01:45–06:43 ↗

QThe host said engineers often assume the behavioral round can be improvised. What should a candidate do to be placed at staff?

Austin McDonald

Austin says the most important task, in any behavioral story and in the first chat with a recruiter, is to establish scope: what size of business problem was solved with technology, how much ambiguity was handled, and what kind of organization the candidate operated in. The recruiter call is effectively a behavioral interview, so the opening “tell me about yourself” should be the greatest hits of the resume, with metrics, and with depth and complexity.

Austin contrasts “I improved performance in the Facebook app” with an account of organizing about 100 engineers across a twelve-month performance project that hit hard technical problems, needed several staff engineers, and ended in three core principles. A candidate should convey technical depth, organizational depth and business impact, because every interviewer in the loop is listening for the same things. Crisp practice on that opening is the first place to land in the right leveling bucket.

Responding to the host's point that staff promotions also require cross-organization work, Austin agrees and says preparing for behavioral interviews makes someone a better engineer. Most of Austin's coaching clients undersell rather than exaggerate. They need to show how hard the problem was and what impact it had on the team, code quality and the organization over time. Telling the whole story takes preparation, but it is the same skill used in weekly one-on-ones and executive updates.

Is the first recruiter call already an evaluation?
Austin McDonald

The host noted that recruiters pitch the first call as a casual chat. Austin answers “always be closing”: the call is evaluative, though softer, since the recruiter wants to find a candidate who gets through. Recruiters at big companies are paid by the hires they deliver. They advocate for candidates but are not friends, and compensation is a topic to handle carefully.

Austin advises against showing up unprepared or disconnected. If not ready, reschedule and spend time preparing what to say, since that is the best route to a higher-level offer.

Source: 17:16–19:23 ↗
Does the final chat with the hiring manager also carry signal?
Austin McDonald

Austin says yes. The pressure is lower, and at companies such as Meta or Google a team-matching phase brings conversations with several managers. These chats are more social than interviews, where a long self-introduction cuts into the interviewer's time for collecting signal. The manager is asking whether they like the candidate, whether they will fit the team, and whether the candidate can solve problems like the manager's own.

So Austin recommends asking the recruiter and sourcer in advance what the manager values and what the team is working on, then telling stories that show the candidate can solve those problems.

Source: 19:25–21:12 ↗
Source: 13:18–17:14 ↗

QWhat is the most common mistake candidates make in compensation conversations with recruiters?

Austin McDonald

Austin says they are not a negotiation expert and recommends getting advice from people who are. Their own view is that early anchoring is dangerous: when asked early about compensation expectations, a candidate should be careful, because whatever is said anchors the rest of the conversation.

Austin tells candidates to learn the local laws and says that in California and New York recruiters are required to share salary and total-comp bands, which a candidate can use to see where they sit (this legal claim is Austin's and was not checked). Austin thinks the biggest mistake is not having multiple offers. Without them, a candidate negotiates from weakness, so Austin urges candidates to time offers to land at about the same moment, even though that is more stressful and more work.

Source: 21:14–22:52 ↗

QIf a candidate who wants only staff roles sees they are being funneled into the wrong loop, can that be corrected mid-process?

Austin McDonald

Austin says that depends on the company and process, but it is a good conversation to have with the recruiter. Companies uplevel candidates as well as downlevel them, and recruiters will usually try to keep someone in the process. Austin suggests pushing to complete as much of the evaluation as possible for the desired level up front, so that follow-up interviews and late changes are not needed. If a team offers only a lower level, it depends on the job and total compensation, but Austin would aim to excel and then ask for consideration at the higher level.

Austin names two methods. The first is to anchor every conversation at the higher level, starting with “tell me about yourself” and then in the behavioral and system design interviews, so that interviewers see large-scope projects and impact and reset what they expect from the rest of the interview. The second is story choice. Behind every behavioral question is a question the interviewer actually cares about: is the candidate operating at the expected level? Interviewers forget the details quickly.

Austin says their book gives four considerations for choosing a story, and scope comes first. The candidate's job is to leave having told the most important stories of their career, and since the interviewer drives, to steer the conversation toward the signal that best represents them.

Source: 22:54–26:51 ↗

QWhat do senior, staff and principal scope look like, and how should a candidate express them?

Austin McDonald

Austin first says to research the specific company's level expectations, then offers a simple rubric for big-tech-style companies, shown in the table below. Levels are really about how much ambiguity a person can handle. Austin notes that the ambiguity facing an intern differs from the ambiguity facing a chief executive, and says that difference is what separates both levels and pay.

Staff versus senior comes down to breadth of impact: a whole team or several teams rather than a small project. Stories involve working across a large organization. For that reason Austin thinks startup engineers struggle to reach staff unless they were founders, because a few engineers and one stakeholder limit how much organizational leadership they can show.

Austin adds two more things to quantify or mention. For technical complexity, a candidate should give a sense of the time involved, the risk, how many people were consulted, and how hard it would have been to back out of a decision. For leadership, which engineers often forget because they love to talk about technology, a candidate should describe influence, getting concessions from other teams, aligning roadmaps, and mentoring people to make the team and organization better. Austin recommends reflecting on one's own career to identify what differentiates it, and talking about those things.

How should a specialist who solves problems no one else can describe their scope?
Austin McDonald

The host asked about people who push the industry forward on their own. Austin says to start with business impact, which technology-focused engineers find hard. There was a reason the technology was needed and a context around it, and Austin encourages people to ask what Steve Jobs would say about the advance and why the project was critical to the company.

Source: 32:27–33:22 ↗
Is it too much to say that a team of staff engineers failed before the candidate succeeded?
Austin McDonald

The host said that framing works when a manager says it in a promotion committee, but that a candidate saying it about themselves may sound like too much. Austin disagrees outright. In Austin's view behavioral interviewers are pattern matchers, and having solved problems others could not is one of the patterns for a higher level.

Austin finds it fine to say a candidate was the third owner of a project and where earlier owners failed, as long as the point is not to boast but to show insight into why those efforts failed, whether a product-market fit that did not work or a technical approach that did not work. Austin sees that judgment and reflection as a mark of seniority, and says many candidates simply tell a problem-solved story with no lesson, which Austin treats as a sign of someone below the level.

Source: 33:23–35:27 ↗
Is it unfair that candidates who sell themselves well do better?
Austin McDonald

The host noted that commenters complain about people who manage optics, and that promotion content draws the same objection. Austin replies that this is how people work, in careers and in personal relationships alike: saying “can't you feel that I love you” does not work, and behaviors must be shown and communicated.

Austin calls self-advocacy an unpleasant but worthwhile tax on progress that candidates can skip only by giving up staff-level promotion or hiring. Austin tells people that a principal engineering job is about a million dollars a year in compensation, so they should be fully ready for the process.

Source: 35:29–37:24 ↗
Source: 27:35–32:19 ↗
Austin McDonald's rubric of scope by level
LevelWhat the person ownsWhat that looks like
New gradTasksTakes a task from the manager or ticket system, completes it, and comes back for the next.
Mid-levelA feature (many tasks, a couple of weeks)Delivers a feature end to end.
SeniorA project (many features)Leads and delegates, often through mid-level or junior engineers, with communication and organization.
Staff (level 6 at Meta)A goal such as an engagement or revenue goalCoordinates several projects, working across teams and a large organization, with influence and mentoring.
Principal or distinguishedAn organization (many goals)Responsibility spans many goals, projects, features and tasks; Austin says names for these levels vary.
Next level upA business or industry (many organizations)Responsibility for an entire business containing many organizations.
Source: 27:35–29:44 ↗

QWho actually makes the hiring decision?

Austin McDonald

Austin lists the decision points. The sourcer, who decides from a LinkedIn profile whether to contact someone, is distinct from the recruiter, who takes over after the phone screen, runs the negotiation, organizes the loop and advocates before the committee. The phone screener is another decision point, whether a sourcer's multiple-choice question or an engineer's coding screen.

The hiring committee then decides, usually by consensus and sometimes by vote, whether to hire at a level, add a follow-up, or drop the candidate. Two or three engineering directors above the committee make the final call, again mostly by consensus and sometimes by vote.

Source: 37:26–39:08 ↗

QDid Austin ever see bias in a hiring committee, such as nepotism, and how much do referrals matter?

Austin McDonald

Austin has never seen overt nepotism or bribery, but has seen referrals play a huge role, especially when the referrer is senior or shows up in the committee room to advocate. The referrer's seniority matters: a VP or director risks personal reputation, while a note that someone knew a candidate at school carries little weight. Content matters as well. A referral saying the person worked directly with the candidate and listing specific strengths helps much more, so Austin tells candidates to write the referral for the referrer.

Austin says referrals matter most for candidates on the bubble. Austin's own phone screens went poorly, and Austin believes a follow-up interview was granted because a former schoolmate who had worked with them directly had referred them.

Could a very strong referral rescue a lukewarm interview performance?
Austin McDonald

The host described a candidate with a lukewarm result and the strongest possible VP referral. Austin says referrals help on the bubble, usually by winning a follow-up, and Austin has never seen a general consensus not to hire overturned for an engineer. It may happen more in leadership hiring, which Austin calls a different matter. At senior manager and director level, Austin thinks who you know sometimes matters more than raw performance, because the number of decision makers shrinks and they are easier to influence.

Austin adds that a good hiring process is not like that: it identifies what makes people successful and evaluates for it without bias.

Source: 41:48–43:47 ↗
Source: 39:10–41:46 ↗

QHow well does interview performance predict performance on the job?

Austin McDonald

Austin says the committee did not track how many interviews someone passed. It looked at the interviewer's stated confidence in a hire-and-level decision, and that confidence correlated with later performance. Austin reads this as evidence that calibrated interviewers who have run hundreds of interviews sense what good looks like even when it is hard to define, and that a rubric reduces bias without removing the gut feel.

Austin also notes that some candidates excel in interviews and then do poorly, and others look rocky and then do well. Interviewing is a skill separate from the job, and Austin says candidates need to spend time getting good at it.

Source: 43:49–45:26 ↗

QWhat does the behavioral rubric look like, and how should a candidate use it?

Austin McDonald

Austin says it varies by company. Well-run large companies often employ industrial-psychology PhDs, called selection scientists, who study what makes engineers successful and codify it into signal areas. At Meta, according to Austin, there are five: driving results, embracing ambiguity, resolving conflicts, growing continuously and communicating effectively. These are not Meta's company values. Candidates should ask the recruiter for the rubric in advance or search for it.

Austin groups the typical five to eight items into eight broader signal areas, described in their book, and tells candidates to categorize their stories by those areas. Inside the interview the core loop is decode, select, deliver: work out why the question is being asked and which area it probes, select a story that supplies that signal, and tell it engagingly. At smaller companies a formal rubric may not exist. There Austin suggests relying on company values and asking recruiters or team members what makes engineers successful and what the hiring process looks for.

How can one story serve different questions, and what does the interviewer need from the candidate?
Austin McDonald

The host says that as an interviewer of hundreds of candidates, including engineering managers, the host often asked a targeted question and watched candidates talk past it into a rehearsed spiel, leaving a blank in the rubric. The host sees the interview as a mutual exercise in filling out that rubric.

Austin agrees and offers a movie-trailer image, credited to PM behavioral coach Robert Hamilton. One story may contain action, romance, ambiguity, communication and conflict, and the candidate can re-cut it into a trailer that fits the question. That has to happen early, in the opening context. Austin says candidates should treat themselves as partners helping the interviewer reach the signal sought.

Source: 47:57–50:12 ↗
Source: 45:39–47:54 ↗
Editorial synthesis
Source: 46:23–50:12 ↗

QHow should candidates tailor behavioral stories for OpenAI and Anthropic?

Austin McDonald

Austin starts by mapping stories onto the eight general signal areas, because most company values reduce to them, and then adds whatever the company's own values contribute. For OpenAI, Austin reads “act with humility” as growth: taking feedback and improving yourself and those around you. “Feel the AGI” is outside the eight areas. Austin reads it as being optimistic about what AI could do for the world.

For Anthropic, the caption renders a value as “hold light and shade”, which Austin takes to mean understanding both the positive and negative implications of AI. A story about using AI at Anthropic should mention the potential harms the candidate thought about and how they assessed and mitigated them. Without that, Austin says, the interviewers will not feel comfortable hiring. At OpenAI a candidate who is not AI-forward or excited about new domains for AI will interest them less. These are Austin's readings of the values, not official definitions.

Source: 50:14–52:20 ↗

QWhat are the most common behavioral interview mistakes for senior engineers?

Austin McDonald

Austin lists several. First, the wrong stories, meaning stories that do not match the target scope. Second, too much context: senior people are good communicators and tend to talk, but only the context needed to understand the behaviors is useful. If about thirty seconds pass without an action in the story, Austin suggests the candidate is giving too much backstory or technical detail. Work stories are not exciting, Austin admits, so the action must keep moving.

Third, inviting uncharitable readings. Interviewers hiring a senior leader are risk-averse, so a candidate should think defensively. Saying the codebase had heavy technical debt may sound like a good story, but a senior engineer in the room invites the question of how it got that way. Austin recommends adding the judgment behind the situation, for example that the team was a startup that had to close its next funding round and so accepted the debt, then chose to prioritize paying it down.

Fourth, too little on non-technical work: mentoring, organizing, delegating, influencing the roadmap, resolving conflicts, working across teams and managing up. Fifth, long, multi-year stories need an organized shape. Austin suggests opening with a short table of contents (the business context, then perhaps five parts such as proposing the idea, aligning stakeholders, solving hard problems and a long rollout), so the candidate can return to the key parts after interruptions.

How should a candidate choose which story to tell?
Austin McDonald

Austin gives four criteria in order. Scope comes first, which Austin says surprises people who assume relevance is first: how can a big-scope story fit the question? Relevance is second, since a story about an unambiguous project cannot answer a question on ambiguity. Recency is third: stories from the last two to three years are fine, beyond three or four years needs a strong reason, and the limit stretches with seniority, so a principal with a 30-year career may use a ten-year-old story. Uniqueness is fourth: across several behavioral rounds a candidate should avoid repeating the same story, for example keeping the project deep dive separate from the general ambiguity answer.

Source: 57:10–58:35 ↗
Is it acceptable to answer like a politician and steer toward a stronger story?
Austin McDonald

The host compared this to a politician delivering a rehearsed answer that fills in the rubric rather than the question asked. Austin says, unfortunately, yes. The aim is to leave having shown the most business value and problem solving, and strictly answering the narrow question can leave a bigger story untold.

Austin's example is a question about a conflict with a product manager. A candidate can say they had one and outline it, then offer that a longer conflict with a director of engineering, involving data collection and many meetings, might be more interesting, and ask whether to tell that instead. The interviewer may constrain the candidate back to the smaller story, but the interviewer may also only be gathering conflict-resolution signal.

Source: 58:37–1:00:39 ↗
How can a candidate tell whether they are talking too long?
Austin McDonald

Austin says interviewers differ. Some, like Austin, listen and take in what the candidate finds interesting. Others interrupt, turn a detail over, ask many follow-ups or move quickly between questions. Candidates should be emotionally prepared for the second type, who can make a candidate feel they are failing when the interviewer is just bouncing around.

Austin advises reading cues such as eye contact and note-taking, and if engagement drops, pausing to ask whether this is what the interviewer wants. A calibrated interviewer will interrupt even if rude in order to collect signal, but weaker ones need the candidate to make stopping easy. Austin recommends talking for no more than two to four minutes at a time, since a monologue longer than four or five minutes has to be very good.

Source: 1:00:04–1:02:29 ↗
Source: 52:22–57:07 ↗

QHow should a candidate split preparation time across coding, system design and behavioral rounds?

Austin McDonald

Austin says most people spend too much time on coding and too little on system design and behavioral, which are murkier to prepare for. For juniors, the technical signal matters most, and the behavioral focus should be on thinking, motivations and ideas tried, as signals of future impact, since juniors have fewer accomplishments.

For mid-level engineers, Austin says the old approach of focusing only on technical work and not flubbing the behavioral no longer works. Austin gives two reasons: layoffs have produced many candidates, so one must shine across all interview types, and more technical work is being done with agentic coding, so employers want mid-level engineers who own problems end to end and keep learning as engineering changes quickly. Austin says that ownership and growth show up in the behavioral interview. Coding practice should come early because coding assessments come first, but some weeks before the on-site a candidate should choose core stories, study values and the rubric, and make sure each key area has a story.

From senior up, Austin says it mostly comes down to behavioral. For a staff packet Austin went straight to the behavioral interview, since there are only so many ways to design a web crawler or solve two-sum, and the behavioral shows organizational impact, influence, conflict handling, scope and business impact. At staff-plus levels, extra rounds may include a cross-functional partner such as a PM or a project deep dive. Austin sees the technical rounds there as checkmarks to pass and the behavioral ones as what gets someone hired.

Austin thinks most people underinvest in behavioral preparation, which takes at least a few weeks. Staff candidates and above should start when they start LeetCode, work on positioning stories, get feedback, and do mocks with a friend or professional. For in-demand companies such as Meta, OpenAI or Anthropic, Austin recommends a mock interviewer calibrated to that company who can give a feel for its culture.

Can a packet with a modest technical result and a strong behavioral result still go through?
Austin McDonald

Austin says yes at the highest levels. At staff, principal and manager levels, where less day-to-day coding is expected, the committee would discount a weak coding performance. That is much harder for junior candidates.

Austin tells of a candidate whose accomplishments were limited and technical performance only okay. Austin kept seeing ideas the candidate had tried to push even though a manager disagreed or the organization blocked them. Austin pushed for the hire and says the person later became a staff engineer. Austin's reading is that the behavioral interview assesses a slope of growth, even for juniors.

Source: 1:07:10–1:08:33 ↗
Source: 1:02:31–1:07:09 ↗

QHow much does subjective likeability matter, and how does presence affect the outcome?

Austin McDonald

Austin says it scales with level. At big companies, behavioral interviews for juniors are structured, with forms, to reduce the “beer test” effect. For seniors the interviewer expects the person to influence others on the job, so how they come across counts. Austin describes a Silicon Valley quality of “casual excellence”: looking calm yet sharply competent. A disheveled or nervous candidate who cannot be present is giving signal about how they will show up in meetings and before a CEO.

Austin adds that cultural norms differ by country and company. The conversation here is about a Silicon Valley or Seattle style that opens with playful banter and then turns to hard-hitting questions, and candidates should learn the expectations of the place they are applying to.

How can a staff engineer who is not a people person come across strongly?
Austin McDonald

Austin starts from the idea that the inside shows on the outside, so the work begins with belief rather than a mask. Austin cites a recent podcast by the author of a book on Silicon Valley etiquette, named in the captions as Sam Lesson (spelling unverified), who stressed lowering heart rate before the conversation. Austin points out that a company that will be around has other chances, so a candidate can give themselves permission to make mistakes and appear calmer.

The second belief is empathy: the interviewer wants to find a great engineer, is not an enemy, and is a human who would be glad to work with the candidate. On the outside, Austin suggests dressing one notch up, checking the video background, and showing care in the first minutes rather than waiting passively. A candidate who is not extroverted can still let their regard for people show through a warm greeting and stated enthusiasm. Austin recommends practicing that opening in mock interviews, noting that the interviewer may be nervous too and that a hiring manager or leader shapes the candidate's view of the team.

Source: 1:11:20–1:15:16 ↗
Does a curt, concise candidate or a warm, bubbly one score better?
Austin McDonald

The host posed this contrast. Austin says it depends on who conducts the interview, and that Austin would favor the warmer person because Austin likes to engage. But rapport does not mean bubbliness, it means connecting with the other person. A candidate should start positive and energetic, then read the interviewer. Someone who skips the introduction and goes straight to “tell me about a time” wants efficiency, so the candidate should be efficient. Someone who opens with several minutes of weather and sports is a different type, and the candidate should match that energy.

Source: 1:15:18–1:17:29 ↗
Source: 1:09:03–1:11:19 ↗

QWhich counts more, the first impression or the last impression?

Austin McDonald

Austin says that if forced to choose, the beginning. Austin often decides within the first ten or fifteen minutes whether to hire, since Austin opens with the biggest-scope questions (favorite project, most ambiguous project, something proud of). If Austin would like to see that performance replicated in the organization, the rest of the interview is a check on other areas such as conflict resolution and growth.

The ending still matters, mainly through the candidate's questions. Austin says candidates often prepare stories but then ask something generic like a day in the life of an engineer, which is similar everywhere. Questions drawn from real thought about the team, organization, product and company, and that help the candidate decide whether to join, leave the impression of an engaged candidate.

What share of the outcome is already set early in the interview?
Austin McDonald

Austin says no social science has been applied directly to tech interviews, and one cannot simply transfer research from a fast-food company. Austin recalls research saying roughly 40 percent of decisions are made in the first 15 percent, about the first ten minutes (Austin's recollection, not verified). In Austin's own experience it is rare to decide against someone early and then be won back at minute 38. More common is feeling unsure, then writing notes against the rubric, which is meant to move the decision from a gut reaction to something more deliberate.

If Austin decided early, it was hard for the candidate to overcome, usually because of poor story choice, work below the expected level, or weak storytelling. The host adds from experience that interviewers seem to zone out halfway once they have already decided, which makes the first half important, and that the closing questions are also evaluative.

Source: 1:19:11–1:21:43 ↗
What makes a good question to ask at the end?
Austin McDonald

Austin says everything is evaluative, from the recruiter call to the closing questions. A candidate should start from what matters to them: worry about the company's long-term product prospects, or, for career growth and a supportive manager, a request such as asking the manager to describe helping someone grow from one level to the next. Technology-stack questions seem more junior to Austin, though in an AI context a question about model construction or evaluation could be strong. One of Austin's favorites is what makes someone in this role successful, which signals interest in succeeding.

Austin would not try to impress with a deep question, but would let a genuine concern read as depth. Questions about the conversation for the role, or about free food, may matter to the candidate but do not belong with a behavioral interviewer.

Source: 1:21:45–1:24:03 ↗
Source: 1:17:40–1:19:09 ↗

QWhat are the best ways to tell a behavioral story with the least effort?

Austin McDonald

Austin says a story needs an arc, with a beginning, middle and end, and must deliver the signal area the interviewer is after: past behavior that can be repeated in the new organization. STAR (situation, task, action, result) is the best-known shortcut. Austin does not love it but says that anyone with prepared STAR stories the night before should use them, since they give an arc, context for the actions, and results.

Austin prefers CALR: context, actions, results, learnings. The difference between situation and task is not useful in a long project, which has many tasks, so context followed by actions is simpler. For senior engineers STAR leaves no room for reflection, judgment or learning, and Austin looks for whether the candidate can see what made them successful or not and apply it forward.

How should a candidate adapt the length of an answer to the question?
Austin McDonald

Austin says senior candidates manage time. A “trunk” question such as a project that was really ambiguous invites a longer story. A “branch” question, such as whom the candidate spoke to for a piece of information, seeks a communication signal and deserves something shorter than a full STAR or CALR story. A “leaf” question, such as which framework was used, only needs the answer before moving on. Austin says detecting how long the interviewer wants to listen is both a mark of seniority and a way to manage the interview.

Source: 1:26:37–1:27:59 ↗
What matters more, what the candidate says or how they say it?
Austin McDonald

Austin says mostly what, because engineering interviews are structured and engineers value substance. A candidate who sounds confident and positive but shows no structured approach to ambiguity or conflict will not win support. Form follows function.

Austin adds that delivery matters more at senior levels, because senior people must tell engaging status stories, for example when a VP asks how a project is going. Details belong only when they serve a purpose, such as technical depth or, in a cross-team story, how another tech lead's hostile look showed the candidate pushing through resistance. Most candidates, Austin thinks, need more work on basic story structure and on naming the repeatable actions they took.

Source: 1:28:01–1:30:24 ↗
Source: 1:24:30–1:26:34 ↗

QThe host asked Austin to explain, in terms of scope, why Austin was promoted to M2 at Meta.

Austin McDonald

Austin says getting to M2 meant solving hard problems in recruiting, with the most important being diversity. Austin left a team building products for teenagers, which Austin calls a hard time for Facebook, to lead teams in the internal recruiting products organization that supports candidates, recruiters and sourcers. What drew Austin was a team working to hire more diverse engineers, and Austin was motivated by opening technology, which Austin calls the largest wealth opportunity, to more people.

Austin says a product team cannot decide school curricula or all hiring decisions, but could move the needle by improving interview preparation, and credits that with helping diversity hiring at Meta. Austin also supported other teams in building high-quality candidate data in Facebook's applicant tracking system. The host heard multiple teams, an ambiguous problem and strong self-motivation. Austin agrees and adds company-wide impact from leading the iOS and Android recruiting pipelines, which scaled Austin beyond the teams directly managed. These are Austin's own account of their record.

Source: 1:30:27–1:33:41 ↗

QLooking back on big tech, does Austin regret anything?

Austin McDonald

Austin does not regret leaving and says they enjoyed working with wonderful people. The regret is the anxiety brought into teams and into their own life. Austin points out that no one at the end of life wishes they had gotten a few more percent of an engagement number, and says people value relationships and connection.

Austin says they made conscious choices to favor life experience over career but were not always honest with themselves about the trade-offs in pay, progression and status. Since leaving big tech to support a spouse's business, income has dropped. Before leaving, Austin decided to accept lower cash flow in exchange for more time with their kids and more community volunteering, and has returned to that choice when money was tight. Austin wishes to have made that kind of values-driven decision earlier.

What did being dishonest with oneself look like?
Austin McDonald

Austin describes frustration and at times bitterness when others were promoted or got jobs. Austin says the honest answer was that those people moved teams faster and worked harder, while Austin prioritized family and community. Austin does not think people can have everything: some may be able to be a level-seven IC and leave at 5:00, depending on talent and skills built, but for most people accomplishing something extraordinary takes extraordinary steps.

Austin says that deciding what mattered, including what their children would remember about them in ten or fifteen years, was clarifying.

Source: 1:35:58–1:37:30 ↗
Did that clarity remove the feelings of envy?
Austin McDonald

Austin says the feelings return on a semi-regular basis, especially in Silicon Valley where people stack wealth quickly. Each time Austin asks whether that is what they want. Being aligned with one's own values, with a mission statement or vision for life, is what Austin finds satisfying.

Source: 1:37:32–1:38:10 ↗
Source: 1:33:42–1:35:56 ↗

QWhat is the best career advice Austin ever received?

Austin McDonald

Austin says it was the importance of creating scope. Many people wait for someone to give them the opportunity, but a manager once told Austin that to get an M2 role, Austin had to create an M2-scope team and solve problems of that size. Advancing does not mean doing the same thing better. It means doing something different, which is creating more scope and room for the organization to succeed.

Austin adds a test: what is the VP saying about your project, and if the VP is not telling peers or their manager, is it the right work? Candidates already work backwards from the signal area they want to show in an interview and from the packet they want in a promotion. Austin suggests working backwards in the same way from what leadership should say about the accomplishment, then finding a way to achieve it. The host adds that promotions built on self-created scope are the most satisfying because they need no one's permission.

Source: 1:38:13–1:40:26 ↗

QWhat advice would Austin give a younger self just after college?

Austin McDonald

Austin says imposter syndrome held them back. After completing a computer science PhD, Austin spent summers doing university research while peers took industry internships at places like Google or Facebook, because Austin did not want to go through interviews and risk rejection. Austin loves their career and would not change much, but says that fear slowed their understanding of how big organizations and large codebases work, coming from academia.

Austin's summary advice is simple: do not give in to fear.
